Title: Product Design Engineering Services

Services

# Product design engineering help from early idea to manufacture.

I support people building physical products through concept development, prototyping, design for manufacture,
production strategy, and the technical-commercial decisions that sit between a promising idea and a viable product.
You can get in touch for a specific question, practical project help, or more strategic product support.

Based in Belfast, with clients and manufacturing partners across Northern Ireland, the UK, Ireland, Europe, North America, Asia and Australasia:
[product design in Belfast and Northern Ireland](https://oriondesign.xyz/product-design-belfast/).

If this is your first product

## You do not need to arrive speaking engineering.

Bring the idea, the problem you want to solve, what you have tried, and what worries you about taking the next step.
I can help translate that into a development plan: what must be learned first, what should be prototyped, and where money should not be committed yet.

[See the product-development roadmap →](https://oriondesign.xyz/ready-to-launch/)

If you already have a product team

## Use Orion as targeted external design capacity.

Bring a specific bottleneck: concept generation, mechanical architecture, DFM, prototyping, manufacturing route, [cost-down](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html), supplier preparation, or an independent design review.
The engagement can stay narrow rather than forcing a full consultancy programme around a problem that only needs one experienced pair of hands.

[Describe the bottleneck →](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)

## Advice call or product review

Useful when you need an experienced second view on a product idea, prototype, manufacturing route, cost assumption, or next-step decision before committing more time or budget.

## Concept and prototype support

Turn a rough product direction into clearer architecture, CAD, prototypes, test priorities, and practical development tasks that answer the most important unknowns first.

## Design-for-manufacture review

Review part strategy, assembly burden, material choices, tooling assumptions, supplier readiness, and cost risks before the product becomes expensive to change.

## Manufacturing route strategy

Compare prototype, bridge, and production routes against demand confidence, design maturity, capital tolerance, quality requirements, and target cost.

## Ongoing strategic product support

For teams that need product design engineering input across several decisions, from concept direction and supplier conversations through launch planning and cost-down work.

Representative engagements

## Services grounded in actual product-development work.

These representative visuals are useful because they show the breadth behind the offer: scientific instruments, soft goods, consumer accessories,
and product architectures that needed more than surface-level [industrial design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/industrial-design-vs-engineering-design.html).

Research and definition

### Technical product framing

Scientific and engineering products need the front end handled carefully: who the user is, what must be proved, and how the product architecture supports that use.

Development and prototyping

### Refining product direction

Development work often sits between mechanism, geometry, soft-goods detail, ergonomics, and testable prototype learning rather than one clean discipline.

Design for manufacture

### Preparing products for production

Design for manufacture means resolving geometry, joining logic, tooling assumptions, and part strategy early enough that manufacturing does not become a late surprise.

Where Orion helps most

## Typical problems this work is designed to solve.

Most enquiries sit somewhere between design uncertainty and manufacturing risk. The service offer is built around that middle ground, with enough flexibility for early advice or deeper involvement.

Concept and scope

### The team has several directions but weak decision structure.

Use concept selection, product-purpose framing, and development planning to narrow the right direction before effort spreads too thin.

Manufacturing and cost

### The product is promising, but route-to-manufacture is still unclear.

Use break-even, production-strategy, and assembly thinking to connect architecture choices to real production implications.

Business and launch

### The concept needs a stronger commercial case.

Use revenue, business-case, route-to-market, and investor metrics to see whether the product supports a viable path beyond engineering.

Engagement shape

Some projects only need a focused review. Others need practical design engineering or strategic support across several stages.

A short, focused review of the product, the decision, and the risks that need attention next.

**2**

**3**

**6**

Bring product, manufacturing, cost, and commercial assumptions together before launch commitments harden.

If you want to explore the same journey yourself first, use the [ready-to-launch roadmap](https://oriondesign.xyz/ready-to-launch/).

## Questions people ask before getting in touch

### Do I need a finished specification or drawings before contacting Orion Design?

No. A short description of the product, the problem it solves, what you have tried so far and what worries you about the next step is enough. Turning that into a clear brief and development plan is part of the work. [Working with a product design consultancy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/working-with-a-product-design-consultancy.html) explains what a useful brief covers.

### Can you help if I am not based in Belfast or Northern Ireland?

Yes. Much product design engineering work happens through CAD reviews, calls and shared prototypes, and clients and manufacturing partners have included businesses in Great Britain, the Republic of Ireland, France, Germany, Sweden, Poland, the United States, China, Taiwan, India, Australia and New Zealand. The [MLT Industries case study](https://oriondesign.xyz/case-studies/mlt-industries-switchmaster.html) shows a product taken from concept into manufacture with the client in Australia.

### What is the difference between product design and product design engineering?

Product design often focuses on form, user experience and appearance. Product design engineering also covers how the product works and how it will be made: mechanical architecture, materials, tolerances, assembly, manufacturing route and cost. Orion Design works across both, with an emphasis on getting the product ready to manufacture.

### How much does product design support cost?

It depends on the decision and the depth of help needed, from a focused review of one question to hands-on development across several stages. Describe where the product is and what you need to decide, and the scope and cost can be agreed before any work begins.

### Can I use the free tools before getting in touch?

Yes, and it often makes the first conversation more useful. Save results from the tools to your [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) and send the plan along with your question.

## Need help with a live product decision?

If you want to test a decision yourself first, the tools are there. If you already have a live question around concept, manufacturability, cost, or launch, send a short note and I can help shape the next step.

Title: MLT Industries Product Design Case Study

Remote concept-to-manufacture case study

# MLT Industries: from an early product concept to manufacture and a growing product family.

This project is a useful example of what end-to-end product design can look like when the client, designer, prototype suppliers, and manufacturers are not in the same place. Orion worked from Belfast with MLT Industries in Australia, connecting the physical product journey from concept through prototypes, supplier sourcing, manufacture, and later product-family development.

Client

MLT Industries, Australia

Orion base

[Belfast, Northern Ireland](https://oriondesign.xyz/product-design-belfast/)

Delivery model

Remote collaboration + international suppliers

Scope

Concept → prototype → manufacture → family

The project journey

## One relationship across the stages where product decisions become expensive.

Many product-development engagements cover one slice of the process. The value of the MLT relationship is continuity: early design intent could be carried forward into prototype learning, manufacturing choices, and later extensions rather than being repeatedly reinterpreted at each hand-off.

01

### Concept definition

The work began by turning an early product idea into a physical architecture that could be discussed, challenged, and developed rather than remaining an abstract intention.

02

### Prototype and learn

Prototype iterations created physical evidence: fit, access, assembly, usability, packaging of the electronics, and the practical questions that are difficult to resolve convincingly in CAD alone.

03

### Design for manufacture and supplier sourcing

As the product matured, the design conversation moved toward manufacturing processes, production detail, and finding suitable prototype and manufacturing suppliers internationally. The objective was not simply to find a supplier, but to make sure the product and process assumptions made sense together.

04

### Manufacture

The project progressed beyond presentation models into a manufactured product. That transition is where design details such as fastening, access, cable routing, enclosure construction, repeatability, and assembly burden stop being theoretical.

05

### Extend the platform

The relationship continued as the original product developed into a broader family. Reusing an established product language and manufacturing logic can reduce the amount that has to be rediscovered when a successful product grows into variants and accessories.

Why this case matters

### Remote does not have to mean fragmented.

Good remote product development depends on clear models, drawings, decisions, photographs, prototype feedback, and supplier communication. Geography changes the communication system; it does not change the engineering fundamentals.

Public outcome

### SwitchMaster is a current MLT Industries platform.

MLT Industries currently publishes the SwitchMaster product and related enclosure resources, including production injection-moulded case options. That public product provides a useful view of the downstream manufactured platform without exposing confidential development material.

[View SwitchMaster at MLT Industries →](https://www.mltindustries.com.au/switchmaster)

A distributed development model

## Client, designer, prototype suppliers, and manufacturers can operate as one product-development system.

**Australia**Client, product need, market context, field feedback
↔

**Belfast**Product design, mechanical development, coordination
↔

**International suppliers**Prototype manufacture, process feedback, production

The important interface is not distance. It is the quality of the information crossing each boundary: what changed, why it changed, which assumptions remain open, and what evidence the next prototype or supplier interaction needs to produce.

For founders

## You do not need to arrive with a finished specification.

A useful first conversation can start with a problem, sketch, existing prototype, or rough idea. The job is to identify the next uncertainty worth resolving rather than pretending every answer is known at the beginning.

[Describe your product idea →](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)

Title: After Launch: Returns, Feedback and Changes

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small teams whose product is on sale and who want to learn from returns, reviews and complaints without losing control of the design

# After launch: returns, feedback and design changes

How to collect and record what customers tell you once a product is on sale, find the real cause of a problem, decide what to change, and make design changes in a controlled way that protects safety, quality and certification.

Quick answer

## Collect every return, review and complaint in one log, find the root cause before you change anything, treat safety issues first, and make each fix a controlled, re-tested design change.

Customers are now running the largest test your product will ever have. Record each report with the failure, the batch or date and how the product was used, so patterns show up.
Reproduce and inspect the problem until you understand why it happened, then change the design, the process or the instructions through a revision that is recorded, shared with suppliers and validated before it ships.

## Contents

- Why the work continues after launch

- Setting up feedback channels

- Logging and classifying returns and complaints

- Finding the root cause

- Deciding what to change

- Controlling the change

- Communicating with customers

- Using what you learn

- Worked example: a cracked clip

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## Why the work continues after launch

However thorough your testing, customers will use the product in ways, places and quantities you could not fully reproduce. Some problems only appear after weeks of use, in a particular climate, or in one production batch. Others are not faults at all, but confusion about how the product works.

The first months on sale are the best chance to catch these while volumes are still small and fixes are cheaper. That only works if feedback reaches the people who can act on it, in a form they can use.

## Setting up feedback channels

Decide where feedback will arrive and who reads it, before launch if you can. The usual channels are:

- **Reviews** on your own site and on marketplaces. Read the low ratings in full; the detail is in the text, not the stars.

- **Support emails, messages and calls.** Use one shared inbox or form so nothing sits in one person's account.

- **Returns.** Ask for a reason with every return, and ask for faulty units back where it is practical, because a physical part tells you far more than a description.

- **Retailer and distributor feedback.** Retailers often see returns and complaints you never hear about. Ask them to pass on reasons and, where possible, the returned units. [Selling on marketplaces](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/selling-on-marketplaces.html) covers how those channels work.

- **Your own production data.** End-of-line test failures and inspection rejects are early warnings of the same problems.

Make it easy for customers to tell you something went wrong: a contact route on the packaging and in the instructions, and a short form that asks the right questions.

## Logging and classifying returns and complaints

Put every report in one log, even a simple shared spreadsheet. One complaint is an anecdote; ten with the same failure from the same batch is a pattern you can act on. Record at least:

|
Field |
What to record |

|
Date and source |
When it arrived and through which channel |

|
Product and batch |
Model, revision, batch or serial number, purchase date |

|
Failure mode |
What happened, in a few standard categories (broken, not working, cosmetic, missing part, confusing, other) |

|
How it was used |
Where, how often, how long before it failed, anything unusual |

|
Safety flag |
Yes or no: could this cause injury, fire, burns, shock or damage? |

|
Unit returned? |
Whether you have the part, and where it is |

|
Status |
Open, investigating, cause found, change made, closed |

Batch numbers make the log far more useful, which is why [product liability basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-liability-basics.html) recommends making products traceable. Keep the failure categories few and consistent so you can count them. Review the log on a regular rhythm, not just when something feels wrong.

## Finding the root cause

The reported symptom is rarely the cause. "The clip broke" could come from a weak design, the wrong material, a moulding fault, an assembly error, damage in transit or a use you did not expect. Each needs a different fix. Work through it in plain steps:

- **Reproduce it.** Try to make the failure happen on purpose, on a good unit, under the conditions the customer described.

- **Inspect returned units.** Look at where and how a part broke, compare dimensions and material against the drawing, and compare returned units with stock from the same and other batches.

- **Ask "why" repeatedly.** The clip broke. Why? It was overstressed. Why? The wall was thinner than drawn. Why? The tool had worn. Stop when you reach something you can change and control.

- **Check your records.** Compare against the original test results and your [test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html): was this condition ever tested? Check supplier records, material certificates and [first-article and batch inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) reports for anything that changed.

Be honest about what you do not know yet. If the cause is unclear, say so in the log and keep investigating, rather than settling on the most convenient explanation.

Each change goes back into the loop: feedback on the revised product is how you confirm the fix worked.

## Deciding what to change

**Safety comes first, every time.** Any report that suggests a risk of injury, fire, burns, shock or damage to property should be escalated immediately, not queued with cosmetic issues. Stop shipping suspect stock while you investigate, as the [quality control guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) describes. You may have obligations to act, and [product liability basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-liability-basics.html) notes that you should plan how you would handle complaints, incidents and, if needed, a recall. Check the GOV.UK guidance on [product safety for manufacturers](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/product-safety-for-manufacturers), and take professional advice from a solicitor and your insurer for your situation.

For everything else, weigh four things together:

- **Severity:** does it stop the product working, shorten its life, or only annoy?

- **Frequency:** how many reports, and is the count growing or tied to one batch?

- **Cost:** the one-off cost of the fix against the cost of returns, replacements, support time and lost reputation if you leave it.

- **Type of fix:** not every problem needs a design change. The cause may be a process or supplier issue, packaging, or instructions that need rewriting.

Severe and frequent problems go to the top. Rare, minor ones may be best saved for the next version, recorded so they are not forgotten.

## Controlling the change

A change made informally, by a phone call to the factory, is how products drift and problems become impossible to trace. Treat every change as a small, recorded project:

- **Raise the revision.** Give the changed part a new revision letter (for example, Rev B to Rev C) and record what changed, why, who approved it and from which batch or date it applies.

- **Update the documents.** Update the drawing, 3D model and bill of materials together, so suppliers never work from mixed versions. [Tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains how drawings carry this information.

- **Tell suppliers in writing.** Send the new revision, ask for confirmation, agree what happens to existing stock and work in progress, and get any tool modification or new price quoted on the same basis as before, as in [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html).

- **Re-validate.** Repeat the tests the change could affect, on parts made by the production process, and run a first-article inspection on the first revised parts.

- **Check certification.** In general terms, [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) notes that design changes and component changes can require a review of your technical file and test evidence. Ask whoever maintains it, or your test house, before the change ships.

The same discipline applies to cost-down changes; [reducing the cost of an existing product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html) covers those.

## Communicating with customers

Reply to each complaint promptly, thank the customer, and explain what happens next: a replacement, a refund or a request to return the unit for investigation. Avoid guessing at causes in public before you know them.

When a fix is in place, say so where it helps: a reply to a review, a note on the product page, or improved instructions. Customers generally respond better to a clear, honest account than to silence. For anything safety-related, follow the advice you have taken on what to say and to whom.

## Using what you learn

The log is a record of how your product really behaves. Use it for:

- **The next version.** Turn recurring issues into requirements and tests, so the next product is designed and checked against them from the start.

- **Repair and spares.** Parts that fail most often are the ones to make easy to replace and to stock as spares. [Design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) shows how.

- **Longer product life.** Fixing the causes of early failure keeps products in use for longer, which is often the biggest environmental gain available; see [why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html).

## Worked example: a cracked clip

Illustrative example only. A small company sells a plastic desk organiser with a snap-on lid. A few weeks after launch, several reviews mention that a clip on the lid cracked, and some units come back through a retailer.

**Log.** The team records each report. Most cracked clips come from one batch, and several customers say the crack appeared after opening and closing the lid many times, not on first use.

**Root cause.** They reproduce the crack by cycling the lid on stock units from that batch, and fail to reproduce it on units from earlier batches. Inspecting returned lids shows the cracks start at a sharp inside corner at the root of the clip. Asking why: the clip cracks because stress concentrates at the corner; the corner is sharper on the newer batch because the moulder repaired the tool and the radius was not reinstated; nobody noticed because the radius was not marked as a critical feature on the drawing, and the original test plan only checked a modest number of opening cycles.

**Change.** The team issues Rev C of the lid drawing, marks the corner radius as a critical feature with an inspection check, and slightly enlarges the radius to give more margin. The moulder confirms in writing, corrects the tool and supplies first-article parts. The test plan gains a longer opening-cycle test, which the revised lids pass. Suspect stock from the affected batch is held and inspected.

**Customers and spares.** Affected customers are offered a replacement lid, and the lid becomes a spare part sold separately. The log is watched over the following batches to confirm the reports stop.

## Common mistakes

**Fixing symptoms, not causes.**
Thickening a broken part without understanding why it broke can move the failure elsewhere, add cost, or miss a process fault that will return.

**Uncontrolled changes.**
Changes agreed by phone, with no revision or record, make it impossible to tell which customers have which version or to trace a later problem.

**Ignoring small signals.**
A handful of similar reports can be the start of a larger problem, especially if they come from one batch. Log them and look for patterns early.

**Changing the design without re-testing.**
A fix for one problem can create another. Repeat the relevant tests on production-process parts before the change ships.

**Treating safety reports like any other.**
Anything that could cause harm needs immediate escalation and professional advice, not a place in the queue.

## Decision rules

- **One log** for every channel, with batch, failure mode and how the product was used.

- **Safety first:** escalate immediately, hold suspect stock and take advice.

- **No fix without a cause** that you have reproduced or confirmed on returned units.

- **Every change is a revision,** shared with suppliers in writing and re-validated before it ships.

- **Check certification** whenever a change touches materials, components, construction or labelling.

- **Close the loop** by watching the log after the change, and feed lessons into the next version.

## FAQ

### What should I do with returned products?

Log each one with its reason, batch and how it was used, and keep faulty units for inspection where you can. Returned parts often show the cause of a problem far more clearly than a written description.

### What is root cause analysis?

Working back from a reported symptom to the underlying reason it happened, by reproducing the problem, inspecting failed parts, asking why repeatedly and checking test, inspection and supplier records. The aim is a cause you can change and control.

### What should I do if a complaint suggests a safety problem?

Escalate it immediately, hold suspect stock and investigate. You may have obligations to act, so check the GOV.UK guidance on product safety for manufacturers and take advice from a solicitor and your insurer.

### What is change control?

A simple process for making design changes on purpose and on the record: a new revision letter, updated drawings and bill of materials, written confirmation from suppliers, re-validation and a note of which batch the change applies from.

### Does a design change affect my product certification?

It can. Changes to materials, components, construction or labelling may require a review of your technical file and test evidence. Check with whoever maintains it, or your test house, before the change ships.

Source: https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/aluminium-extrusions-for-product-enclosures.html
Title: Aluminium Extrusions for Product Enclosures

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers who need a metal enclosure without the cost of a casting or moulding tool

# Aluminium extrusions for product enclosures: profiles, end caps and finishing

A plain-English guide to building a product enclosure from extruded aluminium: how extrusion works, why it suits electronics housings, when an off-the-shelf profile is enough and when a custom die is worth it, how to design a profile an extruder can make, and how end caps, machining and finishes complete the box.

Quick answer

## An extruded enclosure is a length of aluminium profile, cut to size, machined for connectors and closed with end caps. It gives a tough metal housing for a modest die cost.

Start with an off-the-shelf enclosure profile if one fits; move to a custom profile when you need your own shape, PCB slots or screw ports built in.
Design the profile with balanced walls, generous radii and simple hollows, and expect looser tolerances than machining.
Seal the open ends with gasketed end caps screwed into the profile, and anodise the result.

## Contents

- What extrusion is

- Why extrusion suits enclosures

- Standard or custom profiles

- Designing the profile

- End caps and sealing

- Cutting, machining and deburring

- Alloy and temper

- Worked example: a sensor enclosure

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## What extrusion is

Extrusion works much like squeezing toothpaste through a shaped nozzle. A cylinder of aluminium, called a billet, is heated until it is soft but still solid, then a press pushes it through a steel die with the profile's shape cut through it.
What comes out is a long length with the same cross-section all the way along. It is cooled, stretched straight, usually aged to its final strength, and cut to the lengths you need.

The key limit follows from this: an extrusion can only have features that run the full length of the part. Anything that changes along the length, such as a connector hole, a mounting slot or a cut-out, has to be added afterwards.

## Why extrusion suits enclosures

Many electronics products are a [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) in a box, and a constant-section tube open at both ends is exactly what extrusion makes well.

- **Low tooling cost.** An extrusion die is a relatively simple steel disc, so it typically costs a fraction of a die-casting die or an injection mould for a part of similar size. [Manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html) sets it alongside the alternatives in relative terms.

- **Many lengths from one die.** The same profile can be cut short for one product and long for another, so a product family can share one die.

- **A good surface.** Outside faces come out clean and consistent, ready for blasting or brushing.

- **Heat spreading.** Aluminium conducts heat well, so the enclosure itself can carry heat away from hot components, which matters most in sealed products. [Managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html) explains why the housing is often the best heat sink.

- **Anodising.** Extrusion alloys generally anodise well, giving a hard, even finish in clear or dyed colours. [Surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) covers anodising and its alternatives.

The trade-off is shape freedom. An extruded box is a straight-sided tube; if the product needs curved, sculpted or tapered forms, [die casting](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/die-casting-explained.html), moulding or [CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) will suit it better.

## Standard or custom profiles

Several suppliers sell ready-made enclosure extrusions: rectangular and oval tubes with PCB slots, screw ports and matching end plates, often in a range of widths and lengths.
A custom profile means paying for your own die, which you then normally own or have reserved for your use.

|
Route |
Choose it when |
Watch out for |

|
Off-the-shelf enclosure profile |
Prototypes, low volumes, or products where a standard shape is acceptable; you need parts quickly with no tooling |
Board size and connector positions must fit the catalogue sizes; the product looks like others built from the same range |

|
Custom profile |
You need your own shape, branding, fin pattern or internal features; volumes justify a die; the product family will use one section in several lengths |
Die lead time and a sample round; extruders often set a minimum run, so ask about it early |

A common path is to prototype in a standard profile, then commission a custom one once the board outline and look are stable.

## Designing the profile

Limits depend on the alloy, profile size and the extruder's presses. Treat these points as typical guidance and ask your extruder to review the profile before the die is made.

An enclosure profile seen end on, not to scale. The screw ports, PCB slots and even wall run the full length of the extrusion; end caps screw into the ports, and connector holes are machined afterwards.

|
Feature |
Typical guidance |
Why |

|
Wall thickness |
Keep walls as even as possible around the profile |
Metal flows through the die fastest where the opening is widest; balanced walls fill evenly and stay straight |

|
Thin next to thick |
Avoid very thin walls joined to thick sections; blend changes gradually |
Uneven flow distorts the profile, and thin fins next to thick walls are hard to hold in shape and tolerance |

|
Corners |
Round internal and external corners generously |
Radii help the metal flow, strengthen the die and reduce stress; sharp corners wear and crack dies |

|
Hollows |
Keep hollow sections simple and as few as the design allows |
Each fully enclosed hollow needs a more complex die, which costs more and runs slower |

|
Screw ports |
Build ports into the profile, usually in the corners, sized for the screw the extruder and fastener supplier agree |
End caps can then be screwed straight into the extrusion, with no drilling or inserts |

|
PCB slots |
Add pairs of rails to slide the board in; allow clearance for board thickness variation and the finish |
The slots locate the board without extra brackets |

|
Tolerances |
Expect looser tolerances, flatness and straightness than machining; machine features that need precision |
The profile cools and is stretched straight after leaving the die, so it moves more than a machined part |

**Hollow, semi-hollow and solid profiles.**
A **solid** profile has no enclosed spaces, like a flat bar or an angle. A **hollow** profile fully encloses at least one space, like a tube; the die needs a mandrel supported on bridges, and the metal splits around them and welds back together inside the die.
A **semi-hollow** profile nearly encloses a space through a narrow gap, like a C-shaped screw port, and can be harder to make than it looks, because the thin tongue of die steel forming the gap is weak. Discuss screw port shapes with the extruder.

**Practical rule:**
send the extruder a 2D section with critical dimensions and cosmetic faces marked, not just a 3D model, and ask which features they would change to make the die more reliable.

Use your extruder's published tolerances on the profile drawing and keep tight ones for machined features, as [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains.

## End caps and sealing

The open ends carry the connectors, lights and the seal, so they take most of the design work.

- **Machined end plates** in aluminium suit low volumes, need no tooling, are easy to change and anodise to match the body.

- **Moulded end caps** in plastic make sense at higher volumes, can include [light pipes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-buttons-switches-and-controls.html), cable glands and gasket grooves, and avoid machining every plate. They need a mould, so they usually come later.

- **Fixing.** Screws pass through the end plate into the screw ports. Use [thread-forming screws](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) where the fastener supplier agrees they suit the port, or tap the ports, and consider how often the joint will be reopened.

- **Sealing.** A die-cut or moulded gasket between the end cap and the profile's end face, compressed by the screws, seals the joint. The cut end must be square and clean for the gasket to work. [Sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) explains gasket compression and how to seal cables and connectors.

## Cutting, machining and deburring

Most extruded enclosures need some secondary operations, which many extruders or their partners can do:

- **Cutting to length,** with the cut ends kept square and flat so the end caps seal. Some designs face the ends by machining for a better sealing surface.

- **CNC machining** for anything that varies along the length: connector holes, display windows, mounting slots, vents and countersinks. Keep these features simple and reachable, as in the [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html), and group them on as few faces as possible to reduce set-ups.

- **Deburring** of cut ends and machined edges, so there are no sharp edges for users and no burrs to cut gaskets or cables.

- **Finishing**, usually bead blasting and anodising after machining, with bare areas masked where the case needs an electrical contact.

## Alloy and temper

Most extrusions are made from 6000-series alloys, which flow well through a die and respond to heat treatment. As [choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) notes, **6063** is a common choice for extrusion, and **6060** is widely used for similar work; both give a good surface for anodising.
Where the profile must carry more load, extruders often offer **6082**, which is stronger but generally harder to extrude in thin, detailed sections and may not anodise to quite the same appearance.

Specify the temper as well as the alloy: the same alloy can be soft or fully heat-treated, and the strength differs considerably. Ask your extruder which alloy and temper they recommend for your profile and finish, and check the datasheet values they work to.

## Worked example: a sensor enclosure

Illustrative example. A small company makes an environmental sensor for plant rooms. Its first units used an off-the-shelf enclosure extrusion, but the board was a poor fit, a bracket was needed to hold it, and the housing looked generic. With the electronics stable and a product family planned in two lengths, the team commissions a custom profile.

|
Feature |
Designed into the profile, or added afterwards? |

|
Outer shape with shallow fins on the top face for heat spreading and a recognisable look |
Designed into the profile |

|
PCB slots sized to the board, replacing the bracket |
Designed into the profile |

|
Four screw ports in the corners for the end caps |
Designed into the profile, shape agreed with the extruder |

|
A slot along the base for a wall-mounting bracket |
Designed into the profile |

|
Two lengths for the two product versions |
Cut to length from the same profile |

|
Square, clean end faces for the gaskets |
Machined after cutting |

|
Vent hole for a breathable membrane, and a window for a status light |
Machined after cutting |

|
End caps with a cable gland, a connector cut-out and a gasket groove |
Machined from aluminium plate for the first batches; a moulded cap is considered once volumes are known |

|
Deburring, bead blasting and clear anodising, with a masked earth contact inside |
Finishing after machining |

Before ordering the die, the team asks two extruders to review the section and quote the die, minimum run and machining, then builds the first samples into complete units for seal and temperature tests.
This example gives no prices on purpose: get real quotes for your own profile.

## Common mistakes

**Designing the profile like a machined part.**
Thin fins beside thick walls, sharp corners and tight tolerances everywhere make a die that is hard to run. Let the extruder review the section.

**Forgetting what cannot be extruded.**
Holes, cut-outs and anything that changes along the length need machining. Count those operations in the cost, not just the extrusion.

**Leaving the end caps until last.**
The ends carry the connectors, seal and fixings, and the screw ports depend on them. Design them alongside the profile.

**Too little clearance in the PCB slots.**
Board thickness varies and anodising adds material. Leave clearance so the board slides in without forcing.

**Commissioning a custom die too early.**
If the board outline or the look is still changing, prototype in a standard profile first.

## Next steps

- Check whether a standard enclosure profile fits your board and connectors before designing your own.

- Sketch the profile section with balanced walls, screw ports and PCB slots, and mark the critical and cosmetic faces.

- Plan the ends with [sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) and the heat path with [managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html).

- Send the section and drawings to two or three extruders using [finding and briefing a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html), and compare their replies with [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html).

## FAQ

### Is an extrusion die expensive?

Compared with a die-casting die or an injection mould for a similar part, an extrusion die is usually much cheaper, because it is a relatively simple steel disc. Cost rises with profile size, complexity and the number of hollows, so ask extruders for quotes on your own section.

### Can I start with a standard enclosure extrusion and change later?

Yes, and it is often the sensible route. Prototype and sell early units in a standard profile, then move to a custom profile once the board outline, connectors and look are stable. Keep the end caps and board design easy to adapt.

### Which aluminium alloy is used for extruded enclosures?

6063 and 6060 are commonly used, because they extrude well and anodise to a good finish. 6082 is often offered where more strength is needed. Ask your extruder which alloy and temper they recommend for your profile and finish.

### Can an extruded enclosure be waterproof?

Yes. The tube itself has no joints along its length, so sealing comes down to the two ends: gaskets compressed between the end caps and square, clean end faces, plus sealed cable glands and connectors. Test the complete unit, not just the parts.

### What has to be machined after extrusion?

Anything that is not constant along the length: connector holes, windows, vents, mounting holes and sometimes the end faces. Cutting to length and deburring are always needed, and finishing usually follows machining.

Title: Assembly and Work Instructions

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and engineers handing a product to a factory who want every unit built the same way

# Assembly instructions and work instructions for production

Why written build instructions still matter when a contract manufacturer does the assembly, what a good work instruction contains, how to write it for the person at the bench, and how to build, error-proof and control it from the pilot run onwards.

Quick answer

## A work instruction is a short, illustrated, step-by-step sheet that tells an operator exactly how to build one stage of your product, with the parts, tools, settings and checks for each step.

Even when a contract manufacturer assembles the product, you should own or approve the instructions, because they fix how the product is built, what is checked and what the quote was based on.
Give each instruction a document number and revision tied to the bill of materials, keep to one action per step, show rather than tell, prove the instructions during the pilot run, and change them only through the same change process as the design.

## Contents

- Why written instructions matter

- Work instructions, assembly drawings and user instructions

- What a good work instruction contains

- Writing for the person at the bench

- Building them from the pilot run

- Fixtures and jigs

- Error-proofing the design

- Keeping instructions under revision control

- Worked example: a small enclosure

- Common mistakes

## Why written instructions matter

It is tempting to assume that once a contract manufacturer has your drawings and a sample, how they assemble the product is their business. In practice, assembly decides much of how well it works, how long it lasts and what it costs. Written instructions are how you keep control without standing at the line.

- **Consistency.** Without written steps, each operator and shift develops its own method, and small differences, such as screw order or [cable routing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cables-wiring-and-connectors-inside-a-product.html), become variation you cannot explain later.

- **Training.** Factories move people between lines. A clear instruction lets someone new build the product correctly on their first day.

- **Quality.** The instruction is where checks happen. If a critical feature is not checked at the step where it can go wrong, the first chance to find it may be your customer.

- **Cost quotes.** A supplier prices assembly from the steps they expect. Agreeing the instruction gives you a basis to compare and question quotes.

- **Changes.** A controlled instruction is how a design change reaches the bench, rather than a new part sitting beside the old one with nobody told which to use.

The manufacturer will often write the final, line-specific version in their own format. That is fine. What matters is that you supply the design intent, approve what they write and keep a copy at the same revision.

## Work instructions, assembly drawings and user instructions

Three different documents are often called "assembly instructions". They have different readers and should not be merged.

- **Assembly drawing.** An [engineering drawing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) of the finished assembly, usually with an exploded view and a parts list or balloon references to the [bill of materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html). It defines what the assembly is, not the order of work or the checks.

- **Work instruction.** A step-by-step guide for one station or stage of production, written for the operator. It defines how the assembly is built and checked, in sequence.

- **End-user instructions.** The manual or quick-start card for your customer. That is separate work with its own safety and legal content, outside the scope of this guide.

The work instruction refers to the assembly drawing and BOM; it never replaces them. If they disagree, the released drawing and BOM win, and the instruction must be corrected.

## What a good work instruction contains

Each instruction usually covers one station or one sub-assembly, with a header and a short sequence of steps. A useful one includes:

- **Document number and revision.** Its own number, a revision letter, a date and an approval, plus the BOM and assembly drawing revisions it applies to. An operator should be able to see at a glance that the sheet matches the parts in front of them.

- **Parts and quantities for each step.** Part number, name and quantity, taken from the BOM rather than retyped from memory. Listing parts per step, not just at the top, stops a small part being forgotten.

- **Tools and fixtures.** Which driver, bit, press, fixture or test lead is used, identified by name or number so the right one is picked up.

- **Torques and settings.** Screw torques, press forces, adhesive quantities and cure times, heat-staking or welding settings. These come from the design, the fastener or adhesive supplier, or trials, so write them on the instruction as placeholders such as "[torque from drawing]" until the released value is confirmed, never as a guess.

- **One action per step.** "Fit the lid" and "drive the four screws" are two steps. Combined steps hide errors and make it impossible to see which one went wrong.

- **Photos or exploded views.** At least one picture per step, with the part being added highlighted and its orientation obvious.

- **Critical-to-quality checks.** The [critical-to-quality features](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) that can go wrong at this step, with a clear pass or fail criterion: "[gasket](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) visible all round, no folds", not "check gasket".

- **Handling and ESD notes.** Where a step involves bare [circuit boards](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html), sensitive components, cosmetic surfaces or sharp edges, say what precautions apply, such as using the factory's static-safe workstation, wearing gloves, or holding a board by its edges. Keep these general and let the manufacturer's own procedures supply the detail.

One step, one action. The header ties the sheet to a released revision, the picture carries most of the meaning, and the check gives a clear pass or fail before the operator moves on.

## Writing for the person at the bench

The reader is an operator building the product many times a shift, glancing at a screen or sheet above the bench, possibly in a second language. Write for that person, not for an engineer reviewing the document.

- **Start each step with a plain verb:** place, push, fit, drive, route, check. Avoid vague words such as "secure" or "assemble", which can mean several different things.

- **Put pictures before words.** A clear photo with an arrow or a highlighted part often does most of the work, and the text confirms it. Show the correct result, and for steps that often go wrong, a photo of the wrong result marked as such.

- **Keep the text short.** A step that needs a paragraph is usually two or three steps.

- **Use the same name for the same part everywhere**, matching the BOM. "Lid", "cover" and "top housing" on one sheet suggests three parts.

- **Plan for translation when the factory is overseas.** Short, literal sentences translate more reliably than idiomatic ones. Ask the manufacturer to translate, have someone you trust check it, and keep both versions at the same revision. Pictures and part numbers travel better than any wording.

**Practical rule:**
give the draft instruction and a kit of parts to someone who has never seen the product. Watch, without helping. Every hesitation, question or wrong move marks a step to rewrite or a picture to add.

## Building them from the pilot run

Draft the instructions from the CAD model and your prototype builds, but treat that draft as a hypothesis. The [pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) is where it is tested: real operators, real fixtures and parts from production suppliers, at production rate.

- **Watch where operators hesitate, improvise or ask.** Each of those is an unclear step, a missing picture or a design feature that is harder to assemble than it looked.

- **Record defects by step.** If a defect keeps appearing at one step, the instruction, the fixture or the design at that step needs attention.

- **Time each step and each station.** Compare the observed times with the figures your costing assumed, such as a concept-stage estimate from the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html); [estimating assembly time](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) explains how that estimate is built. Update the inputs it shares with the line, such as seconds per join and check time, so your unit cost reflects what the line actually does.

- **Update and re-release.** Revise the instructions from what you observed and release them at a new revision before volume production, so the ramp-up starts from the proven version.

## Fixtures and jigs

A fixture or jig is a holder that locates parts in the right position while they are assembled, glued, pressed or tested. It can be as simple as a 3D-printed nest that holds a housing upside down, or as involved as a powered press with a part-specific tool.

Fixtures make assembly faster and more repeatable because the operator no longer judges alignment by eye, and they act as a check: a part that will not sit in its nest is probably wrong or the wrong way round. Name each fixture in the instruction and treat a change to it like a change to the instruction. Some [joining methods](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html), such as adhesives with a cure time or ultrasonic welding, cannot be done consistently without one, so discuss fixtures with the manufacturer when you choose the joint, not after the pilot.

## Error-proofing the design

Error-proofing, often called by its Japanese name **poka-yoke**, means arranging things so that the wrong action is impossible, or at least immediately obvious. A warning in a work instruction depends on someone reading and remembering it every time. A feature in the design that prevents the mistake works on every unit, on every shift.

The best place to error-proof is the design itself, while it is still easy to change:

- **Asymmetric features.** If a part must go one way, give it a tab, notch or offset hole so it only fits that way. If orientation does not matter, make it fully symmetrical so there is nothing to get wrong.

- **Keyed connectors.** Use cable connectors that only fit one way, and avoid two identical connectors on one board unless they are keyed or coloured differently.

- **Locating features.** Pins, ribs and slots that guide a part into place make correct alignment the easy path.

- **Visible confirmation.** A snap fit that clicks, a connector latch you can see, a window that shows a gasket in its groove: features that tell the operator the step is done.

Where the design cannot prevent an error, the fixture or a test can catch it: a nest that only accepts the correct orientation, or an end-of-line test that detects a missing part. The instruction is the last line of defence, not the first.

## Keeping instructions under revision control

Work instructions are controlled documents, exactly like drawings. Give each one a number and revision, and list it against the assembly it builds, so the BOM, drawings and instructions move together. When a part changes revision, check every instruction that uses it as part of the same [change process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html); the [Change Request Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/change-request-builder.html) can help you record which documents a change affects.

Ask how the factory makes sure only the current revision is on the line and old printed copies are removed. When you [brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html), say who will write and approve the instructions and how changes will be handled, so it is agreed before the quote rather than argued over after.

## Worked example: a small enclosure

Illustrative example. A small battery-powered sensor has a moulded base and lid, a circuit board, a battery with a short lead, a gasket and four screws. The steps below are part of work instruction WI-104 at revision B, applying to the assembly at the matching BOM revision. Part numbers are invented for the example, and the torque is a placeholder to be filled from the released drawing.

The team added photos of a latched and an unlatched connector, logged a design action for a connector with a more visible latch, fed the observed times into the assembly estimate, and released WI-104 at revision C.

## Common mistakes

**Leaving it all to the factory.**
If you never see the instructions, you cannot know which checks are made or what the quote assumed. Supply the design intent and approve the result.

**Several actions in one step.**
Long steps are skimmed and partly done. One action, one picture, one check.

**Vague checks.**
"Check assembly" gives no pass or fail. Say what to look at and what good looks like.

**Guessed settings.**
Torques and cure times typed in from habit can crack bosses or leave joints weak. Take them from the design and confirm them in trials.

**Instructions that drift from the BOM.**
A part changes and the instruction does not. Keep both under the same change process and revision.

**Relying on the instruction to prevent errors.**
If a part can be fitted the wrong way, sooner or later it will be. Fix it in the design or the fixture where you can.

## Next steps

- Draft a work instruction for your main assembly from the CAD model and your last prototype build, one action per step.

- Look for any part that could fit the wrong way and ask whether the design can prevent it.

- Plan to prove the instructions and time each station during your [pilot run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html), and agree the inspection checks with your supplier using [quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html).

- See where this sits in the wider journey in the [manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

Work instructions

Fixtures

## FAQ

### Who should write the work instructions, me or the manufacturer?

Usually both. You supply the design intent: the assembly drawing, BOM, critical features, settings and the order that matters. The manufacturer often writes the line version in their own format. You approve it and keep a copy at the same revision.

### What is the difference between a work instruction and an assembly drawing?

An assembly drawing defines what the finished assembly is, with its parts and key dimensions. A work instruction tells an operator how to build it, step by step, with the tools, settings and checks for each step.

### Do I need work instructions for a small batch I assemble myself?

A simple version, yes. Even a few illustrated steps with the checks keep units consistent, help anyone who helps you, and become the starting point when you hand assembly to a supplier later.

### What does poka-yoke mean?

It is a Japanese term for error-proofing: arranging the design, fixture or process so a mistake cannot be made, or is caught straight away. Asymmetric parts that only fit one way and keyed connectors are common examples.

### When should work instructions be finalised?

Draft them before the pilot run, prove them during it, and release the updated version before volume production. After that, change them only through the same change process as the drawings and BOM.

Title: Estimating Assembly Time During Design

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For engineers and designers reducing assembly cost before the design is fixed

# Estimating assembly time during design.

Assembly cost is often locked in long before the manufacturing line exists. Part count, fastening logic,
awkward handling, and repeated checks all leave early signals if you know how to read them.

**Topic**
Design for assembly

**Audience**
Engineers and product teams

**Tool**
Assembly Time Estimator

**Use it for**
Architecture comparison

Quick answer

## To estimate assembly time during design, count the parts, joins, reorientations and checks in each concept, give each a typical time, and add them up.

Assembly time ≈ (parts × handling and insertion time) + (joins × fastening time) + (reorientations × turn time) + (checks × inspection time)

Multiply the total in seconds by a fully loaded labour rate per second to get labour cost per unit. The result is a comparison tool, not a forecast:
it shows which concept is likely to be quicker and cheaper to build, and which parts and joins are driving the time, long before a production line is planned.

Early-stage assembly estimates are imperfect, but they are still highly useful. The goal is not to predict final takt time to the second.
The goal is to expose which concept directions are likely to become labour-heavy and which ones are quietly removing future cost.

**Best use of the estimate:**
compare concepts, not absolutes. If one architecture removes joins, handling steps, or reorientation, that signal is more valuable than pretending the estimate is exact.

## Contents

- Where the time usually comes from

- Typical times to use at concept stage

- The classic method: design for assembly

- Worked example

- Why this matters before manufacturing engineering starts

- Five design-for-assembly questions to ask in review

- Common mistakes

- Use the estimate as a design conversation starter

- Next steps

- Pair the assembly tool with other decisions

## Where the time usually comes from

In manual or semi-manual assembly, recurring time often accumulates from mundane actions rather than dramatic ones: picking up a part, turning the assembly,
aligning a fastener, checking that a feature has seated correctly, or pausing because the next step is not obvious.

|
Assembly driver |
What it looks like in the design |
Why it matters |

|
Part count |
More individual handled items |
Each extra part creates handling, orientation, and error potential |

|
Handling difficulty |
Small, flexible, slippery, sharp or tangling parts; parts that look symmetrical but are not |
Awkward parts slow the pick and raise the chance of fitting them the wrong way round |

|
Insertion difficulty |
Tight fits with no lead-in, parts that must be held while something else is fitted, obstructed access or poor visibility |
Insertion that needs care or a second hand is slower and less repeatable |

|
Join count |
More screws, clips, adhesives, or repeated fastening steps |
Joining effort scales directly with labour time |

|
Reorientation |
The build must be turned repeatedly during the process |
Operator movement adds non-value time and often increases mistake risk |

|
Inspection burden |
Frequent checks to confirm fit or function |
QA time is recurring cost and often indicates design ambiguity |

## Typical times to use at concept stage

You do not need a stopwatch study to start. Use rough, consistent allowances for each action, and apply the same allowances to every concept you compare.
The ranges below are broad, hedged starting points for manual bench assembly of small products; real times depend on the part, the operator, the fixtures and the batch size.

|
Action |
Rough allowance |
What pushes it up |

|
Pick and place an easy part |
A few seconds |
Small or nested parts, tweezers, holding down while fitting |

|
Snap fit or push fit |
A few seconds |
No lead-in, high insertion force, uncertain engagement |

|
Driving a screw |
Often several seconds or more |
Hand starting, mixed screw types, poor access, torque checks |

|
Adhesive or tape |
Several seconds plus any cure or hold time |
Surface preparation, careful alignment, waiting before the next step |

|
Turning the assembly over |
A few seconds |
Loose parts that must be held in place, heavy or awkward assemblies |

|
Visual or functional check |
A few seconds to much longer |
Hidden features, test equipment, recording results |

If you have timed a similar product, use those figures instead. The [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) applies consistent allowances so you can compare concepts quickly.

## The classic method: design for assembly

Structured design for assembly (DFA) was formalised by Geoffrey Boothroyd and Peter Dewhurst, whose method estimates handling and insertion time for each part from its features
and compares the design against a theoretical minimum number of parts. You do not need the full method to use its core idea. For each part, ask three questions:

- Does the part move relative to the parts it joins during normal use?

- Must it be a different material, or isolated from the others, for a real functional reason?

- Must it be separate so that other parts can be assembled, removed or serviced?

If the answer to all three is no, the part is a candidate for combining with a neighbour. Fasteners, brackets, spacers and covers often fail this test.
Treat the result as a prompt, not a rule: a separate part can still be the right choice for cost, tooling, repair or supply reasons.

A few seconds lost in one unit rarely look alarming. A few seconds repeated across every unit, every batch, and every operator become a design decision with financial consequences.

## Worked example

Illustrative figures only. Imagine two concepts that create similar user value. Concept A uses 12 parts, 8 screwed joins, 3 reorientations and 2 checks.
Concept B uses 9 parts and 5 joins, removes one awkward reorientation, and needs only 1 check because its parts can only fit one way.

Using assumed allowances (lower than the Assembly Time Estimator's defaults of 7 to 18 seconds per part and 6 seconds per reorientation) of 4 seconds to handle and insert each part, 8 seconds per screw, 4 seconds per reorientation and 5 seconds per check:

- Concept A: (12 × 4) + (8 × 8) + (3 × 4) + (2 × 5) = 48 + 64 + 12 + 10 = 134 seconds.

- Concept B: (9 × 4) + (5 × 8) + (2 × 4) + (1 × 5) = 36 + 40 + 8 + 5 = 89 seconds.

With an assumed fully loaded labour rate of £30 an hour, Concept A costs about £1.12 of labour per unit (134 ÷ 3,600 × £30) and Concept B about £0.74 (89 ÷ 3,600 × £30).
The 45-second saving is worth about £0.38 a unit, or roughly £3,750 over 10,000 units, before counting fewer parts to buy, stock and inspect.
The absolute numbers will be wrong in detail; the direction, and the fact that screws account for nearly half of Concept A's time, are the useful findings.

Illustrative allowances from the example above, bars drawn to scale. Screws are nearly half of Concept A's time, and fewer screws give Concept B the largest part of its 45-second saving.

## Why this matters before manufacturing engineering starts

- Assembly cost compounds over [pilot runs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html), launch batches, and production scale-up.

- Complex assembly often hides reliability and quality risk as well as labour cost.

- Many assembly burdens are locked in by architecture decisions long before detailed production planning exists.

- Every part removed also removes a drawing, a supplier line, a stock item and an inspection point, so the saving usually reaches beyond labour. For a product already in production, [reducing the cost of an existing product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html) shows how to weigh that saving against tool changes and retesting.

## Five design-for-assembly questions to ask in review

- Can two parts become one without damaging serviceability?

- Can alignment features become more self-locating?

- Can the join count be reduced without compromising strength or repair? ([Joining methods compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) sets out the trade-offs.)

- Can the build be completed in fewer orientations?

- Does the design force extra checking because the correct state is not obvious?

## Common mistakes

**Treating the estimate as a quote.**
Concept-stage figures compare options. Your manufacturer will set real times from their own process, fixtures and labour rates.

**Merging parts at any cost.**
Combining parts can create a complex, expensive moulding or make repair impossible. Check the tooling cost and the service plan before merging.

**Counting parts but not joins.**
Two designs with the same part count can differ greatly in time if one uses screws and the other uses snap fits or locating features.

**Ignoring mistake-proofing.**
A part that can be fitted the wrong way round adds checking time and rework. Make asymmetric parts clearly asymmetric, or fully symmetrical.

**Using different allowances for different concepts.**
The comparison is only fair if each action is valued the same way in every option.

**Forgetting cables, labels and packing.**
Routing wires, fitting labels and packing the product are real steps and are often missing from early estimates.

## Use the estimate as a design conversation starter

**Look for repeated actions.**
Repetition is where labour hides. One difficult step repeated eight times is usually more important than one obviously awkward step.

**Challenge false precision.**
The point is not to claim that assembly will take exactly 4.6 minutes. The point is to know which concept is directionally better.

**Link time to architecture.**
If the estimate changes substantially after a small architecture change, that is a strong design signal worth acting on.

## Next steps

- List the parts and joins for each concept, ideally in the [BOM Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html).

- Run each concept through the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) using the same allowances.

- Apply the three minimum-part questions above to the parts driving the most time.

- Check that any merged parts are still mouldable or machinable with the [DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html).

- Feed the labour figure into the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) to see its effect on unit cost.

For the wider context, see [how to estimate manufacturing cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html),
[how engineers choose between concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html), and
[design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html), which covers the other side of the same joints.
The [Development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html) and the
[Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html) put this in the wider product journey.

Design review prompt

If the assembly estimate rises mainly because of repeated joins or reorientation, the problem is probably structural, not operational.

## FAQ

### How do engineers estimate assembly time before production?

They use early proxies such as part count, join count, handling difficulty, reorientation, and inspection effort to compare concepts before process engineering is locked.

### What design changes reduce assembly time most?

Reducing part count, removing unnecessary joins, simplifying orientation, and improving part location usually provide the strongest gains.

### Why does assembly time matter so early?

Because recurring seconds become recurring cost across pilot, launch, and scaled production, and those costs are often created by decisions made during architecture and concept development.

### How long does it take to assemble a product?

It depends almost entirely on the design. A small product with a handful of snap-fitted parts may take well under a minute by hand; one with many screws, cables and checks can take several minutes or more. Count the parts, joins, reorientations and checks to get a first estimate.

### What is design for assembly (DFA)?

Design for assembly is the practice of designing parts and products so they are quick, easy and hard to get wrong when assembled. Its core principles are fewer parts, fewer separate fasteners, parts that are easy to handle and self-locating, and an assembly built from one direction with few reorientations. Boothroyd and Dewhurst developed the classic structured method.
