Title: Bills of Materials and Revision Control

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small teams who need their supplier to build exactly the version they approved

# Bills of materials and revision control: making sure everyone builds the same product

What a bill of materials is and who relies on it, the columns worth having, engineering and manufacturing BOMs, simple part numbers, revision letters, release states, a light change process for a small team, and how to send suppliers the right files.

Quick answer

## A bill of materials (BOM) lists every part in the product with its part number, revision and quantity; revision control makes sure everyone is working from the same version of each part.

Give every part a plain, sequential part number and a revision letter, and keep the CAD, drawing and BOM at the same revision. Raise the revision when a change keeps the part interchangeable, and create a new part number when it does not.
Only send suppliers released files, as STEP models plus PDF drawings, log what you sent, and put every change through a short request, impact check and approval with a clear date or serial number from which it applies.

## Contents

- What a BOM is and who uses it

- The columns that matter

- Engineering vs manufacturing BOMs, flat vs indented

- Part numbering

- Revision control

- Release states: draft, released, obsolete

- A simple change process

- Sharing files with suppliers

- Worked example: a bike light BOM and one change

- Common mistakes

## What a BOM is and who uses it

A bill of materials is the parts list for your product: every moulding, fastener, [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html), label, cable and carton needed to make one finished unit, with the quantity of each. It ties the design to what actually gets bought, built and checked, and several people rely on it:

- **You**, to see the whole product in one place, estimate cost and work out what a change will affect.

- **The manufacturer**, to quote, plan assembly and check that every part on the line is the right one.

- **Purchasing**, whether you or the factory, to order the right quantities and spot long lead-time items.

- **Quality control**, to inspect parts and finished units against the correct revision, as in [quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html).

If they read different versions of the list, you get parts ordered to an old drawing and units inspected against the wrong standard. Revision control prevents that.

## The columns that matter

A spreadsheet is enough for most small products. These are the columns worth having from the start:

|
Column |
What it holds |

|Item |A line number, or a position such as 1.2.3 that shows where the part sits in the structure |

|Part number |Your unique identifier for the part; the same part always has the same number |

|Revision |The current released revision of that part, such as B |

|Description |A short, consistent name: noun first, then detail, such as "Screw, M2 x 6, pan head" |

|Quantity |How many are used per parent assembly, with the unit if it is not "each" (grams of adhesive, millimetres of tubing) |

|Material and finish |The material grade, colour and finish, or "see drawing" where the drawing holds the detail |

|Make or buy |Make: made to your drawing. Buy: a catalogue part you order as it is |

|Supplier and manufacturer part number |For bought parts, the maker's own part number, plus approved alternatives if you have them |

|Unit cost |The cost per part at your expected order quantity, with the date of the quote |

|Notes |Anything that affects buying or building: lead time, single source, safety-critical, torque setting |

Include the small things: screws, labels, adhesive, the leaflet and the box. Leaving them off is a common reason an early [manufacturing cost estimate](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html) comes in low.

## Engineering vs manufacturing BOMs, flat vs indented

The **engineering BOM** describes the product as designed. It usually mirrors the assembly structure in your CAD model and is owned by the design team.
The **manufacturing BOM** describes the product as built. It is grouped by how the factory assembles it, and adds things CAD does not show: glue, grease, solder paste, protective film, packing materials and sometimes an allowance for scrap.

For a small company, you usually keep the engineering BOM and the manufacturer creates its own manufacturing BOM from it. Ask to see theirs before the first build and check it against yours; differences are where wrong parts hide.

A BOM can be laid out two ways:

- **Flat:** every part listed once with its total quantity per product. Good for purchasing and costing.

- **Indented (multi-level):** parts grouped under their sub-assemblies, with quantities per parent. Good for assembly planning and for seeing what a change touches.

Keep the indented version as your master and produce a flat list from it when needed: a part's total is its quantity multiplied by the quantity of each assembly above it.

## Part numbering

A part number has one job: to identify a part uniquely and permanently. The simplest scheme that does that is a plain sequential number, such as 1001, 1002, 1003, with a short fixed prefix if you like, issued from a single register so nobody hands out the same number twice.

Resist building meaning into the number. Schemes that encode material, colour, product family or supplier look tidy, but the meaning goes out of date when the part is reused or the material changes, leaving a misleading number or a renumbering job.
Put that information in the description, where it can change. A little grouping, such as a separate range for assemblies, is fine if it never needs to change.

**Practical rule:**
a part number identifies; it does not describe. The revision letter, not the part number, tells you which version you are looking at.

## Revision control

Every made part has a revision, usually a letter: A for the first released version, then B, C and so on. Many teams skip I, O and Q because they look like numbers. Some use numbers or a prefix such as X1, X2 for pre-release drafts and switch to letters at first release; either works if you are consistent.
The revision appears in the drawing title block, in the file names and in the BOM line.

### New revision or new part number?

The usual test is **form, fit and function**. If the changed part can still replace the old one in every product where it is used, without any other change, it is interchangeable: raise the revision. If it no longer fits, works or looks the same in a way that matters, so that mixing old and new parts would cause a problem, give it a new part number.

- **New revision:** a thicker rib inside a housing, a corrected drawing note, a tighter tolerance that old parts also meet.

- **New part number:** a hole that moves so the old screw no longer reaches, a change of colour where both colours will be stocked, a connector that is no longer compatible with the old cable.

When a part gets a new number, the parent BOM needs a new revision too. When in doubt, ask whether anyone, including a repair technician years from now, could pick up the wrong one and get into trouble. If so, it needs a new number.

### Keeping CAD, drawings and BOM in step

The 3D model, the 2D drawing and the BOM line for a part should always carry the same revision. A practical way to keep them together is to name files with part number and revision, such as 1103_C.step and 1103_C.pdf, and never edit a released file: copy it, raise the revision, and work on the copy.
The [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) guide covers what the title block and revision table on a drawing should show.

## Release states: draft, released, obsolete

Each revision of a part sits in one of three states:

- **Draft:** work in progress. It can change without notice. It can be sent out for an early budget quote if it is clearly marked as draft, but never used to cut tooling or order production parts.

- **Released:** approved for quoting, tooling and production. From now on it only changes through the change process, and the change creates a new revision.

- **Obsolete:** replaced by a later revision or no longer used. Keep the files, because you may need them to support products already sold, but mark them clearly so nobody orders from them.

Releasing a part is a decision, often taken at a [design review](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html). Record who released it and when.

## A simple change process

Large companies run formal change requests and change orders through dedicated software. A small team needs the same steps, not the overhead: a spreadsheet log and a folder per change is enough.

The same five steps work for a one-line drawing correction and a new moulding; only the depth of the impact check changes.

- **Change request.** Anyone can raise one. Write down what should change, why, and which part numbers are affected. Give it a number.

- **Impact check.** Before deciding, work out what the change touches: parts in stock and on order, tooling that needs modifying, certification or test results that may no longer hold (see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html)), and the effect on unit and one-off cost. Use the indented BOM to find every assembly that contains the part.

- **Approval.** One named person, usually whoever owns the product, approves or rejects the change and records the decision with the date.

- **Release.** Update the CAD, drawing and BOM together, raise the revision or issue a new part number, and mark the previous revision obsolete or "use up existing stock".

- **Effectivity.** State when the change takes effect: from a date, a production batch or a serial number. Tell suppliers in writing and ask them to confirm. This is what lets you answer "which customers have the old version?" later.

Changes driven by faults found after launch follow the same steps, with root cause and re-testing added; [after launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) covers that side.

## Sharing files with suppliers

Most revision mix-ups start in an email thread. A few habits prevent nearly all of them:

- **Send released revisions only** for anything that will be quoted firmly, tooled or built. If you must send a draft for an early opinion, mark it as draft in the file name and on the drawing.

- **Send STEP plus a PDF drawing** for every made part. STEP gives the geometry in a neutral format any CAD system can open; the PDF drawing gives tolerances, material, finish and the revision. Where they disagree, say which one governs, usually the drawing.

- **Send a matching BOM** that lists the same revisions as the files in the pack.

- **Log what you sent:** date, supplier, part numbers, revisions and the purpose (quote, tooling, production). Ask the supplier to quote the revision back on their quotation and order confirmation.

The [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html) helps you assemble a quote pack with the right files listed, and [must-have documents before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) covers the rest of the pack.

## Worked example: a bike light BOM and one change

Illustrative example. A small company is about to order its first production batch of a rechargeable front bike light: a moulded housing and rear cover sealed with an [O-ring](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html), a lens, a circuit board, a battery cell, a handlebar clip and a retail box. The part numbers, revisions and structure below are invented to show the layout; the material, make-or-buy, supplier and cost columns are left out so the table fits the page.

Illustrative indented BOM for a rechargeable bike light

|
Item |
Part no. |
Rev |
Description |
Qty |

|1 |1000 |A |Bike light, packed |1 |

|1.1 |1100 |A |Light assembly |1 |

|1.1.1 |1101 |B |Housing, PC/ABS, black |1 |

|1.1.2 |1102 |A |Lens, clear PC |1 |

|1.1.3 |1103 |B |Rear cover, PC/ABS, black |1 |

|1.1.4 |1104 |A |O-ring, nitrile |1 |

|1.1.5 |1105 |C |PCB assembly, LED driver |1 |

|1.1.6 |1106 |A |Battery cell with protection |1 |

|1.1.7 |1107 |A |Screw, M2 x 6, pan head |4 |

|1.2 |1200 |A |Handlebar clip assembly |1 |

|1.2.1 |1201 |A |Clip body, nylon |1 |

|1.2.2 |1202 |A |Strap, silicone |1 |

|1.3 |1300 |A |Charging cable, USB-C |1 |

|1.4 |1400 |A |Retail box, printed |1 |

|1.5 |1500 |A |Instruction leaflet |1 |

**The change.** During pilot assembly, two rear covers crack at a screw boss when the screws are driven. The team raises change request CR-007: thicken the boss wall and add a small fillet at its base on 1103.

**Form, fit and function.** The outside of the cover, the screw holes and the sealing face do not move, so a rev C cover fits every housing and uses the same screws. Old and new covers are interchangeable, so this is a new revision, not a new part number.

**Impact check.** Stock: rev B covers already moulded are used up with an extra visual check at assembly, and rev B moulding stops. Tooling: adding plastic means removing steel from the mould, a modification the moulder quotes. Certification: the sealing face is unchanged, but the water test is repeated on first-off rev C parts. Cost: a one-off tool charge; the piece price is unchanged.

**Approval and release.** The founder approves CR-007. 1103 rev C is released with an updated STEP file and drawing; rev B is marked "use up stock, then obsolete". Because the light assembly BOM lists revisions, 1100 is reissued as rev B, and the packed product 1000 as rev B in turn.

**Effectivity and suppliers.** The change applies from serial number 0501. The moulder and assembler receive the rev C files and updated BOM, confirm in writing, and the send log records it.

## Common mistakes

**Part numbers that try to say everything.**
Encoded numbers go out of date as soon as a part changes material or gets reused. Keep the number plain and put the detail in the description.

**CAD, drawing and BOM at different revisions.**
If the drawing says rev C and the STEP file is still rev B, the supplier has to guess. Release all three together, every time.

**Changing a released file in place.**
Overwriting a released revision destroys the record of what was built. Copy, raise the revision and keep the old one.

**A new revision where a new part number was needed.**
If old and new parts are not interchangeable, sharing a number means someone will eventually fit the wrong one.

**Changes agreed by email with no effectivity.**
Without a date or serial number, nobody can tell which units have the change. Record where every change starts.

## Next steps

- Set up your BOM with the columns above and cost it in the [BOM Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html).

- Start a part number register and a change log, even if each is a single spreadsheet tab.

- Put every change to a released part through a numbered request, impact check, approval and effectivity with the [Change Request Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/change-request-builder.html).

- Check that every made part has a drawing with a revision letter; [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains what it should show.

- Assemble your quote pack from released files with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

## FAQ

### Do I need special software to manage a BOM?

Not at first. A well-structured spreadsheet, a part number register and a change log are enough for most small products. Dedicated product data software becomes worthwhile when several people edit the same data, the product range grows or a customer requires it.

### When should a change get a new part number instead of a new revision?

When the old and new parts are no longer interchangeable in form, fit or function. If the new part can replace the old one everywhere without any other change, raise the revision; if mixing them could cause a problem, give the new part its own number.

### Should bought-in parts have my own part numbers?

Usually yes. Your own number stays the same if you change supplier or approve an alternative, while the supplier and manufacturer part numbers sit alongside it in the BOM.

### What is the difference between an engineering BOM and a manufacturing BOM?

The engineering BOM describes the product as designed, usually following the CAD structure. The manufacturing BOM describes it as built, grouped by assembly steps and including consumables such as adhesive and packing materials. Small teams usually keep the engineering BOM and check the manufacturer's version against it.

### What does effectivity mean?

It is the point from which a change applies, given as a date, a production batch or a serial number. Recording it means you can always tell which units contain the old part and which contain the new one.

Title: Building a Hardware Business Case

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders and product teams testing whether a product can pay back its development

# Building a hardware business case.

A credible hardware business case connects market reach, conversion, unit economics, development spend, and payback timing. It should make the opportunity easier to challenge, not easier to oversell.

Quick answer

## A hardware business case shows whether enough reachable buyers will pay a price that recovers development spend in an acceptable time.

Payback (years) = upfront investment / (annual gross profit - annual operating cost)

Build it from reachable market, realistic conversion, unit price and gross margin, then compare the profit that produces with the development,
tooling and operating cost it has to carry. If payback only looks acceptable when every assumption is optimistic, the case is not yet robust.

Early business cases go wrong when they confuse the total market with the reachable market. Hardware businesses do not monetise market size directly. They monetise the portion they can actually reach, convert, and serve.

A good business case is not a sales document. It is a structured argument that the team, an investor or a board can challenge line by line.
Its job is to make the important assumptions visible, show which ones the outcome depends on most, and point to the evidence that would make them stronger.

**Decision test:** if the business case only works when market share, conversion, and pricing all lean optimistic at the same time, the opportunity is not yet robust enough.

## Contents

- What belongs in the first-pass model

- Addressable market versus reachable market

- Why payback matters

- Worked example: a connected air-quality monitor

- Common mistakes in hardware business cases

- Practical next steps

## What belongs in the first-pass model

- **Addressable market and the smaller reachable segment:** who could buy, and who you can realistically get in front of with your channels and budget.

- **Conversion:** the share of that reachable audience that becomes actual unit sales each year.

- **Unit price and gross-profit quality:** the net price you receive after channel deductions, minus landed unit cost.

- **Development and tooling spend:** design, prototypes, tooling, certification and launch work that must be recovered.

- **Annual operating cost:** people, marketing, support, warehousing and overhead that the product has to carry every year.

Keep the first pass small. Five or six well-argued inputs are more useful than a fifty-tab spreadsheet that nobody can explain.
Detail can be added once the shape of the opportunity has survived a first challenge.

## Addressable market versus reachable market

The addressable market is everyone who could plausibly need the product. The reachable market is the part you can actually access in the next two or three years,
given your channels, geography, sales capacity, certification and price point. For most early hardware businesses the reachable segment is a small fraction of the headline figure.

That is not a weakness. A narrow, well-understood segment with a clear reason to buy is easier to convert than a vast, vague one.
The risk lies in multiplying a large market by a small percentage and treating the result as demand. That number has no evidence behind it.
Build demand upwards from the channels you will use and the conversion rates you can defend.

## Why payback matters

A large market story can still hide a poor payback profile. If it takes too long for the product to recover development and operating spend, the risk profile remains weak even if the eventual upside looks attractive.

Payback also connects the business case to cash. A product that recovers its investment in two years needs much less funding, and carries far less risk,
than one that needs six. Hardware product lives are finite, so a long payback can mean the product is superseded before it has earned its keep.

## Worked example: a connected air-quality monitor

Illustrative figures only. A small team is planning a connected air-quality monitor for small offices. They assume an addressable market of 400,000 organisations,
of which 10% (40,000) are reachable through their chosen channels. They expect 6% of that reachable group to buy each year, giving 2,400 units.

The net price received is GBP180 and landed unit cost is GBP81, so gross margin is 55% and gross profit is GBP99 per unit. Annual gross profit is 2,400 x GBP99 = GBP237,600.
The product carries GBP140,000 of annual operating cost, leaving GBP97,600 a year towards the GBP210,000 upfront investment in development, tooling and certification.
Payback is GBP210,000 / GBP97,600, or roughly 26 months.

That looks reasonable, until conversion is tested. The same model with conversion moved up and down tells a very different story.

|
Scenario |
Annual conversion |
Units per year |
Profit after operating cost |
Payback |

|
Conservative |
4% |
1,600 |
GBP18,400 |
Over 11 years |

|
Expected |
6% |
2,400 |
GBP97,600 |
About 26 months |

|

3,200 |
GBP176,800 |
About 14 months |

The lesson is not that the product is good or bad. It is that conversion is the assumption that decides the case, so it is where the team should spend its next round of evidence-gathering:
pilot customers, pre-orders, distributor conversations or a small paid test.

Illustrative figures from the table above, bars drawn to scale. Two points of conversion either side of the expected 6% move payback from about 14 months to over 11 years, so conversion is the assumption to test first.

A useful business case tells you which assumption to test next. A weak one only tells you the answer you hoped for.

## Common mistakes in hardware business cases

**Top-down demand.**
Taking a percentage of a large market instead of building demand from channels, conversion and sales capacity.

**Using retail price as revenue.**
Revenue should be what the business actually receives after VAT, retailer margin or marketplace fees, not the price on the shelf.

**Gross margin based on factory price.**
Unit cost should be landed cost, including freight, duty, packaging and an allowance for scrap and returns.

**Forgetting the operating cost.**
A product can have healthy unit economics and still fail to pay back if support, marketing and overhead are left out.

**One scenario only.**
A single forecast hides fragility. Always show conservative, expected and optimistic cases side by side.

## Practical next steps

- Write down the reachable segment and the channels that reach it, in one sentence each.

- Estimate net price per channel and landed unit cost, even if the cost is a range.

- List the upfront investment as cost blocks rather than a single figure.

- Run three conversion scenarios and note which one the business can survive.

- Identify the single assumption that moves payback most, and plan how to test it before committing to tooling.

The [Hardware Business Case Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/hardware-business-case-builder.html) helps structure that first-pass model so the discussion becomes about evidence and assumptions rather than enthusiasm.
When the case needs monthly detail on margin, stock and cash, [building a hardware financial model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-financial-model.html) shows how to extend it.
For the upfront investment line, the guide to [estimating hardware development costs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html) breaks the budget into blocks you can defend.
If the problem itself still needs proving, start with [how to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html).
Once the case holds up, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) turns it into a staged plan for development, manufacture and launch.

## FAQ

### What should a hardware business case include?

At minimum: the reachable market, expected conversion into unit sales, net price after channel costs, landed unit cost and gross margin, upfront development and tooling spend, annual operating cost, and the resulting payback period. It should also show conservative, expected and optimistic scenarios so readers can see how fragile the outcome is.

### What is the difference between addressable and reachable market?

The addressable market is everyone who could plausibly need the product. The reachable market is the smaller group you can realistically access in the next few years with your channels, geography, budget and certification. Business cases should be built on the reachable market.

### How long should payback be for a hardware product?

There is no universal figure, but shorter is safer because hardware has upfront tooling and certification costs and a finite product life. Many early teams look for payback within two to three years of launch. If payback stretches beyond the expected life of the product, the case needs rethinking.

### How accurate does an early business case need to be?

It does not need to be precise, but it does need to be honest and explainable. Ranges are fine at the start. What matters is that each assumption has a stated source and that the team knows which assumption moves the result most.

### What gross margin should a hardware business case assume?

Use the margin your actual unit cost and channel prices produce, not a target. As a rough guide, many consumer hardware businesses aim for gross margins of around 40 to 60 per cent on direct sales, and less on wholesale. If the case only works at a margin well above that range, check the cost and price assumptions.

Title: Building a Hardware Financial Model

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and small teams who need one set of numbers to decide price, route, volume and funding

# Building a hardware financial model

A hardware financial model is not a forecast to impress anyone. It is a small machine that links what the product costs, what it sells for,
how many you sell and when cash moves, so you can see which decision changes the outcome and how much money the plan really needs.

**Topic**
Financial modelling

**Audience**
Founders, spin-outs, small teams

**Tools**
Cost, margin, break-even and cash tools

**Use it for**
Price, route, volume and funding decisions

Quick answer

## A hardware financial model links unit cost, net price, volume, fixed costs and payment timing to find profit, break-even and the cash low point.

Contribution per unit = net price (after VAT and channel share) - landed unit cost

Build it in blocks: landed unit cost, net price by route to market, monthly volume, fixed costs and upfront spend (development, tooling, certification),
then the timing of stock and customer payments. Contribution and fixed costs give break-even; the monthly cash flow gives the low point, which sets the funding need.
Run conservative, expected and optimistic scenarios, because a single set of numbers hides the assumption that matters most.

Most early teams already have pieces of a model: a costed bill of materials, a target price, a development budget. The pieces are rarely connected.
Change the route to market and margin, break-even, stock and funding need all change. A model is useful when one change flows through to every answer.

## Contents

- What the model is for

- The building blocks and how they connect

- Worked example: one product, one route

- Scenarios and sensitivity

- Which tool covers each block

- Common modelling mistakes

- Practical next steps

## What the model is for

Build the model around the decisions it supports, not around a template:

- **Price:** is there enough margin left after VAT, channel share and selling costs?

- **Route to market:** each route has a different net price and payment delay.

- **Volume:** how many units cover fixed costs, and is that realistic?

- **Funding need:** how much cash the business must have access to before sales carry it.

- **Timing:** when to commit to tooling, how large the first order should be, and when to raise money.

If a line in the spreadsheet does not affect one of these decisions, it can wait. Five or six well-argued inputs beat fifty tabs nobody can explain.

## The building blocks and how they connect

Each block feeds the next. Profit and break-even answer "does it make money?"; the monthly cash flow answers "can we survive until it does?". Scenarios flex the inputs at the top and show how far the low point moves.

### Unit economics: cost of goods and landed cost

Start with what one sellable unit costs you once it is in your warehouse: parts, assembly, packaging, inspection, scrap allowance, freight, duty and insurance.
That landed cost is the cost of goods sold (COGS) the model should use, not the factory price. See [landed cost: freight, duty and VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html).

### Price, VAT and channel margins

Revenue is the net price the business receives, not the shelf price. Remove VAT (UK consumer prices normally include it, at a standard rate of 20%),
then the retailer's margin or marketplace fees and your selling costs. Each route earns a different amount per unit, which is why [revenue and margin planning](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html) works backwards from the price to a target COGS for each route.

Margin = (price - cost) / price. Markup = (price - cost) / cost.

### Volume and demand

Build volume upwards from channels and conversion you can defend, month by month, rather than as a share of a large market.
A launch month, a growth rate and a ceiling set by stock or sales capacity are usually enough for a first pass. The
[hardware business case guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-business-case.html) explains reachable market and conversion.

### Fixed costs, development spend and tooling

Separate monthly fixed costs (people, rent, software, insurance, marketing) from one-off upfront spend (design, prototypes, tooling, certification).
Fixed costs set break-even; upfront spend sets how deep the cash hole is before the first sale. Tooling appears twice: as cash, paid (often in stages) before production,
and as a cost per unit when amortised. Keep both views, and never let the amortised figure hide the cash payment.

Tooling per unit = tooling cost / units the tool is expected to make over the period you choose

### Working capital: stock, MOQs and payment terms

Factories commonly ask for a deposit at order and the balance before shipment, minimum order quantities force larger batches, and retailers may pay
30 to 90 days after delivery. That is working capital: cash tied up between paying for stock and being paid for it.
[Minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) shows how a cheaper unit price can cost more cash.

### Monthly cash flow, the low point and break-even

Break-even is the volume at which contribution covers fixed costs. It does not say whether you survive until then. For that, lay out cash in and out
month by month and carry the balance forward. The lowest closing balance is the cash low point; the business needs enough cash to keep it above zero with a buffer. [Financial break-even for hardware products](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html) and
[calculating hardware start-up cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html) cover each method in depth.

## Worked example: one product, one route

Illustrative figures only, the same ones used in the [cash flow guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html) and the
[break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html), so you can follow them across the site.
A product sells direct for a net price of £49 (about £58.80 to a UK consumer once 20% VAT is added). Landed COGS is £22. Fixed overhead is £9,500 a month.
The business spends £18,000 upfront on development and tooling, starts with £85,000 in the bank, sells 120 units in month 1 and grows 12% a month.
Customers' money arrives one month after the sale, and stock is paid for in the month it is sold.

|

|

Read the rows together. A 55% margin looks healthy, yet sales only cover overhead in month 11, and because sales are paid a month late, cash falls until month 12. The business uses about £74,200 of its £85,000 before it turns, leaving a low point of roughly £10,800, a little over one month's overhead.
If the team wanted three months' overhead (£28,500) in hand at the low point, it would need roughly £102,700 at the start, or a smaller first year of spending.

The upfront spend row shows both views: about £6.20 a unit in the profit view, trimming contribution to about £20.80, while the full £18,000 left the bank in month 1.

## Scenarios and sensitivity

Change one input at a time and watch the low point. These rows rerun the same illustrative model with a single change each.

No change is dramatic on its own, and break-even does not move at all for the last two. The cash low point is far more sensitive, which is why cash is modelled monthly.
The row that moves the outcome most is where to gather evidence next: a firmer quote, a price test, early sales or better payment terms.

**Decision rule:**
if the plan only survives when price, cost, growth and payment timing all go your way, it needs more margin, a smaller first commitment or more funding before tooling is ordered.

## Common modelling mistakes

**Mixing margin and markup.**
A 50% markup is only a 33% margin. Agree which one a supplier, retailer or spreadsheet means before comparing figures.

**Ignoring VAT.**
VAT in a consumer price is not revenue; counting it overstates revenue by a sixth of the price. VAT on imports and sales also moves cash between periods, so check the timing with your accountant.

**Ignoring payment timing.**
Annual totals and same-month payment hide the low point. Model monthly, with real deposit, balance and customer payment terms.

**Single-point estimates.**
One forecast hides fragility. Show conservative, expected and optimistic cases, and note which input moves the result most.

**Forgetting tooling and certification.**
Both are paid before the first sale, may need modifying or repeating, and often land in the same few months as the first stock order.

## Practical next steps

- Write down the decisions the model has to support, and the date each one must be made.

- Get a landed unit cost, even as a range, from the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) and [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html).

- Work out the net price and target COGS for each route you are considering.

- Budget upfront spend with the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html), then find break-even.

- Build the monthly cash flow, find the low point in each scenario, and add contingency to get the funding need.

- Match that need to the options in [funding routes for hardware start-ups in the UK and Northern Ireland](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-routes-uk-northern-ireland.html), allowing for how long each takes to arrive.

The [Funding and cash hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-and-cash.html) sets this model in the wider picture of how much a hardware product needs and where the money can come from.

See how many units cover fixed cost, and how far small price or cost changes move it.

Hardware financial model
Unit economics
Funding need

## FAQ

### What should a hardware financial model include?

Landed unit cost, net price by route to market, monthly volume, fixed costs, upfront spend such as development, tooling and certification, and the timing of stock and customer payments. Together they give contribution, break-even and the monthly cash low point.

### Should I model monthly or annually?

Monthly, for at least the first eighteen months or until cash has clearly turned. The cash low point usually sits inside a single month, and annual totals hide it.

### How do I treat tooling in the model?

Twice. In the cash flow, record the payments when they are made, often in stages before production. In the profit view, spread the cost over the units the tool is expected to make so the unit cost reflects it.

### Do I include VAT in revenue?

No. Use the net price the business keeps after VAT and any channel share. VAT does affect cash timing, though, so check with your accountant how and when it will be paid and reclaimed.

### How does the model tell me how much funding I need?

Find the lowest closing cash balance in a cautious scenario. The cash used to reach that point, plus a contingency buffer, is the minimum the business must have access to. Then match it to funding routes, allowing for how long each takes to arrive.

Title: Cables, Wiring and Connectors in a Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and engineers whose product has a board, battery, motor or display wired together inside a housing

# Cables, wiring and connectors inside a product

Why internal wiring causes so many assembly faults and field failures, how to design out wires in the first place, and how to route, retain, connect, document and test the ones that remain, so they survive assembly, drops and years of use.

Quick answer

## Use as few internal wires as you can, and treat every one that remains as a designed part with a defined route, a fixing and a connector that cannot work loose.

Put parts on the main board or join boards directly where you can. Give the remaining cables moulded routes and clips, keep them clear of sharp edges, screws, moving and hot parts, and make sure any pull is taken by the housing, not a solder joint.
Choose latching, keyed connectors rated from the datasheet, document each harness with a drawing and a part number on the bill of materials, and check every unit for continuity and pin-out in production.

## Contents

- Why internal wiring causes problems

- Fewer wires first

- Routing and retention

- Choosing connectors

- Harnesses and harness drawings

- Mains wiring

- Testing wiring and connectors

- Worked example: a battery lead that fails after drops

- Common mistakes

## Why internal wiring causes problems

On a CAD model a cable is often left out or drawn at the end. In the product it is a flexible part that is fitted by hand and goes wherever it is pushed, which makes wiring a common source of assembly faults and field failures:

- **Assembly time and errors.** Each cable is another manual step and another chance to use the wrong socket, leave a plug half-seated or route the wire wrongly. [Estimating assembly time](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) shows how these steps add up.

- **Pinched or chafed wires.** A wire trapped in a seam, crushed by a screw boss or rubbing on a sharp edge can work for months before the insulation wears through.

- **Connectors working loose.** Drops and vibration shake a friction-held plug until the contact becomes intermittent, one of the hardest faults to find.

- **Solder joints taking cable loads.** A solder joint makes an electrical connection; it is not meant to hold a load. If a tug on the cable or a heavy part pulls on it, it can crack over time.

- **Heat near cables.** Insulation ages faster beside motors, chargers, power parts and heaters. [Managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html) covers finding the hot spots.

- **EMC.** Cables can pick up and give off interference, and loose or inconsistent routes make results hard to repeat. Treat this as a design input, as [electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html#emc) explains, and take layout advice from your electronics partner.

- **Service and repair.** Cables and connectors wear and break at stress points, and wires that are glued down, too short or buried make repair harder. See [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html).

## Fewer wires first

The most reliable cable is the one you do not need. Before designing routes, try to remove wires:

- **Put components on the main board.** Buttons, LEDs, sensors and ports mounted on the board need no wiring, provided the board and housing are laid out together so each part meets its opening.

- **Board-to-board connectors.** Two boards joined directly, stacked or at right angles, need no cable and locate each other. The housing must still hold both boards so the connector does not carry the load.

- **Flexible printed circuits (FPC).** A thin, flat flexible circuit can link boards at different angles or on moving parts, and is the same in every unit. It needs a defined bend shape, no sharp creases and care at assembly, because its connectors are small and easy to fit at an angle.

## Routing and retention

Each cable should have one route, the same in every unit, designed into the housing rather than left to the person at the bench.

The cable has one fixed route. Moulded clips hold it, a small loop of slack lets the board be lifted out for service, and the grommet and strain relief at the wall take any outside pull before it reaches the connector.

- **Moulded channels and clips.** Ribs, slots and small hooks in the housing hold a cable at no extra part cost and show the operator the route. Check them against the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html).

- **Cable ties and tie mounts.** Where clips are not practical, a tie through a moulded slot or onto a mount fixes the bundle. Show its position on the work instruction and say how it is trimmed, so no sharp end is left.

- **Clear of hazards.** Keep routes away from sharp moulded or [sheet metal](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html) edges, screw points, anything that moves (hinges, fans, button stems) and hot parts. Where a wire must pass one, add a rib, sleeve or cover.

- **Service loops.** A little controlled slack lets a board be lifted out and unplugged without straining the cable. Clip the loop so it cannot wander into a seam.

- **Strain relief.** Wherever a cable leaves the product or the board, a pull should be taken by the housing or a clamp, not the connector or a solder joint: a moulded clamp, a tie to a mount, a wrap round a post, or an [overmoulded](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/overmoulding-and-two-shot-moulding.html) boot on an external lead. Inside, fix the cable close to the connector.

- **Grommets and glands at sealed walls.** A grommet protects a cable from the hole edge; in a sealed product a cable gland or sealed connector keeps water out. [Sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html#cables-vents) explains the options.

Wires are often pinched in the last few millimetres as a lid is pressed home over a cable that has lifted from its clip. A rib guarding the seam helps prevent this.

## Choosing connectors

Your electronics partner will propose specific parts. Settle these general points with them, because each affects the mechanical design and assembly:

- **Locking or latching, not just friction.** A latch that clicks into place resists drops and vibration far better than contact pressure alone, and one the operator can see confirms the step is done.

- **Keyed and polarised.** A keyed connector only fits one way round. Where several sit on one board, vary the size, pin count or keying so each plug fits only its own socket. The [error-proofing section of the work instructions guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-and-work-instructions.html#error-proofing) explains why preventing the mistake beats a warning.

- **Current rating and mating cycles from the datasheet.** Take the contact current rating, and how many times the connector can be plugged and unplugged, from the manufacturer's datasheet, not from a similar-looking part. Ratings can change with temperature and with how many contacts carry current, so check the conditions stated.

- **The same connector in prototype and production.** If prototypes use whatever is on the bench, the production part changes the size, latch, access and route late, and the prototypes tell you little about assembly or reliability. Choose the production family by the first integrated prototype.

## Harnesses and harness drawings

A harness is a made-up set of wires cut to length with connectors, terminals and any sleeving fitted. For production, buying made-up harnesses from a specialist is usually worthwhile once there is more than one simple lead, crimped terminals are involved or every unit must be identical, because the supplier has the crimp tooling and test equipment to do it consistently.

The harness drawing is what the supplier builds to. It usually shows:

- **Lengths** of each wire or branch between defined points, with a tolerance.

- **Connectors and pin-out:** connector and terminal part numbers at each end, and a table of which wire runs from which pin to which, with wire size and colour.

- **Labels** and other details such as sleeving, ties or tape, and where they go.

Give each harness its own part number and revision, list it on the bill of materials under its assembly, and change it through the same process as other parts; see [bills of materials and revision control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html). A new connector that will not mate with the old one means a new part number, not just a new revision.

## Mains wiring

Mains-powered products have specific safety requirements for internal wiring, insulation and separation between mains and low-voltage parts. They come from the safety standard that applies to the product and affect routing, fixings and connector choice from the start. Identify that standard at the requirements stage, as [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) explains, and involve a qualified engineer and a test laboratory. A pre-certified external power supply keeps mains wiring out of the product altogether.

## Testing wiring and connectors

- **Continuity and pin-out checks in production.** Every harness should be checked for continuity and correct pin-out, usually by the harness supplier on a fixture. An end-of-line functional test on the assembled product catches connectors left unplugged or half-seated. Write both into your [test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html).

- **Pull tests on strain relief.** Pull external cables, and cables near their connectors, in each likely direction, and check that the housing or clamp takes the load and nothing moves at the joint. Take the force from the applicable standard where there is one, otherwise from realistic use.

- **Drops and vibration.** After each test, open the unit and check every connector is fully seated, every cable is in its clips and nothing is pinched. [Designing for drops and impacts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html#testing) explains why loose heavy parts and unsupported connectors are common drop failures.

## Worked example: a battery lead that fails after drops

Illustrative example. A small handheld product has a rechargeable battery pack whose short lead ends in a friction-fit connector, plugged into a socket at the edge of the main board. The board is screwed down at its corners and the battery sits in a pocket with some clearance.

After a few corner drops, several prototypes stop working; some recover when tapped, which points to an intermittent connection. Opening them shows the connector partly unseated on some, and a cracked solder joint at the socket on others.

|
Finding |
Cause |
Change made |

|
Connector partly unseated |
Friction-only connector; the moving battery tugs on the lead |
A latching, keyed connector, used from the next prototype on |

|
Cracked solder joints at the socket |
Connector at an unsupported board edge; the lead's load goes straight into the joints |
A housing rib under the board at the connector, and a clip holding the lead next to it so the housing takes any pull |

|
Lead taut between battery and board |
Length set from CAD with no slack |
A slightly longer lead in a moulded channel, with its length defined on a harness drawing |

|
Battery free to move |
Clearance in the pocket |
Ribs locating the battery on all sides and a pad under the cover |

The revised design is drop-tested on several units, each opened after every drop, and the lead is pull-tested near the connector. The work instruction gains a check that the latch is engaged and the lead is in its clip, and the battery lead gets its own BOM line with a part number and revision.

## Common mistakes

**Leaving cables out of the CAD.**
Nobody checks a route, length or clearance that is not modelled. Model the main cables as parts.

**Letting solder joints carry loads.**
A joint holding a wire or heavy part in place will eventually crack. Make the housing take the load.

**Friction-only connectors in products that get dropped.**
Use latching connectors wherever drops or vibration are likely.

**Identical connectors side by side.**
Sockets that accept the same plug will be swapped sooner or later. Key them differently.

**Harnesses with no drawing or part number.**
Lengths and pin-outs then drift between batches and suppliers.

## Next steps

- List every cable and ask whether moving a part onto the board, or joining boards directly, would remove it; model the rest in CAD with their routes and clips.

- Confirm each connector's latch, keying, current rating and mating cycles from its datasheet with your electronics partner.

- Give each harness a drawing, a part number and a revision, and cost it in the [BOM Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html).

- Add continuity checks, pull tests and post-drop inspection to your plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- See where this work sits in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

## FAQ

### Should I use a connector or solder wires straight to the board?

A connector makes assembly, testing and repair easier and lets the cable be replaced on its own. Soldering directly can suit a part that will never be removed, but the wire must then be fixed to the housing or board close to the joint so the joint never carries the load.

### When is it worth buying a made-up harness?

Usually once you are past the first prototypes and the product has more than a single simple lead, uses crimped terminals or needs every unit to be identical. A harness supplier has the tooling and test equipment to make and check each one consistently, working from your harness drawing.

### Do internal cables affect EMC?

They can. Cables can pick up and give off interference, and long or loosely routed cables make results harder to repeat from unit to unit. Keep cables short, give them a fixed route and discuss the layout with your electronics partner before pre-compliance testing.

### How do I stop a connector coming loose in a drop?

Use a latching connector rather than one held by friction, fix the cable to the housing close to the connector so it cannot tug on it, support the board under the connector, and stop heavy parts such as batteries from moving. Then confirm it by opening units after drop tests.

### What should a harness drawing include?

The length of each wire or branch with a tolerance, the connector and terminal part numbers at each end, a pin-out table showing which wire runs from which pin to which, wire size and colour, and any labels, sleeving or ties, plus its own part number and revision.

Title: Calculating Hardware Startup Cash Flow

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders planning how much cash a hardware launch needs, and when

# Calculating hardware startup cash flow

Hardware businesses fail on cash more often than on spreadsheet profit. The difference is timing:
when cash leaves for tooling, stock, and overhead versus when customers or channels finally pay you.

**Topic**
Startup cash flow

**Audience**
Founders and commercial leads

**Tool**
Cashflow Projection Tool

**Use it for**
Runway and working-capital planning

Quick answer

## Cash flow is a timing problem, not just a margin problem.

Closing cash = opening cash + cash received - cash paid

To calculate hardware startup cash flow, list each month's cash in (customer and channel payments, when they actually arrive) and cash out
(upfront development and tooling, stock, overhead), then carry the closing balance forward. A business can grow in revenue and still run out of cash
if it pays for stock and overhead before customer cash arrives.

This is especially common in hardware because growth often increases the need for working capital.
You buy more stock, carry more packaging, pay more suppliers, and still wait thirty or sixty days for cash to return.
Software businesses can often scale with little extra cash tied up. Hardware businesses cannot: every extra unit sold usually has to be paid for first.

## Contents

- Key definitions

- The four cashflow traps hardware teams hit early

- What a useful early cashflow model needs

- A worked example

- Common cash flow modelling mistakes

- How to use the model well

- Practical next steps

## Key definitions

Monthly net cash flow = cash received - (stock payments + overhead + one-off spend)

Runway (months) = cash available / average monthly net cash outflow

Cash conversion cycle (days) = days stock is held + days customers take to pay - days you take to pay suppliers

The cash conversion cycle is the most useful single idea here. It measures how long each pound spent on stock is away from the business before it comes back.
The longer the cycle, the more cash growth consumes.

## The four cashflow traps hardware teams hit early

**Inventory is paid before it is sold.**
Even if the business is profitable per unit, the stock still has to be financed first. Many overseas suppliers ask for a deposit at order and the balance before shipment, weeks before the stock reaches a customer.

**Channels pay late.**
Marketplaces, distributors, and retailers often introduce a delay between sale and cash receipt.

**Upfront project spend is treated as one-off and ignored.**
Tooling, development, compliance, and launch assets can create a hole that growth does not refill quickly enough.

**Fixed overhead keeps leaving every month.**
Rent, people, software, contractors, and basic operations do not wait for the revenue curve to mature.

## What a useful early cashflow model needs

- opening cash

- one-off launch or development spend, placed in the month it is actually paid

- monthly unit sales and growth

- COGS per unit, including freight, duty and packaging

- fixed monthly overhead

- payment delay from customers or channels

- supplier payment terms and minimum order quantities, once you have them

The business does not run out of cash because growth is bad. It runs out of cash because growth changes the timing of cash faster than the team planned for.

## A worked example

Illustrative figures only. Start with GBP85,000 in cash, spend GBP18,000 upfront on development or tooling, sell 120 units in month 1,
grow 12% per month, and carry GBP22 of COGS on a GBP49 sale price. Add GBP9,500 of monthly overhead and a one-month payment delay.
Stock is paid in the month it is sold.

Each unit contributes GBP27, so the business needs about 352 units a month just to cover overhead. Sales do not reach that level until month 11,
and because cash arrives a month late, the bank balance keeps falling for the whole first year.

|
Month |
Units sold |
Cash in |
Cash out |
Closing cash |

|

|

The low point is roughly GBP10,800 in month 12, and cash only starts to rise in month 13. The P&L may look healthy later in the year,
but the cash graph dips much earlier because month 1 and 2 outflows happen before revenue arrives.

Now change one input. If customers or channels pay after two months instead of one, the same business runs out of cash in month 10
and is still roughly GBP9,600 short in month 14. Nothing about the product or the margin changed. Only the timing did.

Illustrative figures from the worked example, drawn to scale. The same product and margin either bottoms out at about £10,800 or runs out of cash in month 10: only the payment delay changed.

**Practical rule:**
find the month with the lowest closing cash in your most cautious scenario, then make sure the business can survive it with a buffer of several months' overhead.

## Common cash flow modelling mistakes

**Modelling profit instead of cash.**
Profit records a sale when it happens. Cash records it when the money lands. In hardware the gap can be months.

**Annual or quarterly totals.**
The low point usually sits inside a single month. Model monthly for at least the first eighteen months.

**Ignoring minimum order quantities.**
A supplier MOQ can force you to buy several months of stock at once, which often creates a deeper low point than launch itself.

**Forgetting tax timing.**
VAT and import duty paid on stock, and VAT collected on sales, move cash between periods. Check the timing with your accountant rather than assuming it nets out.

**No re-order lead time.**
If stock takes ten to twelve weeks to arrive, the next order must be paid for well before the current batch is sold.

## How to use the model well

- run a conservative, expected, and optimistic sales case

- test both same-month payment and delayed-payment scenarios

- check whether your first large stock order creates the real low point, not the launch month

- pair the result with startup-cost and break-even tools, not in isolation; [building a hardware financial model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-financial-model.html) shows how the pieces connect

## Practical next steps

- Estimate the pre-launch spend with the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html) and the approach in [estimating hardware development costs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html).

- Ask likely suppliers and channels for their payment terms, deposits and MOQs, even informally.

- Build a monthly model in the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html) and identify the low point in each scenario.

- Check how far away unit break-even is using [financial break-even for hardware products](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html).

- Decide how much funding, or which changes to terms, stock or launch timing, would keep the low point safely above zero.

If you want the cash plan to sit alongside development stages, tooling and launch timing, the
[Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps bring those decisions into one staged plan.

Use the startup-cost planner if you need to estimate how much capital the project needs before sales begin.

Hardware startup cashflow
Working capital
Runway planning

## FAQ

### What is the difference between cash flow and profit?

Profit measures whether sales exceed costs over a period. Cash flow measures when money actually enters and leaves the bank. A hardware business can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash because it pays for stock and tooling long before customers or channels pay it.

### Why do growing hardware businesses run out of cash?

Because each extra unit sold usually has to be bought, shipped and stored before it is paid for. Faster growth means larger stock orders sooner, so more cash is tied up in inventory and unpaid invoices at any one time.

### How do I calculate cash runway?

Divide the cash you have by your average monthly net cash outflow. For an early hardware business, a monthly cash flow model is more reliable than a single average, because burn changes as stock orders, launch costs and sales arrive at different times.

### How much runway does a hardware startup need?

There is no fixed rule, but many founders aim for twelve to eighteen months of runway after a funding round. Hardware often needs the upper end, or more, because tooling, certification and manufacturing lead times make delays common and expensive.

### What is working capital in a hardware business?

Working capital is the cash tied up in running the business day to day, mainly stock, goods in transit and money owed by customers, minus what you owe suppliers. Longer supplier lead times and slower customer payment both increase the working capital you need.

Title: Choosing a 3D Printing Process

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers ordering printed prototype parts

# Choosing a 3D printing process for prototypes: FDM, SLA, SLS, MJF and metal

What the main 3D printing processes are good and bad at, how to pick one by the question your prototype must answer, how to design and prepare parts for printing, and when to move on to machining, casting or tooling.

Quick answer

## Choose the process by the question the prototype must answer: filament (FDM) for quick fit and form checks, resin (SLA) for appearance and fine detail, powder nylon (SLS or MJF) for tougher functional parts and small batches, and metal printing only for complex metal parts.

No printing process behaves exactly like a moulded or machined production part, so treat printed results on strength, stiffness and finish as indicative.
Most products use more than one process across their prototype rounds, and printing usually gives way to machining, vacuum casting or bridge tooling as the design settles.

## Contents

- The main processes in brief

- How they compare

- Choosing by the question the prototype must answer

- Designing parts for printing

- Preparing files and asking for quotes

- Decision rules

## The main processes in brief

"3D printing" covers several different processes. All build a part layer by layer, but their materials, surfaces and strength differ enough to change what a prototype can tell you.

### FDM: filament printing

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) melts a plastic filament and lays it down in lines, layer by layer. It is the process behind most desktop printers and usually the quickest, cheapest way to get a part in your hand.

Layer lines are visible, fine detail is limited, and parts are anisotropic: noticeably weaker between layers than along them, so a clip can snap along a layer line under a load it would otherwise carry. FDM is good for fit checks, form studies, jigs and early mechanism layouts.

### SLA: resin printing

Stereolithography (SLA) and related resin processes cure a liquid photopolymer with light, layer by layer. They give fine detail, crisp edges and smooth surfaces that take paint well, which makes them a common choice for looks-like models, small detailed parts and masters for vacuum casting.

Many standard resins are more brittle than production plastics, and some soften, yellow or embrittle with heat and ultraviolet light. Tougher engineering resins exist but still do not behave quite like a moulded thermoplastic. Parts need washing, curing and support removal.

### SLS and MJF: powder bed nylon

Selective laser sintering (SLS) and Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) fuse fine plastic powder, most commonly nylon, layer by layer. The surrounding unfused powder supports the part as it builds, so no support structures are needed and parts can be nested together in one build.

The result is tough nylon parts that suit functional prototypes, [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) that must flex, trial housings and small batches. The surface is slightly grainy, often dyed or left grey or white, and fine detail is softer than resin.

### Metal printing

Metal powder bed processes melt metal powder, typically steels, aluminium or titanium alloys, to build dense metal parts. They are specialist processes used for complex metal parts that would be hard or impossible to machine, such as internal channels or lightweight lattice structures.

Parts need supports and significant post-processing, often heat treatment, support removal and machining of critical faces. For most consumer product prototypes, a [machined part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) is simpler and cheaper unless the geometry genuinely needs printing.

## How they compare

These are qualitative, typical comparisons. Specific machines, materials and bureaus vary, so ask your supplier about the material they would actually use.

|
Process |
Surface |
Detail |
Strength |
Typical prototype use |

|
FDM (filament) |
Visible layer lines |

Reasonable along layers, weaker between them |

|

Smooth, paints well |

[Prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html) places 3D printing alongside CNC machining, vacuum casting and tooling, where it is typically best for fast learning and geometry checks at quantities of one to tens.

## Choosing by the question the prototype must answer

The most useful starting point is not the process but the question. A prototype that answers the wrong question well is still wasted.
[Looks-like vs works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) explains how to separate appearance questions from function questions; the printing process then follows.

Typical starting points, not rules. If a question depends on the production material, no printing process may be close enough.

- **"Does it fit, and is the size right?"** FDM is usually enough; speed matters more than finish.

- **"Does it look and feel right?"** SLA gives surfaces that can be sanded and painted to represent the final finish for user sessions and photography.

- **"Does it work, flex or survive handling?"** SLS or MJF nylon is the usual printed choice for clips, hinges, brackets and trial housings, with the caveat that nylon is not your production plastic.

- **"Will it survive in the production material?"** This is often a question printing cannot answer. Machined parts in the real material, or vacuum castings in a resin chosen to mimic it, are usually better evidence.

[How many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) shows how to group questions into rounds, so you can see where each process fits in your plan.

## Designing parts for printing

Printing removes many moulding constraints, but it adds a few of its own. These points are qualitative; ask your bureau for the minimum sizes their process and material support.

- **Wall thickness.** Very thin walls can warp or break during cleaning, and very thick sections can distort. Keep walls reasonably even, and if the part will later be moulded, use the wall thickness intended for moulding so the prototype stays honest.

- **Orientation.** Orientation decides where layer lines fall, which faces are smoothest and, for FDM, which directions are weak. Put loaded features such as clips and bosses so the load runs along the layers, and keep cosmetic faces away from supports.

- **Supports.** FDM, SLA and metal printing need supports under overhangs, which leave marks. Chamfers instead of flat overhangs, or splitting a part in two, can reduce them. Powder processes need no supports, but enclosed hollows need escape holes for the powder.

- **Holes and threads.** Small holes often print undersize or out of round; plan to drill or ream holes that matter. Printed threads are weak and wear quickly, so use heat-set or press-fit threaded inserts, or self-tapping screws into bosses, for anything assembled more than once.

- **Clearances.** Parts that must slide or snap together need more clearance than the same parts moulded. Print a quick test piece for critical fits rather than relying on nominal sizes, and see [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) for how to state the fits that matter.

- **Post-processing.** Sanding, painting, dyeing, vapour smoothing and machining critical faces all help. For looks-like models, finishing often takes longer than printing.

## Preparing files and asking for quotes

A print bureau can only quote and build what the files and notes tell them. A clean package avoids delays and surprises:

- **Export the right files.** STL is the common format for printing; export at a fine enough resolution that curves are not faceted. Send STEP as well, because it keeps exact geometry.

- **Check units and scale.** State the units, and give one or two key overall dimensions so the bureau can check the scale.

- **Name the process and material, or ask for advice.** If you are unsure, describe what the part must do and let the bureau suggest options.

- **Add orientation and finish notes.** Mark cosmetic faces, faces that must be free of support marks, loaded features and any holes to be drilled or inserts to be fitted.

- **Give quantity and deadline.** Quantity changes the best process and the price per part.

When quotes come back, check they are for the same process, material, finish and quantity before comparing price. [Getting and comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) explains how to compare like with like.

## When to move beyond printing

Printing is strongest while the design is changing. As questions shift from "what should it be?" to "will it work as made?", other routes usually give better evidence:

- **CNC machining** when you need real materials, tight geometry or durable functional parts, typically from one part up to low hundreds.

- **Vacuum casting** when you need tens of looks-like or trial parts in production-like plastics; a silicone mould typically yields roughly 10 to 25 parts, often from an SLA master.

- **Bridge tooling** when you need hundreds to several thousand moulded parts for pilots or early sales, and the design is stable enough to commit to a tool.

[The risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) explains how to step through these routes without over-committing, and [from 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) covers the design changes a printed part usually needs before it can be moulded.
The [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html) scores printing against CNC, vacuum casting, bridge tooling and pilot injection for a specific build, and the
[Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) shows where a tooled route starts to pay back.

## Worked example: three rounds of a handheld product

Illustrative example. A small team is developing a handheld battery-powered device with a two-part plastic housing, a button, a clip-on cover and a small [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html).
They plan three prototype rounds and choose a printing process, or not, for each based on the question that round must answer.

|
Round |
Question |
Process chosen |
Why |

|
1. Form and fit |
Is the size comfortable in the hand, and do the board and battery fit inside? |
FDM, several variants |
Quick and cheap; layer lines do not matter for grip and packaging checks |

|
2. Appearance and function |
Do users like the look and feel, and does the cover clip survive repeated use? |
SLA for painted looks-like models; SLS nylon for the working clip and housing |
Two questions, two processes: resin for finish, nylon for a clip that must flex |

|
3. Field trial |
Does the product hold up in real use by a small group of users? |
Vacuum cast housings from SLA masters |
Production-like plastic and finish for a few dozen units |

In round 2 the FDM clip from round 1 would have been misleading: it snapped along a layer line, while the nylon clip flexed as intended. The team still treats the nylon result as indicative and plans to re-test the clip in moulded parts before design freeze.

## Common mistakes

**Judging strength from FDM parts.**
A filament part that breaks along a layer line tells you about the print, not the design; one that survives may still fail when moulded. Use FDM for geometry and test strength in more representative material.

**Expecting production finish.**
No printed part comes off the machine looking moulded. If appearance matters, budget for finishing, or use vacuum casting once the form is settled.

**Using one process for every question.**
A single favourite process is convenient but answers some questions badly. Match the process to the question, round by round.

**Ignoring orientation.**
Orientation changes strength, accuracy and where support marks fall. Left to chance, it can put a weak layer line through a clip or a support scar on a cosmetic face.

## Decision rules

- **If the question is fit or size**, use FDM and print variants quickly.

- **If the question is appearance or fine detail**, use SLA and budget for finishing.

- **If the part must flex, carry load or survive handling**, use SLS or MJF nylon and treat results as indicative.

- **If the part is metal and complex**, compare metal printing with machining before choosing.

- **If the answer depends on the production material**, move to machining, vacuum casting or tooling rather than printing again.

- Write down the question each upcoming prototype must answer.

- Prepare STL and STEP files with units, orientation and finish notes before requesting quotes.

- See where these rounds sit in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

## FAQ

### Which 3D printing process is best for prototypes?

It depends on the question the prototype must answer. FDM suits quick fit and form checks, SLA suits appearance and fine detail, SLS or MJF nylon suits tougher functional parts and small batches, and metal printing suits complex metal parts. Many products use several processes across their prototype rounds.

### What is the difference between FDM and SLA printing?

FDM lays down melted plastic filament, giving quick, low-cost parts with visible layer lines and weaker bonds between layers. SLA cures liquid resin with light, giving smoother surfaces and finer detail, but many resins are more brittle.

### Are SLS and MJF parts strong enough for functional testing?

For many functional checks, yes. Powder bed nylon parts are tough and fairly even in strength in all directions, which suits clips, brackets and trial housings. They are still not your production material, so treat results as indicative and re-test critical features in production-intent parts.

### What file format should I send to a 3D print bureau?

STL is the common format for printing, exported at a fine enough resolution that curves are smooth. Send STEP as well where possible, state the units, and add notes on orientation, cosmetic faces, holes to be drilled and inserts to be fitted.

### When should I stop 3D printing and use another process?

When the questions depend on the production material, finish or quantity. CNC machining suits real-material functional parts, vacuum casting suits tens of production-like parts, and bridge tooling suits hundreds to several thousand moulded parts once the design is stable.
