Title: Choosing How to Make an Enclosure

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small teams deciding how the housing of a physical product should be made

# Choosing how to make an enclosure: matching the route to your volume and design

The questions that decide how a product's housing should be made, the eight common routes from a modified off-the-shelf box to an injection-moulded case, how they compare, and how to move from one to the next as your volumes grow.

Quick answer

## Choose the enclosure route by how many you will make, how sure you are of that number, and how settled the design is; then check it against appearance, sealing, heat and strength.

For a handful of units, modify an off-the-shelf box or 3D print or machine your own. For small to medium batches, aluminium extrusion with end caps, sheet metal or CNC machining often fit, with vacuum casting for moulded-looking plastic parts.
Injection moulding and die casting give the lowest cost per part at steady volumes, but need expensive tools and a stable design. Many products move through two or three of these routes, so design with the next one in mind and compare real quotes before you commit to tooling.

## Contents

- The questions that decide it

- A first pass at the decision

- The routes

- How the routes compare

- Moving between routes as volume grows

- Worked example: a small outdoor sensor

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

This guide covers the housing only. For processes in general, see [manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html).

## The questions that decide it

Answer each of these briefly before asking for quotes. The first usually settles most of the decision; the rest rule routes in or out.

- **Volume, and how certain it is.** How many in the first year and over the product's life? A forecast backed by orders can justify tooling; a hopeful one usually cannot.

- **Appearance.** Does it need its own shape, colour and texture, or is a neat, plain box acceptable?

- **Sealing.** Will it get wet or dusty? Some routes leave few joints to seal; others leave many. [Sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) explains why this is a design-stage decision.

- **Heat.** Must the case carry heat away? Metal spreads heat far better than plastic; see [managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html).

- **Strength and drops.** Will it be dropped, stood on or bolted to a wall? See [designing for drops and impacts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html).

- **Size.** Small housings suit moulding and machining; large, flat-sided cabinets suit sheet metal.

- **Time to market.** Tooled routes take longer to the first part; an untooled route can supply trial units meanwhile.

- **Budget for tooling.** Tooling is paid before you sell anything, alongside the first batch of stock.

- **Whether the design will change.** If trials, certification or a new [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) could still change the shape, avoid locking it into steel.

## A first pass at the decision

The flow below gives a shortlist of one or two routes to check against the questions above and real quotes.

A first pass only. Vacuum casting can stand in for moulded parts in small batches, CNC machining suits small runs of metal housings at any stage, and the dashed outcomes need tooling, so check them against real quotes.

## The routes

Each route has one job it does well and one main trade-off; the linked guides cover the detail.

### Off-the-shelf enclosures, modified by machining

Catalogue enclosures in plastic or die-cast aluminium, often with gasketed lids, have holes and cut-outs machined for your connectors, then a label or printed panel added.
This fits prototypes, pilot batches and products where a plain box is acceptable, with no tooling. The trade-off is a generic look and someone else's dimensions. A sealing claim for the empty box does not cover the holes you add, so test the finished unit. Keep machined features simple, as the [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) describe.

### 3D printed

Printing needs no tooling and handles almost any shape, so it suits a changing design and very small batches.
The trade-off is a high cost per part that hardly falls with volume, and properties and finish unlike moulded or machined parts. [Choosing a 3D printing process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html) explains which process answers which question.

### CNC machined

Machining from solid aluminium or engineering plastic gives precise, strong housings in real materials, and [anodised](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) aluminium looks premium. It suits small to medium batches and designs that may still change.
The trade-off is cost per part: deep pockets take machine time, and much of the material ends up as chips. See the [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html).

### Sheet metal

Folded steel or aluminium suits larger box-shaped housings, cabinets and covers. Laser cutting and press-brake bending need no part-specific tooling, which suits one-offs to moderate batches; at high volumes, dedicated press tools can lower the cost per part.
The trade-off is shape: flat panels of even thickness, with folded corners that need welding or a gasketed lid if the product must be sealed. [Sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html) covers bends, holes and reliefs.

### Aluminium extrusion with end caps

A profile cut to length, machined and closed with end caps. Standard profiles need no tooling, and a custom die typically costs far less than a mould or casting die. It gives a tough, heat-spreading metal case with two joints to seal.
The trade-off is a straight-sided tube, with anything that changes along the length machined afterwards. [Aluminium extrusions for product enclosures](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/aluminium-extrusions-for-product-enclosures.html) covers profile design and end caps.

### Vacuum casting

Silicone moulds taken from a master produce tens of parts in resins that imitate production plastics, for samples, trials and pilot batches of a housing that will later be moulded.
The trade-off is that the materials are not the moulding grade and moulds wear out, so the cost per part stays well above moulding. [From 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) describes it as a bridge while the tool is made.

### Die cast

Molten aluminium or zinc forced into a steel die gives detailed, rigid housings with ribs and fins at a low cost per part once the die is paid for. It suits steady volumes of housings that need metal for heat, screening or feel.
The trade-off is a high up-front die cost and long lead time, plus machining of sealing faces and coating afterwards. See [die casting explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/die-casting-explained.html), and [choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) for the alloys.

### Injection moulded

Plastic injected into a machined tool gives a low cost per part at volume and great freedom of shape, with [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html), textures and colour moulded in. It is the usual route for consumer housings in steady thousands.
The trade-off is the tool: expensive, slow to make and costly to change, so the design must be stable and the demand believable. See [injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) and [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html).

## How the routes compare

These are relative, typical characteristics for an enclosure, in line with [manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html). They are for planning, not quotes: size, complexity, finish and supplier all move the answer.

|

## Moving between routes as volume grows

Few products stay on one route. A common, low-risk path for an enclosure has three stages, each committing only when the evidence supports it:

- **Printed or machined** (or an off-the-shelf box) while the design is changing and you are building prototypes and the first trial units.

- **Extrusion or sheet metal** for pilot batches and early sales, where a modest die or no tooling at all gives real production parts.

- **Moulded or die cast** once the design has stopped changing and demand is steady enough to repay the tool.

Not every product needs the last stage; an extruded or sheet-metal housing can serve for the product's whole life.

Design so the next change is easier:

- Keep the circuit board outline, mounting points and connector positions the same across routes, so the electronics do not change when the housing does.

- Add draft and even walls early where you expect to mould later; [from 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) lists the changes a printed part usually needs.

- Choose a sealing method that can carry across, such as a compressed gasket at the lid or end caps.

To decide when to take the next step, put real quotes for two routes into the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html). It compares a low-volume route against a tooled one, which you can set to injection moulding or die casting, and shows where the tool pays back. The [risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) explains how to stage these commitments.

## Worked example: a small outdoor sensor

Illustrative example. A start-up is developing a small, battery-powered sensor for outdoor posts. It must survive rain and sun and be opened yearly for a new battery. Volumes are uncertain: a pilot with one customer, then perhaps a wider launch.

- **Printed prototypes.** Early rounds are printed to settle the size, battery door and internal fit. Each round changes the shape, so tooling would be wasted.

- **Machined off-the-shelf box for the pilot.** The team buys a gasketed die-cast aluminium catalogue box, has the sensor port and cable gland holes machined, and fits a breathable vent. Complete units are water-tested, because the box's own claim does not cover the new holes. It looks generic, but the customer is testing function.

- **Custom extrusion for launch.** With the board stable, the team commissions a custom profile with PCB slots, screw ports and a mounting slot, closed by gasketed, machined end caps. It looks like their own product, spreads heat and has two joints to seal.

- **When to revisit moulding or die casting.** If orders become steady and a redesign is due anyway, the team will get quotes for a die-cast or moulded housing and compare them with the extrusion. Plastic would need checks on sunlight and heat; a casting would need its sealing faces machined.

This example gives no prices on purpose. Get real quotes for your own housing and enter them in the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

## Common mistakes

**Tooling on a hopeful forecast.**
A mould paid for on sales that never come is cash you cannot get back. Use an untooled route until demand is proven.

**Choosing on unit cost alone.**
Tooling, lead time and minimum orders can outweigh a lower part price. Compare total cost at realistic volumes.

**Leaving sealing and heat until last.**
Both depend on the route. A plastic case that later needs to shed heat, or a folded box that must be waterproof, can force a late change.

**Designing for the prototype process.**
A housing that prints well may not mould, cast or extrude. Keep the next route in mind from the first serious prototype.

**Assuming an off-the-shelf box is already sealed.**
Every hole you add is a new leak path. Seal each opening and test the finished unit.

## Next steps

- Write a short answer to each of the questions above, especially volume and how certain it is.

- Use the decision flow to pick one or two routes, then read their detailed guides.

- Ask two or three suppliers to quote, using [finding and briefing a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html).

- Compare the quotes in the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) before committing to a tool.

This guide answers

Enclosures
Process choice
Tooling
Scaling up

## FAQ

### What is the cheapest way to make a small number of enclosures?

Usually a modified off-the-shelf box, or a printed or machined housing, because none of them needs tooling. Which is cheapest depends on size, finish and the features you need, so ask for quotes on two of them.

### Should my enclosure be plastic or metal?

Plastic is lighter, usually cheaper at volume and allows almost any shape and colour. Metal spreads heat, screens electronics, resists impact and feels solid. Start from what the housing must do, then choose the material and route together.

### When should I move to injection moulding or die casting?

When the design has stopped changing and demand is steady enough for the tool to pay for itself. Compare real quotes for your current route and the tooled one in the Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser rather than relying on a rule of thumb.

### Can I start with one route and change later?

Yes, and most products do. Keep the circuit board, mounting points and connector positions the same across routes, and design early parts with the later process in mind, so the change affects the housing and not everything inside it.

### Is an extruded enclosure a halfway house or a final answer?

It can be either. For products with a box-like shape, modest volumes or a need for a metal case, an extrusion with end caps can be the right route for the product's whole life. Move on only if the shape, look or cost at volume calls for it.

Title: Choosing Lower-carbon Materials for Products

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers and engineers choosing materials with climate impact in mind

# Choosing lower-carbon materials: less material, better material, longer life

A practical approach to lower-carbon material choices: compare parts that do the same job, reduce mass first, use recycled content and better sources, and check durability and end of life so savings are real.

Quick answer

## The lowest-carbon material is usually the one that does the job with the least mass, lasts the longest and can be recovered, not simply the one with the lowest figure per kilogram.

Compare materials per part, not per kilogram: a stiffer or stronger material may need much less of it. Use less material through better geometry, prefer recycled content
where performance allows, consider where and how the material is made, and check durability, because a part that fails early wastes everything that went into it.
Use consistent data sources and treat early figures as estimates.

## Start with the part, not the material

A material's footprint per kilogram is only the starting point. What matters is the footprint of the part that meets the requirement.
A higher-footprint material can win if it allows a much lighter or longer-lasting part. Define the requirement first: load, stiffness, temperature, environment, lifetime.
See [choosing materials for plastic products](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html).

## Five levers

|
Lever |
In practice |

|
Use less material |
Ribs instead of thick walls, hollow sections, optimised geometry, fewer parts |

|
Recycled content |
Recycled metals and plastics often have lower footprints than virgin material; check grades meet the requirement and supply is consistent |

|
Production source |
The energy used to make a material, and where it is made, can change its footprint substantially; ask suppliers for data |

|
Durability |
A part that lasts twice as long can justify a higher initial footprint; see [design for repair](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) |

|
End of life |
Materials that are widely recycled, easy to separate and clearly marked keep their value |

**Practical rule:**
reduce mass first, then improve the material. Removing material removes its footprint entirely, whatever it was made from.

## Watch for trade-offs

- **Bio-based is not automatically lower-carbon.** Farming, processing and end of life all count, and some bio-based plastics are hard to recycle.

- **Lighter can mean shorter-lived.** Thin walls and weaker materials can fail sooner.

- **Mixed materials** may perform well but be impossible to separate for recycling.

- **Transport** matters most for heavy, bulky products moved long distances, but is often smaller than material and manufacturing impacts.

- **Other impacts** such as water use or toxicity may rise when carbon falls; see [product carbon footprint vs LCA](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-carbon-footprint-vs-lca.html).

## Getting reliable data

Footprint figures for materials vary between databases, regions and production routes. Use one consistent source for comparisons, ask suppliers for environmental product
declarations or footprint data where available, and present early results as ranges. The [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html)
helps compare options at design stage.

## Common mistakes

**Comparing per kilogram.**
Compare parts that meet the same requirement.

**Mixing data sources.**
Differences between databases can be larger than the difference you are measuring.

**Assuming "natural" means low impact.**
Check the evidence for each material.

**Ignoring lifetime.**
The greenest part is the one that does not need replacing.

## Next steps

- Shortlist materials that meet the requirement with the [Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html).

- Compare the footprint of each option with the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

- Check how lifetime changes the picture with the [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html).

Filter plastics by the properties your part needs.
[Open Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html)

### Compare footprints

Estimate the carbon of each material option.
[Open Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html)

## FAQ

### How do I choose a lower-carbon material?

Compare the footprint of parts that meet the same requirement rather than footprints per kilogram, reduce mass first, prefer recycled content where performance allows, ask suppliers for data, and check durability and end of life.

### Are recycled materials always lower-carbon?

Recycled metals and plastics often have lower footprints than virgin material, but it depends on the material, the recycling process and the data source. Check the grade meets your requirements.

### Are bio-based plastics better for the climate?

Not automatically. Farming, processing and end of life all count, and some bio-based plastics are hard to recycle in existing systems. Compare them on evidence like any other material.

### Does reducing weight reduce carbon footprint?

Usually, because less material is made and transported, as long as the lighter part still lasts as long. A part that fails early can undo the saving.

### Where can I find carbon data for materials?

Use a consistent database for comparisons and ask suppliers for environmental product declarations or footprint data. Figures vary by source and region, so present early estimates as ranges.

Title: Choosing Metals for a Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers choosing a metal for a bracket, housing, frame or fitting

# Choosing metals for a product: common alloys, trade-offs and how to decide

How to choose a metal for a physical product: what drives the decision, when to use aluminium, mild steel, stainless steel, brass, zinc or titanium, how the manufacturing process narrows the field, and how to avoid corrosion and finishing problems.

Quick answer

## Choose the metal and the process together, starting from what the part must do: load, weight, environment, finish, volume and cost.

For most product parts the shortlist is short. Aluminium alloys (6082 or 6061 for machined parts, 5052 for bent sheet) when weight and appearance matter;
mild steel with a protective coating when cost and stiffness matter most; 304 stainless for wet or food-contact use indoors, and 316 near salt water or chlorides;
brass for small machined fittings; zinc die-casting alloys for detailed parts at volume. Check the datasheet for the specific alloy and temper, and keep dissimilar metals apart where they can get wet.

## Contents

- What drives the choice

- Common metals compared

- How the process shapes the choice

- Corrosion and galvanic pairs

- Finishes

- Metal or plastic?

- Worked example: a bracket for an outdoor sensor

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## What drives the choice

Write down what the part must cope with before looking at alloys. Six questions settle most decisions:

- **Strength and stiffness for the weight.** Steel is stiffer than aluminium and usually stronger, but aluminium is roughly a third of the density of steel and about a third as stiff. For a part that must be light, aluminium usually wins; for a part that must be stiff in a small space, steel often does.

- **Corrosion.** Where will the part live: indoors, outdoors, in a kitchen, near the sea, in contact with sweat or cleaning chemicals? This decides whether you need stainless steel, a coating, or neither.

- **Process.** Each process suits particular alloys. A metal that machines beautifully may crack when bent, and few alloys suit die casting.

- **Finish.** Some finishes only work on some metals. Anodising, for example, is mainly an aluminium process.

- **Cost.** Raw material price matters, but for small parts the cost of machining, forming and finishing usually matters more.

- **Recyclability.** Steel and aluminium are among the most widely recycled materials, and recycled aluminium needs only a small fraction of the energy of new metal. Using one metal throughout, and avoiding permanent joints between different metals, keeps that value at end of life.

Approximate densities of common product metals. A part made in aluminium weighs roughly a third of the same part in steel; zinc alloy is nearly as heavy as steel, and brass slightly heavier. Exact values vary by alloy, so check the datasheet.

## Common metals compared

Relative comparisons for typical grades. Use this to shortlist, then check the supplier datasheet for the specific alloy and temper, because properties within a family vary widely.

|
Metal |
Strengths |
Watch out for |
Typical uses |

|
Aluminium alloys |
Light, machines quickly, good natural corrosion resistance, can be anodised |
Less stiff than steel; some alloys crack when bent; soft surface scratches |
Housings, brackets, [heat sinks](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html), frames, extruded profiles |

|
Mild (low-carbon) steel |
Cheap, stiff, strong, easy to weld and form |
Rusts unless coated; heavy |
Chassis, frames, sheet enclosures, furniture, brackets |

|
Stainless steel (304, 316) |
Corrosion resistant without coating, hygienic, attractive bare finish |
Costs more than mild steel; much slower to machine; heavy |
Food equipment, outdoor fittings, fasteners, medical and marine parts |

|
Brass |
Machines very easily, low friction, good corrosion resistance, decorative |
Heavy and expensive per kilogram; some machining grades contain lead |
Fittings, valves, [threaded inserts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html), small turned parts, trim |

|
Zinc die-cast alloys |
Fine detail, thin walls, long tool life, good base for plating |
Heavy; weaker than steel; creeps under load when warm |
Handles, knobs, buckles, lock parts, small housings |

|
Titanium |
Very high strength for its weight, excellent corrosion resistance, biocompatible |
Expensive and slow to machine; few suppliers for small runs |
Medical implants, aerospace, premium sports and outdoor gear |

### Aluminium: which alloy?

For machined parts, **6082** (common in the UK and Europe) and **6061** (common in North America) are the usual general-purpose choices. They are heat-treated to a hard temper, machine cleanly and anodise well.
For bent sheet parts, **5052** is the usual choice: it bends tightly without cracking and resists corrosion well, including in damp and marine air. 6061 or 6082 in a hard temper tends to crack on tight bends, so do not specify it for sheet work without checking with the fabricator.
Extruded profiles usually use alloys from the same 6000 series chosen for extrusion, such as 6063. Very high-strength alloys such as 7075 exist, but cost more and are rarely needed for consumer products.

### Stainless steel: 304 or 316?

**304** is the general-purpose stainless steel used for kitchen equipment, sinks and indoor fittings. **316** adds molybdenum, which makes it much more resistant to pitting from chlorides: salt water, sea air, swimming pools, de-icing salt and some cleaning chemicals.
For anything near the coast or regularly wetted by salt, choose 316. Fasteners follow the same pattern, sold as A2 (304 type) and A4 (316 type).
Both are largely non-magnetic, which can matter around magnets and sensors, though cold working makes them slightly magnetic. Ferritic grades such as 430 are cheaper and magnetic but less corrosion resistant.

### The others in brief

**Mild steel** is the default for low-cost structural parts, provided it is protected by paint, powder coating, zinc plating or galvanising.
**Brass** is the easiest common metal to machine and suits small turned parts, but check restrictions on lead content if the part touches drinking water or sits in certain consumer products.
**Zinc die-cast alloys** suit small, detailed parts made in volume, often plated or painted.
**Titanium** is worth its cost only when weight, corrosion or biocompatibility truly demand it.

## How the process shapes the choice

The metal and the process should be chosen together. See [manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html) for the wider picture.

- **CNC machining:** works with almost any metal, but cost tracks machining time. Brass and aluminium cut quickly; mild steel is slower; stainless steel and titanium are much more expensive to machine. The [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) cover the geometry side.

- **Sheet metal:** laser cutting, punching and bending suit mild steel, stainless steel and formable aluminium such as 5052, at low tooling cost. Bend radii depend on the material and thickness, as explained in [sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html).

- **Die casting:** high-volume parts with complex shapes, mostly in zinc or aluminium casting alloys. Tooling is expensive, so it pays only at volume. Cast aluminium alloys contain silicon to help them flow, which also makes them anodise poorly. [Die casting explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/die-casting-explained.html) covers the process, design rules and finishing in more detail.

- **Extrusion:** long, constant-section aluminium profiles such as frames, rails and heat sinks, cut to length and machined. Die costs are modest, which makes extrusion attractive even at moderate volumes. [Aluminium extrusions for product enclosures](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/aluminium-extrusions-for-product-enclosures.html) covers profile design, end caps and finishing.

**Practical rule:**
specify the alloy and the temper, not just "aluminium" or "stainless". 6082 in its hard temper and 5052 in a soft temper behave very differently on a press brake, and 304 and 316 behave very differently by the sea.

## Corrosion and galvanic pairs

Mild steel rusts unless protected. Aluminium and stainless steel protect themselves with a thin oxide layer, but that layer can break down: stainless steel can pit in chloride environments, and aluminium can corrode in strongly alkaline or salty conditions.

**Galvanic corrosion** happens when two different metals touch and are bridged by water, particularly salt water. The less noble metal, such as aluminium or zinc, corrodes faster; the more noble one, such as stainless steel, is protected. In general terms:

- In dry indoor products it is rarely a problem.

- Outdoors or in wet use, prefer the same metal throughout, or metals close together in the galvanic series.

- Where different metals must meet, insulate them with plastic washers, sleeves, sealant or a coating, and keep water out of the joint.

- Area ratio matters. Small stainless screws in a large aluminium panel are usually tolerable; aluminium rivets in a large stainless sheet will corrode quickly.

## Finishes

Finishes protect the metal, set its appearance and affect cost. Common pairings: anodising for aluminium; powder coating for mild steel and aluminium; zinc plating or galvanising for steel; brushed, bead-blasted, passivated or electropolished surfaces for stainless; plating or painting for zinc die-castings.
Plan the finish when choosing the metal, not after, and allow for its thickness on tight fits and threads. The [surface finishes guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) covers each process in more detail.

## Metal or plastic?

Metal suits parts that must be stiff, strong, hot, conductive, hard-wearing or premium to the touch, and processes such as machining and sheet metal need little tooling at low volume.
Plastic suits complex shapes with clips, bosses and integrated features, light weight, electrical insulation and radio transparency, and becomes very cheap per part once a mould is paid for.
Many products use both: a plastic housing with a metal chassis or bracket inside. For the plastic side of the decision, see [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html), and shortlist polymers with the [Plastic Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html).

## Worked example: a bracket for an outdoor sensor

Illustrative example. A small company needs a wall bracket to hold a sensor unit of about 2 kg on buildings, including coastal sites. Requirements: no visible rust for at least ten years, little or no maintenance,
fixing with stainless steel screws, a clean appearance, and a few hundred brackets a year, so low tooling cost matters.

|
Candidate |
Assessment |

|
Mild steel sheet, powder coated |
Cheapest and stiff, but any chip or cut edge will rust at a coastal site. Rejected for the long life required |

|
Machined 6082 aluminium, anodised |
Light and attractive, but machining from solid is slow for a simple bracket, and stainless screws in sea air create a galvanic pair. Rejected on cost |

|
5052 aluminium sheet, powder coated |
Light, bends well, resists marine air. Workable, but needs insulating washers at the screws and relies on the coating staying intact. Kept as the lower-cost alternative |

|
304 stainless sheet |
No coating needed, but prone to staining and pitting at coastal sites. Rejected for the coastal sites |

|
316 stainless sheet |
Resists chlorides, matches A4 stainless screws so there is no galvanic pair, and needs no coating to chip. Higher material cost, but the bracket is small and simple. Chosen |

The team specifies a laser-cut and bent 316 bracket with a brushed finish and passivation, checks the bend radii with the fabricator, and asks for a material certificate with each batch.
Before committing, they fit samples to a test site and inspect them over a winter. Prices and lead times come from real quotes, not from this example.

## Common mistakes

**Writing "aluminium" or "stainless" on the drawing.**
Without the alloy and temper, the supplier will choose, and their choice may not suit your bends, finish or environment.

**Using 304 by the sea.**
304 stainless can stain and pit in salt air. Use 316 where chlorides are present.

**Mixing metals in wet places.**
Aluminium parts with stainless or brass fixings, left wet, can corrode quickly at the joint. Insulate them or use one metal.

**Choosing on price per kilogram.**
Machining time, scrap and finishing often cost more than the metal. A cheaper alloy that is slow to machine can make a dearer part.

**Choosing metal by habit.**
A metal part copied from a prototype may be cheaper and lighter as a moulded plastic part at volume, or vice versa. Revisit the choice when volumes change.

## Next steps

- Write the requirements for your part: load, weight, environment, finish, volume and cost target.

- Choose the likely process, then shortlist two or three metals that suit it, and ask suppliers for datasheets for the specific alloy and temper.

- Check the geometry against the [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) or [sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html).

- Estimate how far a bracket or beam will bend in each candidate metal, and how stressed it is, with the [Bracket Deflection Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bracket-deflection-calculator.html). Use the elastic modulus and yield strength from the datasheet for your alloy and temper.

- Estimate the part cost with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html), then confirm it with real quotes.

- Compare the footprints of candidate materials with the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

For the wider picture, see the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## FAQ

### Should I use aluminium or steel for my product?

Use aluminium when weight, natural corrosion resistance or an anodised finish matters, and steel when stiffness in a small section, weldability or low material cost matters more. Aluminium is roughly a third of the density of steel but also about a third as stiff, so an aluminium part often needs thicker sections to match.

### What is the difference between 304 and 316 stainless steel?

316 contains molybdenum, which gives it much better resistance to pitting from chlorides such as salt water, sea air and some cleaning chemicals. 304 is cheaper and fine for most indoor and kitchen use; 316 is the usual choice for marine, coastal and pool environments.

### Which aluminium alloy should I use for sheet metal parts?

5052 is the usual choice because it bends tightly without cracking and resists corrosion well. Heat-treated alloys such as 6061 and 6082 machine well but tend to crack on tight bends, so check with the fabricator before specifying them for sheet work.

### Can I use stainless steel screws in aluminium?

Often, yes, indoors and in dry conditions. Outdoors or in wet use the pair can cause galvanic corrosion of the aluminium, so isolate the screws with plastic washers or sealant, keep water out of the joint, and check the coating covers the hole.

### Is titanium worth it for a consumer product?

Usually only when weight, corrosion resistance or skin contact genuinely demand it, or the premium is part of the product's appeal. It is expensive and slow to machine, so a well-designed aluminium or stainless part is normally the better value.

Title: Choosing Plastic Materials for Products

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For designers, engineers and founders choosing plastics for moulded or machined parts

# Choosing materials for plastic products: common polymers, trade-offs and how to decide

How to choose a plastic for a physical product: start from the requirements, shortlist from the common polymers, understand grades and additives, and test in the real material before committing to tooling.

Quick answer

## Choose a plastic from the product's requirements, not its reputation: load, temperature, chemicals, appearance, regulation, cost and end of life.

For many consumer and enclosure parts, the shortlist is polypropylene (PP), ABS, polycarbonate (PC) or a PC/ABS blend; for wear parts and gears, acetal (POM) or nylon (PA);
for soft-touch grips and seals, a thermoplastic elastomer (TPE). Write the requirements down first, shortlist two or three materials, check the datasheets for the specific grade,
and test prototypes in the intended material before the tool is cut, because each plastic shrinks differently.

## Contents

- Start with the requirements

- Common plastics compared

- Grades, fillers and additives

- Worked example: choosing a material for a handheld device housing

- Recycling and end of life

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## Start with the requirements

Before looking at materials, write down what the part must cope with. These questions eliminate most candidates quickly:

- **Loads:** static, impact, fatigue or long-term load (plastics creep under sustained load).

- **Temperature:** the highest and lowest temperatures in use, storage and shipping, including inside a hot car or near a heat source.

- **Chemicals and environment:** cleaning products, oils, sunscreen, food, outdoor UV and moisture.

- **Appearance:** gloss, texture, colour, transparency, scratch resistance.

- **Assembly:** [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html), [living hinges](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html), screws, ultrasonic welding, bonding, painting or printing.

- **Regulation:** flammability ratings for electrical enclosures, food contact, toys, medical use.

- **Cost and supply:** price per kilogram, availability of the grade, and whether recycled grades exist.

- **End of life:** whether the material can be identified, separated and recycled.

## Common plastics compared

Relative comparisons for typical unfilled grades. Properties vary widely between grades and suppliers, so use this to shortlist, then check the datasheet of the actual grade.

|
Material |
Strengths |
Watch out for |

|

|

|

Enclosures, consumer products, appliance housings |

|

|

High temperature, chemical resistance and strength |
High cost; harder to process |
Demanding industrial, medical and automotive parts |
High to very high |

## Grades, fillers and additives

Each plastic comes in many grades. Glass or mineral fillers increase stiffness and heat resistance but make parts more brittle and the tool wear faster.
Additives give UV stabilisation, flame retardancy, colour, impact modification or antistatic properties. For electrical products, flammability ratings
(often to the UL 94 scale, such as V-0) may be required by the product's safety standard. Always specify the grade, not just the polymer family, on drawings and purchase orders.

**Practical rule:**
choose the material before the tool is designed. Plastics shrink by different amounts as they cool, and the tool is cut oversize to suit one specific material. Changing material later can mean changing the tool.

## Worked example: choosing a material for a handheld device housing

Illustrative example. A rechargeable handheld device needs a two-part housing. Requirements: survive a 1 m drop, stay rigid at up to 60 °C in a parked car,
resist hand cream and common cleaning wipes, take a smooth painted-look finish, and meet the flammability rating required by its safety standard.

|
Candidate |
Assessment |

|
ABS |
Good finish and low cost, but marginal on heat and chemical resistance for this use |

|
Polycarbonate |
Excellent toughness and heat resistance; risk of stress cracking with some chemicals; harder to get the finish |

|
PC/ABS |
Balances toughness, heat and finish; flame-retardant grades are widely available. Shortlisted, with chemical tests against the actual creams and wipes |

|
Polypropylene |
Tough and chemical resistant, but too flexible for a rigid housing and harder to finish |

The team chooses a flame-retardant PC/ABS grade, makes prototype housings from it (vacuum casting resins only approximate it, so a few machined or bridge-moulded parts are worth having),
and tests drop, heat and chemical resistance before the production tool is cut.

## Recycling and end of life

Mark parts with their material identification code so they can be sorted later; the codes used on products and packaging include 1 (PET), 2 (HDPE), 3 (PVC), 4 (LDPE), 5 (PP), 6 (PS) and 7 (other).
Avoid permanently joining different plastics where you can, use one material family across parts where possible, and consider recycled grades where they meet the requirement.
In practice, recycling of durable products is far less established than packaging, so durability and repairability usually matter more; see the
[Sustainability and product life hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html).

## Common mistakes

**Choosing a material because a similar product uses it.**
The other product may have different loads, chemicals or cost targets.

**Specifying the family, not the grade.**
"Nylon" or "ABS" covers materials with very different properties.

**Testing only in printed prototypes.**
3D-printed and cast parts behave differently from moulded parts in the same nominal material.

**Forgetting chemical exposure.**
Sun cream, cleaning products and oils crack some otherwise suitable plastics.

**Ignoring moisture.**
Nylon changes size and stiffness as it absorbs water; several plastics must be dried before moulding.

## Next steps

- Write the requirements list above for your part.

- Shortlist two or three materials, for example with the [Plastic Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html), and ask suppliers or your moulder for datasheets of specific grades.

- Check the part design against [the injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html), since wall thickness and draft depend on the material.

- Estimate material cost per part with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html).

- Compare footprints of candidate materials with the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

For products that touch food, check the Food Standards Agency's guidance on food contact materials and ask suppliers for declarations of compliance for the specific grade.
If a part needs to be stiffer, stronger or more heat resistant than a plastic allows, see [choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html).
For the wider picture, see the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## FAQ

### What is the best plastic for a product enclosure?

There is no single best choice. ABS is a common starting point for indoor enclosures thanks to its finish and cost; PC/ABS adds toughness and heat resistance and is widely available in flame-retardant grades; polycarbonate suits very tough or transparent parts; polypropylene suits parts needing chemical resistance or living hinges. Choose from the requirements and test.

### What is the difference between ABS and polycarbonate?

ABS is cheaper, easier to mould and finish, and takes paint and plating well, but has lower heat and [impact resistance](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html). Polycarbonate is much tougher, has better heat resistance and comes in transparent grades, but costs more, needs drying before moulding and can stress-crack with some chemicals.

### Which plastic is best for gears and moving parts?

Acetal (POM) and nylon (PA) are the usual choices. Acetal has low friction and stays dimensionally stable; nylon is tougher but absorbs moisture, which changes its size and stiffness. Both are available in filled and lubricated grades.

### Can I change the plastic after the mould is made?

Sometimes, but it is risky. Different plastics shrink by different amounts, so a tool cut for one material may produce parts out of tolerance in another. Choose the material, and ideally the grade, before the tool is designed.

### Are recycled plastics suitable for products?

Often, for parts where their properties are adequate and consistent supply is available. Recycled grades can vary more between batches, so test them, agree specifications with the supplier, and avoid them where regulation requires specific virgin grades, such as some food-contact or medical uses.

Title: CNC Machining Design Rules

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For designers and engineers preparing machined parts for prototypes or production

# CNC machining design rules: designing parts that are quick to machine

Practical rules for designing CNC-machined parts: what round cutting tools mean for corners and pockets, sensible walls, holes and threads, fewer set-ups, and tolerances and finishes that control cost. Figures are typical shop guidance to confirm with your machinist.

Quick answer

## Design CNC parts around round cutting tools: give internal corners a radius, keep pockets and holes shallow relative to their width, avoid very thin walls, and only tighten tolerances where they matter.

CNC machining removes material with rotating tools, so every internal corner has a radius, deep narrow features need long tools that deflect, and each extra set-up or special tool adds cost.
Use standard hole and thread sizes, minimise the number of sides that must be machined, and agree a general tolerance with a few tighter callouts on critical features.
The figures below are typical shop guidance, not fixed limits; confirm them with your machinist.

## When CNC machining suits a product

CNC is ideal for prototypes, low to medium volumes, precise metal parts and parts in engineering plastics. There is no tooling cost, so it is often used before or instead of moulding or casting.
Unit cost stays relatively high as volumes grow; compare routes with the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

## Key design rules

|
Feature |
Typical guidance |
Why |

|
Internal corners |
Add a radius slightly larger than the cutter radius; larger is cheaper |
Round tools cannot cut sharp internal corners; a slightly larger radius lets the tool move smoothly |

|
Pocket depth |
Commonly up to about 3 to 4 times the cutter diameter |
Longer tools deflect and chatter, slowing cutting and hurting accuracy |

|
Wall thickness |
Avoid very thin walls; plastics need thicker walls than metals |
Thin walls vibrate and deform during cutting |

|
Holes |
Standard drill sizes; depth commonly up to about 4 times the diameter for easy drilling |
Standard drills are faster and cheaper than milling a custom size |

|
Threads |
Standard sizes; thread depth rarely needs to exceed about 1.5 to 2 times the diameter |
Extra depth adds little strength and raises the risk of tap breakage |

|
Text and fine detail |
Engraved rather than raised, with a simple, bold font |
Raised text needs material removed around it |

**Practical rule:**
if a feature could only be made with a very small or very long tool, change the feature. Small, long tools are slow, fragile and expensive to run.

## Reduce set-ups

Each time a part has to be turned over or re-clamped, there is set-up time and a chance of misalignment. Where possible, put features on as few sides as possible,
align them with the main axes, and avoid undercuts that need special cutters. Parts that need features on many faces may need 5-axis machining, which costs more per hour.

## Tolerances and finishes

- **Use a general tolerance**, for example to a recognised standard such as ISO 2768, and call out tighter tolerances only on critical features. [Tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains general tolerances, fits and datums.

- **Tight tolerances cost more:** slower cutting, more inspection and sometimes extra operations. Check how tolerances combine with the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html).

- **Specify surface finish only where it matters.** As-machined is cheapest; bead blasting, anodising and polishing add cost and can change dimensions. [Surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) compares the options.

## Materials

Aluminium alloys are popular because they machine quickly and well. Steels and [stainless steels](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) are stronger but slower to cut. Engineering plastics such as acetal and nylon machine well but
move with heat and moisture, so allow for that in tolerances. Material choice also affects finishes: anodising, for example, is mainly used on aluminium (and a few other metals such as titanium), not on steel. The
[Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html) compares material properties.

## Common mistakes

**Sharp internal corners.**
They cannot be milled; the part comes back with radii or needs costly extra operations.

**Tight tolerances everywhere.**
They raise cost without improving the product.

**Designing a moulded part, then machining it.**
Thin ribs and deep pockets that suit moulding are slow to machine; design for the process you will use.

**No drawing.**
A 3D model alone does not say which features are critical, which threads are needed or what finish is expected.

- Compare machining with moulding or casting at your volumes with the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

- Prepare drawings and quote requests with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

## FAQ

### Why do CNC parts need internal corner radii?

Milling cutters are round, so they leave a radius in every internal corner. Designing a radius slightly larger than the cutter lets the tool move smoothly and keeps cost down; truly sharp internal corners need extra processes.

### How deep can a CNC pocket be?

As typical shop guidance, pockets up to about 3 to 4 times the cutter diameter are straightforward. Deeper pockets need longer tools that deflect, which slows machining and reduces accuracy. Check with your machinist.

### What tolerance should I use for CNC parts?

Use a general tolerance, for example to ISO 2768, for most features and call out tighter tolerances only on critical fits. Tighter tolerances add machining and inspection cost.

### Is CNC machining good for production?

It suits prototypes and low to medium volumes, precise metal parts and engineering plastics, as there is no tooling cost. At higher volumes, moulding, casting or sheet metal are often cheaper per part.

### How can I reduce CNC machining cost?

Use generous corner radii, shallow pockets, standard hole and thread sizes, fewer set-ups, a general tolerance and as-machined finishes where possible, and choose an easily machined material.

Title: Getting and Comparing Manufacturing Quotes

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams requesting quotes from manufacturers and choosing between them

# Getting and comparing manufacturing quotes

How to ask manufacturers for quotes you can compare, what to check in each reply, and how to turn different quotes into a landed cost per unit and the cash needed before the first sale.

**Topic**
Quotes and supplier choice

**Audience**
Founders, engineers, small teams

**Tools**
RFQ pack, landed cost, payoff

**Use it for**
Choosing a supplier on the full picture

Quick answer

## Send three to five suitable suppliers the same request, then compare their quotes on landed cost per unit, tooling and who owns it, and the cash you must pay before you sell anything.

Cash for the first commitment = tooling + (minimum order quantity × landed cost per unit)

A quote is only comparable when it states the quantity, delivery terms, what is excluded, lead times and payment terms. Add freight, duty,
packaging and inspection to each unit price to reach a landed cost, then add tooling and the minimum order to see the cash involved.
The lowest unit price is often not the lowest landed cost, and rarely the least cash.

Quotes rarely arrive in the same shape: one delivered, one priced at a port, one at the factory gate with packaging left out, each at a different quantity.
Comparing headline unit prices is the most common way first-time teams choose the wrong supplier.

## Contents

- What to send

- How many suppliers to ask

- Making quotes comparable

- From quote to landed cost and cash

- Worked example: three quotes

- Red flags

- Questions to ask before you choose

- Clarifying and negotiating respectfully

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## What to send

The quality of a quote depends on the quality of the request. Send every supplier the same pack, so differences in the replies come from the suppliers and not from what you told them:

- 3D CAD and [2D drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) with materials, finishes and the tolerances that matter

- quantities: the first order, expected annual volume, and the price breaks you want quoted (for example 500, 1,000 and 3,000)

- quality and compliance requirements, including inspection and test reports

- packaging and labelling, and the delivery terms you want the price on

- when you need samples and first production

- a list of the items you need back, so every reply covers the same ground

The [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html) turns this into a request for quotation document, and
[the documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) explains each item.
Named price breaks matter most: they stop each supplier quoting at a quantity that suits them.

## How many suppliers to ask

Three to five well-chosen suppliers is usually enough. Fewer gives little sense of what is normal; many more takes weeks to manage and
rarely changes the answer. Shortlist before you ask: check they make parts of your size, material and quality, and that your volumes matter to them.
[How to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html) covers where to look and what to check.

Include at least one supplier from each route you are seriously considering, because a nearby and an overseas supplier differ on cost, cash, lead time and how easily the design can change; [UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html) sets out that trade-off.

## Making quotes comparable

Put every quote into the same table before forming a view. These are the lines that most often differ:

|
Line |
What to check |

|
Tooling cost and ownership |
Total cost, how it is paid, who owns the tool, whether you can move it, how many parts it is expected to make, and who pays for repairs |

|
Unit price at stated quantities |
The quantity each price applies to; a price at 3,000 cannot be compared with one at 1,000 |

|
Minimum order quantity (MOQ) |
The smallest order accepted, per order or per colour or variant |

|
Lead times |
Separately for tooling, first samples and production, plus shipping if not included |

|
Payment terms |
Deposits, stage payments and when the balance is due: at order, at sample approval, before shipment or after delivery |

|
Delivery terms |
The Incoterm the price is quoted on, and the named place |

|
What is excluded |
[Retail packaging](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html), cartons, testing and inspection, freight, duty, and any set-up charge per order |

|
Validity |
How long the price holds, and whether material price changes can be passed on |

Delivery terms decide how much you still have to add. Under the [Incoterms rules](https://iccwbo.org/business-solutions/incoterms-rules/),
an EXW (ex works) price ends at the factory, so you pay for everything after that; FOB (free on board) covers loading onto the ship; DDP (delivered duty paid) brings the goods to you with duty paid.
[Landed cost: freight, duty and VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) explains each cost that sits between those points.

## From quote to landed cost and cash

Two numbers make quotes comparable. The first is what one unit costs once it is in your warehouse, ready to sell:

Landed cost per unit = quoted price + anything excluded (packaging, inspection) + freight and insurance + duty + clearance and UK delivery

The second is the cash you must find before the first unit is sold:

Cash for the first commitment = tooling + (MOQ × landed cost per unit)

Then check when that cash leaves: a balance due before shipment is paid weeks before the goods arrive.
The [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html) does the per-unit sum, and
[minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) explains why a lower unit price can cost more cash.
To see how tooling changes the picture as volume grows, enter each quote in the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

## Worked example: three quotes

Illustrative figures only, reused from other guides so you can follow them across the site. A team plans a first order of 1,000 units of a small moulded product and expects to sell about 150 a month.
Unit prices and minimum orders for A and B come from the [MOQ guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html); the £16,000 and £6,500 tooling from the
[hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html) and [mould break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html).
Freight, insurance, clearance and delivery use the [landed cost guide's](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) per-unit allowances (£0.70, £0.06, £0.12, £0.18), with duty assumed at 4% of the customs value (price plus freight and insurance) and inspection at £0.20 a unit.
Replace these with a forwarder's quote; larger shipments usually cost less per unit. Import VAT is left out, as a VAT-registered business can normally reclaim it.

|
|
Supplier A (UK) |
Supplier B (overseas) |
Supplier C (overseas) |

|
Quoted unit price |
£7.50 delivered |
£6.00 FOB |
£5.60 EXW |

|
Minimum order |
1,000 |
3,000 |
2,000 |

|
Tooling and ownership |
£16,000, yours, can be moved |
£6,500, stays the supplier's property |
£9,000, yours on final payment |

|
Excluded from the price |
Nothing listed |
Freight, duty, inspection |
Retail packaging (£0.30), transport to port (£0.20), freight, duty, inspection |

|
Duty at 4% |
None |
£0.27 |
£0.27 |

|
Landed cost per unit |
£7.50 |
£7.53 |
£7.63 |

|
Cash for the first commitment |
£23,500 |
£29,091 |
£24,269 |

|
Paid to the supplier before goods arrive |
£19,750 (tooling, 50% deposit) |
£24,500 (tooling, full order before shipment) |
£20,800 (tooling, full order before shipment) |

|
Stock at 150 a month |
About 7 months |
20 months |
About 13 months |

|
Cost per unit over 3,000 units, tooling included |
£12.83 |
£9.70 |
£10.63 |

Illustrative figures from the example above, bars drawn to scale within each chart. The cheapest quote lands as the dearest per unit, and the lowest tooling needs the most cash because of its minimum order.

Read the rows together. Supplier C's £5.60 is the lowest price on paper, but once packaging, transport to the port, freight, duty and inspection are added it lands at £7.63, the highest of the three.
Supplier B lands within 3p of the UK quote, so the real differences are tooling, cash and risk, not unit cost.

Supplier A needs the least cash and stock, and you own a tool you can move, but its £16,000 tooling makes it the dearest per unit over 3,000 units.
Supplier B is cheapest over 3,000 units, yet needs the most cash, locks up 20 months of stock and keeps the tool.
For an early, still-changing product, A for the first batches is a reasonable choice, while asking B about tool transfer and a price at 1,000.
With firmer demand or cheaper funding, B could be the better call. The table does not decide; it makes the trade-off visible.

## Red flags

**A price far below the others.**
Usually a misread specification, a cheaper material, or extras that appear later.

**No questions about the design.**
Suppliers who have looked closely ask about tolerances and finishes.

**Tooling ownership left vague.**
If it is not in writing, assume you do not own the tool and cannot move it.

**Full payment before any samples.**
Deposits are normal; paying everything before you have approved a part is a large risk.

**Missing lines.**
No delivery term, validity date or lead time usually means the quote is a starting point, not a commitment.

## Questions to ask before you choose

- What quantity does each price assume, and what is the price at our first order quantity?

- Who owns the tooling, can it be moved, how many parts is it expected to make, and who pays for repairs and changes?

- What are the lead times to tooling, first samples and production, and what usually delays them?

- What exactly is excluded: packaging, cartons, testing, inspection, freight, duty?

- When is each payment due, and is any of it linked to sample approval or inspection?

- How long is the price valid, and what would change it?

- Which design changes would lower cost or risk?

Keep the answers in writing with the quote. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) covers how to agree what "acceptable" means before production.

## Clarifying and negotiating respectfully

Most quote problems are misunderstandings, so clarify before you negotiate. Send every supplier the same questions and any specification change, and let them requote.

When you negotiate, solve the supplier's problem rather than just asking for less: offer a realistic forecast, a standard material they already run, or payments linked to sample approval.
Ask what drives the minimum order and whether a smaller first batch is possible at a slightly higher price.
Do not invent competing quotes or inflate volumes; the relationship has to survive the tenth order. Tell unsuccessful suppliers promptly, as you may need them later.

Once you have chosen, write down what was agreed, including tooling ownership, quality and payment, before you pay for tooling; [supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html) lists the topics to cover.

**Decision rule:**
choose on landed cost, cash needed and risk together. If two quotes are close on landed cost, prefer the one with the smaller cash commitment, clear tool ownership and shorter lead time.

## Common mistakes

**Comparing unit prices only.**
Delivery terms and exclusions can move a unit price by a quarter or more, as supplier C shows.

**Ignoring tooling ownership.**
A cheap tool that stays with the supplier can tie your product to them for its whole life.

**Mismatched quantities.**
A price at 3,000 units says nothing about the price at 1,000. Ask for the same price breaks from everyone.

**Ignoring payment timing.**
Two quotes with the same total can need cash on very different dates. Model payments month by month.

## FAQ

### How many manufacturers should I ask for a quote?

Usually three to five suppliers you have already checked for fit. Fewer gives little sense of what is normal; many more takes time to manage and rarely changes the answer.

### Why are manufacturing quotes so different from each other?

They usually assume different quantities, delivery terms, exclusions, tooling and payment terms, and sometimes a different reading of the specification. Put them on the same basis before comparing.

### Should I always choose the lowest unit price?

No. Compare landed cost per unit, tooling and its ownership, the minimum order and the cash needed before the first sale. The lowest unit price is often not the lowest landed cost.

### Who owns the injection mould tool?

Whoever the contract says. Many suppliers transfer ownership once the tool is paid for, but some keep it or tie it to an order volume. Get ownership, transfer rights and maintenance responsibility in writing.

### How long is a manufacturing quote valid?

It varies by supplier and is usually stated on the quote. If it is missing, ask, and ask whether material or currency changes can alter the price before you order.

Author

## Andrew Hunter

Product design engineer working across manufacturability, sustainability, and hardware commercial decisions in Belfast, Northern Ireland.

Source and Attribution

This article was created by Orion Design as part of a human-first engineering knowledge resource for product teams. Use it to structure a quote comparison, then confirm freight, duty and terms with your forwarder, the [UK Trade Tariff](https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff) and the suppliers themselves. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Title: Competitor and Patent Landscape Review

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and product teams checking what already exists before investing in development

# Competitor and patent landscape review: mapping what already exists

How to map the products customers can already buy and the patents and designs around your idea: where to look, what to record, and how to turn findings into positioning, requirements, price and IP decisions.

Quick answer

## Before investing in development, map what already exists: the products customers can buy today, how they compare, and the patents and designs around the idea.

A landscape review shows where there is room for your product, what customers already accept on price and features, which ideas have been tried, and which rights might
limit you. Keep it proportionate: a few focused days early can save months of developing something that already exists or cannot be sold freely.

## Why review the landscape

- **Avoid reinventing** something already on sale, or already tried and abandoned.

- **Find the gap:** what existing products do badly, and who they leave out.

- **Set expectations** for price, features and quality from what customers already buy.

- **Spot IP risks early,** while the design is easy to change.

- **Strengthen your case** for investors, grant applications and retailers.

## Part 1: the competitor review

Include direct competitors, indirect alternatives and the do-nothing or workaround option customers use today.

|
Look at |
Where to find it |

|
Products, features and prices |
Retailers, marketplaces, brand websites, trade catalogues |

|
What customers like and dislike |
Reviews, forums, social media, [customer interviews](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/customer-discovery-for-hardware.html) |

|
How products are made |
Buying and taking apart key competitors (a teardown) |

|
Where they are sold |
Retail and online channels, distributors, trade shows |

|
Failed or abandoned products |
[Crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) archives, discontinued listings, industry news |

Summarise the findings in a simple comparison grid of features, price, strengths and weaknesses, and note where your concept is clearly better.
The [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html) can score your concepts against the best existing product as a baseline.

**Practical rule:**
read the one- and two-star reviews of the leading products. They are often the clearest list of unmet needs you will find.

## Part 2: the patent and design landscape

- Describe the product's key features and functions in plain words, and list alternative terms for each.

- Search patents and published applications through the official [patent search](https://www.gov.uk/search-for-patent) routes and the international databases they link to.

- Search [registered designs](https://www.gov.uk/search-registered-design) for similar-looking products.

- Note who holds patents in the area, how recent they are, and the countries they cover.

- Flag anything close to your product for professional review.

Patent documents are also a rich source of technical ideas and of approaches others have tried. An early search is not a legal opinion; see
[freedom to operate explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/freedom-to-operate-explained.html) and
[design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html).

## Turn findings into decisions

- **Positioning:** which customers and needs you will serve better than the alternatives.

- **Requirements:** must-have features customers already expect, and the differences that matter. Add them to your [product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html).

- **Price range:** where your product can sit; check the margins with the [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html).

- **IP actions:** features to design around, protect or have checked.

## Common mistakes

**"There is no competition."**
There is almost always an alternative, even if it is a workaround or doing nothing.

**Only looking at direct competitors.**
Customers compare across categories when they solve the same problem.

**Searching patents with one keyword.**
Patents often use unusual terms; search by function and use several phrasings.

**Doing it once.**
Markets and patent filings change; refresh the review at major decisions.

- Define who the product is for with the [Product Purpose tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html).

- Build a comparison grid and score concepts with the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html).

- Check price positioning with the [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html).

- Read [how to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html).

## FAQ

### What is a competitor and patent landscape review?

A review of the products customers can already buy, how they compare on features, price and quality, and the patents and registered designs in the same area, done early to find the gap and spot risks.

### How do I find competitors for a new product?

Look at retailers, marketplaces, brand websites, trade catalogues and shows, crowdfunding archives and reviews, and ask target customers what they use today, including workarounds and doing nothing.

### How do I search for patents?

Describe the product's features in plain words with alternative terms, then search official patent databases, starting from the GOV.UK patent search pages and the international databases they link to. Flag anything close for professional review.

### Is a patent search the same as a freedom to operate opinion?

No. An early search helps you understand the landscape and spot obvious risks; a freedom to operate opinion is a professional judgement on whether your specific product infringes rights in force where you sell it.

### How long should a landscape review take?

Keep it proportionate to the investment. A few focused days early in a project is often enough to make better decisions, with deeper reviews before major commitments such as tooling.

Title: Crowdfunding a Hardware Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders considering crowdfunding or pre-orders to fund a first production run

# Crowdfunding a hardware product: funding a first run and delivering it

A practical guide to crowdfunding a physical product: what it is good for, what to have in place before launch, how to set a goal that covers delivering every reward, and how to manage cash, manufacturing and backers after the campaign.

Quick answer

## Crowdfunding can fund a first production run and prove demand, but only if the goal covers the real cost of making and delivering every reward.

Launch with a design that is largely finished, quotes from manufacturers, and an audience already waiting. Set the goal from the full cost of fulfilment,
including tooling, unit cost, packaging, shipping, platform and payment fees, VAT where it applies, and contingency, not from what seems achievable.
Plan for delays, communicate openly with backers, and remember that a successful campaign is the start of manufacturing, not the end of development.

## What crowdfunding is good for

- **Funding tooling and a first batch** with customer money rather than equity.

- **Testing demand** with real payments, which is stronger evidence than interest or surveys.

- **Building an audience** and gathering feedback before retail.

It is less suited to products that are still early in development, very expensive to make in small numbers, or hard to ship.

## Before you launch

|
Ready? |
What it means |

|
Design |
A working, near-final prototype; the main technical risks resolved |

|
Costs |
Quotes for tooling, parts, assembly, packaging and freight at your likely quantities |

|
Compliance |
Known safety and certification requirements, and time and budget to meet them; see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) |

|
Audience |
An email list or community ready to back on day one, since early momentum matters |

|
Fulfilment |
A plan for packing, shipping to each country, customs and returns |

|
IP |
Protection decided before public disclosure; see [design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html) |

## Setting the goal and reward prices

Work out what you need to deliver every reward, then set the goal and prices so the campaign still works if it only just succeeds:

- Tooling and set-up costs, which do not depend on the number of backers.

- Unit cost of each reward at the quantity you expect, including packaging.

- Shipping to backers, which can vary a lot by country and is often underestimated.

- Platform and payment fees, taken from the money raised; check each platform's current fees.

- VAT and other taxes that may apply to pledges for rewards; take advice from an accountant.

- Certification, marketing, and contingency for delays and cost increases.

The [Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html) works through these and shows what each backer leaves after costs.

**Practical rule:**
if the campaign only works at the stretch goal, the base goal is too low. Make sure you can deliver at exactly the minimum.

## All-or-nothing or flexible funding

Some platforms only collect pledges if the goal is reached; others let you keep what is raised either way. All-or-nothing protects you from being committed to deliver
without enough money; flexible funding can leave you with obligations you cannot afford. Check each platform's current rules.

## After the campaign

- **Cash arrives once,** but costs continue for months; plan it with the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

- **Lock the design** before tooling; changes after launch are expensive.

- **Update backers regularly,** especially with bad news. Silence damages trust more than delays.

- **Plan quality checks** before shipping; see [quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html).

## Common mistakes

**Launching too early.**
Unresolved technical problems become delays that backers have paid for.

**Underestimating shipping.**
International delivery, customs and damaged parcels can wipe out the margin.

**Too many reward options.**
Each colour, size or bundle adds stock and complexity.

**No audience at launch.**
Campaigns rarely find their audience from the platform alone.

## Next steps

- Model the campaign with the [Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html).

- Check tooling readiness with [Ready for Tooling](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html).

- Plan the cash after the campaign with the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

- Read [minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html).

### Plan the campaign

See what each backer leaves after making and shipping their reward.
[Open Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html)

### Plan the cash

Map costs month by month after the money arrives.
[Open Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html)

## FAQ

### Is crowdfunding a good way to fund a hardware product?

It can fund tooling and a first batch with customer money while proving demand, if the design is nearly finished, costs are quoted, and you have an audience ready at launch. It suits early-stage ideas poorly.

### How should I set a crowdfunding goal?

From the full cost of delivering every reward at the minimum: tooling, unit and packaging costs, shipping, platform and payment fees, taxes that apply, certification, marketing and contingency. Make sure you can deliver at exactly the goal.

### When should I launch a crowdfunding campaign?

When you have a working, near-final prototype, [manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html), a plan for compliance and fulfilment, IP decisions made, and an audience ready to back on the first day.

### Why are crowdfunded hardware products often late?

Common causes include launching before technical risks are resolved, underestimated tooling and certification time, supplier delays and design changes after the campaign. Planning contingency and updating backers openly helps.

### Do I need to charge VAT on crowdfunding pledges?

VAT may apply where backers receive a reward in return for their pledge. Rules depend on your circumstances, so take advice from an accountant before setting reward prices.
