Title: Customer Discovery for Hardware Products

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders exploring a product idea before committing to design and development

# Customer discovery for hardware: learning what matters before you design

How to learn from the people who have the problem before you design a physical product: who to talk to, questions that give evidence rather than politeness, observing real use, and turning conversations into decisions.

Quick answer

## Customer discovery means talking to the people who have the problem, about their past behaviour, before you design the product.

Find people who experience the problem, ask how they deal with it today and what it costs them, and listen for patterns. Avoid pitching your idea or asking whether they would buy it;
people are polite and bad at predicting their own behaviour. For hardware, add observation in the real environment, because use conditions shape the design.
Then test the strongest signals with something that asks for commitment, such as a pre-order or a pilot.

## Why it matters more for hardware

Changing a physical product after tooling is slow and expensive, so learning what matters before design starts saves far more than it does for software.
Discovery also reveals the use environment, who buys versus who uses, and the price people already pay for alternatives. It is the first step of
[validating a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html).

## Who to talk to

- **Users** who experience the problem directly.

- **Buyers,** if different: parents, purchasing teams, gift buyers.

- **Influencers and gatekeepers:** retailers, installers, clinicians, facilities managers.

- **People who have given up** on existing solutions, and those who rely on workarounds.

Find them through communities, forums, trade associations, events, your own network and introductions from earlier interviews. Aim for variety, not just friendly contacts.

## How to run a good interview

|
Ask about |
Example question |

|
The last time it happened |
"Tell me about the last time you had to deal with this." |

|
What they do now |
"How do you handle it at the moment? What have you tried?" |

|
What it costs them |
"What does that cost you in time, money or hassle?" |

|
What they have spent |
"Have you paid for anything to solve it? What happened?" |

|
The context |
"Where are you, and what else is going on, when it happens?" |

**Practical rule:**
ask about the past, not the future. "What did you do last time?" gives evidence; "Would you buy this?" gives politeness.

## Questions to avoid

- "Would you buy a product that…?" — hypothetical and leading.

- "How much would you pay?" — stated prices are unreliable; see [how to price a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-price-a-physical-product.html).

- "Do you like my idea?" — invites compliments, not information.

## Observe as well as ask

For physical products, watch people in the real setting where possible: the kitchen, workshop, ward or vehicle. Note the space, lighting, gloves, mess, noise and interruptions.
These become requirements in your [product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html).
Once you have a model to put in people's hands, the same habits of watching rather than asking carry into [usability testing a prototype](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html).

## Make sense of what you hear

- Write up each conversation the same day, separating what was said from your interpretation.

- Look for patterns across interviews: repeated problems, workarounds and spending.

- Rank problems by how often they occur, how painful they are, and whether people already pay to solve them.

- Keep going until new conversations stop revealing new themes, then test the strongest with a commitment: a pre-order, deposit, pilot or letter of intent.

## Common mistakes

**Pitching instead of listening.**
Once you describe your solution, people respond to it instead of telling you about their problem.

**Only asking friends and family.**
They want to be supportive, not accurate.

**Counting compliments as evidence.**
Enthusiasm without commitment is a weak signal.

**Stopping after a handful of chats.**
Keep going until the patterns are clear and stable.

## Next steps

- Write down who has the problem and how you will reach them.

- Capture purpose and user insights in the [Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html).

- Compare concepts against what you learn with the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html).

- Test commitment with pre-orders; plan a campaign with the [Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html).

### Clarify the purpose

Turn what you learn into a clear statement of who the product is for.
[Open Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)

### Test real commitment

Plan pre-orders or a crowdfunding campaign.
[Open Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html)

[Opportunity and concept: the hub guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/opportunity-and-concept.html)

[Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)

[Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html)

[Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html)

Related guides

[Validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html)

[Competitor and patent landscape](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/competitor-and-patent-landscape-review.html)

## FAQ

### What is customer discovery?

Talking to people who have the problem you want to solve, about how they experience and deal with it today, before designing the product. It finds out whether the problem matters, to whom, and what they already do and pay.

### How many customer interviews should I do?

There is no fixed number. Keep going, with a varied group of users and buyers, until new conversations stop revealing new themes, then test the strongest findings with something that asks for commitment.

### What questions should I ask in a customer interview?

Ask about specific past experiences: the last time the problem happened, what they did, what it cost them, what they have tried or paid for, and the context. Avoid hypothetical questions about buying your idea.

### Should I show people my product idea?

Not at first. Once you describe a solution, people react to it rather than telling you about their problem. Show concepts later, and look for commitment rather than compliments.

### How is customer discovery different for hardware?

The use environment, physical constraints and the split between buyer and user matter more, and design changes after tooling are expensive. Observing people in the real setting is especially valuable.

Title: Design for Repair and Disassembly

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers and engineers who want products to last longer and be easier to repair

# Design for repair and disassembly: making products that last longer

A practical approach to repairable products: find the parts that will fail first, design so they can be reached and replaced, support repair after sale, and plan for separating materials at the end of life, while managing the trade-offs with cost, sealing and safety.

Quick answer

## Design so the parts most likely to fail can be reached, removed and replaced with ordinary tools, and so materials can be separated at the end of life.

Identify which parts wear out or fail first, such as batteries, buttons, seals, hinges and cables, and make those easy to access. Prefer screws and clips to glue,
use standard fasteners and few tool types, make spare parts and repair information available, and avoid permanently joining different materials.
A longer, repairable life usually does more for a product's environmental impact than recyclable materials alone.

## Why repairability matters

The impact of making a product is spent once, so every extra year of use spreads it further. Products that cannot be opened or repaired are often replaced for the sake of one failed part.
Repairability also reduces warranty costs, supports a reputation for quality, and is increasingly expected by customers and regulators. See
[why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html).

## Step 1: find the parts that will fail first

Before choosing fixings, list the likely failure points. Typical candidates:

- **Batteries** lose capacity with charge cycles and age.

- **Moving parts:** buttons, switches, hinges, latches, motors and bearings.

- **Seals and gaskets** harden and crack over time; [sealing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) with replaceable O-rings or gaskets keeps them serviceable.

- **Cables and connectors** flex, wear and break at stress points.

- **Cosmetic surfaces** that scratch, such as lenses, screens and covers.

- **Consumables** such as filters, blades and brushes.

Field returns from similar products (see [after launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) for how to log them), accelerated life tests and your own [design reviews](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html) show which matter most. Plan these in your [test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

## Step 2: design for access and disassembly

|
Principle |
In practice |

|
Reversible fixings |
Screws, clips and snap fits that can be undone, rather than adhesives and welds, for parts that may need replacing |

|
Few, common tools |
Standard screw heads and as few different types and sizes as possible |

|
Short disassembly paths |
The parts that fail first should come out first, without removing everything else |

|
Modular sub-assemblies |
Group parts into modules that can be swapped as a unit, such as a battery pack or a switch module |

|
Connectors, not solder |
Plug-in connections for parts likely to be replaced |

|
Clear and robust |
Fixings and clips that survive being opened more than once, with features that guide reassembly |

**Practical rule:**
for each likely failure, count the steps and tools needed to replace it. If replacing the most common failure needs more than a few steps or a special tool, look for a better design.

## Step 3: support repair after sale

- **Spare parts** for the common failures, available for a reasonable period after the product goes off sale.

- **Repair information:** exploded views, part numbers and short guides, for professional repairers and, where safe, users.

- **Software and firmware** that does not block genuine replacement parts without a safety reason.

## Step 4: design for end of life

- Avoid permanently joining different materials, such as over-moulding incompatible plastics or bonding metal to plastic, where separation matters. [Joining methods compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) shows which joints can be undone.

- Mark plastic parts with their material, and use fewer material types overall.

- Make batteries easy to remove; battery and electrical producer responsibilities may apply (see the [Sustainability and product life hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html)).

## Trade-offs to manage

Repairable designs can conflict with other goals: screws add parts and assembly time, opening a product can affect water resistance or safety, and modularity can add size and cost.
The answer is rarely all or nothing; target repairability at the failures that actually happen, and check the assembly effect with the
[Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html). Where sealing or safety rule out user repair, make professional repair practical instead.

## Regulation

Repairability requirements are growing, especially for energy-related products under ecodesign rules, which can include spare-part availability and repair information.
Requirements differ by product category and between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the EU, so check current guidance on
[energy-related products](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/placing-energy-related-products-on-the-uk-market) for your category, and see the [right to repair and ecodesign rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/right-to-repair-and-ecodesign-rules.html) overview.

## Common mistakes

**Gluing everything for a slimmer product.**
It often ends the product's life at the first battery or button failure.

**Making the wrong parts repairable.**
Focus on what actually fails, not what is easiest to make removable.

**One-time clips.**
Clips that break when opened turn a repair into a replacement.

**No spare parts plan.**
A repairable design without available parts is not repairable in practice.

## Next steps

- List likely failure points and their repair steps.

- Compare lifetime and repair scenarios with the [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html).

- Estimate the footprint effect with the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

- Add life and durability tests with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

Make sure repairable fixings do not add too much assembly time.

## FAQ

### What is design for repair?

Designing a product so the parts most likely to fail can be reached, removed and replaced with ordinary tools, and supporting that with spare parts and repair information. It extends product life and reduces waste.

### Which parts should be easy to replace?

The ones that fail or wear first: typically batteries, buttons and switches, hinges and latches, seals, cables and connectors, cosmetic covers and consumables. Use field returns and life testing to decide.

### Does design for repair cost more?

It can add parts or assembly time, for example screws instead of glue. Targeted at the failures that actually happen, the cost is often modest, and can be offset by lower warranty costs and a longer-lasting reputation.

### Is design for repair required by law?

For some product categories, ecodesign rules include repair-related requirements such as spare-part availability and repair information, and these are expanding. Requirements differ by category and between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the EU, so check current guidance.

### How do repair and recycling relate?

Repair keeps the product in use, which usually saves far more than recycling at the end of life. Designing for disassembly helps both: it makes repair easier and lets materials be separated for recycling.

Title: Design Registration vs Patents

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and designers deciding how to protect a new product (an overview, not legal advice)

# Design registration vs patents: protecting how a product looks and works

An overview of the two main registered rights for physical products: what patents and registered designs each protect, how they compare, where unregistered rights fit, and why timing and disclosure matter. Take professional advice before relying on any of them.

Quick answer

## A patent protects how something works; a registered design protects how it looks. Many products need to consider both, and timing matters for each.

Patents cover new, inventive technical features, such as a mechanism, process or function. Registered designs cover appearance: shape, contours, pattern, texture or ornamentation.
Design registration is generally quicker and cheaper; patents are harder to get but can protect the underlying idea more broadly.
In both cases, avoid public disclosure before filing, and take professional advice before relying on either. This guide is an overview, not legal advice.

## Side by side

|
|
Patent |
Registered design |

|
Protects |
Technical inventions: how a product works or is made |
Appearance: how a product or part looks |

|
Main tests |
New, involves an inventive step, capable of industrial application |
New and has individual character |

|
Process |
Detailed application, examination and usually several years to grant |
Simpler application, usually much quicker |

|
Cost |
Higher, especially with attorney fees and overseas filings |
Usually lower |

|
Maximum term in the UK |
Up to 20 years from filing, if renewal fees are paid |
Up to 25 years, renewed every 5 years |

|
Good for |
A genuinely new mechanism, function or method |
A distinctive shape or look that copiers would imitate |

Durations, fees and rules are set by each country and change over time; check the current details on GOV.UK for
[patents](https://www.gov.uk/patent-your-invention) and
[registered designs](https://www.gov.uk/register-a-design).

## Unregistered rights

Some protection for appearance and shape can arise automatically, without registration, through
[design right](https://www.gov.uk/design-right) and, in more limited cases, copyright. Unregistered protection is generally narrower,
shorter and harder to enforce, because you must prove copying and when the design was created. Keep dated records of design work either way.

## Which do you need?

- **Does the product work in a new, non-obvious way?** Discuss a patent with a patent attorney before showing it publicly.

- **Is the look what makes it sell?** A registered design may be the most practical protection.

- **Both?** Many products have a new feature and a distinctive look, and can be protected in both ways.

- **Neither?** Speed to market, brand, [trade marks](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/trade-marks-and-product-names.html), relationships with retailers and know-how may matter more than registration.

**Practical rule:**
decide on protection before you publish, crowdfund, exhibit or pitch publicly. Disclosure before filing can destroy the novelty a patent needs, and grace periods for designs are limited and vary by country.

## Timing and confidentiality

- Use non-disclosure agreements when sharing details before filing; the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html) creates a starting draft.

- Plan filing dates around launches, trade shows and [crowdfunding campaigns](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html), using the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html) and [Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html).

- Protection is territorial: decide which markets matter, including where products are made and sold.

## Check you are free to sell

Owning a patent or design does not mean you are free to sell your product; someone else's rights may cover part of it. A [freedom-to-operate](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/freedom-to-operate-explained.html) review checks this.
See [how to protect product IP](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) and the
[IP, partners and compliance hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html).

## Common mistakes

**Showing it before filing.**
A public post, pitch or campaign can make a later patent impossible.

**Patenting the look.**
Appearance is usually better protected by design registration.

**Filing everywhere, or nowhere.**
Choose territories by where you will sell and where copies may be made.

**Treating registration as a business plan.**
Protection only has value if you can afford to enforce it and the product sells.

## Next steps

- List what is new about your product, function, method or appearance, and record IP decisions in the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

- Prepare an NDA for early conversations with the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html).

- Speak to a registered patent or trade mark attorney before any public disclosure.

- Read the official [intellectual property overview](https://www.gov.uk/intellectual-property-an-overview).

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a patent and a registered design?

A patent protects a technical invention, meaning how something works or is made. A registered design protects appearance, such as shape, contours, pattern or texture. A product can have both.

### Which is cheaper, a patent or a registered design?

Design registration is usually much cheaper and quicker. Patents involve a detailed application and examination, often with attorney fees, and cost more again when filed in several countries. Check current official fees.

### Can I patent the shape of my product?

Shape and appearance are normally protected by design registration or unregistered design right (and, in limited cases, copyright) rather than patents. A shape may be part of a patent only where it gives a new technical effect.

### Is my design protected without registering it?

Some protection can arise automatically through unregistered design right and copyright, but it is generally narrower, shorter and harder to enforce than a registered design. Rules differ between countries.

### Should I file before launching or crowdfunding?

Yes, decide before any public disclosure. Disclosure before filing can prevent a patent, and grace periods for designs are limited. Take professional advice on timing.

Title: Designing Buttons, Switches and Controls

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and designers choosing and detailing the buttons, switches and controls on a product

# Designing buttons, switches and controls: controls that feel right and keep working

How to start from the person pressing the button, the main types of switch and control and their trade-offs, the mechanical details that stop buttons feeling mushy or sticking, sealing, graphics and backlighting, switch life, and how to prototype and test the feel.

Quick answer

## A good control starts with how it will be used, then chooses a switch type to suit, and only then gets detailed in CAD around a checked tolerance stack-up.

Decide how often the control is used, whether people will wear gloves or have wet hands, how to prevent accidental presses and how the user will know it worked.
Choose between tactile switches with a plastic actuator, silicone keypads, membrane switches, capacitive touch, rotary controls and toggles on feel, sealing, cost and life.
Then check the gap between the button and the switch at the tolerance extremes, guide the button so it cannot wobble or rub, keep side loads off the switch, and test the feel on prototypes with real users.

## Contents

- Start with the user

- The main options

- Mechanical design of a button

- Sealing buttons

- Graphics, legibility and backlighting

- Switch life

- Prototyping and testing the feel

- Worked example: a mushy, sticking button

- Common mistakes

## Start with the user

Buttons are often designed last and touched first. Before choosing a switch, write down what each control does and for whom:

- **What it does and how often.** A power button pressed twice a day, a reset button pressed once a year and a volume control turned constantly need different switches.

- **Gloves and wet hands.** Gloved fingers need larger, well-spaced buttons and a clear click. Gloves and water can stop capacitive touch working reliably.

- **Accessibility.** Allow for weak grip, limited sight or tremor: a modest operating force, buttons that can be told apart by touch, good contrast and no meaning carried by colour alone.

- **Accidental presses.** Keep important buttons away from where the hand grips or the product rests, recess or guard them, or ask for a long press for anything that switches off or erases.

- **Feedback.** The user needs to know the press worked: tactile (a click you feel), audible (a click or beep) or visual (an LED or screen change). Use more than one where users may not be looking.

Record these in your [product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html) so the switch choice can be checked against them.

## The main options

Each option trades feel, sealing, cost, tooling and life against each other:

|
Option |
Feel |
Sealing |
Cost, tooling and life |

|
Board-mounted tactile switch with a plastic actuator |
Crisp click |
Needs a separate seal |
Cheap switches; actuator is part of the housing tooling. Sensitive to tolerances |

|
Silicone rubber keypad with carbon pills |
Softer press, set by the moulded web |
Good: the keypad seals the openings |
Own silicone mould and contact pads on the board; printed legends can wear |

|
Membrane switch and printed overlay |
Flat; metal domes can add a click |
Good: one bonded face |
Low tooling; graphics printed behind the film. Adhesive and edges need care |

|
Capacitive touch |
No movement; needs light, sound or vibration |
Excellent: behind a solid wall |
Nothing to wear, but needs careful electronics and testing with water and gloves |

|
Rotary encoder or potentiometer |
Turning, often with detents |
Shaft needs a seal |
An encoder counts steps; a potentiometer gives a position. Keep side loads off the board |

|
Toggle or rocker switch |
Clear, visible on/off state |
Sealing boots available |
Usually panel-mounted; check the electrical rating if it switches main power |

Agree the choice with your electronics designer early, because it changes the board. The [electronics in a physical product guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers designing the board and housing together.

## Mechanical design of a button

The commonest control is a plastic button pressing a tactile switch on the board. Most complaints about mushy, rattling, sticking or dead buttons come from a few details.

### Travel and the tolerance stack-up

A tactile switch has only a small travel before it clicks. If the actuator already presses on it at rest, the switch is half-pressed: the click disappears and the button feels mushy. If the gap is too large, the user pushes through dead travel first.

The gap is set by a chain of parts: the button, the stop that holds it in the housing, the bosses the board sits on, the board and the switch. Check it at both tolerance extremes, not just nominal, as the [tolerances and engineering drawings guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains, and shorten the chain by locating the board next to the button.

The gap between the stem and the switch depends on every part in the chain. Check it at both tolerance extremes so the button never preloads the switch and never has excessive dead travel.

### Captive buttons and wobble

A separate button needs a stop so it cannot fall or be pulled out, usually a flange inside the housing larger than the hole, or a snap or retaining plate. At rest it should sit against that stop, not on the switch. A button held only at its top edge rocks under an off-centre press and rattles when shaken, so guide it with ribs or a sleeve, as long as space allows, with a small, even clearance.

### Buttons moulded into the housing

Some products mould the button into the wall as a flap or tongue. This saves a part, but the flexing section must suit the material: a true living hinge is normally polypropylene, as the [snap fits and living hinges guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html) explains. In a rigid plastic, use a longer tongue that bends only slightly, and check the strain.

### Avoiding sticking buttons

Buttons stick when clearance is too tight once draft and moulding variation are included, when an off-centre press tilts the button onto an edge, when the switch alone is too weak to return a large cap against friction, or when dirt gets into the gap. Long guides, even clearance and, for large caps, a separate spring or rubber return prevent most of it.

### Side loads and drops

Tactile switches are made to be pressed straight down. Sideways pushes, users leaning on a knob or a button hitting the switch in a drop all end up in the solder joints. Give the button an end stop on the housing, support the board directly under each switch, and hold knobs and shafts in the housing rather than the board. The [drops and impacts guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html) covers board support more widely.

## Sealing buttons

Every button is a hole in the housing. Common ways to seal it are a **membrane or overlay** bonded to a flat face over the switches, a **silicone keypad** clamped around its edge so it is both button and seal, or a **boot or O-ring** on each rigid button or shaft. The keypad clamp is a seal like any other, so its squeeze depends on tolerances; the [sealing and waterproofing guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) explains how to design and test it. Sealing also changes the feel, so test the two together.

## Graphics, legibility and backlighting

Legends must stay readable for the product's life. **Pad or screen printing** is common, but printed legends on a top surface wear, so a protective coating may be needed. **Laser etching** marks the plastic itself or removes a painted layer to let light through. **In-mould decoration** moulds a printed film into the part; it is durable but adds tooling effort. **Printed overlays** carry the graphics on the back face, where they cannot rub off. The [surface finishes guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) covers these in more detail. Check legend size and contrast in real lighting.

Backlighting usually uses an LED on the board and a light pipe, a clear part that carries the light to the button. Watch for light leaking into neighbouring buttons and bright spots over the LED; opaque walls and a diffusing texture help. Prototype it early in a dark room.

## Switch life

Use the rated life from the switch datasheet, and check its test conditions match your use. Estimate the presses over the product's life from how often each control is used, and choose a switch with a comfortable margin. Actuators, hinges, keypads and legends wear too, so test the whole assembly with a **simple cycling rig**: a motor and cam, or a small linear actuator, pressing the real button in the real housing, with a counter. Stop at intervals to check function, feel and legend.

## Prototyping and testing the feel

- **Printed actuators.** Print several versions with different lengths, clearances and guides, and try them on the real board. [Printed parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html) are rougher than mouldings, so treat friction as approximate.

- **Feel panels.** Mount candidate switches or keypad samples side by side so people can compare force, travel and click directly.

- **Usability testing.** Give real users realistic tasks, with gloves, wet hands or dim light where those are normal, and watch for missed, accidental or repeated presses. See the [usability testing guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html).

Confirm the feel again on the first moulded samples.

## Worked example: a mushy, sticking button

Illustrative example. A handheld device has two moulded buttons, power and mode, pressing tactile switches on the main board. On the first moulded samples the mode button feels mushy on some units and sometimes stays down on others. The team cut a sample through the button and measured the parts in the chain.

|
Finding |
Cause |
Fix |

|
Mushy, no click on some units |
The gap had only been checked at nominal; at one extreme the stem half-pressed the switch |
Re-ran the stack-up at both extremes and shortened the stem so the smallest gap is still positive |

|
Long tolerance chain |
The board was located by bosses at the far end of the housing |
Added a locating feature and support next to the switch |

|
Button sometimes stays down |
Guided only at its top edge, the cap tilted and rubbed on the drafted edge of the hole |
Added guide ribs, slightly increased the hole clearance and rounded the cap edge |

They checked the changes with printed actuators before agreeing the tool changes with the toolmaker. Adding guide ribs only removes steel, but shortening the stem and opening up the hole take plastic off the part, which means adding steel to the tool, so they asked how best to make those. They then ran a short cycling test on the new samples.

## Common mistakes

**Designing the buttons last.**
Button positions, switch types and board layout are linked; settle them together.

**Checking the gap only at nominal.**
Check the stack-up at both extremes.

**Letting the switch take the load.**
Add an end stop and support the board under each switch.

**Capacitive touch without feedback.**
Add light, sound or vibration, and test with water and gloves.

**Testing the switch, not the button.**
Cycle-test the whole assembly.

## Next steps

- List every control with what it does, how often it is used, and any gloves, wet hands or accessibility needs.

- Choose a switch type for each and agree the board layout with your electronics designer.

- Check each button gap at the tolerance extremes with the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html).

- Add feel, life and sealing tests to your plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- See where this sits in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

## FAQ

### Should I use tactile switches or a silicone keypad?

Tactile switches with plastic actuators give a crisp click and suit products with a few buttons, but need a separate seal. A silicone keypad seals the openings and suits several buttons together, with a softer feel and its own mould. A keypad over tactile switches combines a seal with a firmer click.

### Does capacitive touch work with gloves or wet hands?

Often not reliably. Gloves can stop a touch registering, and water can cause false presses. It can be tuned to cope better, but if gloves or wet hands are normal for your users, a mechanical button or a combination is usually safer. Test with real gloves and water early.

### How do I stop a button rattling or wobbling?

Guide it along its length with ribs or a sleeve in the housing rather than only at the top edge, keep the clearance small and even, and make sure it rests against a stop in the housing when not pressed. A longer guide resists tilting better than a tighter one.

### How many presses should a button be designed for?

Estimate it from how often each control is used and how long the product should last, then choose a switch whose datasheet rating sits comfortably above that. Check the rest of the button, such as hinges, keypads and legends, with a cycling test on the real assembly.

### Can I prototype the feel of a button with 3D printing?

Yes, for travel, gaps, guides and overall layout, especially by printing several variants at once. Printed parts are rougher and less consistent than mouldings, so confirm the final feel and any moulded hinge on the first tool samples.

Title: Designing a Product to Survive Drops

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and engineers whose product will be carried, handled or knocked off a table

# Designing a product to survive drops and impacts

Why products break when they are dropped, the design changes that make the biggest difference, how to set a realistic drop requirement from the way the product is used, and how to test prototypes so the results mean something.

Quick answer

## A product survives a drop when the energy of the impact is spread out, absorbed or steered away from the weak points, and when nothing heavy inside is free to move.

Round the corners, tie bosses and ribs into the walls, choose a tough material that stays tough in the cold, hold batteries and boards firmly, and give the corners something to absorb the hit.
Set the drop heights, surfaces and orientations from how the product is really used, then drop prototypes on faces, edges and corners, open them up after each drop and record what you find.

## Contents

- Why products fail when dropped

- Design responses

- Defining the drop requirement

- Testing drops on prototypes

- Where simulation helps

- Worked example: a handheld device that cracks at a corner

- Common mistakes

## Why products fail when dropped

In a drop, the product's energy has to go somewhere in a fraction of a second, and it goes into whatever bends, breaks or moves first. Most failures fall into a handful of patterns:

- **Cracks at stress raisers.** Sharp internal corners, the roots of bosses and ribs, holes near edges and sudden changes in wall thickness concentrate stress, and cracks start there.

- **Snap fits and clips letting go.** The housing flexes, the halves spread for an instant and the hooks slip off their catches, so the product pops open without breaking.

- **Screw bosses splitting.** A boss already stressed by its screw splits under a shock load, especially when it stands free of the wall or sits in a corner.

- **Heavy internal parts moving.** Batteries, magnets, motors and populated boards keep travelling when the housing stops, hammering whatever holds them.

- **Solder joints and connectors.** Board flex can crack joints under large or heavy components, and connectors can unseat or pull pads off the board.

- **Displays and glass.** Glass often cracks from an edge, especially if the housing twists or a hard point presses on it.

- **Seals shifting.** A housing that flexes and springs back can leave a gasket out of its groove, so a product that was waterproof is no longer.

Several of these are not cracks at all. A product that looks fine outside can hide a loose battery, a cracked joint or a displaced seal, which is why inspection after each test drop matters.

The same drop height can do very different damage depending on what hits first. Corner drops usually find the weak points, so test all three orientations.

## Design responses

Toughness is designed in through geometry, material and how the inside is held together. Each change below is cheap in CAD and expensive once a mould has been cut.

### Generous radii

Round the outside corners and edges of the housing, and round the inside corners too. A sharp internal corner is a ready-made crack starter, and larger external radii can help the product skid on impact rather than stop dead on a point.

### Ribs and bosses tied into the walls

A free-standing boss behaves like a post that can snap off at its base. Connect bosses to the nearest wall with a short rib or gussets, keep a radius at every root, and avoid putting a boss right in a corner where the impact load arrives first.
Size ribs and bosses to the wall as described in the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html#ribs-bosses), so the part still moulds without sink marks or voids, which are weak points of their own.

### Tough materials, and the effect of temperature

Tough plastics bend and absorb energy before breaking; brittle ones are stiff but crack with little warning. Fillers such as glass fibre usually add stiffness at some cost to toughness, and many plastics become more brittle in the cold, so a housing that survives indoors may crack on a winter morning.
Tougher grades can be less stiff, less heat resistant or dearer, so shortlist against all the requirements using the guide to [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html), and check the supplier's data for the exact grade at the lowest temperature the product will see.

### Wall thickness

Walls that are too thin flex too far and crack; walls that are too thick mould poorly and can hide voids. Aim for even, adequate walls with ribs for stiffness rather than thickening everything, and avoid sudden steps in thickness.

### Securing heavy parts

Anything with mass needs a positive location in every direction, not just friction or a strip of foam tape. Cradle batteries with ribs or a moulded pocket, clamp them with a cover or bracket, and leave little room for them to gain speed. Magnets, weights and motors need the same. Battery safety adds its own requirements, covered in [electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html).

### Board mounting and heavy components

Support the circuit board near its heavy components and connectors, not just at its four corners, so it cannot flex like a trampoline. Large components may need adhesive staking or a support rib. Keep tall parts clear of the walls and retain cables and connectors so they cannot shake loose.

### Bumpers, overmoulds and corner protection

A soft material at the corners spreads the impact over a longer time, lowering the peak force: an [overmoulded](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/overmoulding-and-two-shot-moulding.html) rubber-like layer, clip-on bumpers or a sleeve. Raised corners can keep a display off the floor in a face-down drop. Overmoulding adds tooling cost, so weigh it against geometry changes.

### Letting energy go somewhere deliberate

Sometimes the best answer is to choose where the energy goes. A flexible rib, a sprung mount or a crumple feature on a cheap replaceable part can take the hit so the housing and electronics do not. The [snap fits guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html) covers keeping hooks within the strain the material can take.

**Practical rule:**
if a drop breaks the product, find out where the energy went first. The fix is usually to spread the load, slow it down or redirect it, rather than to make everything thicker.

## Defining the drop requirement

"It must survive being dropped" cannot be designed or tested to. Write down:

- **Height:** from real use: a handheld device from pocket or ear height, a desk product from a table, a tool from a bench or ladder.

- **Surface:** carpet, wood, tile and concrete differ greatly. Use the hardest surface the product is likely to meet.

- **Orientation:** faces, edges and corners, prioritising the most likely ones.

- **Number of drops and temperature:** one drop or many, at room temperature or in the cold.

- **Pass criteria:** still works, no cracks, cosmetic marks allowed or not, still sealed, and safe if it does break.

Some product standards include a drop or impact test. Check whether the standard that applies to your product specifies one, because that becomes a minimum; the guide to [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) explains how to find it.

Keep this separate from packaging transit tests, which check the boxed product during handling and delivery and tell you about the packaging, not about the product being dropped by its user. Plan those with the guide to [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html).

## Testing drops on prototypes

Drop early. A crude test on the first integrated prototype shows where the battery moves or which boss is wrong while those are easy to change.
Treat the results with care: 3D-printed parts are usually weaker between layers, behave differently from the moulded material and lack its knit lines. A printed part that cracks might be fine moulded, and one that survives is not proof. Use prints to find obvious problems, then repeat the decisive tests on samples from the production tool.

A useful drop test looks like this:

- **Every orientation:** faces, edges and corners, starting with the likeliest and the ones you suspect are weakest.

- **Cold testing:** condition some units to the lowest expected temperature and drop them before they warm up.

- **Repeated drops:** damage accumulates, so a unit that survives one drop may crack on a later one.

- **Inspect inside after each drop:** check function, then open the unit for cracks, loose parts, moved cables and displaced seals.

- **Record everything:** unit, build state, material, temperature, height, surface, orientation, result and photographs. Slow-motion phone video shows what flexes and moves.

Test more than one unit and retest after any design, material or supplier change. Fit drop testing into the wider [product test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) with clear pass criteria, and use the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html) to set it out. For sealed products, repeat the water test after the drop sequence, because a drop can undo a good seal; see [sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html).

## Where simulation helps

Drop simulation can show where stresses peak and how parts move, which helps compare options, spot a weak boss before parts exist and understand a failure seen in testing.
It depends on material data that is often limited for plastics under impact and in the cold. Treat it as a complement that narrows the options, not a replacement for dropping real parts.

## Worked example: a handheld device that cracks at a corner

Illustrative example. A start-up is developing a handheld battery-powered gauge with a two-part moulded housing held together by four screws into bosses at the corners. A rechargeable battery sits loose in a pocket between two ribs.
The requirement is to keep working with no cracks after a sequence of drops from typical hand height onto a hard floor, on every face, edge and corner, at room temperature and in the cold.

In early drops on printed prototypes, the housing cracks on a corner drop, starting at the root of the free-standing corner screw boss. Opening the unit also shows the battery has moved and marked the ribs.
Because prints can exaggerate cracking, the team treats this as a warning about geometry rather than a verdict on the material.

|
Finding |
Change made |

|
Crack starts at a sharp root on a free-standing corner boss |
Move the boss slightly inboard from the corner, tie it to both walls with gussets and add a radius at the root |

|
Small external corner radius concentrates the impact |
Increase the outside corner radius and add matching internal radii |

|
Battery moves and hammers the ribs |
Add a rib cage that locates the battery on all sides and a foam pad under the cover to take up clearance |

|
The chosen grade loses toughness in the cold |
Review tougher grades with the material supplier, keeping heat and chemical requirements in view |

|
Unprotected corners take each corner drop directly |
Add an overmoulded soft corner band, priced against the extra tooling cost before committing |

The retest plan uses several units of the revised design, each taken through the full sequence of faces, edges and corners, with half conditioned in the cold first. Every unit is checked and opened after each drop, with results logged and photographed.
Once the revised prints pass, the same sequence is scheduled on first samples from the production tool before they are approved.

## Common mistakes

**No written drop requirement.**
Without a height, surface, orientation and pass criteria, nobody can say whether a result is good enough.

**Only testing flat face drops.**
Corners and edges usually find the weak points. Test them all.

**Testing only at room temperature.**
Many plastics are more brittle in the cold, which is often when products get dropped outdoors.

**Judging only from the outside.**
A unit that looks fine may have a loose battery, a cracked joint or a displaced seal. Open it up.

**Trusting printed prototypes too far.**
Use them to find problems early, then confirm on moulded samples.

**Confusing product and packaging drops.**
A boxed product surviving a transit test tells you nothing about the product surviving its user.

## Next steps

- Write a drop requirement with heights, surfaces, orientations, temperatures, number of drops and pass criteria.

- Review the CAD for sharp internal corners, free-standing bosses and unsecured heavy parts.

- Add the drop sequence to your plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- See where drop testing sits in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

## FAQ

### What height should I drop-test my product from?

Start from how the product is used: the height it is usually held, carried or placed at, and the hardest surface it is likely to land on. Then check whether a standard that applies to your product specifies a drop test, because that sets a minimum.

### Is a product drop test the same as a packaging drop test?

No. A product drop test checks the unpackaged product being dropped by its user. A packaging transit test checks the boxed product surviving handling and delivery. Most products need both, planned separately.

### Can I drop-test 3D-printed prototypes?

Yes, and it is worth doing early to find loose parts and weak features. Printed parts behave differently from moulded ones, usually weaker between layers, so confirm the results on samples from the production tool.

### Why test drops in the cold?

Many plastics become more brittle at low temperatures, so a housing that survives indoors can crack outdoors in winter. Condition units to the lowest temperature the product will see and drop them before they warm up.

### Can simulation replace physical drop testing?

No. Simulation is useful for comparing options and finding weak points before parts exist, but it relies on material data that is often limited for plastics. Use it alongside physical tests, not instead of them.

Title: Designing Snap Fits and Living Hinges

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and designers adding clips, catches and hinges to moulded plastic parts

# Designing snap fits and living hinges: flexible features that last

How snap fits work, the simple strain check that stops a cantilever snap from cracking, the angles that decide whether it can be undone, what they mean for the mould, how to test them on prototypes, and how to design a polypropylene living hinge.

Quick answer

## A snap fit works only if the plastic can bend far enough to clear the catch without being strained beyond what the material can take. Check that strain before the tool is cut.

For a cantilever snap, the strain at the root is roughly 1.5 × thickness × deflection ÷ length². Keep it below the permissible strain in your material supplier's design data, add a radius at the root, and choose the angles to suit whether the joint must come apart.
Living hinges are thin flexible webs, almost always moulded in polypropylene, that need careful gating so the plastic flows straight across the hinge.

## Contents

- Types of snap fit

- The cantilever rule: checking strain

- Root radius and stress concentration

- Assembly angle, retention angle and friction

- What snap fits mean for the mould

- Designing for disassembly and repair

- Testing snap fits on 3D-printed prototypes

- Living hinges

- Worked example: checking a battery-door snap

- Common mistakes

## Types of snap fit

A snap fit is a flexible feature that deflects as two parts are pushed together and springs back behind a catch. It needs no screws or loose parts. The [joining methods guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) sets snap fits against screws, welding and adhesives; this guide goes into how to design them.

- **Cantilever:** a hook on the end of a short flexible beam. The most common type, and the easiest to calculate.

- **Annular:** a continuous bead or groove around a round part, as on a pen cap or a container lid. It can be strong and help to seal, but needs more force to assemble.

- **Torsional:** a lever held on a short bar that twists. Pressing one end of the lever lifts the hook at the other, which makes it a natural choice for a catch that the user releases by hand.

## The cantilever rule: checking strain

When a cantilever snap deflects, the plastic on the outside of the bend is stretched, most of all at the root, where the beam meets the wall. If it goes beyond what the material can take, the beam cracks or stays permanently bent.

For a beam of constant rectangular section, the strain at the root is approximately:

**ε = 1.5 × t × y ÷ L²**
where **t** is the beam thickness at the root, measured in the direction it bends; **y** is the deflection, how far the hook must move to clear the catch; and **L** is the beam length, from the root to the point where the catch acts on the hook. Use the same units for all three. The answer is a fraction, so multiply by 100 for a percentage.

Side view, not to scale. The dashed outline shows the beam bent by y as the hook rides over the catch. Strain rises with thickness and deflection, and falls with the square of the length.

The result must stay below the **permissible strain** for your material, taken from the supplier's design data for the exact grade. Plastics differ widely here: tough, unfilled grades usually tolerate far more than brittle or glass-filled ones, and some supplier guides give a higher value for a snap that is assembled once than for one that will be opened again and again.

Because L is squared, **lengthening the beam** is the most powerful way to reduce strain. **Tapering the beam**, so it is thicker at the root and thinner towards the hook, spreads the bending more evenly and also lowers the peak strain; supplier design guides give adjusted formulas for tapered beams. A shallower catch reduces deflection too, but leaves less engagement.

The formula is a simplified beam calculation that assumes a rigid wall and modest deflections. Treat it as a design check and confirm it by testing real parts.

## Root radius and stress concentration

A sharp internal corner where the beam meets the wall concentrates stress, so the local strain can be much higher than the formula suggests, and it is where most snap fits crack. A radius at the root spreads the load; a radius of around half the beam thickness is a commonly cited starting point, and larger is generally better if the space allows.

Keep the beam's wall junction consistent with the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html): a beam much thicker than the wall it grows from will sink, and a beam much thinner may not fill.

## Assembly angle, retention angle and friction

A cantilever hook has two working faces. The **assembly angle**, or lead-in, is the sloping face that rides over the catch as the parts go together. A shallow slope makes assembly easier but needs a longer hook. The **retention angle** is the face that holds the parts together once assembled, and it decides whether the joint can come apart:

- **Permanent:** a retention face at or near 90° to the pull will not push the beam aside, so the joint cannot be separated by pulling. Something must break first, or the hook must be lifted by hand or with a tool.

- **Releasable:** a retention face set at a shallower angle lets the hook slide out under a firm pull, so the joint can be opened without a tool. The shallower the slope, the lower the force needed to separate it.

**Friction** matters more than people expect. The force to push a snap together comes from bending the beam, multiplied by a factor that depends on the angle and the friction between the two surfaces. A commonly used relationship is W = P × (μ + tan α) ÷ (1 − μ × tan α), where P is the force to deflect the beam, α is the angle of the face and μ is the coefficient of friction. The same expression with the retention angle gives the force to pull it apart.
As the angle steepens, the term (1 − μ × tan α) approaches zero and the force rises sharply, which is why a steep retention face behaves as if it were locked. Friction varies with the materials and [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html), so take values from supplier data and confirm forces by testing.

## What snap fits mean for the mould

A hook that faces sideways is an **undercut**: it would lock the part on the tool when the mould opens. As [injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) describes, undercuts are formed by moving parts of the tool. **Sliders** (side actions) move out sideways before the part is ejected, and **lifters** move at an angle as the part is pushed off the core. Both add tool cost and maintenance.

Often the better answer is to design them out. Putting a **through-hole** in the wall behind the hook lets a **bypass core** pass through and form the hook's underside, so the hook can be moulded with a straight pull. Shallow annular snaps in a flexible material can sometimes be pushed off the core without a side action; your moulder will know whether that suits the part. Agree every snap detail at the DFM review, before the steel is cut, and check draft on the beam faces.

Removing steel from the tool, which makes a feature thicker or deeper, is usually easier than adding steel back. So start with a beam on the thin side and a slightly shallow catch: if first samples are too weak or too easy to release, the toolmaker can thicken the beam or deepen the catch by removing steel.

## Designing for disassembly and repair

A housing held shut by hidden one-way snaps cannot be opened without breaking it, which turns a battery change into a new product. If the product may ever be serviced, follow [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html):

- Use releasable angles, or provide a slot where a flat tool can press the hook back, and show where it is.

- Design for the number of openings expected and check the permissible strain for repeated use, not single assembly.

- Make sure the closed snap is relaxed, not left bent: plastics creep under constant load.

## Testing snap fits on 3D-printed prototypes

3D-printed prototypes are a good way to check that a snap engages, how it feels, and whether a hand or tool can release it. They are a poor guide to how long it will last. Printed parts are usually **anisotropic**: they are weaker between layers than along them, so a beam whose layers run across the root can snap at a strain a moulded part would shrug off. Many printed materials also tolerate **less strain** than the moulded grade, and their surface and friction differ.

Print beams with the layers running along their length where you can, and do not change a sound design only because a print failed; equally, a print that survives is not proof. Make the decisive tests on first samples from the tool. [From 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) covers the wider changes, and [choosing a 3D printing process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html) compares the processes, some of which give tougher parts than others.

## Living hinges

A living hinge is a thin, flexible web of plastic that joins two parts of the same moulding, as on a flip-top bottle cap. It saves a separate hinge and its assembly, but only works in the right material with the right detail.

- **Material:** polypropylene is the usual choice because it can flex many times without cracking; polyethylene is sometimes used. Most other common plastics, such as ABS and polycarbonate, crack after a few flexes. Check the grade with the supplier; [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) explains how plastics differ.

- **Geometry:** the web is very thin compared with the walls either side, short in the direction of bending, and blends into the thicker sections with smooth radii rather than sharp steps. The supplier's design guide or your moulder will give the starting dimensions for the grade.

- **Gate location:** plastic should flow straight across the hinge, from one side to the other, in a single front. The molecules then line up across the hinge, which gives it its strength. Avoid a gate that sends flow along the hinge or makes two flow fronts meet in it, because the resulting weld line is weak.

- **Flexing after moulding:** a commonly cited practice is to flex the hinge a few times soon after the part leaves the tool, while it is still warm, to set the orientation. Practice varies, so ask your moulder whether they recommend it for your grade.

Living hinges are hard to prototype faithfully: printed versions rarely behave like moulded polypropylene, so treat them as fit checks and plan to prove the hinge on tool samples.

## Worked example: checking a battery-door snap

Illustrative example, with round numbers chosen to show the method. A moulded battery door has a cantilever snap with a beam **t = 1.5 mm** thick at the root and **L = 15 mm** long. The hook must move **y = 1 mm** to clear the catch.

ε = 1.5 × 1.5 × 1 ÷ 15² = 2.25 ÷ 225 = 0.010, or **about 1.0%** strain at the root.

The next step is to compare that 1.0% with the permissible strain for the exact grade, taken from the supplier's design data. If the supplier's figure is comfortably higher, the beam is likely to be fine. If it is lower, or only just higher, change the design. Lengthening the beam to 20 mm, for example, gives 1.5 × 1.5 × 1 ÷ 400, about 0.56%; reducing the deflection to 0.8 mm gives about 0.8%. Tapering the beam would also help.

Because the door will be opened for battery changes, the team uses the permissible strain for repeated use, adds a root radius, gives the hook a releasable retention angle and a slot for a coin, then proves it by opening and closing moulded samples many times.

## Common mistakes

**A sharp corner at the root.**
It concentrates strain where it is already highest. Add a radius.

**Checking strain against the wrong figure.**
A value from a different grade, a general table or a single-assembly figure for a snap that is opened often. Use the supplier's data for your grade and use case.

**Short, stiff beams.**
Halving the length quadruples the strain. Find the space for a longer beam early in the layout.

**Judging durability from 3D prints.**
Printed parts are weaker between layers and tolerate less strain. Use them for fit and feel, and moulded samples for durability.

**Every snap needing a side action.**
Ask whether a through-hole and bypass core can form the hook instead.

**A living hinge in the wrong plastic, or with a weld line across it.**
Use a suitable polypropylene and gate so the flow crosses the hinge in one front.

## Next steps

- List every snap and hinge in the design and note whether each must be opened again.

- Get the design data for your chosen grade from the supplier and check each cantilever with the formula above, or with the [Snap-fit Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/snap-fit-calculator.html), which also estimates the assembly and separation forces.

- Check walls, draft and undercuts with the [Injection Moulding DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html), then review the snap details with your moulder.

- See where this sits in the wider picture in the [manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## FAQ

### Where do I find the permissible strain for my plastic?

In the material supplier's design data or snap-fit design guide for the exact grade. Ask the supplier or your moulder if it is not published. Use the figure for repeated use if the snap will be opened more than once.

### Can I use snap fits in glass-filled plastics?

Sometimes, but glass-filled grades usually tolerate much less strain than unfilled ones, so the beam must be longer, thinner or deflect less. Run the strain check with the supplier's figure for the filled grade before committing.

### Why did my 3D-printed snap fit break?

Printed parts are often weaker between layers and tolerate less strain than moulded parts, so a beam that breaks in a print may be fine when moulded. Print the beam with layers along its length and confirm durability on moulded samples.

### Do snap fits always make the mould more expensive?

Not always. A hook facing sideways is an undercut that needs a slider or lifter, but a through-hole behind the hook often lets a bypass core form it with a straight pull. Agree the approach with your moulder at the DFM review.

### Can a living hinge be made in ABS?

Not one that flexes repeatedly: ABS and most other common rigid plastics crack after a few cycles. Polypropylene is the usual material for living hinges. For an ABS part, use a separate pin hinge or a moulded snap-in hinge instead.

Title: Product Development and Prototyping Explained

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders, engineers and spin-out teams planning how to take a product from concept to production-ready design

# Development and prototyping: how a hardware product gets from idea to production-ready

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about developing a physical product: [the stages most products pass through](https://oriondesign.xyz/idea-to-manufacture/), which prototype answers which question, how many rounds to plan, and how testing and design freeze keep the project under control. Each section links to a deeper guide or a free tool.

Quick answer

## Product development is a sequence of questions, each answered by the cheapest build that can answer it.

A hardware product typically moves from requirements and concepts, through proof-of-principle, looks-like and works-like prototypes,
to engineering prototypes, design verification and a pilot production run. Plan each prototype round around the specific risk it must retire,
expect to go round the loop more than once, and keep the expensive commitments, such as production tooling and certification, until the design has stopped moving.

## Contents

- The stages of hardware development

- Types of prototype and what each is for

- How many prototype rounds to plan

- Testing and validation

- Worked example: planning the rounds for a handheld device

- Keeping the design under control

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## The stages of hardware development

Different companies use different names, but most physical products pass through the same stages. Electronics teams often call the last three
EVT, DVT and PVT (engineering, design and production validation test). What matters is not the label but the question each stage answers
and the evidence it leaves behind.

Each stage exists to answer one question. When a test says no, the team goes back round the loop, which is far cheaper before tooling than after it.

|
Stage |
Main outputs |
Typical builds |
Ready to move on when… |

|
1. Define |
User needs, a requirements list with measurable targets, constraints (cost, size, regulation) |
Sketches, cardboard or foam models |
The team agrees what "good" looks like and how it will be measured |

|
2. Concept |
Several distinct directions, a scored comparison, a chosen concept |
Quick mock-ups, simple rigs |
One direction clearly beats the others against the requirements |

|
3. Proof of principle |
Evidence that the core mechanism, sensor or process works |
Bench rigs, breadboards, off-the-shelf parts |
The riskiest technical question has a convincing yes |

|
4. Looks-like and works-like |
User feedback on form and use; a functional model of the system |
Appearance models; separate functional prototypes |
Users understand and want it; the system works end to end |

|
5. Engineering prototype |
An integrated design that combines form and function; detailed CAD |
3D-printed, CNC or vacuum-cast parts with real components |
It meets the specification on the bench and in early user trials |

|
6. Design verification |
Test reports against requirements; pre-compliance results; design freeze |
Production-intent parts, sometimes from bridge tooling |
Tests pass with margin and the design is frozen under [change control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html) |

|
7. Pilot production |
Production process, [work instructions](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-and-work-instructions.html), inspection plan, first-article reports |
Parts from production tools, assembled on the real line |
The factory can build it repeatably at the quality and cost planned |

The [Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html) lets you place your own product on these stages,
and [mapping the product design process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mapping-the-product-design-process.html) explains how to plan the work in each.

## Types of prototype and what each is for

|
Prototype |
Question it answers |
Common methods |

|
Proof of principle |
Does the core idea work? |
Bench rigs, development boards, modified existing products |

|
Looks-like |
Is the size, shape, feel and appearance right? |
SLA printing, CNC, painted and finished models |

|
Works-like |
Does the full system function? |
Functional parts in a rough housing, wired-up electronics |

|
Engineering (alpha) |
Does the integrated design meet the specification? |
Printed, machined or vacuum-cast parts with production-intent components |

|
Field trial (beta) |
What happens in real use, over time? |
Small batch for trusted users, often vacuum-cast or bridge-tooled |

|
Pre-production |
Do production parts and processes give the right result? |
Parts from production or bridge tools, built on the intended line |

Separating looks-like from works-like is one of the most useful habits in early development: each can be built quickly and cheaply
when it does not have to do the other's job; [looks-like vs works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) explains when to combine them. The [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html)
suggests the build method for each question, and [prototyping versus production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html)
compares the processes in detail.

## How many prototype rounds to plan

Many products need two or three rounds between first concept and production-intent parts, and complex, connected or safety-critical products often need more.
Rather than fixing a number, list the questions that must be answered before tooling and group them into rounds:

- **Answer the riskiest question first.** If the product fails because the core function does not work, nothing else matters.

- **One round, one purpose.** A round that tries to prove function, appearance and manufacturability at once usually proves none of them well.

- **Use the cheapest build that can answer the question.** A rig on a bench can settle a mechanism long before a housing exists.

- **Plan for at least one surprise.** Budget time and money for a round you cannot yet name; one is often needed.

**Practical rule:**
write down, before each build, the question it answers and the result that would change your plan. If you cannot, the build is probably not needed yet.

## Testing and validation

Testing turns prototypes into evidence. A simple test plan lists each requirement, how it will be tested, the pass criterion and the result; the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html) gives you a starting list.
Typical areas include function and performance, user testing, durability and life cycles, drop and impact, temperature and humidity,
and, for products that need it, pre-compliance checks for electrical safety and electromagnetic compatibility before formal certification.

Pre-compliance testing is worth doing early for any electrical product: problems found at a test house after tooling are among the most expensive to fix.
For which rules apply to your product, start from official guidance such as GOV.UK's
[guidance on UKCA marking](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukca-marking), and take specialist advice for regulated categories. [Product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) explains the process.

## Worked example: planning the rounds for a handheld device

Illustrative example. A start-up is developing a rechargeable handheld device with a sensor, a small display and a two-part plastic housing.
Instead of commissioning "a prototype", the team lists its open questions and plans four rounds.

|
Round |
Question |
Build |
Decision it unlocks |

|
1 |
Can the sensor give a stable reading in real conditions? |
Development board and sensor on a bench rig |
Choose the sensor and electronics architecture |

|
2 |
Is the size and grip right; can users read the display? |
Three printed looks-like models; a works-like unit in a rough box |
Fix the form, display size and button layout |

|
3 |
Does the integrated design fit, work, charge and survive a drop? |
Five engineering prototypes with printed housings and a custom circuit board |
Release the design for production-intent detailing |

|
4 |
Do production-intent parts pass the tests and pre-compliance checks? |
Twenty vacuum-cast units for testing and a short field trial |
Freeze the design and commit to tooling |

Each round is small and has a single job. If round 3 shows the housing cracks in a drop test, the fix costs a reprint rather than a tool modification.
The plan also gives the team a clear point, after round 4, at which committing to tooling is justified. Because the product contains a custom circuit board, the board and housing were developed side by side;
[electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers what to plan early.

## Keeping the design under control

As prototypes multiply, keep a light but disciplined record: a requirements list with test results against it, a revision number on every part and drawing,
and a short change log saying what changed and why. At design freeze, any further change should go through a simple change-control step,
because from that point changes ripple into tooling, suppliers, test reports and cost.

The same records are what a manufacturer will ask for. See [the documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html).

## Common mistakes

**Building a beautiful prototype too early.**
High-finish models are slow and expensive, and teams become reluctant to change them.

**Testing to confirm rather than to learn.**
A test that cannot fail tells you nothing. Set pass criteria before you see the result.

**Skipping design for manufacture until the end.**
Wall thickness, draft, part count and assembly should shape the engineering prototype, not be retrofitted after it.

**Leaving compliance to the end.**
Early pre-compliance checks are much cheaper than redesign after a failed formal test.

**No written record of why decisions were made.**
Six months later nobody remembers why a material or dimension was chosen, and the same question gets answered again.

## FAQ

### What are the stages of hardware product development?

Most products pass through defining requirements, concept development, proof of principle, looks-like and works-like prototypes, engineering prototypes, design verification and pilot production. Electronics teams often call the last three EVT, DVT and PVT. Each stage answers one main question before money is committed to the next.

### What is the difference between a looks-like and a works-like prototype?

A looks-like prototype shows the size, shape, finish and feel of the product but may not function. A works-like prototype proves the product functions but may look nothing like the final design. Building them separately is faster and cheaper than trying to make one model do both jobs early on.

### How many prototypes does a hardware product need?

Many products need two or three rounds before production-intent parts, and complex or regulated products often need more. Plan rounds around the questions that must be answered rather than a fixed number, and allow for at least one unplanned round.

### When should a design be frozen?

When testing on production-intent parts shows the requirements are met with some margin, and before committing to production tooling and formal certification. After the freeze, changes should go through a simple change-control step because they affect tools, suppliers and test reports.

### How long does hardware product development take?

It varies widely with complexity, regulation and how quickly decisions are made. A simple mechanical product can move from concept to production in months, while connected, medical or safety-critical products commonly take considerably longer. Map your own stages and rounds to get an estimate you can defend.
