Title: Die Casting Explained: Process and Design

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers with a metal part that may be outgrowing CNC machining

# Die casting explained: the process, alloys, design rules and when it pays

A plain-English explanation of die casting for people considering it for the first time: how the process works, the alloys you will be offered, the design rules that make a part castable, what happens to a casting afterwards, and how to tell whether a die will pay for itself.

Quick answer

## Die casting forces molten metal under pressure into a hardened steel die, giving detailed, near-finished metal parts at a low cost per part once the die is paid for.

Part cost ≈ metal + (machine rate × cycle time ÷ cavities) + trimming + machining + finishing + scrap allowance + tooling ÷ volume

Zinc is usually cast in hot-chamber machines and aluminium in cold-chamber machines.
Design the part much like a moulding: even walls, draft, radii, ribs instead of thick sections, few undercuts.
Castings contain some porosity, so sealing faces and threads are usually machined afterwards.
The die is expensive and slow to change, so die casting suits stable designs at volumes that can share its cost.

## Contents

- How die casting works

- Hot-chamber and cold-chamber machines

- Common die-casting alloys

- When die casting makes sense

- Design rules for die-cast parts

- Trimming, machining and finishing

- Dies, die life and trials

- Worked example: a housing moving from CNC to die casting

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## How die casting works

A die-casting die is a pair of hardened steel blocks with the shape of the part cut into them, much like an injection mould but built to survive molten metal.
The die is clamped shut, molten metal is driven into the cavity at high speed and pressure, and once it solidifies the die opens and ejector pins push the casting out, with its runner, overflows and flash still attached for trimming.

Fast, pressurised filling gives fine detail, thin walls and short cycles. It also traps some gas and leaves shrinkage porosity, which shapes several design rules below.

A simplified section through a die. Metal flows along the runner and through the gate into the cavity. The overflow beside the cavity collects the first, coldest metal and some trapped air. Ejector pins in the moving half push the casting out and leave small round marks on it.

## Hot-chamber and cold-chamber machines

There are two main kinds of die-casting machine. The alloy usually decides which is used, but knowing the difference helps you follow a quote.

|
Machine |
How the metal gets to the die |
Usually used for |

|
Hot-chamber |
The injection mechanism sits in the molten metal; a plunger pushes each shot straight into the die, keeping cycles short |
Zinc and other low-melting alloys, some magnesium |

|
Cold-chamber |
Metal is ladled from a separate furnace into a shot sleeve, then a plunger drives it into the die |
Aluminium, which would attack parts left sitting in it, and much magnesium |

Some die casters specialise in one alloy family, so ask early whether a supplier casts the alloy you need.

## Common die-casting alloys

Few alloys suit die casting, and they differ from the wrought alloys used for machined and sheet parts: they are formulated to flow and fill the die, so their properties and finishes differ too.
[Choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) covers the wider choice.

|
Alloy family |
Strengths |
Watch out for |
Typical uses |

|
Aluminium die-casting alloys |
Light, stiff for the weight, conduct heat well, reasonable corrosion resistance |
Contain silicon to help them flow, which also tends to make them anodise poorly; dies wear faster than for zinc |
Housings, enclosures, heat-sinking covers, brackets, frames |

|
Zinc die-casting alloys |
Fine detail, thin walls, long die life, good base for plating |
Heavy, nearly as dense as steel; weaker than steel; creeps under load when warm |
Handles, knobs, buckles, lock parts, small housings and decorative trim |

|
Magnesium die-casting alloys |
The lightest of the three for a given size |
Needs specialist handling and corrosion protection; fewer suppliers |
Housings and frames for portable equipment where every gram counts |

**Practical rule:**
do not put a wrought alloy such as 6082 on a die-casting drawing. Ask the die caster which casting alloy they recommend and check your design against its datasheet.

## When die casting makes sense

Die casting is a tooled process: expensive to start, cheap to repeat. It makes sense when the design is stable, volumes can share the die cost, and the part needs metal.
[Manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html) sets it alongside the alternatives in relative terms.

|
Alternative |
Choose the alternative when |
Die casting tends to win when |

|
[CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) |
Volumes are low, the design is still changing, or the look depends on anodised wrought aluminium |
Volumes grow and the shape has pockets, ribs and bosses that are slow to machine |

|
[Sheet metal](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html) |
The part is a folded shell, panel or bracket of even thickness |
The part needs ribs, bosses or rounded 3D forms |

|
Investment casting |
Volumes are lower, or the part must be steel or another alloy that cannot be die cast; its tooling generally costs less |
Volumes are higher and the part suits aluminium, zinc or magnesium, where faster cycles cut the cost per part |

|
[Plastic injection moulding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) |
The part does not need metal; plastic is lighter and usually cheaper per part |
The part must be stiff in thin sections, carry heat, screen electronics or feel solid |

[When does injection moulding become cheaper?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) explains why demand confidence and design stability matter as much as break-even volume; the same applies to a die.

## Design rules for die-cast parts

Many rules echo the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html). Treat this as typical guidance and confirm values with your die caster, who will set them by alloy, part size and process.

|
Feature |
Typical guidance |
Why |

|
Wall thickness |
Keep walls uniform and change thickness gradually; zinc generally allows thinner walls than aluminium |
Thick sections freeze last and gather porosity and sink |

|
Draft |
Draft faces parallel to the die opening, more on internal walls |
The casting shrinks onto cores and would drag or stick |

|
Radii |
Round internal and external corners; avoid sharp edges |
Better flow, lower stress, and sharp die corners are prone to cracking |

|
Ribs |
Stiffen with ribs rather than thicker walls; keep ribs thinner than the wall they join |
Stiffness without a thick, porous section |

|
Bosses |
Core bosses hollow and tie them to walls with ribs |
A solid boss is a thick, porous spot; a cored hole can be tapped afterwards |

|
Undercuts |
Avoid them, for example by moving a hole to a face in line with the die opening; otherwise the die needs a slide |
Each slide adds cost, maintenance and flash to trim |

|
Parting line |
Agree it early; keep it simple and away from cosmetic and sealing faces |
Flash forms there and trimming leaves a witness line |

|
Ejector pins |
Leave flat areas for pins on hidden faces, spread across the part |
Pins leave marks, and uneven pushing can distort the casting |

**Porosity, and why some features are machined afterwards.**
Every die casting contains some porosity, from trapped gas and from shrinkage where thick sections freeze last; the skin that freezes against the die is usually the soundest metal.
As-cast surfaces carry draft and parting lines, so they are rarely accurate enough for a [gasket](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) face, bore or thread. Those features are machined, which cuts through the skin and can open pores: a leak path on a sealing face, or weak engagement in a thread.

**Practical rule:**
keep machined features in even sections, not thick lumps, with a small machining allowance. Ask the die caster where porosity is likely and, for parts that must seal, about leak testing and impregnation.

## Trimming, machining and finishing

- **Trimming:** runner, overflows and flash are removed, at volume in a press with its own trim tool, a separate cost to check for in the quote.

- **Machining critical features:** sealing faces, bores and threads need fixtures to locate the casting. Mark which features are as-cast and which machined, keep tight tolerances to machined ones, and pick datums found on the raw casting (see [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html)).

- **Finishing:** powder coating, paint and plating are common; zinc takes decorative plating well. [Surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) covers each finish and masking.

Anodising is commonly reported to suit die-cast aluminium poorly compared with wrought alloys: the silicon tends to give a darker, uneven finish, and surface porosity can show through.
If the look depends on anodising, test it on sample castings, or plan for powder coat or paint.

## Dies, die life and trials

A die is hardened tool steel that is heated sharply by every shot and cooled again. Over time this causes fine surface cracks, called heat checking, which show as raised lines on castings until the die is repaired.

Die life varies with the alloy, part, steel and maintenance. Zinc casts at a much lower temperature, so zinc dies generally last much longer than aluminium dies.
Ask each die caster for the life they expect, what maintenance is included and who pays for repairs, and put that and die ownership in writing (see [supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html)).

Die cost follows part size, complexity, slides and cavities, plus the trim tool and machining fixtures.

New dies are proved in trials, like moulds. Many suppliers call the first shots T0 and the first customer samples T1, but labels vary, so agree what each means.
Ask for samples machined as in production, a porosity check on critical areas (by sectioning or X-ray, for example), and a leak test if the part must seal.
Ask for each die caster's lead time to first samples, and plan for at least one modification round.
[Mould tool trials and sample approval](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html) covers reading samples and signing them off, and most of it applies to dies.

## Worked example: a housing moving from CNC to die casting

Illustrative example. A small company makes a handheld measuring instrument with a housing machined from 6082 aluminium and anodised. Sales are growing, the housing is the most expensive part on the bill of materials, and the design has been stable for a year. Would die casting cut the cost, and what must change?

|
Feature of the machined housing |
What changes for die casting |

|
Straight pocket walls and corners sized for the cutter |
Draft on every wall; larger internal radii |

|
Thick floor and walls left by the machining strategy |
Even walls; floor thinned and ribbed |

|
Solid bosses, drilled and tapped |
Cored bosses tied to walls; threads tapped after casting |

|
Side port for a cable connector |
An undercut that cannot move, so the team accepts one slide |

|
Gasket groove and lid sealing face |
Still machined, with a small allowance; samples leak tested |

|
6082 aluminium, anodised |
The die caster's recommended casting alloy, powder coated instead of anodised |

The team gets quotes from their machining shop and two die casters for the same volumes, and enters them in the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html): machining in the CNC fields, and die casting in the tooled route, after switching that route from injection moulding to die casting.
The tool cost is the die, trim tool, fixtures and redesign work, and the unit cost is the casting with trimming, machining and powder coat. They run conservative, expected and optimistic volumes.

If the crossover sits well inside the conservative case, the die is likely to pay back; if only the optimistic case reaches it, keep machining for now.
This example gives no prices on purpose: get real quotes for your own part.

## Common mistakes

**Sending the machined part for a die-casting quote.**
A part designed for machining has no draft and too many thick sections. Redesign it for casting first, or ask for a DFM review alongside the quote.

**Expecting cast surfaces to seal.**
Plan to machine sealing faces, keep them in sound metal, and leak test samples.

**Keeping the wrought alloy and anodised finish by habit.**
Agree a casting alloy and a finish that suits it before the die is cut.

**Tight tolerances on as-cast features.**
Hold tight tolerances only on machined features, and say which is which on the drawing.

**Comparing the casting price with the machined price.**
Include the die, trim tool, fixtures, machining, finishing and redesign in the comparison, not just the raw casting.

## Next steps

- Check whether a die could pay back at your volumes with the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html), using quoted figures.

- Shortlist the alloy with [choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) and the die caster's datasheets.

- Brief two or three die casters, using [finding and briefing a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html), and ask each for a DFM review with the quote.

- Compare the quotes like for like with [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html), then plan the die trials and sample approval.

For the wider picture of processes and cost, see the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## FAQ

### What is the difference between die casting and injection moulding?

Both force a liquid into a closed steel tool and eject the finished part. Die casting uses molten metal, so the die must survive far higher temperatures, the castings usually need trimming and some machining afterwards, and they contain some porosity that the design has to allow for.

### Is die casting cheaper than CNC machining?

Per part, usually yes once volumes are high enough, but the die, trim tool and fixtures must be paid for first and the design must stop changing. Compare the total cost of each route at realistic volumes using real quotes.

### Can die-cast aluminium be anodised?

It can be, but it is commonly reported to give a darker, less even finish than wrought aluminium, because of the silicon in casting alloys and porosity near the surface. Powder coat or paint are more usual; if anodising matters, test it on sample castings first.

### Why do die castings need machining?

As-cast surfaces carry draft, parting lines and small variations, so they are rarely flat or accurate enough for sealing faces, bearing bores or threads. Those features are machined afterwards, and the casting is designed so the cuts land in sound metal.

### How long does a die-casting die last?

It depends on the alloy, the part, the die steel and maintenance. Zinc dies generally last much longer than aluminium dies, because zinc casts at a lower temperature. Ask each die caster for the life they expect and how repairs are handled.

Title: Planning Electronics in a Physical Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders whose product contains electronics and who need the board, the enclosure and production to fit together

# Electronics in a physical product: what to plan early

A product design engineer's view of the decisions between the circuit and the housing: board and enclosure together, batteries, heat, EMC and radio,
assembly, test access, prototyping, supply risk and what to hand to an electronics partner. It is about planning and integration, not circuit design.

Quick answer

## Design the circuit board and the enclosure together from the first layout, because each sets limits on the other.

Agree the board outline, mounting points, component heights, connector and button positions, battery space, antenna zone and the path heat will take out, before either side is frozen.
Treat EMC, radio performance, test access, programming and component supply as design inputs rather than late checks. Most expensive surprises in electronic products come from integration, not from the circuit itself.

## Contents

- Why integration is where the risk sits

- Design the board and enclosure together

- Power and batteries

- Heat needs a path out

- EMC and radio as design inputs

- Cables, connectors and assembly

- Firmware, test points and programming in production

- How electronics prototypes usually progress

- Component supply and second sources

- What to hand to an electronics partner

- Worked example: a small battery-powered handheld device

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## Why integration is where the risk sits

Often an electronics engineer designs a circuit that works on the bench while a designer draws a housing that looks right. Both can succeed and the product still fail:
the board does not fit, the antenna sits behind metal, the battery is too small, or the assembled board cannot be programmed. These problems are cheap to avoid early and expensive to fix after tooling.

## Design the board and enclosure together

The printed circuit board (PCB) and the enclosure share one space, so treat their interface as a design item with an owner. In practice that means a shared 3D model: the mechanical designer exports the board outline and keep-outs,
the electronics designer places parts within them and exports the populated board back. Agree, and revise together:

- **Board outline and mounting.** Shape, thickness and fixing points (screws, bosses, clips or slots), with clearance around fixings.

- **Keep-out zones.** Where no parts or tracks may go: under ribs and bosses, near the antenna and along edges that slide into guides.

- **Component heights.** Height limits for each region, so tall capacitors, connectors and modules sit where the housing has room.

- **Openings that line up.** Connectors, buttons, LEDs, displays and sensors must meet a hole, window or actuator, within the tolerance of both parts, including light pipes and button actuators. [Designing buttons, switches and controls](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-buttons-switches-and-controls.html) covers choosing switches and getting the button stack-up right.

Five items to agree between the electronics and mechanical sides before either design is frozen. Each one is cheap to change in CAD and expensive to change after tooling.

Neither side should be frozen first. Freezing the enclosure forces the board into awkward shapes or extra cables; freezing the board forces the housing to grow around it. Iterate both, then freeze them together.

## Power and batteries

The battery is often the largest and heaviest part inside, so power decisions shape the product. At a planning level:

- **Runtime and capacity.** Estimate average power across real use, including standby and radio activity, then size the battery for the runtime you promise. Capacity scales roughly with cell size, so the runtime target sets the size of the product.

- **Type and charging.** Replaceable cells, a built-in rechargeable pack or mains power each change the enclosure; for charging, decide the port position, the indicator and what charger you supply or specify.

- **Access.** Whether the battery can be reached for replacement, and how it is held so it cannot move, rub or be crushed. See [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html).

Lithium cells also bring battery safety, transport and producer-responsibility requirements, which [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) lists among the things to identify at the requirements stage.

## Heat needs a path out

A board that runs cool in open air on a bench can run much hotter inside a closed housing. Identify the parts that get warm (processors, regulators, chargers, motor drivers and the battery while charging)
and decide how their heat reaches the outside: board copper, a thermal pad to the case wall, a metal part, vents or airflow. Plastics conduct heat poorly, and a surface safe for the electronics may still feel too hot in the hand.
Measure temperatures inside a representative enclosure early.
The guide to [managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html) covers thermal paths, simple temperature estimates and testing in more detail.

## EMC and radio as design inputs

Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) means the product neither emits too much interference nor is upset by it. It depends largely on layout, grounding, cabling and the enclosure, so it belongs in the mechanical design too.

- **Cables act as antennas.** Keep internal cables short and consistently routed, and plan where external cables leave.

- **Grounding and shielding.** Decide early whether the enclosure is plastic, metal or coated, and how the board connects to any metal parts.

- **Antenna placement.** An antenna needs clear space near an outside wall, away from the battery, metal parts, displays and the user's hand. Metal housings block radio unless the design provides a window or non-metal section; plastics are more forgiving.

A pre-certified radio module can greatly reduce the radio testing needed, but it does not certify the whole product, and its antenna guidance still applies in your enclosure.
Book pre-compliance checks on engineering prototypes while the layout can still change. [Product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) explains how EMC and radio testing fit into conformity,
and the [Certification Readiness Checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html) helps you see what is still open.

## Cables, connectors and assembly

Every internal cable is a part to buy, route, fit and inspect, and a common source of faults; fewer boards and cables usually mean easier assembly. Where cables are needed:

- Fix them so they cannot be pinched, rub on sharp edges or move near hot parts.

- Give external cables strain relief, so a pull is taken by the housing, not the solder joints.

- Use keyed connectors that cannot be fitted the wrong way round and can be reached during assembly.

- Plan the assembly order, and whether the product can be reopened for rework or repair.

The [guide to estimating assembly time](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) shows how fixings and cable connections add up.
[Cables, wiring and connectors inside a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cables-wiring-and-connectors-inside-a-product.html) covers routing, strain relief, choosing connectors and harness drawings in more detail.

## Firmware, test points and programming in production

In production every unit must be loaded with firmware, tested and often serialised or calibrated, quickly and repeatably. Plan for this in the first custom board:

- **Test points** for power, programming and key signals, placed so a fixture can reach them, usually from one side.

- **A programming route** that works before the board goes into the enclosure, and ideally a way to update firmware afterwards.

- **A board-level functional test**, so faults are found before assembly.

- **Firmware version control**, so you know which version is in which batch.

Write these into your test plan alongside product-level tests. [Product testing and validation plans](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) covers the wider testing picture, and the
[Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html) turns requirements into a test list.

## How electronics prototypes usually progress

Electronics prototyping usually moves from off-the-shelf parts towards a custom board, in step with the
[looks-like and works-like](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) streams described elsewhere.

|
Stage |
What it is |
What it answers |

|
Development boards |
Off-the-shelf boards and modules wired together on a bench |
Can the chosen sensors, radio and processor do the job? Early firmware and power measurements |

|
Breakout or interim board |
A simple custom board or carrier for the chosen parts, not yet in the final shape |
Does the chosen circuit work together, and what does it really draw in power? |

|
Custom PCB in an integrated prototype |
A board in the real outline, fitted in a printed or cast housing |
Fit, heat, antenna performance, assembly, test access and pre-compliance checks |

Expect more than one revision of the custom board. [How many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) explains how to plan rounds so each answers a clear question.

## Component supply and second sources

A board is only as available as its scarcest part. Before committing, check that each part is in active production, stocked by more than one distributor and not marked as not recommended for new designs.
Prefer parts with a second source or drop-in alternative, and list approved alternatives on the bill of materials. Processors, radio modules, displays, batteries and custom parts are hardest to replace without redesign.
Discuss stock and lead-time risk with your manufacturer before setting a launch date.

## What to hand to an electronics partner

Whether briefing an electronics design partner or an assembly manufacturer, a clear pack avoids quotes based on guesses:

- **Requirements:** functions, power and runtime, environment, interfaces, markets and known regulations.

- **Mechanical interface:** outline, keep-outs, height limits, mounting and opening positions, ideally as a 3D model.

- **Bill of materials** with part numbers and approved alternatives.

- **Manufacturing files** for the board and assembly, plus programming and test instructions.

- **Volumes, timing and target cost**, including prototype and pilot quantities.

[The documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) covers the wider pack, and the
[RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html) helps you assemble a request for quotation.

## Worked example: a small battery-powered handheld device

Illustrative example. A start-up is developing a small handheld device with a rechargeable battery, a Bluetooth link to a phone, two buttons, a status LED and a sensor at one end.
The [industrial design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/industrial-design-vs-engineering-design.html) has a slim, rounded form that users liked in looks-like testing.

|
Question |
Decision |

|
Will the battery give the runtime promised? |
Power measured on a development-board rig; the battery needed was larger than assumed, so the housing was lengthened slightly rather than cutting runtime |

|
Where does the antenna go? |
A pre-certified module placed at the end opposite the sensor, near a plastic wall, away from the battery and outside the area covered by the user's hand |

|
Do buttons, LED and charging port line up? |
Board outline and heights shared as a 3D model; light pipe and actuators designed with the housing; charging port backed by a housing rib |

|
How does heat get out while charging? |
Charger placed away from the battery, with a thermal pad to the housing wall; temperature checked inside a printed housing |

|
How will each unit be programmed and tested? |
Test pads on the underside for a fixture, programming before assembly, and a short functional test of buttons, LED, sensor and radio |

|
What if a part becomes hard to get? |
Alternatives listed for the passive parts and charger; the module and battery flagged as single-source risks to monitor |

None of these decisions needed advanced circuit design; they needed both sides working from one model early enough that each change was made in CAD, not in a tool.

## Common mistakes

**Freezing the enclosure before the board.**
The board is then forced into a shape that may need more layers, extra cables or a second board.

**Leaving no room for the antenna.**
An antenna squeezed beside the battery or metal, or under the hand, can perform poorly, and the fix may mean a housing change.

**No test access.**
Without test points and a programming route, units are slow to program and faults surface only after assembly.

**Single-source parts everywhere.**
One unavailable part can stop production. Check availability and alternatives before the design is frozen.

**Ignoring heat.**
A board that is fine on the bench can overheat in a sealed housing. Measure temperatures in a representative enclosure.

## Decision rules

- **If different people design the board and housing**, share one 3D model and agree the interface list first.

- **If the product has a radio**, reserve the antenna zone in the first layout.

- **If runtime is a selling point**, measure power on a rig before fixing the product's size.

- **If a part has no alternative**, accept the risk, hold stock or design it out, and record the decision.

- **Freeze the board and enclosure together**, after an integrated prototype passes fit, heat and pre-compliance checks.

## FAQ

### Should the circuit board or the enclosure be designed first?

Neither should be finished first. Agree a rough board outline, mounting points, height limits and connector positions early, then develop both together using a shared 3D model and freeze them at the same time.

### Do I need an electronics engineer if I use development boards?

Development boards are a good way to prove the function, but a product usually needs a custom board to fit the enclosure, reach the cost target, and be tested and certified. Most teams bring in electronics design skills when moving from a rig to a custom board.

### Does a pre-certified radio module mean my product is certified?

No. A pre-certified module can greatly reduce the radio testing needed, but the finished product still has to comply as a whole, and the module's antenna guidance must be followed in your enclosure.

### Can a metal enclosure be used for a wireless product?

It can, but metal blocks radio signals, so the design needs a window, a non-metal section or an external antenna. Plan this before the enclosure design is fixed, and check radio performance in the real housing.

### What are test points and why do they matter?

Test points are pads on the board that a test fixture or programmer can touch. They let every board be programmed and checked quickly in production, so faults are found before assembly, when they cost least to fix.

Title: How Much Does It Cost to Develop a Hardware Product?

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and teams budgeting for development before launch

# How much does it cost to develop a hardware product?

Founders often ask what it costs to develop a hardware product as if there is one number. There is not.
The useful question is which cost blocks are likely to matter for this product, at this stage, on this route to launch.

Quick answer

## Pre-launch cost is usually a stack, not a single project fee.

Pre-launch requirement = engineering + prototypes + tooling + compliance + inventory + launch work + contingency

To estimate hardware development cost, price each block separately for your product and route to market, then add a contingency,
commonly 15 to 25 per cent and more for novel technology. Teams usually under-budget because they remember the exciting parts and forget the expensive supporting work around them.

A simple mechanical accessory and a connected, battery-powered device can differ in development cost by an order of magnitude.
The number that matters is not an industry average. It is your own stack, built from the decisions your product actually requires,
with the uncertain parts clearly marked.

## The six blocks most teams should expect

- **Design and engineering:** concept development, CAD, iteration, testing support, and supplier-ready detail.

- **Prototype builds:** multiple prototype rounds, fixtures, sample tools, and validation parts.

- **Tooling and setup:** mould tools, jigs, fixtures, or production setup costs.

- **Compliance:** test labs, standards work, documentation, and re-test risk.

- **First inventory:** stock, packaging, inserts, and pre-launch working capital.

- **Launch work:** imagery, packaging, copy, early commercial assets, and market-entry effort.

Contingency then sits on top of the whole stack, not inside one block.

## What pushes development cost up or down

|
Cost driver |
Tends to raise cost |
Tends to lower cost |

|
Electronics |
Custom [PCBs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html), radios, batteries, firmware and an app |
No electronics, or proven off-the-shelf modules |

|
Enclosure and parts |
Many moulded parts, tight tolerances, cosmetic finishes |
Few parts, standard materials, forgiving tolerances |

|
Regulation |
Medical, child-facing, food-contact, mains-powered or wireless products |
Low-risk categories with well-understood standards |

|
Novelty |
New mechanisms or technology with unknown failure modes |
Familiar architecture adapted to a new use |

|
Volume and route |
Retail launch needing large first stock and [retail-ready packaging](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html) |
Small direct launch with bridge production |

## Worked example: a small connected consumer device

Illustrative figures only. A team is developing a battery-powered household device with a two-part plastic enclosure, a custom PCB using a pre-certified Bluetooth module,
and a simple companion app supplied by a partner. They plan three prototype rounds and a first production batch of 1,000 units.

|
Cost block |
Estimate |
Main assumption |

|
Design and engineering |
GBP45,000 |
[Industrial design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/industrial-design-vs-engineering-design.html), mechanical and electronics engineering to production release |

|
Prototype builds |
GBP14,000 |
Three rounds, from [looks-like and works-like](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) models to near-production samples |

|
Tooling and setup |
GBP38,000 |
Injection mould tools for enclosure parts plus test and assembly fixtures |

|
Compliance |
GBP16,000 |
Safety, EMC and radio testing for UKCA and CE marking, plus one re-test allowance |

|
First inventory |
GBP26,000 |
1,000 units at GBP24 unit cost, plus packaging and inbound freight |

|
Launch work |
GBP9,000 |
Photography, packaging artwork, product page and early marketing |

|
Subtotal |
GBP148,000 |
All six blocks |

|
Contingency at 20% |
GBP29,600 |
Moderate novelty, first product for this team |

|
Pre-launch requirement |
GBP177,600 |
Before any sales income |

Notice that design and engineering is only about 30 per cent of the subtotal. Founders who budget only for the design fee are often surprised by the other 70 per cent.
Note too that the estimate covers pre-launch spend only. Monthly overhead and the cash needed to fund the second stock order belong in the [cash flow model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-financial-model.html).

Illustrative figures from the worked example, drawn to scale. Design and engineering is the largest block but only about 30 per cent of the six; the other five make up about 70 per cent, and contingency sits on top of the whole stack.

**Practical rule:**
treat the first estimate as a range. If the low and high ends are far apart, the gap usually points to one or two decisions, such as the number of moulded parts or the certification route, that are worth settling early.

## How much contingency to hold

Contingency is the acknowledgement that physical product development creates surprises: a failed test, a tool modification, a component going out of stock, an extra prototype round.
A common working range is 15 to 25 per cent of the subtotal. Use the lower end for a simple product built on a proven architecture,
and the upper end, or more, for new technology, regulated categories, or a team building its first product. Contingency should be released deliberately as risks close, not spent by default.

## Common budgeting mistakes

**Prototype count is usually underestimated.**
The first build rarely answers every important question. Budget for at least two or three rounds.

**Compliance arrives later than expected.**
Teams often budget the first test but not the cost of fixing and re-testing.

**First inventory is not just product cost.**
Packaging, labels, inserts, and freight decisions often land here too.

**Tooling changes are not free.**
Modifications after first samples are normal. Allow for them rather than assuming the first shots will be right.

**Contingency is not optional.**
Leaving it out does not remove the risk. It only moves the surprise to a point where it is harder to fund.

## How to use the estimate well

- separate pre-launch cost from recurring monthly overhead

- keep the cost blocks visible instead of collapsing them too early

- connect the total to runway and cashflow, not just fundraising ambition

- stage the spend so that the largest commitments, usually tooling and first inventory, come after the riskiest questions are answered

## Practical next steps

- List the six blocks for your product and mark each figure as quoted, estimated or guessed.

- Plan your prototype rounds with the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html), so each round has a clear question to answer.

- Estimate unit cost for the first inventory using the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html).

- Add contingency and check the total against runway using the guide to [calculating hardware startup cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html).

- Decide whether bridge production could delay the tooling commitment, as described in [prototyping versus production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html).

The [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) can then lay the cost blocks against development stages, so the team can see when each commitment falls due.

### Check the runway after that

Use the cashflow model to see whether the pre-launch requirement and growth timing can actually be financed.

## FAQ

### How much does it cost to develop a hardware product?

It depends heavily on complexity, regulation and launch volume. A simple non-electronic product can reach launch for a modest budget, while a connected or regulated device can cost several times more. The reliable way to answer it for your product is to estimate each cost block separately and add contingency.

### How much contingency should a hardware budget include?

A common working range is 15 to 25 per cent of the estimated cost blocks, added on top. Use more for new technology, regulated products or a first-time team, and less for a simple product on a proven architecture.

### How many prototype rounds should I budget for?

Most products need at least two or three rounds, moving from proof of concept to looks-like and works-like models and then near-production samples. Each round should answer a specific question. More complex or safety-critical products often need more.

### Is tooling a development cost or a production cost?

For budgeting, treat it as an upfront pre-launch cost because it has to be paid before production starts, often in stages. In the business case it is part of the investment the product must recover, alongside design and certification.

### What hardware costs do founders most often forget?

The usual gaps are extra prototype rounds, compliance re-testing, tooling modifications, packaging, inbound freight and duty on first stock, and launch assets. Contingency is also frequently left out entirely.

Title: Estimating Product Carbon Footprint During Design

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers, engineers and founders comparing concepts before the design is fixed

# Estimating product carbon footprint during design.

You do not need a full lifecycle assessment to make better early decisions. A concept-stage carbon estimate can already show whether
the main burden sits in materials, manufacturing, transport, or the use phase.

**Topic**
Concept-stage carbon

**Audience**
Designers and engineering teams

**Tool**
Carbon Footprint Estimator

**Use it for**
Option comparison

Quick answer

## Estimate a product's carbon footprint during design by multiplying each material mass, process, journey and kilowatt-hour by an emission factor, then adding the results by lifecycle stage.

Footprint (kg CO2e) ≈ Σ(material mass × material factor) + manufacturing + Σ(shipped mass × distance × transport factor) + (annual energy × lifetime × grid factor) + end of life

At concept stage the aim is not a precise number but a reliable ranking: which stage dominates, and which design change would move the total most.
Use one consistent set of emission factors, state your assumptions, and treat the result as a comparison tool rather than a figure for public claims.

Teams often delay carbon thinking until supplier data is available, but that is usually too late to influence the architecture.
By then material choice, form factor, assembly logic, and use-phase behaviour are already harder to change.
You do not need a full lifecycle assessment to make better early decisions: a rough model built from the bill of materials and a few honest assumptions is usually enough to show where the burden sits.

**Useful principle:**
early carbon estimates are not for reporting. They are for comparison. The goal is to identify which option is directionally lighter and why.

## Contents

- Embodied carbon and use-phase carbon

- What to estimate first

- A simple method you can repeat

- Where emission factors come from

- Worked example

- Common mistakes

- Use the estimate to compare choices, not to make claims

- Connect carbon to lifecycle quality

- Next steps

## Embodied carbon and use-phase carbon

A product's footprint is usually reported in kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent (kg CO2e), which converts other greenhouse gases into the warming effect of an equivalent mass of CO2.
It is helpful to split the total into two broad parts.

- **Embodied carbon** is everything emitted to make and deliver the product: extracting and refining materials, making components, manufacturing and assembly, packaging, and transport. It is fixed the moment the product is built.

- **Use-phase carbon** comes from running the product: electricity, fuel, consumables, and sometimes maintenance and spare parts. It accumulates every year the product is in service.

End-of-life treatment (landfill, incineration, recycling or reuse) adds or offsets a smaller amount for most products, and is the least certain part of an early estimate because nobody yet knows where the product will end up.

The boundary you choose matters. A **cradle-to-gate** estimate stops when the product leaves the factory, covering materials and manufacturing only.
A **cradle-to-grave** estimate follows the product through distribution, use and disposal. Cradle-to-gate figures are common in supplier data, but for anything that uses energy they can miss most of the footprint.
Always say which boundary a number uses before comparing it with another.

## What to estimate first

|
Carbon driver |
What to ask |
Why it matters |

|
Material mass |
How much material is the product actually carrying? |
Heavy, high-impact materials create embodied burden immediately |

|
Manufacturing process |
Is the route materially or energy intensive? |
Process choice changes both waste and energy profile |

|
Transport |
How far is the product moving and by which mode? |
Transport can be a major penalty, especially when air freight appears |

|
Use phase |
Does the product consume energy over years of operation? |
Use-phase carbon can dominate the total for active products |

|
Lifetime |
How long does the product stay useful before replacement? |
Short lifetime makes embodied impact harder to justify |

## A simple method you can repeat

- **Define the functional unit.** Decide what you are comparing: one product, or one product delivering a service for a stated time (for example, five years of daily use). Comparing per year of service stops a cheap, short-lived option looking better than it is.

- **List the bill of materials by mass.** Weigh or estimate each significant part and group it by material. Electronics, batteries and metals deserve their own lines because their factors are usually much higher per kilogram than common plastics.

- **Assign emission factors from one dataset.** Use the same source for every option so that the differences you see come from the design, not from mixing databases.

- **Add manufacturing.** Include process energy and waste, such as machining swarf, moulding runners and offcuts. At concept stage a per-kilogram allowance by process is often enough.

- **Add transport.** Multiply shipped mass (including packaging) by distance and a factor for each mode. Note every leg: factory to port, sea or air, port to warehouse, warehouse to customer.

- **Add the use phase.** Annual energy in kWh = power in watts × hours of use per day × days per year ÷ 1,000. Multiply by lifetime and by a grid electricity factor for the market where the product will be used.

- **Sum by stage and find the hotspot.** The largest stage is where design effort pays back most.

- **Test sensitivity.** Change one assumption at a time (lifetime, power, transport mode, material) and see which ones change the ranking. Those are the assumptions to firm up first.

## Where emission factors come from

Emission factors are published in lifecycle inventory databases, government conversion factor sets, industry association data and suppliers' environmental product declarations.
Values for the same material can differ noticeably between sources because they assume different production routes, energy mixes, recycled content and system boundaries.
That is normal, and it is why a single unexplained number should never be treated as authoritative.

- Record the source and version of every factor you use.

- Keep to one dataset for a comparison wherever possible.

- Prefer supplier-specific data once you have chosen a supplier, and note when you switch to it.

- Use the grid factor for the country where the product will be used, not where it is designed, and remember grid factors change over time.

Formal studies follow recognised standards: ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 for lifecycle assessment, and ISO 14067 for the carbon footprint of products.
An early design estimate does not need to meet those standards, but borrowing their discipline about boundaries, functional units and documented assumptions makes the estimate far more useful later.

A rough carbon model is valuable when it changes a design decision. It does not need to be perfect to be useful.

## Worked example

A compact electronic product may look low impact because it uses little material, but if it runs every day for five years the use phase can exceed the embodied footprint.
A passive product can behave the opposite way, where material choice and transport dominate almost everything.

Illustrative figures only. The factors below are rounded placeholders chosen to show the method, so they differ slightly from the Carbon Footprint Estimator's built-in factors (for example 0.2 here against its 0.193 kg CO2e per kWh); real values depend on the dataset, supplier and country, and should be replaced with sourced figures.
Consider a mains-powered desk lamp with a 0.4 kg ABS housing, a 0.1 kg aluminium heatsink and a small LED driver board, shipped 20,000 km by sea at 0.8 kg packed, drawing 10 W for 4 hours a day over a five-year life.

|
Stage |
Illustrative assumption |
kg CO2e |

|
ABS housing |
0.4 kg × 3.5 kg CO2e/kg |
1.40 |

|
Aluminium heatsink |
0.1 kg × 9.0 kg CO2e/kg |
0.90 |

|
Electronics |
Lumped allowance for the LED and driver board |
4.00 |

|
Manufacturing and assembly |
Lumped allowance for moulding, finishing and assembly |
1.00 |

|
Transport |
0.0008 t × 20,000 km × 0.015 kg CO2e per tonne-km (sea) |
0.24 |

|
Use phase |
10 W × 4 h × 365 days ÷ 1,000 = 14.6 kWh a year × 5 years = 73 kWh × 0.2 kg CO2e/kWh |
14.60 |

|
**Total** |
Cradle-to-grave, excluding end of life |
**22.14** |

On these assumptions, embodied carbon is 7.54 kg CO2e (about 34 per cent) and the use phase is 14.60 kg CO2e (about 66 per cent). The hotspot is energy in use, not the housing. Now test the alternatives one at a time:

- **A more efficient 7 W LED design** uses 10.22 kWh a year, or 51.1 kWh over five years, which is 10.22 kg CO2e. That saves 4.38 kg and brings the total to 17.76 kg CO2e.

- **Recycled ABS** at an assumed 2.0 kg CO2e/kg cuts the housing from 1.40 to 0.80, saving 0.60 kg. Worth doing, but about a seventh of the efficiency gain.

- **Air freight instead of sea** at an assumed 0.6 kg CO2e per tonne-km gives 0.0008 × 20,000 × 0.6 = 9.60 kg, raising the total to 31.50 kg CO2e, an increase of about 42 per cent.

- **Halving the lifetime** to two and a half years leaves the embodied 7.54 kg unchanged but spreads it over half the time: about 3.02 kg CO2e per year of service instead of 1.51.

The example shows why ranking matters more than precision. Even if individual factors were 30 per cent out, the conclusions would very likely stand: keep it off air freight, design for low power, and make it last.

Illustrative figures from the example above, in kg CO₂e, bars drawn to scale. Energy in use is the largest stage, so designing for low power saves far more than recycled plastic, and air freight undoes both.

## Common mistakes

**They compare materials but ignore lifetime.**
A lower-carbon material is useful, but not if the product becomes less durable and gets replaced sooner.

**They focus on recycling before reducing burden.**
If the design is heavy, energy-hungry, or over-engineered, recycling will not rescue the concept.

**They overlook logistics.**
A small product moved inefficiently over long distances can still carry a disproportionate footprint.

**They mix datasets and boundaries.**
Comparing a cradle-to-gate figure from one source with a cradle-to-grave figure from another produces a difference that has nothing to do with the design.

**They leave out electronics and batteries.**
These are often small by mass but large by footprint. A model built only from the plastic and metal parts can badly understate the embodied total.

**They assume the use phase away.**
Standby power, chargers and consumables are easy to forget and can add up over years of service.

**They quote the estimate as a fact.**
A concept-stage number with placeholder factors is not evidence for a marketing claim.

## Use the estimate to compare choices, not to make claims

- Compare one material system against another.

- Test whether manufacturing-route changes alter the picture meaningfully.

- Stress-test lifetime and use-phase assumptions.

- See whether the product improves more by consuming less energy than by changing polymer grade.

If you later want to make a public environmental claim, it needs a properly bounded assessment with sourced data, and the claim itself must be accurate, clear and substantiated.
In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority's [Green Claims Code](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/green-claims-code-making-environmental-claims) sets out what that means in practice.

## Connect carbon to lifecycle quality

Carbon is one lens, not the whole answer. The [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html) shows where the emissions burden is likely to sit.
The [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html) helps test whether lifetime, repairability, and recovery design make the concept more defensible overall.
[Why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html) explains why durability so often beats material substitution,
and [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) covers how to make a longer life realistic.

## Next steps

- Write down the functional unit, boundary and lifetime you are assuming, before choosing any factors.

- Run your main concept options through the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html) and note which stage dominates for each.

- If materials dominate, compare candidates with the [Plastic Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html) and the guide to [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html), checking durability as well as carbon.

- If the use phase dominates, set a power budget early and treat it as a design requirement.

- Repeat the estimate when supplier data arrives, and commission a formal assessment only when you need a figure for reporting or claims.

For the wider picture, see the [Sustainability and product life hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html).

## FAQ

### Can you estimate product carbon footprint before doing a full lifecycle assessment?

Yes. Early estimates use material mass, process route, transport, product lifetime, and energy use to compare directions before a formal LCA is needed.

### What usually drives product carbon footprint most?

The biggest drivers are usually embodied material burden, energy-intensive manufacturing, transport distance and mode, and use-phase energy over the product lifetime.

### What is the difference between a product carbon footprint and a lifecycle assessment?

A carbon footprint measures one impact, greenhouse gas emissions, expressed in kg CO2e. A lifecycle assessment can cover many impacts, such as water use, toxicity and resource depletion, as well as climate. ISO 14067 covers product carbon footprints, while ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 cover lifecycle assessment.

### What does cradle-to-gate mean compared with cradle-to-grave?

Cradle-to-gate covers emissions from raw materials up to the point the product leaves the factory. Cradle-to-grave also includes distribution, use and end of life. For products that use energy, cradle-to-gate figures can leave out most of the total.

### Can I use an early carbon estimate in marketing or sustainability claims?

Not on its own. A design-stage estimate with placeholder factors is for comparing options. Public claims need a properly bounded assessment with sourced data, and in the UK they should meet the Competition and Markets Authority's Green Claims Code.

Title: Financial Break-even for Hardware Products

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders and product leads checking how many units must sell before profit

# Financial break-even for hardware products

Break-even analysis answers a very narrow question: how many units must be sold to recover fixed cost at the current contribution margin.
It becomes useful only when the product cost is credible and the team understands what fixed costs are actually being recovered.

Quick answer

## Break-even happens when total contribution equals fixed cost.

Break-even units = fixed costs / (selling price - variable cost)

Subtract the variable cost of each unit from the net price you actually receive, then divide the fixed costs you need to recover by that contribution.
The trap is treating the result as a full business decision when it is really one checkpoint inside a wider model.

For hardware, the inputs need care. The selling price should be the net price the business receives after VAT and any retailer or marketplace share.
Variable cost should include everything that rises with each unit sold, not just the factory price. Get those two numbers right and break-even becomes a sharp test of whether the commercial model is viable.

## Key definitions

Contribution per unit = net selling price - variable cost per unit

Break-even revenue = fixed costs / contribution margin ratio, where the ratio = contribution per unit / net selling price

Margin of safety = (forecast units - break-even units) / forecast units

|
Cost type |
Typical hardware examples |

|
Variable cost |
Components, assembly, packaging, inbound freight and duty, payment fees, pick and pack, outbound shipping, returns allowance, channel commission |

|
Fixed cost |
Tooling, design and engineering, certification, launch assets, and the overhead you choose to recover over the period being tested |

Be explicit about which fixed costs are in the calculation. A **project break-even** asks how many units recover the one-off investment in development, tooling and certification.
An **operating break-even** asks how many units a month cover recurring overhead. Both are useful, but mixing them without saying so makes the result hard to interpret.

## What break-even is good at

- testing whether the current contribution per unit is strong enough

- showing whether the sales target is plausible at all

- comparing how price or cost changes move the required volume

- comparing routes to market on a like-for-like basis

## What break-even is bad at

- capturing payment timing and working-capital pressure

- showing whether the first production run can be financed

- including channel fees, returns, or route-to-market complexity unless those are already in variable cost

- reflecting that unit cost usually falls as volume grows and changes when components are re-sourced

## Worked example

Illustrative figures only. Recover GBP65,000 of fixed cost with a GBP49 net sale price and GBP22 of variable cost. Contribution per unit is GBP27,
so break-even arrives at roughly 2,408 units, or about GBP118,000 of revenue. The contribution margin ratio is about 55%.

If the team forecasts 3,500 units in the first year, the margin of safety is about 31%: sales could fall by almost a third before the fixed cost is no longer recovered.
At 200 units a month, break-even takes roughly twelve months to reach.

Now test the same product against the changes that commonly happen during development and launch.

|
Scenario |
Net price |
Variable cost |
Contribution |
Break-even units |

|
Base case, direct sales |
GBP49.00 |
GBP22.00 |
GBP27.00 |
2,408 |

|
Unit cost rises by GBP3 |
GBP49.00 |
GBP25.00 |
GBP24.00 |
2,709 |

|
Price cut to GBP45 |
GBP45.00 |
GBP22.00 |
GBP23.00 |
2,827 |

|
Sold through a retailer keeping 40% |
GBP29.40 |
GBP22.00 |
GBP7.40 |
8,784 |

The last row is the one that catches teams out. Retailer margins commonly sit somewhere between 30 and 50 per cent of the retail price before VAT,
so a product designed for direct sales can need more than three times the volume to break even once it moves into retail. That is a design and cost problem, not just a sales problem.

Illustrative figures from the table above, bars drawn to scale. Small cost and price changes move break-even by a few hundred units; a retailer's 40% share more than triples it, far past the 3,500-unit forecast.

**Practical rule:**
if small changes in cost or price move the break-even point dramatically, the business model probably needs more margin headroom.

## Common break-even mistakes

**Using RRP instead of net price.**
VAT and channel share are not yours to keep, so they cannot contribute to fixed cost.

**Factory price as variable cost.**
Freight, duty, packaging, fulfilment, payment fees and returns all scale with volume and belong in the calculation.

**Leaving tooling out.**
Tooling is often the largest single fixed cost in a moulded product. If it is excluded, say so and check it separately.

**Ignoring time.**
Break-even volume means little without a realistic sales rate. Two thousand units in a year and two thousand units in four years are very different businesses.

**Treating break-even as the goal.**
Breaking even only recovers cost. The business still needs margin to fund the next product, stock growth and overhead.

## Use break-even in the right order

- estimate product cost bottom-up with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html)

- check break-even volume with the [Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html)

- test the result against each route to market you are considering

- model cashflow and route-to-market pressure, using [calculating hardware startup cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html)

If tooling is a major part of the fixed cost, the guide to [when injection moulding becomes cheaper](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) covers the related question of when that investment is worth making.
[Building a hardware financial model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-financial-model.html) shows how break-even connects to unit cost, working capital and the cash low point.
To see where break-even sits alongside development stages and launch timing, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) brings those decisions into one plan.

Use the cashflow tool if sales timing and working capital are more likely to break the plan than the margin itself.

## FAQ

### How do you calculate break-even for a product?

Divide the fixed costs you need to recover by the contribution per unit, which is the net selling price minus the variable cost of each unit. Round up to the next whole unit. Multiply by the net price if you want the answer as revenue.

### Should tooling be included in break-even?

Usually yes, because tooling is a fixed cost the product has to recover and is often one of the largest. Some teams calculate an operating break-even without it as well, but they should state clearly which version they are using.

### What is a good contribution margin for a hardware product?

It depends on the category and channel, but a product needs enough headroom that modest changes in price or cost do not multiply the break-even volume. If a small cost increase or a move into retail makes break-even several times harder, the margin is probably too thin.

### What is the difference between break-even and payback?

Break-even is a volume: the number of units needed to recover fixed cost. Payback is a time: how long it takes for profit to recover the investment. A product can have an achievable break-even volume and still a long payback if sales build slowly.

### Does break-even analysis include VAT?

No. In the UK, VAT collected on sales is passed to HMRC rather than kept by the business, so break-even should use the price net of VAT and of any retailer or marketplace share.

Title: Freedom to Operate Explained

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and product teams checking IP risks before tooling or launch (an overview, not legal advice)

# Freedom to operate explained: checking you can make and sell your product

An overview of freedom to operate: how it differs from protecting your own idea, which rights can block a product, how to make an early informal check, when to get a formal opinion and what to do if you find a problem.

Quick answer

## Freedom to operate (FTO) asks whether you can make and sell your product without infringing someone else's rights, in the countries where you will make and sell it.

It is a different question from whether you can protect your own idea. Your product could be patentable and still infringe an older patent.
An early, informal search helps you spot obvious problems and design around them; a formal FTO opinion from a patent attorney is worth considering before major investment such as tooling or launch.
This guide is an overview, not legal advice.

## Freedom to operate vs patentability

|
|
Patentability |
Freedom to operate |

|
Question |
Is my invention new and inventive enough to protect? |
Can I make and sell this without infringing others' rights? |

|
Looks at |
Everything published before your filing date, anywhere |
Rights that are in force, or may be granted, where you make or sell |

|
Focus |
What is new about your idea |
Every feature of your actual product |

## What can block you

- **Patents** in force in the countries where you make, import or sell, and published applications that may still be granted.

- **Registered designs** covering the appearance of similar products.

- **Unregistered design rights and copyright**, where you have copied another product.

- **Trade marks**, for your product name and branding; see [trade marks and product names](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/trade-marks-and-product-names.html).

Rights are territorial and time-limited: an expired patent, or one not in force in your markets, does not block you there. See [design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html).

## An early, informal check

- Break your product into its key features: mechanism, functions, shape, materials and methods.

- Search patents and published applications for those features, using the official [patent search](https://www.gov.uk/search-for-patent) routes and international databases they link to.

- Search [registered designs](https://www.gov.uk/search-registered-design) for similar-looking products.

- Note competitors' patents marked on their products and packaging.

- Record what you find and when, and flag anything close for professional review.

**Practical rule:**
search early, while the design is still easy to change. Designing around a problem patent at concept stage is cheap; after tooling it is expensive.

## When to get a formal opinion

Reading patent claims and judging infringement is specialist work, and an informal search cannot give certainty. Consider a formal FTO review by a registered patent attorney
before committing to tooling, a large production order, a [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) launch, or investment, and when entering a new market. Investors and retailers may ask what checks you have made.

## If you find a problem

- **Check it properly:** is it in force where you sell, and do its claims really cover your product?

- **Design around it:** change the feature so the claims no longer apply.

- **License it** from the owner.

- **Get advice** on whether it could be challenged.

## Common mistakes

**Assuming your own patent gives freedom.**
Owning a patent does not stop you infringing someone else's.

**Searching only for your main idea.**
Infringement can come from any feature of the product.

**Leaving it until launch.**
Problems found late are the most expensive to fix.

**Forgetting manufacturing countries.**
Making a product somewhere can infringe rights there, even if you sell elsewhere.

## Next steps

- List your product's key features and the countries where it will be made and sold.

- Record IP checks and decisions in the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

- Protect early conversations with the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html).

- Schedule professional review before tooling with the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html), and check tooling readiness with [Ready for Tooling](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html).

Make sure IP and design checks are done before committing to tools.
[Open Ready for Tooling](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html)

### Protect your own idea

Compare patents and registered designs.
[Read design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html)

## FAQ

### What is freedom to operate?

Whether you can make, use and sell a product in particular countries without infringing someone else's patents, designs or other rights that are in force there.

### Is freedom to operate the same as patentability?

No. Patentability asks whether your invention is new enough to protect; freedom to operate asks whether your product infringes others' rights. A product can be patentable and still infringe an older patent.

### When should I check freedom to operate?

Start with an informal search early, while the design can still change, and consider a formal review by a patent attorney before major commitments such as tooling, launch, crowdfunding or investment.

### Can I do a freedom to operate search myself?

You can do an informal search of patents and registered designs to spot obvious issues. Judging whether claims actually cover your product is specialist work, so get professional advice on anything close.

### What if a patent covers my product?

Check it is in force where you make and sell and that its claims really apply, then consider designing around it, licensing it, or taking advice on whether it could be challenged.
