Title: 3D-Printed Prototype to Moulded Part

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers with a printed prototype that works and a plan to injection mould it

# From 3D-printed prototype to injection-moulded part: what has to change

Why a part that prints well can be impossible or expensive to mould, the design changes moulding usually needs, how to sequence the redesign with your moulder, and the bridge options that keep you moving while the tool is made.

Quick answer

## A printed part proves the idea, not the mouldability: before tooling it usually needs draft, even cored-out walls, properly proportioned ribs and bosses, radiused corners and fewer undercuts.

Printing builds a part layer by layer, so almost any shape can be made. Moulding fills a steel or aluminium tool and must then pull the part straight out of it, so the geometry has to suit flow, cooling and ejection.
Redesign the CAD for moulding, review it with your moulder, choose the moulding grade, and expect the first tool samples to need some adjustment.

## Contents

- Why a good print can be a bad moulding

- Draft on faces in the direction of pull

- Even walls: coring out thick sections

- Ribs, bosses and corners

- Undercuts: side actions or redesign

- Parting lines, gates and ejector marks

- Shrinkage, warp and tolerances

- Splitting or merging parts

- Printing materials are not moulding grades

- Sequencing the redesign

- Bridge options while the tool is made

- Worked example: a printed enclosure lid

- Common mistakes

## Why a good print can be a bad moulding

A printer adds material only where the file says, so a solid block, a sharp corner, a sideways hook or an untapered wall costs it nothing extra. Those are exactly the features that cause trouble in a mould tool.

In moulding, molten plastic is forced into a closed tool, cools against its walls, shrinks slightly, and is pushed out once the tool opens. [Injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) covers the cycle. The plastic must **flow** into every feature, **cool evenly** (cooling is usually the longest step, set by the thickest wall), and **come straight out** of the tool. A print that ignores these can mould with sink marks, voids and warping, stick in the tool, or need costly moving tool parts.

Changes are also cheaper on the model than on the tool: once it is cut, removing material from the part can mean welding and re-machining the tool, or a new insert.

## Draft on faces in the direction of pull

Draft is the slight taper on faces that run in the direction the tool opens. Prints rarely have it. Without it, a moulded part drags and sticks on ejection and scuffs its cosmetic faces. The [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) gives a common starting point of at least 0.5 to 1 degree on every face parallel to the direction the tool opens, with more for deep features and textured surfaces; a textured face can need several degrees, and the texture supplier will usually state a minimum.

Add draft in CAD early: retrofitting it ripples through mating dimensions and clearances.

## Even walls: coring out thick sections

Prototypes are often printed thick, for strength or because solid was easier to model. In moulding, even wall thickness is the most important single rule. A thick section stays molten longest and, as it cools and shrinks, pulls the surface into a sink mark or leaves an internal void, and lengthens the cycle every part pays for.

The fix is to core thick features out so they are made of walls close to the nominal thickness, and to blend any change in thickness gradually rather than in steps. The checklist's typical range is around 1 to 4 mm for many small and medium parts, depending on material and size; the material datasheet and your moulder set the actual figure.

Cross-sections, not to scale. The printed block is fine for a printer but would sink, cool slowly and stick in a tool. Moulded, the same job is done by even walls, a cored boss joined to the plate by gussets, thin ribs for stiffness, and draft on faces in the direction of pull.

## Ribs, bosses and corners

With thinner walls, stiffness and fixings come from ribs and bosses; too thick, they sink the face opposite. The DFM checklist's typical starting points are:

- **Ribs:** thickness about 40 to 60 per cent of the adjoining wall; height up to about 3 times the wall; spaced at least about 2 wall thicknesses apart; drafted.

- **Bosses:** outside diameter around twice the hole; boss wall thinner than the main wall; supported by gusset ribs or joined to nearby walls; cored from below. Follow the screw manufacturer's hole size for your chosen plastic, not the hole that happened to work in the print.

- **Corners:** inside radius at least about half the wall; outside radius about inside radius plus the wall, so the wall stays even around the bend. Sharp printed corners concentrate stress, restrict flow and are harder to fill and eject.

The [Injection Moulding DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html) applies these rules to your own dimensions and explains each result.

## Undercuts: side actions or redesign

An undercut is anything that stops the part pulling straight out of the tool: a side-facing clip, a side hole, an internal groove. Prototypes collect them freely. In a tool each usually needs a side action, a lifter or another moving part, which adds cost, lead time and maintenance.

Before accepting a side action, ask whether the feature can be redesigned. A snap-fit hook can often be moulded straight-pull by putting a hole in the wall behind it, so a core passes through and forms the hook's underside. Some joins are better changed altogether, to screws into bosses, heat-set inserts or a different snap arrangement; [joining methods compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) sets out the options. Keep a side action only where the feature earns its cost.

## Parting lines, gates and ejector marks

A moulded part carries three marks a print never has:

- **Parting line:** a fine line where the two halves of the tool meet, usually around the widest outline of the part.

- **Gate:** a small blemish where the plastic entered, left when the feed channel is cut or broken off.

- **Ejector marks:** small round witness marks from the pins that push the part out, usually on the inside faces.

Agree gate, ejector and parting-line positions with the moulder, away from cosmetic faces; moving them after the tool is cut is costly. [Surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) covers polish and texture choices, and why texture needs extra draft.

## Shrinkage, warp and tolerances

Every moulded plastic shrinks as it cools, by an amount that depends on the material, the wall thickness and the process. The toolmaker allows for it when cutting the tool, which is one reason the tool is cut for a specific material and choosing the material late causes trouble. Uneven walls and large flat areas shrink unevenly and can warp; ribs or gentle curvature help flat areas stay flat.

Fits proven in a print do not carry over: printed clearances reflect the printer, orientation and finishing, so a snap that works printed may be tight or loose moulded. Call up tight tolerances only where the function needs them, check critical fits with the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html), and state them on a drawing as described in [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html).

## Splitting or merging parts

A prototype's split into parts often reflects the printer's build volume rather than production. Merging parts can remove assembly steps and fasteners but makes a more complex tool; splitting one can turn deep pockets or undercuts into two simple straight-pull parts. Each part normally needs its own tool or cavity, so balance tool cost, assembly time and servicing.

## Printing materials are not moulding grades

Printing filaments, powders and resins are formulated for printing. Even where a material shares a name with a moulding plastic, such as nylon, its strength, stiffness, toughness and heat resistance differ, and resins can behave quite unlike any moulded thermoplastic. Prints are also weaker between layers, so a printed failure, or success, may not repeat when moulded.

Choose the moulding grade from the product's requirements, not from what printed well, using [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) and the [Plastic Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html). Then re-check the wall thickness, ribs and snap fits against that grade's datasheet, since materials flow and shrink differently.

## Sequencing the redesign

- **Freeze the function first.** Use prints to settle what the part must do. Redesigning for moulding while the requirements are still moving means doing it twice.

- **Redesign the CAD for moulding.** Choose the material, set the nominal wall, add draft, core out thick sections, then size ribs, bosses and radii, and remove undercuts where you can.

- **Print the redesigned part** to confirm assembly, treating strength and fits as indicative.

- **DFM review with the moulder.** Most toolmakers provide a DFM report proposing gate, parting line and ejector positions; for complex parts, ask for a mould-flow simulation as well. Read it before approving the tool design.

- **First samples (T1).** Check the first parts off the tool against your drawings and plan for at least one modification round. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) explains how parts are signed off.

## Bridge options while the tool is made

If you need parts before the production tool is ready, two common bridges are:

- **Vacuum casting:** silicone moulds, often made from a printed master, produce tens of parts in production-like plastics. Good for samples and trials, though not in the moulding grade.

- **Aluminium or soft-steel bridge tools:** real injection-moulded parts in the production material for the first few thousand parts, at lower tool cost and shorter lead time, with a shorter tool life. They need the same DFM as a production tool.

The [risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) explains how to stage these commitments, and [prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html) compares the routes by volume and cost.

## Worked example: a printed enclosure lid

Illustrative and qualitative. A start-up's handheld device has a lid printed in nylon powder that fits and survived early [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html). They plan to mould it in PC/ABS. The redesign changes:

- **Thick walls thinned to an even nominal wall,** avoiding sink and shortening the cycle, with three internal ribs to restore stiffness.

- **Solid screw pillars cored out** into bosses joined to the side walls with gussets, so the outer face does not sink and the bosses do not crack under screw torque.

- **Draft added to the side walls,** with more on the textured top face, so the lid releases cleanly without drag marks.

- **Sharp inside corners radiused** relative to the wall, for better flow and lower stress.

- **Two sideways clips redesigned** as straight-pull snaps with pass-through cores, removing two side actions from the tool.

- **Snap and lid-to-base clearances re-specified** on the drawing for the moulded material, rather than copied from what worked printed.

- **Gate and ejector positions agreed** on the inside of the lid, and the parting line placed on an edge where it will not be seen.

None of these changes alters what the lid does. The team prints the redesign to check assembly, then requests quotes and a DFM review.

## Common mistakes

**Sending the print file as the tooling file.**
A print mesh, or a model with no draft and solid sections, gives the toolmaker nothing sound to quote or cut from. Send a CAD model redesigned for moulding, with a drawing.

**Keeping thick printed walls.**
Walls made thick to strengthen a print will sink, void and lengthen every cycle when moulded. Core them out and stiffen with ribs.

**Zero draft.**
Prints need none, so prototypes rarely have it. Without it, parts stick and scuff; adding it late changes every mating dimension.

**Assuming printed fits will match moulded fits.**
Clearances, snap forces and stiffness all change with the process and material. Re-specify critical fits and confirm them on the first moulded samples.

## FAQ

### Can I injection mould my 3D-printed design as it is?

Rarely. Printed designs usually lack draft, have thick or uneven walls, sharp corners and undercuts that printing makes freely. Those cause sink, warping, sticking and costly side actions in a tool, so the CAD normally needs redesigning for moulding first.

### How much draft do I need to add to a printed part?

A common starting point is at least 0.5 to 1 degree on faces parallel to the direction the tool opens, with more for deep features and textured surfaces. Textured faces can need several degrees; the texture supplier will usually state a minimum.

### Will a moulded part be stronger than my 3D print?

Often, but not always, and not in a predictable way. Printed parts are weaker between layers and printing materials differ from moulding grades. Choose the moulding grade from the requirements and test critical features on the first moulded samples.

### Will snap fits that work printed also work moulded?

Not necessarily. Clearances, stiffness and snap forces change with the material and process. Re-specify the fit for the moulding grade, design the snap to mould straight-pull where possible, and confirm it on the first samples.

### What can I use while the injection mould is being made?

Vacuum casting gives tens of parts in production-like plastics from silicone moulds, and an aluminium or soft-steel bridge tool gives real moulded parts in the production material for the first few thousand, at lower tool cost but with a shorter tool life.

Title: Funding and Cash for Hardware Start-ups

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders, spin-outs and small teams working out how much money a hardware product needs and how to fund it

# Funding and cash: how much a hardware product needs, and where the money can come from

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about paying for a physical product: why the funding requirement is set by the cash low point, how the main funding sources compare, how to stage funding to milestones, and why stock and payment terms can strain even a profitable business. Each section links to a deeper guide, a free tool or an official source.

Quick answer

## A hardware business needs enough cash to reach the lowest point of its cash curve, plus contingency, and should raise it in stages tied to risk.

Funding needed ≈ deepest cumulative cash shortfall (development + tooling + first stock + overheads − early sales) + contingency

Development is only part of the requirement: tooling and the first stock order are usually paid for months before the money from selling them arrives.
Model the cash month by month to find the low point, then match funding to milestones, using cheaper, less dilutive sources such as grants, pre-orders and tax relief
for early, risky work and equity or loans once the product and market are better proven.

## Contents

- How much funding a hardware product needs

- Funding sources compared

- Matching funding to stages and risk

- Working capital: the cost of stock and slow payment

- What investors and funders look for

- Support in the UK and Northern Ireland

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## How much funding a hardware product needs

The question "how much do we need to raise?" is answered by a cash flow forecast, not a budget. Lay out, month by month, the money going out
(design, prototypes, tooling, certification, stock, overheads) and coming in (sales, grants, pre-orders). The deepest point of the cumulative total is the cash low point,
and that, plus a contingency, is the minimum the business must have access to.

Illustrative figures only. The funding needed is set by the lowest point of the curve, not by the development budget: here development costs £108k, but the business needs about £186k before sales carry it, plus contingency.

Notice the second dip at month 18 when the next stock order is paid for. Growth needs cash too: every time sales rise, stock has to be bought before the extra sales are paid for.
The [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html) builds the pre-launch budget, the
[Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html) finds the low point, and
[calculating hardware start-up cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html) explains the method.
[Building a hardware financial model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-financial-model.html) shows how unit cost, margin, break-even and cash timing connect into one set of numbers.

## Funding sources compared

Each source has a cost, whether in equity given up, interest, time spent applying or obligations to customers. Terms, eligibility and schemes change,
so check current details with the official sources linked below before relying on any of them.

|
Source |
Fits best when… |
What it costs you |
Watch out for |

|
Founders, friends and family |
The idea is early and unproven |
Your own money, or relationships if it goes wrong |
Put terms in writing, even with family |

|
Customer money (pre-orders, deposits, pilots) |
Demand can be shown before stock is made |
A promise to deliver, often by a date |
Delays and refunds; only take what you can deliver |

|
Crowdfunding |
A consumer product with a clear story and an audience |
Platform and payment fees, campaign effort, public commitment |
Underpriced rewards and shipping costs; manufacturing delays in public |

|
Grants and innovation funding |
Genuinely innovative technical work with a defined project |
Time to apply and report; often match funding required |
Competitive, slow, and usually paid in arrears |

|
R&D tax relief |
The company spends on qualifying research and development |
Record-keeping and claim preparation |
Rules change; arrives after the spend; get qualified advice |

|
Start-up and business loans |
There is a credible plan to repay from trading |
Interest and repayments, sometimes personal guarantees |
Repayments start before the product may be profitable |

|

Valuation and terms; SEIS and EIS reliefs can matter to UK angels |

|

Significant equity and expectations of rapid growth |
Many hardware businesses do not fit the model; that is not a failure |

## Matching funding to stages and risk

Raising everything at once is rarely possible and usually expensive: before risks are retired, investors price them in. A staged approach raises enough for the next milestone that materially reduces risk, then raises again on better terms.

|
Stage |
Main risk being retired |
Funding that often fits |

|
Idea and evidence |
Is there a real problem and market? |
Founders' time and money; small grants or competitions |

|
Proof of principle and prototypes |
Does it work, and can it be made? |
Innovation grants, R&D tax relief, friends and family, early angels |

|
Pre-production and launch |
Will customers buy at the planned price? |
Pre-orders, crowdfunding, angels, start-up loans |

|
Growth |
Can sales scale profitably? |
Equity rounds, stock and invoice finance, trading profits |

**Practical rule:**
tie each round of funding to a milestone a funder can see: a working prototype, a passed test, a signed retailer, a sold-out batch. Milestones are what make the next round cheaper.

## Working capital: the cost of stock and slow payment

Working capital is the cash tied up between paying for stock and being paid for it. For hardware it is often larger than founders expect, because
factories commonly want a deposit at order and the balance before shipping, minimum order quantities force larger batches, goods spend weeks in transit,
and retailers may pay 30 to 90 days after delivery. A profitable order can therefore still require a lot of cash. Plan batch sizes, deposits and payment terms
alongside the route to market, as described in the [Route to market and margins hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html).

## What investors and funders look for

Funders want to see that you understand your own numbers: unit cost and margin by route, the cash low point, what the money is for, and which milestone it buys.
Equity investors also look at the size of the opportunity and the team. Hardware-specific questions often include the tooling plan, certification route, supplier risk and gross margin.
The [Investor Metrics and KPIs](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/investor-metrics-kpis.html) tool and
[hardware investor metrics that actually matter](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-investor-metrics.html) explain which figures to prepare,
and the [Hardware Business Case Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/hardware-business-case-builder.html) brings them together.

## Support in the UK and Northern Ireland

Starting points for official information (eligibility and terms change, so always check the current details). [Funding routes for hardware start-ups in the UK and Northern Ireland](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-routes-uk-northern-ireland.html) explains how to choose and apply for each.

- [Innovate UK](https://www.ukri.org/councils/innovate-uk/): the UK's innovation agency, which runs competitions for innovation funding.

- [Invest NI](https://www.investni.com/): Northern Ireland's economic development agency, with support for innovation, R&D and growing businesses.

- [R&D tax relief](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-research-and-development-rd-relief): HMRC guidance on Corporation Tax relief for research and development.

- [Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme (SEIS)](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/seed-enterprise-investment-scheme-background): tax reliefs for investors in early-stage companies, which can make angel investment easier to raise.

- [Start Up Loans](https://www.gov.uk/start-up-loans): government-backed personal loans for starting a business.

- [GOV.UK business finance and support finder](https://www.gov.uk/business-finance-support): searches grants, loans and support by location and sector.

University spin-outs should also talk to their institution's technology transfer office about proof-of-concept funding and investment routes.

## Common mistakes

**Raising the development budget instead of the cash low point.**
Tooling, stock and the months before sales are paid for often need more money than the design work.

**Treating grants as quick money.**
Applications take time, many are competitive, and payment is often in arrears against spend.

**Forgetting the second stock order.**
Success needs cash too: more sales mean more stock bought in advance.

**Taking pre-order money without a delivery plan.**
Customer money is the cheapest funding until delivery slips; then it becomes the most expensive.

**No contingency.**
A failed test, a tool modification or a delayed shipment can each move the low point by months.

## FAQ

### How much money do I need to launch a hardware product?

Enough to reach the lowest point of your cumulative cash forecast, plus contingency. That includes development, prototypes, tooling, certification, first stock and overheads until sales income catches up, not just the design budget. It varies enormously with the product, so build your own forecast rather than relying on an average.

### What funding is available for hardware start-ups in Northern Ireland?

Options include Invest NI support, Innovate UK competitions, R&D tax relief, Start Up Loans, angel investment (where SEIS and EIS reliefs can help) and customer funding such as pre-orders. Availability and terms change, so check the official sources and use the GOV.UK business finance and support finder for current schemes.

### Should I use crowdfunding to fund manufacturing?

It can work well for consumer products with a clear story and an existing audience, because it provides money and evidence of demand before stock is made. Price rewards to cover the full landed cost, fees and shipping, and only promise delivery dates your manufacturing plan can meet.

### Why do profitable hardware businesses run out of cash?

Because stock is paid for before it is sold, and customers such as retailers may pay weeks or months after delivery. Rapid growth makes this worse, as each larger order needs more cash up front. A month-by-month cash forecast shows the problem before it happens.

### When should a hardware start-up raise equity investment?

Usually once there is evidence that reduces risk, such as a working prototype, test results or early sales, so the business can raise on better terms. Equity suits businesses with a route to substantial growth; many good hardware businesses are better funded through customers, grants, loans and profits.

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and spin-outs in the UK and Northern Ireland deciding where development and launch money will come from

# Funding routes for hardware start-ups in the UK and Northern Ireland

A practical guide to the main funding routes for hardware start-ups in the UK and Northern Ireland: what each needs, how long it takes, and how to combine them, with links to the official sources. It contains no invented figures; schemes and terms change, so always check the current details.

Quick answer

## Match each funding route to the stage and the risk you are trying to retire, and start applications well before the money is needed.

Early technical work in the UK is commonly funded by founders, innovation grants and competitions, R&D tax relief and early angel investors (where SEIS and EIS reliefs can help).
Launch is often funded by pre-orders or crowdfunding, start-up loans and angels; growth by equity rounds, stock finance and trading profits.
In Northern Ireland, Invest NI is a central source of support, and university spin-outs have their own routes through technology transfer offices.
Most routes take weeks to months to secure, so plan the timeline into the cash forecast. Schemes and terms change: check the official sources linked below. This is general information, not financial or tax advice.

|

## Innovation grants and competitions

UK-wide, [Innovate UK](https://www.ukri.org/councils/innovate-uk/) runs competitions for innovation funding; open competitions are listed on the
[Innovation Funding Service](https://apply-for-innovation-funding.service.gov.uk/competition/search) and on [UKRI's funding finder](https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/).
Applications are scored against published criteria, so read the scope and scoring guidance closely and answer every question directly.

- **Be specific about the innovation:** what is technically uncertain, and why existing solutions do not solve it.

- **Show the market:** who will buy, why, and the evidence you already have.

- **Plan and budget in detail:** work packages, milestones, risks and a realistic budget.

- **Plan the cash:** grants are commonly paid in arrears against claims, and many require a contribution from the company, so you still need working capital.

## R&D tax relief

Companies spending on qualifying research and development can claim Corporation Tax relief, which can return part of that spending or provide a payable credit for some loss-making companies.
Qualifying work must seek an advance in science or technology by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty; some hardware development meets that test and some does not. The rules have changed several times,
so read [HMRC's R&D relief guidance](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-research-and-development-rd-relief) and take advice from an accountant who knows the current scheme.
Keep records as you go: what was uncertain, what you tried, and what it cost.

## Northern Ireland support

- [Invest NI's support for business](https://www.investni.com/support-for-business) covers innovation, research and development, skills and growth support for eligible businesses.

- [HBAN](https://www.hban.org/), the Halo Business Angel Network, connects early-stage companies with angel investors across the island of Ireland.

- University spin-outs should talk to their institution's commercialisation or spin-out support; at Queen's University Belfast, [QUBIS](https://www.qubis.co.uk/) is the university's spin-out company.

- The [GOV.UK business finance and support finder](https://www.gov.uk/business-finance-support) lists grants, loans and support by location and sector.

## Angel investment, SEIS and EIS

Angels invest their own money, often alongside others in a syndicate or network. Many UK angels look for companies that qualify for the
[Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme (SEIS)](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/seed-enterprise-investment-scheme-background) or the
[Enterprise Investment Scheme (EIS)](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/venture-capital-schemes-apply-for-the-enterprise-investment-scheme), which give investors tax reliefs.
Companies can apply to HMRC for advance assurance that they are likely to qualify, which many investors expect before committing. Eligibility conditions and limits apply and change, so check the current guidance.

For hardware, angels typically want to understand the unit economics by route to market, the cash low point, the tooling and certification plan, and what milestone their money buys.
[Hardware investor metrics that actually matter](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-investor-metrics.html) explains what to prepare.

## Customer money: pre-orders and crowdfunding

Money from customers is often the cheapest funding for a first batch, and the strongest evidence of demand. It works best when you can show a convincing product,
price it to cover the full landed cost, fees and shipping, and deliver on a date your manufacturing plan can actually meet. Delivery delays are not unusual in hardware,
so build slack into the promised date and communicate early when things change.

## Start-up loans and other debt

[Start Up Loans](https://www.gov.uk/start-up-loans) are government-backed personal loans for starting a business, with mentoring support. Other options include bank lending,
asset finance for equipment, and stock or invoice finance once the business is trading. Debt does not dilute ownership, but repayments start before many hardware products are profitable,
so test them in the cash forecast.

**Practical rule:**
start funding conversations at least two to three months before the cash forecast says you need the money, and longer for grants and equity. Late funding forces poor terms or cuts at the worst moment.

## Combining routes

Many hardware businesses combine several sources. One possible pattern is founders' money and a grant for early technical work, R&D tax relief recovering part of that spend,
pre-orders or an angel round for the first production batch, and stock finance or a larger equity round to grow. Check how sources interact:
some grants restrict other public funding on the same costs, and investors will want to see the full funding plan.

## Common mistakes

**Applying for everything.**
Poorly targeted applications waste time; pick the routes that fit the stage and the project.

**Forgetting match funding and arrears.**
A grant can still leave a cash gap until claims are paid.

**No records for R&D relief.**
Reconstructing what was uncertain a year later is hard; keep notes as you work.

**Raising equity too early.**
Before key risks are retired, investors price them in, which costs founders more of the company.

**Relying on figures from old articles.**
Scheme limits and rates change; always check the current official guidance.

## FAQ

### What grants are available for hardware start-ups in the UK?

Innovation funding competitions run by Innovate UK are the main UK-wide source, listed on the Innovation Funding Service and UKRI's funding finder. Regional agencies such as Invest NI also offer innovation and growth support. Competitions open and close through the year, so check the official listings regularly.

### Can a hardware start-up claim R&D tax relief?

It may, if it spends on work that seeks an advance in science or technology by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty. Some hardware development meets that test and some does not. The rules have changed several times, so read HMRC's guidance and use an accountant familiar with the current scheme. Keep records as you go.

### What is SEIS advance assurance?

Confirmation from HMRC, requested by the company, that its planned share issue is likely to qualify for the Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme. Many angel investors expect it before investing because it gives them confidence of their tax relief.

### How long does it take to raise money for a hardware product?

It varies by route. Start-up loans can take weeks; grants commonly take months from competition opening to funds and are paid in arrears; angel rounds often take several months from first meeting to money. Start well before the cash forecast says you need it.

### Where can a Northern Ireland start-up get funding support?

Starting points include Invest NI, Innovate UK competitions, R&D tax relief, Start Up Loans, HBAN for angel investment across the island of Ireland, and, for university spin-outs, the institution's commercialisation or spin-out support, such as QUBIS at Queen's University Belfast.

Title: Hardware Investor Metrics That Actually Matter

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For hardware founders preparing to talk to investors

# Hardware investor metrics that actually matter.

Investors do not just want growth. They want to know whether growth improves the business, buys time, and demonstrates a repeatable commercial engine.

Quick answer

## Investors in hardware look for real demand, healthy gross margin, efficient acquisition and enough runway to reach the next milestone.

CAC payback (orders) = customer acquisition cost / gross profit per order after fulfilment

The core set is monthly revenue, gross margin, customer acquisition cost (CAC), payback and runway. Together they show whether growth makes the business stronger
or simply consumes cash faster.

Early hardware businesses often report vanity signals because they feel easier to defend. The stronger story usually sits in fewer numbers: revenue quality, gross margin, acquisition efficiency, payback, and runway.

Hardware brings its own complications. Stock is paid for before it is sold, unit cost changes with volume, and most products are bought once rather than paid for monthly.
That means investor metrics built for software need adapting, and some hardware-specific numbers deserve a place alongside them.

**Good reporting discipline:** every metric should help answer one of three questions. Is demand real? Is the margin good enough? Is the company buying enough time to prove the next stage?

## The core metrics to watch

|Metric |What it reveals |Why it matters |

|Monthly revenue |Demand converted into cash generation |Shows the scale of the commercial engine |

|Gross margin |Quality of each sale after unit cost |Weak margin makes scale less useful |

|CAC |Cost of acquiring a customer |Tests whether demand can be repeated efficiently |

|Payback |How quickly gross profit recovers acquisition cost |Shows whether growth is buying strength or just spend |

|Runway |How long the current cash can support the business |Defines how much time exists to improve the model |

## How to calculate them

Gross margin % = (revenue - landed cost of goods sold) / revenue

CAC = sales and marketing spend in the period / new customers in the period

Runway (months) = cash in the bank / net monthly burn

For a one-off hardware purchase, payback is usually best expressed in orders rather than months: does the first order recover the cost of winning the customer?
If the product has consumables, accessories or a subscription, repeat gross profit can be added, but only on evidence of actual repeat behaviour.

## Hardware-specific metrics worth adding

**Contribution after fulfilment.**
Gross profit minus pick and pack, shipping, payment fees and returns. This is what each order really leaves behind.

**Inventory days or turns.**
How long stock sits before it sells. Slow-moving stock is cash the business cannot use.

**Return and warranty rate.**
An early signal of quality or expectation problems that will erode margin as volume grows.

**Current versus target COGS.**
Investors will want to see today's landed cost and a credible, evidenced path to the cost at scale.

**Attach rate.**
For products with consumables or accessories, the share of customers who buy again. This is often where lifetime value comes from.

## Worked example: two versions of the same month

Illustrative figures only. A direct-to-consumer hardware brand sells 600 units in a month at a net price of GBP120, giving GBP72,000 of revenue.
Landed COGS is GBP54, so gross profit is GBP66 per unit and gross margin is 55%. Marketing spend of GBP18,000 brings in those 600 customers, so CAC is GBP30.

Fulfilment and payment costs add GBP12 per order, leaving GBP54 of contribution after fulfilment. After CAC, each order leaves GBP24, or GBP14,400 for the month.
Fixed overhead is GBP45,000, so net burn is GBP30,600. With GBP420,000 in the bank, runway is about 13.7 months. The first order more than recovers CAC.

Now suppose the same 600 sales were only achieved with a 20% discount, at GBP96. Gross profit falls to GBP42 per unit, margin drops to under 44%,
and after fulfilment and CAC each order leaves nothing at all. Revenue still looks healthy at GBP57,600, but net burn rises to GBP45,000 and runway shrinks to about nine months.

Illustrative figures from the example above, bars drawn to scale. The discount takes £24 off every order, exactly what was left after costs and CAC, so revenue still looks healthy while runway falls by more than four months.

A business with rising revenue but weak gross margin and poor payback may look busy while becoming more fragile. Investors usually see that contradiction quickly.

Growth is only good news if each extra sale leaves the business stronger than before it was made.

## Common reporting mistakes

**Reporting units shipped instead of revenue received.**
Shipments to a retailer on sale-or-return or long payment terms are not the same as cash.

**Gross margin on factory price.**
Margin should use landed cost, including freight, duty and packaging, or it will flatter the business.

**Blended CAC hiding paid CAC.**
Mixing organic and paid customers can make acquisition look cheaper than it will be once growth depends on paid channels.

**Quoting future COGS as current.**
Cost at scale is a target. Show it separately from the cost you are paying today.

**Ignoring stock in runway.**
A planned stock order can shorten runway sharply. Runway should reflect committed purchases, not just overhead.

## Practical next steps

- Calculate gross margin on landed cost and contribution after fulfilment for your current product.

- Separate paid and organic CAC, and check whether the first order recovers paid CAC.

- Build runway from a monthly cash model that includes stock orders, as set out in [calculating hardware startup cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html).

- Show current COGS next to target COGS, with the steps that close the gap.

- Tie the numbers back to the opportunity in [your hardware business case](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-business-case.html).

The [Investor Metrics and KPIs](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/investor-metrics-kpis.html) tool helps turn monthly sales, unit economics, burn, and acquisition assumptions into a clearer board-level or investor-facing view.
For margin by channel, the [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html) shows how route mix changes the picture.
If investors ask how the next stage of development, tooling and launch will be sequenced, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps set that out as a staged plan.

### Calculate the core KPI view

Model revenue, gross margin, CAC, payback, and runway in one place.[Open Investor Metrics Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/investor-metrics-kpis.html)

### Strengthen the underlying business case

If the KPI picture is weak, revisit the opportunity model and the unit economics before trying to improve the narrative.[Open Business Case Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/hardware-business-case-builder.html)

## FAQ

### What metrics do investors look for in a hardware startup?

Most start with monthly revenue, gross margin, customer acquisition cost, payback and runway. For hardware they also look closely at landed unit cost and the path to lower cost at scale, inventory levels, return rates and any repeat revenue from consumables or accessories.

### What gross margin do investors expect for hardware?

Expectations vary by category and channel, but many investors look for a credible path to gross margins of roughly 40 per cent or more on landed cost. Lower margins can work with strong repeat revenue or very efficient distribution, but they leave less room for mistakes.

### How do you calculate CAC payback for a one-off hardware purchase?

Divide the cost of acquiring a customer by the gross profit from their order after fulfilment costs. A result below one means the first order recovers the acquisition cost. Only include repeat purchases if you have evidence customers actually make them.

### What is a good LTV to CAC ratio?

A commonly quoted rule of thumb is a lifetime value of at least three times CAC. For one-off hardware purchases with little repeat business, lifetime value is close to first-order gross profit, so the more useful test is whether that first order clearly covers CAC.

### How is runway calculated for a hardware business?

Runway is cash in the bank divided by net monthly burn. For hardware, burn should include committed stock purchases and supplier deposits, not just overhead, because a single stock order can shorten runway by months.

Title: How to Turn RRP into Target COGS

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders and product teams setting a target cost from the retail price

# How to turn RRP into target COGS.

If you know the retail price the market can support, you can work backwards to the COGS the product needs.
The mistake is stopping too early and forgetting how much of that price gets consumed before profit appears.

Quick answer

## Target COGS is the amount left after VAT, route costs, hidden selling costs, and the margin the business needs to keep.

Target COGS = net selling price - channel deductions - selling costs - required margin

Start from the RRP, remove VAT, remove what the retailer or marketplace keeps, remove fulfilment, acquisition and returns costs, then remove the margin the business needs.
What remains is the most the product can cost to make and land. Working backwards like this gives founders and engineers a clearer cost target than treating the retail price as if it belongs to the factory.

Product teams often set a target retail price and then ask engineering to make the cost work. That only becomes useful once the target COGS is derived properly.
Retail price is not factory value. It has to absorb VAT, route-to-market fees, warehousing, packaging, logistics, selling costs, and the margin the business needs to keep.

**Practical rule:** target COGS is what is left after everyone else has been paid and the business still has a worthwhile margin.

## Contents

- Start with the money you do not keep

- A simple way to think about it

- Margin and markup are not the same

- Worked example: one RRP, three routes

- Why this matters for design teams

- Common mistakes when working back from RRP

- Practical next steps

## Start with the money you do not keep

|Cost layer |Typical examples |Why it matters |

|Tax and channel take |VAT, marketplace fees, retailer margin |This can remove a large share of the top line before operations even start |

|Operational selling cost |Warehousing, pick and pack, secondary packaging, outbound logistics |These costs rise with every unit sold |

|Commercial cost |Site and payment fees, paid acquisition, trade spend, account support |These are often split across teams and missed in the product economics |

|Business margin |The profit needed to fund growth, overhead, and future product work |If nothing is left here, the product is not commercially healthy |

## A simple way to think about it

- Remove VAT if the RRP includes it. UK consumer prices normally do, and the standard rate is 20%, so divide by 1.2.

- Remove the route-to-market share you do not keep.

- Remove the hidden selling and fulfilment costs attached to that route.

- Remove the margin the business needs to keep.

- What remains is the maximum landed COGS the product can afford.

## Margin and markup are not the same

Margin = (price - cost) / price. Markup = (price - cost) / cost.

A product that costs GBP50 and sells for GBP100 has a 50% margin but a 100% markup. Suppliers and retailers sometimes talk in different terms,
so confirm which one is meant before agreeing a number. Confusing the two is one of the quickest ways to set a cost target that is far too generous.

## Worked example: one RRP, three routes

Illustrative figures only. A home product has an RRP of GBP180 including VAT, so the net retail price is GBP150. The business wants to keep 30% of the revenue it actually receives
as margin to cover overhead and future development. Fees and costs below are plausible assumptions, not quotes. The marketplace commission here is charged on the VAT-inclusive price; the Target COGS tool applies its fee to the price before VAT, which leaves slightly more.

|
Step |
Direct to consumer |
Marketplace |
Retailer |

|
Net of VAT |
GBP150.00 |
GBP150.00 |
GBP150.00 |

|
Channel take |
None |
15% commission on GBP180: GBP27.00 |

|

GBP123.00 |

|

The same GBP180 product can afford about GBP62 of landed cost when sold direct, but under GBP50 through retail.
If the product is engineered to the direct-sales target and later needs to go into retail, it may need [cost-down](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html) work or redesign because the original cost target was based on the wrong commercial model.
Note too that direct sales only support the higher figure if acquisition cost stays under control. If paid acquisition doubles, the direct target falls sharply.

Illustrative figures from the table above, bars drawn to scale. The retailer's share is the largest single slice, so the same product has about £12 less to spend on making it than when sold direct.

Design to the cost target of the most demanding route you realistically expect to use, not the most generous one.

## Why this matters for design teams

- It sets a clearer brief for cost-down and design-for-manufacture work.

- It shows whether the route-to-market idea and the product architecture fit each other.

- It helps avoid late commercial surprises that force rushed redesign.

- It gives founders and engineers a shared number to design toward.

A target COGS can then be split into a budget for each major sub-assembly: enclosure, electronics, packaging, assembly labour. That turns a commercial number into engineering decisions
about part count, materials, finishes and supplier choice. The guide to [estimating manufacturing cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html) shows how to build the bottom-up figure to compare against it.

## Common mistakes when working back from RRP

**Forgetting VAT.**
Treating a VAT-inclusive RRP as revenue overstates what the business receives by a sixth at the standard rate.

**Comparing against ex-works price.**
Target COGS should be compared with landed cost: factory price plus freight, insurance, duty and packaging.

**Confusing margin and markup.**
A 50% markup is only a 33% margin. Mixing them up can hide a large gap.

**Leaving out acquisition cost for direct sales.**
Direct sales keep more of the price, but advertising and returns can absorb much of that advantage.

**Setting the target once.**
Fees, freight and channel terms change. Revisit the target at each major design review.

## Practical next steps

- Agree the realistic RRP range with evidence from comparable products.

- Decide which routes to market are likely in the first two years, and which is the most demanding.

- Work back to target landed COGS for each route using the [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) tool.

- Compare the target with a bottom-up estimate from the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html).

- If the gap is large, decide early whether to change the specification, the price or the route. The guide to [how route to market shapes product design and cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-hardware-product.html) covers that choice in more depth.

The [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) tool works backwards from RRP to the COGS ceiling for DTC, marketplace, and retailer routes.
The [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html) then shows what those assumptions mean at annual launch level once route mix and overhead are included.
Once the cost target is agreed, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps carry it into a staged development and launch plan.

## FAQ

### How do you calculate target COGS from RRP?

Remove VAT from the RRP, then subtract the channel's share, the selling and fulfilment costs for that route, and the margin the business needs to keep. The remainder is the maximum landed cost the product can carry. Repeat it for each route you expect to use.

### What is the difference between margin and markup?

Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. A product that costs GBP50 and sells for GBP100 has a 50% margin and a 100% markup.

### What percentage of RRP should COGS be?

It depends on the route, category and selling costs, so there is no single answer. A common rule of thumb for consumer products sold through retail is an RRP of roughly three to five times landed cost. Direct sales can support a higher share, provided acquisition and fulfilment costs are included.

### Should target COGS include freight and duty?

Yes. Compare the target with landed cost, which includes the factory price plus freight, insurance, import duty and packaging. Comparing against the ex-works factory price makes the product look cheaper than it really is.

### Does RRP include VAT in the UK?

Prices shown to UK consumers normally include VAT, which is 20% at the standard rate. Some products qualify for reduced or zero rates, so check the rate for your category before working back to a cost target.

Title: Choosing Between Concepts: Pugh Decision Matrix

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For design teams choosing which concept to develop

# How engineers choose between concepts.

Good concept selection is not about defending a favourite idea. It is about comparing options against the same criteria,
surfacing the real trade-offs, and deciding what needs to be de-risked next.

Quick answer

## Engineers choose between concepts by scoring each option against the same agreed, weighted criteria, then testing the assumptions behind the leader.

Concept decision = agreed criteria + honest weights + evidence-based scores + a plan to de-risk the leading option

A Pugh matrix or weighted scoring matrix makes the trade-offs visible. It does not make the decision for you: its real output is a shortlist
and a clear view of what still needs to be proven before more design effort is committed.

Teams rarely struggle because they have no ideas. They struggle because several ideas remain plausible at the same time and each stakeholder is weighting success differently.
The founder may be thinking about the customer, the engineer about technical risk, and the investor about unit cost. That is when a structured concept-selection matrix becomes useful.

**Better question:**
not “which concept wins?” but “which concept is strongest under the criteria we actually agree matter, and what evidence would change that answer?”

## Contents

- How concept selection works in practice

- What a strong decision matrix includes

- Typical criteria for a physical product

- Worked example: three concepts for a rechargeable bike light (illustrative)

- Common concept-selection mistakes

- What to do after the matrix

- Use weighted comparison to improve decision quality

## How concept selection works in practice

Most engineering teams use two passes. The first is **concept screening**, often done with a Pugh matrix: one concept, or an existing product,
is chosen as the reference (the datum), and every other concept is marked better (+), the same (0) or worse (−) against each criterion.
Screening is quick and is good at removing weak options and spotting strengths that could be combined.

The second pass is **concept scoring**. The remaining two to four concepts are rated on a scale, typically 1 to 5, and each criterion carries a weight
that reflects its importance to the project. Multiplying scores by weights gives a total that is easier to discuss, as long as everyone remembers that the precision is only as good as the inputs.

## What a strong decision matrix includes

- stable criteria used across every concept, agreed before anyone scores

- weights that reflect the real project priorities and add up to 100%

- scores grounded in evidence such as tests, quotes, user sessions or calculations, not just preference

- a note of the confidence behind each score, so weak evidence is visible

- a follow-up view of what the matrix does not yet know

## Typical criteria for a physical product

|
Criterion |
What it asks |
Evidence that supports a score |

|
User value |
How well does the concept solve the problem the customer actually has? |
User interviews, rough prototype trials, observed workarounds |

|
Technical feasibility |
Can it be made to work reliably with known technology? |
Calculations, rig tests, supplier data sheets |

|
Manufacturability |
Can it be made repeatably with sensible processes and tolerances? |
Early DFM review, supplier conversations, part count |

|
Unit cost |
Does the likely cost leave room for the target selling price? |
Rough BOM, process estimates, indicative quotes |

|
Development risk |
How many unknowns stand between the concept and a working product? |
Count of unproven functions, dependence on new suppliers or technology |

|
Compliance |
What standards or approvals will it need? |
Initial regulatory screen for safety, EMC, radio or food contact |

|
Lifetime and repair |
Will it last, and can it be serviced when parts wear? |
Wear-part analysis, fastening strategy, battery access |

Five to seven criteria is usually enough. More than that and the weights become thin, the scoring slows down, and criteria start to overlap.

## Worked example: three concepts for a rechargeable bike light (illustrative)

Imagine a startup with three concepts for a clip-on rechargeable rear bike light. Concept A is a sealed one-piece moulded housing with a built-in battery.
Concept B uses a two-part housing with a user-replaceable battery. Concept C puts a bought-in LED and battery module inside a simple custom shell.
The figures below are illustrative, not data from a real project.

|

|

|
**Weighted total** |
**3.55** |
**3.60** |
**3.75** |

On paper Concept C leads. But the totals sit within 0.2 of each other, which is well inside the uncertainty of the scores. A quick sensitivity check makes the point:
raise user value to 40% and drop unit cost to 10%, and Concept B moves to the top with 3.70 while A and C tie on 3.55.
The matrix is telling the team that the decision hinges on how much customers value brightness, mounting and battery life against price.

Illustrative scores from the table above. One reasonable change of weights reverses the order, so the matrix points to a test of what customers value rather than to a winner.

One concept might lead on customer value but lag on manufacturability. Another may be technically safer but commercially weaker.
The right response is often to identify the best de-risking experiment, not to declare the discussion over. Here, that might be a short [user test](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html)
with rough prototypes of B and C, plus an indicative quote for the bought-in module at the expected volumes.

## Common concept-selection mistakes

**Changing the criteria mid-discussion.** That usually means the team is trying to defend a preferred solution after the fact.

**Weighting everything highly.** If every criterion is critical, none of them are helping make the decision.

**Scoring as a group from the start.** The loudest voice anchors everyone else. Score individually first, then discuss the differences.

**Double counting.** Criteria such as “part count” and “assembly cost” often measure the same thing and quietly inflate one concept.

**Ignoring hybrids.** The best answer is often a combination, such as the low-risk electronics of one concept inside the better housing of another.

**Treating the output as final truth.** The matrix should guide the next test, not replace engineering judgement.

A concept matrix is most useful when it shows the team where it disagrees. The disagreement is usually where the next experiment belongs.

## What to do after the matrix

- Name the leading concept and a credible runner-up, so there is a fallback if testing goes badly.

- List the assumptions behind the leader’s highest scores, starting with the ones that carry the most weight.

- Design the cheapest test that could prove each assumption wrong: a rough prototype, a calculation, a [supplier quote](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) or a user session.

- Set a date to rescore with the new evidence, using the same criteria and weights.

- Record the decision and the reasoning, so later design changes can be traced back to it.

If the problem itself is still uncertain, step back before scoring concepts. The guide on
[how to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html) covers the evidence to collect first.

## Use weighted comparison to improve decision quality

The [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html) gives the team a visible way to compare concepts and adjust weights to see how robust the result is.
Pair it with the [Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html) if the chosen concept still needs structured development gates,
and read [Mapping the product design process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mapping-the-product-design-process.html) for how concept selection fits the wider project.
Once a direction is settled, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) can turn it into a staged plan with costs and milestones.

Run a weighted matrix so value, feasibility, manufacturability, and commercial logic are compared in one place.

### Map the next stage after selection

Use the process map if the winning concept now needs clearer planning rather than more debate.

## FAQ

### What is a Pugh matrix in product design?

A Pugh matrix compares several design concepts against a reference concept, called the datum, across a fixed set of criteria. Each concept is marked better, the same or worse than the datum for each criterion. It is a fast way to screen out weak options and spot strengths worth combining before more detailed scoring.

### How many concepts should you compare in a selection matrix?

Screening can handle a wider set, but detailed weighted scoring works best with around two to four serious concepts. Beyond that, the scoring takes longer than the insight it produces. Use quick screening to cut the list down first.

### How do you choose weights for concept selection criteria?

Agree the weights before scoring, based on what the project genuinely needs to succeed, and make sure they add up to 100%. A useful check is to ask which criterion you would sacrifice first if forced. Then test whether reasonable changes to the weights change the winner.

### What is the difference between concept screening and concept scoring?

Screening uses simple better, same or worse judgements against a reference to narrow a long list quickly. Scoring uses weighted numerical ratings on a short list to compare finalists in more detail. Most teams screen first and score second.

### What should you do if two concepts score almost the same?

Treat a close result as a sign that the evidence is not yet strong enough to separate them. Identify the criteria driving the difference and run a quick test, prototype or supplier enquiry to firm up those scores. Look for a hybrid that keeps the strengths of both.

Title: How Many Prototypes Do You Need?

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and teams planning prototype rounds, budgets and time

# How many prototypes do you need? Planning prototype rounds

Why the number of prototypes depends on the questions you need to answer, the typical rounds from rough models to pre-production samples, what makes a product need more, and how to keep prototyping fast and affordable.

Quick answer

## There is no fixed number: plan prototypes by the questions you need to answer, and build each one to answer a specific question as cheaply and quickly as possible.

Most physical products go through several rounds: rough models to explore ideas, looks-like and works-like prototypes to test appearance and function,
an integrated prototype that combines them, and pre-production samples made with production processes. Simple products may need few rounds; products with electronics,
safety requirements or tight fits usually need more (see [electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html)). Budget for at least one round more than you expect, because testing nearly always finds something.

## Plan by question, not by count

Each prototype should answer something you do not yet know: does the mechanism work, is it comfortable, will users understand it, does it fit together, will it survive a drop?
List the questions first, then group them into prototype rounds. The [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html) helps match questions to prototype types, and [usability testing a prototype](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html) explains how to answer the "will users understand it?" questions in each round.

## Typical prototype rounds

|
Round |
Answers |
Typical methods |

|
Sketch and rough models |
Size, form, basic idea, early user reactions |
Card, foam, quick 3D prints, existing parts |

|
Works-like |
Does the mechanism, electronics or function work? |
3D prints, machined parts, development boards, test rigs |

|
Looks-like |
Appearance, feel, size and user appeal |
Finished 3D prints or machined models, painted and assembled |

|
Integrated (looks-and-works-like) |
Do function and form fit together in one product? |
Higher-quality prints, machining, urethane casting, custom electronics |

|
Pre-production samples |
Can it be made, assembled and tested at volume, and does it pass certification? |
Production tooling and processes, pilot batches |

Each round may involve several iterations. See [prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html) for the methods in more detail, and [looks-like vs works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) for how to brief and combine those two streams. Where a round uses 3D printing, [choosing a 3D printing process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html) helps match filament, resin or powder printing to the question.

Each round answers its own question, and each may take several iterations. Works-like and looks-like prototypes are often built separately before being combined, and the cost of a round rises sharply towards production.

## What drives the number of rounds

- **Complexity:** moving parts, electronics, software and fluids each add questions.

- **Risk:** products that are safety-critical, worn on the body or used by children need more testing.

- **Novelty:** a new mechanism or use needs more learning than a variation on a known product.

- **Precision:** tight fits, seals and [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) often need iterations in the production material.

- **Certification:** formal testing may need units made exactly like production.

- **Evidence needed:** investors, [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) or retailers may need a convincing looks-like model earlier.

**Practical rule:**
test the riskiest question first, with the cheapest prototype that can answer it. A rough model that kills a bad idea in a week is worth more than a beautiful model of the wrong product.

## Budget and time

Prototype costs rise sharply through the rounds: rough models are cheap, integrated prototypes and pre-production samples cost far more, and changes after tooling are the most expensive.
Plan time for testing and changes between rounds, not just building. Ending each round with a short [design review](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html) turns what the prototype showed into recorded decisions before the next one is built. Add prototype rounds to your plan with the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html)
and budget them in the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html).

## Common mistakes

**Polishing too early.**
High-quality models of an untested idea cost time and money and make change feel harder.

**Combining everything too soon.**
An integrated prototype that fails is harder to diagnose than separate works-like and looks-like tests.

**Building without a test plan.**
A prototype without defined tests answers nothing; plan them with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

**Budgeting for one perfect round.**
Testing almost always leads to changes; plan for iterations.

## Next steps

- List the questions your product must answer, riskiest first.

- Choose prototype types with the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html).

- Plan tests for each round with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Add rounds and time to the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html).

Match what you need to learn to the right type of prototype.
[Open Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html)

### Plan the timeline

Add prototype rounds, testing and changes to your schedule.
[Open Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html)

## FAQ

### How many prototypes does a product need?

There is no fixed number. Most physical products go through several rounds, from rough models to works-like, looks-like, integrated and pre-production samples, each with its own iterations. Complexity, risk, novelty and certification drive how many.

### What is the difference between looks-like and works-like prototypes?

A looks-like prototype shows appearance, size and feel without necessarily working. A works-like prototype proves the function, mechanism or electronics without necessarily looking right. They are often built separately before being combined.

### Which prototype should I build first?

The cheapest one that answers your riskiest question. If the main risk is whether the mechanism works, start with a works-like rig; if it is whether people want it, a rough model or looks-like prototype may come first.

### When should I stop prototyping?

When the integrated design meets its requirements, passes its tests and has been checked with production processes in pre-production samples. Moving to tooling earlier risks expensive changes.

### How do I keep prototyping costs down?

Test one question at a time with the simplest prototype that can answer it, use quick and cheap methods early, avoid polishing untested ideas, and plan tests before building.

Title: How to Estimate Manufacturing Cost

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders, engineers and product leads setting a first realistic cost target

# How to estimate manufacturing cost for a hardware product

Early cost work is rarely about finding the exact number. It is about building a cost structure that is accurate enough
to guide the product architecture, route to market, and target price before expensive assumptions spread through the project.

**Topic**
Bottom-up product costing

**Audience**
Founders, engineers, and product leads

**Tool**
Product Cost Estimator

**Use it for**
Setting a first realistic COGS target

Quick answer

## Manufacturing cost is more than materials and process.

COGS = materials + bought-in parts + process + labour + packaging + scrap + overhead

To estimate it, build the cost bottom-up from the bill of materials at the volume you expect to order, add assembly time, packaging, a scrap allowance and overhead,
then spread tooling over the units it will make and add freight and duty to get a landed cost.
If one of those terms is missing, the estimate is probably too low and the commercial model built on top of it will be fragile.

Many early hardware cost estimates look neat because they are incomplete. The team prices the obvious physical part,
then mistakes that for a product cost. A working estimate needs to include the recurring cost of making the product repeatedly, not just the raw geometry.

**Practical rule:**
cost the product at the level you expect to build and ship it, not the level you first imagine it in CAD.

## Contents

- The seven blocks that usually matter first

- Two more lines: tooling and landed cost

- A step-by-step method

- Typical allowances and how to treat them

- A simple worked example

- Common mistakes: where teams usually under-price the product

- Why this matters before pricing

- Next steps

## The seven blocks that usually matter first

- **Raw materials:** resin, metal, fabric, or other base material directly consumed.

- **Bought-in parts:** electronics, fasteners, seals, inserts, packaging inserts, and other purchased components.

- **Process cost:** moulding, machining, printing, cutting, finishing, or external conversion work.

- **Assembly labour:** manual assembly, test steps, inspection, and packing effort.

- **Packaging:** [retail packaging](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html), shipping cartons, instructions, labels, and secondary packing.

- **Scrap and rework:** process losses, cosmetic rejects, yield loss, or damaged components.

- **Overhead:** factory burden, quality support, management time, and operating costs absorbed into production.

## Two more lines: tooling and landed cost

The seven blocks give the recurring cost of building one unit. Two further lines decide what each unit really costs the business.

-
**Tooling amortisation.** Moulds, press tools, fixtures and test jigs are one-off costs, but they exist only to make the product.
Dividing the tooling cost by the number of units you expect it to produce gives a per-unit figure to carry alongside COGS. Keep it as a separate line so you can see how it changes with volume.

-
**Landed cost.** A price quoted ex-works or free on board stops at the factory or the port. Freight, insurance, customs clearance, import duty and delivery to your warehouse all come on top.
For a VAT-registered business, import VAT is usually reclaimable and so is normally left out of unit cost, but check this with your accountant.
[Landed cost: freight, duty and import VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) covers this in detail.

Unit cost to the business = COGS + (tooling ÷ units the tooling will make) + landed-cost additions per unit

Development, certification and design fees are also real costs, but they are not usually part of unit cost. Plan them separately as project costs; the guide to
[estimating hardware development costs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html) covers them.

## A step-by-step method

- **Fix the volume and the version.** State the order quantity and the configuration you are costing. Prices for 500 units and 10,000 units can be very different.

- **Build a bill of materials.** List every part, including fasteners, labels, adhesives and packaging, with quantity per product. The [BOM Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html) gives a structure to start from.

- **Cost each made part.** Material is mass × price per kilogram, plus an allowance for runners, offcuts or swarf. Process cost is usually machine rate × cycle time ÷ parts per cycle, plus any finishing.

- **Price bought-in parts at your volume.** Use distributor price breaks or supplier quotes for the quantity you will actually order, and note any minimum order quantities.

- **Estimate assembly, test and pack time.** Multiply minutes per unit by a fully loaded labour rate. The [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) helps break the build into steps.

- **Add packaging, scrap and overhead.** Apply scrap as a percentage of direct cost, then overhead as a loading, and state both assumptions.

- **Add tooling and landed cost.** Spread tooling over a realistic volume and add freight and duty per unit.

- **Run a low and high case.** A single number hides uncertainty. A range shows where to spend effort firming up quotes.

## Typical allowances and how to treat them

The figures below are broad, hedged starting points for an early model, not benchmarks. Replace them with supplier figures as soon as you have them.

|
Line |
Early-model starting point |
What moves it |

|
Scrap and rework |
Often a few per cent for a mature process; more for new processes, cosmetic parts or first runs |
Process maturity, cosmetic standard, tolerance demands, handling damage |

|
Overhead |
A percentage loading, commonly in the tens of per cent, or already built into a supplier's rate |
Whether you build in-house or buy finished units; check quotes so overhead is not counted twice |

|
Material waste |
A small allowance for runners and purging in moulding; more for machining from solid |
Process route, hot or cold runners, part nesting |

|
Bought-in parts |
Distributor price at your order quantity |
Volume, lead time, minimum order quantities, currency |

|
Overall estimate accuracy |
At concept stage, treat the total as uncertain by perhaps a third either way |
Narrows as the design freezes and real quotes replace assumptions |

## A simple worked example

Illustrative figures only. Imagine a small consumer device with £4.80 of material, £2.40 of process cost, £5.50 of bought-in parts,
£4.80 of labour (12 minutes at an assumed fully loaded rate of £24 an hour), and £1.20 of packaging. Before scrap or overhead, the direct build cost is £18.70.

Add a 6% scrap allowance (£1.12) to reach £19.82, then a 14% overhead loading on that (£2.77), and the fully loaded COGS becomes £22.59.
That is the figure the commercial model should be tested against, not the £12 to £15 number that a partial estimate of material, process and bought-in parts (£12.70) might suggest.

Now add the lines that sit outside COGS. An assumed £12,000 of tooling spread over a planned 10,000 units adds £1.20, giving £23.79.
If the product is made overseas and freight, insurance, clearance and duty together add an assumed £1.60 per unit, the landed unit cost is £25.39, roughly double the partial estimate.

|
Line |
Per unit |
Running total |

|

£12.70 |
£12.70 |

|
Labour + packaging |
£6.00 |
£18.70 |

|

£1.12 |

|

|

£1.60 |
