Illustrative figures from the worked example, drawn to scale. Each line the partial estimate leaves out adds to the unit cost, and the landed cost ends up roughly double the £12.70 that material, process and bought-in parts alone suggest.

Two quick sensitivity checks show where the effort should go:

- **Volume:** if only 2,000 units sell, the same tool adds £6.00 a unit instead of £1.20, and the landed cost rises to £30.19.

- **Assembly time:** cutting the build from 12 to 8 minutes saves £1.60 of labour, or about £1.93 once scrap and overhead are applied, which is around £19,300 over 10,000 units.

## Common mistakes: where teams usually under-price the product

**Bought-in parts are missing.**
The estimate focuses on the moulded or machined enclosure and forgets the electronics, fasteners, inserts, or accessories.

**Assembly is treated as free.**
Even a short manual build time compounds quickly at scale, especially when reorientation, test, or inspection are required.

**Scrap is set to zero.**
Real processes waste material, parts, or labour. Early models should acknowledge that instead of pretending perfect yield.

**Packaging is added too late.**
Secondary packaging, instructions, labels, and pack-out often arrive after the selling price has already been discussed.

**Tooling is left out or spread too thinly.**
Amortising a tool over a volume you have not yet sold makes the unit cost look better than the cash position will feel.

**Prices from different volumes are mixed.**
Using a 10,000-unit component price with a 500-unit first order understates what the first batch will cost.

**Ex-works prices are treated as landed.**
Freight, duty and clearance can add a noticeable share to the unit cost, especially for bulky or low-value products.

**Currency is fixed.**
If parts or assembly are bought in another currency, test the estimate at a less favourable exchange rate.

## Why this matters before pricing

Route-to-market decisions, gross-margin targets, and retail pricing all depend on a credible product cost.
If the cost model is weak, the business case will only look healthy because the wrong number is holding it up.

The best sequence is usually:

- estimate the build cost bottom-up

- check break-even and cash-flow pressure

- work backwards from the route to market into target COGS

[How to price a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-price-a-physical-product.html) picks up from here, and
[when injection moulding becomes cheaper](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) helps decide whether tooling is justified at your volume.

## Next steps

- List every part in the [BOM Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html), including packaging and fasteners.

- Turn it into a loaded unit cost with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html), stating your scrap and overhead assumptions.

- Estimate build time with the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) if labour is more than a small share of the total.

- Check whether tooling pays back at your volume with the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

- Add freight and duty with the [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html) if you are importing.

- Replace the largest assumptions with supplier quotes first; [how to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html) explains how to ask for comparable quotes.

- If the product is already in production and costs too much, use the breakdown to rank changes with [reducing the cost of an existing product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html).

For the wider picture of processes and cost, see the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

If the number still changes wildly between scenarios, the project probably needs more design or supplier clarity before pricing discussions become meaningful.

## FAQ

### What is usually missing from an early manufacturing cost estimate?

Bought-in parts, packaging, scrap, labour burden, and overhead are among the most common omissions.

### Should retail price be set before product cost is understood?

No. Product cost should be understood well enough first that the margin model and route-to-market discussion are based on something credible.

### How do you calculate the cost per unit of a product?

Add the cost of materials, bought-in parts, processing, assembly labour and packaging for one unit, add a scrap allowance and an overhead loading, then add tooling divided by the units it will make and any freight and duty per unit. Always state the order volume the figure applies to.

### Should tooling cost be included in the unit cost?

Keep it as a separate line next to COGS. Divide the tooling cost by a realistic number of units the tool will make, and check the result at a lower volume too, because tooling is paid for up front whether or not the units sell.

### How accurate does an early manufacturing cost estimate need to be?

Accurate enough to make decisions, not to quote from. At concept stage it is sensible to treat the total as uncertain by perhaps a third either way and to show a low and high case. The range should narrow as the design freezes and supplier quotes replace assumptions.

Title: How to Find and Brief a Manufacturer

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams looking for their first manufacturer or comparing suppliers

# How to find and brief a manufacturer, in the UK or overseas

How to find the right manufacturer for a physical product and brief them well: the types of supplier, where to look, what to check, what to send, and how to compare quotes fairly once delivery terms, freight, duty and minimum orders are included.

Quick answer

## Find the right type of manufacturer, brief them with a complete pack, and compare quotes on landed cost and risk, not unit price.

Decide whether you need a specialist part supplier, a contract manufacturer that assembles the whole product, or a design-and-make partner.
Build a shortlist through referrals, trade directories and trade shows, then send each the same request for quotation: drawings and CAD, quantities, target cost,
quality and compliance requirements, packaging and delivery terms. Compare the replies like for like, including tooling, minimum order quantities, payment terms,
freight, duty and lead time, and meet or audit the finalists before committing.

- Where to find manufacturers

## Which kind of manufacturer do you need?

|
Type |
What they do |
Suits |

|
Specialist process supplier |
Makes parts by one process: moulding, machining, [sheet metal](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html), casting, [PCB](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) assembly |
Teams that will manage assembly themselves or through another partner |

|
Contract manufacturer |
Sources parts, assembles, tests and packs the finished product to your design |
Products with several parts and processes; teams without their own production |

|
Electronics manufacturing services (EMS) |
Contract manufacturing focused on circuit boards and electronic products |
Products where the electronics are the main manufacturing challenge |

|
Design-and-make (ODM) partner |
Develops and manufactures a product, often adapting an existing design |
Speed and lower development cost, at the price of less control and ownership |

|
Sourcing agent or trading company |
Finds and manages factories for you, usually overseas |
Teams without the time or language to manage factories directly; check who owns the relationship |

## Where to find manufacturers

- **Referrals:** other founders, product designers, component distributors and your existing suppliers usually know who is good at what.

- **Trade bodies and directories:** national and regional manufacturing associations, industry directories and economic development agencies such as [Invest NI](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-routes-uk-northern-ireland.html) in Northern Ireland.

- **Trade shows:** subcontract manufacturing and sector shows let you meet many suppliers and see sample work.

- **Online sourcing platforms:** useful for overseas suppliers, but verify that you are dealing with the factory, not just a reseller.

- **The products you admire:** markings, teardowns and published case studies can point to the suppliers behind similar products.

## Shortlisting: what to check

|
Check |
What good looks like |

|
Relevant experience |
Similar size, materials, processes and quality level; examples they can show |

|
Fit with your volumes |
Your quantities matter to them; [minimum order quantities](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) you can afford |

|
Quality system |
Documented inspection, traceability and corrective action; certification such as ISO 9001 where relevant |

|
Engineering support |
A design-for-manufacture review with useful suggestions, not just a price |

|
Communication |
Clear, prompt answers from someone technical; a named contact |

|
Commercial terms |
Clear tooling ownership, payment terms, lead times and what happens when parts are rejected |

|
Stability |
A business that will still be there for your second and tenth order |

## Briefing: the request for quotation

A good brief gets better quotes faster and shows the supplier you are worth taking seriously. Send every supplier the same pack so the replies can be compared:

- 3D CAD and [2D drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) with materials, finishes, critical dimensions and tolerances

- quantities: first order, expected annual volume and how it may grow

- a target price or cost range, if you have one

- quality requirements: inspection, acceptance criteria, cosmetic standards

- compliance needs: marking, test reports, material declarations

- packaging, labelling and delivery requirements, including the delivery terms you want quoted

- timeline: when you need samples and first production

- what you want them to propose: process suggestions, design changes, alternative materials

[The documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) covers each item in detail,
and [how to protect product IP](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) explains what to have in place before you share it.

**Practical rule:**
tell suppliers the truth about volumes. Inflated forecasts get you a price you will not see in practice and a relationship that sours when the orders do not arrive.

## Comparing quotes like for like

Quotes arrive in different shapes. Before comparing, put them on the same basis. Delivery terms matter most: the internationally used Incoterms rules
(published by the [International Chamber of Commerce](https://iccwbo.org/business-solutions/incoterms-rules/))
define who pays for what. "EXW" (ex works) means you collect from the factory and pay everything after that; "FOB" (free on board) means the supplier pays to get goods onto the ship;
"DDP" (delivered duty paid) means the supplier delivers to you with duty paid.

Illustrative figures only. A team receives three quotes for 2,000 units of an assembled product. Freight, duty and inspection costs are planning assumptions;
check duty rates for your product code on the [UK Trade Tariff](https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff). Import VAT is left out because a VAT-registered business can normally reclaim it.

|
|
UK supplier |
Overseas supplier A |
Overseas supplier B |

|
Quoted price per unit |
£8.40 delivered |
£4.90 FOB |
£4.20 EXW |

|
Freight and insurance per unit |
Included |
£0.65 |
£0.85 (including inland transport to port) |

|
Duty per unit (assumed 4% of price plus freight and insurance) |
None |
£0.22 |
£0.20 |

|
Customs clearance and handling per unit |
None |
£0.15 |
£0.15 |

|
Pre-shipment inspection per unit |
None |
£0.20 |
£0.20 |

|
Landed cost per unit |
£8.40 |
£6.12 |
£5.60 |

|
Minimum order and lead time |
500 units, 3 weeks |
2,000 units, 8 weeks plus 5 to 6 weeks shipping |
5,000 units, 10 weeks plus shipping |

Supplier B looks cheapest, but its minimum order is two and a half times the planned quantity, so the real cash commitment is far higher.
Supplier A saves about £2.28 a unit against the UK quote, or about £4,560 on this order, but ties up cash for roughly two to three months longer and makes design changes slower.
A reasonable plan might start with the UK supplier for the first batches, then move volume overseas once the design and demand are stable. The right answer depends on cash, volumes and risk, not just the per-unit figure.
[Getting and comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) adds tooling ownership, payment timing and the cash each quote needs.

## UK or overseas?

|
Factor |
UK and nearby |
Further overseas |

|
Unit price |
Often higher |
Often lower, before freight, duty and inspection |

|
Lead time and stock in transit |
Shorter; less cash tied up |
Longer; more stock and cash in the pipeline |

|
Minimum order quantities |
Often more flexible |
Often larger |

|
Communication and visits |
Easier, same time zone and language |
Harder; needs planning or local support |

|
Design changes and problem solving |
Faster |
Slower and more costly to iterate |

|
Supply chain depth |
Varies by process |
Very deep for some sectors, such as electronics |

Importing brings customs and duty obligations; GOV.UK's [guidance on importing goods into the UK](https://www.gov.uk/import-goods-into-uk) is the starting point.

## Before you commit

- **Get samples** of their work, and of your own part once tooling exists.

- **Visit or audit** the factory, in person or through a third-party inspection company.

- **Agree the quality plan:** inspection points, acceptance criteria, a signed-off [golden sample](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html) and first-article inspection.

- **Put the terms in writing:** prices, payment schedule, lead times, tooling ownership, warranty and what happens with rejected parts. [Supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html) lists what to cover.

- **Start small:** a pilot batch tests the relationship before large orders. [Planning a pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) covers what to measure and agree in advance.

## Red flags

**A price far below every other quote.**
Usually a misunderstanding of the specification, or costs that will appear later.

**No questions about your design.**
Good manufacturers ask; silence often means they have not looked closely.

**Reluctance to put tooling ownership in writing.**
It can leave your tools, and your product, tied to one supplier.

**Full payment up front with no samples.**
Deposits are normal; paying everything before seeing parts is a large risk.

**Unclear who actually makes the product.**
A trading company presenting itself as the factory can hide quality and IP risks.

## FAQ

### How do I find a manufacturer for my product?

Decide first whether you need a specialist part supplier, a contract manufacturer or a design-and-make partner. Then use referrals from designers and other founders, trade bodies and directories, regional agencies such as Invest NI, trade shows and, for overseas suppliers, sourcing platforms, verifying that you are dealing with the actual factory.

### What should I send a manufacturer to get a quote?

CAD and drawings with materials, finishes and critical tolerances, realistic quantities for the first order and per year, quality and compliance requirements, packaging and delivery terms, a timeline, and a target cost if you have one. Send every supplier the same pack so the quotes can be compared.

### What do EXW, FOB and DDP mean on a quote?

They are Incoterms rules that define who pays for transport, insurance and duty. EXW (ex works) means you take responsibility from the factory door; FOB (free on board) means the supplier pays to load the goods onto the ship; DDP (delivered duty paid) means the supplier delivers to your premises with duty paid.

### Is it cheaper to manufacture overseas?

The unit price is often lower, but freight, duty, inspection, larger minimum orders, longer lead times and slower design changes all add cost or cash requirements. Compare landed cost and the cash tied up, not just the factory price; for early, changing products a nearby supplier can be cheaper overall.

### How do I check a manufacturer is reliable?

Ask for examples of similar work and references, review their quality system, request samples, visit or commission a third-party audit, and start with a pilot batch. Make sure tooling ownership, payment terms and rejection procedures are agreed in writing.

Title: How to Price a Physical Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams setting a launch price for a physical product

# How to price a physical product: value, competitors, margins and testing

A practical method for pricing a physical product: start from the value to customers and their alternatives, check comparable products, work out the price floor from costs and margins, and test the price before committing to it.

Quick answer

## Price from the value to the customer and their alternatives, then check that cost and every margin in the chain still work at that price.

Ceiling = what customers will pay, given their alternatives
Floor = landed cost ÷ (1 − your margin) ÷ (1 − channel margins) × (1 + VAT)
A viable price sits between the floor and the ceiling

Cost-plus pricing on its own tends to under-price good products and over-price weak ones. Start with what the product is worth to the buyer and what they pay today to solve the problem,
look at comparable products, then work through the margins your route to market needs. If the floor is above the ceiling, change the cost, the channel or the product before launching.

## Three ways to think about price

|
Approach |
How it works |
Strength |
Weakness |

|
Cost-plus |
Add a standard markup to the unit cost |
Simple; guarantees a margin on paper |
Ignores what customers will pay and what competitors charge |

|
Competitor-based |
Position against similar products |
Grounded in what buyers already accept |
Copies others' assumptions; weak if your product is genuinely different |

|
Value-based |
Price from the benefit to the customer and the cost of their alternative |
Captures the value you create |
Needs evidence about customers; harder to estimate |

In practice the best answer uses all three: value and competitors set the ceiling, cost and margins set the floor.

## Step 1: understand the value and the alternatives

- **What does the customer do today?** The current workaround, and what it costs in money, time or frustration, is the real reference point.

- **What is the benefit worth?** Time saved, cost avoided, risk reduced, enjoyment or status gained. For business buyers, this is often measurable.

- **Who decides and who pays?** A gift buyer, a parent, or a purchasing department each weigh price differently.

[How to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html) covers how to gather this evidence.

## Step 2: look at comparable products

List the products customers will compare yours with, including indirect alternatives, and note their prices, features, reviews and where they are sold.
Decide deliberately where you sit: cheaper with fewer features, similar with a clear advantage, or premium with a reason customers can see.

## Step 3: work out the floor

The floor is the lowest shelf price at which everyone in the chain earns their margin. Start from the landed unit cost, add your margin, then the margins of any distributor and retailer,
then VAT. The [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html) calculates this, and
[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) works the other way, from a price down to the cost you can afford.

Illustrative figures only. A product lands at £8.00 a unit. Selling to a retailer that wants a 45% margin, with the brand keeping 50%, the shelf price needs to be about £34.91 including VAT.
Comparable products sell for £29.99 to £39.99, and interviews suggest buyers value the time it saves highly, so £39.99 is credible and leaves about £5 of headroom.
Through a distributor taking 30% as well, the floor rises to about £41.56 at a 40% brand margin, above the comparable range: that route would need a lower landed cost or a lower margin somewhere.

Illustrative figures from the example above, on one price scale. Through a retailer the floor sits inside the range buyers already accept, so £39.99 works; adding a distributor pushes the floor above that range, even with the brand's margin cut to 40%.

## Step 4: check the business still works

A price that covers margins can still fail if volumes are too low to recover fixed costs. Check break-even with the
[Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html) and the overall picture with the
[Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html). Leave room for promotions, returns and marketing, which come out of someone's margin.

## Step 5: test before you commit

- **Pre-orders or a small batch** at the intended price are the strongest evidence.

- **A landing page with the price shown** measures interest at a price, not just interest in the idea.

- **Conversations with retailers or distributors** reveal what they believe the product can sell for in their channel.

**Practical rule:**
it is far easier to lower a launch price than to raise it. If you are unsure, start at the higher end of a credible range and use offers, bundles or a second model to reach lower price points.

## Keeping prices consistent across channels

If you sell both direct and through retailers, set prices so every channel works. Undercutting your retailers on your own website damages the relationship;
many brands keep the same recommended price everywhere and compete on service, bundles or exclusives instead. See
[Route to market and margins](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html).

## Common mistakes

**Pricing from cost alone.**
You may leave money on the table, or price a product nobody values at that level.

**Forgetting channel margins and VAT.**
The shelf price is often several times the landed cost once everyone is paid.

**Pricing for launch, not for scale.**
A direct-only price may not survive the move into retail.

**Asking people what they would pay.**
Stated willingness to pay is unreliable; test with real offers.

**No room for promotions.**
Discounts and offers are part of retail; plan for them in the margin.

## Next steps

- List the alternatives and comparable products, with their prices.

- Build the floor with the [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html).

- Check the target cost with [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html).

- Check break-even with the [Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html).

- Test the price with pre-orders or a small batch.

### Build the price ladder

From landed cost through every margin to the shelf price.
[Open Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html)

### Work back to a target cost

From a shelf price to what the product can cost to make.
[Open Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html)

[Route to market and margins: the hub guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html)

[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html)

[Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html)

Related guides

[Turn RRP into target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html)

[Why route to market matters](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-hardware-product.html)

[Validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html)

This guide answers

Pricing
Margins
Value
Competitors

## FAQ

### How do I price a physical product?

Start with the value to the customer and the price of their alternatives to find the ceiling, then work out the floor from landed cost plus your margin, channel margins and VAT. A viable price sits between the two; test it with pre-orders or a small batch before committing.

### What markup should I use on a product?

There is no single right markup, because channel margins and costs differ by product and route. Work out the margins each party needs as a share of their selling price; selling through retail commonly requires a shelf price several times the landed cost.

### Should I price lower to win customers at launch?

Usually not by default. It is much easier to lower a price than to raise it, and a low launch price can leave too little margin for retail later. Use time-limited offers or bundles instead of a permanently low price.

### How do I know if my price is too high?

Test it: pre-orders, a landing page showing the price, or a small batch will show whether people buy. Compare with what customers pay for alternatives. Stated willingness to pay in surveys is a weak signal.

### Should my website price match retail prices?

Many brands keep the same recommended price across channels to protect retailer relationships, and compete on service, bundles or exclusives rather than undercutting their own retailers.

Title: Protect Product IP Before Manufacturing

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders about to share designs with manufacturers or partners

# How to protect product IP before talking to manufacturers

Protecting product IP is not just a legal document exercise. It is a practical operating discipline:
decide what is sensitive, disclose it in stages, control the files properly, and make ownership explicit before work starts.

**Topic**
IP and supplier readiness

**Audience**
Founders and hardware teams

**Tool**
NDA Generator

**Use it for**
Early supplier conversations

Quick answer

## An NDA helps, but IP protection is a system rather than a single document.

IP protection = staged disclosure + file control + supplier due diligence + clear ownership + appropriate agreements

The risk is usually not one dramatic act of theft. It is a series of avoidable habits:
sending too much too early, sharing uncontrolled files, and leaving ownership vague when outside parties contribute design work.

If any part of the product might be patentable, decide on filing before you share it outside a confidential circle: in general an invention must be new when the patent application is filed,
and public disclosure first can prevent a valid patent. This guide is general information, not legal advice; have agreements reviewed by a solicitor, and take patent and design questions to a registered patent attorney.
[Design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html) explains the options.

Early supplier conversations are necessary. They are often how teams learn what is manufacturable, what looks expensive, and what needs to change.
But “talk to manufacturers” should not mean “email the whole design pack and hope for the best.” The goal is to share enough information
to get useful feedback while keeping control of what actually matters.

**Practical rule:**
only release the information needed for the current decision. If the supplier does not need the full pack yet, do not send the full pack yet.

## What usually needs protecting

- product architecture, CAD, drawings, and toleranced details

- firmware, electronics choices, and test methods

- BOM structure, supplier relationships, and costing assumptions

- commercial plans, customer data, pricing logic, and launch timing

- know-how that sits in process detail rather than in a patent filing

## What an NDA does and does not do

|
NDA helps with |
NDA does not fix |

|
Setting confidentiality expectations early |
Over-sharing information the supplier does not need |

|
Defining the basic scope of confidential material |
Poor file control or weak revision discipline |

|
Supporting a professional conversation with a new partner |
Unclear ownership of design work created during development |

|
Making disclosure feel structured rather than casual |
Choosing the wrong supplier or asking the wrong questions |

## The common ways teams leak IP by accident

**Full file packs go out too early.**
A supplier asked for a rough feasibility comment does not usually need every CAD model, drawing, and sourcing note.

**Revision control is poor.**
Once multiple versions are circulating, teams lose track of who has what and what the current truth actually is.

**Ownership of contributed design work is assumed, not written down.**
If a supplier changes the design, tooling, or process, the contract must be clear about what belongs to whom.

## Worked example: the difference between careless and controlled disclosure

A startup wants feedback on a plastic enclosure. In the careless version, it emails the full CAD assembly, internal layouts,
BOM notes, and commercial forecast to several suppliers at once. In the controlled version, it first sends a short scope note,
external renders, key dimensions, target volume, and the specific questions it needs answered. Only after the shortlist is clearer,
and confidentiality has been addressed, does the team release the deeper geometry and cost-sensitive detail. The second approach tends to produce better conversations,
not slower ones, because the supplier receives a clearer brief and the team stays in control.

The controlled route still starts the conversation early, but each supplier only sees what the current decision needs, and the sensitive detail goes out once there is a shortlist and confidentiality in place.

## A practical release sequence before supplier engagement

- Define what is confidential and what can be shared more freely.

- Prepare a clean summary pack for first conversations: scope, stage, target volumes, and the questions you need answered.

- Use an NDA where it is appropriate for the sensitivity and stage of discussion.

- Release deeper files in stages as the conversation becomes more serious and more specific.

- Track exactly which version of which files went to which party.

- Make ownership explicit if the supplier, contractor, or consultant is contributing design work.

Good IP protection does not block supplier conversations. It makes those conversations more intentional, more professional, and easier to manage.

## When the supplier is doing design work too

The risk increases once external parties are not just quoting manufacture but actively changing geometry, optimising tools, selecting components,
or contributing engineering detail. At that point, confidentiality is only one part of the job. The agreement also needs to state
who owns the resulting design changes, tooling data, manufacturing know-how, and any project-specific deliverables created during the engagement.
[Supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html) covers this alongside the other terms to agree before production.

## Protecting IP still requires a good document pack

Strong IP discipline and strong supplier preparation sit together. If you need help deciding what belongs in the first supplier pack,
read
[Must-have documents before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html).
The best conversations happen when the brief is clear and the disclosure is deliberate.

### Generate a cleaner NDA draft

Use the NDA Generator as a structured starting point for one-way or mutual confidentiality discussions.
[Open NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html)

### Prepare the supplier pack next

Once confidentiality is framed properly, tighten the files, scope notes, and open questions you send to suppliers.

[Read Document Guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html)
[Open Cost Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html)

## Need help preparing a supplier conversation without over-sharing?

Orion Design can help frame the technical pack, decide what to share at each stage, and make the manufacturer conversation clearer before sensitive detail goes out. Legal agreements and IP filings still need a solicitor or patent attorney.

Review prompt

If you cannot explain why each file is being shared, you are probably sharing too much too early.

## FAQ

### Is an NDA enough to protect product IP?

No. An NDA helps set confidentiality expectations, but strong protection also depends on staged disclosure, file control, supplier due diligence, and explicit ownership terms.

### What should you send a manufacturer first?

Start with the minimum information needed for the current discussion: product scope, high-level visuals or geometry, target volumes, and the specific questions you need answered.

### How do hardware teams usually leak IP by accident?

They send full CAD packs too early, lose [revision control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html), assume ownership is obvious when external design work is added, and share sensitive detail without a clear commercial purpose.

Title: How to Validate a Product Idea

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 10 September 2026 · For first-time founders deciding whether an idea deserves investment

# How to validate a product idea before you build it

Product idea validation is not about collecting polite encouragement. It is about finding out, early and honestly,
whether a real customer problem exists, whether the buyer cares enough to switch or pay, and whether the team can deliver the answer credibly.

**Topic**
Idea validation

**Audience**
Founders and hardware teams

**Tool**
Product Purpose Framework

**Use it for**
Early concept review

Quick answer

## A validated idea has evidence behind the problem, the buyer, and the route to delivery.

Strong idea = real problem + specific buyer + reason to switch + viable route to build and support

If the team cannot show who needs the product, why current alternatives are failing, and what makes the offer believable,
the idea is not ready for expensive development.

Teams often move too fast from enthusiasm into specification. Someone sketches a product, a few people say it sounds useful,
and suddenly the conversation is about CAD, tooling, apps, and packaging. That is backwards. Before the detail work starts,
the team needs to prove that the opportunity is strong enough to deserve it.

**Validation is not the search for approval.**
It is the search for disconfirming evidence early enough to save time, cash, and attention if the idea is weaker than it first appears.

## What product idea validation is really testing

|
Test |
What good evidence looks like |
Warning sign |

|
Problem strength |
People describe the pain clearly, repeatedly, and with consequences |
The problem sounds nice to solve, but not urgent |

|
Buyer clarity |
You know who decides, who pays, and who uses the product |
The target user is broad or vague |

|
Willingness to switch or pay |
There is evidence of current spend, workaround pain, or budget |
Interest disappears when price or effort becomes real |

|
Delivery credibility |
The product can be built, supplied, and supported without breaking the value proposition |
The concept only works if key risks are ignored |

## What weak validation usually looks like

**Friends like it.**
Friendly reactions do not equal customer evidence, especially when no trade-off has been asked of them.

**The problem is described in solution language.**
If the pitch starts with features before the underlying pain is clear, the team may be validating a concept, not a need.

**The economics are treated as someone else’s problem.**
A product that looks exciting but needs an impossible selling price or support burden is not validated.

## Worked example: polite enthusiasm versus real evidence

Imagine a team developing a premium countertop food-waste appliance. Early conversations sound encouraging:
people say the concept is clever, sustainable, and visually attractive. But stronger validation questions reveal the real picture.
Many households do not feel enough pain to give up counter space. Filter replacement looks inconvenient. The likely selling price feels high
compared with existing behaviour. That is useful learning, not failure. It tells the team to change the concept, narrow the audience,
or stop before cost and complexity expand.

## The five questions every serious idea review should answer

- Who has the problem often enough that solving it changes behaviour, saves money, or reduces risk?

- What are they doing today instead, and what is broken about that workaround?

- Why would they choose this product over the next-best alternative, not just over doing nothing?

- What price, support burden, and delivery model still leave the business case intact?

- What evidence would make the team slow down, pivot, or kill the concept?

A strong idea becomes easier to explain as it is tested. A weak idea usually becomes more decorated, more complicated, and more dependent on optimism.

## What evidence is worth collecting before development starts

The point is not to build a giant research programme before any design work happens. The point is to gather enough sharp evidence
to avoid designing the wrong thing well.

- problem interviews that reveal repeated pain in the customer’s own language

- evidence of current spend, friction, delay, waste, or failure in the existing workaround

- early price or budget conversations that make the commercial reality visible

- an initial feasibility screen around product architecture, regulation, and manufacturing logic

- a clear reason this concept should win against alternatives already available

## Validation is also a sustainability question

If a product does not solve a meaningful problem well enough to justify its material, energy, and support burden,
it is not just commercially weak. It may be hard to justify at all. That is why validation and sustainability belong in the same early conversation.
The deeper framing is explored in
[The most sustainable product is the one you never make](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html).

## Where the Product Purpose Framework helps

Once the basic evidence is on the table, the
[Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)
gives the team a harder way to review the concept. It scores the idea across human value, planetary impact, economic viability, and technical feasibility,
which helps separate ideas that are merely interesting from ideas that deserve momentum.

### Score the concept properly

Use the Product Purpose Framework to test whether the idea is balanced enough to justify further work.
[Open Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)

### Stress-test the business case next

Once the problem and buyer look credible, pressure-test demand, pricing, and payback assumptions before the build plan expands.

[Open Business Case Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/hardware-business-case-builder.html)
[Compare Concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html)

Orion Design can help structure the early decision: clarify the value proposition, challenge weak assumptions,
and turn a broad idea into a buildable, commercially sensible brief.

## FAQ

### How do you validate a product idea properly?

Prove that the problem is real, the buyer is specific, the customer would switch or pay, and the product can be delivered credibly without breaking the business model.

### Is positive feedback enough to validate a product idea?

No. Positive feedback matters less than evidence of repeated pain, current workarounds, budget, and a believable reason the product will win.

### What should a hardware team validate before development starts?

Validate the problem, the buyer, willingness to pay, the likely route to manufacture and support, and the major technical or supply-chain risks that could undermine the offer.

Title: How to Write a Product Requirements Document

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams turning an idea into a brief that can be designed and tested

# How to write a product requirements document for a physical product

A practical guide to writing requirements for a physical product: what to include, how to make each requirement specific and testable, and how to keep the document useful as the project moves from idea to production.

Quick answer

## A product requirements document says what the product must do, for whom, and how you will know it does it, without deciding how it will be designed.

Write down the user and the problem, the use environment, the functional and performance requirements, regulatory and safety needs, cost and volume targets, and constraints.
Make each requirement specific and testable, mark which are essential, and keep it short enough that people actually read it. Update it as you learn, and use it to brief designers, judge concepts and plan tests.

## Why write one

A product requirements document (PRD), sometimes called a product specification or design brief, turns an idea into something a team can design, cost and test against.
Without one, decisions drift, each person imagines a different product, and nobody can say when the design is good enough.
It is also the basis for a clear brief to a consultancy; see [working with a product design consultancy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/working-with-a-product-design-consultancy.html).

## What to include

|
Section |
What it answers |

|
Purpose and user |
Who the product is for, the problem it solves and why they will choose it over their current alternative |

|
Use environment |
Where and how it is used: indoors or outdoors, temperature, moisture, drops, cleaning, who handles it |

|
Functional requirements |
What it must do |

|
Performance requirements |
How well: capacity, speed, battery life, accuracy, strength, with numbers |

|
Usability and appearance |
Size and weight limits, controls, accessibility, brand and finish expectations; check them through [usability testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html) |

|
Regulatory and safety |
Markets, likely regulations and standards, and safety requirements |

|
Commercial targets |
Target retail price, target unit cost, launch volumes and timing |

|
Life and sustainability |
Expected lifetime, servicing and repair, materials and end-of-life expectations |

|
Constraints and assumptions |
Fixed decisions, existing parts or platforms, and what you have assumed but not yet confirmed |

## How to write good requirements

- **Specific and testable.** "Survives a 1 m drop onto concrete on any face" can be tested; "robust" cannot.

- **What, not how.** "Holds 500 ml" leaves room for design; "a 70 mm diameter cylinder" decides too early, unless it is a genuine constraint.

- **Prioritised.** Mark each requirement as must-have or nice-to-have, so trade-offs are clear.

- **Justified.** Note where each requirement comes from: user research, regulation, a retailer or a cost target.

- **Numbered.** Give each requirement an ID so tests, concepts and decisions can refer to it.

Illustrative example for a portable outdoor light. Weak: "long battery life, tough, affordable".
Better: "R1 Must give at least 8 hours on the medium setting. R2 Must survive a 1 m drop onto concrete on any face. R3 Must resist rain (target rating to be confirmed against the relevant standard).
R4 Should retail at or below £40, with a target landed cost set from the route to market."

**Practical rule:**
for every requirement, ask "how would we test this?" If there is no answer, rewrite it until there is.

## Keep it alive

A PRD is not written once and filed. Early on it will contain targets and open questions; as research, prototypes and quotes come in, firm them up and record what changed and why.
Use it to score concepts with the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html), and turn the testable requirements into a test plan with the
[Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

## Common mistakes

**Writing the solution, not the need.**
It closes off better designs before anyone has explored them.

**Vague words.**
"Durable", "premium" and "easy to use" mean different things to everyone until you add numbers or tests.

**Everything is essential.**
Without priorities, the team cannot make sensible trade-offs.

**No cost target.**
Designing without a target unit cost often leads to a product that cannot be sold profitably.

**Too long to read.**
A focused few pages that people use beats a long document nobody opens.

## Next steps

- Define the user, problem and purpose with the [Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html).

- Set a target cost from your price with [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html).

- Collect the requirements and decisions in the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

- Read [how to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html) to back the requirements with evidence.

### Start with purpose

Clarify who the product is for and the problem it solves.
[Open Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)

### Turn requirements into tests

Plan how each requirement will be checked.
[Open Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html)

## FAQ

### What is a product requirements document?

A document that sets out what a product must do, for whom, in what conditions and to what standard, along with cost, volume and regulatory targets, so a team can design, cost and test against it. It describes the need rather than the design.

### How long should a product requirements document be?

Long enough to cover the essentials and short enough to be read and used. For many physical products, a focused few pages with numbered, prioritised requirements works better than a long document.

### What makes a good requirement?

It is specific, testable, prioritised and says what is needed rather than how to achieve it. If you cannot describe how you would test it, rewrite it.

### Is a PRD the same as a design brief?

They overlap. A design brief often focuses on the project, scope and goals for a designer, while a PRD focuses on the product's requirements. Many small teams combine them into one document.

### When should the requirements be updated?

Whenever research, prototypes, testing or quotes change what you know. Record what changed and why, so decisions can be traced back to evidence.

Title: Industrial Design vs Engineering Design

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and small teams working out what design and engineering help a physical product needs

# Industrial design vs engineering design: who does what

What industrial designers, product and mechanical design engineers, electronics and firmware engineers, and manufacturers each typically focus on, where the roles overlap, who you need at each stage of development, how to brief them so hand-offs do not fail, and what to ask when choosing help.

Quick answer

## Industrial design shapes what a product is like to see, hold and use; engineering design makes it work reliably and makes it possible to manufacture.

Industrial designers usually lead on form, ergonomics, user experience, colour, material and finish (CMF) and brand. Product and mechanical design engineers lead on architecture, mechanisms, materials, tolerances, design for manufacture and production CAD, with electronics and firmware engineers alongside where the product needs them.
The roles overlap heavily, many people work across both, and most products need both kinds of thinking from the start, in different proportions at each stage.

## Contents

- What industrial designers focus on

- What product and mechanical design engineers focus on

- Electronics and firmware engineers

- Manufacturers and toolmakers

- Where the roles overlap

- Who you need at each stage

- Briefing, and how hand-offs go wrong

- Questions to ask when choosing help

- Worked example: a consumer gadget

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What industrial designers focus on

Industrial design is about the relationship between the product and the person using it. An industrial designer typically asks: what should this look and feel like, how will people understand it, and does it fit the brand and the setting it lives in?

- **Form and proportion:** the overall shape, how parts read together and how the product sits on a shelf, a desk or in a hand.

- **User experience and interaction:** how people pick it up, start it, understand controls and feedback, and recover from mistakes.

- **Ergonomics:** grip, reach, weight balance, forces and comfort across the range of intended users.

- **CMF (colour, material and finish):** the visible materials, colours, textures and [surface finishes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html), and how they feel and age.

- **Brand and product character:** making the product recognisably part of a family and right for its price point and market.

Typical outputs are sketches, mood and CMF boards, foam and looks-like models, renders and surface CAD that defines the visible shape.

## What product and mechanical design engineers focus on

Engineering design is about making the product work, keeping it working and making it buildable at a sensible cost. A product or mechanical design engineer typically asks: how is it arranged inside, what holds it together, what will break, and how will it be made and assembled?

- **Architecture:** how the product is divided into parts and sub-assemblies, where components sit and how they connect.

- **Mechanisms:** hinges, latches, buttons, springs, seals and anything that moves or takes load.

- **Materials:** choosing grades for strength, stiffness, temperature, chemical resistance and cost, often from the shortlist the CMF work suggests.

- **Design for manufacture and assembly (DFM/DFA):** shaping parts for the chosen process, such as draft and wall thickness for [injection moulding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html), and reducing parts, fasteners and assembly steps.

- **Tolerances:** deciding how much each dimension may vary and checking parts still fit and function; see [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html).

- **CAD for manufacture:** solid models, drawings and data packs that suppliers can quote and make from.

Typical outputs are works-like prototypes, detailed CAD, engineering drawings, a bill of materials, calculations and test results.

## Electronics and firmware engineers

If the product has a circuit board, battery, sensor, motor or radio, electronics engineers design the circuits and board layout, and firmware engineers write the software that runs on it. Their work constrains the enclosure as much as the enclosure constrains them: board size and shape, battery space, heat, antenna placement and test access all need agreeing with the mechanical and industrial design early.
[Electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers what to plan and what to hand over to an electronics partner.

## Manufacturers and toolmakers

Manufacturers, toolmakers and other suppliers know their own processes in depth: what their machines and tools can hold, where defects tend to appear and what drives their cost. Their feedback on a design is valuable, especially before tooling. But a factory's job is usually to make what it is given. It may suggest changes that suit its process, which are not always the changes that suit your product, so someone on your side needs to judge them against your requirements.
[How to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html) covers working with them.

## Where the roles overlap

The boundary is blurred in practice. Ergonomics, materials, finishes, parting lines and the position of every button affect both appearance and engineering, so the best results come when both kinds of thinking happen together rather than in sequence.
Many industrial designers are comfortable with mechanisms and manufacturing, and many engineers have a strong eye for form and use. Job titles vary between companies and countries, so ask what someone actually does rather than relying on the title.

"Product design engineer" is a common name for someone who works across the two. Product design often focuses on form, user experience and appearance; product design engineering also covers how the product works and how it will be made: mechanical architecture, materials, tolerances, assembly, manufacturing route and cost. Orion Design works across both, with an emphasis on getting the product ready to manufacture.

## Who you need at each stage

Every discipline has some role throughout, but who leads tends to shift as the product moves from idea to production.

A typical pattern, not a rule: on a mechanism-heavy product engineering may lead from day one, and on a consumer product where appearance sells it, industrial design stays closely involved until production.

|
Stage |
Main question |
Skills usually most needed |

|
[Opportunity and concept](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/opportunity-and-concept.html) |
What should we build, for whom, and could it work? |
Industrial design for direction and use; engineering for feasibility, rough architecture and early cost |

|
Prototypes |
Does it work, can people use it, and does it look right? |
Separate or combined [looks-like and works-like](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) builds; engineering and electronics leading, industrial design refining |

|
Detailed design and production |
Can it be made consistently, at the target cost? |
Engineering for DFM, tolerances and data packs; manufacturer and toolmaker input; industrial design signing off CMF and appearance |

The [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html) sets out the stages in more detail, and
[how many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) helps plan which questions each round should answer.

## Briefing, and how hand-offs go wrong

Most problems between disciplines are not about skill but about hand-offs: one person finishes a stage and passes it on, and the next discovers that something important was never agreed. Common failures include:

- A beautiful shape that leaves no room for the battery, board or fixings, or cannot be moulded without costly tooling.

- An engineered layout that changes the proportions or controls the users liked in testing, without anyone checking.

- CMF choices that look right on a render but have no matching production finish or material grade.

- CAD sent to a supplier without drawings, tolerances, materials or quantities, so quotes and parts vary.

To avoid them:

- **Share one set of requirements.** A [product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html) gives every discipline the same targets for use, appearance, function, cost and compliance.

- **Overlap, do not relay.** Bring engineering into concept reviews and industrial design into engineering reviews, even briefly.

- **Agree who owns each decision,** such as the visible surfaces, the internal layout and the final material, and how changes are approved.

- **Hand over complete information,** including CAD revisions, decisions made and open questions. [Must-have documents before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) lists what suppliers need.

**Practical rule:**
if a change in one discipline would surprise someone in another, it needs a review, not just an updated file.

## Questions to ask when choosing help

Whether you are looking at an industrial design studio, an engineering consultancy, a freelancer or someone who spans both, these questions help show what you would actually get:

- Which parts of the work will you do yourselves, and which would you expect another discipline or supplier to do?

- Can you show examples of work taken through to production, not just concepts or renders?

- How do you work with electronics engineers and manufacturers, and who manages those hand-offs?

- What will you hand over at the end of each stage, and in what file formats?

- Who will actually do the work, and who makes design decisions day to day?

[Working with a product design consultancy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/working-with-a-product-design-consultancy.html) covers briefing, engagement structures and intellectual property in more depth.

## Worked example: a consumer gadget

Illustrative example. A founder has an idea for a small, rechargeable desk gadget that sits in view and is handled several times a day. It has a button, a light and a simple mechanism. Appearance matters because it will sell partly on how it looks in photographs.

|
Stage |
Skills the founder needs |
Why |

|
Concept |
Industrial design to explore form, size and interaction; a short engineering feasibility check of the mechanism, battery and likely processes |
So the favoured concept is one that can work and be made, not just one that looks good on paper |

|
Prototype |
Mechanical engineering for architecture and the mechanism; an electronics partner for the board, battery and charging; industrial design refining looks-like models and testing them with users |
Function and handling are tested in parallel, then combined in an integrated prototype |

|
Production |
Engineering for DFM, tolerances and drawings; manufacturer and toolmaker reviews; industrial design approving colour and finish samples |
So the parts that come off the tool match the design that was tested and the look that was promised |

The founder could hire each skill separately, or work with someone who spans industrial design and engineering and brings in electronics and manufacturing partners as needed. Either way, one shared requirements document and regular joint reviews keep the disciplines pointing at the same product.

## Common mistakes

**Polishing looks before the architecture works.**
Detailed renders and CMF work on a shape that cannot fit the internals end up being redone. Prove the layout roughly before refining the surface.

**Engineering a product nobody wants to use.**
A product can be robust and cheap to make yet awkward to hold, confusing to start or unappealing on the shelf. Keep users and appearance in the reviews throughout.

**Hand-offs without shared requirements.**
Each discipline then optimises for its own idea of success, and the conflicts surface late, when changes are most expensive.

**Assuming the factory will "sort out" design for manufacture.**
A manufacturer may adjust parts to suit its process, but not necessarily your product, cost target or appearance. DFM decisions need an owner on your side before tooling.

## Decision rules

- **If people will choose the product partly on how it looks or feels**, involve industrial design from the start, not as a finishing step.

- **If the product has moving parts, loads, seals or tight internal space**, bring engineering in at concept, not after the shape is fixed.

- **If it contains electronics**, agree board size, battery and antenna space with the mechanical layout before the form is frozen.

- **If two or more parties are involved**, write down the requirements and who owns which decisions before work starts.

- **Before tooling**, have an engineer on your side review DFM, tolerances and the manufacturer's suggested changes.

## FAQ

### What is the difference between industrial design and engineering design?

Industrial design focuses on how a product looks, feels and is used: form, ergonomics, interaction, colour, material and finish, and brand. Engineering design focuses on how it works and is made: architecture, mechanisms, materials, tolerances and design for manufacture. Most products need both, and the work overlaps.

### Do I need an industrial designer and an engineer?

Most physical products need both kinds of skill, but not always two people. Some designers and engineers work across both, and the balance depends on the product: appearance-led consumer products lean on industrial design, while mechanism-heavy or technical products lean on engineering.

### What is a product design engineer?

A product design engineer usually works across industrial design and engineering: considering how a product is used and how it looks, while also designing the mechanical architecture, materials, tolerances and assembly so that it can be manufactured. The exact scope varies between people and companies.

### Who should I hire first?

Start with whoever addresses your biggest unknown. If the risk is whether people want and can use it, start with industrial design and [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html); if the risk is whether it can work or be made at the target cost, start with engineering. Bring the other in early rather than at the end.

### Can the manufacturer do the engineering design?

Some manufacturers offer design services, and their process knowledge is valuable. But their priorities are not always yours, and you may have less control over the design and its ownership. Keep requirements, key decisions and design files under your own control, and have suggested changes reviewed against your requirements.

Title: When Does Injection Moulding Become Cheaper?

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 10 September 2026 · For teams deciding when injection moulding tooling is worth paying for

# When does injection moulding become cheaper?

Teams often ask for a single magic volume where tooling suddenly becomes the right answer. In practice the decision sits at the intersection
of setup cost, unit cost, demand confidence, design stability, and how painful a late change would be.

**Topic**
Break-even volume

**Audience**
Hardware teams and founders

**Tool**
Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser

**Use it for**
Timing tooling decisions

Quick answer

## Injection moulding becomes cheaper when lower unit cost outweighs tooling cost.

Break-even volume = tooling cost / (prototype unit cost - moulded unit cost)

Example: GBP6,500 / (GBP18 - GBP0.70) = roughly 376 units. That figure is only useful if the design and forecast are stable enough to trust.

Break-even volume is the point where a process with a higher upfront investment but lower recurring unit cost overtakes a process that is cheap to start but expensive to repeat.
Injection moulding usually wins late, not early. That does not make it wrong. It makes it timing-sensitive.

**Practical rule:**
if the design is still moving, forecast confidence is weak, or the first production volume is unclear, it is usually safer to stay with additive,
machining, or bridge tooling until the product proves it deserves a mould.

## The wrong question teams often ask

“When is moulding cheaper?” sounds precise, but it hides the real issue: “When is moulding safer and more profitable than the alternatives?”
Cost alone is not enough. A route that looks cheapest at 20,000 units can still be the wrong move if you only sell 4,000, change the geometry twice,
or need to ship [pilot builds](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) before tooling is ready.

Break-even is not a number to memorise. It is a timing decision about when your confidence in the product becomes strong enough to justify commitment.

## Example calculation

Assume 3D printing costs GBP18 per part with no tooling, while injection moulding costs GBP0.70 per part with a GBP6,500 tool.
The cost gap per part is GBP17.30. On paper, the moulded route starts to win at roughly 376 units.

That sounds early, but only if the design is stable, the forecast is credible, and the first few hundred parts will not be scrapped by engineering changes.

Example figures from the calculation above. The mould starts £6,500 behind but adds only £0.70 a part, so it overtakes 3D printing at roughly 376 units, provided the design and forecast hold.

## What each manufacturing route is buying you

|
Process |
What you gain |
What you give up |
Typical trigger to move on |

|
3D printing |
Speed, flexibility, almost no setup commitment |
High unit cost, weaker cosmetic and process repeatability |
When learning slows and recurring unit cost starts to dominate |

|
[CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) |
Durable parts, predictable quality, useful functional prototypes |
Moderate cost and slower repetition at higher quantities |
When volume grows beyond the point where machining remains economical |

|
Vacuum casting |
Bridge-volume flexibility and better appearance than many prototype routes |
Limited life and not the final production process |
When demand and geometry justify real production tooling |

|
Injection moulding |
Lowest recurring cost and repeatable scale production |
High upfront commitment and painful late-stage changes |
When both demand and product architecture are genuinely stable |

## Five questions to answer before cutting steel

- How strong is the forecast, and who owns that confidence?

- What is the cost of one major geometry change after tooling starts?

- Can a bridge process carry the first launch or pilot batch more safely?

- Are the quality and finish requirements already stable enough to tool against?

- Does the team have enough cash and lead-time tolerance to absorb tooling delays?

## Common decision traps

**Trap 1: believing the spreadsheet too early.**
A break-even line is only as good as the demand and cost assumptions behind it.

**Trap 2: ignoring bridge production.**
Many teams do not need to choose between prototype and final tooling immediately. Bridge routes often buy better evidence.

**Trap 3: underestimating the cost of change.**
A late design change can erase the unit-cost advantage that justified tooling in the first place.

Run at least three cases:

- a conservative demand scenario

- your expected case

- an optimistic case with a more stable design and better process efficiency

Then compare the cost curves against what you know about launch timing, cash, and engineering maturity. That is where the real decision sits.

## FAQ

### When does injection moulding become cheaper than 3D printing?

When the tooling investment has been diluted enough that the lower unit cost outweighs the zero-tooling advantage of additive manufacturing.

### Is break-even volume the only factor that matters?

No. Demand confidence, design maturity, lead-time tolerance, and the risk of rework after tooling can matter just as much.

### What should teams check before committing to tooling?

Check forecast confidence, product stability, quality requirements, bridge-production options, and whether the cash position can absorb tooling lead time and change risk.

Title: Injection Moulding DFM Checklist

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For engineers, designers and founders preparing plastic parts for injection moulding

# DFM checklist for injection-moulded parts: walls, draft, ribs, bosses and undercuts

Use this checklist on your CAD model before asking for [tooling quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html). It covers the features that most often cause sink marks, warping, sticking parts and expensive tooling, with typical starting values and the reason behind each rule.

Quick answer

## Keep walls even, add draft, size ribs and bosses to the wall, round the corners, avoid undercuts, and agree cosmetic faces with the moulder.

Most injection-moulding problems, such as sink marks, warping, parts sticking in the tool and expensive side actions, come from a short list of design features.
Checking those features before the tool is cut is one of the cheapest ways to reduce tooling cost, cycle time and rejected parts.
The figures below are widely used starting points; the material datasheet and your moulder's design-for-manufacture review have the final say.

## Contents

- Why design for manufacture matters most in moulding

- The checklist

- Walls and draft

- Ribs and bosses

- Worked example: reviewing an enclosure lid

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## Why design for manufacture matters most in moulding

An injection-mould tool is machined from aluminium or steel to the exact shape of the part. Once it is cut, adding material to the part is usually easy (the toolmaker removes steel),
but removing material from the part can mean welding and re-machining the tool, or making a new insert. Features that need moving tool parts, such as undercuts,
add cost to every tool and complexity to every cycle. That is why the checks below are worth doing on the CAD model, not on the first samples. If your part started as a 3D print, [from 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) walks through the changes in order.

## The checklist

|
Feature |
Typical starting point |
Why it matters |

|
Wall thickness |
As uniform as possible; commonly around 1 to 4 mm for many small and medium parts, depending on material and size; blend changes gradually rather than in steps |
Thick and uneven sections cool unevenly, causing sink marks, voids, warping and long cycle times |

|
Draft |
On every face parallel to the direction the tool opens: commonly at least 0.5 to 1 degree, more for deep features and textured surfaces |
Without draft, parts drag and stick on ejection, scuffing cosmetic faces |

|
Ribs |
Thickness about 40 to 60 per cent of the adjoining wall; height up to about 3 times the wall; spaced at least about 2 wall thicknesses apart; drafted |
Ribs add stiffness without thick sections; too thick and they sink the opposite face |

|
Bosses |
Outside diameter around twice the hole; boss wall thinner than the main wall; supported by gusset ribs or joined to nearby walls; cored from below |
Solid bosses cause sink and voids; unsupported bosses crack when screws are driven |

|
Corners |
Inside radius at least about half the wall; outside radius about inside radius plus the wall |
Sharp corners concentrate stress, restrict flow and are harder to fill and eject |

|
Undercuts |
Avoid where possible; otherwise use side actions, lifters, flexible bump-offs, or a pass-through core redesign |
Anything that stops the part pulling straight out needs moving tool parts, which add cost and maintenance |

|
Holes and slots |
Prefer through holes; keep blind holes shallow relative to their diameter; keep holes away from edges |
Long slender core pins deflect and break; holes near edges weaken the part |

|
Text, logos and texture |
Raised lettering on the part (engraved into the tool) is easier to make and change; add extra draft for texture (see [surface finishes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html)) |
Engraving can be added to a tool later; texture without enough draft scrapes on ejection |

|
Gates, ejector pins, parting line |
Agree their positions with the moulder, away from cosmetic faces |
All leave visible marks; moving them after the tool is cut is costly |

|
Tolerances and flatness |
Tight tolerances only where the function needs them; add ribs or curvature to large flat areas |
Plastics shrink and can warp; unnecessary tight tolerances raise tool and inspection cost (check critical fits with the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html)) |

## Walls and draft

Even wall thickness is the most important single rule. The plastic in a thick section stays molten longest, and as it cools it shrinks and pulls the surface inwards (a sink mark)
or leaves an internal void. The fix is almost always to core the thick feature out so that it is made of walls close to the nominal thickness.

Cross-sections, not to scale. Coring out thick features keeps walls even, shortens cooling time and removes the cause of sink marks and voids.

Draft is the slight taper on faces that run in the direction the tool opens. It lets the part release cleanly. The amount needed rises with depth and surface texture:
a textured cosmetic surface can need several degrees, and the texture supplier will usually specify a minimum. Add draft in CAD from the start;
retrofitting it changes every dimension that depends on those faces.

### Try it: draft and undercuts

Draft angle

1.5°

Add an undercut (e.g. a snap catch)

At 1.5° a small gap opens as soon as the part moves, so it releases cleanly. Around 1° to 2° is a common starting point for many plastics; deep or textured faces usually need more.
Cross-section, not to scale; the draft angle is drawn eight times steeper than real so it can be seen. With no draft the walls rub on the core all the way out. An undercut, such as a snap catch, locks the part on the core and needs a side action, a lifter or a design change.

## Ribs and bosses

Ribs and bosses are how moulded parts get stiffness and fixing points without thick walls. Their proportions are a balance: thick enough to fill and to do their job,
thin enough not to cause sink marks on the visible face opposite them.

Typical starting proportions only; your moulder and the material datasheet may recommend different values. Thin ribs and bosses avoid sink marks on the opposite face.

For screw bosses, follow the screw manufacturer's recommendations for hole size in your chosen plastic: thread-forming screws for plastics are designed for specific hole diameters,
and the right hole matters more for joint strength than the boss's outside size. Heat-set or moulded-in inserts are an alternative where the joint is opened often; [joining methods compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) sets screws and inserts against snap fits, welding and adhesives.

**Practical rule:**
if a feature needs a side action, ask whether it can be redesigned. A snap-fit hook can often be moulded straight-pull by putting a hole in the wall behind it, so a core passes through and forms the hook's underside.

## Worked example: reviewing an enclosure lid

Illustrative example. A start-up sends a moulder its CAD for a two-part plastic enclosure. The lid has 4 mm walls, four solid screw bosses 9 mm across,
no draft on its 25 mm side walls, sharp internal corners, and two side-facing clips that would each need a side action.

|
Issue found |
Change made |
Effect |

|
Walls thicker than the part needs |
Reduced to a uniform 2.5 mm, with three internal ribs for stiffness |
Less material, shorter cooling time, no sink marks |

|
Solid screw bosses |
Cored bosses joined to the side walls with gussets |
No sink on the outer face; stronger under screw torque |

|
No draft on side walls |
1 degree on smooth faces, more on the textured top |
Clean ejection, no drag marks |

|
Sharp internal corners |
Radii added, sized to the wall thickness |
Better flow, lower stress at the corners |

|
Two clips needing side actions |
Redesigned as straight-pull snaps with pass-through cores |
Simpler, cheaper tool with fewer moving parts |

None of these changes alters what the lid does, but together they make the tool simpler, the cycle shorter and the parts more consistent. That is typical of a good DFM review.

## Common mistakes

**Designing as if the part will be machined.**
Solid blocks and sharp internal corners that are easy to machine make poor moulded parts.

**Adding draft at the end.**
It ripples through every mating dimension; design it in from the start.

**Using one wall thickness rule for every plastic.**
Materials flow and shrink differently; check the datasheet and ask the moulder.

**Ignoring where the tool will leave marks.**
Gate, ejector and parting-line marks end up on the cosmetic face unless they are agreed.

**Skipping the moulder's DFM report.**
Most toolmakers provide one, often with a mould-flow simulation; read it before approving the tool.

- Estimate the part cost with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html).

## FAQ

### What wall thickness should an injection-moulded part have?

As uniform as possible, at the thinnest value that meets the strength and filling requirements. Many small and medium parts fall somewhere around 1 to 4 mm, but the right figure depends on the material, the part size and the flow length, so check the material datasheet and ask your moulder.

### How much draft angle does an injection-moulded part need?

A common starting point is at least 0.5 to 1 degree on faces parallel to the direction the tool opens, with more for deep features and textured surfaces. Textured surfaces can need several degrees; the texture supplier will usually state a minimum.

### How thick should ribs be on a plastic part?

Typically about 40 to 60 per cent of the wall they join, up to about three times the wall thickness tall, with draft and a small radius at the base. Thicker ribs tend to cause sink marks on the opposite face.

### What is an undercut in injection moulding?

Any feature that stops the part being pulled straight out of the tool, such as a side hole, a clip or an internal groove. Undercuts need side actions, lifters or flexible ejection, which add cost, so they are worth designing out where possible.

### What causes sink marks on moulded parts?

Thick sections, such as solid bosses or heavy ribs, cool more slowly than the surrounding wall and shrink as they do, pulling the surface inwards. Keeping walls even and coring out thick features is the usual cure.
