Title: Injection Moulding Explained: Process and Cost

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers preparing to commission their first injection-mould tooling

# Injection moulding explained: the process, tooling types, lead times and cost drivers

A plain-English explanation of injection moulding for people commissioning tooling for the first time: how the process works, the tooling choices you will be asked about, the steps from quote to production parts, and what really drives tool and part cost.

Quick answer

## Injection moulding forces molten plastic into a machined metal tool, cools it, and ejects a finished part, repeating every few seconds to a minute.

Part cost ≈ material + (machine rate × cycle time ÷ cavities) + finishing and handling + scrap allowance + tooling ÷ volume

It gives low, consistent part costs and fine detail at volume, but needs an expensive tool that takes weeks to make and is costly to change.
Tool cost is driven by part size, complexity, number of cavities, moving parts for undercuts, and steel grade; part cost by material, cycle time and machine size.
It suits stable designs with enough volume to share the tooling cost.

## Contents

- How the process works

- Types of tooling

- The tooling project, step by step

- What drives tool cost

- What drives part cost

- When injection moulding is, and is not, the right choice

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## How the process works

Plastic pellets are dried if needed, melted and mixed by a rotating screw in a heated barrel, then injected under high pressure into the cavity of a closed tool.
The plastic cools against the tool's water-cooled walls, shrinks slightly, and is pushed out by ejector pins once the tool opens. The same tool can make hundreds of thousands of parts or more.

Choose a step to see what happens, what the designer controls, and how it affects cycle time.

What happens

What the designer controls

Effect on cycle time

One cycle typically takes from several seconds to a minute or more, depending mainly on wall thickness, material and part size. Every second of cycle time is paid for on every part.

## Types of tooling

|
Choice |
Options |
Trade-off |

|
Tool material |
Aluminium; pre-hardened steel; hardened steel |
Aluminium is quicker and cheaper but wears sooner; hardened steel costs most and lasts longest, especially with abrasive filled plastics |

|
Cavities |
Single cavity; multi-cavity; family tool (different parts in one tool) |
More cavities cut cost per part but raise tool cost; family tools save tooling but can be harder to balance |

|
Runner system |
Cold runner; hot runner |
Hot runners waste less material and can shorten cycles but cost more to build and maintain |

|
Moving parts |
Straight-pull; side actions; lifters; unscrewing mechanisms |
Every moving part adds cost, lead time and maintenance; design them out where possible |

|
Inserts and modularity |
Master unit die (MUD) frames with interchangeable inserts |
Cheaper for small parts and early runs; less suitable for large or complex parts |

Many start-ups begin with an aluminium or soft-steel "bridge" tool for the first few thousand parts, then move to a hardened multi-cavity tool once the design and demand are proven.
[The risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) explains that sequence.

## The tooling project, step by step

- **Quote and DFM review:** the toolmaker reviews your CAD for mouldability and proposes gate, parting line and ejector positions.

- **Tool design:** the tool is designed in detail; you approve the layout and any changes to the part.

- **Tool manufacture:** machining, spark erosion, polishing or texturing, and fitting.

- **First samples (T1):** the first parts off the tool, checked against your drawings.

- **Modifications and further samples (T2, T3…):** adjustments to dimensions, fit, finish or process.

- **Approval and first-article inspection:** you sign off production-representative parts; the process settings are recorded.

- **Production:** parts are moulded, inspected and packed to the agreed quality plan.

Lead times vary widely with the toolmaker, the country, the part's complexity and the workload of the shop. As a broad guide, simple aluminium tools are often quoted in a few weeks,
and production steel tools commonly take from several weeks to a few months to first samples, before any modification rounds and shipping.
Treat any lead time as a range in your plan, and ask each toolmaker for their own figures.

## What drives tool cost

- **Part size:** larger parts need larger blocks of steel and bigger machines.

- **Complexity:** deep ribs, fine detail and tight tolerances take more machining and fitting.

- **Moving parts:** each side action or lifter adds design and build work.

- **Number of cavities:** more cavities, more cost, but lower cost per part.

- **Steel grade and expected life:** hardened steel costs more but lasts longer.

- **Surface finish:** high polish and specified textures add finishing time.

- **Runner system:** hot runners add cost to the tool.

- **Where it is made:** toolmaking rates differ considerably between countries; compare the full cost, including shipping, modifications and communication.

## What drives part cost

Once the tool exists, the price of each part depends mainly on the plastic used (weight times price per kilogram, plus a small allowance for runners and scrap),
the cycle time, the hourly rate of the moulding machine (larger parts need larger, more expensive machines), the number of cavities, and any secondary operations
such as printing, inserts or assembly.
Adding a soft grip or seal as a second material is covered in [overmoulding and two-shot moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/overmoulding-and-two-shot-moulding.html).

Illustrative figures only. A small enclosure part weighs 40 g in ABS. With material at an assumed £3 per kilogram and a 5 per cent allowance for scrap and runners,
material is about £0.13 per part. The tool has two cavities and a 30-second cycle on a machine charged at an assumed £50 per hour:
£50 ÷ 3,600 seconds × 30 seconds ÷ 2 cavities ≈ £0.21 per part. Before packing, overhead and the moulder's margin, the part costs about £0.33.
Cutting the cycle to 24 seconds by thinning the walls saves about £0.04 a part, roughly £4,000 over 100,000 parts.

Illustrative figures from the example above, before packing, overhead and the moulder's margin. Machine time is the larger share of this part's cost, which is why a shorter cycle, set mainly by wall thickness, pays back on every part.

The [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) builds this kind of estimate for your own part,
and [the injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) covers the design features that set cycle time.

## When injection moulding is, and is not, the right choice

|
Good fit |
Poor fit |

|
Volumes high enough to share the tool cost |
A few dozen or a few hundred parts |

|
A design that has stopped changing |
A design still changing after [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html) or certification |

|
Parts needing consistent quality, fine detail or [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) |
Very large, simple parts better suited to vacuum forming or rotational moulding |

|
Enough cash to pay for tooling before sales |
A cash position that cannot absorb the tool and first stock together |

[When does injection moulding become cheaper?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) and the
[Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) help find the volume at which a tool pays for itself.

## Common mistakes

**Comparing tool quotes on price alone.**
Check tool material, expected life, cavities, ownership, included sample rounds and modification costs.

**Assuming T1 parts will be right.**
Plan time and money for at least one modification round.

**Ordering more cavities than the volume needs.**
A four-cavity tool for a few thousand parts a year ties up cash for little saving.

**Not agreeing who owns the tool.**
Put ownership, storage, maintenance and transfer terms in writing before paying.

**Choosing the material late.**
Shrinkage differs between plastics; the tool is cut for a specific material.

[When injection moulding becomes cheaper](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html)

[Risk-progressive manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html)

[Manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html)

[Quality control and FAI](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html)

This guide answers

Injection moulding
Tooling
Cycle time
Part cost

## FAQ

### How does injection moulding work?

Plastic pellets are melted in a heated barrel and injected under pressure into a closed metal tool. The plastic cools and solidifies against the tool walls, the tool opens and ejector pins push the part out. The cycle then repeats, typically every few seconds to a minute.

### How long does it take to make an injection mould tool?

It varies with complexity, tool material, the toolmaker and the country. Simple aluminium tools are often quoted in a few weeks, while production steel tools commonly take from several weeks to a few months to first samples, plus time for modifications and shipping. Ask each toolmaker for their own lead time.

### What is the difference between aluminium and steel moulds?

Aluminium tools are quicker and cheaper to make but wear sooner, so they suit prototypes and lower volumes. Steel tools cost more and take longer but last much longer, especially hardened steel, and suit high volumes and abrasive filled plastics.

### What is a multi-cavity mould?

A tool that makes several identical parts in each cycle. It costs more to build than a single-cavity tool but reduces the cost per part, so it suits higher volumes. A family tool makes several different parts in one cycle.

### What are T1 samples?

The first parts moulded from a new tool. They are checked against the drawings, and the tool is usually adjusted before later samples (T2, T3 and so on) are approved for production. Plan for at least one modification round.

Title: Product IP, Partners and Compliance Explained

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams preparing to share, protect, make and sell a physical product in the UK

# IP, partners and compliance: protecting a product, working with partners and meeting the rules

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about protecting a physical product and putting it on the market legally: the types of intellectual property, the disclosure mistake to avoid, what to agree with designers and manufacturers, and how UK product compliance and safety duties work. It is general information with links to official sources, not legal advice.

Quick answer

## Decide early what to protect and how, put partner relationships in writing, and design for the regulations that apply from the start.

Patents protect how a new invention works and must be applied for before the idea is made public. Registered designs protect appearance; trade marks protect the brand;
copyright and unregistered design right arise automatically but give narrower protection. Use confidentiality agreements and clear contracts with designers and manufacturers,
especially on who owns the design and the tooling. And identify the product regulations and standards that apply before the design is fixed, because compliance problems found after tooling are expensive.
This page is general information, not legal advice.

## Contents

- Types of intellectual property for physical products

- Disclosure: the mistake that cannot be undone

- Working with designers, manufacturers and distributors

- Product compliance in the UK

- Northern Ireland and Great Britain

- Product safety and liability

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## Types of intellectual property for physical products

|
Right |
What it protects |
How you get it |
Points to know |

|
[Patent](https://www.gov.uk/patent-your-invention) |
How a new invention works: a mechanism, process or technical solution |
Application to the Intellectual Property Office, examination, fees |
Must be new and inventive; can last up to 20 years with renewal fees; expensive to file and defend internationally |

|
[Registered design](https://www.gov.uk/register-a-design) |
The appearance of a product: shape, lines, contours, decoration |
Application to the Intellectual Property Office |
Cheaper and quicker than a patent; renewable every 5 years up to 25 years |

|
[Unregistered design right](https://www.gov.uk/design-right) |
The shape and configuration of a product |
Automatic |
Protects against copying only, and is harder to prove than a registration |

|
[Trade mark](https://www.gov.uk/how-to-register-a-trade-mark) |
Brand names, logos and other signs |
Registration for specific classes of goods and services |
Renewable every 10 years; check availability before you invest in a name |

|
Copyright |
Drawings, manuals, software, artwork, photographs |
Automatic |
Make sure contracts say who owns work produced for you |

|
Confidential information |
Know-how, unpublished designs, processes, supplier details |
Keeping it secret, supported by confidentiality agreements |
Lost once it becomes public |

Many physical products rely on a combination: perhaps a patent on one key mechanism, a registered design on the appearance, a [trade mark on the name](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/trade-marks-and-product-names.html),
and confidentiality for manufacturing know-how. The Intellectual Property Office's [overview of intellectual property](https://www.gov.uk/intellectual-property-an-overview)
is a good starting point, and [how to protect product IP before talking to manufacturers](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) covers the practical steps.

## Disclosure: the mistake that cannot be undone

An invention generally needs to be new when a patent application is filed. Showing it publicly first, through a [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) page, a trade show, a social media post or an unprotected pitch,
can prevent you from patenting it. Registered designs have different rules on disclosure, but the safest approach is the same: take advice and decide what to file
**before** the product is shown outside a confidential circle.

**Practical rule:**
until you have decided on protection, share only under a confidentiality agreement, share only what the other party needs, and keep a dated record of what you shared and with whom.

## Working with designers, manufacturers and distributors

Many IP problems with partners come from things that were never written down. Agree these points before work starts:

- **Confidentiality:** a non-disclosure agreement before sharing designs. The [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html) produces a starting draft to review.

- **Ownership of design work:** make sure work done for you by a designer or consultancy is assigned to your company, not just licensed.

- **Tooling:** who owns the tools you paid for, where they are kept, maintenance, and how you can move them to another supplier.

- **Quality and specifications:** drawings, tolerances, inspection and what happens when parts are out of specification.

- **Exclusivity and territory:** for distributors and licensees, which products, which countries, for how long, and what targets apply.

Good documents also make partners more effective. See [the documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html).
[Supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html) sets out the topics to agree before tooling and the first order. For contracts with real value, have them reviewed by a solicitor.

## Product compliance in the UK

Consumer products placed on the UK market must be safe, and many categories have specific regulations: electrical equipment, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), radio equipment,
toys, machinery, medical devices and others. For many of these, the manufacturer must show conformity, keep a technical file, sign a declaration of conformity and apply a marking.

The general shape of conformity for many UK product regulations. Which regulations apply, and whether a third party must be involved, depends on the product: check the official guidance.

Identify the regulations at the requirements stage, not after the design is finished ([product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) covers the process in more detail): they can affect materials, enclosures, labelling, instructions and test budgets.
Pre-compliance testing during development, described in the [Development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html), reduces the risk of failing formal tests.
Official starting points: [using the UKCA marking](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukca-marking),
[CE marking](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/ce-marking), and the
[Office for Product Safety and Standards](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/office-for-product-safety-and-standards).

## Northern Ireland and Great Britain

Product marking rules differ between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Broadly, products for Northern Ireland follow the EU rules and use CE marking, with
[UKNI marking](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukni-marking) in some cases, while Great Britain uses UKCA marking and also recognises CE marking for many product types. General consumer product safety in Northern Ireland is also covered by the EU General Product Safety Regulation, which has applied there since 13 December 2024.
The rules have changed several times and differ by product category, so check the current guidance for your product before printing labels or packaging.

## Product safety and liability

Whoever places a product on the market is responsible for it being safe, and producers can be liable for harm caused by defective products.
Practical protection comes from a documented risk assessment, testing to recognised standards, clear instructions and warnings, traceability of batches,
a process for handling complaints and recalls, and appropriate product liability insurance. Insurers and retailers may ask for evidence of these.
GOV.UK's [product safety guidance for manufacturers](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/product-safety-for-manufacturers) sets out the duties.

## Common mistakes

**Showing the product before deciding on protection.**
A public post or pitch can prevent a later patent.

**Assuming you own work you paid for.**
Without an assignment, a designer may own the copyright or design rights in their work.

**No written agreement on tool ownership.**
Moving production becomes difficult or impossible.

**Discovering regulations at the test house.**
Requirements that should have shaped the design arrive as expensive changes.

**Relying on an NDA as complete protection.**
An NDA helps keep information confidential but does not stop independent development and is only as useful as your ability to enforce it.

## FAQ

### Should I patent my product idea?

Only if the invention is genuinely new and inventive, the protection would be commercially valuable, and you can afford to file and enforce it in the markets that matter. Many products are better protected by a registered design, a trade mark, speed to market and confidentiality. Take advice from a registered patent attorney before you disclose the idea.

### Does an NDA protect my product idea?

It helps keep shared information confidential and makes clear the other party may not use it, but it does not stop someone developing a similar idea independently, and enforcement can be costly. Use an NDA alongside sharing only what is necessary and deciding on formal protection early.

### Who owns the design if I pay a designer or consultancy?

Not automatically you. Copyright and design rights can stay with the person who created the work unless the contract assigns them to you. Make sure your agreement includes an assignment of intellectual property in the work produced for you.

### Do I need UKCA or CE marking?

Many product categories, including electrical equipment, radio equipment, toys and machinery, need a conformity marking. Great Britain uses UKCA and recognises CE marking for many products; Northern Ireland uses CE marking, with UKNI in some cases. Check the official GOV.UK guidance for your product category.

### Who is responsible if my product causes harm?

Whoever places the product on the market has duties to make sure it is safe, and producers can be liable for harm caused by defective products. A documented risk assessment, testing, clear instructions, traceability and product liability insurance are the usual protections. This is general information; take legal advice for your situation.

Title: Joining Methods: Screws, Snap Fits, Welding

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers deciding how the parts of a product will be held together

# Joining methods: screws, snap fits, adhesives and welding

How the common ways of joining plastic and metal parts compare on strength, whether they can be undone for repair, assembly time, tooling, cost and recycling, and how to choose between them for your product.

Quick answer

## Choose a joining method by asking whether the joint must ever come apart, how strong and sealed it must be, and how many products you will build.

Screws and threaded inserts are slower to assemble but can be undone again and again, which suits anything that will be serviced or repaired. Snap fits are quick and need no extra parts, but they add features to the mould and must suit the material.
Ultrasonic welding, staking and adhesives make strong, permanent joints, which is right for sealed or tamper-proof products and wrong for products that need repair.

## Contents

- Five questions that decide the joint

- Screws into plastic: bosses, thread-forming screws and inserts

- Machine screws in metal

- Snap fits

- Heat and ultrasonic staking

- Ultrasonic welding of plastics

- Adhesives and tapes

- Welding, brazing, rivets and clinching for metal

- The methods side by side

- Worked example: closing a small plastic enclosure

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## Five questions that decide the joint

Every joint trades assembly speed against ease of undoing it. For each joint, ask:

- **Must it come apart?** For repair, battery replacement, servicing or separating materials at the end of life. If yes, rule out permanent joints there.

- **What load and environment does it see?** Drops, vibration, heat, moisture, and whether it must seal (see [sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html)).

- **Which materials meet?** Two parts in the same plastic can be welded; different plastics, or plastic and metal, usually need a mechanical fixing or an adhesive.

- **How many will you build?** Dedicated equipment and mould features pay back over volume; at low volume, simple fasteners usually win.

- **Should it be visible?** Screw heads and weld lines affect appearance; hidden snap fits do not.

## Screws into plastic: bosses, thread-forming screws and inserts

A screw into a plastic part needs a **boss**, a hollow post moulded into the part. The [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) gives the usual starting proportions: outside diameter around twice the hole, a boss wall thinner than the main wall, cored from below and supported by gusset ribs or joined to nearby walls.
Solid bosses cause sink marks and voids; unsupported bosses crack when screws are driven.

- **Thread-forming screws for plastics** form their own thread in a plain moulded hole, with no extra parts or operations. The hole size matters more than the boss size, so follow the screw maker's recommendation for your plastic. The thread wears each time the screw is removed, so they suit joints opened occasionally.

- **Threaded inserts**, usually brass, give a machine thread that survives repeated assembly. **Heat-set** inserts are pressed in with a heated tip that melts the plastic into their knurls; **ultrasonic** inserts use vibration instead; **moulded-in** inserts are placed in the tool before each shot, adding handling to every cycle.

Inserts add a part, an operation and cost, but suit products that will be opened for service or repair. A metal insert left in a plastic part complicates recycling, so make it removable or accept that the plastic may be downgraded.

## Machine screws in metal

In machined or cast metal, a tapped hole takes a standard machine screw that can be undone many times; allow enough thread engagement for the load, and a thread-locking compound where vibration could loosen it.
[Sheet metal](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html) is usually too thin to tap, so self-clinching nuts, studs and standoffs pressed into the sheet give strong threads without welding.

Screws are reliable, repairable and join different materials. Their costs are the parts and the time: driving a screw is one of the slower steps in a manual build, as the [assembly time guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) explains.

## Snap fits

A snap fit is a flexible feature moulded into one part that deflects as the parts are pushed together and springs back behind a catch on the other. It needs no screws, tools or extra parts, which makes it one of the quickest joints to assemble.
**Cantilever** snap fits, a hook on a short flexible beam, are the usual choice for lids and battery doors. **Annular** snap fits, a continuous bead around a round part as on a pen cap, are strong and can help to seal, but need more force to assemble.

**Design for the material's strain.** As the beam deflects, the plastic at its root is stretched. Every plastic has a limit on the strain it can take without cracking or permanently bending, and tough plastics such as polypropylene and nylon tolerate much more than brittle or glass-filled grades.
Longer or tapered beams, smaller deflections and a generous root radius all lower the strain; check the allowable value on the datasheet, and see [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) for how plastics differ. Plastics creep under constant load, so a closed snap fit should be relaxed, not left bent.
To check a hook's root strain and its assembly and separation forces, try the [Snap-fit Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/snap-fit-calculator.html).

**One-way or releasable.** A square retaining face is effectively permanent: the catch must break to open. An angled face, or a slot where a flat tool can press the hook back, makes it releasable. For anything that may be repaired, design releasable snap fits and test them through repeated opening.

**Tooling.** A snap hook is an undercut, and undercuts need side actions or lifters that add cost and maintenance. As the DFM checklist notes, a hook can often be moulded straight-pull by putting a hole in the wall behind it, so a core passes through and forms its underside. Agree snap-fit details with your moulder before the tool is cut. For the strain calculation, angles and living hinges, see [designing snap fits and living hinges](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html).

## Heat and ultrasonic staking

Staking fixes a part with a hole, such as a [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) or metal bracket, onto a plastic post. The post's tip is melted and reformed into a head, like a rivet, with a heated tool or ultrasonic vibration.
It needs no fasteners and joins different materials, but removing the part means cutting off the heads, so keep it away from batteries and other parts that wear out.

## Ultrasonic welding of plastics

Ultrasonic welding presses two plastic parts together and vibrates them at high frequency until the interface melts and fuses. The joint is designed into the moulding, usually with a small ridge called an energy director, and the plastics must be the same or compatible. Amorphous plastics such as ABS and polycarbonate generally weld more easily than semi-crystalline ones such as polypropylene and nylon.

The weld cycle is short and the joint can be strong and sealed, with a clean exterior. The costs are a welding machine, a horn and fixture made for the part, and joint features that must be right in the mould. The product cannot be opened for repair, though a housing welded from one plastic may still recycle as one material.

## Adhesives and tapes

Adhesives spread load, join almost any pair of materials and can seal. Their weak point is the process: bond strength depends on **surface preparation**, removing grease and mould release and sometimes abrading or priming. Low-surface-energy plastics such as polypropylene and polyethylene are hard to bond without special adhesives or treatment.

Many adhesives need a **cure time** with the parts held or fixtured, and that wait is assembly cost. Double-sided tapes give handling strength straight away, and some are designed to release when stretched so a part can be removed.
Most structural adhesives are in practice **permanent**: a glued housing or battery is a common barrier to repair, as the [design for repair and disassembly guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) explains, and adhesive on mixed materials makes them harder to separate for recycling.

## Welding, brazing, rivets and clinching for metal

- **Welding** fuses the parent metal. It is strong and can seal, but adds heat distortion, finishing work and labour, damages coatings such as galvanising, and is permanent.

- **Brazing** uses a filler metal that melts below the parts' melting point. It distorts less and can join different metals, but is permanent.

- **Rivets**, including blind rivets fitted from one side, are quick, need no heat and join different materials. They can be drilled out for repair.

- **Clinching** presses overlapping sheets into an interlocking button. It needs no consumables or heat, so it suits pre-coated sheet, but it is permanent.

Joints between the same metal do not usually stop it being recycled as scrap; the bigger end-of-life concern is plastic, foam or adhesive permanently attached to the metal.

## The methods side by side

A qualitative comparison; strength and cost depend on the joint design, material and volume.

## Worked example: closing a small plastic enclosure

Illustrative example. A handheld sensor has a moulded ABS base and lid, a circuit board and a replaceable battery. The team compares closing the lid with four screws into heat-set inserts, snap fits around the edge, or an ultrasonic weld.

|
Option |
Serviceability |
Assembly time |
Tooling |
Appearance |

|
Screws and heat-set inserts |
Best: opens with a screwdriver, many times |
Slowest: four screws plus inserts |
Bosses; insertion equipment |
Screw heads visible unless covered |

|
Releasable snap fits |
Good if designed for repeated opening |
Quickest: one push |
Snap features in the mould |
Clean, with a release slot |

|
Ultrasonic weld |
None |
Short machine cycle |
Welder, horn and fixture |
Cleanest; can seal |

Using the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html)'s own defaults of 14 seconds per join and £28 an hour, four screws add 56 seconds, about £0.44 of labour per unit (56 ÷ 3,600 × £28), before fitting the inserts.
The assembly time guide puts a snap fit at a few seconds. These are defaults, not measured times; time a prototype build to replace them.

Welding is ruled out because the battery must be replaceable. The team chooses releasable snap fits plus two screws into inserts near the battery, so the lid stays secure after a drop, survives many openings and needs half the screw time. A sealed product with no wear parts could reasonably choose the weld.

## Common mistakes

**Welding or gluing shut a product that needs repair.**
A permanent joint around a battery or other wear part turns a repair into a replacement.

**Snap fits in brittle materials.**
A beam that is fine in polypropylene can crack in a brittle or glass-filled grade. Check the material's allowable strain before the tool is cut.

**Screws straight into soft plastic without a boss designed for them.**
Wrong hole sizes and solid or unsupported bosses strip, crack or sink. Size the hole to the screw maker's recommendation.

**Adhesive with no surface preparation.**
Mould release, grease and low-surface-energy plastics stop adhesives bonding, and the failure often appears only in the field.

## Decision rules

- **Use screws, ideally into inserts,** wherever the joint must be opened for repair or service.

- **Use releasable snap fits** where speed matters and the material is tough enough.

- **Use welding, staking or adhesives** only for joints that never need opening, or where sealing or tamper resistance is required.

- **Avoid permanently joining different materials** where they will need separating at the end of life.

- **Count the joins** in each concept and estimate their assembly time.

## FAQ

### Are snap fits strong enough for a product enclosure?

Often, yes, if they are designed for the material and the loads, with enough engagement and a relaxed state once closed. Many enclosures combine snap fits with one or two screws where drop loads or tamper resistance matter.

### Should I use thread-forming screws or threaded inserts in plastic?

Thread-forming screws are cheaper and fine for joints opened rarely. Threaded inserts cost more and add an operation, but give a durable machine thread for products that will be opened repeatedly for service or repair.

### Can ultrasonically welded parts be repaired?

Not without damage. The joint fuses the two parts, so opening it means cutting or breaking the housing. Use it for sealed products with no parts that need replacing.

### Why did my glued joint fail?

The most common causes are poor surface preparation, such as mould release or grease left on the parts, a plastic that is hard to bond such as polypropylene, or moving the parts before the adhesive had cured.

### Which joining method is best for recycling?

Joints that can be undone, such as screws and releasable snap fits, make it easiest to separate materials. Permanent joints between the same material matter less for recycling than adhesives or inserts that bind different materials together.

Title: Landed Cost: Freight, Duty and Import VAT

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams importing products or components into the UK

# Landed cost explained: freight, duty and import VAT for physical products

What it really costs to get a product from a factory to your warehouse: the parts of landed cost, how UK import duty and import VAT are worked out, and an illustrative calculation from factory price to landed cost per unit.

Quick answer

## Landed cost is everything it costs to get a product from the factory to your warehouse, ready to sell, not just the price on the supplier's quote.

Landed cost = goods + packaging + freight + insurance + import duty + clearance and port charges + inland delivery (+ import VAT if you cannot reclaim it)

For goods made overseas these extras can add a substantial share on top of the factory price. Duty is charged on the customs value, which in the UK usually includes freight and insurance to the UK border,
at a rate set by the product's commodity code. Import VAT is charged on top but can normally be reclaimed by VAT-registered businesses. Build landed cost into the unit cost from the first quote,
and check duty rates on the official UK Trade Tariff. This is general information, not tax or customs advice.

## The parts of landed cost

|
Cost |
What it covers |
Notes |

|
Goods |
The supplier's price on the agreed delivery terms (Incoterms) |
An EXW price leaves more for you to pay than a FOB or DDP price |

|
Packaging |
[Retail packaging](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html), inner cartons, shipping cartons, pallets |
Sometimes quoted separately from the product |

|
Freight |
Sea, air, rail, road or courier, plus origin charges |
Sea is usually cheapest per unit but slow; air and courier are fast and expensive |

|
Insurance |
Cover for loss or damage in transit |
Check whose responsibility it is under the Incoterms used |

|
Import duty |
Customs duty at the rate for the product's commodity code |
May be reduced or zero under a trade agreement if the goods meet the rules of origin |

|
Import VAT |
VAT on imported goods, normally at the standard rate |
Usually reclaimable by VAT-registered businesses; it still affects cash unless accounted for on the VAT return |

|
Clearance and port charges |
Customs broker fees, terminal handling, documentation |
Often several separate small invoices; easy to forget |

|
Inland delivery |
From port or airport to your warehouse or fulfilment centre |
Can be significant for small shipments |

|
Other |
Pre-shipment inspection, currency exchange costs, financing the stock in transit |
Not always in the unit cost, but real |

## How import duty is worked out

- **Find the commodity code.** Every product has a code that sets its duty rate. See GOV.UK's guidance on [finding commodity codes](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/finding-commodity-codes-for-imports-or-exports).

- **Look up the rate** for that code and the country of origin on the [UK Trade Tariff](https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff).

- **Work out the customs value.** Usually the price paid plus the cost of transport and insurance to the UK border. GOV.UK explains [how to value imports](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/how-to-value-your-imports-for-customs-duty-and-trade-statistics).

- **Check for preferences.** Goods from a country with a UK trade agreement may pay less or no duty if they meet the [rules of origin](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-your-goods-meet-the-rules-of-origin).

- **Duty = customs value × duty rate.** Import VAT is then charged on the customs value plus duty and certain other costs.

VAT-registered businesses can usually account for import VAT on their VAT return rather than paying it at the border; see GOV.UK on
[accounting for import VAT on your VAT return](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-when-you-can-account-for-import-vat-on-your-vat-return).
Different arrangements apply to some goods moving into Northern Ireland, so check current GOV.UK guidance if you sell there. A customs broker or freight forwarder can confirm codes and costs for your shipments.

## Worked example: from factory price to landed cost

Illustrative figures only. A start-up imports 1,000 units of a small product at £6.00 each FOB (the supplier pays to load the goods onto the ship).
The goods share a container (a "less than container load" shipment). The duty rate is assumed at 4 per cent; the real rate depends on the commodity code and origin.

|
Step |
Calculation |
Amount |

|
Goods (FOB) |
1,000 × £6.00 |
£6,000.00 |

|
Sea freight and insurance |
Quoted by the forwarder |
£760.00 |

|
Customs value |
Goods + freight + insurance |
£6,760.00 |

|
Import duty |
4% × £6,760 |
£270.40 |

|
Clearance and UK delivery |
Broker fee + haulage |
£300.00 |

|
Landed cost (excluding reclaimable VAT) |
Total ÷ 1,000 units |
£7,330.40, or about £7.33 a unit |

|
Import VAT (reclaimable) |
20% × (customs value + duty), simplified |
£1,406.08 |

Illustrative figures only. Each bar starts where the last ended; together they make the landed cost, about 22 per cent above the factory price. Import VAT is not shown because a VAT-registered business can normally reclaim it.

The landed cost is about 22 per cent above the factory price. On a shipment half the size, the fixed charges (clearance, delivery and the minimum freight charge) would weigh more heavily per unit.
The VAT line is simplified: in practice some costs after the border, such as onward delivery, can also count towards the value import VAT is charged on.
The [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) includes freight and duty in the unit cost.

**Practical rule:**
compare suppliers on landed cost, not factory price. A cheaper quote on EXW terms from further away can cost more on arrival than a dearer quote delivered to your door.

## Common mistakes

**Using the factory price in the business case.**
Margins calculated on the quote, not the landed cost, are too high.

**Guessing the duty rate.**
Rates differ widely between commodity codes; look the code up or ask a broker.

**Forgetting the small charges.**
Port handling, documentation and broker fees add up, especially on small shipments.

**Ignoring cash timing.**
Freight, duty and VAT can be due before the goods are sold; plan them in the cash flow.

**Comparing quotes on different Incoterms.**
Put every quote on the same delivered basis before comparing; [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) shows how, with tooling and cash included.

## FAQ

### What is landed cost?

The total cost of getting a product from the supplier to your warehouse ready to sell: the goods, packaging, freight, insurance, import duty, customs and port charges and inland delivery, plus import VAT if you cannot reclaim it. It is the figure to use in margins and pricing, not the factory price.

### How is UK import duty calculated?

Find the commodity code for the product, look up the duty rate for that code and the country of origin on the UK Trade Tariff, and apply it to the customs value, which is usually the price paid plus transport and insurance to the UK border. Trade agreements can reduce the rate if the goods meet the rules of origin.

### Do I have to pay VAT on imported goods?

Import VAT is normally charged, but VAT-registered businesses can usually reclaim it and can often account for it on their VAT return rather than paying at the border. It still matters for cash planning, and non-registered businesses bear it as a cost.

### How much does freight add to the cost of a product?

It depends on size, weight, distance, mode and shipment size. Sea freight is usually cheapest per unit but slow; air and courier are much faster and more expensive. Fixed charges make small shipments relatively expensive, so get forwarder quotes for your expected shipment sizes.

### What is the difference between FOB and landed cost?

A FOB price covers the goods loaded onto the ship at the origin port. Landed cost adds everything after that: sea freight, insurance, duty, customs and port charges, and delivery to your warehouse.

Title: Looks-Like vs Works-Like Prototypes

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers deciding what their next prototype should prove

# Looks-like vs works-like prototypes: what each is for and when to combine them

What a looks-like prototype and a works-like prototype each answer, why they are usually built separately at first, when to bring them together into an integrated prototype, the methods commonly used for each, and how to brief them so the build answers the right question.

Quick answer

## A looks-like prototype tests appearance, size, ergonomics and how people react; a works-like prototype tests whether the function, mechanism or electronics actually work.

Building them separately early on lets each be quick and cheap, because neither has to do the other's job. Once both have answered their questions, combine them into an integrated (often called alpha or engineering) prototype that looks and works like the product,
then test that against your requirements before design freeze. Never present a looks-like model as if it works.

## Contents

- What each prototype answers

- When to build them separately and when to combine

- What each typically costs in effort

- Typical methods for each

- How they feed into testing and design freeze

- How to brief a looks-like or works-like build

- Worked example: a countertop kitchen gadget

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What each prototype answers

The names describe the job, not the quality. A looks-like prototype is built to be seen and handled; a works-like prototype is built to be run, loaded and measured.
Each answers a different kind of question, and each can be convincing in its own area while saying nothing about the other.

|
|
Looks-like |
Works-like |

|
Main question |
Is the size, shape, finish and feel right, and do people want it? |
Does the mechanism, electronics or process do what it must? |

|
Typical tests |
User reactions, grip and reach, how it sits in its setting, colour and finish choices, photography |
Performance against requirements, forces and speeds, power use, heat, sensor readings, early life cycling |

|
What it usually looks like |
The final product, often hollow or with dummy buttons and screens |
A bench rig, an open frame or a rough box with exposed wiring |

|
What it cannot tell you |
Whether anything inside will fit, work or survive |
Whether people will like it, understand it or find it comfortable |

Some products lean heavily one way. A handheld tool whose value is comfort may need several looks-like rounds and only a simple works-like check; a sensing device with a plain enclosure may be almost entirely a works-like problem.
[How many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) explains how to group questions into rounds.

## When to build them separately and when to combine

Early in development, separate streams are usually faster. A works-like rig can be rearranged on a bench without worrying about a housing, and a looks-like model can be reshaped without rerouting wires.
When one stream finds a problem, only that stream has to change.

Each stream can iterate on its own until it has answered its question. Merging them too early means every change in one forces rework in the other.

Combine them into an integrated prototype when:

- **Both streams have answered their main questions.** The mechanism or electronics work on the bench, and users have accepted the form.

- **The remaining risks are about interaction.** Fit, heat inside the enclosure, sealing, [cable routing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cables-wiring-and-connectors-inside-a-product.html), assembly order and how the product behaves in a drop only show up when form and function share the same space.

- **You need realistic use.** User trials of how the product is set up, carried and cleaned need something that both looks and works roughly like the real thing.

Some simple products can combine from the start, for example a mostly mechanical product with few parts where the housing is the mechanism. That is reasonable when the function is low risk; it becomes expensive when a failure could come from either side and the team cannot tell which.

## What each typically costs in effort

These are qualitative comparisons, not prices. Effort depends heavily on size, complexity and how much finish is needed.

|
Build |
Where the effort goes |
Typical relative effort |

|
Rough looks-like |
Quick CAD, printing or foam, little finishing |
Low |

|
Finished looks-like |
Surface preparation, paint, texture, graphics and assembly |
Moderate to high; finishing time often exceeds making time |

|
Works-like rig |
Off-the-shelf parts, wiring, firmware and test fixtures |
Low to moderate, rising with electronics and software |

|
Integrated (alpha) |
Packaging everything into the real form, custom circuit boards, detailed CAD and tolerances |
High; usually the most expensive round before production-intent parts |

Budget these rounds in the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html), and see
[how much it costs to develop a hardware product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html) for the wider picture.

## Typical methods for each

|
Method |
Common use |

|
3D printing |
Both: fast looks-like forms and functional brackets, housings and test parts. Resin printing gives finer surfaces for looks-like models; printed parts may not behave like the production material. See [choosing a 3D printing process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html). |

|
[CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) |
Works-like parts that need precision, strength or real materials; high-quality looks-like models when finish matters. |

|
Vacuum casting |
Small batches of looks-like or integrated housings in production-like plastics, for user trials or field tests. |

|
Off-the-shelf development boards |
Works-like electronics: proving sensors, power, connectivity and firmware before designing a custom circuit board (see [electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html)). |

|
Card, foam and existing products |
Very early looks-like checks of size and grip, and quick works-like hacks using parts from existing products. |

[Prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html) compares these routes in more detail, and the
[Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html) suggests a method for each build from quantity, fidelity, urgency and budget.

## How they feed into testing and design freeze

Each stream should end with evidence, not just a model. Looks-like rounds produce user feedback and agreed form decisions; works-like rounds produce measurements against requirements.
Write both down against your [requirements](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html) so the integrated prototype starts from settled answers.
[Usability testing a prototype](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html) explains how to run user sessions on either kind of build without leading people.

The integrated prototype is where fuller testing starts: function in the real enclosure, heat, drop, sealing, usability and early durability.
Problems found here are still cheap compared with changes after tooling. Once production-intent parts pass, the design can be frozen under [change control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html).
[Product testing and validation plans](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) explains which tests belong at each stage, and the
[Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html) turns requirements into a test list.

**Practical rule:**
test function in a material and geometry close enough to production that the result means something. A printed snap fit or hinge can fail, or pass, for reasons that will not apply to a moulded part.

## How to brief a looks-like or works-like build

Whether the build is in-house, with a model maker or with a design consultancy, a short written brief avoids paying for the wrong kind of quality:

- **The question it must answer**, and the result that would change your plan.

- **Which type it is**: looks-like, works-like or integrated, and what it does not need to do.

- **Fidelity needed**: which surfaces, colours and details must be right, and which can be rough.

- **What it will go through**: user sessions, bench tests, drops, photography or a demonstration.

- **Quantity, deadline and budget**, and whether more copies may be needed for trials.

- **Inputs supplied**: CAD revision, requirements, reference products and any parts you will provide.

[Working with a product design consultancy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/working-with-a-product-design-consultancy.html) covers briefing outside help more generally, and
[industrial design vs engineering design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/industrial-design-vs-engineering-design.html) explains who usually leads each kind of build.

## Worked example: a countertop kitchen gadget

Illustrative example. A small team is developing a mains-powered countertop gadget with a motor, a heating element, two buttons and a removable bowl.
Their two biggest unknowns are whether the motor and heater can reach the required performance together, and whether people find the bowl easy to lift out and clean.

|
Build |
Question |
Method |
Outcome |

|
Works-like rig |
Do the motor and heater meet the performance target without overheating? |
Off-the-shelf motor and heater on a frame, development board, temperature logging |
Motor choice confirmed; heater needs more space for airflow |

|
Looks-like models |
Is the size right on a worktop, and can users lift and clean the bowl? |
Two printed, lightly finished variants with a dummy bowl |
Users prefer the taller variant; bowl handle enlarged |

|
Integrated (alpha) |
Does everything fit, stay cool enough and survive normal handling? |
Printed housing around the chosen components, first custom circuit board |
Airflow space from the rig carried into the taller form; ready for production-intent detailing |

Because the airflow problem was found on a bench rig, the fix was a change to a frame rather than to a finished housing. Because the form was settled separately, the integrated round started with fewer open questions.
For a mains-powered product the team would also plan electrical safety and EMC checks; see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html).

## Common mistakes

**Polishing the looks-like too early.**
A painted, perfect model of an untested form is slow and costly, and it makes the team reluctant to change it when users push back.

**Testing function in the wrong material.**
Printed plastics, machined blocks and moulded parts differ in strength, stiffness and surface. Treat early functional results on substitute materials as indicative, and re-test in production-like material.

**Showing investors a looks-like as if it works.**
It damages trust when found out, and it can set expectations about timing and readiness the team cannot meet. Say clearly what each model is, and show the works-like evidence alongside.

**Merging the streams too soon.**
An integrated prototype that fails is harder to diagnose than separate tests, and every fix touches both form and function.

**Leaving the works-like without space limits.**
A rig that only works with components spread across a bench may never fit the chosen form. Give the works-like stream a rough space envelope early.

## Decision rules

- **If the biggest risk is "does it work?"**, build a works-like rig first and keep appearance rough.

- **If the biggest risk is "will people want or use it?"**, build a looks-like model first, even a rough one.

- **If the function is low risk and the parts are few**, a combined prototype from the start can be reasonable.

- **Merge into an integrated prototype** when both streams have answered their main questions and the remaining risks are about fit and interaction.

- **Only freeze the design** after production-intent parts pass the tests that matter, not after a looks-like model is approved.

## Next steps

- List your open questions and mark each as looks-like, works-like or interaction.

- Plan how each build will be tested with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- See where these rounds sit in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a looks-like and a works-like prototype?

A looks-like prototype shows the appearance, size, finish and feel of a product so you can test ergonomics and user reaction, but it may not function. A works-like prototype proves the function, mechanism or electronics but may look nothing like the final product.

### Should I build a looks-like or a works-like prototype first?

Build first whichever answers your riskiest question. If you are unsure the product can work, start with a works-like rig; if the main doubt is whether people will want or be able to use it, start with a looks-like model. Many teams run both in parallel.

### What is an integrated or alpha prototype?

A prototype that combines the looks-like form and the works-like internals into one unit, so you can test fit, heat, assembly and real use together. It usually comes after both separate streams have answered their main questions, and before production-intent parts.

### Can I show a looks-like prototype to investors?

Yes, as long as you say clearly that it shows appearance only, and back it up with evidence from works-like testing. Presenting a looks-like model as a working product damages trust and can set expectations you cannot meet.

### Can one prototype be both looks-like and works-like?

Yes, for simple, low-risk products, or once both streams have settled their main questions. Early on, combining them usually makes each change slower and failures harder to diagnose.

Title: Managing Heat in a Product Enclosure

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small teams putting electronics, batteries or motors inside a housing

# Managing heat in a product enclosure: giving heat a path out

Why heat matters in a physical product, where it comes from, how it moves in plain terms, the trade-off between venting and sealing, simple first estimates you can do on paper, and how to test temperatures on a prototype before the design is frozen.

Quick answer

## Almost all the power your product uses ends up as heat, and that heat has to find a way out of the housing. Design that path on purpose rather than hoping the enclosure copes.

List the parts that get warm and how much power each one uses, then give the hottest ones a solid route to the outside: a thermal pad to the case wall, a metal lid or panel, more surface area, or vents if the product does not need to be sealed.
A rough estimate of temperature rise (power multiplied by thermal resistance) tells you early whether you have a problem. Then measure a prototype at its worst-case temperature and load, and check the results against the component datasheets and the touch-temperature limits in your product's safety standard.

## Contents

- Why heat matters

- Where the heat comes from

- How heat moves, in plain terms

- What that means for the design

- Venting versus sealing

- Heat sinks and spreaders

- Fans, and when to avoid them

- Simple first estimates

- Testing temperatures on a prototype

- Touch temperature

- Worked example: a sealed outdoor sensor

- Common mistakes

## Why heat matters

A circuit that runs happily on an open bench can run much hotter inside a housing, as the [electronics guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) points out. Heat causes problems in four ways:

- **Component ratings.** Every electronic part has a maximum operating temperature in its datasheet. Near it, parts may slow down, shut off, drift or wear out early.

- **Battery temperature limits.** The cell maker sets temperature ranges for charging and for use. The charging range is often narrower, and a battery next to a warm charger can be pushed outside it.

- **Touch temperature.** A surface that is safe for the electronics may still be too hot to hold; see below.

- **Plastic softening and creep.** Plastics lose stiffness as they warm, and under a steady load, such as a screw boss, they slowly deform. Warm plastic creeps faster. The [plastics guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) covers choosing a grade with enough heat resistance.

## Where the heat comes from

Almost all the electrical power a product uses becomes heat inside it. The usual sources are:

- **Processors and radio modules**, especially when busy or transmitting.

- **Voltage regulators.** A linear regulator turns the whole voltage drop into heat; a switching one wastes less.

- **Battery chargers** and the battery itself while charging.

- **Motors and motor drivers**, especially when stalled or working hard.

- **LEDs**, which turn much of their power into heat, not light.

- **Sunlight.** Sunshine on a dark housing can add more heat than the electronics do, and it never appears on the circuit diagram.

Ask your electronics engineer for each part's power in its worst realistic mode, not the average. That list starts every estimate below.

## How heat moves, in plain terms

Heat always flows from hotter to cooler, in three ways:

- **Conduction** is heat passing through solid material, or between two surfaces pressed together. Metals conduct well; plastics and still air conduct poorly, so even a small air gap insulates.

- **Convection** is heat carried away by moving air or liquid. Warm air rises, so even without a fan there is a gentle flow over a warm surface.

- **Radiation** is infrared given off by any warm surface, and received from the sun.

In a closed housing, heat conducts from a component into the board, crosses air or a pad to the wall, passes through it, then leaves the outer surface by convection and radiation. Each step resists the flow, and the slowest one tends to set the temperature.

Section through a sealed housing, not to scale. A thermal pad and a boss on the lid give the hot chip a solid conduction path to the aluminium lid, which then loses heat to the air. Sunlight on the lid works against it.

## What that means for the design

- **Give hot parts a thermal path to the housing.** Connect the hottest component to the case wall or a metal part through solid material, rather than letting heat soak into trapped air. Board copper also spreads heat sideways.

- **Use thermal pads or gap fillers to bridge gaps.** These soft, conductive pads fill the air gap between a component and the case. The gap must stay within the pad's range across your [tolerances](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html).

- **Metal versus plastic housings.** A metal housing, or just a metal lid, spreads heat over its surface far better than plastic, which tends to leave a hot spot. Metal has trade-offs, such as blocking radio; see [choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html).

- **Surface area.** The outer surface hands heat to the air, so more area, ribs or fins lower the temperature.

- **Colour and finish.** Outdoors, a light colour or a shade often helps more than any internal change. A matt or [anodised](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) finish radiates better than shiny bare metal.

## Venting versus sealing

Vents let warm air out and cool air in: cheap and effective. Put inlets low and outlets high so rising warm air does the work, away from where a hand or surface could block them.

But every opening also lets in water and dust. If the product must be [sealed against water and dust](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html), heat must leave by conduction through the walls, so the thermal path and housing material matter much more. A membrane vent equalises pressure as the air inside warms and cools, but moves very little heat. Decide early whether the product is vented or sealed; they lead to different designs.

## Heat sinks and spreaders

A **heat sink** is finned metal, usually aluminium, fixed to a hot component to give it more surface area. It needs moving air around it, so it suits vented products; in a small sealed box it mostly warms the trapped air.

A **heat spreader** is a plate that moves heat sideways from a small hot spot to a larger area. A metal lid, chassis or bracket can do this alongside its structural job. In sealed products, the best heat sink is often the housing itself.

## Fans, and when to avoid them

A fan moves far more heat than natural convection, and some products need one. For most small products, try hard to avoid it:

- **Noise.** Users notice it, and it changes as the fan ages.

- **Dust.** A fan pulls dust in, where it coats the board and blocks vents.

- **A failure point.** Its bearings wear out, and its life may set the product's life.

It also needs openings, which rules it out for most sealed products. Reduce power and improve the conduction path first. If a fan is still needed, plan for filters, cleaning and a [replaceable fan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html), and make the product protect itself if it stops.

## Simple first estimates

You can catch most heat problems with two simple ideas and a calculator.

**Power in equals heat out.** Once the product has settled, all the power going in leaves as heat. If the board uses 2 W, the housing must shed 2 W, plus any sunshine.

**Temperature rise follows thermal resistance.** Each heat path has a thermal resistance, **Rθ**, in degrees Celsius per watt (°C/W): how many degrees warmer one end gets per watt flowing through it.

Temperature rise ΔT (°C) = power P (W) × thermal resistance Rθ (°C/W)

Resistances in a chain add together. The result is a rise above the surrounding air, so add your worst-case ambient temperature.

**Illustrative example, round numbers.**
A regulator uses 1 W and its datasheet gives a thermal resistance from the chip to the surrounding air of 50 °C/W on a typical board. ΔT = 1 × 50 = 50 °C. At an ambient of 40 °C, the chip would reach about 40 + 50 = 90 °C. Compare that with the datasheet maximum, with a margin.

**Check the datasheets.** Datasheets usually give thermal resistances, such as junction to case or junction to ambient, and the test board they were measured on. That rarely matches your housing, so treat them as a starting point. Pad datasheets give a figure too. The estimates are rough, but show quickly whether you are clear or need a change.

## Testing temperatures on a prototype

Estimates point the way; measurements decide. Build temperature tests into your [test and validation plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html), on a prototype with the real housing material, walls, pads and seals.

- **Thermocouples on the hottest parts.** Small wire sensors fixed to the processor, regulator, charger, battery and the housing above them, recorded on a logger.

- **Worst-case ambient and load.** Test at the highest ambient the product must work in, with the heaviest realistic load, such as charging while transmitting, and in sun for outdoor products. A temperature chamber helps.

- **Steady state.** Keep going until readings stop rising, which can take an hour or more.

- **A thermal camera as an aid.** It finds hot spots quickly and shows where to put thermocouples, but its readings depend on surface finish, so confirm with thermocouples.

## Touch temperature

How hot a surface may safely get depends on the material, how long it is touched and the type of product. Metal feels hotter than plastic at the same temperature because it conducts heat into the skin faster.
The limits come from your product's applicable safety standard, so this guide does not quote them. Identify that standard early, as described in [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html), and design to it from the first prototype. A metal lid that cools the electronics can make the outside hotter, so check both.

## Worked example: a sealed outdoor sensor

Illustrative example, with round numbers chosen to show the method. A start-up is developing a sealed outdoor sensor with a 2 W circuit board inside a moulded plastic housing. The product must work in shaded outdoor air up to 40 °C, and the team has set a target of keeping the hottest component below 65 °C, taken from its datasheet with a margin.

**Before.** The board sits in still air inside the sealed plastic box. Heat must warm the trapped air, cross the plastic wall and leave the outer surface. The team estimates the whole path at about 25 °C/W, to be confirmed on a prototype.
ΔT = 2 W × 25 °C/W = 50 °C. Component temperature ≈ 40 + 50 = 90 °C, well above the 65 °C target.

**After.** The lid is changed to aluminium, about 100 × 100 mm, with a boss on its underside and a thermal pad pressing on the hottest chip. The path is now: pad and contact surfaces about 1 °C/W, then the lid's outer surface to the air.
For a surface in still air, engineers often use a rough combined convection and radiation figure of around 10 W per square metre per °C. The lid's area is 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01 m², so its resistance to air is about 1 ÷ (10 × 0.01) = 10 °C/W.
Total ≈ 1 + 10 = 11 °C/W. ΔT = 2 W × 11 °C/W = 22 °C. Component temperature ≈ 40 + 22 = 62 °C, just under the target.

|
Design |
Rθ |
Rise |
At 40 °C |

|
Plastic, no thermal path |
25 °C/W |
50 °C |
90 °C |

|
Aluminium lid and pad |
11 °C/W |
22 °C |
62 °C |

Some heat still leaves through the plastic walls, so reality should be slightly better. But 62 °C leaves little margin, and the estimate assumed shade. The team chooses a light-coloured lid finish, checks the lid against the touch limits in their safety standard, and plans a thermocouple test in sun before freezing the design.

## Common mistakes

**Testing the board on the bench.**
Open-air temperatures say little about a closed housing. Measure inside a representative enclosure.

**Using average power.**
Heat problems happen in the worst case, such as charging while transmitting on a hot day. Estimate and test at that load.

**Forgetting the sun.**
A dark housing in sunshine can gain more heat than the electronics produce. Choose the colour and test outdoors.

**Leaving an air gap.**
A small gap between a hot part and the case wall acts as insulation. Bridge it with a pad sized for the tolerance range.

**Treating touch temperature as an afterthought.**
Fixing a hot outer surface after tooling is expensive. Check the limits in your standard from the start.

## Next steps

- List the parts that get warm and their worst-case power, and add them up.

- Decide whether the product is vented or sealed, and sketch the path heat will take to the outside.

- Do a rough ΔT = P × Rθ estimate for the hottest part at your highest ambient temperature, using the [Enclosure Temperature Rise Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/temperature-rise-estimator.html).

- Add worst-case temperature tests to your plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Identify your safety standard, and its touch-temperature limits, with the [Certification Readiness Checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html).

## FAQ

### Do I need thermal simulation software?

Not usually at the start. A list of power figures and a simple ΔT = P × Rθ estimate show whether you have a problem. Simulation becomes worthwhile for products that run hot, are tightly packed or must be sealed with little margin, and its results should still be checked with measurements on a prototype.

### Is a metal housing always cooler than a plastic one?

Inside, usually yes, because metal spreads and conducts heat far better. But a metal surface can feel hotter to touch, can block radio signals and, if dark, can absorb a lot of sunlight. A metal lid or panel on a plastic housing is often a good compromise.

### Can I seal a product that gets warm?

Yes, but the heat must then leave by conduction through the walls. Give the hot parts a solid path to the housing with thermal pads, use metal for at least part of the enclosure if needed, and add a membrane vent so the seal is not strained as the air inside warms and cools.

### Where do I find the touch-temperature limits for my product?

In the safety standard that applies to your product type. They vary with the material, how long the surface is touched and the kind of product, so identify your standard early through the certification process and design to it from the first prototype.

### How long should a temperature test run?

Until the readings stop rising and stay level, which is called steady state. For a small product that can take an hour or more. Run it at your highest expected ambient temperature and heaviest realistic load.
