Title: Manufacturing and Cost for Hardware Products

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders, engineers and product teams choosing how a product will be made

# Manufacturing and cost: how physical products are made, and what drives the price

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about making a physical product: which processes suit which volumes,
what actually sets the unit cost, when tooling is worth paying for, and how to get to a number you can plan around.
Each section links to a deeper guide or a free tool.

Quick answer

## Unit cost is materials, process time and labour, plus tooling shared across the volume you will really sell.

Unit cost ≈ materials + process time × machine rate + assembly labour + packaging + (tooling ÷ lifetime volume) + supplier overhead and margin

The manufacturing route you choose decides which of those terms dominates. Low-volume processes such as 3D printing and CNC machining
need little or no tooling but cost more per part. High-volume processes such as injection moulding and die casting need expensive tooling
but make each part cheaply. The right route is the one that fits your realistic volume, how settled the design is, and how much cash you can commit before you sell.

## Contents

- Manufacturing processes compared

- How volume changes cost

- What drives unit cost

- Tooling decisions

- Worked example: one enclosure part, three routes

- From factory price to landed cost

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## Manufacturing processes compared

Most physical products are made from a handful of process families. The table gives typical working ranges, not hard limits:
the right answer for a given part depends on its size, material, tolerances and finish, and a supplier quote will always beat a rule of thumb.

|
Process |
Typical volumes |
Upfront tooling |
Cost per part |
Typical use |

|
3D printing ([FDM](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html), SLA, SLS, MJF) |
One-offs to a few hundred |
None |
High, and roughly flat with volume |
Prototypes, complex low-volume parts, jigs and fixtures |

|
CNC machining |
One-offs to low thousands |
Fixtures and programming only |
High, falling slowly as set-up is shared |
Metal parts, precise features, [works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) |

|
Vacuum (urethane) casting |
Tens to a few hundred |
Low: a master pattern and silicone moulds, each good for a limited number of shots |
Medium |
Production-looking prototypes, pilot batches, early sales units |

|
Injection moulding, aluminium tool |
Hundreds to tens of thousands |
Medium |
Low |
Bridge production while demand and design settle |

|
Injection moulding, steel tool |
Tens of thousands to millions |
High |
Lowest |
Stable designs at volume |

|
Sheet metal (laser cutting and bending) |
One-offs to tens of thousands |
None for laser and press-brake work; press tools only at high volume |
Medium |
Enclosures, brackets, chassis (see [sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html)) |

|
Vacuum forming and thermoforming |
Tens to thousands |
Low to medium |
Low to medium |
Covers, trays, large thin shells, packaging inserts |

|
Die casting |
Thousands upwards |
High |
Low |
Metal housings and structural parts at volume |

Processes are not either-or for the life of a product. Many products start in 3D printing or vacuum casting, move to an aluminium
tool for the first production runs, and only commit to hardened steel tooling once sales and design have settled. How tooling works is covered in [injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html). That sequence is described in
[the risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) and
[prototyping versus production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html).

## How volume changes cost

Every route has a fixed part (tooling, fixtures, set-up, programming) and a variable part (material, machine time, labour per unit).
Cost per part is the fixed part divided by the number of parts, plus the variable part. Low-tooling routes keep the fixed part small,
so they win at low volume. Tooled routes have a large fixed part but a much smaller variable part, so they win once volume is high enough.

3D printing (no tooling, about £14 a part)
CNC machining (£300 set-up, about £9 a part)
Injection moulding (£16,000 tool, about £1.20 a part)
Illustrative figures for one small plastic part, not quotes. The shape of the curves is the point: tooling is a fixed cost that only becomes cheap when it is shared across enough parts.

The crossover point is a simple calculation: **tooling cost ÷ (cost per part on the cheaper-to-start route − cost per part on the tooled route)**.
The [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) draws these curves for your own figures, and
[when does injection moulding become cheaper?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) explains why the break-even line alone is not enough to decide.

## What drives unit cost

The same product can cost very different amounts depending on decisions made in design. These are the drivers that most often move the number:

|
Driver |
Why it matters |
What usually reduces it |

|
Part count |
Every part needs its own tool or set-up, its own stock, and assembly time |
Combine parts, use snap fits or living hinges where they suit the load and life |

|
Material |
Material price per kilogram varies many-fold between commodity and engineering grades |
Choose the least demanding grade that meets the real requirement (see [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html)); reduce part mass |

|
Cycle time |
In moulding and casting, thick sections cool slowly and machine time is charged by the hour |
Even, appropriate wall thickness; ribs instead of solid sections |

|
Tolerances |
Tight tolerances need slower processes, extra operations and more inspection |
Hold tight tolerances only on features that genuinely need them |

|
Finishes |
Painting, plating, texturing and printing add operations, handling and scrap |
Moulded-in colour and texture; fewer cosmetic surfaces |

|
Assembly |
Labour is paid on every unit, for the life of the product |
Fewer fasteners, self-locating parts, one assembly direction (see [estimating assembly time](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html)) |

|
Yield and scrap |
Rejected parts are paid for by the good ones |
Robust design margins and a stable, well-documented process |

|
Order quantity |
Suppliers price set-up and minimum order quantities into small batches |
Plan batch sizes against cash, storage and demand rather than unit price alone |

**Practical rule:**
most of a product's cost is decided in design, long before a factory quotes it. Changes are cheap on a CAD model, expensive on a prototype and very expensive once a tool is cut.

## Tooling decisions

Tooling is often one of the largest single commitments between prototype and launch, and one that is easy to make too early.
A few principles help:

- **Tool life should match the plan.** As a broad rule of thumb, aluminium injection-mould tools suit volumes in the thousands to tens of thousands of shots, and hardened steel tools suit hundreds of thousands or more. Actual life depends heavily on the plastic, the part geometry and how the tool is built, so ask the toolmaker to state it.

- **Expect modifications.** First samples (often called T1) rarely come off a new tool perfect. Budget time and money for at least one round of changes before production approval.

- **Agree ownership in writing.** Make sure the contract says who owns the tool, where it is kept, what maintenance is included, and how you can move it to another supplier.

- **Check the design before quoting.** Run the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) on your CAD so the tool is quoted on a mouldable design.

- **Tool when the design has stopped moving.** If [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html), certification or a key component could still change the geometry, a cheaper bridge route usually costs less overall than modifying a production tool.

- **Count the whole set.** A product with eight moulded parts may need eight tools (or multi-cavity and family tools with their own trade-offs), plus assembly and test fixtures.

The [Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html) helps decide whether to tool now, bridge first or stay with low-volume processes,
based on demand confidence, design maturity and cash.

## Worked example: one enclosure part, three routes

Illustrative figures only. A start-up needs a palm-sized plastic enclosure part. Quotes come back at about £14 a part for SLS 3D printing,
about £9 a part plus £300 set-up for CNC machining, and £16,000 for an injection-mould tool with parts at about £1.20 each.
The team expects to sell 600 units in the first year and is fairly confident of 3,000 over three years.

|
Volume |
3D printing |
CNC machining |
Injection moulding |

|
100 parts |
£1,400 (£14.00 each) |
£1,200 (£12.00 each) |
£16,120 (£161.20 each) |

|
600 parts |
£8,400 (£14.00 each) |
£5,700 (£9.50 each) |
£16,720 (£27.87 each) |

|
1,250 parts |
£17,500 (£14.00 each) |
£11,550 (£9.24 each) |
£17,500 (£14.00 each) |

|
3,000 parts |
£42,000 (£14.00 each) |
£27,300 (£9.10 each) |
£19,600 (£6.53 each) |

On paper, moulding beats 3D printing at about 1,250 parts and beats CNC machining at about 2,000. But the team only has confident demand for 600 units this year,
and the enclosure may still change after user testing. A sensible plan would be to launch on the low-tooling route, keep the design stable for a few months of real use,
then tool once the three-year volume looks real. The cash that is not tied up in a tool can fund stock and marketing instead.
That is the judgement the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) and the
[injection moulding break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) are designed to support.
To see the same kind of decision made for one product across every stage, with the figures carried from tool to tool, read the
[walkthrough from idea to manufacture](https://oriondesign.xyz/walkthrough/).

## From factory price to landed cost

The price a supplier quotes is rarely what a unit costs you. Depending on the terms of the quote, you may still need to add packaging,
freight, insurance, import duty and VAT, customs brokerage, inbound handling, and warehousing before a unit is ready to sell.
For parts and products made overseas these can add a substantial share on top of the ex-works price, so build them into the cost model from the start rather than discovering them on the first invoice.
For duty rates and import VAT, use the official [UK Trade Tariff](https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff) rather than estimates.

The [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) builds the full unit cost, and
[how to estimate manufacturing cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html) walks through each line. [Landed cost explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) covers freight, duty and import VAT in detail.

## Common mistakes

**Choosing the process by unit price alone.**
The cheapest part at 100,000 units is often the most expensive at 1,000. Use the volume you will realistically sell, not the volume you hope for.

**Tooling before the design is stable.**
Tool modifications cost time and money, and some changes cannot be made to an existing tool at all.

**Forgetting assembly, packaging and logistics.**
These are paid on every unit and are often larger than the difference between two part quotes.

**Tolerances copied from a default title block.**
Blanket tight tolerances raise cost on every feature. Specify what the function needs.

**Briefing suppliers with incomplete information.**
Quotes are only as good as the drawings, quantities and requirements you send. See
[the documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html).

## FAQ

### What is the cheapest way to manufacture a small number of products?

For tens to a few hundred units, processes with little or no tooling are usually cheapest overall: 3D printing, CNC machining, vacuum casting, sheet metal fabrication or vacuum forming, depending on the part. The cost per part is higher, but you avoid paying for tooling that a small volume cannot recover.

### At what volume does injection moulding become worth it?

There is no single number. Divide the tooling cost by the saving per part compared with your low-volume route to find the break-even volume, then ask whether you are confident of selling well beyond it and whether the design is stable enough to tool. In this page's illustrative example it falls at about 1,250 parts against 3D printing; for your own part it depends on the tool cost and the saving per part, so work it out from real quotes.

### How is tooling cost included in the unit cost?

Spread it across the number of units you expect the tool to make for you, either over its expected life or over a planning horizon such as the first two or three years. In cash terms, though, tooling is paid up front, usually in stages, so it also belongs in the start-up budget and cash flow.

### What has the biggest effect on manufacturing cost?

Usually decisions made in design: the number of parts, the material, wall thickness and cycle time, tolerances, finishes and how easily the product assembles. Volume and the choice of process then decide how those decisions turn into a price.

### Should I manufacture in the UK or overseas?

Compare landed cost rather than the factory price: freight, duty, VAT, lead time, minimum order quantities, communication and the cost of quality problems all count. Local suppliers often suit prototypes, early batches and products that change often; overseas suppliers can suit stable products at higher volume.

# Manufacturing processes compared: volumes, tooling, cost and constraints

A side-by-side reference of common manufacturing processes, from 3D printing to injection moulding, comparing volumes, tooling, unit cost, lead time and design constraints in relative terms, with how to choose and when to move between them.

Quick answer

## Choose a process by volume, tooling budget, unit cost and the design features you need; low-volume processes avoid tooling but cost more per part.

At one-offs and small batches, 3D printing, CNC machining and vacuum casting avoid expensive tooling. As volumes grow, processes with tooling, such as injection moulding,
die casting and pressed sheet metal, bring the unit cost down but need investment and a stable design. The table compares common processes in relative terms;
real break points depend on the part, material and supplier, so use quotes to decide.

Relative, typical characteristics for planning, not quotes. Volumes and lead times vary widely by part size, complexity and supplier.

The interactive chart needs JavaScript. The sentence below gives the figures for 1,000 parts.
At 1,000 parts, with a £12,000 mould, injection moulding is cheapest at about £12.80 a part, against 3D printing £14.00, vacuum casting £16.75, CNC machining £22.25. In this example injection moulding becomes cheaper than 3D printing above about 909 parts; a cheaper mould moves that point lower.

Vacuum casting is rarely the cheapest option in a chart like this; it is chosen for moulding-like appearance and materials in small batches, before a production mould is justified.

## How to choose

- **Volume over the product's life,** not just the first order.

- **Design stability:** tooling locks in the design; keep flexible processes while it is still changing.

- **Cash:** tooling is paid up front; low-volume processes spread cost per part instead.

- **Features and quality:** surface finish, tolerances, materials and strength may rule processes in or out.

- **Lead time:** tooled processes take longer to the first part but are faster per part after.

**Practical rule:**
compare total cost (tooling plus unit cost times volume) at your realistic volumes, and remember that many products move from one process to another as they scale.

## Moving between processes

A common path is 3D printing for early prototypes, CNC or vacuum casting for pilot batches, then tooling once demand and design are stable.
Designing early with the final process in mind avoids redesign later; see [prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html).
The [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) shows where tooling pays back, and the
[Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html) suggests a route for each stage.
For a product's housing specifically, [choosing how to make an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-how-to-make-an-enclosure.html) narrows these options to the routes that suit enclosures.

## Common mistakes

**Choosing on unit cost alone.**
Tooling, minimum orders and lead time can outweigh a lower part price.

**Tooling too early.**
Design changes after tooling are slow and expensive.

**Designing for the prototype process.**
A part that prints well may not mould or machine well.

[Sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html)

This guide answers

Processes
Tooling
Volumes
Reference

## FAQ

### Which manufacturing process is cheapest?

It depends on volume. Processes without tooling, such as 3D printing and CNC machining, are usually cheapest for small quantities; tooled processes such as injection moulding become cheaper per part at higher volumes once tooling is paid for.

### When should I switch from 3D printing to injection moulding?

When the design is stable and expected volumes make the tooling cost worthwhile. Compare total cost, tooling plus unit cost times volume, at realistic volumes, and use quotes rather than rules of thumb.

### What is vacuum casting used for?

Making small batches of moulding-like parts from silicone moulds taken from a master pattern, often for [pilot runs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html), testing and pre-production samples.

### Is CNC machining suitable for production?

Yes, for low to medium volumes, precise metal parts and engineering plastics, as it needs no tooling. At higher volumes, tooled processes are usually cheaper per part.

### Why do lead times differ so much between processes?

Tooled processes need moulds or dies to be designed, made and tested before the first part, which takes weeks to months. Untooled processes can start within days but take longer per part.

Title: Mapping the Product Design Process

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders and teams planning the stages of a product development project

# Mapping the product design process.

Projects slow down when teams cannot see what should happen next. A process map helps prioritise discovery, prototyping, verification, industrialisation, and launch work based on the actual project context.

Quick answer

## A product design process map shows the stages from discovery to launch and which of them deserve emphasis now.

Stage emphasis = biggest open uncertainty + cost of getting it wrong + time available

Most hardware projects move through discovery, concept development, prototyping, verification, industrialisation and launch. The [idea-to-manufacture explainer](https://oriondesign.xyz/idea-to-manufacture/) covers each stage in turn, and the [walkthrough](https://oriondesign.xyz/walkthrough/) follows one product through all of them.
The stages overlap, and the time spent in each depends on product complexity, regulatory burden and how new the manufacturing route is.

No two hardware projects follow the exact same path, but almost all of them suffer when the team confuses stage pressure with process clarity.
Mapping the process makes dependencies visible before the schedule starts making bad decisions for you.

**Useful process rule:** the right next stage is defined by what uncertainty matters most, not by which activity feels most familiar to the team.

## The typical stages of hardware product development

|
Stage |
Main question |
Typical outputs |
Evidence to move on |

|
Discovery |
Is there a real problem worth solving, for whom? |
User research, problem statement, early requirements |
A specific user and buyer with a clear, repeated need |

|
Concept development |
Which approach best solves it? |
Sketches, rough models, concept selection matrix |
A chosen direction with its key risks named |

|
Prototyping and detailed design |
Does it work, and can it be made? |
CAD, works-like and [looks-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html), draft BOM |
Critical functions proven on representative prototypes |

|
Verification and validation |
Does it meet the specification, standards and user needs? |
Test plans, test reports, pre-compliance results |
Design passes testing with production-intent parts |

|
Industrialisation |
Can it be made repeatably at the right cost? |
DFM changes, tooling, supplier agreements, [pilot builds](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) |
Pilot run meets quality and yield targets |

|
Launch and support |
Can it be sold, delivered and supported? |
Production orders, packaging, service and spares plan |
Stable supply, returns and feedback being tracked |

Teams with electronics often describe the later stages as EVT, DVT and PVT: engineering validation, design validation and production validation builds.
The labels matter less than the principle. Each build should answer a defined question, and the next stage should not start in earnest until that question has a reasonable answer.

## What changes the process emphasis

- **Product complexity and system interactions.** More subsystems mean more integration work and more prototype loops.

- **Regulatory burden and verification load.** Products with mains power, radios, food contact or medical claims need compliance planning from the concept stage, not the end.

- **Manufacturing novelty and supply-chain learning.** A new process or a first-time supplier relationship needs more industrialisation time and earlier conversations.

- **Launch pressure.** Schedule compression pushes stages to overlap, which is manageable only if the team knows which overlaps carry the most risk.

## Illustrative example: two products, two maps

A low-complexity product with a long launch window can stay discovery and prototyping heavy for longer. A regulated product with manufacturing novelty may need earlier verification and industrialisation planning than the team expects.

Consider two illustrative projects. The first is a mechanical camping accessory made from two moulded parts and a stainless pin, with no electronics.
Its map puts weight on discovery and prototyping, because the main risks are whether users want it and whether it survives rough handling.
Verification is mostly drop and load testing, and industrialisation centres on one tooling decision.

The second is a mains-powered kitchen device with Wi-Fi. Here, electrical safety, EMC and radio requirements shape the electronics architecture, enclosure and labelling.
Its map should start compliance planning during concept development, run pre-compliance checks on prototypes, and allow more time for verification and supplier qualification.
Following the first project’s map would leave the second team discovering test failures after tooling has started.

## How to build a process map for your project

- List the open uncertainties: user need, technical function, cost, compliance, supply and demand.

- Rank them by the cost of getting each one wrong late in the project.

- Match each high-ranking uncertainty to the stage and activity that resolves it.

- Define a simple gate for each stage: the evidence needed before committing more money.

- Hold a short [design review](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html) at each gate and record the decision and actions.

- Plan the next three to six months in detail and the rest in outline only.

- Revisit the map at every gate, because the biggest uncertainty will change.

## Common process-mapping mistakes

**Treating the process as a straight line.** Real projects loop back. A failed test can send a team from verification back to detailed design, and the plan should expect that.

**Skipping discovery because the founder knows the user.** Personal experience is a good starting point, not a substitute for talking to other buyers.

**Leaving compliance to the end.** Late test failures are among the most expensive surprises in hardware because they can force changes to tooled parts.

**Starting tooling while verification is unresolved.** Tooling against an unproven design locks in geometry that may still need to change.

**Planning every stage in equal detail.** Detailed plans for stages a year away usually turn out wrong. Effort is better spent on the next gate.

A good process map does not predict the project. It makes the next decision obvious and the cost of skipping a stage visible.

## Turning the map into a working plan

The [Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html) helps teams convert those project signals into a clearer stage emphasis so the next 3-6 months of work become easier to plan.

If the team is still choosing between directions, read
[How engineers choose between concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html) first.
For the manufacturing side of the map, [The risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html)
explains how to stage the move from prototype to bridge to scale, and the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html)
helps pick the right build method for each stage. When the stages are clear, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html)
can pull timing, cost and milestones into one plan to share with the team or investors.

### Map the next phase of work

Use the process map to see which stages deserve emphasis now and which ones should wait.[Open Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html)

### Use concept selection before process detail

If the team is still debating options, narrow the concepts first so the process map is built around the right direction.[Open Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html)

Part of a hub

[Development and prototyping: the hub guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

Related tools

[Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html)

[Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html)

[Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html)

Typical questions

Product design process mapHardware development processProduct development stages

## FAQ

### What are the stages of the product design process?

For physical products the usual stages are discovery, concept development, prototyping and detailed design, verification and validation, industrialisation, and launch. In practice the stages overlap and loop back when testing reveals problems. The balance between them depends on the product’s complexity, regulation and manufacturing route.

### How long does it take to develop a physical product?

It varies widely. A simple mechanical product with a stable concept can often reach production in well under a year, while a connected or regulated electronic product commonly takes a year or more. Compliance testing, tooling lead times and the number of prototype loops are usually what decide the timeline.

### What do EVT, DVT and PVT mean?

They are common names for build stages in hardware development. EVT (engineering validation test) checks that the design works, DVT (design validation test) checks that production-intent parts meet the specification and standards, and PVT (production validation test) checks that the production line can make it repeatably.

### Is the product design process linear?

No. It is usually drawn as a sequence, but real projects iterate. Prototyping often sends teams back to concept decisions, and verification can send them back to detailed design. A good process map plans for those loops instead of pretending they will not happen.

### When should you start thinking about manufacturing?

From the concept stage. Choices about materials, part count and process shape cost and feasibility long before tooling is ordered. An early design for manufacture review is far cheaper than changing a design after it has been tooled.

Title: Minimum Order Quantities and Cash

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders planning and funding a first production order

# Minimum order quantities and cash: planning your first production order

Why suppliers set minimum order quantities, how much cash a first order really needs, how to compare a lower unit price with the stock it creates, and practical ways to negotiate and fund the first run.

Quick answer

## A minimum order quantity (MOQ) decides how much cash you must spend before you sell anything, so plan it alongside your sales forecast, not just your unit cost.

Suppliers set MOQs because each production run has set-up costs. Larger orders usually lower the unit price, but tie up cash in stock that may take months to sell.
Work out the cash needed for the first order, deposits, tooling, freight and duty, and compare it with realistic sales. Then negotiate: smaller first runs, staged deliveries,
shared materials or a higher unit price for a lower quantity are often possible.

## Why suppliers set MOQs

- **Set-up costs:** changing a mould, a print run or a production line takes time and creates scrap, which must be spread over enough units.

- **Material buying:** raw materials, colours and components are often bought in minimum quantities themselves.

- **Capacity:** small runs take up line time that could go to larger customers.

Understanding which reason applies tells you what to negotiate.

## The cash picture

The first production order is often the biggest single cash outlay in a hardware start-up. Add up:

|
Cost |
When it is usually paid |

|
Tooling |
Often in stages, for example on order and on sample approval |

|
Production deposit |
On order, commonly a share of the order value |

|
Production balance |
Before shipment or on delivery, depending on terms |

|
Freight, duty and import VAT |
On shipping and at import, before you can sell |

|
Packaging, inspection and storage |
Around production and after delivery |

Payment terms vary by supplier and relationship; agree them in writing. Then set the outlay against when sales actually arrive, with the
[Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html). Landed cost per unit comes from the
[Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html).

Illustrative figures only. A supplier quotes £6.00 a unit at an MOQ of 3,000 or £7.50 at 1,000. The larger order costs £18,000 against £7,500, before tooling, freight and duty.
If realistic sales are about 150 a month, 3,000 units is 20 months of stock: the lower unit price saves £4,500 but ties up £10,500 more cash for well over a year, with the risk of design changes or slow sales.
For many start-ups, the smaller order is the safer first step.

Illustrative figures from the example above, bars drawn to scale. The £4,500 unit-price saving costs £10,500 of extra cash, locked in stock for well over a year.

**Practical rule:**
compare the order with months of realistic sales, not with the unit price saving. Stock you cannot sell is cash you cannot use.

## How to negotiate a lower MOQ

- **Ask what drives the MOQ** and offer to solve that: use a standard colour or material the supplier already stocks.

- **Pay more per unit** for a smaller first run.

- **Commit to an annual volume** delivered in smaller call-off batches.

- **Pay for the set-up** separately, so the supplier is covered for a short run.

- **Reduce variants:** fewer colours and sizes at launch means larger quantities of each.

- **Choose the right process:** some processes suit low volumes better. The [Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html) and [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) help compare options.

## Funding the first order

Pre-orders and [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) can fund production with customer money while also testing demand; see the [Crowdfunding Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/crowdfunding-planner.html).
Other options include trade or stock finance, retailer orders with agreed payment terms, and grants or investment; see
[funding routes in the UK and Northern Ireland](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-routes-uk-northern-ireland.html).

## Common mistakes

**Chasing the lowest unit price.**
A big first order can leave no cash for marketing, which is what sells the stock.

**Forgetting the extras.**
Freight, duty, import VAT, packaging and inspection can add substantially to the order value.

**Too many variants at launch.**
Each colour or size may carry its own minimum.

**Ignoring design changes.**
Early customer feedback often leads to changes; a large first batch locks in the first version.

- Model the order against sales with the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

- Check total launch costs with the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html).

- Read [calculating hardware start-up cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html).

## FAQ

### What is a minimum order quantity?

The smallest order a supplier will accept for a part or product, usually because each production run has set-up, material and capacity costs that must be spread over enough units.

### Should I order more to get a lower unit price?

Only if you can sell the stock in a reasonable time and still have cash for marketing and running the business. Compare the order with months of realistic sales, not just the unit price saving.

### How can I negotiate a lower MOQ?

Find out what drives the minimum, then offer to address it: use stocked materials or colours, accept a higher unit price, pay for set-up separately, reduce variants, or commit to an annual volume delivered in smaller batches.

### How much cash do I need for a first production order?

Add tooling, the production deposit and balance, freight, duty, import VAT, packaging, inspection and storage, and set them against when sales arrive. A cash flow projection shows the peak amount you need.

### How do start-ups fund their first order?

Common routes include pre-orders and crowdfunding, retailer orders with agreed terms, trade or stock finance, grants and investment. Pre-orders have the advantage of testing demand at the same time.

Title: Mould Tool Trials and Sample Approval

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small teams who have ordered an injection mould and need to judge the first parts that come off it

# Mould tool trials and sample approval: from first shots to signed-off parts

What happens between approving a tool design and starting production, what to ask the toolmaker for with each round of trial samples, how to read common moulding defects, how tool changes are handled and paid for, and how to sign off the parts that production will be judged against.

Quick answer

## A new mould is tried, adjusted and tried again until its parts match the drawing; only then are samples signed off as the reference for production.

Expect at least one round of changes. For each trial, ask for the shot count, the recorded process settings, the material and colour batch, a short trial report and a dimensional report against the drawing's critical dimensions.
Fix dimensions and defects first, texture the tool after the dimensions are approved, then sign off approved samples and limit samples, record the approved revision and move on to a pilot run.

## Contents

- From steel to first shots

- What to ask for with trial samples

- Reading the samples: common defects

- Tool modifications and who pays

- Texturing comes after the dimensions

- Signing off the samples

- Approving samples remotely

- Worked example: one housing through two trials

- Common mistakes

## From steel to first shots

Once you approve the tool design, the toolmaker orders steel and starts cutting the cavity, core, slides and cooling. [Injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) covers the process and the tooling project as a whole; this guide picks up when the tool is first put in a moulding machine.

At the first trial the toolmaker fills the tool for the first time, checks it opens, ejects and cools properly, and starts to find workable process settings. These first shots are rarely right, and that is normal: the trial tests the tool, not yet your product.

Trials are usually labelled with a T and a number. Many toolmakers call the very first shots **T0** and the first samples sent to the customer **T1**, with **T2**, **T3** and so on after each round of changes. Others start at T1 for the first shots. The naming varies by toolmaker, so ask what yours means by each label and write it into the quote or order, along with how many trial rounds are included.

Steps 3 and 4 repeat until the parts meet the drawing. Labels such as T0 and T1 vary between toolmakers, so agree what each one means.

## What to ask for with trial samples

A box of parts on its own tells you little. Ask for the following with every trial round, and put the list in your order:

- **Shot count:** how many shots were run and which shots your samples came from.

- **Recorded process settings:** temperatures, pressures, times and the machine used, so you can tell whether the tool or the process changed between rounds.

- **Material and colour batch:** the grade, the supplier and the batch or lot of material and colourant, so you know the samples were made in the material you specified and not a substitute.

- **A trial report:** a short note of what the toolmaker saw, what they think caused it and what they propose to change.

- **A dimensional report:** measurements against the critical dimensions marked on your drawing, on more than one part, with each result shown as in or out of tolerance. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) explains how critical features and inspection reports fit into the wider quality plan.

Ask for enough parts to measure, assemble and keep a few as a record, and label each set with its trial number and date.

**Practical rule:**
judge trial parts against the drawing and the agreed sample list, not against how the CAD model looked on screen. If a requirement is not on the drawing or in the order, it is hard to hold the toolmaker to it.

## Reading the samples: common defects

Most first-trial problems fall into a short list. The same defect can come from the process (how the machine runs the tool), the tool steel or the part design, so treat the table as a starting point for a conversation with the toolmaker, not a diagnosis.

|
Defect |
What it looks like |
What it usually points to |

|
Short shot |
The part is incomplete, often at the end furthest from the gate or at thin features |
Process first (pressure, speed, temperature); if it persists, venting, gate size or wall thickness in the steel or design |

|
Sink |
Shallow dips on a surface opposite a thick section, rib or boss |
Thick sections in the design; process (hold pressure and time) can reduce it but rarely removes it |

|
Flash |
Thin fins of plastic along the parting line or around inserts and ejectors |
Process (too much pressure) or steel that does not seal, such as a worn or poorly fitted shut-off |

|
Warp |
The part bows or twists, so flat faces are not flat or mating edges do not meet |
Uneven cooling or uneven walls; process changes help, but cooling layout or design changes may be needed |

|
Weld lines |
Fine lines where two flow fronts meet, often around holes |
Gate position and part geometry in the steel; process can make them fainter. They can also be weaker points |

|
Gate marks |
A small blemish or raised stub where the plastic entered the part |
Gate type and position in the steel; trimming and process settings affect its size |

|
Ejector marks |
Round witness marks or shiny spots where ejector pins pushed the part out |
Pin position and fit in the steel; process (cooling time, sticking) if the marks are deep or stressed |

|
Flow lines |
Wavy lines or rings on the surface, often near the gate |
Mostly process (speed, melt and tool temperature); sometimes gate design or sudden wall changes |

|
Colour or texture mismatch |
The colour, gloss or texture differs from the agreed reference |
Material or colourant batch and process temperature for colour; the steel finish for texture and gloss |

Check parts in even light at the distance a customer would view them, and assemble them with their mating parts.
Many of these defects are designed out before steel is cut; [from 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) covers draft, wall thickness, gates and shrinkage at the design stage.

## Tool modifications and who pays

After each trial, the toolmaker proposes changes. Process changes cost little. Steel changes take longer, and there is one rule that shapes them: **taking steel off is much easier than adding it back**. Removing steel adds plastic to the part; adding steel usually means welding or inserting metal, which is slower and riskier.

That is why experienced toolmakers and designers leave critical features **steel-safe**: the tool is first cut so that any likely correction is a matter of removing steel. A hole might be cut slightly small so it can be opened up after measuring. Ask which features have been left steel-safe.

Agree who pays for each kind of change before the first trial. A common split is that the toolmaker pays to correct its own errors and to bring the tool into line with the agreed drawing, while you pay for changes to the design itself. Write this down, along with how many trial rounds the quote includes; [supply agreements with a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html#tooling) covers tooling terms, and the right wording for your situation may be worth checking with an adviser.

## Texturing comes after the dimensions

If the part has a textured or grained surface, the texture is usually applied once the dimensions are approved. Texturing changes the surface of the steel, and any later steel change on that face may mean re-texturing it. Textured faces also need extra draft; [surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) explains the choices.

Approve texture and colour against physical references, such as texture plaques or a colour sample, rather than a screen or a printed photo. Expect a further trial after texturing to confirm the finish and release.

## Signing off the samples

Sign-off turns a good trial into the standard production is judged against. It usually has four parts:

- **Approved or golden samples:** parts made on the production tool, in the production material and colour, that meet the drawing. Sign, date and keep a set at both ends. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) covers how golden samples are then used.

- **Limit samples for cosmetics:** parts that show the worst acceptable version of a cosmetic feature, such as the largest acceptable gate mark or the faintest acceptable weld line.

- **A record of the approved revision:** note which drawing and model revision the samples were approved against, and any agreed deviations. Update the part's revision in your [bill of materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html).

- **The next step:** with samples approved, the process is proven for a single part. A [pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) then proves the whole line makes good, packed products repeatedly.

## Approving samples remotely

An overseas toolmaker is no barrier to good approval, but it takes planning:

- **Photos** taken in agreed lighting, of agreed faces, with a scale or ruler in shot.

- **Video** of the tool opening and the parts ejecting, and of the parts being assembled, flexed or fitted.

- **Samples by courier** for anything you need to handle, measure or fit to other parts. Allow for transit and customs.

- **A third-party inspection** service local to the toolmaker can witness a trial, measure parts against your drawing and report back.

[UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html) covers the wider trade-offs of working with a distant supplier.

## Worked example: one housing through two trials

Illustrative example. A start-up is tooling the lower housing of a small handheld device: a moulded shell with four screw bosses, a battery opening and a long, flat side wall that mates with the top cover. The drawing marks three critical dimensions: boss spacing, battery opening width and the flatness of the mating edge.

**T0 (first shots).** The toolmaker reports short shots at the corner furthest from the gate and warp along the long side wall, so the housing does not close fully against the top cover. Process changes improve the fill but do not cure it. The battery opening measures slightly narrow, as intended, because it was cut steel-safe.

**Modification.** The toolmaker adds venting at the corner that filled short and adjusts the cooling and process to reduce the warp. Steel is removed to open the battery opening to its nominal size. Both changes bring the tool into line with the agreed drawing, so under the agreed terms the toolmaker pays.

**T1.** The parts fill fully, all three critical dimensions are within tolerance on every part measured, and the housing closes against the top cover. The only issue is a gate mark on the inside face, slightly larger than the founder hoped. It is hidden once assembled and moving the gate would mean new steel, so both sides accept it and keep a part as a **limit sample** showing the largest acceptable gate mark. The tool is then textured, a short trial confirms the finish, golden samples are signed, the BOM records the approved revision, and the project moves on to its pilot run.

## Common mistakes

**Expecting the first samples to be right.**
A first trial is a test of the tool. Plan time and money for at least one round of changes.

**Accepting parts with no reports.**
Without the process settings, material batch and dimensional report, you cannot tell what changed between rounds or whether the parts meet the drawing.

**Texturing too early.**
Texture applied before the dimensions are approved may need redoing after a steel change.

**Leaving payment for changes vague.**
Agree before the first trial who pays for toolmaker errors and who pays for design changes, and how many trial rounds are included.

**Approving on looks alone.**
Measure the critical dimensions and fit the part to its mating parts; a part can look perfect and still warp out of tolerance.

## Next steps

- Mark the critical dimensions on each drawing and check they are clear before the first trial.

- Write the trial sample list, reports and number of included trial rounds into your tooling order.

- Agree in writing who pays for each kind of tool modification.

- Before ordering steel, work through the [Ready for Tooling self-check](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html).

- See where tool trials sit in the wider picture in the [manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

Catch draft, wall and rib issues that cause sink, warp and short shots.
[Open DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html)

T0 and T1 samples
Moulding defects
Steel-safe design
Limit samples

## FAQ

### What is the difference between T0, T1 and T2 samples?

They label successive trial rounds of a new mould. Many toolmakers call the first shots T0 and the first samples sent to the customer T1, with T2 and later numbers after each round of changes. Others start at T1, so ask your toolmaker what each label means.

### How many tool trials should I expect?

It depends on the part, the tool and how settled the design was when steel was cut. Plan for at least one round of modifications, agree how many rounds the quote includes, and allow a further trial if the tool is textured after the dimensions are approved.

### Who pays for tool modifications?

It is whatever you agree. A common arrangement is that the toolmaker corrects its own errors and brings the tool into line with the agreed drawing, while the customer pays for design changes. Put the split in writing before the first trial.

### What is a limit sample?

A part kept to show the worst acceptable version of a cosmetic feature, such as the largest acceptable gate mark. Production parts are compared with it, so cosmetic decisions do not depend on memory or opinion.

### Can I approve samples without visiting the toolmaker?

Yes, with planning. Ask for photos in agreed lighting, video of the tool running and parts being assembled, and samples by courier for anything you need to handle or measure. A local third-party inspector can also witness a trial and measure parts for you.

Title: Documents Before Talking to a Manufacturer

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders and engineers preparing to request quotes from manufacturers

# Must-have documents before talking to a manufacturer

Manufacturer conversations go badly when the team brings a vague idea, a half-defined file pack, and no shared view of what is confidential.
The fastest route to better feedback is better preparation.

Quick answer

## An NDA is useful, but it is not the only document that matters.

Useful supplier pack = NDA + product scope + drawings + BOM + volumes and target cost + prototype evidence + decision questions

Before talking to a manufacturer, prepare a short scope note, current 3D CAD and drawings, a bill of materials, realistic volumes and a target cost,
plus any prototype evidence and the specific questions you need answered. Suppliers respond better when the technical brief is clear, the scope is explicit, and the commercial conversation is framed properly from the start.

A manufacturer can only quote what it can understand. A vague enquiry tends to produce a vague quote, a long list of questions, or no reply at all,
because the supplier cannot judge whether the work suits them. A clear, well-organised pack signals that the team is serious and makes quotes from different suppliers easier to compare.

## Contents

- The core documents most teams need first

- Manufacturer document checklist

- What to send at each stage of the conversation

- Illustrative example: a moulded sensor enclosure

- Where the NDA fits

- Common mistakes when approaching manufacturers

- Practical next steps

## The core documents most teams need first

- **NDA:** sets the confidentiality baseline if the discussion is sensitive.

- **Product scope note:** explains what the product is, what stage it is at, and what kind of help is being requested.

- **Drawings or 3D files:** enough geometry to discuss manufacturability meaningfully.

- **BOM or major component list:** shows the parts and bought-in items likely to matter.

- **Prototype evidence:** photos, test results, or lessons from existing builds.

- **Open questions:** what you actually want the supplier to comment on.

## Manufacturer document checklist

|
Document |
What it contains |
When you need it |

|
NDA |
Who is disclosing, what counts as confidential, how long the obligation lasts |
Before sharing anything sensitive, usually at first contact |

|
Product scope note |
One or two pages: what the product does, development stage, the parts or services you need, timeline |
First contact |

|
3D CAD |
Neutral files such as STEP for each part, at the current revision |
Feasibility and DFM review, quoting |

|
2D drawings |
Critical dimensions, tolerances, material, finish, colour, revision letter |
Formal quotation and production |

|
Bill of materials (BOM) |
Every part and bought-in component, quantities per unit, make or buy, preferred suppliers |
Quoting for assembly or sourcing; useful earlier as a summary |

|
Specification |
Performance requirements, operating environment, relevant standards, cosmetic expectations |
Feasibility review onwards |

|
Volumes and target cost |
First order quantity, expected annual volume, batch sizes, target part or unit cost |
Any meaningful quote; tooling and process choices depend on it |

|
Prototype evidence |
Photos, test results, known issues and what has already changed |
Feasibility and DFM review |

|
Question list |
The specific decisions you want supplier input on |
Every conversation |

|
Quality and inspection criteria |
Critical-to-quality features, acceptance criteria, approved samples |
Before first production order |

|
Packaging and labelling |
Pack format, labels, markings, regulatory information, carton quantities |
Before production, if the supplier assembles or packs |

## What to send at each stage of the conversation

Not every document belongs in the first email. A staged approach protects sensitive information and keeps the conversation focused.

- **First contact:** scope note, an image or overview drawing, rough volumes, and the NDA if needed.

- **Feasibility or DFM review:** 3D CAD, a draft BOM, prototype evidence and your question list.

- **Formal quotation:** fully toleranced drawings, material and finish specifications, volumes and delivery expectations.

- **Pre-production:** inspection criteria, approved samples, packaging and labelling details.

**Do not send everything by default.**
Send the right amount for the conversation you need, not every file you have.

**Revision control matters.**
Suppliers lose confidence when they cannot tell which file is current.

**Asking better questions improves quotes.**
If you need feedback on tooling risk, tolerances, or yield, ask that directly.

## Illustrative example: a moulded sensor enclosure

Imagine a startup that needs a two-part injection-moulded enclosure for an outdoor wall-mounted sensor. A weak enquiry says “please quote for our enclosure” and attaches a single native CAD file.
A stronger pack, sent after an NDA, includes a one-page scope note, STEP files for both parts, a drawing showing the critical dimensions around the seal groove and [snap fits](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html),
a preferred material with UV stabilisation, the texture finish, a first order of a few thousand units with expected growth, and a target part cost range.

It closes with three questions: are the draft angles and wall thicknesses suitable for moulding, would a family tool make sense for both parts, and what tool life should the team specify for the expected volumes.
The figures and choices here are illustrative, but the effect is typical: suppliers can quote on the same basis, and their DFM comments arrive before tooling, not after.

## Where the NDA fits

An NDA is usually about setting expectations, not about making a weak brief safe. If the product definition is still vague,
the real problem is often not legal. It is that the supplier cannot respond properly because the pack does not yet make sense.

If your main concern is protecting sensitive information before the conversation starts, read
[How to protect product IP before talking to manufacturers](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html).
It covers staged disclosure, file control, and the practical limits of NDAs on their own.

## Common mistakes when approaching manufacturers

**Leaving out volumes.** Without quantities, a supplier cannot choose between processes or size tooling, so the quote becomes guesswork.

**Tolerancing everything tightly.** Tight tolerances on non-critical features raise cost. Mark only what genuinely matters to function or fit.

**Sending native CAD only.** Not every supplier uses the same software. A STEP file and a PDF drawing are the safer default.

**Reusing file names across revisions.** Add a revision letter to every file name and drawing title block. [Bills of materials and revision control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html) sets out a simple scheme for part numbers, revisions and changes.

**Asking only for the best price.** Price without context invites shortcuts. Ask about lead time, tool ownership, tool life and what is excluded.

The quality of a quote rarely exceeds the quality of the brief that requested it.

## Practical next steps

- Draft a one-page scope note and decide what stays confidential until a later stage.

- Export current parts as STEP files and create drawings for critical parts, with revision letters; [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) covers what each drawing should show.

- Build a simple BOM and a first estimate of unit cost; the guide on [how to estimate manufacturing cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html) can help.

- Write down the volumes you can defend and the questions you need answered.

- Prepare an NDA with the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html) if the discussion is sensitive.

If you are not sure which build method suits the next batch, the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html) helps frame the request.
For a wider view of costs, timing and milestones around the supplier conversation, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) brings the plan together in one place.

Create a simple one-way or mutual confidentiality draft for early product and manufacturing conversations.

### Pressure-test the product pack

Use costing, prototype, and manufacturing tools so the supplier conversation is built around clearer decisions.

NDA for manufacturers
Supplier pack
Product documents

## FAQ

### Do I need an NDA before talking to a manufacturer?

If you are sharing unpublished designs or sensitive technical detail, an NDA is a sensible baseline and most established suppliers will sign a reasonable one. It sets expectations but does not replace careful, staged disclosure. For a general first enquiry with no sensitive detail, it is often not needed yet.

### What file format should I send to a manufacturer?

STEP is the most widely accepted neutral 3D format for machined and moulded parts, with a PDF drawing for dimensions, tolerances and finishes. STL files suit 3D printing but lose the precise geometry most other processes need. Ask the supplier if they prefer native files.

### What should a request for quotation (RFQ) include?

An RFQ should include the part files and drawings, material and finish, quantities and batch sizes, required delivery dates, quality expectations and the specific items you want priced, such as tooling, samples and unit cost. The clearer the RFQ, the easier it is to [compare quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) fairly.

### What is a bill of materials?

A bill of materials, or BOM, is a structured list of every part, component and material in a product, with the quantity used per unit. It usually shows whether each item is made or bought and who supplies it. Manufacturers use it to quote assembly and sourcing, and teams use it to estimate unit cost.

### How much detail does a manufacturer need to give a quote?

For a budgetary quote, 3D files, material, finish and realistic volumes are often enough. For a firm quote, they also need toleranced drawings, quality requirements and delivery expectations. If a detail is missing, the supplier will either ask, assume, or add margin to cover the uncertainty.

Title: Product Opportunity and Concept: Where to Start

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For first-time founders, inventors and product teams deciding whether an idea is worth developing

# Opportunity and concept: how to test a product idea and choose what to build

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about the earliest stage of a physical product: proving there is a real problem, checking what already exists, writing requirements that can be tested and choosing the right concept. Each section links to a deeper guide or a free tool.

Quick answer

## Prove the problem before you design the product, then choose the concept against written requirements.

The opportunity stage is about evidence, not engineering. Confirm that a specific group of people has a problem they care about,
understand what they do about it today, check what already exists (including patents), and turn what you learn into measurable requirements.
Only then generate several concepts and choose between them with a structured comparison. This is the cheapest stage to change your mind in, so use it.

## Contents

- Start with the problem, not the product

- Gathering evidence: the evidence ladder

- What already exists: competitors, patents and designs

- Turning evidence into requirements

- Generating and choosing concepts

- A first commercial sense check

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## Start with the problem, not the product

Most product ideas arrive as a solution: a gadget, a mechanism, a better version of something. The questions that decide whether it is worth developing are about the problem behind it:

- **Who exactly has the problem?** A named group you can find and talk to, not "everyone".

- **How often, and how badly?** Frequent, painful problems justify a purchase; occasional mild annoyances rarely do.

- **What do they do today?** The current workaround is your real competitor, even if it is a cardboard box and some tape.

- **Who pays?** In many markets the user, the buyer and the budget holder are different people.

- **Should it exist at all?** A physical product uses materials and energy for its whole life. [The most sustainable product is the one you never make](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html) explains how to test that honestly.

The [Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html) walks through these questions and scores how well the idea is defined.

## Gathering evidence: the evidence ladder

Evidence comes in strengths. What people say in a friendly conversation is weak; what they do, and especially what they pay, is strong.
Climb the ladder only as far as the next decision needs: a weekend of interviews may be enough before spending on a sketch model, but not before ordering tooling.

Each rung costs more to reach and is harder to fake. Climb only as far as you need before the next spending decision.

In problem conversations, ask about past behaviour rather than future intentions: "tell me about the last time this happened" is far more reliable than "would you buy this?".
Avoid describing your idea until late in the conversation, so you hear about their problem rather than their politeness.
[How to validate a product idea](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html) covers interviews, smoke tests and pre-orders in more detail.

## What already exists: competitors, patents and designs

Before investing in development, spend a few hours on what already exists. You are looking for direct competitors, adjacent products that solve the same problem differently,
and protected rights that might limit what you can make.

|
Search |
Where to look |
What it tells you |

|
Products on sale |
Retailers, marketplaces, trade catalogues, [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) platforms |
Price points, features, reviews and complaints you could answer |

|
Patents |
The [UK patent search](https://www.gov.uk/search-for-patent) and the European Patent Office's Espacenet database |
Prior ideas, active protection you may need to avoid, and expired patents you may be free to use |

|
Registered designs |
The [UK registered design search](https://www.gov.uk/search-registered-design) |
Protected appearances you should not copy |

|
Failed attempts |
Discontinued products, closed campaigns, forum threads |
Why earlier versions did not work, and whether that has changed |

A search like this is a sense check, not legal clearance. If a patent looks close to your product, take advice from a registered patent attorney before committing significant money.
[How to protect product IP](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) explains the options for protecting your own idea.

## Turning evidence into requirements

Requirements are the bridge between what you learned and what the design team builds. Good requirements are specific, measurable and traceable to evidence;
vague requirements cannot be tested and quietly grow cost.

|
Vague |
Measurable |

|
Lightweight |
Under 250 g including battery |

|
Long battery life |
At least 5 days of typical use (defined as 20 readings a day) between charges |

|
Durable |
Survives repeated drops from 1 m onto concrete without loss of function |

|
Easy to use |
A first-time user completes setup in under 3 minutes without instructions |

|
Affordable |
Retail price at or below the target set by the route-to-market model |

The figures above are examples of the form, not recommendations. Mark each requirement as essential or desirable, note the evidence behind it,
and keep the list short enough that the team can remember it. It will become the basis of your test plan in the
[development and prototyping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html) stage.

## Generating and choosing concepts

Generate several genuinely different concepts before choosing: different working principles, architectures or ways of using the product, not three styling variations of the first idea.
Quick sketches, cardboard models and simple rigs are enough at this point.

Then compare them against the requirements in a structured way. A Pugh matrix scores each concept against a reference design, criterion by criterion,
which makes trade-offs visible and stops the loudest opinion from winning by default. Often the best outcome is a hybrid that combines the strengths of two concepts.

**Practical rule:**
if one concept wins on every criterion, check the criteria. Real choices involve trade-offs, and a matrix with no trade-offs usually means the criteria were written around a favourite.

[How engineers choose between concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html) explains the method, and the
[Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html) runs it for your own concepts.

## A first commercial sense check

Before development money is committed, do a rough check that the numbers could work. You need three figures, even as ranges:
the price customers would pay, the margins taken by the route to market (retailers, distributors, marketplaces), and therefore the most the product can cost to make.
If that target unit cost looks impossible for anything like the product you have in mind, it is far better to find out now.

[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) works out the cost ceiling from a price,
and the [Hardware Business Case Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/hardware-business-case-builder.html) brings price, cost, volume and investment together.
[Building a hardware business case](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-business-case.html) explains what a credible case contains.

## Common mistakes

**Asking friends whether they like the idea.**
Politeness is not demand. Ask strangers about their past behaviour instead.

**Falling in love with the first concept.**
Without alternatives there is nothing to compare, and the first idea is rarely the best.

**Skipping the search for what exists.**
Discovering a close competitor or patent after tooling is expensive and avoidable.

**Writing requirements that cannot be tested.**
"Premium", "robust" and "simple" mean different things to everyone until they are measured.

**Leaving the numbers until the end.**
A rough price-and-cost check takes an afternoon and can save a year.

## A step-by-step path through this hub

- **Define the problem and purpose** with the [Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html).

- **Search what exists** and read [how to protect product IP](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html).

- **Choose a concept** with the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html) and [its guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html).

Save results as you go to the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html): its first section, the product and the opportunity, is built from these steps.

## FAQ

### How do I know if my product idea is worth pursuing?

Look for evidence that a specific group of people has the problem, cares enough to act on it today, and would pay for a better answer. Conversations about past behaviour, observed workarounds and, above all, small commitments such as sign-ups, letters of intent or pre-orders are much stronger evidence than people saying they like the idea.

### Should I check for patents before developing a product?

Yes, a basic search is worth doing early. Use the UK patent search and Espacenet to look for close prior ideas and active protection. A search is a sense check rather than legal clearance, so take advice from a registered patent attorney if anything looks close.

### What should a product requirements document contain?

Who the product is for and the problem it solves, the essential and desirable requirements written as measurable targets, constraints such as target cost, size and regulation, and the evidence behind each requirement. Keep it short and update it as you learn.

### How many concepts should I develop before choosing one?

Enough to represent genuinely different approaches: commonly three to five. They only need to be developed far enough to compare against the requirements, usually sketches, simple models or rigs.

### When should I think about cost and price?

At the opportunity stage, as a rough range. Working back from a realistic retail price through the route-to-market margins gives a target unit cost. If that looks impossible for the product you have in mind, change the idea before spending on development.
