Title: Overmoulding and Two-Shot Moulding

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and engineers deciding whether a soft grip, seal or bumper should be moulded on or fitted separately

# Overmoulding and two-shot moulding explained

What overmoulding, two-shot and insert moulding mean, why products use them, how the two materials stay together, the design rules to agree with your moulder, the tooling trade-offs, and how to prototype a two-material part before committing to steel.

Quick answer

## Overmoulding moulds a second material, often a soft thermoplastic elastomer (TPE), over or around a first part so the two come out of the tool as one component.

It gives grip, impact protection, a seal or strain relief without separate parts to fit. It works only when the materials bond well or are locked together, and it costs more in tooling than a separate part.
At low volumes a glued or pressed-in part is often the better choice; at higher volumes, or where a loose part would be a reliability problem, overmoulding usually earns its place.

## Contents

- What the terms mean

- Why use a second material

- Bonding between materials

- Design guidance

- Cost and tooling trade-offs

- Prototyping a two-material part

- Worked example: from glued sleeve to overmoulded grip

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## What the terms mean

All three processes are variations on standard [injection moulding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html). The difference is what is already in the tool when the plastic is injected, and how it got there.

- **Overmoulding** is the general term for moulding a second material over a first part, called the substrate. The most common case is a rigid plastic housing with a soft TPE grip, bumper or seal moulded onto it. The substrate may be made in a separate tool and moved across, by hand or by robot, which is often called pick-and-place overmoulding.

- **Two-shot moulding**, also called 2K or multi-shot moulding, makes both materials in one machine and one tool. The machine has two injection units. The first shot forms the substrate, the tool rotates or shuttles it to a second cavity, and the second shot is moulded onto it while it is still warm.

- **Insert moulding** moulds plastic around a part that is not itself moulded in that tool: a threaded metal insert, a pin, a cable, or an electronic part such as a sensor or small [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html). The insert is placed in the tool before each shot.

Illustrative cross-section. The overmould stops at a defined shut-off edge, and where the chemical bond may be weak, the material flows through a hole and forms a small head behind the substrate so it cannot peel away.

## Why use a second material

- **Grip and feel.** A soft-touch grip on a handheld tool or device feels better, is less slippery and can hide fastener heads and joins.

- **Bumpers and impact protection.** A soft band at the corners spreads the force of a drop over a longer time. The [drops and impacts guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html) explains when that beats a geometry change.

- **Seals moulded in place.** A TPE seal moulded onto a housing flange cannot be lost or fitted wrongly, though it cannot be replaced on its own. The [sealing and waterproofing guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) compares it with gaskets and O-rings.

- **Cable strain relief.** An overmoulded boot where a lead leaves a plug or housing takes the bending and pulling away from the conductors, as described in [cables, wiring and connectors](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cables-wiring-and-connectors-inside-a-product.html).

- **Integrated buttons.** A flexible membrane moulded into a rigid housing can act as a sealed button over a switch. See [designing buttons, switches and controls](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-buttons-switches-and-controls.html) for the feel and travel side.

- **Fewer assembly steps.** One component instead of two means no adhesive, no fitting operation and nothing to fall off in use.

## Bonding between materials

The two materials hold together in two ways: a chemical bond, where the hot second material partly fuses with the surface of the substrate, and a mechanical lock, where the geometry stops them separating. Most reliable parts use both.

Chemical compatibility is the first check. TPEs are commonly overmoulded onto PP, ABS or PC, for example, but whether a particular pair bonds well depends on the grades, not just the families. TPE suppliers publish compatibility data and offer grades intended to bond to specific substrates.
Check that data for the exact grades you plan to use, tell your moulder which pair you have chosen, and confirm the bond with peel tests on trial parts. The [choosing plastic materials guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) covers the substrate side of that choice.

Where bonding is weak, or peel forces will be high, add **mechanical interlocks**: holes through the substrate that the second material flows through and caps behind, undercuts or grooves it wraps into, or a wrap over an edge. They are also a sensible backstop for parts that will be handled roughly or heat cycled.

**Practical rule:**
never rely on a chemical bond you have not tested on real moulded parts. Design in at least some mechanical interlock wherever a peeled edge would be a product failure.

## Design guidance

These are typical guidelines; the right values depend on the materials, part size and the moulder's equipment, so confirm each one with your moulder before the tool is designed. The general rules in the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) still apply to both shots.

- **Shut-off edges.** The second material needs a crisp line on the substrate where the tool seals against it and the soft material stops. A small step, groove or raised lip gives the tool a positive edge to clamp on; a shut-off on a smooth, flat surface is more likely to flash.

- **Avoid thin, feathered edges.** A soft layer that tapers to nothing at its edge is likely to lift, peel or tear. End it against a step so it keeps a sensible thickness right to the edge.

- **Flow paths.** The second material must be able to fill the whole area from its gate. Long, thin runs of soft material may not fill, so keep flow lengths reasonable or add gates, and make sure air can escape at the far end.

- **Uniform overmould thickness.** As with any moulding, even thickness helps the part fill and cool evenly. Very thin areas may not fill; very thick areas can sink and take longer to cool.

- **Gates and parting lines.** Agree early where each material's gate and parting line will go. Gate marks and witness lines on a soft grip are visible and can be felt, so keep them away from where the hand rests or a seal must seal.

## Cost and tooling trade-offs

In relative terms, from cheapest tooling to most expensive, the options usually run like this:

|
Route |
Tooling |
Usually suits |

|
Separate part, glued or pressed in |
A simple tool or bought-in part for the soft piece |
Low volumes, early production, parts that must be replaceable |

|
Pick-and-place overmoulding |
Two tools: one for the substrate, one for the overmould; a standard machine can run each |
Moderate volumes; moulders without two-shot machines |

|
Two-shot moulding |
One more complex tool, run on a specialised two-shot machine |
Higher volumes, where the shorter cycle and lack of handling pay back the tool |

Two-shot tools are more complex to design and trial, and fewer moulders have the machines. Pick-and-place adds handling time to every part.
At low volumes, a separately moulded grip or seal that is glued or pressed into a groove often does the job for far less tooling. You can move to overmoulding later once sales justify it, as part of a [risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html).

## Prototyping a two-material part

You can approximate an overmoulded part before tooling, but none of the methods fully reproduces the real thing:

- **Cast urethane overmoulding.** A soft urethane is cast in a silicone mould around a printed or machined substrate. It gives a good impression of feel and appearance and is useful for [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html), but the bond and the material are not those of the production pair.

- **Multi-material printing.** Some printers can combine rigid and flexible materials in one build. Good for checking shape, layout and rough feel quickly, but the soft materials, [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) and bond strength differ from moulded TPE.

Use prototypes to decide shape and feel, not as evidence of the production bond or durability; that comes only from trial parts off the real tool.

## Worked example: from glued sleeve to overmoulded grip

Illustrative example. A small company makes a handheld measuring device with a rigid moulded housing and a rubber sleeve glued around the handle. Returns showed sleeves lifting at one end after a few months, and gluing was a slow, messy assembly step.

With volumes now steady, they ask their moulder about a TPE overmould onto the existing housing material. The moulder suggests pick-and-place overmoulding, so the existing housing tool can be modified rather than replaced, with a second tool for the grip.

The design changes agreed before the tool was made:

- **Material pair:** a TPE grade the supplier lists as bonding to the housing grade, confirmed with the moulder.

- **Interlocks:** a row of small holes through the handle wall at each end of the grip, where peeling had started on the old sleeve, with a recess inside so the soft material forms a head behind each hole.

- **Shut-offs:** a small step around the handle at both ends of the grip, so the overmould ends at a defined edge instead of feathering out.

- **Thickness and gating:** an even grip thickness, with the gate placed on the underside away from the thumb rest.

At the [tool trials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html), the team checked trial parts for flash at the shut-offs, short shots at the far end of the grip, and sink in the thicker areas. They ran simple peel tests by hand and after a few days of heat and cold cycling, and checked that the housing had not distorted in the second shot. One shut-off showed light flash and was corrected before the samples were signed off. The gluing step was removed from the assembly line.

## Common mistakes

**Choosing materials by family, not grade.**
"TPE on ABS" says little on its own. Check the suppliers' compatibility data for the exact grades and test the bond.

**No mechanical interlock.**
Relying only on the chemical bond leaves nothing to stop an edge lifting once it starts.

**Feathered edges and vague shut-offs.**
A soft layer that thins to nothing peels, and a shut-off with no edge to clamp on flashes.

**Overmoulding too early.**
Committing to a two-shot tool before the design and volumes have settled makes every change expensive. A separate part is often better for the first batches.

**Trusting the prototype bond.**
Cast or printed parts show the feel, not how the production materials will hold together.

## Next steps

- Write down what the second material must do: grip, protect, seal or relieve strain. That sets the material and thickness.

- Shortlist material pairs using the suppliers' compatibility data, then discuss them with your moulder.

- Decide between a separate part, pick-and-place and two-shot based on your expected volumes, and revisit it as volumes grow.

- Add interlocks and shut-off steps to the CAD, and check both parts with the [DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html).

- Plan bond, flash and fill checks into the [tool trials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html).

Run both the substrate and the overmould through the main moulding rules.

## FAQ

### What is the difference between overmoulding and two-shot moulding?

Overmoulding is the general term for moulding a second material over a first part. Two-shot moulding is one way of doing it, with both materials made in one machine and one tool. Pick-and-place overmoulding uses two separate tools instead.

### Will a soft grip stay bonded to a hard plastic housing?

It can, if the two grades are compatible and the part is designed well. Check the material suppliers' compatibility data for the exact grades, add mechanical interlocks where peeling would matter, and test the bond on trial parts from the real tool.

### Is overmoulding worth it at low volumes?

Often not. The extra tooling is shared over few parts, so a separately moulded grip or seal that is glued or pressed in is usually cheaper at first. Overmoulding tends to pay back once volumes are steady or a loose part causes problems.

### What is insert moulding used for?

Moulding plastic around a part placed in the tool before each shot, such as a threaded metal insert, a pin, a cable or a small electronic part. It gives a strong, sealed joint without a separate assembly step.

### Can I prototype an overmoulded part without a mould tool?

Yes, approximately. Cast urethane over a printed substrate, or multi-material printing, shows shape and feel well enough for user testing. Neither shows how the production materials will bond, so the bond is proven only at tool trials.

Title: Packaging Design for Shipping

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and product teams planning packaging for retail or direct-to-customer sales

# Packaging design for shipping: protecting products from factory to customer

How to design packaging that protects a product all the way from the factory to the customer: mapping the journey, designing the layers, fitting cartons and pallets, testing before production, and meeting sustainability and producer responsibilities.

Quick answer

## Design packaging for the whole journey, from factory to customer, not just the shelf: protect the product, fit the shipping system, sell the product, and use as little material as possible.

Start early, because pack size affects freight cost, pallet and carton counts, and sometimes the product itself. Work out how the product will travel, which drops, vibration,
compression and temperatures it will meet, and design inner protection and outer cartons to suit. Test with recognised transit tests before production, and check your packaging
responsibilities, which in the UK include extended producer responsibility for many businesses.

## What packaging has to do

|
Job |
What it means |

|
Protect |
Survive drops, vibration, stacking, humidity and temperature on the way to the customer |

|
Fit the system |
Work with carton, pallet and container sizes, parcel carriers and warehouse handling |

|
Sell and inform |
Retail presence or a good unboxing, plus required labels, barcodes, safety and disposal information |

|
Minimise waste and cost |
Right-sized, with as little and as simple material as the protection allows |

## Map the journey

List each stage: factory, container or air freight, warehouse, retailer or fulfilment centre, parcel carrier, customer. Each has its own hazards.
Products sold by parcel direct to customers are handled individually and dropped more often than products shipped on pallets to shops,
and [online marketplaces](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/selling-on-marketplaces.html) and retailers may have their own packaging requirements. Ask them early; [retail-ready packaging and barcodes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html) covers what retailers commonly ask for.

## Design the layers

- **Primary pack:** the box the customer sees. It may be the shipping box too, for direct-to-customer products.

- **Inner protection:** moulded pulp, folded card or foam inserts that hold the product away from the walls and stop it moving.

- **Shipper carton:** holds several units for freight; its strength must suit how high cartons will be stacked.

- **Pallet:** carton sizes that fill a pallet well reduce freight cost and damage.

**Practical rule:**
decide the pack size before you finalise the product. A few millimetres can change how many units fit a carton or pallet, which affects every shipment's cost.

## Test before production

Transit test procedures, such as those published by the [International Safe Transit Association (ISTA)](https://ista.org/test_procedures.php),
simulate drops, vibration and compression in a repeatable way. Test packaging samples with real products inside, and include it in your
[test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html). Fix weak points before ordering packaging in volume.

## Sustainability and responsibilities

- Right-size the pack and avoid void fill where you can.

- Use materials that are widely recycled, and avoid mixing materials that cannot be separated.

- Mark materials and disposal guidance clearly.

-
Check your obligations: in the UK, many businesses that supply packaging have
[extended producer responsibility for packaging](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-who-is-affected-and-what-to-do)
duties, depending on size and role.

Packaging also adds to the product's footprint; see the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

## Cost

Packaging carries tooling for inserts and print set-up, a unit cost and [minimum order quantities](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) of its own, and it changes freight cost through size and weight.
Include it in the unit cost with the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) and in landed cost with the
[Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html).

## Common mistakes

**Leaving packaging until last.**
It can delay launch and leave an oversized, expensive pack.

**Designing for the shelf only.**
Retail boxes that look good may not survive parcel delivery.

**No transit testing.**
Damage found by customers costs far more than a test.

**Ignoring pallet and carton fit.**
Poor fit means paying to ship air.

## Next steps

- Map the journey and the hazards at each stage.

- Add packaging and transit tests to the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Include packaging in the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) and [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html).

- Include packaging requirements in quotes with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

Add drop, vibration and compression tests to your plan.
[Open Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html)

### Count the cost

See how packaging and freight change the landed cost.
[Open Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html)

Packaging
Transit testing
Freight
EPR

## FAQ

### When should packaging design start?

Early, alongside the product. Pack size affects how many units fit a carton and pallet, freight cost and sometimes the product design, and packaging has its own lead times, tooling and minimum orders.

### How do I test packaging for shipping?

Use recognised transit test procedures, such as those published by ISTA, which simulate drops, vibration and compression. Test real products in production-representative packaging before ordering in volume.

### Is direct-to-customer packaging different from retail packaging?

Usually. Parcels are handled individually and dropped more, so they need more protection, while retail packs are mainly shipped in cartons on pallets and need shelf presence. Some products need both.

### What are my packaging responsibilities in the UK?

Many businesses that supply packaging have extended producer responsibility duties, depending on their size and role. Check the current official guidance on GOV.UK for what applies to you.

### How can I make packaging more sustainable?

Right-size it, use less material, choose widely recycled materials, avoid mixing materials that cannot be separated, and label disposal clearly, while still protecting the product, because damage wastes far more.

Title: Planning a Pilot Production Run

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and engineers with approved first-article parts who are about to place their first production order

# Planning a pilot production run

What a pilot run is for, where it sits between first-article approval and volume production, how large to make it, what to plan and measure, how to run it with a supplier you cannot visit every day, and how to decide whether you are ready to ramp up.

Quick answer

## A pilot run is a small batch built on the real production line, at production rate, to prove the process rather than the design, before you commit to volume.

It comes after design freeze and first-article approval. Plan it like an experiment: agree in advance what you will measure, including yield, defect types, assembly time, test results and how packed units survive transit, and what result counts as a pass.
Then decide go, fix and repeat, or stop, and feed what you learned into your cost, quotes and cash plan before placing the volume order.

## Contents

- What a pilot run is for

- Where it sits in the journey

- How large should it be?

- What to plan and measure

- Who attends, and running it with a remote supplier

- Using the pilot units

- Go/no-go criteria and what happens if it fails

- Feeding the results into cost and plan

- Worked example: a small consumer product made overseas

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What a pilot run is for

By the time you reach a pilot run, the design should already be proven and the first parts from production tools checked against the drawings. What is not yet proven is whether the whole system can make the product repeatedly, at the rate and quality you need. That system includes:

- **The process:** settings that hold steady over hours, not just for a handful of careful samples.

- **The tooling and fixtures:** tools that run at their intended cycle, and the jigs, fixtures and test stations that assembly depends on.

- **The assembly line:** operators who have not built your product before, working from written instructions at normal speed.

- **Packaging and labelling:** the real box, inserts, labels and documents, packed the way production will pack them.

- **The supply chain:** bought-in parts arriving from production suppliers, in production quantities, on time.

Electronics teams often call this stage production validation, or PVT. The question is the same: if we place the volume order tomorrow, will what arrives be what we approved?

## Where it sits in the journey

A pilot run follows two earlier gates. First, **design freeze**: the design has met its requirements, its tests are complete and further changes go through [change control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html). The [testing and validation plans guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) covers the evidence you need, and [Am I Ready to Commit to Tooling?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html) checks whether you are ready to cut tools at all.

Second, **first-article approval**: parts from production tools and processes are measured and checked in full, and [golden samples](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html) are signed off. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) explains how. A first article proves that the process can make a good part; a pilot proves that it does, repeatedly, when the line is running normally.

The pilot is the last gate before volume. A failed gate sends you back a step to fix the cause, not forward with a hope that the next batch will be better.

The pilot is also the bridge into the wider staged approach described in the [risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html): it supplies the yield, defect and process evidence that justifies the next, larger commitment.

## How large should it be?

There is no standard number. The batch needs to be large enough for the line to run as it will in production, long enough to settle and show drift, and for occasional problems to have a fair chance of appearing. A handful of units built slowly by the best technician proves very little.

But every pilot unit is built before the process is proven, so a very large pilot carries the risk it was meant to reduce. A sensible size usually follows from the process: a shift or a few hours of continuous assembly, a full cycle of any batch process such as painting, and enough units for the tests and samples you have planned. Agree the quantity with your supplier, and what happens to units that fail.

## What to plan and measure

Write a short pilot plan before the run and share it with the supplier. It should name what will be built, how, and what will be recorded:

- **Work instructions.** Illustrated steps for each station, written for operators new to the product. Where they hesitate or improvise, the instructions are unclear. [Assembly instructions and work instructions for production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-and-work-instructions.html) explains what each step should contain.

- **Fixtures and test stations.** Check that jigs hold parts repeatably and end-of-line tests catch faults without rejecting good units. Record each unit's results, not just pass or fail.

- **Yield and defect types.** Count units that pass first time, need rework or are scrapped, and record each defect by type and station. The pattern matters more than the total: one recurring defect usually has one fixable cause.

- **Cycle and assembly time.** Time each station and compare it with the estimate your costing assumed. The [assembly time guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) and the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) give the baseline to compare against. Note the bottleneck station, because it sets the rate of the whole line.

- **Packaging and transit.** Pack units exactly as production will, then ship or drop-test them and inspect what arrives. [Packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html) covers the checks.

- **Labelling and documents.** Check rating labels, [barcodes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html), serial numbers, warnings and instructions against your specification and required markings.

- **Supply chain.** Note any bought-in part that arrived late, short, in the wrong revision or with quality problems.

## Who attends, and running it with a remote supplier

On the supplier side, the process engineer, line leader and quality lead should own the run. On your side, someone who knows the design should be present: ideally its engineer, or a trusted representative or inspection company if you cannot travel. Their job is to observe, record and answer questions, not to fix problems by hand.

With a distant supplier, agree the plan, quantity and acceptance criteria in writing before the run. Ask for photos or video of each station, a daily summary of yield and defects, the test data and measured times, and some finished, packed units sent to you. [UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html) discusses the wider trade-offs of distance.

## Using the pilot units

Pilot units are the first that truly represent production, which makes them valuable:

- **Testing.** Repeat the key tests from your validation plan on production-made units, especially durability, drop, temperature and anything sensitive to process settings.

- **Certification samples, where appropriate.** Test houses generally want samples that represent what you will sell, so pilot units can be a good source. Confirm with your test house what they need and when; [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) outlines how conformity is shown.

- **Early customers.** A few units with friendly customers can reveal set-up and instruction problems that factory tests miss. Tell them these are early units, and only sell units that passed the same checks as production.

- **Reference samples.** Keep a few as reference units for comparing future batches.

## Go/no-go criteria and what happens if it fails

Agree the criteria with the supplier before the run, so the decision is about evidence rather than opinion. Typical criteria: first-pass yield at or above an agreed level; no safety or critical-to-quality defects; every recurring defect understood and fixable; assembly time close enough to the estimate to support your costing; packed units surviving transit checks; correct labelling; and bought-in parts available in production quantities.

The outcome is usually one of three:

- **Go:** the criteria are met, perhaps with minor actions that can be closed during ramp-up.

- **Fix and repeat:** the causes are understood and fixable, such as a fixture, an instruction or a process setting, but the fix must be proven, often with a smaller, focused re-run.

- **Stop:** a problem points back to the design or tooling. Treat it as a controlled design change, with new first articles where parts change, rather than patching it on the line.

Agree in advance who pays for a repeat run: often the supplier for process faults, and you for design or specification issues.

## Feeding the results into cost and plan

The pilot replaces assumptions with measurements. Update your unit cost with measured assembly time, real yield and scrap, and actual packaging in the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html). If the numbers have moved, revisit your quotes using [getting and comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html), since a supplier's price was based on their own assumptions about time and yield.

Then check timing and cash. A repeat run delays first stock, and the volume order may carry a minimum quantity and a deposit due well before sales arrive. [Minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) shows how to plan for that.

## Worked example: a small consumer product made overseas

Illustrative and qualitative. A start-up's small battery-powered kitchen gadget has two moulded housing parts, a bought-in [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html), a battery, a button and a printed retail box. The supplier is overseas, and first articles were approved from video and samples.

The team and supplier agree a written plan: roughly a shift's output, yield recorded by defect type, every station timed, every unit tested, and a carton of packed units sent by the normal freight route. The criteria are no safety defects, recurring defects understood, times close to the estimate and packed units arriving undamaged. An inspection company attends for the team.

What the pilot finds:

- **A recurring button defect.** Several buttons stick, because a fixture lets the housing close slightly off-centre. The supplier modifies the fixture; the design does not change.

- **Assembly slower than estimated.** Operators struggle to route a cable around a boss. Clearer instructions and a pre-formed cable bring the time down, though not fully to the estimate, so the team updates its costing.

- **Transit damage.** In the shipped carton, some retail boxes are crushed at the corners. A stronger shipping carton and a change of pallet pattern solve it, and the change is checked with a drop test.

- **A late bought-in part.** The battery arrives late from its supplier. The team agrees a buffer stock and a second approved source.

The decision is fix and repeat: a short re-run proves the fixture, cable and carton changes before the volume order is placed. A few pilot units go to the test house, and a few to friendly early customers, who find the quick-start card unclear; it is reprinted before launch.

## Common mistakes

**Treating the pilot as a sales batch.**
When pilot units are already promised to customers, the pressure is to ship them whatever the results show. Plan the pilot to learn, and size and promise units accordingly.

**No agreed acceptance criteria.**
Without criteria written down beforehand, every result can be argued either way, and the volume order goes ahead by default.

**Design changes slipped in during the pilot.**
A "small tweak" on the line means the pilot no longer represents what was approved, and the change has not been tested. Route any change through change control and re-prove it.

**Skipping packaging and transit checks.**
A product that leaves the factory perfect can arrive damaged. Pack and ship pilot units the way production will be packed and shipped.

## Decision rules

- **Prove the process, not the design:** freeze the design and approve first articles before the pilot.

- **Write the plan and criteria first,** and agree them with the supplier.

- **Run at production rate** with normal operators, fixtures, packaging and suppliers.

- **Record yield by defect type and time by station,** then fix causes, not symptoms.

- **Update cost, quotes and cash** from the measured results before placing the volume order.

## Next steps

- Confirm you are ready with [Am I Ready to Commit to Tooling?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html) and a completed first-article inspection.

- Plan the tests the pilot units will go through in the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Agree the pilot plan, quantity and go/no-go criteria with your supplier in writing, as part of the brief described in [how to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html).

- See where this sits in the wider picture in the [manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

### Plan the pilot tests

Choose which tests production-made units must pass before ramp-up.

Go/no-go

## FAQ

### What is a pilot production run?

A small batch built on the real production line, with production tools, fixtures, operators, packaging and suppliers, at normal rate. Its purpose is to prove the manufacturing process before committing to volume, not to prove the design.

### How is a pilot run different from first-article inspection?

First-article inspection checks the first parts from production tools in full, to show the process can make a correct part. A pilot run builds complete, packed products at production rate, to show the process does so repeatedly.

### How many units should a pilot run be?

There is no standard number. Make it large enough for the line to run normally for a sustained period and for occasional problems to show, and enough to cover planned tests and samples, but not so large that a process problem becomes expensive.

### Can I sell units from a pilot run?

Units that pass the same checks as production can be sold, often to friendly early customers. Do not plan the pilot as a sales batch, though, because the pressure to ship can override what the results are telling you.

### What happens if the pilot run fails?

Find the cause of each problem. Process, fixture and instruction problems are fixed and proven with a focused re-run; design or tooling problems go through change control, with new first articles where parts change, before you try again.

Title: Product Carbon Footprint vs LCA

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers and founders deciding how to measure a product's environmental impact

# Product carbon footprint vs LCA: what each measures and when to use it

The difference between a product carbon footprint and a life cycle assessment, the standards behind each, how boundaries change the result, and when a quick design-stage estimate is enough.

Quick answer

## A product carbon footprint measures one impact, greenhouse gas emissions; a life cycle assessment (LCA) looks at many impacts across the product's whole life.

For early design decisions, a simple carbon estimate is usually enough to compare options and find the biggest contributors.
A full, standards-based footprint or LCA takes far more data and effort, and is worth it when you need to make public claims, meet a customer's requirements,
or compare options where the differences are small or the trade-offs involve impacts other than carbon.

## The difference at a glance

|
|
Product carbon footprint |
Life cycle assessment |

|
Measures |
Greenhouse gas emissions, usually as kg CO₂e |
Several impact categories, such as climate change, water use, resource depletion and toxicity |

|
Main standards |
ISO 14067; the GHG Protocol Product Standard; PAS 2050 |
ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 |

|
Effort |
Lower, especially for a design-stage estimate |
Higher: more data, more modelling, often external review |

|
Good for |
Comparing design options on climate impact; finding hotspots |
Avoiding trade-offs where reducing carbon raises another impact; formal comparisons and claims |

## Boundaries: what is included

- **Cradle to gate:** materials and manufacturing, up to the product leaving the factory.

- **Cradle to grave:** adds distribution, use, maintenance and end of life.

- **Functional unit:** what is being compared, for example "one year of use" rather than "one product", so products with different lifetimes compare fairly.

Results only compare fairly when the boundaries, functional unit and data sources are the same. For products that use energy, the use phase is often large,
so leaving it out can be misleading; see [why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html).

**Practical rule:**
use a quick estimate to steer design, and a formal study to support claims. Don't publish a number from an early estimate as if it were a verified footprint.

## When an estimate is enough

- Comparing two materials, processes or transport options early in design.

- Finding which parts or life stages dominate, so effort goes where it matters.

- Setting internal targets and tracking improvements between design versions.

The [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html) is built for this kind of design-stage comparison; see [estimating carbon footprint during design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-product-carbon-footprint-during-design.html).

## When you need more

- **Public environmental claims** must be accurate and supported by evidence; see the CMA's [Green Claims Code](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/green-claims-code-making-environmental-claims).

- **Customer or retailer requirements** for footprints to a named standard.

- **Close comparisons** where differences are within the uncertainty of an estimate.

- **Possible trade-offs** beyond carbon, such as water use or toxicity, where an LCA is needed.

## Common mistakes

**Comparing results with different boundaries.**
A cradle-to-gate figure cannot be compared with a cradle-to-grave one.

**Ignoring the use phase.**
For products that use energy or consumables, it can outweigh manufacturing.

**False precision.**
Early estimates carry wide uncertainty; present them as ranges.

**Making claims from estimates.**
Public claims need robust evidence.

## Next steps

- Estimate the main contributors with the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

- Compare lifetime and repair scenarios with the [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html).

- Read [the most sustainable product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html) and [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html).

### Estimate the footprint

Compare design options and find the hotspots.
[Open Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html)

### Explore product life

See how lifetime and repair change the picture.
[Open Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html)

Part of a hub

[Sustainability and product life: the hub guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html)

Use these tools next

[Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html)

[Material Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/material-selector.html)

Related guides

[Why lifetime matters](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html)

Carbon footprint
LCA
Standards
Green claims

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a carbon footprint and an LCA?

A product carbon footprint measures greenhouse gas emissions only, usually in kg CO₂e. A life cycle assessment looks at several environmental impacts, such as climate change, water use and resource depletion, across the product's life.

### Which standards apply to product carbon footprints and LCAs?

Product carbon footprints are commonly calculated to ISO 14067, the GHG Protocol Product Standard or PAS 2050. Life cycle assessments follow ISO 14040 and ISO 14044.

### What does cradle to gate mean?

A boundary that covers raw materials and manufacturing up to the product leaving the factory. Cradle to grave adds distribution, use and end of life.

### Is a design-stage estimate good enough?

For comparing options and finding hotspots during design, usually yes. For public claims, customer requirements or close comparisons, a formal study to a recognised standard is more appropriate.

### Can I publish my product's carbon footprint?

Environmental claims must be accurate and supported by evidence. In the UK, the CMA's Green Claims Code sets out what businesses should consider. Early estimates should not be presented as verified figures.

Title: Product Certification Basics: UKCA, CE and Safety

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers bringing electrical, connected or consumer products to the UK market for the first time

# Product certification basics for hardware start-ups: UKCA, CE, safety and EMC

An overview of how product certification works in the UK for start-ups: which regulations commonly apply, how conformity is assessed and documented, the marking rules for Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and how to plan testing into development. It is general information with official links, not legal advice.

Quick answer

## Find out which product regulations apply, design and test to the standards that show compliance, then document it, declare it and mark the product.

Many products sold in the UK, including electrical equipment, anything with a radio, toys and machinery, must meet specific product regulations and carry a conformity marking:
UKCA in Great Britain (where CE marking is also recognised for many products) and CE in Northern Ireland, with UKNI in some cases. For most products the manufacturer assesses conformity itself,
usually by testing against recognised standards; some higher-risk products need an independent conformity assessment body. Identify the rules at the requirements stage, because they affect the design.
This is general information, not legal advice.

## Contents

- Who this applies to

- Common product regulations in Great Britain

- How conformity is shown

- UKCA, CE and UKNI

- Planning certification into development

- Worked example: a small rechargeable Bluetooth device

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## Who this applies to

The person who places a product on the market carries most of the responsibility. If you design a product and sell it under your name, you are usually the manufacturer in law,
even if a factory makes it for you. Importers and distributors have their own, lighter duties, such as checking the marking and documents are in place and that their name and address appear on the product or its packaging.

## Common product regulations in Great Britain

Which regulations apply depends on what the product is and does; one product can fall under several. Common examples:

|
Regulation |
Applies to |

|
[Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2016/1101/contents) |
Electrical equipment within certain voltage limits (often called the low voltage rules) |

|
[Electromagnetic Compatibility Regulations 2016](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2016/1091/contents) |
Electrical and electronic equipment that could cause or be affected by electromagnetic interference |

|
[Radio Equipment Regulations 2017](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2017/1206/contents) |
Products that intentionally transmit or receive radio waves, such as Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or cellular devices |

|
[RoHS Regulations 2012](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2012/3032/contents) |
Restriction of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment |

|
[Toys (Safety) Regulations 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2011/1881/contents) |
Products designed or intended for play by children under 14 |

|
[General Product Safety Regulations 2005](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1803/contents) |
Consumer products generally, especially where no specific regulation covers a risk, in Great Britain. In Northern Ireland, the EU General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988 has applied since 13 December 2024 |

Other categories, including machinery, medical devices, pressure equipment, personal protective equipment and construction products, have their own regimes, as do producer-responsibility rules for waste electricals, batteries and packaging
(see the [Sustainability and product life hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html)). Connectable consumer products can also be subject to security requirements under the
[Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2022/46/contents); EU cybersecurity requirements for radio equipment may also apply to products sold in the EU or Northern Ireland.
Rules change, so check the current GOV.UK guidance for your category.

## How conformity is shown

- **Identify the regulations and essential requirements** that apply to the product.

- **Identify the standards.** Designated standards (in Great Britain) and harmonised standards (in the EU) give a presumption of conformity when you meet them. GOV.UK lists [designated standards](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/designated-standards); standards themselves are published by BSI and other standards bodies.

- **Choose the conformity assessment route.** For most electrical, EMC and many radio products the manufacturer can self-assess. Some products, such as certain radio equipment tested without the relevant standards or some toys, need a third-party conformity assessment body.

- **Design and test.** Test against the standards, in-house or at a test laboratory. Laboratories accredited by [UKAS](https://www.ukas.com/) (or equivalent bodies abroad) give confidence in the results.

- **Compile the technical documentation:** description, drawings and circuit diagrams, risk assessment, list of standards applied, test reports and the production controls that keep products consistent.

- **Sign a declaration of conformity** listing the product, the regulations and standards, and the manufacturer's details.

- **Mark and label:** conformity marking, manufacturer (and importer) name and address, product identification for traceability, and instructions and safety information in English.

- **Keep it up to date:** design changes, component changes and new versions of standards can all require a review.

**Practical rule:**
use pre-certified radio modules and power supplies where you can. A pre-certified module does not certify your whole product, but it can greatly reduce the radio testing needed and the risk of failure.

## UKCA, CE and UKNI

Broadly, products placed on the market in Great Britain use UKCA marking, and CE marking continues to be recognised there for many product types; products in Northern Ireland follow EU rules and use CE marking,
with UKNI marking added in some cases. The detail differs by product category and has changed several times, so check GOV.UK's guidance on
[UKCA](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukca-marking), [CE](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/ce-marking) and [UKNI](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukni-marking) marking before printing labels.
Selling into the EU requires CE marking and, for manufacturers outside the EU, usually an EU-based representative or importer.

## Planning certification into development

|
Development stage |
Certification work |

|
Requirements |
List applicable regulations and standards; note design requirements such as creepage distances, enclosure ratings, labelling and battery rules |

|
Engineering prototypes |
Pre-compliance checks, especially EMC and radio; [design reviews](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html) against the standards |

|
Design verification |
Formal testing on production-intent units; fix failures before tooling is final |

|
Pilot production |
Complete the technical file, sign the declaration, finalise labels and instructions |

|
After launch |
Control changes, monitor complaints and incidents, keep documentation for the required period |

Budget for at least one round of fixes and re-tests: failing a formal EMC or safety test at the first attempt is not unusual, and the cost of a re-test is small next to a late redesign.
The [Development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html) places this work in the wider development plan, and
[how much it costs to develop a hardware product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html) includes compliance in the budget.

Certification work runs through development, not just at the end. Pre-compliance checks on engineering prototypes, and formal tests before tooling is final, mean a failure does not turn into tool changes and delays; design or component changes after launch can need a fresh review.

## Worked example: a small rechargeable Bluetooth device

Illustrative example. A start-up is launching a battery-powered household device with a Bluetooth link to a phone app, sold online in Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Working through the questions above, it identifies:

- radio equipment rules (it has a Bluetooth radio), which also bring in electrical safety and EMC requirements;

- RoHS restrictions on hazardous substances in the electronics;

- battery safety, transport and producer-responsibility requirements for the lithium cell;

- waste electrical equipment (WEEE) and packaging obligations as a producer;

- CE marking for Northern Ireland and UKCA (or recognised CE) for Great Britain.

By using a pre-certified Bluetooth module and a certified charger, the team reduces the radio and mains-safety testing on its own product. It books a pre-compliance EMC scan on its engineering prototypes,
fixes an emissions problem with a layout change before the circuit board is finalised, then completes formal tests on production-intent units.
[Electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers the design decisions, such as antenna placement and cabling, that make this easier.

## Common mistakes

**Assuming a certified module certifies the product.**
It helps, but the finished product still has to comply as a whole.

**Leaving testing until after tooling.**
Fixes then mean tool changes and delays.

**Relying on a supplier's certificate without checking it.**
Check that it covers your product, version and standards, and comes from a credible laboratory.

**Forgetting labels and instructions.**
Required markings, addresses, warnings and English instructions are part of compliance.

**Treating certification as one-off.**
Component or design changes can invalidate earlier test results.

## Next steps

- List the regulations that may apply and check the GOV.UK guidance for each.

- Ask a test laboratory for a review of your design and a test plan; book pre-compliance testing early.

- Add certification to your development plan with the [Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html).

- Include testing and re-test allowances in the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html).

For the wider legal picture, see the [IP, partners and compliance hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html). For regulated categories such as medical devices, take specialist advice.

### Budget for compliance

Include testing, re-tests and documentation in the pre-launch budget.
[Open Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html)

### Plan it into development

See where pre-compliance and formal testing fit in the stages.
[Open Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html)

[IP, partners and compliance: the hub guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html)

## FAQ

### Does my product need UKCA or CE marking?

If it falls under a product regulation that requires a conformity marking, such as electrical equipment, electromagnetic compatibility, radio equipment, toys or machinery, yes. Great Britain uses UKCA and recognises CE marking for many products; Northern Ireland uses CE marking, with UKNI in some cases. Check GOV.UK guidance for your product category.

### Can I certify my own product?

For many products, yes: the manufacturer carries out the conformity assessment, usually by testing to designated or harmonised standards, prepares technical documentation and signs a declaration of conformity. Some higher-risk products, or products not fully covered by standards, need an independent conformity assessment body.

### Do I need to use an accredited test laboratory?

It is not always a legal requirement for self-assessed products, but test reports from a laboratory accredited by UKAS or an equivalent body carry more weight with retailers, marketplaces, insurers and regulators, and the laboratory's experience helps avoid mistakes.

### If I use a pre-certified Bluetooth or Wi-Fi module, is my product certified?

No. A pre-certified module can greatly reduce the radio testing needed, but the finished product must still meet the radio, EMC and safety requirements as a whole, and you still need the technical file, declaration and marking.

### When should I start thinking about certification?

At the requirements stage. Regulations can affect materials, enclosure design, circuit layout, labels and instructions. Pre-compliance testing on engineering prototypes, before tooling is finished, is far cheaper than redesign after a failed formal test.

Title: Printable Product Development Checklists

Reference

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders and teams preparing for manufacturer meetings, tooling, certification and launch

# Printable product development checklists

Six free, printable checklists for the main decision points in developing a physical product, each linked to the interactive tool or guide behind it. No sign-up needed.

Quick answer

## Six printable checklists for the main decision points in developing a physical product, free to print and use, with no sign-up.

Use them before talking to a manufacturer, before committing to tooling, while preparing for certification, when reviewing moulded parts, when sending a quote request and before launch.
Each links to an interactive version or a guide that explains the reasoning. To print, use your browser's print option; the checklists print with tick boxes.

- Ready to talk to a manufacturer

- Ready to commit to tooling

- Certification readiness

- Injection-moulded part review

- Quote request (RFQ) pack

- Launch readiness

## Ready to talk to a manufacturer

Can a manufacturer quote from what you send, without guessing? Score yourself with [Ready to Talk to a Manufacturer?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-manufacturer.html)

- Do you have 3D CAD of the parts in a standard format such as STEP?

- Do you have drawings showing materials, finishes and critical tolerances?

- Is there a bill of materials listing every part and quantity?

- Do you know realistic quantities for the first order and per year?

- Do you have a target unit cost worked back from your price and route to market?

- Has the design been tested in a prototype that works as intended?

- Have you checked the design against the process's design-for-manufacture rules?

- Do you know which regulations and markings apply to the product?

- Is a confidentiality agreement ready to sign before you share files?

- Have you decided what you will ask suppliers to quote, and on what delivery terms?

## Ready to commit to tooling

Tooling locks in the design and the spending. Score yourself with [Ready to Commit to Tooling?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html)

- Have production-intent parts passed testing against your requirements?

- Is the design frozen, with changes now going through [change control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html)?

- Have you done pre-compliance or formal compliance testing where required?

- Has a moulder or toolmaker reviewed the parts for manufacturability?

- Is there evidence of demand beyond the break-even volume for the tooling?

- Have you compared bridge tooling or low-volume routes with production tooling?

- Is the material and grade chosen and tested?

- Are tool ownership, life, modifications and samples agreed in writing?

- Can you fund the tooling and the first stock order together?

- Is there time and budget for at least one round of tool modifications?

## Certification readiness

Preparing for compliance testing and documentation (a self-check, not legal advice). Score yourself with [the Certification Readiness Checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html)

- Have you listed the product regulations that apply (for example electrical safety, EMC, radio, toys)?

- Have you identified the designated or harmonised standards you will test against?

- Do you know whether you can self-assess or need a conformity assessment body?

- Have you done pre-compliance testing on engineering prototypes?

- Is formal testing planned with a laboratory, with time for a re-test?

- Is there a documented risk assessment for the product?

- Is the technical documentation being compiled as you go (drawings, test reports, standards list)?

- Are labels, markings, addresses and English instructions designed?

- Is there a way to keep production consistent with the tested design (change control, traceability)?

- Have you covered producer responsibilities (waste electricals, batteries, packaging) where they apply?

## Injection-moulded part review

Points to check on each moulded part before asking a toolmaker for a review. Explained in the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html)

- Draft on every face that is parallel to the direction the mould opens

- Walls as even in thickness as the design allows, with gradual transitions

- Ribs thinner than the walls they support, to avoid sink marks

- Bosses supported by ribs and cored out rather than solid

- Internal and external corners radiused

- Undercuts removed, or agreed with the toolmaker if side actions are needed

- Gate, ejector pin and parting line positions acceptable on cosmetic faces

- Critical dimensions and tolerances marked; [general tolerances](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) realistic for moulding

- Material and grade chosen with shrinkage allowed for

- Texture and colour specified, with draft suited to the texture

## Quote request (RFQ) pack

What to send so suppliers can quote accurately and comparably. Build one with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html)

- Covering note: what the product is and what you are asking for

- 3D CAD in a standard format, such as STEP

- 2D drawings with materials, finishes and critical tolerances

- Bill of materials with quantities

- Quantities: first order, annual volume and how they may change

- Quality requirements: inspection, testing, cosmetic standard and samples

- Packaging and labelling requirements

- Compliance requirements the supplier must support

- Delivery terms, location and target dates

- What to quote: tooling, unit price at each quantity, lead times and payment terms

- Confidentiality agreement and contact details

## Launch readiness

Before the first units reach customers. Background in [product liability basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-liability-basics.html)

- Price checked against every margin in the chain and VAT

- Compliance confirmed, with technical documentation and markings complete

- Instructions, warnings and labels final and checked by real users

- Packaging tested for transit and sized for cartons and pallets

- First-article inspection passed and production checks agreed

- Batch or serial numbers in place for traceability

- Product liability insurance in place

- Returns, warranty and customer support process ready

- Stock, fulfilment and delivery promises agreed

- Listings, product pages and retailer information ready

- Cash plan covers the period until sales income arrives

- Packaging and producer responsibilities checked where they apply

**Practical rule:**
a "partly" is a "no" until it is finished. The gaps you are unsure about are often the ones that cause delays.

### Score your readiness

The interactive version weights each question and lists the gaps in order.
[Open Ready to Talk to a Manufacturer?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-manufacturer.html)

### Collect it in a plan

Save results from every tool into one plan you can print or share.

Title: Product Liability Basics for Product Developers

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders bringing a physical product to market in the UK (an overview, not legal advice)

# Product liability basics: what product developers should know

An overview of product liability for people developing physical products: who can be responsible when a product causes harm, the kinds of defect, and practical steps from design to insurance that reduce the risk. Take professional advice for your situation.

Quick answer

## If your product causes harm because it is defective, you may be liable even if you were not careless, so design, test, document and insure with that in mind.

In the UK, product liability law can make producers, including importers and businesses that put their own brand on a product, responsible for damage caused by defective products.
Reduce the risk through safe design, testing, clear instructions and warnings, traceability and good records, and talk to an insurer and a solicitor before launch.
This guide is an overview, not legal advice.

## What product liability means

Product liability is responsibility for harm caused by a product. In Great Britain, Part 1 of the
[Consumer Protection Act 1987](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/43) sets out liability for damage caused by defective products,
without the injured person needing to prove negligence, with equivalent provisions in Northern Ireland. Claims can also arise under contract and negligence.
Separately, product safety regulations require that products placed on the market are safe; see the official guidance on
[product safety for manufacturers](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/product-safety-for-manufacturers).

## Who can be liable

- **The manufacturer** of the finished product or a component.

- **The importer** that brings the product into the UK from outside.

- **An own-brander** that presents itself as the producer by putting its name or brand on the product.

- **Suppliers** in some circumstances, for example if they cannot identify who supplied them.

For a start-up having products made by a contract manufacturer and sold under its own brand, this usually means the start-up carries producer responsibilities.

## Kinds of defect

|
Defect |
Example |
How to reduce the risk |

|
Design |
A hinge that can trap fingers in normal use |
Risk assessment, [design reviews](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/running-a-design-review.html), foreseeable misuse, testing |

|
Manufacturing |
A batch moulded in the wrong material that cracks |
Specifications, first-article inspection, production checks, traceability |

|
Warnings and instructions |
Missing guidance on safe charging |
Clear instructions, warnings and labels, tested with real users |

**Practical rule:**
design out hazards first, guard against what remains, and only then rely on warnings. A warning does not make an unsafe design acceptable.

## Reducing the risk

- **Assess risks** early, including foreseeable misuse and vulnerable users such as children.

- **Design for safety** and meet the regulations and standards that apply; see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html).

- **Test** with a structured plan; see [product testing and validation plans](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html).

- **Control production quality**; see [quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html).

- **Write clear instructions and warnings.**

- **Make products traceable** with batch or serial numbers, so problems can be traced and recalls targeted.

- **Keep records** of design decisions, risk assessments, tests and supplier certificates.

- **Agree responsibilities** in supply contracts, including quality, indemnities and insurance.

- **Insure:** discuss product liability insurance with a broker before you sell.

- **Plan for problems:** how you would handle complaints, incidents and, if needed, a recall. [After launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) covers logging complaints and controlling fixes.

## Common mistakes

**Assuming the factory is responsible.**
If you sell under your brand or import the product, you may be treated as the producer.

**Relying on warnings.**
Warnings support a safe design; they do not replace it.

**No traceability.**
Without batch records, a small problem can mean recalling everything.

**Insurance as an afterthought.**
Retailers and marketplaces may ask for proof of cover before listing your product.

## Next steps

- Check your compliance route with [Certification Readiness](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html).

- Plan safety and abuse tests with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Add insurance and compliance costs to the [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html).

- Speak to an insurance broker and a solicitor before launch.

### Check compliance readiness

See what is needed before certification and launch.
[Open Certification Readiness](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html)

### Plan safety tests

Include abuse, misuse and safety tests in your plan.
[Open Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html)

Safety
Insurance
Compliance

## FAQ

### What is product liability?

Legal responsibility for harm caused by a product. In the UK, producers of defective products that cause damage can be liable without the injured person proving negligence, and claims can also arise in contract and negligence.

### Am I liable if a factory makes my product?

Possibly. If you import the product into the UK or present yourself as the producer by putting your brand on it, you may be treated as a producer with liability for defects, even though another company made it.

### Do I need product liability insurance?

It is strongly advisable for most physical products, and retailers and marketplaces may require it. Discuss the cover you need with an insurance broker before you start selling.

### Do warnings protect me from liability?

Clear warnings and instructions matter, but they do not make an unsafe design acceptable. Design out hazards first, guard against what remains, then warn about residual risks.

### How can I reduce product liability risk?

Assess risks early, design for safety, meet applicable regulations, test thoroughly, control production quality, write clear instructions, make products traceable, keep records, agree supplier responsibilities and insure.

Title: Product Testing and Validation Plans

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For product teams planning tests from first prototype to production

# Product testing and validation plans: proving a product works

How to plan testing for a physical product: the difference between verification and validation, what goes into a test plan, the main types of test, and which tests belong at each stage from early prototypes to production.

Quick answer

## Verification checks you built the product right; validation checks you built the right product. A good test plan covers both, linked to your requirements.

Turn each requirement into a test with a method, a sample size and a pass or fail criterion. Plan which tests happen at which prototype stage, from quick engineering checks on early models
to formal testing on production-representative units. Include user testing, durability and life tests, transit tests and any certification testing, and record results so decisions can be traced.

## Verification and validation

|
|
Verification |
Validation |

|
Question |
Does the product meet its requirements? |
Does the product meet users' real needs in real use? |

|
Examples |
Dimensions, strength, battery life, drop tests, temperature, electrical safety |
User trials, in-home or field testing, usability sessions |

|
Based on |
The [product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html) |
The user, problem and use environment |

A product can pass every verification test and still fail validation, if the requirements were wrong. That is why both matter.

## What a test plan contains

- **Requirement or question** being tested, with its ID.

- **Method:** how the test is done, ideally to a named standard or a written procedure.

- **Samples:** how many units, made how, at which build stage.

- **Pass criteria:** agreed before testing, not after seeing the results.

- **Who and where:** in-house, at a supplier or at an accredited test lab.

- **Timing and cost:** so tests fit the schedule and budget.

## Types of test to consider

|
Type |
Examples |

|
Functional |
Does every feature work as specified? |

|
Performance |
Capacity, speed, accuracy, battery life |

|
Durability and life |
Cycle tests on buttons, hinges and latches; wear; fatigue |

|
Environmental |
Temperature, humidity, water and dust, UV |

|
Mechanical abuse |
Drops, impacts, crush and misuse |

|
Transit |
Packaged drop, vibration and compression; see [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html) |

|
Usability |
Can target users set up, use, clean and maintain it without help? |

|
Compliance |
Safety, EMC and other tests for the regulations that apply; see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) |

For setting drop heights and orientations and designing the product to pass, see [designing a product to survive drops and impacts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html).

**Practical rule:**
run informal pre-compliance and abuse tests on prototypes before booking formal certification testing. Failing at an accredited lab costs time and money that an early check could have saved.

## Test at the right stage

- **Early prototypes:** quick checks of the riskiest functions and user reactions.

- **Integrated prototypes:** fuller functional, performance, durability and [usability tests](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html).

- **Pre-production samples:** repeat key tests on units made with production processes, plus formal compliance testing.

- **Production:** ongoing checks; see [quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html).

See [how many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) for planning the rounds.

## Common mistakes

**Testing without pass criteria.**
Results become a matter of opinion.

**Testing one unit.**
One pass may be luck; test enough units to be confident, especially for safety.

**Testing only in the lab.**
Real users and real environments reveal problems lab tests miss.

**Not retesting after changes.**
A design or supplier change can undo earlier results.

- List requirements and risks, then build the plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- Check compliance testing needs with [Certification Readiness](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/certification-readiness.html).

- Add test time to your schedule with the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html).

Verification
Validation
Durability

## FAQ

### What is the difference between verification and validation?

Verification checks that the product meets its specified requirements. Validation checks that it meets users' real needs in real use. A product can pass verification and still fail validation if the requirements were wrong.

### What should a product test plan include?

For each test: the requirement or question, the method, the number and build stage of samples, pass criteria agreed in advance, who will do it and where, and the timing and cost.

### When should testing start?

As soon as there is something to test. Early prototypes test the riskiest functions and user reactions; later stages add fuller performance, durability, usability and compliance testing.

### What is pre-compliance testing?

Informal testing against the requirements of a regulation or standard before formal certification testing, so problems are found and fixed before paying for accredited lab tests.

### How many units should I test?

Enough to be confident the result is not luck, which depends on the test, the risk and the variation between units. Safety-critical tests usually need more units than quick engineering checks.
