Title: Prototyping vs Production: A Startup Guide

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For start-ups moving from prototypes towards production

# Prototyping vs production: a startup guide

The wrong prototype route wastes time because it answers the wrong question. Before choosing the process,
decide whether this build is meant to prove appearance, function, manufacturability, pilot demand, or all of the above.

Quick answer

## The right prototype method depends on what you need to learn, not what process feels most advanced.

Best route = build objective + quantity + fidelity needs + urgency + budget + commitment tolerance

Prototyping is for learning quickly while the design can still change; production is for making the same part repeatably at the lowest sustainable unit cost.
If the objective is still learning, flexible low-commitment processes usually beat more production-like routes, and production tooling should wait until the design and demand are stable.

Startups often feel pressure to look “production ready” early, whether for investors, [crowdfunding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) or retail buyers. That pressure can push a team into tooling,
[minimum order quantities](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) and fixed geometry before the product has earned them. Understanding what each route is really buying helps the team spend money on learning first and commitment second.

## Prototyping vs production at a glance

|
Factor |
Prototyping |
Production |

|
Main goal |
Learn and reduce uncertainty |
Repeatable quality at target cost |

|
Typical quantity |
One to a few hundred |
Thousands upwards |

|
Upfront cost |
Low; little or no tooling |
High; tooling, fixtures and setup |

|
Unit cost |
High |
Low |

|
Lead time |
Days to a few weeks |
Weeks to months before the first parts |

|
Cost of a design change |
Small |
Often large, especially after tooling |

## What each route is best at

|
Route |
Best for |
Typical quantities |
Weakest point |

|
3D printing |
Fast learning, geometry checks, concept demos |
One to tens |
Surface quality and scalable unit economics |

|
[CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) |
Functional validation, precise geometry, durable prototypes |
One to low hundreds |
Higher unit cost at larger quantities |

|
Vacuum casting |
Looks-like parts and low-volume bridge production |
Roughly 10 to 25 parts per silicone mould; tens to low hundreds overall |
Not a final mass-production route |

|
Bridge tooling |
[Pilot runs](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) and early market validation |
Hundreds to several thousand |
Still requires more commitment than true prototype routes |

|
Pilot injection |
Production-like learning when volume and confidence are high |
Hundreds to thousands from the production tool |
Painful if the design is still moving |

These quantity ranges are typical rules of thumb, not limits. Part size, material, geometry and the supplier’s equipment all shift them.
Within 3D printing, filament, resin and powder processes suit quite different questions; [choosing a 3D printing process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-a-3d-printing-process.html) compares them.

A prototype is not successful because it looks like production. It is successful because it teaches the team what the next decision should be.

## The kinds of prototype a startup usually needs

- **Looks-like prototypes** show form, size and finish for user feedback, photography and investor conversations.

- **Works-like prototypes** prove the mechanism or electronics, often with no attention to appearance.

- **Integrated prototypes** combine the two so the team can test the real product in use.

- **Pre-production samples** come from production or bridge processes and test repeatability, assembly and quality.

Splitting looks-like and works-like early is usually faster and cheaper than trying to make every build do everything. [Looks-like vs works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) explains when to merge them into an integrated prototype.

## Questions to answer before choosing a route

- What must this build prove?

- How many units are genuinely needed?

- How much cosmetic fidelity matters right now?

- How painful would a late design change be?

- Is the team optimising for learning speed or production realism?

## Illustrative example: a flip-top drinks bottle lid

Imagine a startup developing a leak-proof flip-top lid for a reusable bottle. Early on, resin 3D prints let the team try a dozen hinge and latch variations in a few weeks.
Next, a small batch of machined or high-detail printed lids in near-final materials checks the seal under pressure and repeated opening.

For user trials, the team vacuum casts a few dozen lids in a polyurethane chosen to mimic the target plastic. The trials reveal that users struggle to open the latch with wet hands, which is cheap to fix at this stage.
Only once the latch, seal and hinge are stable does the team commission a production mould. One lesson is typical: some properties, such as the fatigue life of a moulded polypropylene hinge,
only show up properly in the production material and process, so the plan allows for sample testing after the first moulded parts. This example is illustrative.

## When to move from prototyping to production

- critical features are frozen and further changes are cosmetic or minor

- representative parts have passed the functional and [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html) that matters

- a design for manufacture review has been done with the intended supplier

- there is credible demand evidence, such as orders, pre-sales or a committed channel

- the team can fund tooling and first inventory, and can absorb the lead time

Production injection mould tools commonly take several weeks to a few months to build, depending on complexity, followed by sampling and adjustment.
Planning for that gap is part of the decision. The [injection mould break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) covers the cost side in more detail.

## Common mistakes

**Over-building early prototypes.** Paying for production-like finish before the mechanism works spends money on the wrong question.

**Tooling too early.** Committing to a mould before the design is stable often leads to tool modifications that cost time and erode the expected savings.

**Assuming prototype materials behave like production ones.** Printed and cast parts differ in strength, stiffness and wear. Test critical features in the real material before launch.

**Skipping DFM.** A part that prints well may be hard or impossible to mould without draft, uniform walls and sensible undercuts; [from 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html) explains what to change.

**Ignoring the time after first samples.** First moulded samples rarely go straight to production; allow time for corrections.

## Practical next steps

Write down what the next build must prove, then use the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html) to compare routes against that brief.
If the product is close to the prototype-to-production boundary, the [Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html)
and [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) show when committing makes sense.
[The risk-progressive manufacturing strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html) explains the staged path in more depth,
and the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps fit prototyping, tooling and launch into one timeline and budget.

### Compare prototype routes

Score 3D printing, CNC, vacuum casting, bridge tooling, and pilot injection against the actual build brief.
[Open Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html)

### Plan the next production step

Use the production planner if you are moving from prototype intent into low-volume manufacture or scale-up.
[Open Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html)

Related guides

[How many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html)

[Manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html)

This article answers

Prototype method
3D printing vs CNC
Bridge production

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a prototype and a production part?

A prototype is made to answer a question about the design, such as whether it works, fits or appeals to users, usually with flexible processes and little tooling. A production part is made with the final process and tooling to be repeatable at the target cost and quality. The two can look similar but often differ in material behaviour and tolerances.

### How many prototypes do you need before manufacturing?

There is no fixed number. Most physical products go through several rounds, from rough concept models to works-like, looks-like and pre-production builds. The right point to stop is when critical functions and user needs have been proven on representative parts, not when a set count is reached.

### Is 3D printing suitable for production?

For low volumes, complex geometry or customised parts, it can be. For most consumer products at higher volumes, unit cost, cycle time and [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) usually favour moulding or machining. Many teams use 3D printing for production of small batches while volumes are uncertain.

### What is bridge tooling?

Bridge tooling is lower-cost, faster-to-make tooling, often aluminium or simplified steel, used to produce real moulded parts in modest volumes before full production tooling. It lets a team run pilots and early sales in the production material while keeping commitment lower. Tool life is shorter, so it is not normally the long-term answer for high volumes.

### When should a startup invest in injection mould tooling?

When the design is stable, testing on representative parts is complete, a DFM review has been done, and demand evidence supports the volume needed to recover the tooling cost. If any of those are weak, a bridge route usually buys better evidence first.

Title: Quality Control and First-Article Inspection

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers moving a product into production with a manufacturer

# Quality control and first-article inspection for new products

A practical approach to quality for a new product: define what good looks like, check the first production parts in full, inspect during production and before shipment, and agree how problems will be handled before they happen.

Quick answer

## Agree in writing what "good" means before production, check the first parts against it in full, then sample every batch against the same standard.

Quality control starts with a clear specification: drawings with tolerances, critical-to-quality features, cosmetic standards and golden samples.
A first-article inspection (FAI) measures and tests the first production parts against every requirement before volume production is approved.
After that, incoming, in-process and pre-shipment inspections catch problems while they are still cheap to fix.

## Why quality control needs planning

A factory can only meet a standard it has been given. Many disputes between brands and manufacturers come from requirements that were never written down:
a colour that was "close enough", a gap that was within the drawing but felt wrong, or a function nobody tested. Planning quality early is far cheaper than sorting or reworking a shipment.

## Step 1: define what good looks like

- **Drawings and tolerances** for every part, with the critical dimensions marked. See the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html).

- **Critical-to-quality (CTQ) features:** the few dimensions and functions that decide whether the product works, is safe or looks right.

- **Cosmetic standards:** which surfaces matter, which defects are acceptable, at what viewing distance and lighting.

- **Golden samples:** approved reference units, signed off and kept by both you and the factory.

- **Functional tests:** what each unit, or each sample, must do before it ships.

- **Packaging and labelling** requirements, including drop and transit expectations.

## Step 2: first-article inspection

A first-article inspection checks the first parts made with production tooling, materials and processes against every requirement on the drawings and specification.
It confirms that the process can make the part correctly before you commit to volume.

|
FAI covers |
What to check |

|
Dimensions |
Every dimension on the drawing, with the critical ones measured on several parts, and results recorded in an inspection report |

|
Materials |
Material grade, colour and finish match the specification, with supplier certificates where relevant |

|
Assembly and fit |
Parts assemble as intended, with correct gaps, alignment and fastener torque |

|
Function |
The product passes its functional tests and any safety checks |

|
Cosmetics |
Surfaces compared with the golden sample and cosmetic standard |

For moulded parts this usually follows tool trials (T1, T2 and so on) and texture or colour approval. See
[Ready for Tooling](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html) and the
[injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html). Repeat the FAI whenever the tool, material, process or supplier changes.
[Mould tool trials and sample approval](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html) explains what to ask for with each trial round and how to read the first moulded samples.
Once first articles are approved, a [pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) checks that the full line makes good, packed products repeatedly before volume.

**Practical rule:**
do not approve volume production from a sample that was hand-finished or made on a different process. Approve parts made exactly as production parts will be made.

## Step 3: inspection during production

|
Stage |
Purpose |

|
Incoming inspection |
Check bought-in parts and materials before they are used |

|
In-process checks |
Catch drift early, for example measuring critical dimensions at set intervals |

|
End-of-line testing |
Functional or safety tests on each unit, or on a defined sample |

|
Pre-shipment inspection |
A sample from the finished, packed batch checked before it leaves the factory, often by an independent inspector |

## Sampling and acceptance levels

Inspecting every unit is rarely practical, so batches are usually checked by sampling. Acceptance sampling standards such as ISO 2859-1 set how many units to inspect for a given batch size
and how many defects are acceptable, expressed as an acceptance quality limit (AQL), the term ISO 2859-1 uses (older texts say acceptable quality level). Agree the AQL for critical, major and minor defects with your manufacturer before production,
with critical defects (safety or regulatory) usually allowed none.

## When things go wrong

- **Contain:** stop shipment and separate suspect stock.

- **Find the root cause:** tool wear, material change, process drift or an unclear specification.

- **Correct and prevent:** fix the cause, update the specification or checks, and confirm with a fresh inspection. For problems found by customers, see [after launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html).

- **Agree responsibility** in advance in your [supply agreement](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/supply-agreements-with-a-manufacturer.html): who pays for sorting, rework and replacement.

## Common mistakes

**No written cosmetic standard.**
"It looks wrong" is hard to enforce without agreed criteria and golden samples.

**Skipping FAI to save time.**
Problems found in a full shipment are far more expensive than in the first parts.

**Only checking at the end.**
Pre-shipment inspection finds problems after the batch is made; earlier checks prevent them.

**Not repeating checks after changes.**
A new material, tool repair or second supplier can change the parts without anyone noticing.

- Include quality requirements in your quote request with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

- Check your handover with [Ready for Manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-manufacturer.html).

- Read [how to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html).

## FAQ

### What is a first-article inspection?

A full check of the first parts made with production tooling, materials and processes against every requirement on the drawings and specification, covering dimensions, materials, fit, function and cosmetics, before volume production is approved.

### When should a first-article inspection be repeated?

Whenever something that could change the part changes: a new or repaired tool, a different material or supplier, a process change or a move to another factory.

### What is AQL in quality control?

The acceptance quality limit (often still called the acceptable quality level): the defect level used with a sampling standard such as ISO 2859-1 to decide whether a batch passes, based on inspecting a sample. Brands usually set separate limits for critical, major and minor defects, with none allowed for critical defects.

### What is a golden sample?

An approved reference unit, signed off by the brand and the manufacturer, that production is compared against, especially for colour, finish and feel that drawings cannot fully describe.

### Do I need an independent inspector?

Not always, but an independent pre-shipment inspection is common when [manufacturing overseas](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html) or with a new supplier, because it gives an objective check before you pay for and ship the goods.

Title: Reducing the Cost of an Existing Product

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers whose product is already in production and costs more to make than it should

# Reducing the cost of an existing product

How to find where the cost of a product in production really sits, which kinds of change usually lower it, how to make those changes without breaking function, safety or certification, and how to decide which ones are worth doing first.

Quick answer

## Start from a full cost breakdown, not a hunch, then rank possible changes by saving per unit times volume, against the effort, one-off cost and risk of making each one.

Cost in a product that is already being made often hides in bought-in parts, assembly time, scrap, packaging and freight rather than in the main moulded or machined parts.
The best cost-down changes remove parts, operations or over-specification that customers do not value, and every change is validated and controlled before it reaches production, because a cheaper product that fails, or no longer meets its certification, is not cheaper.

## Contents

- What value engineering means for a product in production

- Start from a cost breakdown

- Where cost hides

- Cost-down ideas by category

- Protecting function, safety and brand

- Talking to suppliers

- Prioritising: saving × volume against effort and risk

- Worked example: three changes to a small device

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What value engineering means for a product in production

Value engineering asks what each part, feature and process step does for the customer, and whether the same function can be delivered for less. Once a product is in production that is harder to act on: tools are cut, suppliers are set up, test reports and certificates refer to the current design, and customers know how it looks and feels.

So cost reduction on an existing product is a balance. Every change saves something per unit but costs something once: engineering time, tool changes, new samples, retesting and the risk of a fault reaching customers. A change is worth making when the first comfortably outweighs the second at the volumes you will actually sell.

## Start from a cost breakdown

Before choosing changes, rebuild what one unit really costs, line by line, at your current order volume. The [guide to estimating manufacturing cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html) sets out the method: materials, process, bought-in parts, assembly labour and packaging, then a scrap allowance and an overhead loading, then tooling and landed costs on top.

List every part in the [BOM Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html) with its quantity and current price, then load the totals into the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html), which shows the largest cost driver and how sensitive the result is to each input. Use real invoice prices and measured build times: that is the advantage of a product already in production. The breakdown is also the baseline every saving is measured against.

## Where cost hides

The main enclosure or chassis gets the attention, but it is often not where most of the money goes. Look hardest at:

- **Bought-in parts.** Electronics, cables, fasteners, inserts, labels and accessories add up, and many were chosen quickly during development.

- **Process and cycle time.** A moulding with thick walls cools slowly; a machined part with tight features takes longer and needs more setups. Cycle time is usually priced into each part.

- **Assembly labour.** Each screw, cable, label and reorientation takes seconds, and seconds multiply across every unit. The [assembly time guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) shows how to estimate them, and [joining methods compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) shows the faster alternatives.

- **Scrap and quality.** Parts rejected for cosmetic marks, units failing end-of-line test and rework all add cost that may sit inside an allowance nobody questions. [Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) covers how to find the causes.

- **Packaging and freight.** An oversized box costs more to make, fits fewer units on a pallet and can cost more to ship. See [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html) and [landed cost: freight, duty and VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html).

- **Tooling amortisation.** If tooling cost is being recovered per unit, low sales mean each unit carries more of it. That is a volume problem, not a design one, so do not try to fix it with redesigns that need new tools.

## Cost-down ideas by category

How much each is worth depends entirely on your product, volumes and suppliers, so treat these as places to look, not promises.

- **Part consolidation.** Two parts that never move relative to each other can sometimes become one moulding, removing a part, a join and an assembly step. The new part may need a new or modified tool.

- **Material changes.** A lower-cost grade, an unfilled resin in place of a glass-filled one, or a standard sheet thickness can save money, but material changes affect strength, appearance, flammability and sometimes certification. [Choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) explains the trade-offs.

- **Tolerance relaxation.** Tight tolerances on features that do not need them add machining time, inspection and scrap. Review the drawing against what each feature actually does, as described in [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html).

- **Finish simplification.** A moulded-in texture in place of paint, one print colour instead of two, or a finish only on visible faces can remove whole operations. See [surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html).

- **Fastener reduction.** Fewer screws, one screw type throughout, or snap fits where the joint is not opened for service all cut parts and assembly time.

- **Packaging size.** A smaller box, fewer inserts and instructions printed on the box itself can reduce material and freight cost, provided the product still survives transit.

- **Supplier and route changes.** Re-quoting a part, combining parts with one supplier or moving where the product is made can change cost substantially, but a cheaper unit price can bring higher freight, [minimum order quantities](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) or quality risk. Compare like for like using [getting and comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) and [UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html).

## Protecting function, safety and brand

A product in production has already been proven. Each change reopens part of that proof, so treat it as a small design project:

- **Validate before you switch.** Decide which tests the change could affect, such as drop, strength, temperature, ingress, transit or user feel, and repeat them on parts made by the production process. The [testing and validation plans guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) and the [Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html) help you choose.

- **Use change control.** Record each change with a reason, a new part or [drawing revision](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html), the date or batch it takes effect, and who approved it, so that a field problem can be traced to the build it came from.

- **Check certification.** Changes to materials, the enclosure, electronics, power supply, labelling or construction may affect the evidence behind a declaration of conformity or a test report. Ask whoever holds your technical file, or your test house, whether the change needs assessing before you make it. [Product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) outlines how conformity is shown.

- **Protect what customers value.** The feel of a button, the weight in the hand and the unboxing can be part of why people buy. Ask customers, or check reviews and returns, before removing something that looks like a cost but works as a reason to buy.

## Talking to suppliers

Your suppliers make these parts every day and often know where the cost is. Ask them openly: which features slow the cycle, cause rejects or need extra operations, and what they would change if they could. A supplier who can plan longer runs from an honest forecast may lower the price without any design change.

Ask for any new price to be quoted against the same specification, volume and terms as the current one, and to show the one-off cost of tool changes and new samples separately. Agree who pays for tool modifications and who owns the modified tool. A brief like the one in [how to find and brief a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-find-and-brief-a-manufacturer.html) keeps the request clear.

## Prioritising: saving × volume against effort and risk

Annual saving = loaded saving per unit × units per year

Compare that annual saving with the one-off cost of the change (engineering, tool modification, samples, retesting, any certification work) to find how many units it takes to pay back. Then weigh the risk: a packaging change that a drop test can prove is lower risk than a material change to a load-bearing part.

If scrap and overhead are charged as percentages, a direct saving is worth slightly more once they are applied. Start with changes that are high in saving × volume, low in risk and quick to prove.

## Worked example: three changes to a small device

Illustrative figures only. This continues the worked example in the [manufacturing cost guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html): £4.80 of material, £2.40 of process, £5.50 of bought-in parts (£12.70 together), £4.80 of labour (12 minutes at £24 an hour) and £1.20 of packaging (£6.00 together). The direct cost is £18.70; a 6% scrap allowance (£1.12) gives £19.82, and a 14% overhead loading (£2.77) gives a COGS of £22.59.

The team tests three assumed changes, each priced with the same method and rounding:

|
Change (assumed) |
Direct cost |
New COGS |
Saving |

|
Snap fits replace four screws |
Labour −£1.20 (12 to 9 min); screws −£0.30 |
£20.78 |
£1.81 |

|
Smaller box, one fewer insert |
Packaging −£0.25 |
£22.30 |
£0.29 |

|
No paint on a hidden face |
Process −£0.30 |
£22.23 |
£0.36 |

|
All three together |
£18.70 to £16.65 |
£20.12 |
£2.47 |

With all three, the direct cost falls to £16.65; scrap at 6% is £1.00, giving £17.65, and overhead at 14% is £2.47, giving a COGS of £20.12. The individual savings add up to £2.46 rather than £2.47 because each figure is rounded to the penny.

Illustrative figures from the worked example, drawn to scale. Most of the saving comes from assembly time; scrap and overhead fall too because they are charged as percentages.

At an assumed 10,000 units a year, the three changes save £24,700 a year. Suppose the tool modification for the snap fits costs £2,500, and samples, a transit drop test and retesting cost another £1,500. The £4,000 of one-off cost is repaid after about 1,620 units (£4,000 ÷ £2.47), well inside the first year.

At 500 units a year the same changes save £1,235 a year, and the payback takes more than three years. The packaging change on its own, at £0.29 a unit, would save £145 a year at that volume, which is unlikely to cover even a drop test.

Two cautions. The overhead saving assumes overhead is charged as a percentage, as a supplier's loading usually is; a fixed overhead of your own will not fall. And the snap fits must still allow any service access the product needs, proven by drop and opening tests.

## Common mistakes

**Cutting cost that customers value.**
A thinner wall that flexes, a cheaper switch that feels loose or a flimsier box can lose more in returns, reviews and price than it saves.

**Changes without validation.**
A part that looks equivalent can behave differently in a drop, in heat or after months of use. Prove each change on production-process parts before switching.

**Chasing small savings on low-volume parts.**
A few pence on a part made a few hundred times a year rarely repays the engineering, samples and testing it needs.

**Ignoring tooling change costs.**
Tool modifications, new tools, scrapped stock of the old part and supplier set-up charges all belong in the payback calculation.

**Forgetting certification.**
A material, component or construction change can affect the evidence behind your declaration. Check before the change, not after.

## Decision rules

- **Measure first:** rebuild the full unit cost before choosing any change.

- **Rank by annual saving** (saving per unit × units per year), then by risk and one-off cost.

- **Prefer removing** parts, operations and unneeded precision over cheapening what remains.

- **Validate and record** every change, and check whether it touches certification.

- **Leave alone** what customers notice and value, unless they tell you otherwise.

- Plan the tests each change needs in the [Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

## FAQ

### What is value engineering?

A structured review of what each part, feature and process step does for the customer, looking for ways to deliver the same function for less cost. On a product in production it is usually called cost reduction or cost-down.

### Where should I look first to reduce product cost?

Rebuild the full unit cost and look at the largest lines first. Bought-in parts, assembly time, scrap and packaging are often bigger than expected, and changes that remove parts or operations usually save more than squeezing the price of what remains.

### Do I need to retest after a cost-down change?

Usually, yes, for whatever the change could affect. A new material, a different joint or smaller packaging should be checked with the relevant drop, strength, temperature or transit tests on parts made by the production process.

### Can a cost-down change affect my product certification?

It can. Changes to materials, the enclosure, electronics, power supply, labelling or construction may affect the evidence behind your declaration of conformity. Check with whoever maintains your technical file, or your test house, before making the change.

### How do I know if a cost saving is worth making?

Multiply the saving per unit by the units you expect to sell each year, then compare it with the one-off cost of tooling changes, samples and testing to find the payback. Favour changes that pay back quickly and carry little risk.

Title: Retail and Distributor Margins Explained

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders preparing to sell a physical product through retailers or distributors

# Retail and distributor margins explained: from shelf price to what you receive

How margins work when a physical product is sold through retailers and distributors: the difference between margin and markup, how to work back from the shelf price, and the terms beyond the headline margin that affect what you actually keep.

Quick answer

## Each business in the chain takes its margin as a share of its own selling price, so work backwards from the shelf price to see what you receive.

Margin = (selling price − buying price) ÷ selling price
Markup = (selling price − buying price) ÷ buying price
Markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin)

Retailers and distributors usually talk in margin, while many founders think in markup, and confusing the two is a common source of pricing mistakes.
Start from the shelf price, remove VAT, then remove each party's margin in turn to find what you will be paid. Then check that covers your landed cost and your own margin,
plus any promotions, marketing contributions and payment terms the buyer asks for.

## Margin and markup

|
Margin |
Equivalent markup |
Selling price if the buying price is £10 |

|
20% |
25% |
£12.50 |

|
25% |
33.3% |
£13.33 |

|
40% |
66.7% |
£16.67 |

|
50% |
100% |
£20.00 |

|
60% |
150% |
£25.00 |

When a buyer asks for "a 50% margin", they mean half of their selling price, which is double your price to them, not 50% more.

## The chain from factory to shelf

|
Stage |
What happens |

|
Landed cost |
What each unit costs you once made, packed, shipped, duty-paid and in your warehouse; see [landed cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) |

|
Your margin |
Must cover overheads, development, marketing, returns and profit |

|
Distributor (if used) |
Buys from you, stocks and sells to retailers; takes a margin for logistics, sales reach and credit risk |

|
Retailer |
Buys from you or the distributor and sets the shelf price; takes a margin for space, staff, marketing and risk |

|
VAT |
Added to the shelf price for consumers; see current [VAT rates](https://www.gov.uk/vat-rates) |

Margins vary widely by category, retailer and the services each party provides, so ask buyers and distributors directly rather than relying on a rule of thumb.

Illustrative figures only. A product sells at £39.99 including 20% VAT, so £33.33 before VAT. A retailer taking a 40% margin pays £20.00. A distributor taking a 25% margin pays the brand £15.00.
With a landed cost of £8.00, the brand keeps £7.00, a 46.7% margin, from which overheads, marketing and returns must be paid. Selling direct to the retailer instead, the brand would receive £20.00.
The retailer's 40% margin is a 66.7% markup, and the distributor's 25% is a 33.3% markup.

Illustrative figures from the example above, bars drawn to scale. Each business takes its margin from its own selling price, so a £39.99 shelf price pays the brand £15.00, and only £7.00 of that is left once the £8.00 landed cost is covered.

**Practical rule:**
build your price from the shelf down, not from your cost up. If the shelf price customers will pay cannot support every margin in the chain, change the cost, the route or the product.

## Beyond the headline margin

- **Payment terms:** buyers often pay weeks after delivery, which affects your cash; model it with the [Cash Flow Projection](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

- **Promotions:** discounts are frequently funded partly or wholly by the supplier.

- **Marketing contributions:** some retailers ask for fees or co-funded marketing for listings or displays.

- **Returns and damages:** agree who pays for faulty, damaged or unsold stock.

- **Sale or return:** occasionally offered to new brands, but you carry the stock risk until it sells.

- **Settlement discounts:** a small discount for early payment can help cash flow.

Agree these in writing; they can take more of the price than the headline margin suggests. Retailers also set packaging, barcode and outer case requirements of their own; see [retail-ready packaging and barcodes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html).

## Common mistakes

**Confusing margin and markup.**
A "40% markup" leaves far less room than a buyer's "40% margin" requires.

**Forgetting VAT.**
Margins are worked on prices before VAT.

**Pricing direct sales below retail.**
Undercutting your retailers damages the relationship; see [how to price a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-price-a-physical-product.html).

**Ignoring the extras.**
Promotions, contributions and terms can cut your real margin significantly.

## FAQ

### What is the difference between margin and markup?

Margin is profit as a share of the selling price; markup is profit as a share of the buying price. A 50% margin equals a 100% markup. Retailers and distributors usually quote margin.

### How do I convert margin to markup?

Markup equals margin divided by one minus the margin. For example, a 40% margin is 0.4 ÷ 0.6, a 66.7% markup.

### What margin do retailers expect?

It varies widely by category, retailer and the services involved, so ask buyers directly. Work backwards from the shelf price to check that every margin in the chain still leaves you enough.

### Do I need a distributor?

Not always. Distributors add reach, logistics and credit management in return for a margin. Selling direct to retailers keeps more of the price but means more sales and admin work for you.

### Are margins calculated before or after VAT?

Before VAT. Remove VAT from the shelf price first, then work back through each party's margin.

Title: Retail-Ready Packaging and Barcodes

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders preparing a physical product for its first retailer or distributor

# Retail-ready packaging and barcodes: the basics

What changes when a product moves from your website onto a shop shelf: what retailers commonly ask for, barcodes, outer cases, on-pack information, display, sustainability, and how print, tooling and minimum orders affect cash and the schedule.

Quick answer

## Retail packaging must sell the product on a shelf and fit the retailer's systems: a barcode for each variant, a clear outer case specification, accurate dimensions and weights, and the right information and marks.

Ask your first retailer or distributor for their supplier requirements early, because they shape the box, carton and schedule. Retailers commonly require a GS1 barcode, carrying a number called a GTIN, on every product; a business obtains these through GS1 membership in its country, and each variant needs its own.
Design the pack alongside the product, sample and test it, and keep the first print run modest until pilot feedback is in.

## Contents

- How retail packaging differs from shipping-only packaging

- What retailers and distributors commonly ask for

- Barcodes: the essentials

- Information on the pack

- Shelf presence: hanging or standing

- Sustainability

- Print, tooling, minimum orders and cash

- Working with packaging suppliers

- Fitting packaging into the schedule

- Worked example: a small gadget's first retailer

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## How retail packaging differs from shipping-only packaging

Packaging for parcels sent direct to customers is mostly about protection and unboxing; [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html) covers that journey. Retail packaging must still protect, but takes on extra jobs:

- **Sell without you there.** On a shelf or a hook, the box is the only salesperson: a shopper should grasp what the product is and does within seconds.

- **Work in someone else's systems.** Retailers receive, count and sell stock using barcodes, case labels and data you supply. Packaging that does not fit causes delays or refused deliveries.

- **Survive handling in store.** Boxes are handled, opened by curious shoppers and restocked, so seals, windows and hang tabs need to cope.

- **Travel in cases and on pallets.** Retail stock usually moves in outer cases on pallets, so case and pallet fit matter as much as the box.

Some products need a retail box for shops and a different pack for online orders; decide early whether one design can do both.

Retailers ask for details at every level, so a change to the unit pack ripples through the case quantity and the pallet.

## What retailers and distributors commonly ask for

Each retailer and distributor sets its own requirements, usually in a supplier manual or new-product form; ask for it as soon as talks become serious. In general terms, expect questions about:

|
Item |
What it usually means |

|
Barcodes |
A barcode on each product, and often on the outer case, with numbers registered to your business |

|
Outer case specification |
The carton the units ship in: material, size, strength and how it is closed |

|
Case quantity |
How many units in each case, and in each inner pack if used, often chosen to suit the retailer's ordering |

|
Case labelling |
Description, product code, quantity, barcode and sometimes batch information on the carton |

|
Dimensions and weights |
Measured size and weight of the unit pack, inner and outer case |

|
Pallet arrangement |
Cases per layer, layers per pallet, and any height or weight limits |

|
Drop or transit testing |
Sometimes, evidence that the packed product survives handling |

|
Product information |
Images, descriptions, materials and compliance documents for listings and their own checks |

Plan any drop or transit tests in your [test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) so the evidence is ready when asked. [Retail and distributor margins explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-and-distributor-margins-explained.html) covers the commercial terms that come alongside.

## Barcodes: the essentials

Retailers commonly require a GS1 barcode on each product. The number behind it is a GTIN (Global Trade Item Number), identifying one specific product to tills and stock systems. A business obtains GTINs through membership of GS1, the organisation that runs the system, in its own country; in the UK that is [GS1 UK](https://www.gs1uk.org/). Check the current membership terms with GS1 directly.

- **One number per variant.** Each colour, size, kit or pack quantity a shopper could buy needs its own GTIN, or nobody can tell variants apart in stock or sales.

- **Ask about cases.** Retailers may also want an identifier on the outer case so a whole case can be scanned.

- **Keep a register.** Record which number belongs to which variant and pack, and never reuse one for a different product.

- **Print and check.** Place it on a flat, clear area, follow your printer's and GS1's guidance on size and clear space, and scan printed samples before approving the run.

Set barcodes up before artwork is finalised: the numbers have to be in the print files.

## Information on the pack

At a general level, the pack and the product together need to tell a shopper and a retailer:

- **Product name and what it is,** clear enough to understand at a glance from the shelf.

- **What is in the box:** product, accessories, batteries and instructions.

- **Who you are and how to reach you:** your business name and contact details.

- **Required marks and information.** [Product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) describes these in general terms: conformity marking where it applies, the manufacturer's (and importer's) name and address, product identification for traceability, and instructions and safety information in English. Check that guide and its official links before artwork is signed off.

- **A batch or date code,** so a problem can be traced to a production run later.

Labelling is part of compliance, not decoration: ask whoever maintains your technical file to check the pack copy.

## Shelf presence: hanging or standing

How the product will be displayed shapes the box from the start. Ask the retailer which they expect:

- **Hanging display, on pegs or hooks.** A strong hang tab, a pack that hangs straight, and a front that works at eye level. Common for small, light products.

- **Standing display, on shelves.** A stable base, a front that reads side by side with others, and information on more than one face.

- **Shelf-ready cases.** Some retailers prefer outer cases that open into a display tray. Agree this before the case is specified.

The box should say what the product does from a distance, then give detail close up. Windows show the product but add material; a good image on card often does the same job.

## Sustainability

Retail packs tend to use more print and more mixed materials than a plain shipping box. The principles in [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html) apply here too: right-size the pack, use materials that are widely recycled, avoid combining materials that cannot be separated, and mark materials and disposal guidance clearly. That guide also points to the official guidance on packaging producer responsibilities.

Card or moulded pulp inserts in place of plastic trays are a common simplification. Packaging is part of the product's footprint, so read [sustainable product design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html) and the [sustainability and product life hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainability-and-product-life.html), and print only environmental claims you can evidence.

## Print, tooling, minimum orders and cash

Retail packaging has its own costs and minimum orders, separate from the product:

- **Print set-up.** Printed boxes carry set-up costs and get cheaper per unit in larger runs.

- **Tooling.** Cutting dies (cutters) for the box shape, and tools for moulded inserts or trays, are one-off costs that take time to make. Changing the box shape later usually means a new cutter.

- **Minimum order quantities.** Packaging suppliers set their own minimums, which may not match your product order, and boxes bought ahead of sales tie up cash like any stock; see [minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html).

- **Unit cost and freight.** Packaging adds to unit cost, and its size and weight change freight, so include both in your [landed cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html).

Then check the price still works all the way to the shelf with the [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html).

## Working with packaging suppliers

Treat packaging as a component with its own drawing, specification and supplier. Brief it with the product's dimensions, display type, case quantity, the retailer's requirements, materials, print, quantities and testing. Ask several suppliers to quote on the same basis, as in [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html), and check which costs are one-off and which are per unit.

Sample in stages:

- **Plain samples** to check size, fit, inserts and closure with real products.

- **Printed proofs** to check colours, text, marks and that the barcode scans.

- **Pre-production samples** made by the production process and packed with production-intent products, for fit, transit testing and retailer approval where they ask for it.

## Fitting packaging into the schedule

Packaging tends to be planned last and needed first: retailers may want samples, dimensions and barcodes before ordering, and boxes must reach the factory before packing. Work backwards from the first delivery:

- Retailer requirements and display type known before the box is designed.

- Pack size fixed while the product can still change slightly, because a few millimetres can change how many units fit a case or pallet.

- Barcodes allocated and compliance text agreed before artwork is finalised.

- Sampling, testing and approval before the print order.

- Lead times for cutters, inserts, printing and delivery to the factory.

Use the real packaging in your pilot batch; [planning a pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) explains how a pilot tests packing alongside the product. Add these steps to your plan with the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html).

## Worked example: a small gadget's first retailer

Illustrative example only. A start-up sells a small rechargeable desk gadget through its own website, in a plain shipping box. A gift retailer agrees to stock it in two colours and sends its requirements.

**Questions first.** The retailer uses shelves, so a standing box; it wants a case quantity that suits its store orders, in a labelled outer case. It also asks for unit and case dimensions and weights, images, and confirmation the product meets the rules that apply.

**Checklist the team works through:**

- GS1 membership arranged; one GTIN for each colour, a case identifier if the retailer wants one, and a register of which number belongs to which variant.

- A standing retail box with a card insert: a front face showing the product, a "what's in the box" panel, contact details, the marks and information identified with the certification guide, a batch code area and recycling information.

- An outer case sized for the agreed quantity, checked against the pallet before the size is fixed, with a label showing description, code, quantity and barcode.

- Plain samples to check fit, printed proofs scanned with a barcode reader, and a drop test of a packed case added to the test plan.

**Decisions.** The team keeps its website box for online orders rather than forcing one pack to do both jobs. It orders a modest first print run to cover the pilot batch and the retailer's first order, accepting a higher unit cost, because feedback from store staff and shoppers may change the artwork. It does not share one barcode across both colours, which would have mixed their stock and sales from day one.

## Common mistakes

**One barcode for all variants.**
Variants become impossible to tell apart in stock and sales, and fixing it means relabelling stock.

**Carton sizes that do not suit pallets or retailers.**
Cases that overhang or underfill a pallet waste freight and get damaged; quantities that do not suit the retailer cause rework.

**Designing the box last.**
It delays launch, squeezes out sampling and testing, and can force compromises on the product.

**Printing large runs before pilot feedback.**
Big runs are cheaper per box, but one error or product change can leave you with boxes you cannot use.

## Decision rules

- **Ask for supplier requirements first,** before the box is designed.

- **One GTIN per variant,** recorded in a register and set up before artwork.

- **Fix pack and case sizes early,** checked against the pallet and the retailer's needs.

- **Treat packaging as a component:** brief, quotes, samples and approval.

- **Test the packed product** the way it will travel.

- **Keep the first print run modest** until pilot feedback is in.

## FAQ

### Do I need a barcode to sell through retailers?

Usually. Retailers commonly require a GS1 barcode on each product, carrying a GTIN registered to your business. Ask each retailer what they need, and set barcodes up before your artwork is finalised.

### How do I get a GS1 barcode?

Through membership of GS1 in your country; in the UK that is GS1 UK. Membership gives your business numbers to allocate to its products. Check the current terms directly with GS1.

### Does each colour or size need its own barcode?

Yes. Each variant a shopper can buy, including different colours, sizes, kits and pack quantities, needs its own GTIN so retailers can track stock and sales separately.

### What is an outer case specification?

The details of the carton your products ship in: its size, material and strength, how many units it holds, how it is labelled and how cases sit on a pallet. Retailers and distributors commonly ask for it before the first order.

### Can my retail box also be used for online orders?

Sometimes, but not always. Parcels are handled individually and dropped more often, so a retail box may need an extra outer or different protection. Decide early whether one pack can do both jobs, and test it.

Title: Right to Repair and Ecodesign Rules

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers and founders planning products for UK and EU markets (an overview, not legal advice)

# Right to repair and ecodesign rules: an overview for product designers

An overview of repair and ecodesign requirements for physical products: what they cover, how they differ between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the EU, and the design decisions that prepare a product for them. Check official sources for your product group.

Quick answer

## Repair and ecodesign rules are spreading from a few energy-using products to many more, so design products that can be repaired and documented, even where the law does not yet require it.

In Great Britain, ecodesign rules for some energy-related products already include requirements such as spare parts and repair information. In the EU, a broader ecodesign
framework and a right-to-repair directive have been adopted, with detailed requirements set product by product over time. Northern Ireland follows some EU product rules.
Requirements depend on the product category and market, so check the official sources. This guide is an overview, not legal advice.

## What these rules cover

|
Type of requirement |
Examples |

|
Energy and performance |
Minimum efficiency, standby power, product information |

|
Repairability |
Spare parts available for a period, repair information for repairers, parts replaceable with common tools |

|
Durability |
Minimum lifetimes or performance after use, for some categories |

|
Information |
Labels, product information and, in the EU, a planned digital product passport for some products |

|
Materials and recyclability |
Recycled content, substances of concern and design for recycling, where set for a product group |

## Great Britain

Ecodesign requirements in Great Britain apply to specific energy-related product groups, and for some of them include repair-related requirements such as spare parts availability
and repair information for professional repairers. Check whether your product group is covered on GOV.UK:
[placing energy-related products on the UK market](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/placing-energy-related-products-on-the-uk-market).

## The EU and Northern Ireland

The EU has adopted the [Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU) 2024/1781](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1781/oj),
a framework that extends ecodesign beyond energy-related products, with requirements set for individual product groups over time, and the
[right-to-repair Directive (EU) 2024/1799](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1799/oj), which strengthens repair obligations for certain products.
Northern Ireland applies some EU product rules under the Windsor Framework, so products for NI or EU markets may face different requirements from those for Great Britain.
Check which rules apply to your product and market, and take professional advice.

**Practical rule:**
design as if repairability will be required. It is far cheaper to plan accessible fixings, spare parts and repair information at concept stage than to redesign later.

## What designers should plan for

- Identify the parts most likely to fail and make them replaceable with common tools; see [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html).

- Keep a list of spare parts and decide how long you can supply them.

- Prepare repair information: exploded views, part numbers and procedures.

- Avoid software or design features that block genuine replacement parts without a safety reason.

- Record materials and substances so information requirements can be met.

- Track which product groups in your markets have, or are getting, requirements.

## Common mistakes

**Assuming it only affects big brands.**
Rules apply to products placed on the market, whoever makes them.

**Treating GB, NI and EU as one market.**
Requirements and timings can differ.

**Waiting for the law.**
Retrofitting repairability into a finished design is expensive.

**Relying on summaries.**
Check the official text and current guidance for your product group.

- Explore repair and lifetime scenarios with the [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html).

- Add durability tests to your plan with the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

## FAQ

### What are ecodesign rules?

Product requirements that set minimum environmental performance for specific product groups, such as energy efficiency, and for some products repairability, durability and information requirements.

### Is there a right to repair in the UK?

In Great Britain, ecodesign rules for some energy-related products include repair-related requirements such as spare parts availability and repair information for professional repairers. Check GOV.UK guidance for your product group.

### What is the EU Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, a framework that extends ecodesign beyond energy-related products. Detailed requirements, which can include durability, repairability and a digital product passport, are set for individual product groups over time.

### Do EU repair rules apply in Northern Ireland?

Northern Ireland applies some EU product rules under the Windsor Framework, so requirements can differ from Great Britain. Check current official guidance and take professional advice for your product.

### How should designers prepare for repair rules?

Make likely-to-fail parts replaceable with common tools, plan spare parts and repair information, avoid blocking genuine parts without a safety reason, and record materials and substances.

Title: The Risk-Progressive Manufacturing Strategy

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For teams deciding how to scale manufacturing without over-committing

# The risk-progressive manufacturing strategy.

The best manufacturing route is rarely chosen in one jump. Most teams need a staged path that learns quickly first, validates repeatability second, and only then commits hard to scale.

Quick answer

## A risk-progressive manufacturing strategy commits money in stages as evidence improves.

Prototype (buy learning) → Bridge (buy evidence) → Scale (buy repeatable economics)

The product moves from prototype to bridge to scale manufacturing only when demand, design stability and quality evidence justify the next commitment.
It accepts a higher unit cost early in exchange for a much lower chance of expensive tooling changes, unsellable inventory or a launch built on unproven processes.

Too many hardware teams frame the decision as prototype route versus final production route. In practice there is usually a more sensible sequence: prototype, bridge, and scale.
Each phase is buying a different kind of confidence, and each one makes the next commitment safer.

**Useful framing:** prototype manufacturing buys learning speed, bridge manufacturing buys evidence, and scaled manufacturing buys repeatable economics.

## What each stage is for

|Stage |Primary goal |Typical processes |Main risk if skipped |

|Prototype |Learn fast and change often |3D printing, [CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html), hand assembly, development boards |Teams lock decisions before the design has earned it |

|Bridge |Test demand, process capability, and quality repeatability |Vacuum casting, aluminium or simplified tooling, small-batch [PCB](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) assembly, manual assembly with simple fixtures |Scale investment arrives before the product proves itself |

|Scale |Reduce recurring unit cost and increase throughput |Hardened steel and multi-cavity moulds, dedicated fixtures, automated test, contract manufacturing |Capex gets committed against weak evidence or unstable geometry |

## What should trigger movement between stages

- demand certainty improving, not just optimism increasing

- product geometry stabilising enough that tooling changes are unlikely

- quality requirements becoming clear and testable

- the team being able to tolerate the lead time and capex of the next commitment

## Stage gates: the evidence to collect

|Gate |Evidence to collect before moving |

|Prototype to bridge |Critical functions verified on representative parts; positive [user testing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/usability-testing-a-prototype.html); a DFM review with likely suppliers; a costed BOM that supports the target price |

|Bridge to scale |Orders, pre-sales or channel commitments; no open changes to critical geometry; yield, defect and [returns data](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) from the bridge run; a supplier able to meet volume and quality; cash for tooling, inventory and lead time |

The gates are not paperwork. They are the points where the team decides whether the next, larger cheque is justified, or whether one more round of cheaper learning is the better use of money. Before scale, a
[pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) is a good way to collect the yield and defect evidence the last gate asks for.

Each stage buys a different kind of confidence. Move on only when the gate's evidence is in, because each step down commits more money and makes changes slower and dearer.

## Illustrative example: a desk lamp startup

A product may appear ready for tooling because the cost curve is attractive, yet still benefit from a bridge run if the quality regime is immature or demand is not proven. That extra stage can prevent a much more expensive mistake.

Imagine a startup making an LED desk lamp with a moulded arm, a machined base and a small control PCB. In the prototype stage, the team builds a handful of lamps from printed and machined parts to test the hinge, heat and light quality.
For the bridge stage, it orders aluminium tooling for the arm and a small PCB batch, and sells a few hundred lamps to early customers.

Returns data shows the arm hinge loosening with repeated use. The fix is a modest change to the aluminium tool, made in days rather than weeks. The bridge run also shows that assembly takes longer than planned,
which feeds into fixture design. Only then does the team order hardened multi-cavity tooling for scale. Had it gone straight to steel, the same hinge fix would have meant modifying a far more expensive tool
after inventory had already been built. The scenario is illustrative, but the pattern is common.

## Moving too early versus moving too late

**Too early:** capex is locked against unstable geometry, tool changes erase the planned savings, and inventory may be built for a version customers do not want.

**Too late:** high bridge unit costs eat margin, supply struggles to keep up with demand, and quality can vary between small batches.

**The balance:** move when the evidence for the next stage is stronger than the cost of being wrong, not when the spreadsheet first says the unit cost is lower.

Bridge manufacturing is not a delay. It is the cheapest place to find the problems that would otherwise be found in steel.

## Common mistakes

- treating bridge production as a failure to commit rather than a deliberate evidence stage

- using bridge runs without measuring anything: yields, defects, assembly time and returns should all be recorded

- ordering scale tooling on forecast optimism rather than orders or channel commitments

- forgetting that tooling lead time, first samples and corrections often add weeks to months before saleable stock exists

- planning the scale stage around one supplier without understanding their capacity and quality systems

## Practical next steps

The [Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html) is useful here because it connects volume, stability, quality, lead time, and capex posture in one staged recommendation.

Use the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) to see where the cost curves cross, and read the
[injection mould break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html) and
[Prototyping vs production](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/prototyping-vs-production-startup-guide.html) for the decisions either side of the bridge stage.
To set the stages against cash and milestones, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) pulls the manufacturing plan into the wider product plan.

### Plan the staged route

Use the planner to decide whether the product should remain in prototype, move into bridge, or justify harder production commitment.[Open Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html)

### Check the manufacturing economics too

Use the payoff visualiser if you also need to understand when the cost curve begins to favour a more committed route.[Open Manufacturing Payoff](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html)

## FAQ

### What is bridge manufacturing?

Bridge manufacturing is low-to-mid volume production that sits between prototyping and full-scale manufacturing. It typically uses processes such as vacuum casting or aluminium tooling to make real, saleable units in modest quantities. Its purpose is to test demand, quality and assembly before committing to expensive scale tooling.

### How long does injection mould tooling take?

Tool manufacture commonly takes from several weeks for simple tools to a few months for large or complex ones, depending on the supplier’s workload. First samples then usually need checking and adjustment before production approval. Plan for that whole sequence, not just the quoted tool build time.

### Is an aluminium mould good enough for production?

For lower volumes it often is. Aluminium tools are typically quicker and cheaper to make and modify than hardened steel, but they wear faster, particularly with abrasive or glass-filled materials. They suit pilot runs and modest annual volumes; high-volume products usually move to steel.

### When should a startup move from bridge to mass production?

When there is real demand evidence such as orders or channel commitments, critical geometry has stopped changing, bridge-run data shows acceptable yield and quality, and the business can fund tooling, inventory and lead time. Lower unit cost on its own is not enough.

### What is the biggest risk of scaling manufacturing too early?

Locking expensive tooling and inventory around a design or demand forecast that later proves wrong. Changes to hardened tools are slow and costly, and stock built to an earlier revision may be hard to sell. Staging the commitment keeps those mistakes small.

Title: Route to Market and Margins for Hardware Products

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams setting a price and choosing how a physical product will reach customers

# Route to market and margins: how sales channels shape price, cost and cash

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about selling a physical product: how each route to market changes the share of the price you keep, how to work back from a retail price to a target cost, and how margins, payment terms and volume decide whether the product pays its way. Each section links to a deeper guide or a free tool.

Quick answer

## Your route to market decides how much of the price you keep, when you are paid, and therefore what the product can cost to make.

Target landed COGS = retail price − VAT − channel share − selling costs − the margin the business needs

Selling direct keeps most of the price but carries the costs of finding customers, fulfilment and returns. Marketplaces take a commission and fees.
Retailers commonly keep 30 to 50 per cent of the retail price before VAT and may pay on 30 to 90 day terms. Work out the target cost for the routes you will actually use,
before the product is engineered, so the design is built to a cost it can afford.

- The main routes to market compared

- Where the retail price goes

- Margin, markup and the numbers people mix up

- Setting the price

- Cash timing and stock

- Volume and break-even

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## The main routes to market compared

Many hardware businesses use more than one route, and the mix changes as the business grows. Each route has a different share of the price,
a different cost of selling, and a different effect on cash.

|
Route |
What you keep |
Main costs to allow for |
Cash and stock |

|
Direct to consumer (own website) |
Most of the price |
Payment fees, paid marketing, fulfilment, customer service, returns |
Paid at order; you hold the stock |

|
Marketplace |
The price less commission and fees |
Commission, advertising to stay visible, fulfilment fees, returns |
Paid on a settlement cycle; may need stock in their warehouse |

|
Retailer |
The wholesale price: commonly 50 to 70 per cent of the net retail price |
Retail-ready packaging, delivery to their depots, promotions, deductions |
Credit terms, often 30 to 90 days; larger, earlier stock commitments |

|
Distributor then retailer |
Less than selling to retailers directly, because both take a share |
Distributor margin on top of retailer margin; less control of pricing |
Fewer, larger orders; useful for reaching new countries |

|
Business-to-business or OEM supply |
A negotiated price, often lower per unit but for larger volumes |
Longer sales cycles, specifications, quality and contract terms |
Purchase orders and payment terms; forecasts help plan production |

|
Crowdfunding |
The pledge less platform and payment fees |
Campaign marketing, rewards, shipping to backers, delivery risk |
Money before manufacture, but a public promise to deliver |

[How route to market shapes product design and cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-hardware-product.html) works through a change in the route mix,
and [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) calculates the cost ceiling for each route from your own figures.

## Where the retail price goes

The clearest way to see a route's effect is to follow one retail price down to the money left for making the product.
UK consumer prices normally include VAT (standard rate 20 per cent), which never belongs to the business; then the channel takes its share,
selling costs are paid, and the business keeps the margin it needs. What is left is the target landed cost of goods.

Illustrative figures from the [target COGS guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html). Each bar starts where the last one ended; together they make up the £180 retail price. Under a third of it is available to make and deliver the product.

**Practical rule:**
set the target cost from the least generous route you expect to use at scale. A product engineered to the direct-sales target can become unprofitable the day a retailer lists it.

## Margin, markup and the numbers people mix up

- **Margin** is profit as a share of the selling price: (price − cost) ÷ price.

- **Markup** is profit as a share of the cost: (price − cost) ÷ cost. A product bought for £50 and sold for £100 has a 50 per cent margin but a 100 per cent markup.

- **Gross margin** usually means after the cost of goods only; **contribution** also takes off the variable selling costs of each sale. Contribution is what actually pays for overheads.

- **Retail price with and without VAT**: a £120 price including VAT is £100 to the business before anyone else takes a share.

Retailers, distributors and suppliers do not always use these words the same way, so confirm which one is meant before agreeing a number.

## Setting the price

Price is set by customers' alternatives and the value the product delivers, not by cost plus a markup. Cost sets the floor; the market sets the ceiling. A few principles:

- **Anchor on alternatives.** What does the customer pay today, in money and effort, to solve the problem another way?

- **Keep prices consistent across routes.** Undercutting your retailers on your own website damages the relationship; plan the price so every route works.

- **Leave room for promotions.** Retail promotions and marketplace discounts come out of someone's margin, usually yours.

- **Test before committing.** Pre-orders or a small batch at the intended price tell you far more than a survey.

The [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html) shows how price, cost and volume combine, and
[how to turn RRP into target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html) works through the calculation step by step.

## Cash timing and stock

Margin is only half of the route decision. A retailer order can be excellent for the brand and still strain cash: you pay the factory before shipping,
the stock spends weeks in transit, and the retailer may pay one to three months after delivery. Model when money goes out and comes in, not just how much,
with the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html) and
[calculating hardware start-up cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html).

## Volume and break-even

Once the contribution per unit is known for each route, the break-even volume follows: fixed costs (development, tooling, overheads) divided by the blended contribution per unit.
If the break-even volume is far beyond what the business can realistically sell, the answer is usually to change the route, the price or the product cost, not to hope for more sales.
Use the [Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html) and
[financial break-even for hardware products](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html).

## Common mistakes

**Treating the retail price as the factory's budget.**
VAT, the channel and selling costs can take well over half of it before production is paid for.

**Forgetting the costs of selling direct.**
Direct sales keep more of the price, but advertising, fulfilment and returns can take much of the difference.

**Confusing margin and markup.**
A "50 per cent" that means markup to one party and margin to another moves the target cost a long way: on a £100 price, the cost is £50 at a 50 per cent margin but about £66.67 at a 50 per cent markup.

**Ignoring payment terms.**
Profitable growth through retail can still run out of cash.

**Setting the target cost after the design.**
By then most of the cost is locked in. Set it before engineering starts.

## FAQ

### How much margin do retailers take on hardware products?

Retailers commonly keep 30 to 50 per cent of the retail price before VAT, depending on the category, the retailer and the support they expect. Promotions, deductions and retail-ready packaging requirements can add to that, so ask for the full terms rather than the headline margin.

### What is the difference between margin and markup?

Margin is profit as a share of the selling price; markup is profit as a share of the cost. A product bought for 50 pounds and sold for 100 pounds has a 50 per cent margin but a 100 per cent markup. Confirm which one is meant before agreeing terms.

### Is selling direct always more profitable than selling through retail?

Not necessarily. Direct sales keep more of the price, but paid marketing, fulfilment, customer service and returns can absorb much of the difference. Retail can bring volume and visibility with lower selling cost per unit, but at a lower price to you and with slower payment.

### How do I work out the target cost for my product?

Start from the retail price, remove VAT, remove the channel's share, remove the selling costs of that route and the margin the business needs. What is left is the most the product can cost to make and land. Use the least generous route you expect to use at scale.

### Should I use a distributor?

A distributor can open markets and retailers you could not reach alone, especially abroad, but takes its own margin on top of the retailer's. It suits products with proven demand and enough margin to share; check the target cost works with both margins included.
