Title: How Route to Market Shapes Product Design and Cost

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 24 November 2026 · For founders choosing how to sell a physical product and what it means for cost

# How route to market shapes product design and cost.

A retail price on its own tells you very little. What matters is how much of that price survives the route to market,
and how much disappears into warehousing, packaging, logistics, platform fees, marketplace charges, and retailer margin.

Quick answer

## Route to market matters because it changes the COGS target the product must hit.

Target COGS = retained price - channel deductions - hidden selling costs - required margin

The same retail price can support very different factory costs depending on whether the product is sold DTC, through a marketplace, or through retail.
Retailers commonly keep 30 to 50 per cent of the retail price, while direct sales keep more of the price but carry acquisition, fulfilment and returns costs, so the channel choice should shape the product brief from the start.

Founders and product teams often ask whether the product can sell for a certain RRP. The harder question is whether the product still works
once the chosen route to market takes its share. That is where many products become commercially weak without anyone noticing early enough.

**Core point:** route to market is not a downstream sales decision. It directly changes the COGS target the product must hit.

## Contents

- The same RRP can support very different COGS

- Routes also change when you get paid

- Why hidden costs matter so much

- Worked example: what happens when the route mix shifts

- Common route-to-market mistakes

- Questions worth asking before you lock the design

- Use route-to-market thinking to guide engineering

- Practical next steps

## The same RRP can support very different COGS

|
Route |
What you keep |
What usually gets missed |

|
Direct to consumer |
Most of the retail price |
Site fees, payment charges, warehousing, pick and pack, customer service, returns, and paid acquisition |

|
Marketplace |
Less than DTC, often more than wholesale |
Marketplace commission, promoted listings, fulfilment surcharges, and reduced control over pricing |

|
Retailer |
The smallest share of the RRP |
Wholesale discount, account management, chargebacks, [retail-ready packaging](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html), and inbound logistics |

## Routes also change when you get paid

Margin is only half of the route decision. Each route also changes cash timing and stock commitment. Direct sales are usually paid at the point of order.
Marketplaces typically pay out on a regular settlement cycle and may require stock to be held in their warehouses. Retailers commonly buy on credit terms of 30 to 90 days,
may expect larger and earlier stock commitments, and can apply deductions for promotions or non-compliant deliveries.
A route with acceptable margin can still strain cash, which is why route choice and the
[cash flow model](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html) should be reviewed together.

## Why hidden costs matter so much

Hidden costs are usually not hidden because they are rare. They are hidden because they sit in different teams or budgets.
Operations owns warehousing. Marketing owns customer acquisition. Ecommerce owns hosting and transaction fees. Sales owns retailer terms.
The product still has to carry all of it.

## Worked example: what happens when the route mix shifts

Illustrative figures only. A kitchen product has an RRP of GBP120 including VAT, so GBP100 net, and a landed COGS of GBP30. The business plans to sell 50% direct,
30% through a marketplace and 20% through a retailer. Fees and costs below are plausible assumptions, not quotes.

Contribution per unit = retained price - hidden selling costs - landed COGS

|
Route |
Retained price |
Hidden selling costs |
Contribution per unit |

|
Direct to consumer |
GBP100 |
GBP36 (payment, fulfilment, returns, acquisition) |
GBP34 |

|
Marketplace |
GBP82 (15% commission on GBP120) |
GBP20 (fulfilment, advertising, returns) |
GBP32 |

|
Retailer |
GBP55 (45% retailer margin) |
GBP7 (retail packaging, inbound freight, promotional support) |
GBP18 |

At the planned 50/30/20 mix, blended contribution is about GBP30.20 per unit. Now suppose a large retail listing arrives and the mix becomes 25% direct, 15% marketplace and 60% retail.
Blended contribution falls to about GBP24.10, a drop of roughly 20%, even though more units may be sold. To restore the original contribution at the new mix, landed COGS would need to fall by about GBP6.10, to roughly GBP23.90.

Notice also that direct sales only narrowly beat the marketplace here, because acquisition cost absorbs much of the advantage of keeping the full price. That is why the right answer depends on the real cost stack, not on channel mythology.

Illustrative figures from the table above, bars drawn to scale. Direct and marketplace leave similar contribution, but the retailer's 45% cuts it to £18, so a big retail listing lowers what every unit earns on average.

A retail listing can be a commercial success and a margin problem at the same time. Plan for both before it arrives.

## Common route-to-market mistakes

**Choosing the route for volume, then fixing the margin later.**
Once tooling and the bill of materials are fixed, there is little room left to recover a missing 20%.

**Assuming direct sales are cheap.**
Direct sales keep more of the price, but paid acquisition, returns and customer service can absorb most of that gain.

**Ignoring price consistency across channels.**
Retailers and marketplaces generally expect the direct price not to undercut them, which limits how differently each route can be priced.

**Packaging designed for one channel only.**
Retail-ready packaging, marketplace requirements and direct-mail shipping often need different solutions. Retrofitting adds cost.

**Overlooking payment terms.**
A route with good margin and slow payment can still starve the business of cash.

## Questions worth asking before you lock the design

- If this product needs to work through retail, what wholesale price does that imply?

- What level of packaging, fulfilment, and account cost is really required for each route?

- Does the product architecture leave enough room for a sensible COGS at the target route?

- Would a channel shift force a redesign later because the product cost is too high?

- Can the business finance the stock and payment terms the route requires?

## Use route-to-market thinking to guide engineering

Route-to-market choice should influence the brief early. If the likely route is retail, the product may need a much more aggressive [cost-down](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html) strategy,
fewer parts, simpler assembly, or a different specification. If the likely route is DTC, the product may be able to carry more value and margin, but only if
acquisition and fulfilment do not absorb the gain.

## Practical next steps

- List the routes you expect to use in the first two years, with a rough share for each.

- Work out retained price and hidden selling costs per route using the [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) tool.

- Set the cost target from the most demanding realistic route, using the method in [how to turn RRP into target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html).

- Model blended contribution and a retail-heavy scenario in the [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html).

- Check the volume needed to recover fixed cost at each mix with the [Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html).

The route decision then feeds the wider plan for development, tooling and launch, which the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps set out in stages.

## FAQ

### What is a route to market for a hardware product?

It is the path a product takes from the business to the end customer, such as selling direct through your own website, through an online marketplace, through retailers, or through distributors. Each route has different fees, costs, payment terms and stock requirements.

### Is direct to consumer or retail better for a hardware startup?

Neither is better in general. Direct sales keep more of the price and give closer customer contact, but need marketing spend and fulfilment capability. Retail offers reach and credibility, but takes a large share of the price and often demands longer payment terms and more stock.

### How much margin do retailers take?

Retailer margins commonly sit somewhere between 30 and 50 per cent of the retail price before VAT, depending on the category and the retailer. Promotional contributions and other deductions can add to that, so check the full terms rather than the headline margin.

### How much do online marketplaces charge?

Most charge a commission on each sale, often in the region of 8 to 15 per cent depending on category, plus optional fulfilment, storage and advertising fees. Rates change, so check the current fee schedule for your category before setting a cost target.

### Can I change route to market after launch?

Yes, but moving to a route that keeps less of the price can leave the product with too little margin. Setting the cost target from the most demanding route you realistically expect avoids being forced into a redesign later.

Title: Running a Design Review

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders, designers and engineers who need a design review to end in decisions, not just slides

# Running a design review: catching problems while they are cheap to fix

What a design review is for, which reviews to hold from concept selection to pilot production, who should be in the room, how to prepare, a simple agenda, and how to record decisions and actions so they actually get done.

Quick answer

## A design review is a short, structured meeting where the right people check a design against its requirements and risks, then decide whether it is ready to move to the next stage.

Hold one at each major commitment: choosing a concept, freezing the design, agreeing manufacturability with the supplier, ordering tooling and approving pilot production.
Circulate the requirements, risk list, open issues, drawings and prototypes beforehand, include at least one person who did not do the design, and finish with a recorded decision and a list of actions, each with an owner and a date.

## Contents

- What a design review is for

- Reviews at each stage

- Who should attend

- Preparing the review

- A simple agenda

- Recording decisions and actions

- Using checklists

- Remote reviews and how often to hold them

- Worked example: a design-freeze review

- Common mistakes

## What a design review is for

Every change to a product gets more expensive the further the project goes. Moving a screw boss on a CAD model takes minutes; moving it after a steel mould has been cut can mean weeks of rework and a large bill.
A design review exists to find problems at the point where they are still cheap to fix, by putting the design in front of people who will look at it differently from the person who drew it.

The second purpose matters just as much: a review is where the project **decides**. The outcome should be one of three things: proceed, proceed once named actions are closed, or go back and rework.
A meeting that ends with "looks good, thanks everyone" has not done its job, however polished the slides were.

**Practical rule:**
if nobody could change their mind as a result of the meeting, it is a presentation, not a review. Spend the time on the open questions and risks, not on what is already settled.

## Reviews at each stage

Reviews belong at the points where the project commits time or money that is hard to get back. Most physical products need five, though small projects can combine some of them.

Each review sits just before a commitment that is costly to reverse. The cost of a change found at the review rises at every step down the timeline.

|
Review |
Main question |
Useful inputs |

|
Concept selection |
Which concept should we develop, and why? |
Concept sketches or rough models, weighted criteria, a [structured comparison](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html) such as the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html) |

|
Design freeze |
Does the integrated design meet its requirements well enough to stop changing it? |
The [requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html), test results against the [test plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html), risk list, integrated prototypes |

|
DFM review with the supplier |
Can each part be made reliably by the chosen process and supplier? |
3D models, drawings with [tolerances](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html), the [DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) or [DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html), the supplier's own feedback |

|
Pre-tooling |
Is everything closed that would be expensive to change once steel is cut? |
Final released data, closed DFM actions, the [Ready for Tooling self-check](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html) |

|
Pre-production or pilot |
Is the process ready for a pilot, and did the pilot prove it? |
First-article results, pilot plan and go/no-go criteria from [planning a pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html) |

Smaller, informal reviews between these points are useful too, for example a quick check of a prototype round before ordering parts. Keep the five above as the formal gates.

## Who should attend

Keep the group small enough to talk, usually three to six people. Each person should be there for a reason:

- **The designer or design engineer** who can explain the choices made and answer detailed questions.

- **Another engineer** who knows the relevant discipline, such as mechanical, electronics or materials.

- **Someone independent** who did not work on the design. Fresh eyes find the assumptions the team stopped noticing.

- **The supplier or manufacturer** for DFM, pre-tooling and pre-production reviews, because they know what their process can and cannot do.

- **The person who owns the requirements**, often the founder or product owner, who can decide whether a shortfall is acceptable.

Name a chair who keeps time and makes sure a decision is reached, and a note-taker who is not the person presenting.

## Preparing the review

Send the material at least a few working days ahead, so people come with questions rather than reading for the first time in the meeting:

- **Requirements:** the current version, with each one marked as met, not yet met or not yet tested.

- **Risk list:** the main technical, user, cost and supply risks, with what has been done about each.

- **Open issues:** known problems and actions carried over from the last review.

- **Models and prototypes:** CAD files or viewer links, and physical prototypes people can handle on the day.

- **Drawings:** current drawings for parts that are being released or quoted.

Ask reviewers to send written comments before the meeting where they can. The meeting can then concentrate on the points that need discussion.

## A simple agenda

An hour to ninety minutes is enough for most stage reviews of a simple product. A plain structure works well:

- **Purpose and decision needed** (a few minutes): what stage this is and what the group must decide.

- **Actions from last time**: closed, open or dropped, with reasons.

- **Requirements status**: concentrate on anything not met or not tested.

- **Risks and open issues**: the bulk of the time, worked through in order of importance.

- **Hands-on time** with prototypes or models, if not already covered.

- **Decision**: proceed, proceed with conditions, or rework.

- **Actions**: read back each one with its owner and date before people leave.

## Recording decisions and actions

The record is what turns a conversation into progress. Write it during the meeting, circulate it the same day, and keep it with the project files so later reviews can refer back to it. It needs only a few parts:

- **The decision** in one sentence, with any conditions attached.

- **Findings**: each problem raised, written as an observation, with its agreed severity.

- **Actions**: what will be done, by whom and by when. One named owner per action, not a team.

- **Decisions not to act**: issues the group accepted, and why, so the same debate does not restart next month.

Settled findings that change what the product must do belong in the requirements document, so they are checked again at the next review rather than remembered.

## Using checklists

A checklist makes sure the obvious things are looked at every time, especially by a tired team close to a deadline: wall thicknesses, fastener access, labelling, battery safety, packaging, test access.
Use one as a prompt during preparation, not as the agenda itself, and add to it when a problem slips through. The [product development checklists](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-development-checklists.html) give a starting point for each stage.

## Remote reviews and how often to hold them

Remote reviews work well for drawings, CAD and documents, and make it easier to include an [overseas supplier](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html). Share the model live so people can ask for a section or a different view, and post prototypes to key reviewers ahead of time, or hold a short in-person session for the physical parts.
Physical products still benefit from being handled; if you are working with Orion Design, reviews can be held in person in Belfast or remotely.

As for frequency, hold the formal reviews at each stage gate and short informal ones whenever the design changes significantly. Far more projects suffer from too few reviews, held too late, than from too many.

## Worked example: a design-freeze review

Illustrative example. A two-person start-up is developing a small, rechargeable desk lamp with a moulded plastic body, a weighted base and a touch dimmer. They have three integrated prototypes and want to freeze the design before asking their supplier for [tooling quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html).
The review includes the founder (who owns the requirements), the design engineer, an independent electronics engineer and, for the last half hour, the supplier's tooling engineer by video call.

Agenda: purpose and decision needed; actions from the previous prototype review; requirements status; risks and open issues; handling the prototypes; decision and actions.

|
Finding |
Severity |
Decision and action |

|
The base housing has no draft on two internal ribs; the supplier says the part will stick in the mould |
Must fix before tooling |
Add draft to the ribs and re-check against the DFM checklist. Owner: design engineer, before the quote request |

|
The touch dimmer misfires on one prototype when the charging cable is plugged in |
Must understand before freeze |
Freeze the enclosure but not the [circuit board](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html); investigate and retest on all three units. Owner: electronics engineer, within two weeks |

|
The founder would prefer a slightly warmer colour finish |
Preference; no effect on tooling |
Accepted as a later colour decision, recorded so it is not reopened at the next review |

The decision recorded was "freeze the enclosure design once the rib draft is added; freeze the electronics after the dimmer retest". Two weeks later a short follow-up review closed both actions, and the requirements document gained a new line on dimmer behaviour while charging.

## Common mistakes

**Treating the review as a presentation.**
A rehearsed walk-through of what went well leaves no time for the risks. Send the material in advance and spend the meeting on the open questions.

**No decision recorded.**
Without a written decision, people leave with different ideas about what was agreed. End every review with a one-sentence decision.

**The wrong people in the room.**
A review made up only of the people who did the design will confirm it. Include someone independent, the requirements owner and, where relevant, the supplier.

**Reviewing too late.**
A first review held after the tooling order is placed can only find expensive problems. Review at concept and design freeze, not just before production.

**No follow-up on actions.**
Actions without owners and dates quietly expire. Start every review by checking the previous actions.

## Next steps

- Mark your next commitment point, such as design freeze or tooling, and schedule a review just before it.

- Bring your requirements up to date and mark each one as met, not met or not tested.

- Before any tooling review, work through the [Ready for Tooling self-check](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html).

- See where reviews sit in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

Stage gates
DFM review

## FAQ

### How long should a design review take?

For a simple product, an hour to ninety minutes is usually enough if the material was circulated beforehand. If a review regularly runs much longer, split it by subsystem or hold a separate session for the supplier.

### Do I need a formal design review if I am a small team?

Yes, though it can be light. Even a two-person team benefits from stopping before a big commitment, asking someone independent to look, and writing down the decision and actions. The formality should match the cost of getting it wrong.

### What is the difference between a design review and design freeze?

Design freeze is a decision that the design will stop changing except through a controlled change process. A design review is the meeting where that decision, and others like it, is made on the evidence available.

### Should the manufacturer be at the design review?

For DFM, pre-tooling and pre-production reviews, yes, because they know what their process can do. For concept and early reviews it is optional, though an early conversation about manufacturing often saves rework later.

### What if the review finds a serious problem late in the project?

Record it honestly, work out what fixing it would cost now against the cost of fixing it after launch, and decide. Delaying a commitment such as tooling is almost always cheaper than changing the product after it has been made.

Title: Sealing and Waterproofing an Enclosure

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers designing a product that has to keep out water, dust or dirt

# Sealing and waterproofing an enclosure: gaskets, O-rings and IP ratings

How the common ways of sealing a product housing work, what makes a seal reliable, how to deal with cables, buttons and vents, what an IP rating does and does not tell you, and how to keep a sealed product repairable.

Quick answer

## A reliable seal is a compressed seal: a gasket or O-ring squeezed by a controlled, even amount between stiff, smooth faces, with every opening in the housing sealed as carefully as the main joint.

Decide the sealing method while the housing is being designed, because it sets the wall flanges, fastener positions, grooves and how the parts fit together.
Gaskets and O-rings can be opened and resealed; welding, adhesives and potting seal permanently. An IP rating describes how a finished product performed in standard tests, usually at a test lab, so plan to test prototypes early rather than assume a rating from the seal you chose.

## Contents

- Why sealing is a design-stage decision

- Compressed gaskets

- O-rings: face seals and radial seals

- Labyrinths, drip edges, potting and coating

- Cables, connectors and vents

- What makes a seal work

- Buttons, displays and other openings

- IP ratings in plain terms

- Sealed or serviceable?

- Worked example: a handheld outdoor device

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## Why sealing is a design-stage decision

Sealing is often treated as something to add once the housing works. In practice the seal shapes the housing. A gasket needs a continuous flat flange, a groove to locate it and enough fasteners to squeeze it evenly. An O-ring needs a precisely sized groove and a tighter fit than an ordinary enclosure. Every button, screen, cable and connector is another opening that needs its own seal.

These features drive part count, assembly and mould design, so they are expensive to add after tooling. Write the environment into your [product requirements](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html) early: rain, splashes, hosing down, immersion, dust, sweat, cleaning chemicals, and whether the product will be opened later for service.

## Compressed gaskets

A gasket is a soft rubber or foam squeezed between two parts so it fills the small gaps between them. The squeeze, called compression, is what makes it seal, and the design must control it.

- **Die-cut gaskets** are cut from sheet rubber or closed-cell foam. They need little tooling, suit flat flanges and low volumes, and are easy to replace, but need locating features so they do not shift during assembly.

- **Form-in-place gaskets** are a bead of liquid dispensed onto the flange by machine, which cures into a soft seal on one part. They follow complex shapes but need dispensing equipment and a groove or stop to set the compression.

- **Overmoulded or two-shot seals** mould a soft thermoplastic elastomer directly onto the rigid housing part, as described in [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html). The seal cannot be lost or fitted wrongly, but tooling is more complex and the seal cannot be replaced on its own.

Specify closed-cell foam, which keeps water out where open-cell foam soaks it up, and check the material suits the temperatures, chemicals and sunlight it will see.

## O-rings: face seals and radial seals

An O-ring is a moulded rubber ring sitting in a groove. It is one of the most dependable seals because the groove controls how much it is squeezed, and standard sizes are widely available. Size the groove from the O-ring maker's design guidance rather than guessing.

- In a **face seal** the ring sits in a groove in a flat face and is squeezed as the two faces are pulled together, usually by screws. It depends on the faces closing fully and evenly.

- In a **radial seal** the ring sits around a plug or spigot and is squeezed against the wall of a bore as one part slides into the other. The fit sets the squeeze, so it depends less on fastener force, which suits round lids and end caps. It needs close tolerances on both diameters and a lead-in chamfer so the ring is not cut.

Simplified cross-sections, not to scale. In a face seal the closing force sets the squeeze; in a radial seal the fit between the parts does.

## Labyrinths, drip edges, potting and coating

Not every product needs a full seal. A **labyrinth**, overlapping walls that force water to take a winding path, and a **drip edge** that sheds water away from a joint, can keep out splashes and rain from above with no seal at all. They cost little and do not wear out, but will not stop water under pressure or immersion.

For electronics, an alternative is to protect the board itself. **Conformal coating** is a thin film over the assembled board that resists moisture and condensation; **potting** fills the space around the electronics with resin that sets solid. Potting protects well against water and vibration but adds weight and makes the board unrepairable. The [electronics guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers how these choices fit with board layout and heat.

## Cables, connectors and vents

- **Cable glands** clamp a seal around a cable where it passes through the wall. They suit round cables of a known diameter and need a flat, smooth area around the hole; flat cables are a common leak path.

- **Sealed connectors** carry their own seals, both to the housing and between the mating halves. Many need a cap to stay sealed when unplugged.

- **Membrane vents** are small patches of a microporous membrane that let air through but block liquid water. A sealed housing heats and cools, so the trapped air expands and contracts. Without a vent, that pressure difference strains the seal and can draw moist air or water in past it. A vent equalises the pressure.

## What makes a seal work

- **Even, controlled compression.** Too little squeeze and the seal leaks; too much and it takes a permanent set or pushes the parts apart. A groove, a hard stop or compression limiters fix the squeeze so it does not depend on how tightly the screws are driven.

- **Stiff flanges.** A thin plastic flange bows between fasteners, squeezing the seal hard at each screw and barely in between. Ribs or a deeper flange keep the faces flat.

- **Enough fasteners or clips around the seal.** Space them closely enough that the flange cannot bow open. The [joining methods guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html) compares screws, inserts and snap fits for holding a lid closed.

- **A smooth, continuous sealing face.** Texture, sink, ejector and gate marks and a parting line across the seal path all create leak channels. Keep the sealing face smooth and specify it on the drawing.

- **Tolerances that hold the squeeze.** The squeeze depends on the tolerances of both parts, so check it at the extremes, not just at nominal, as explained in the [tolerances and engineering drawings guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html); flatness of the sealing faces often matters as much as their size.

## Buttons, displays and other openings

Openings are where many sealed products leak. Common approaches:

- **Buttons** are often a moulded rubber keypad that both seals the opening and acts as the button, or a flexible membrane over a switch. Separate plastic buttons need an O-ring or boot behind each.

- **Displays and windows** are usually bonded in with adhesive tape or a gasket around a flat, clean frame.

- **Speakers, microphones and sensors** can sit behind an acoustic membrane that passes sound but blocks water.

- **Battery doors and charging ports** need their own gaskets or caps, or can be avoided with wireless charging.

## IP ratings in plain terms

An IP (ingress protection) rating such as IP54 or IP67 summarises how well an enclosure keeps out solids and water. The **first digit** describes protection against solid objects and dust; the **second digit** describes protection against water. Higher numbers mean more demanding conditions. An **X** in place of a digit, as in IPX4, means that aspect was not tested, not that it failed.

The ratings are defined by standard tests on finished products, usually done by a test lab. A rating describes how a specific product performed in those tests, not a property of the seal you chose. Choose the rating from how the product will really be used, check the standard's definitions, and plan the testing with the [Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html). The [testing and validation plans guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) explains how to stage tests through development, and [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) covers how environmental testing fits with safety and other compliance work.

## Sealed or serviceable?

The most robust seal is often a permanent one, such as a welded or glued housing or potted electronics. It is also the least repairable: a failed battery or button inside a welded housing turns a repair into a replacement, and seals themselves harden over time.

If the product will be opened, use an O-ring or replaceable gasket held by screws into durable threads, and make the replacement seal available. The [design for repair and disassembly guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) explains how to make wear parts reachable without giving up the protection the product needs.

## Worked example: a handheld outdoor device

Illustrative example. A start-up is designing a handheld outdoor device with a moulded two-part housing, a small display, two buttons, a charging port and a replaceable battery. It must survive rain and being dropped in a puddle. The team compares three ways to seal the main joint.

|
Option |
Sealing reliability |
Serviceability |
Design and tooling impact |

|
Die-cut or form-in-place gasket |
Good if the flange is stiff and fasteners are closely spaced |
Good: reopens, but the gasket may need replacing |
Wide flat flange and many screws add size and assembly time |

|
O-ring in a groove |
Very good: the groove fixes the squeeze |
Good: reopens and reseals with a standard ring |
Groove and tighter tolerances; a radial seal needs a suitable shape |

|
Ultrasonic weld |
Very good once the joint is right |
None: the battery cannot be replaced |
Welder, horn, fixture and joint features in the mould |

The weld is ruled out because the battery must be replaceable, and a gasket would need a wide flange on a small handheld. The team chooses a face-sealing O-ring in a continuous groove, with screws into threaded inserts at each corner and along the sides, and ribs to stiffen the flange.

The openings are handled separately: a rubber keypad, the display bonded with gasket tape, a capped charging connector and a membrane vent. Early prototypes in near-production materials are leak-tested before tooling, rather than waiting for a formal IP test at the end.

## Common mistakes

**Relying on a sealant bead without compression control.**
Its squeeze varies with how tightly the screws are driven. Use a groove or hard stop.

**Too few fasteners.**
A thin flange held only at the corners bows open along the sides.

**A sealing face on a parting line or textured surface.**
Both create leak paths. Keep the seal path smooth and continuous.

**Forgetting pressure equalisation.**
A sealed housing that heats and cools strains its own seal. Consider a membrane vent.

**Not testing early prototypes.**
A simple leak check on early prototypes is far cheaper than a failed lab test after tooling.

## Decision rules

- **Define the environment first,** and whether the product will be opened.

- **Use labyrinths and drip edges** for splashes and rain from above; use compressed seals for water under pressure or immersion.

- **Prefer an O-ring or replaceable gasket** where the product must be opened; reserve welding, adhesives and potting for products that never will be.

- **Design the compression** with grooves or stops, stiff flanges and enough fasteners.

- **Count every opening** and give each its own seal, plus a vent if the housing is fully sealed.

- **Test prototypes early,** then confirm the IP rating with formal testing on production-representative parts.

- See where this sits in the wider picture in the [manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## FAQ

### Should I use a gasket or an O-ring?

An O-ring in a well-designed groove is usually the more dependable seal, because the groove fixes how much it is squeezed. A gasket suits large, flat or irregular flanges and lower volumes, but needs a stiff flange and closely spaced fasteners to compress it evenly.

### What does the X in IPX4 mean?

It means the product was not tested for that aspect, here protection against solids and dust. It does not mean the product failed; it simply makes no claim either way.

### Can I claim an IP rating without testing?

An IP rating describes how a product performed in the standard's defined tests, so a claim should be backed by testing to that standard, usually at a test lab. Using a seal or connector with its own rating does not by itself give the whole product that rating.

### Why does a waterproof product need a vent?

A sealed housing heats and cools, so the air inside expands and contracts. A membrane vent lets air through but blocks liquid water, so the pressure difference does not strain the seal or draw moisture in past it.

### Can a waterproof product still be repairable?

Yes, if it is sealed with O-rings or replaceable gaskets held by screws into durable threads, rather than welded, glued or potted. Make the seal easy to inspect and replace, and make replacement seals available.

Title: Selling a Physical Product on Marketplaces

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For founders considering selling a physical product through online marketplaces

# Selling on marketplaces: fees, fulfilment, listings and responsibilities

What to know before selling a physical product on an online marketplace: the full set of fees, whether to fulfil orders yourself, listings and reviews, keeping prices consistent across channels, and the responsibilities that stay with you.

Quick answer

## Marketplaces give a new product instant reach, but fees, fulfilment, advertising and returns can take a large share of the price, and you stay responsible for the product.

Work out what you keep per sale after referral fees, fulfilment and storage, advertising and returns before listing. Choose between fulfilling orders yourself and using
the marketplace's fulfilment service, prepare clear listings and compliance documents, and protect your pricing so it works across all your channels.
Check each marketplace's current fees and rules, which change often.

## Why sell on a marketplace

- **Reach:** shoppers already searching for products like yours.

- **Trust:** familiar checkout, delivery and returns.

- **Evidence:** real sales and reviews early, which can help with retailers and investors.

The trade-offs are fees, less control over the customer relationship, price competition and dependence on one platform's rules.

## What you will pay

|
Cost |
What to check |

|
Referral or selling fees |
Usually a percentage of the sale price, varying by category; sometimes with a minimum per item |

|
Account or subscription fees |
Monthly fees for professional seller accounts |

|
Fulfilment and storage |
Per-unit fees if the marketplace stores and ships for you, plus storage charges that can rise for slow-moving stock |

|
Advertising |
Sponsored listings are often needed to be seen, especially at launch |

|
Returns |
Return shipping, damaged or unsellable returns, and refunds |

Model these with the [Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) tool, which includes a marketplace route.

## Fulfilling yourself or using the marketplace

- **Self-fulfilment:** more control and no storage fees, but you handle packing, delivery promises and returns.

- **Marketplace fulfilment:** faster delivery options and less admin, but fees, preparation rules for inbound stock, and storage charges.

Packaging must survive parcel networks; see [packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html).

**Practical rule:**
calculate what you keep per sale after every fee, advertising and returns, at a realistic price. If the marketplace route only works at full price with no advertising, it does not work.

## Listings, reviews and pricing

- **Clear listings:** accurate titles, real photographs, dimensions, materials, what is in the box and how to use it. If you also sell through shops, [retail-ready packaging and barcodes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-ready-packaging-and-barcodes.html) covers barcodes and retail packs.

- **Honest reviews only:** never buy or incentivise fake reviews; it is unlawful and breaches marketplace rules.

- **Consistent pricing:** undercutting your retailers on a marketplace damages those relationships; see [retail and distributor margins](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-and-distributor-margins-explained.html).

## Your responsibilities

Selling through a marketplace does not move your legal responsibilities onto it. You still need a safe, compliant product with correct markings, labelling and documents,
and marketplaces may ask for evidence such as test reports or declarations of conformity. Consumer rules on distance selling, cancellations and refunds apply; see
[online and distance selling for businesses](https://www.gov.uk/online-and-distance-selling-for-businesses) and
[accepting returns and giving refunds](https://www.gov.uk/accepting-returns-and-giving-refunds).
For product safety, see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) and
[product liability basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-liability-basics.html).

## Common mistakes

**Pricing without all the fees.**
Fulfilment, storage, advertising and returns can turn a profitable price into a loss.

**Sending too much stock.**
Slow-moving stock in marketplace warehouses can attract rising storage fees.

**Relying on one platform.**
Account suspensions or rule changes can stop sales overnight.

**Missing compliance documents.**
Listings can be removed if you cannot show the product meets the rules.

## FAQ

### Should I sell my product on a marketplace?

Marketplaces offer reach, trust and early sales evidence, but fees, fulfilment, advertising and returns can take a large share of the price. Calculate what you keep per sale before deciding, and avoid relying on one platform.

### What fees do marketplaces charge?

Typically a referral or selling fee as a percentage of the price, account fees, optional fulfilment and storage fees, and advertising costs. Fees vary by marketplace and category and change often, so check current rates.

### Should I use marketplace fulfilment?

It can give faster delivery and less admin, but adds per-unit and storage fees and inbound preparation rules. Self-fulfilment gives more control. Compare the full cost of both at your volumes.

### Is the marketplace responsible for my product's safety?

Not instead of you. As the seller and usually the producer, you remain responsible for a safe, compliant product and correct information. Marketplaces may ask for evidence of compliance.

### Do consumer return rules apply to marketplace sales?

Yes. Distance-selling rules, including cancellation rights and refunds, apply to online sales to consumers. Check current GOV.UK guidance on online selling and returns.

Title: Sheet Metal Design Basics: Bends and Holes

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers, engineers and founders designing brackets, enclosures and chassis in sheet metal

# Sheet metal design basics: bends, holes, reliefs, materials and tolerances

The essentials of designing parts for laser cutting and press-brake bending: how the process works, the rules of thumb that keep parts accurate and cheap, material and joining choices, and what to agree with your fabricator.

Quick answer

## Design sheet-metal parts around the bending process: consistent bend radii, enough distance between holes and bends, bend reliefs, realistic flanges and tolerances.

Sheet-metal parts are cut flat (usually by laser or punch) and then folded on a press brake. Most problems come from features too close to bends, flanges too short to bend,
missing reliefs, and tolerances tighter than bending can hold. The values below are common starting points that depend on material, thickness and the fabricator's tooling,
so share your CAD with the fabricator early and use their bend radii and allowances.

## How sheet-metal parts are made

- **Cutting:** the flat pattern is cut from sheet by laser, punching or waterjet. No part-specific tooling is needed for laser cutting, which suits prototypes and moderate volumes.

- **Forming:** bends are made on a press brake with standard punches and dies; the available tools set the practical bend radii and minimum flanges.

- **Joining and hardware:** welding, rivets, screws, or self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet.

- **Finishing:** for example powder coating or plating for steel, anodising for aluminium, or brushed and passivated [stainless steel](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html).

At high volumes, dedicated press tools can replace laser cutting and press-brake bending, trading tooling cost for lower part cost, the same trade-off described in the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html).

## Design rules of thumb

Flat pattern, not to scale. Reliefs stop the corner tearing as it bends; holes kept away from bends and edges stay round and in position.

|
Feature |
Typical starting point |
Why it matters |

|
Inside bend radius |
Commonly around the material thickness; use one radius throughout the part |
Too tight a radius can crack the outside of the bend; one radius means one set of tools |

|
Flange length |
Several times the material thickness, as set by the fabricator's die |
A flange too short cannot be gripped and bent accurately |

|
Holes near bends |
Keep holes a few material thicknesses plus the bend radius away from the bend |
Holes too close distort into ovals as the metal stretches |

|
Holes near edges and each other |
At least about the material thickness or more between edges |
Thin webs distort or tear when cut or formed |

|
Hole size |
Generally no smaller than the material thickness |
Very small holes are hard to cut cleanly, especially in thicker sheet |

|
Bend relief |
A small notch where a bend meets an edge or another bend |
Prevents tearing and bulging at corners |

|
Grain direction |
Bend across the grain where possible, especially for harder aluminium alloys |
Bending along the grain is more likely to crack |

|
Tolerances |
Looser across bends than within a flat cut feature |
Each bend adds variation; dimension critical features from the same face |

The flat pattern depends on the bend allowance (often expressed as a K-factor), which varies with material, thickness and tooling. CAD sheet-metal tools calculate it,
but use your fabricator's values so the folded part comes out the right size.

**Practical rule:**
send the fabricator a 3D model and a drawing showing only the critical dimensions and tolerances. Let them adjust bend allowances and reliefs to suit their tooling, and ask them to confirm any changes. See [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) for what that drawing should show.

## Choosing a material

|
Material |
Strengths |
Watch out for |

|
Mild steel |
Low cost, strong, easy to form and weld |
Needs a protective finish such as powder coat or plating |

|
Galvanised steel |
Corrosion protection built in |
Welding damages the coating; cosmetic finish is limited |

|
Stainless steel |
Corrosion resistant, good appearance |
More expensive and harder to form; springs back more |

|
Aluminium |
Light, corrosion resistant, can be anodised |
Some alloys crack on tight bends; choose a formable grade |

## Joining and hardware

- **Self-clinching fasteners** (nuts, studs and standoffs pressed into the sheet) give strong threads in thin material without welding.

- **Tabs and slots** help locate parts for welding or assembly and reduce the need for fixtures.

- **Welding** is strong but adds cost, heat distortion and finishing work; spot welds suit overlapping sheets.

- **Rivets and screws** allow disassembly and joining different materials.

## Common mistakes

**Different bend radii on one part.**
Each radius may need a different tool set-up.

**Holes and slots too close to bends.**
They distort as the bend forms.

**Machining-level tolerances on bent features.**
Bending cannot hold them economically.

**Forgetting the finish thickness.**
Powder coating adds thickness to holes, threads and mating faces; mask or allow for it, as [surface finishes for plastic and metal parts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) explains.

**Designing a box that cannot be folded.**
Later flanges can collide with earlier ones or the press brake; ask the fabricator to check the bend sequence.

## Next steps

- Ask your fabricator for their standard bend radii, minimum flange lengths and K-factor for your material and thickness.

- Roll up part costs with the [Bill of Materials Cost Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/bom-builder.html).

- Prepare the request for quotation with the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

## FAQ

### What bend radius should I use for sheet metal?

A common starting point is an inside radius around the material thickness, but it depends on the material, thickness and the fabricator's tooling. Use one radius throughout the part and confirm it with your fabricator.

### How close can a hole be to a bend?

Keep holes a few material thicknesses plus the bend radius away from the bend so they do not distort. If a feature must be closer, ask the fabricator about cutting it after bending or adding a relief.

### What is a bend relief?

A small notch cut where a bend meets an edge or another bend. It lets the metal fold without tearing or bulging at the corner.

### What is a K-factor in sheet metal?

A value that describes where the neutral axis sits within the material as it bends, used to calculate the flat pattern. It varies with material, thickness and tooling, so use your fabricator's value.

### Is sheet metal cheaper than injection moulding?

At low to moderate volumes it often is, because laser cutting and press-brake bending need no part-specific tooling. At high volumes, moulding or press-tooled sheet metal can be cheaper per part. Compare routes for your volumes.

Title: Supply Agreements with a Manufacturer

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders and small brands about to pay for tooling and place a first production order (general information, not legal advice)

# Supply agreements with a manufacturer: what to cover

Why the relationship with your manufacturer belongs in writing, when to agree it, and the topics a supply agreement usually needs to address, explained in plain terms so you can prepare well and get more from a solicitor's time.

Quick answer

## Agree the relationship in writing before you pay for tooling or place the first production order, and make sure it covers more than price.

Cover what "good" looks like (specification, approved samples, inspection, rejects), who owns the tools and data and how you get them back, how pricing, orders, delivery and payment work, how changes are controlled, and who is responsible for faults, compliance and insurance.
This guide is general information, not legal advice: use it to prepare, then have a solicitor draft or review the agreement.

## Contents

- Why put it in writing, and when

- The topics at a glance

- Specification, samples and quality

- Tooling: ownership, storage, maintenance and transfer

- IP, confidentiality and supplier design changes

- Pricing, orders, delivery and payment

- Change control

- Liability, warranty, insurance and compliance

- Ending the relationship

- Worked example: tooling a moulded product overseas

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## Why put it in writing, and when

Many small brands run first production on quotes and purchase orders alone. A purchase order says what you are buying this time, at what price and by when. It rarely says who owns the mould you paid for, what happens when a batch fails inspection, or how you move production elsewhere. Those questions become urgent only when something goes wrong, the worst time to negotiate them.

A supply agreement sets the rules for the whole relationship, so each purchase order only deals with quantities, dates and prices. It need not be adversarial: a clear agreement helps a good supplier too, because it removes guesswork.

The right moment is **before you pay for tooling and before the first production order**. Once a tool is paid for and your launch depends on the next delivery, you have far less room to ask. The main points are often agreed in outline while [comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html), then written up once you have chosen the supplier.

**Important:**
this guide is general information, not legal advice. Contract law and the right approach differ between countries and situations, especially with an overseas supplier. Have a solicitor draft or review the agreement, and use this guide to arrive knowing what you need.

## The topics at a glance

|
Topic |
The question it answers |

|Specification and approved samples |What exactly is the supplier making? |

|Quality, inspection and rejects |How is "good" checked, and what happens to parts that are not? |

|Tooling |Who owns it, who looks after it, and can it be moved? |

|IP and confidentiality |Who owns the design, data and improvements? |

|Pricing and currency |How long does the price hold, and how can it change? |

|Forecasts, orders and MOQs |What are you committed to buy, and what is only a forecast? |

|Lead times and delivery terms |When, where, and who pays for which part of the journey? |

|Payment terms |When does cash leave your business? |

|[Change control](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html) |Who can change what, and how is it approved? |

|Liability, warranty and insurance |Who carries the cost when products are faulty? |

|Compliance and documentation |Who provides which certificates and records? |

|Ending the relationship |How do you leave with your tools, files and stock? |

## Specification, samples and quality

Many disputes with a manufacturer come back to what was ordered. The agreement should point to a controlled specification: drawings with revision numbers, materials and grades, finishes and colours, cosmetic standards, packaging and labelling.
It should also refer to **approved samples**, often called [golden samples](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html), signed off by both sides and kept as the physical reference for appearance and fit.

Then cover how quality is checked: first-article inspection before production, inspection during and after production, who carries it out (you, the supplier or an inspection company), the acceptance criteria, and what happens to rejects, including who pays for rework, replacement, scrap and freight on faulty parts.
[Quality control and first-article inspection](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) explains the checks themselves.

## Tooling: ownership, storage, maintenance and transfer

For moulded or cast parts, tooling is often the largest early payment and what ties you to a supplier. As [comparing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) notes, ownership is whatever the contract says: some suppliers transfer it once the tool is paid for, some keep it, and some tie it to an order volume. Write down:

- **Ownership:** who owns the tool, and from when (on full payment, for example).

- **Identification and storage:** that the tool is marked as yours, where it is kept, and that it will not be used for anyone else's parts.

- **Maintenance and life:** who pays for routine maintenance, repairs and refurbishment, and what happens when the tool wears out. [Injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html) covers how tool steel and design affect tool life.

- **Insurance:** who insures the tool while it is at the supplier's premises.

- **Transfer:** how you can collect or move the tool, how much notice is needed, and whether any costs apply, such as packing or outstanding invoices.

## IP, confidentiality and supplier design changes

An NDA protects information you share while talking to suppliers. It is a sensible start, and the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html) can produce a draft to review, but **an NDA is not a supply agreement**. It usually says nothing about tooling, quality, orders or exit.

The supply agreement should confirm that your design, drawings and data remain yours, and say who owns anything created during the relationship, such as supplier design changes, tooling data, fixtures and test software. It should also say whether the supplier may change materials, processes, sub-suppliers or factory without your approval.
[How to protect product IP](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) covers staged disclosure and ownership of supplier design work, and [design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html) explains the rights you may want to secure before sharing.

## Pricing, orders, delivery and payment

- **Pricing, price reviews and currency.** What the price includes, how long it holds, when it can be reviewed (for example, if material costs move), and the currency. Paying in a foreign currency leaves exchange-rate risk with you unless agreed otherwise.

- **Forecasts, firm orders and MOQs.** Separate a forecast, which helps the supplier plan, from a firm order, which commits you to pay. Agree minimum order quantities, when orders become firm, and whether you pay for materials bought against a forecast. [Minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) shows why these commitments matter so much to a small business.

- **Lead times and delivery terms.** Lead times for samples, first and repeat orders, and what happens when delivery is late. State the delivery term using the [Incoterms rules](https://iccwbo.org/business-solutions/incoterms-rules/) with a named place, so it is clear where cost and risk pass to you. [Landed cost: freight, duty and VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) explains what you still pay after that point.

- **Payment terms.** Deposits, stage payments and when the balance is due, ideally linked to milestones you can verify, such as a passed inspection. [Calculating hardware start-up cash flow](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html) helps you see when each payment hits your bank account.

## Change control

Products change after launch: a fix, a [cost reduction](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html), a component going obsolete. The agreement should say how either side proposes a change, who approves it, how cost and timing are agreed, and when new samples or first articles are needed.
Above all, the supplier should not change anything affecting form, fit, function or compliance without your written approval. [After launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) covers how to run changes on your side.

## Liability, warranty, insurance and compliance

If you sell under your own brand or import the product, you may be treated as its producer, as [product liability basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-liability-basics.html) explains. The agreement cannot remove those duties, but it can set out how responsibility is shared: the supplier's warranty on its work, what happens if a manufacturing defect leads to returns or a recall, any limits on liability, and what insurance each side holds. This is where a solicitor's and an insurance broker's input matters most.

Compliance responsibilities belong here too. Agree who provides material declarations, test reports, certificates for bought-in components and traceability records such as batch or date codes, and how long records are kept. The detail depends on your product and market; [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) gives a general overview of what conformity involves.

## Ending the relationship

The ending is easy to forget while everyone is getting along. Cover how long the agreement lasts and how either side can end it, with what notice. Then cover the practical exit: open orders, paying for materials and finished stock, and above all returning your tools, fixtures, samples and files in working order, on a reasonable timetable. Without a route to get your tools back, a better supplier is of little use to you.

## Worked example: tooling a moulded product overseas

Illustrative and qualitative. A small brand has chosen an [overseas supplier](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html) for a two-part moulded product and is about to pay a tooling deposit. With limited time and legal budget, it decides what matters most before asking a solicitor to draft the agreement.

- **Tooling first.** The tool is the largest early payment and hard to replace, so ownership, storage, maintenance and the right to collect it come top.

- **Specification and approved samples.** The brand cannot visit often, so it relies on controlled drawings, signed golden samples and pre-shipment inspection, with a clear rule on who pays when a batch fails.

- **Change control.** The supplier proposes helpful moulding tweaks. The brand welcomes them, but no material, colour or geometry change happens without written approval and new samples.

- **Orders and payment.** The brand gives a forecast but keeps firm orders to what it can afford, and links payments to sample approval and passed inspection rather than paying everything up front.

- **Exit.** It agrees how the tool, samples and files come back if it moves production, so the relationship can end cleanly if it needs to.

Price reviews, currency and liability still go into the agreement, but the brand spends its preparation time where a gap would be hardest to recover from.

## Common mistakes

**No written tooling ownership.**
Paying for a tool does not by itself make it yours to move. If it is not in writing, assume you cannot take it elsewhere.

**Relying on an NDA alone.**
An NDA covers confidential information. It does not cover quality, tooling, ownership of new work, orders or exit.

**Vague specifications.**
"As per sample" or an uncontrolled drawing leaves every quality argument open. Point to revision-controlled documents and signed samples.

**No route to get tools and files back.**
Without agreed terms for returning tools and files, leaving a supplier can mean starting again.

## Decision rules

- **Agree the terms before money is committed:** before the tooling payment and the first production order.

- **Define "good" in documents and samples,** not in conversations.

- **Treat tooling as an asset** you need to own, find, maintain and move.

- **Separate forecasts from firm commitments,** and link payments to verifiable milestones.

- **Plan the exit while relations are good,** and have a solicitor draft or review the agreement.

## Next steps

- Prepare a clear, revision-controlled pack using [the documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) and the [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html).

- Check you are ready to commit money with [Am I Ready to Commit to Tooling?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html)

- Plan the first batch with [planning a pilot production run](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/planning-a-pilot-production-run.html).

- Write down your answers to each topic above, then take them to a solicitor.

## FAQ

### Do I need a supply agreement if I already have purchase orders?

A purchase order covers one order: what, how many, what price and when. A supply agreement sets the rules for the whole relationship, including quality, rejects, tooling ownership, changes, liability and how it ends, which purchase orders rarely address.

### When should I agree a supply agreement?

Before you pay for tooling and before the first production order. Agree the main points in outline while comparing quotes, then write them up properly once you have chosen the supplier, while you still have room to negotiate.

### Is an NDA enough when working with a manufacturer?

No. An NDA covers confidential information shared during discussions. It does not usually deal with specifications, quality, tooling, ownership of new work, pricing, orders or ending the relationship, which a supply agreement should cover.

### Who owns the tooling I pay for?

Whoever the agreement says. Some suppliers transfer ownership once the tool is paid for, others keep it or tie it to an order volume. Put ownership, storage, maintenance, insurance and your right to move the tool in writing.

### Can I write a supply agreement myself?

You can prepare for it by deciding what you need on each topic, which makes a solicitor's work quicker and better targeted. Contract law differs between countries and situations, so have a solicitor draft or review the agreement, especially with an overseas supplier.

Title: Surface Finishes for Plastic and Metal Parts

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers choosing how plastic and metal parts should look, feel and last

# Surface finishes for plastic and metal parts

The common finishes for moulded plastic and metal parts, what each one changes, how finishes affect fits, masking and colour matching, and how to specify a finish so suppliers quote and make the same thing.

Quick answer

## Choose a finish for what it must do (look, feel, wear, corrosion or cleaning) and apply cosmetic finishes only to the faces people see and touch.

For moulded plastics, the cheapest finish is usually the one built into the tool: a texture or polish level with colour in the material. For metals, bead blasting, brushing, anodising, powder coating, painting, plating and passivation each solve a different problem.
Coatings add thickness, need masking and hanging points, and must be matched to an agreed colour reference, so write the finish, the faces it applies to and any masking on the drawing and in the quote request.

## Contents

- What a finish is for

- Finishes for moulded plastic parts

- Finishes for metal parts

- What each finish changes

- Designing for the finish

- Specifying a finish on a drawing and in a quote request

- Finishes, repair and recycling

- Worked example: a metal enclosure and a plastic housing

- Common mistakes

## What a finish is for

A surface finish is anything done to a part's surface as or after it is formed: a moulded texture, a blasted or brushed surface, a conversion such as anodising, or a coating such as paint, powder or plating.
It has one or more of five jobs: **appearance** (colour, gloss, hiding marks), **feel** (grip, warmth, softness), **wear** (resisting scratches and handling), **corrosion protection**, and **function** (electrical insulation or conductivity, cleanability, friction).

Start from the job, not the finish. A face nobody sees rarely needs more than the process gives naturally, and each extra step adds cost, handling, lead time and another thing that can go wrong.

## Finishes for moulded plastic parts

### Texture and polish in the tool

An injection-moulded part copies the surface of the tool. A polished tool gives a gloss part; a blasted, etched or laser-textured tool gives a matt or patterned one. Texture hides small flow lines, sink and scratches and adds grip, at no cost per part once the tool is made.
Agree polish and texture by the moulder's or texture supplier's reference and a physical sample, not a description such as "light matt".

Texture needs more draft. As the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) explains, a plain face commonly needs at least 0.5 to 1 degree of draft, but a textured face can need several degrees, and the texture supplier will usually state a minimum. Without it the texture scrapes as the part is ejected.
A high gloss is the hardest finish to keep perfect: it shows every sink mark, weld line and scuff.

### Colour: in the material or painted

Colouring the plastic itself, by buying a pre-coloured grade or adding a masterbatch at the press, is usually cheapest and most durable: a scratch shows the same colour underneath. Painting suits high gloss, metallic or soft-touch effects that moulded colour cannot give, or several colours on one part, but it adds a process, masking, reject risk and a coating that can chip or wear.
[Choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) covers which plastics take paint well.

### Printing and decoration

**Pad printing** transfers ink from a soft silicone pad, so it can print logos and markings onto curved or recessed surfaces. **Screen printing** pushes ink through a mesh and suits flat or gently curved faces and larger areas.
Both need a fixture and agreed ink colours. **In-mould decoration** places a printed film in the tool and moulds it into the part, giving durable graphics; it adds tooling and set-up effort, so it is worth asking about at higher volumes or where graphics must not wear off.
Lettering engraved into the tool is often the simplest and most durable marking of all.

## Finishes for metal parts

- **Bead blasting** fires fine media at the surface for an even matt texture that hides machining marks. It is often done before anodising and removes a very small amount of material.

- **Brushing** gives fine parallel lines by rubbing with abrasive in one direction. It suits flat or simple faces; state the grain direction.

- **Anodising** (aluminium, and a few other metals) grows a hard oxide layer out of the metal itself, partly into the surface and partly on top. Clear or dyed, it resists wear and corrosion and does not chip like paint. Hard anodising gives a thicker, tougher layer. It is electrically insulating.

- **Powder coating** sprays a dry powder onto the part, then bakes it into a tough, even coat. Common on steel and aluminium sheet metal, it comes in many colours and textures, but it is noticeably thicker than other finishes and also insulates.

- **Wet painting** gives thinner coats and a wide choice of colours and effects, on metal or plastic, but needs good preparation and is usually less hard-wearing than powder.

- **Plating** deposits a thin metal layer, such as zinc on steel for corrosion protection or nickel and chrome for a decorative, hard-wearing surface. Some plating processes need an extra treatment for high-strength steels; ask the plater.

- **Passivation** is a chemical treatment for stainless steel that removes surface contamination, such as iron from tools, so the steel's own corrosion resistance works as intended. It barely changes the look and is often specified after machining or welding.

## What each finish changes

The comparison below is qualitative; the right choice depends on the material, the supplier and how the product is used.

|
Finish |
Main benefit |
What to watch |

|
Moulded texture or polish |
Look and grip built in; no extra cost per part |
Needs draft; changing it means reworking the tool |

|
Paint on plastic |
Gloss, metallic and soft-touch effects |
Extra process, masking and rejects; can chip or wear |

|
Anodising |
Hard, wear and corrosion resistant, part of the metal |
Aluminium only in practice; insulates; dyed colours can vary between batches |

|
Powder coating |
Tough, wide colour range, good protection for steel |
Thickest build-up; masking; hanging points; insulates |

|
Plating |
Corrosion protection or decorative metal look |
Uneven thickness in holes and corners; process choice for the steel |

Every added finish adds cost and lead time, more so when parts travel to a separate finisher. Finishes built into the tool or material cost least per part.

## Designing for the finish

**Thickness build-up affects fits.** Coatings and anodising add material to every surface they cover, including the walls of holes and the sides of tabs. A hole gets smaller and a shaft or tab gets bigger, so a fit that worked bare can bind once finished.
Decide whether each critical dimension applies before or after finishing, and allow for it; [tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html) explains fits and how tolerances add up.

Not to scale: the coating is drawn thick so it can be seen. Coatings build up on every covered surface, so mask threads, fits and earthing points, or allow for the build-up in their tolerances.

- **Masking.** Threads, bearing seats, sealing faces and earth points usually stay bare. Masking is often manual, so keep masked areas few and simple and show them on the drawing.

- **Hanging and contact points.** Parts are hung on hooks or racks for coating, plating and anodising, leaving a mark. Provide a hole or edge on a hidden face and say where marks are acceptable.

- **Electrical paths.** Anodising and powder coating insulate. If a metal case needs earthing or shielding, mask the contact areas; [electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html) covers enclosure decisions that affect this.

- **Edges and corners.** Coatings thin on sharp edges and pool in sharp inside corners; small radii help.

- **Order of operations.** Either allow for the build-up on precise features, or finish first and machine them afterwards, accepting bare metal there.

- **Colour matching.** The same colour on plastic and metal, or from two suppliers, rarely matches by name alone. Agree a physical colour and gloss reference, then approve [golden samples](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/quality-control-and-first-article-inspection.html) made on the production process, and check against them at inspection.

## Specifying a finish on a drawing and in a quote request

A clear specification lets suppliers quote, and inspectors check, the same thing. On the drawing, state:

- **The finish and process**, such as "anodise, black" or "powder coat, fine texture", plus any type, class or thickness the product needs.

- **The colour and gloss reference**: a named colour system reference or, better, an approved physical sample.

- **Which faces it applies to**, and which faces are cosmetic, often shown by shading or a note such as "cosmetic face A".

- **Masked areas**, contact points and where rack or hanging marks are acceptable.

- **Whether dimensions apply before or after finishing**, at least for the critical ones.

- **A cosmetic standard**: how blemishes are judged, at what distance and lighting.

In the request for quotation, repeat the finish for each part and ask whether suppliers finish in house or subcontract it. The [RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html) assembles the request around your drawings and specification, so put the finish there, and [getting and comparing manufacturing quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html) explains how to check that every supplier has priced the same thing.

## Finishes, repair and recycling

Finishes can extend a product's life by protecting it from wear and corrosion, usually the bigger environmental win. But some make recycling and repair harder: paint and plating on plastics can contaminate recycled material, bonded films are hard to separate, and coatings over fasteners or joints make a product hard to open without damage.
Prefer colour and texture built into the material, avoid finishes that serve no purpose, and keep fasteners and service points uncoated and accessible. [Design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) goes further.

## Worked example: a metal enclosure and a plastic housing

Illustrative example, qualitative choices only. A team has two products: a handheld measuring device with a machined aluminium enclosure, used outdoors and sometimes dropped, and a desktop unit with an injection-moulded housing that is wiped clean.

|
Decision |
Aluminium handheld |
Moulded desktop housing |

|
Main jobs of the finish |
Wear, corrosion, grip, hide machining marks |
Look, hide moulding marks, easy cleaning |

|
Chosen finish |
Bead blast then anodise, dyed dark grey |
Light texture in the tool on visible faces, colour in the material, internal faces as moulded |

|
Rejected options |
Powder coat: thicker, chips on drops, covers the edges unevenly |
Painted gloss: extra process, shows scratches, hinders recycling |

|
Design changes |
Mask the earth contact and the threaded screw holes; allow for the layer on the lid fit; radius sharp edges |
Increase draft on textured faces to the texture supplier's minimum; moulded-in logo instead of a print |

|
Colour control |
Approved anodised sample; check batches against it |
Approved moulded colour and texture sample from the production tool |

The aluminium part needs a finish for protection and feel; the plastic part gets almost everything from the tool and material. Both are specified face by face, with a physical reference, and fits are checked after finishing.

## Common mistakes

**Specifying a cosmetic finish everywhere.**
It raises cost and rejects on faces nobody sees. Mark cosmetic faces and leave the rest.

**Forgetting thickness build-up.**
Coated holes shrink and coated tabs grow, so parts that fitted as prototypes can bind once finished.

**No colour reference.**
A colour name or screen image is not a specification. Without a physical sample, batches and suppliers can differ.

**Finishing tolerance-critical features without allowance.**
A precise bore or thread coated with no masking or allowance may need reworking or rejecting.
