## FAQ

### What is the cheapest finish for an injection-moulded part?

Usually a texture or polish built into the tool, with colour in the material. Once the tool is made it adds no cost per part, and scratches show the same colour underneath. Painting and printing add processes, handling and rejects.

### Should I anodise or powder coat aluminium?

Anodising grows a thin, hard layer from the metal itself, so it suits wear-prone, precise or handheld parts and does not chip. Powder coating is thicker, comes in more colours and suits larger sheet metal parts, but it changes fits more and can chip on impact.

### Does a coating change the size of a part?

Yes. Coatings and anodising add material to every covered surface, so holes get smaller and tabs or shafts get larger. Mask critical features or allow for the build-up in the tolerances, and state whether dimensions apply before or after finishing.

### What is passivation of stainless steel?

A chemical treatment that removes contamination such as iron from tools from the surface, so the steel's natural corrosion resistance works as intended. It barely changes the look, so it is easy to forget to specify after machining or welding.

### How do I make sure the colour is right in production?

Agree a physical colour and gloss reference rather than a name or screen image, approve [golden samples](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mould-tool-trials-and-sample-approval.html) made on the production process, and check batches against them at inspection.

Title: Sustainable Product Design and Product Life

Hub guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For designers, engineers and founders who want to reduce a physical product's environmental impact in ways that are real and defensible

# Sustainability and product life: where a product's impact comes from and how design reduces it

This is the starting point for everything on Orion Design about the environmental side of physical products: where impact comes from across the life cycle, which design decisions reduce it most, how to estimate it early, and the UK rules on producer responsibility and environmental claims. Each section links to a deeper guide, a free tool or an official source.

Quick answer

## The biggest environmental levers are decided in design: whether the product is needed, how much material it uses, how much energy it consumes, and how long it lasts.

Impact per year of use ≈ (materials + manufacture + distribution + end-of-life impact) ÷ years in service + yearly use-phase impact

For products that do not use energy, materials and manufacture usually dominate, so lighter, simpler and longer-lasting designs help most.
For energy-using products, the use phase often dominates, so efficiency matters most. Recycling helps at the end of life but cannot recover the impact of making the product.
Make a rough estimate early, while the design can still change, and make only the claims you can back with evidence.

## Contents

- The product life cycle

- Which stage dominates for your product

- Design levers that reduce impact

- Why lifetime matters so much

- Estimating impact: footprints and LCA

- Producer responsibility, regulation and claims

- Common mistakes

- A step-by-step path through this hub

## The product life cycle

Every physical product has an impact at each stage of its life. Looking at the whole life cycle stops one improvement simply moving the impact somewhere else:
a lighter material that needs replacing twice as often, or a recyclable part that makes the product impossible to repair.

Design decisions set the impact at every stage. Which stage dominates depends on the product, so estimate before optimising.

## Which stage dominates for your product

The pattern below is a general guide, not a rule; a screening estimate for your own product is the only reliable way to know where to focus.

|
Product type |
Stage that often dominates |
Where to focus first |

|
Passive products: furniture, tools, accessories, housewares |
Materials and manufacture |
Material quantity and type, durability, repairability |

|
Energy-using products: appliances, heaters, powered equipment |
Use (energy over the product's life) |
Efficiency in typical use, standby power, controls, lifetime |

|
Electronics with short replacement cycles |
Manufacture, especially electronic components |
Longevity, upgradeability, battery replacement, repair |

|
Products with consumables (cartridges, filters, refills) |
Consumables over the product's life |
Consumable design, refill and return systems |

|
Light, bulky or air-freighted goods |
Distribution can become significant |
Packaging volume, flat-packing, shipping mode |

## Design levers that reduce impact

|
Lever |
What it means in practice |

|
Question the need |
Could an existing product, a service or a smaller product meet the need? See [the most sustainable product is the one you never make](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html). |

|
Use less material |
Right-size walls and sections, remove parts, avoid over-engineering for rare loads |

|
Choose materials deliberately |
Prefer lower-impact and recycled materials where they meet the requirement; avoid mixing materials that cannot be separated |

|
Design for durability |
Test against real use, protect the parts that wear, avoid fragile features that end the product's life early |

|
Design for repair |
Screws instead of glue, accessible wear parts and batteries, spare parts and repair information (see [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html)) |

|
Reduce energy in use |
Efficient components, low standby power, sensible defaults and controls |

|
Design for end of life |
Easy disassembly, marked plastics, fewer material types, take-back where practical |

|
Right-size packaging |
Less volume and material, recyclable packaging, protection matched to the real shipping route |

**Practical rule:**
many sustainability improvements also cut cost: less material, fewer parts, smaller packaging and fewer returns. Look for those first; they are the easiest to justify.

## Why lifetime matters so much

The impact of making a product is spent once, however long it lasts. Spreading it over more years of use is often the most effective improvement available.

Illustrative figures only. Product A has a manufacturing footprint of 20 kg CO₂e and typically lasts 3 years: about 6.7 kg CO₂e per year of use.
Product B uses more robust materials and a replaceable battery, with a footprint of 26 kg CO₂e, but typically lasts 8 years: about 3.3 kg CO₂e per year.
The "heavier" product has roughly half the impact per year of service.

[Why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html) explains this in depth,
and the [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html) compares lifetime, repair and end-of-life options for your product.

## Estimating impact: footprints and LCA

A **screening estimate** uses typical emission factors for materials, processes and transport to find the biggest contributors quickly. It is ideal during design,
when the aim is to compare options rather than publish a number. A full **life cycle assessment (LCA)** follows a recognised method such as ISO 14040 and ISO 14044,
covers several impact categories rather than carbon alone, and is needed if you want to publish robust figures or claims. The
[GHG Protocol Product Standard](https://ghgprotocol.org/product-standard) is a widely used method for product carbon footprints.

The [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html) gives a screening estimate, and
[estimating product carbon footprint during design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-product-carbon-footprint-during-design.html) explains how to use one well.

## Producer responsibility, regulation and claims

Depending on the product, UK producers and importers can have legal responsibilities for the product's end of life, its packaging and its energy performance.
These are overviews to check against; take advice for your specific product.

- **Electrical and electronic equipment:** [WEEE producer and distributor responsibilities](https://www.gov.uk/electricalwaste-producer-supplier-responsibilities).

- **Batteries:** [waste batteries producer responsibility](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/waste-batteries-producer-responsibility).

- **Packaging:** [extended producer responsibility for packaging](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/extended-producer-responsibility-for-packaging-who-is-affected-and-what-to-do).

- **Energy-related products:** [ecodesign and energy labelling requirements](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/placing-energy-related-products-on-the-uk-market).

- **Environmental claims:** the Competition and Markets Authority's [Green Claims Code](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/green-claims-code-making-environmental-claims) sets out how to make claims that are truthful, clear and substantiated.

## Common mistakes

**Optimising the visible thing instead of the big thing.**
Recycled packaging matters less than energy in use for an appliance, or lifetime for a durable product.

**Making the product harder to repair to make it greener.**
Glued, sealed designs can be lighter but shorten the product's life.

**Estimating impact after the design is fixed.**
A footprint that can no longer change the design is a report, not a design tool.

**Claims without evidence.**
"Eco-friendly" and "sustainable" without substantiation risk misleading customers and breaching consumer law.

**Ignoring producer responsibility costs.**
Compliance schemes and fees for electrical products, batteries and packaging belong in the cost model.

## FAQ

### What is the most effective way to make a product more sustainable?

It depends on where the product's impact comes from. For products that do not use energy, using less material and making the product last longer usually help most. For energy-using products, efficiency in use often matters most. A quick screening estimate shows which applies before you start optimising.

### Is recycled material always the better choice?

Often, but not always. Recycled material usually has a lower footprint, but only helps if it meets the requirement: a recycled part that fails early can cause more impact than it saves. Check strength, durability and availability, and avoid mixing materials in ways that block recycling later.

### What is the difference between a carbon footprint and a life cycle assessment?

A carbon footprint estimates greenhouse gas emissions only. A life cycle assessment follows a standard method such as ISO 14040 and 14044 and covers several environmental impacts across the product's life. A screening footprint is ideal during design; a full LCA is needed for robust published figures.

### Do I have legal responsibilities for my product's end of life?

Possibly. In the UK, producers and importers of electrical and electronic equipment, batteries and packaging can have producer responsibility obligations (some schemes apply only above size or tonnage thresholds), and energy-related products can face ecodesign requirements. Check the official GOV.UK guidance for your product and take advice if unsure.

### How can I make environmental claims about my product?

Only make claims that are truthful, specific and backed by evidence you can share, as set out in the Competition and Markets Authority's Green Claims Code. Avoid vague terms such as eco-friendly unless you can substantiate exactly what they mean.

Title: Sustainable Product Design: A Practical Guide

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers and founders who want lower environmental impact to shape the product early

# The most sustainable product is the one you never make.

Sustainability is not just a materials conversation. It starts with a harder question:
should this product exist at all, and is its value strong enough to justify the impact required to create and support it?

**Topic**
Product legitimacy

**Audience**
Founders, designers, and engineers

**Tool**
Product Purpose Framework

**Use it for**
Early concept review

Quick answer

## Sustainable product design means making a product whose value justifies its impact, then cutting that impact across its whole life: materials, manufacture, energy in use, lifetime, repair and end of life.

Impact per year of useful service ≈ (materials + manufacture + transport + end of life) ÷ years of use + energy and consumables per year

The biggest levers are usually decided early: whether the product should exist, how long it will last and be repaired, and how much energy it uses.
Recycled content and recyclable packaging help, but rarely outweigh a short life or a heavy energy draw. Any environmental claim you make should be specific and backed by evidence.

Product teams often jump straight to recycled material percentages, circularity claims, or packaging changes. Those things matter, but they come later.
The first test is legitimacy: does the product solve a real human problem, with defensible impact, in a way the team can actually build and support?

If you need the more tactical version of that question, read
[How to validate a product idea before you build it](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html).
This article goes deeper on customer evidence, buyer clarity, and the signs an idea still needs more proof.

**Useful review lens:**
score product concepts across human value, planetary impact, economic viability, and technical feasibility before significant development effort is committed.

## Contents

- Why “should this exist?” is the right starting point

- The four-part test

- Worked example: two products with very different legitimacy

- Where a product's impact comes from

- A practical method

- Worked example: lifetime against recycled content

- Questions worth asking in the concept review meeting

- How to improve a weak concept before it becomes an expensive one

- Making environmental claims

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

- Turn the review into next-step decisions

## Why “should this exist?” is the right starting point

A weak product can still be profitable. A fashionable concept can still be environmentally poor. A clever technical solution can still add noise rather than value.
Sustainable design begins by refusing to separate product success from product justification.

Sustainability is strongest when it acts as a filter on what deserves to be built, not just as a decoration added after the business case is approved.

## The four-part test

|
Dimension |
What strong looks like |
Warning sign |

|
Human value |
Clear problem solved, frequent use, meaningful benefit |
Novelty or convenience without lasting value |

|
Planetary impact |
Impact is proportionate to benefit and can be reduced over time |
High material or energy burden disguised by shallow green claims |

|
Economic viability |
The concept can survive without distorting the original purpose |
Margin depends on overselling, overproducing, or planned replacement |

|
Technical feasibility |
The team can build, verify, and support it reliably |
Technical complexity is being mistaken for innovation |

## Worked example: two products with very different legitimacy

A diagnostic medical device and a novelty desk gadget might both be manufacturable and commercially attractive. The difference appears when the value question is made explicit.
One product can justify material, energy, and support burden because the utility is high and sustained. The other may only survive if the team ignores that its value evaporates quickly.

## Where a product's impact comes from

Once a concept clears the legitimacy test, look at its whole life. Which stage dominates varies a great deal between products, so find out before choosing where to spend design effort.

|
Life stage |
Design levers |
Often dominant for |

|
Materials |
Use less material, choose lower-impact materials, avoid unnecessary mixed materials and coatings |
Unpowered products, products with metals, electronics or batteries |

|
Manufacture |
Fewer processes and parts, less scrap, sensible finishes |
Products with energy-intensive processes or high scrap rates |

|
Transport and packaging |
Smaller, lighter packs; avoid air freight; flat-pack where it makes sense |
Bulky, low-value products shipped long distances |

|
Use |
Lower power draw, efficient standby, fewer consumables |
Products that use energy, heat, water or consumables over many years |

|
Lifetime and repair |
Durable design, replaceable wear parts and batteries, available spares, updatable software |
Almost every product: a longer life spreads all the other impacts |

|
End of life |
Easy disassembly, marked plastics, separable materials, take-back or refurbishment |
Products with valuable or hazardous materials |

For powered products, energy in use frequently outweighs everything else, so efficiency is often the first lever. For unpowered products, materials and lifetime usually matter most.
The [guide to estimating a product carbon footprint during design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-product-carbon-footprint-during-design.html) shows how to put rough numbers on each stage.

## A practical method

- **Justify the product.** Run the four-part test above. If human value is weak, fix that first.

- **Find the dominant stage.** Make a rough estimate of impact across the life stages and identify the one or two that matter most.

- **Set a lifetime target.** Decide how many years of useful service the product should give, and design and test to it.

- **Design for repair.** Make the parts most likely to fail or wear out easy to reach, replace and buy.

- **Choose materials with the whole life in mind.** Lower-impact materials are good; materials that let the product last longer may be better.

- **Plan the end of life.** Make materials easy to separate and identify, and decide what you will do with returned products.

- **Check your claims.** Only say what you can prove, in specific terms.

## Worked example: lifetime against recycled content

Illustrative figures only, in kilograms of CO₂ equivalent (kg CO₂e); they do not describe any real product. A small powered household product is offered in two versions.
Version A takes 20 kg CO₂e to make and deliver and lasts 3 years. Version B uses sturdier parts and replaceable wear items, takes 26 kg CO₂e and lasts 6 years. Both use 5 kg CO₂e of electricity a year.

- Version A: 20 ÷ 3 + 5 ≈ 6.7 + 5 = 11.7 kg CO₂e per year of service.

- Version B: 26 ÷ 6 + 5 ≈ 4.3 + 5 = 9.3 kg CO₂e per year of service.

Over 6 years a user needs two of Version A (2 × 20 + 6 × 5 = 70 kg CO₂e) or one of Version B (26 + 6 × 5 = 56 kg CO₂e), a reduction of 14 kg, or 20 per cent.
Switching Version A to recycled plastic and cutting its making impact to an assumed 17 kg CO₂e brings it to about 10.7 kg CO₂e per year (17 ÷ 3 + 5), still worse than Version B.
The lesson is not that recycled content is unimportant; it is that lifetime is a larger lever here, and the two can be combined.

Illustrative figures from the example above, bars drawn to scale within each panel. Doubling the life spreads the making impact over more years, which saves more than recycled plastic does on the short-life version.

[Why product lifetime matters more than recycling](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/why-product-lifetime-matters-more-than-recycling.html) explores this trade-off in more depth,
and [design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html) covers how to make a longer life practical.

## Questions worth asking in the concept review meeting

- What real human problem does this solve, and for whom?

- What energy, material, and service burden does the product create over time?

- Would the business model still work if we made the product last longer and need replacing less often?

- Can the team reliably build, support, repair, and improve it?

- Which life stage dominates the impact, and is our design effort aimed at it?

## How to improve a weak concept before it becomes an expensive one

**Clarify the job to be done.**
Sustainability improves when the product solves one important problem well instead of trying to manufacture demand with features.

**Reduce lifecycle burden, not just material guilt.**
Lifetime, power draw, maintenance, and logistics often matter more than a single recycled-content claim.

**Design the business model around longevity.**
If profitability depends on fast replacement cycles, the sustainability story is probably weak.

## Making environmental claims

In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority's [Green Claims Code](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/green-claims-code-making-environmental-claims)
sets out how businesses should make environmental claims. In summary, claims should be truthful and accurate, clear and unambiguous, not omit or hide important information,
make only fair and meaningful comparisons, consider the full life cycle of the product, and be substantiated.
In practice, avoid vague words such as "eco-friendly" or "green", say exactly what is better and by how much, and keep the evidence ready to share. If in doubt, read the code itself or take advice.

## Common mistakes

**Starting with materials.**
Swapping to a recycled or bio-based material before checking which life stage dominates can leave the biggest impact untouched.

**Assuming bio-based or recyclable means lower impact.**
It depends on the material, the product and what really happens at end of life. Recyclable in principle is not the same as recycled in practice.

**Making a product harder to repair to make it sleeker.**
Glued housings and sealed batteries can shorten useful life far more than they save in material.

**Ignoring energy in use.**
For powered products, a small change in standby or running power can outweigh large changes in materials.

**Making vague claims.**
Broad green claims without evidence can mislead customers and breach consumer protection law.

**Treating sustainability as a late review.**
By the time tooling is cut, most of the important decisions about lifetime, repair and materials are fixed.

## Good sustainability strategy starts before tooling, sourcing, and launch.

Review prompt

If a concept scores high on viability and feasibility but low on human value, do not treat that as a design detail. Treat it as a business warning.

## FAQ

### What is sustainable product design really about?

It is about creating products whose human value is strong enough to justify their material, energy, and operational impact.

### Can a product be technically feasible but still be a bad idea?

Yes. Technical feasibility and commercial viability do not guarantee meaningful human value or defensible planetary impact.

### How can teams improve a weak sustainability concept early?

Clarify the real user problem, reduce lifecycle burden, design for longer use and support, and challenge whether the business model depends on unnecessary replacement.

### What are the principles of sustainable product design?

Make products that are worth making, use fewer and lower-impact materials, cut energy and consumables in use, design for a long life and easy repair, plan for reuse and recycling at end of life, and make only claims you can prove. Start with whichever life stage dominates your product's impact.

### Is recycled material always the most sustainable choice?

No. Recycled content often reduces material impact, but it can matter less than how long the product lasts, how much energy it uses, and whether it can be repaired. A recycled material that shortens product life or makes repair harder may be a worse choice overall.

Title: Tolerances and Engineering Drawings

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers preparing parts for prototype or production quotes

# Tolerances and engineering drawings: the basics

What a tolerance is, why every dimension has one, how tolerances drive cost, what fits and datums mean, how tolerances add up across an assembly, and what a drawing must show before a supplier can quote it properly.

Quick answer

## A tolerance is the amount a dimension is allowed to vary and still be acceptable. Every dimension has one, either written next to it or set by the general tolerance in the title block.

Keep most dimensions on a sensible general tolerance and call out tighter tolerances only on the few features that control fit, function or safety, measured from clearly stated datums.
Tighter tolerances cost more to make and inspect, so a drawing for a quote should show material, finish, critical dimensions and their tolerances, revision and quantities, and nothing tighter than the product needs.

## Contents

- What a tolerance is and why every dimension has one

- General tolerances vs specific callouts

- Tolerances, processes and cost

- Fits: clearance, transition and interference

- Datums: where measurement starts

- Geometric tolerancing in concept

- Tolerance stack-ups

- What a drawing for a quote must show

- Worked example: a sliding insert in a housing

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What a tolerance is and why every dimension has one

No process makes two parts exactly the same: tools wear, plastics shrink as they cool and sheet springs back after bending.
A tolerance accepts that and states how far a dimension may move from its nominal (intended) size before the part stops working or stops fitting.

A dimension written as 20 ± 0.1 mm means any part measuring between 19.9 and 20.1 mm is acceptable. Tolerances can also be one-sided, such as 20 +0.1/−0, or written as two limits.
The total allowed variation, here 0.2 mm, is the tolerance band. A dimension without a tolerance is not exact; the supplier simply has to guess, and two suppliers may guess differently.

## General tolerances vs specific callouts

Rather than writing a tolerance next to every dimension, most drawings state a **general tolerance** in the title block, the box of information in the corner of the sheet.
It applies to every dimension that has no tolerance of its own. Many drawings do this by referring to a recognised standard such as ISO 2768, which sets general tolerances by size range in a few classes from fine to coarse.

**Specific callouts** are then added only where the general tolerance is not good enough: a bearing bore, a sealing face, a hole pattern that must line up with another part.
A good drawing has few of these, and each one should be traceable to a reason. If you cannot say why a dimension needs a tight tolerance, it probably does not.

## Tolerances, processes and cost

Each manufacturing process holds some dimensions easily and others only with extra effort. Asking for more than a process naturally gives means slower cutting, extra operations, more inspection, more rejected parts, or a change of process altogether.
The comparison below is qualitative and consistent with the process guides on this site; always confirm what a particular supplier can hold.

|
Process |
What it holds well |
Where tight tolerances get expensive |

|
[CNC machining](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) |
Generally the tightest of common processes; features cut in the same set-up hold well relative to each other |
Tight callouts mean slower cutting, more inspection and sometimes extra operations; features on different sides add set-up variation |

|
[Sheet metal](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html) |
Features cut in the same flat blank, such as holes in one face |
Dimensions across bends are looser, because each bend adds variation; machining-level tolerances on bent features are not economic |

|
[Injection moulding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) |
Very repeatable once the tool and process are settled |
Plastics shrink and can warp, so tight tolerances raise tool and inspection cost and may need tool adjustment after trials |

**Practical rule:**
cost rises much faster than precision. Halving a tolerance that the process already holds comfortably may cost little; halving one that is already near the process limit can mean a different process or full inspection of every part.

## Fits: clearance, transition and interference

Where one part goes into another, such as a shaft in a hole or a pin in a slot, what matters is how the two tolerance bands relate. There are three kinds of fit:

- **Clearance fit:** the largest shaft is always smaller than the smallest hole, so there is always a gap. Used for parts that slide, rotate or must assemble by hand.

- **Interference fit:** the smallest shaft is always larger than the largest hole, so the parts must be pressed or shrunk together. Used for parts that must stay put without fasteners, such as bearings or dowels.

- **Transition fit:** the bands overlap, so some pairs have a small gap and some a slight press. Used for accurate location where parts still need to come apart.

The fit depends on where the two tolerance bands sit relative to each other, not on the nominal sizes alone.

For round parts, the ISO system of limits and fits (ISO 286) gives standard hole and shaft codes for each kind of fit, so you can choose a recognised fit rather than inventing limits.

## Datums: where measurement starts

A dimension is a distance between two things, so every measurement has to start somewhere. A **datum** is the feature, usually a face, edge, hole or axis, that the drawing declares as the reference.
Datums are normally the features that locate the part in the assembly: the face it sits on, the hole a pin goes through.

Without stated datums, the supplier and the inspector may measure from different faces and get different answers, both right by their own reading.
Dimensioning critical features from the same datum also stops tolerances accumulating along a chain of dimensions.

## Geometric tolerancing in concept

Plus-or-minus tolerances control size and distance, but not shape or orientation. A plate can measure correctly in thickness everywhere and still be bowed; a hole can be the right diameter and still be in the wrong place.
Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (often called GD&T, defined in ISO 1101 and ASME Y14.5) adds controls for this, written in a small frame on the drawing that refers to datums.

- **Flatness** limits how far a surface may deviate from a perfect plane, which matters for [sealing faces](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html) and mounting surfaces.

- **Position** defines a zone, measured from the datums, within which the centre of a hole or pin must lie. It suits hole patterns that must line up with another part better than chains of ± dimensions do.

You do not need every symbol to start; know that shape, orientation and location can be controlled separately from size, and ask for that control only where a function depends on it.

## Tolerance stack-ups

In an assembly, tolerances add up. A gap between a lid and a housing depends on several dimensions on several parts, and the gap varies by the combined variation of all of them.
A **worst-case** stack-up adds every tolerance, assuming every part is at its limit at the same time; it guarantees assembly but can demand tight, expensive tolerances on long chains.
An **RSS** (root sum of squares) stack-up assumes independent, random, centred variation, so it predicts a narrower range that most assemblies will fall within. Use worst case for safety-critical fits, short chains and low volumes; RSS suits longer chains from stable processes in reasonable volumes, and many engineers check both.
The formulas are on the [engineering estimation formulas](https://oriondesign.xyz/knowledge/engineering-estimation-formulas.html) page, and the
[Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html) works through both for up to six dimensions.

## What a drawing for a quote must show

A 3D model shows the shape; the drawing tells the supplier what matters. For a firm quote, each part drawing should include:

- **Material**, specific enough to buy (grade, not just "aluminium" or "plastic").

- **Finish**: [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html), coating, colour or texture, and which faces are cosmetic.

- **Critical dimensions**, clearly marked, with their tolerances and datums.

- **General tolerance** in the title block for everything else.

- **Revision** letter or number, matching the 3D file name.

- **Quantities**, either on the drawing or in the request, including prototype and production batch sizes.

Send the drawing as a PDF alongside a neutral 3D file such as STEP. [The documents to prepare before talking to a manufacturer](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/must-have-documents-before-talking-to-a-manufacturer.html) covers the rest of the pack, and the
[RFQ Pack Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/rfq-pack-builder.html) helps you assemble a request for quotation that suppliers can compare like for like.

## Worked example: a sliding insert in a housing

Illustrative example, using the default figures in the Tolerance Stack-up Calculator. A removable insert slides into a pocket in a machined housing. The pocket is 60 ± 0.15 mm long and the insert is 59.4 ± 0.15 mm.
The insert must slide in by hand without rattling, which the team defines as a gap of 0.2 to 1.0 mm.

The nominal gap is 60 − 59.4 = 0.6 mm. Worst case, it is 0.6 ± 0.30 mm, so 0.30 to 0.90 mm, inside the required range. RSS gives about 0.6 ± 0.21 mm, roughly 0.39 to 0.81 mm.
If both lengths had instead been left on a looser tolerance of, say, ± 0.3 mm each (an illustrative figure), the worst-case gap would be 0.0 to 1.2 mm: some inserts would jam and some would rattle.

The useful decision is which dimensions earn a callout:

|
Feature |
In the gap chain? |
Tolerance decision |

|
Pocket length |
Yes |
Specific callout, ± 0.15 mm, measured from the pocket end wall as datum |

|
Insert length |
Yes |
Specific callout, ± 0.15 mm |

|
Housing outside size and wall thickness |
No |
General tolerance |

|
Chamfers, finger recess, label area |
No |
General tolerance; mark the label face as cosmetic |

|
Mounting holes in the housing base |
No, but they must line up with another part |
Positional tolerance from the base datums, not a tight ± on every hole |

Two callouts and one positional control cover what the function needs; everything else stays on the general tolerance.

## Common mistakes

**Tolerancing everything tightly.**
It feels safe, but it raises machining, tooling and inspection cost on features that do not matter, and it hides the few that do.

**No datums.**
Without a stated reference, the supplier and the inspector can measure the same part differently and disagree about whether it passes.

**Missing material or finish.**
Suppliers either guess, which makes quotes hard to compare, or come back with questions, which delays them.

**Sending CAD only, with no drawing.**
A 3D model shows nominal geometry but not which features are critical, what the tolerances are, or which faces are cosmetic. Suppliers then quote to their own assumptions.

## Decision rules

- **Start from a general tolerance** that the chosen process holds comfortably, and state it in the title block.

- **Add a specific callout** only where you can name the fit, function or safety reason for it.

- **Choose datums** from the features that locate the part in the assembly, and dimension critical features from them.

- **Use geometric controls** such as flatness or position where shape or location matters more than size.

- **Check every critical gap** with a stack-up, worst case first for short or safety-critical chains.

- **Ask the supplier** which callouts drive their price.

## Next steps

- List the fits and gaps your product depends on, and the dimensions in each chain.

- Check each chain with the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html).

## FAQ

### What is a tolerance on an engineering drawing?

The amount a dimension may vary from its nominal size and still be acceptable, for example 20 ± 0.1 mm. Every dimension has one, either written next to it or covered by the general tolerance in the title block.

### What is a general tolerance?

A tolerance stated once in the title block, often by reference to a standard such as ISO 2768, that applies to every dimension without its own tolerance. It keeps the drawing readable and leaves specific callouts for the features that matter.

### Why do tight tolerances cost more?

Holding a tighter tolerance than the process naturally gives means slower cutting, extra operations, more inspection and more rejected parts, or a different process altogether. Cost rises much faster than precision.

### What is a datum?

The feature, usually a face, hole or axis, that a drawing declares as the reference that measurements start from. Datums are normally the features that locate the part in the assembly.

### Do I need a drawing if I send a 3D model?

For a rough budget price, a 3D model with material, finish and volumes may be enough. For a firm quote or production, send a drawing too: it shows the critical dimensions, tolerances, datums, finish and revision that a model alone does not.

Title: Trade Marks and Product Names: The Basics

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 27 November 2026 · For founders choosing a name for a physical product before packaging, tooling or launch (an overview, not legal advice)

# Trade marks and product names: the basics

What a trade mark protects and what it does not, why a product name should be checked before it is printed on a box or moulded into a part, how to make basic checks yourself, what registration involves in general terms, and what to do if someone objects to your name.

Quick answer

## A trade mark protects your brand, such as a product name or logo, not the product's design or how it works. Check a name is free to use before you commit to packaging, tooling or domains.

Basic checks are quick: search the official trade mark register for the countries you will sell in, then look at marketplaces, domain names, social media handles and a general web search. Registration is made for particular goods and services and only covers the countries or regions where you register.
Use ™ to show you treat a name as a trade mark, and ® only once it is registered. This guide is general information, not legal advice: for anything close or contested, talk to a trade mark attorney or other IP professional and read the national IP office's guidance.

## Contents

- What a trade mark protects

- Why check a name early

- Basic checks you can make yourself

- Registering a trade mark, in general terms

- ™ and ®

- Using the mark consistently

- Domain names and marketplace brand registries

- If someone objects to your name

- Worked example: naming a kitchen gadget

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What a trade mark protects

A trade mark is a sign that tells customers whose product they are buying. For a physical product that usually means the product or brand name and the logo. Its job is to stop others using a confusingly similar sign for similar goods, so customers are not misled about who made what they buy.

A trade mark does not protect the product itself. It says nothing about the shape, the mechanism or the way the product works. Those are the territory of other rights:

- **Patents** protect how a new invention works: a mechanism, a process or a technical solution.

- **Registered designs** protect appearance: shape, lines, contours and decoration.

- **Trade marks** protect the brand: the name and signs customers use to recognise you.

Many products rely on a combination. [Design registration vs patents](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-registration-vs-patents.html) compares the first two, and the [IP, partners and compliance hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html) sets out the full range, including copyright and confidential information. The Intellectual Property Office's [overview of intellectual property](https://www.gov.uk/intellectual-property-an-overview) is a good official starting point.

## Why check a name early

A name spreads quickly. Within weeks of choosing it, a team has often bought a domain, set up social accounts, briefed a packaging designer and, sometimes, added the logo to a moulded part. All of that depends on the name being free to use.

Changing a name on a website is a nuisance. Changing it after packaging is printed, a [crowdfunding campaign](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/crowdfunding-a-hardware-product.html) has launched or a logo has been cut into a mould tool is expensive and slow. As the [freedom to operate guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/freedom-to-operate-explained.html) puts it for patents: check before you commit, while changing course is still cheap.

**Practical rule:**
shortlist several names, check them all, and only commit packaging, tooling and launch materials to a name that has passed the basic checks and, where the investment justifies it, a professional search.

## Basic checks you can make yourself

Informal checks will not give certainty, but they quickly rule out names that are plainly taken and show which names deserve a closer look.

- **The official trade mark register.** Search the national IP office's register for each country you plan to sell in. In the UK, the Intellectual Property Office provides a [trade mark search](https://www.gov.uk/search-for-trademark). Look for similar names as well as identical ones, including different spellings and names that sound alike, and note what goods and services each mark covers.

- **Marketplaces.** Search the online marketplaces where you expect to sell. A name in active use on similar products is a warning even if you cannot find a registration.

- **Domain names.** See whether the obvious domains are taken and, if so, what they are used for.

- **Social media handles.** Check the platforms you expect to use, and whether existing accounts sell anything like your product.

- **A general web search.** Search the name alone and with words describing your product. Unregistered businesses can still have rights from using a name, so use matters, not just registrations.

Record what you searched, where and when. If anything looks close, in either the name or the goods, take advice before going further.

## Registering a trade mark, in general terms

You can use a name without registering it, but registration generally makes your rights much clearer and easier to enforce. GOV.UK explains [how to register a trade mark](https://www.gov.uk/how-to-register-a-trade-mark) in the UK. Two general ideas matter most when planning:

- **Classes of goods and services.** A registration covers particular goods and services, grouped into classes. The same word can be registered by different owners for unrelated goods. Choose the goods and services you actually sell, and plan to sell.

- **Territories.** Protection is national or regional. A registration in one country does not protect you in another. Think about where you will sell, including online and through distributors abroad, and take advice on which routes cover those markets.

Not every name can be registered. Names that simply describe the product or its qualities are generally hard to protect, because other traders need to be free to use ordinary descriptive words. Distinctive or invented names tend to be stronger.

## ™ and ®

**™** can be used next to a name you treat as a trade mark, whether or not it is registered. It signals that you regard the name as your brand. **®** indicates a registered trade mark and should only be used once the mark is registered, and only in the countries where it is registered. Using ® for an unregistered mark can be misleading and, in some countries, an offence. If you sell in several markets, check each one.

## Using the mark consistently

A trade mark is strongest when it is used consistently as a brand. Use the same spelling and form across packaging, the product, the website and listings. Use the name as a brand alongside a description of the product, such as "the [Name] herb keeper", rather than as the word for the product itself, so it does not drift into a general term. If the logo changes significantly, check your registration still covers it.

## Domain names and marketplace brand registries

Owning a domain or registering a company name does not, on its own, give you trade mark rights, or stop you infringing someone else's mark. It only shows nobody else has registered that exact name in that registry.

Some large marketplaces run brand registry programmes that help brand owners manage listings and report copies. They generally require a trade mark, registered or applied for, in the relevant country. If you plan to [sell on marketplaces](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/selling-on-marketplaces.html), check each one's requirements early, because they can affect where and when you register.

## If someone objects to your name

If you receive a letter saying your name infringes someone else's rights, or your application is opposed, take it seriously but do not reply in haste. Note any deadline, keep the correspondence, and get advice from a trade mark attorney or solicitor before responding. Whether there is a real problem depends on details such as how similar the names and goods are, who used the name first, and where. Outcomes range from no action, to an agreement on how each party uses its name, to a change of name, which is far cheaper before launch than after.

## Worked example: naming a kitchen gadget

Illustrative and qualitative. A founder has developed a small kitchen gadget for keeping fresh herbs. Prototypes are working, a packaging designer is about to start, and the plan includes the name moulded into the lid.

The founder's favourite name plainly describes what the product does. A quick search shows several sellers using similar words, and a descriptive name would be hard to protect, so it is rejected.

The founder shortlists three invented names and checks each: the official registers for the UK and the other first-year markets, the main marketplaces, domains, social handles and a web search. One is registered by another company for kitchenware, so it is dropped. A second is free on the register but used by an active online shop selling garden products, which feels too close. The third shows no conflicts the founder can find, and a suitable domain is available.

Before briefing the packaging designer and toolmaker, the founder asks a trade mark attorney to advise on the third name, applies to register it for the relevant goods in the planned markets, and uses ™ on samples. The logo stays off the mould until the position is clear, so an unexpected objection would cost new artwork, not a tooling change.

## Common mistakes

**Moulding a logo into a tool before checking the name.**
A name cut into steel is expensive to change. Check and, where justified, register the name before it reaches tooling, and consider a printed or applied logo until you are confident.

**Assuming a company name or domain is a trade mark.**
Registering a company or buying a domain does not give trade mark rights or prove the name is free to use for your goods.

**Choosing a descriptive name.**
Names that simply describe the product are generally hard to protect and hard to stand out with. Distinctive names are usually stronger.

**Ignoring other countries you will sell into.**
Protection is national or regional. A name that is clear at home may already belong to someone else in a market you plan to enter through a distributor or a marketplace.

## Decision rules

- **Treat the name as a decision with a deadline:** settle it before packaging, tooling, domains and launch materials.

- **Check several names, not one favourite,** on the official register, marketplaces, domains, social handles and the web.

- **Prefer distinctive names** over descriptive ones.

- **Register for the goods you sell, in the places you sell,** and take professional advice on scope and routes.

- **Use ™ until registered, ® only after,** and get advice before answering any objection.

## Next steps

- Record your shortlisted names, searches and decisions in the IP, partners and compliance section of the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

- Read [freedom to operate explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/freedom-to-operate-explained.html) to check that the product itself is clear to make and sell.

- Put the name decision ahead of packaging and tooling in the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html), and confirm readiness with [Am I Ready to Commit to Tooling?](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html)

- See how trade marks fit with patents, designs and contracts in the [IP, partners and compliance hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html).

Make sure the name, IP and design checks are done before cutting tools.
[Open Ready for Tooling](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/ready-for-tooling.html)

Compare patents and registered designs for the product itself.

## FAQ

### What does a trade mark protect?

A trade mark protects signs that identify your brand, such as a product name or logo, against confusingly similar use on similar goods. It does not protect the product's design or how it works; registered designs and patents cover those.

### When should I check my product name?

Before you commit money to it: before packaging is printed, a logo is moulded into a tool, domains and accounts are built up, or the product is announced. Changing a name gets more expensive with every step.

### Does owning the domain or company name mean I own the trade mark?

No. A domain or company registration only shows nobody else has registered that exact name in that registry. It does not give trade mark rights or prove the name is free to use for your goods.

### Can I use the ® symbol before my trade mark is registered?

No. Use ™ for a name you treat as your brand. Use ® only once the mark is registered, and only in the countries where it is registered; misusing it can be misleading and, in some places, an offence.

### Does a UK trade mark protect me abroad?

No. Trade mark protection is national or regional, so you need protection in each country or region where you sell. Take advice from an IP professional on which routes cover your markets.

### What should I do if someone says my name infringes their trade mark?

Note any deadline, keep the correspondence and get advice from a trade mark attorney or solicitor before replying. Whether there is a real conflict depends on the details, and outcomes range from no action to an agreement or a change of name.

Title: UK vs Overseas Manufacturing

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and product teams deciding where to manufacture a new product

# UK vs overseas manufacturing: choosing where to make your product

How to choose between manufacturing close to home and further away: comparing landed cost rather than factory price, the effect on cash and lead times, quality and communication, Northern Ireland trade rules, and a staged approach many products follow.

Quick answer

## Compare total landed cost, cash tied up, speed, control and risk, not just the factory unit price.

Overseas manufacturing often gives a lower unit price, especially at higher volumes and for labour-intensive assembly, but adds freight, duty, longer lead times,
larger orders and more distance for quality and communication. Local manufacturing in the UK or Ireland often costs more per unit but can mean smaller batches, faster changes and less cash tied up.
Many products use a mix: local for prototypes, early batches or critical parts, and overseas once the design and demand are stable.

## The factors that matter

|
Factor |
Closer to home |
Further away |

|
Unit price |
Often higher, especially for labour-intensive work |
Often lower, especially at volume |

|
Freight and duty |
Lower, or none from UK suppliers |
Added to every shipment, with import VAT to pay up front (normally reclaimable if you are VAT-registered); see [landed cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) |

|
Lead time |
Shorter, so less stock and faster reorders |
Longer, especially by sea |

|
Minimum orders |
Often more flexible for small batches |
Often larger; see [MOQs and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html) |

|
Communication and visits |
Same time zone, easy to visit |
Time zones, language and travel make problems slower to resolve |

|
Design changes |
Quicker and cheaper to iterate |
Changes take longer and may involve stock in transit |

|
Supply chain depth |
May need to source some components abroad anyway |
Some regions have dense clusters of component suppliers |

|
Brand and sustainability |
Local manufacture can be a selling point; less transport |
Depends on the factory, materials and transport mode |

## Compare like with like

A quote from an overseas factory and a quote from a local one rarely include the same things. Bring both to a landed cost per unit at your realistic volumes, including tooling,
freight, duty, inspection, packaging and the cost of holding stock. The [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html) does this,
and the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html) shows the effect of larger orders and longer lead times on cash.

Illustrative figures only. An overseas quote is £5.00 a unit and a local quote £7.00. Adding freight, duty and inspection brings the overseas part to about £6.20 landed,
with a 3,000-unit minimum and a long lead time, against a 500-unit minimum locally. At early volumes, the £0.80 saving may be outweighed by the cash tied up and the cost of changes;
once sales are steady, the saving may justify moving.

**Practical rule:**
decide on landed cost per unit plus cash and risk at your actual volumes. A lower factory price is not a saving if it ties up cash you need to sell the product.

## Northern Ireland, Great Britain and the EU

For businesses in Northern Ireland, trading rules with Great Britain and the EU differ from the rest of the UK, which can affect where you manufacture, how goods move and which product markings apply.
Check current official guidance on [moving goods into, out of or through Northern Ireland](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/moving-goods-into-out-of-or-through-northern-ireland)
and the [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html) guide.

## A staged approach

- **Prototypes and pilot batches** close to the design team, where changes are fast.

- **Early production** where batch sizes and cash are manageable, often local or nearby.

- **Scale** once the design and demand are stable, choosing on landed cost and risk.

- **Review** regularly: costs, freight, tariffs and your volumes change.

The [Production Strategy Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/production-strategy-planner.html) helps choose a route for each stage.

## Common mistakes

**Comparing factory prices only.**
Freight, duty, inspection and stock holding can close much of the gap.

**Moving too early.**
Offshoring an unstable design multiplies the cost of every change.

**No presence or inspection.**
Distance makes quality problems slower and costlier to find; plan inspection from the start.

**One supplier, no backup.**
Consider what happens if a factory, route or tariff changes.

## FAQ

### Is it cheaper to manufacture overseas?

The factory unit price is often lower, especially at volume and for labour-intensive assembly. Once freight, duty, inspection, larger minimum orders and stock holding are included, the gap can be much smaller, and sometimes reverses at low volumes.

### When does UK manufacturing make sense?

Often for prototypes, pilot batches and early production, when batches are small, the design is still changing and cash is limited, and for products where local manufacture, speed or close control matters.

### Should I move production overseas later?

Many products start local and move once the design and demand are stable and volumes justify larger orders. Compare landed cost, cash and risk at your actual volumes before deciding.

### What extra costs come with importing?

Freight, insurance, customs duty where it applies, import VAT (normally reclaimable if you are VAT-registered, but paid before you sell), customs brokerage, inspection and the cost of holding more stock for longer lead times. Check current official guidance for your goods.

### Does Northern Ireland have different rules?

Yes, trading arrangements for goods moving between Northern Ireland, Great Britain and the EU differ from the rest of the UK. Check current official guidance before choosing where to make and ship from.

Title: Usability Testing a Prototype

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and engineers who want to know whether real people can use their prototype

# Usability testing a prototype: how to find out whether people can actually use it

What usability testing is and how it differs from customer discovery and technical testing, what to test at each prototype stage, who to recruit, how to plan and run task-based sessions without leading people, and how to turn what you see into prioritised design changes.

Quick answer

## Usability testing means watching representative users try to do realistic tasks with your prototype, without help, and noting where they hesitate, make mistakes or work around the design.

Start early with rough models and repeat at each prototype round. A handful of sessions with people outside the team usually reveals the main problems.
Give tasks rather than asking opinions, ask people to think aloud, do not help or explain, and then rank what you saw by how often it happened and how badly it affected the task. Fix the serious problems, update your requirements and test again.

## Contents

- What usability testing is, and what it is not

- What to test at each prototype stage

- Who to test with

- Planning a task-based session

- Running the session

- Simple measures, used qualitatively

- Turning findings into changes

- Remote or in person

- Accessibility and inclusive design

- Worked example: a handheld kitchen gadget

- Common mistakes

- Decision rules

## What usability testing is, and what it is not

Usability testing asks one question: can the intended users do what the product is for, easily and without help? You give people a prototype and a set of realistic tasks, then watch.
It is about behaviour, not opinion: what people do with the object in their hands is far more reliable than what they say about it.

It sits between two other activities that are often confused with it:

|
Activity |
Main question |
Typical evidence |

|
[Customer discovery](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/customer-discovery-for-hardware.html) |
Is the problem real, and how do people deal with it now? |
Interviews and observation, usually before there is a design |

|
Usability testing |
Can people use this design to do the job? |
Observed tasks with a prototype: hesitations, errors, workarounds, comments |

|
[Technical verification](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) |
Does the product meet its measurable requirements? |
Bench, durability, environmental and compliance tests |

A product can pass every bench test and still fail the moment someone tries to open it.

## What to test at each prototype stage

You do not need a working product to start, and the earlier a problem is found, the cheaper it is to change.

|
Prototype |
Good for testing |
Limits |

|
Paper, card and foam models |
Overall size, grip, reach, where controls should go, the order of steps, labels and instructions |
Weight, feel and mechanisms are not realistic |

|
Looks-like prototypes |
Handling, first impressions, whether people understand what it is and how to start, button and display layout |
Nothing works, so tasks have to be talked through or simulated |

|
Works-like and integrated prototypes |
Real tasks end to end: set-up, use, cleaning, charging, recovering from mistakes |
Rough appearance can distract; later and more costly to change |

[Looks-like vs works-like prototypes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/looks-like-vs-works-like-prototypes.html) explains what each kind of build is for, and
[how many prototypes do you need?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-many-prototypes-do-you-need.html) shows how to plan usability questions into each round.

## Who to test with

Test with people who match your intended users: their experience, physical abilities, setting and the job they are trying to do. A handful of representative participants per round is usually enough to show the main problems, and several small rounds teach more than one large one.

- **Avoid testing only with friends, family and colleagues.** They know too much, want to be kind and often do not match the users.

- **Never treat the team as users.** You already know how it works, so you cannot see what is confusing.

- **Include the edges of your user group,** such as first-time users, older users, left-handed users or people wearing gloves, if they will use the product.

- **Reuse your discovery contacts** where they fit, and recruit fresh people for later rounds so earlier sessions do not teach them the answers.

## Planning a task-based session

Write a short plan before the first session, so every participant gets the same tasks and the results can be compared:

- **Goals.** Two or three questions this round must answer, such as "can people fit the attachment without instructions?"

- **Tasks.** Realistic goals written in the user's language, not yours: "Make a smoothie for one" rather than "press the pulse button". Do not name controls in the task.

- **A short script.** A welcome, a reminder that you are testing the product rather than the person, the tasks in order, and a few closing questions.

- **Set-up.** A realistic setting where possible, any props needed (food, water, a worktop, a bag), and a way to record notes.

- **Consent and privacy.** Explain what the session involves, what you will record and how you will use and store it, and that people can stop at any time. Ask before photographing or filming, keep personal details separate from notes, and only keep what you need.

Sessions of around 30 to 60 minutes are typical for a simple product. Run one practice session with someone outside the team to find unclear tasks before the real ones.

## Running the session

Hand over the prototype, read the first task and then mostly stay quiet. Ask the participant to think aloud: what they are looking for, what they expect and what surprises them.

- **Do not help, explain or lead.** If someone is stuck, ask "what would you do now?" or "what are you looking for?". Only step in if they cannot continue, and note that you did.

- **Watch for hesitation,** not just failure. A pause, a second look or a tentative press often marks a problem that people will not mention.

- **Note errors and workarounds,** such as holding the product a way you did not intend or using two hands where one was planned.

- **Separate what you saw from what you think it means.** Write "turned it over twice looking for the switch" rather than "switch hard to find".

**Practical rule:**
when a participant asks you a question, answer with a question. Every time you explain the design, you remove the evidence you came for.

## Simple measures, used qualitatively

With small numbers of participants, measures are for spotting patterns, not for statistics. Record the same few things for every task:

- **Completion:** completed without help, completed with help, or not completed.

- **Time:** roughly how long the task took, which mostly flags tasks that dragged.

- **Errors:** wrong actions, false starts and recoveries.

- **Comments:** what people said while doing it, in their own words.

A simple grid of participants against tasks makes patterns obvious. Avoid quoting percentages from a handful of sessions; say "four of five participants" instead.

## Turning findings into changes

Write each problem as an observation, then rate it by how many participants it affected and how severe it was: did it stop the task, slow it down, cause a risk to safety, or just irritate?
Fix problems that stop tasks or create safety risks first, then frequent slowdowns, then minor irritations.

Each round should end with a short list of changes and updated requirements, then the loop repeats on the next prototype.

Look for the cause, not just the symptom: if people miss a button, the answer might be its position, shape, label or the order of steps, not simply making it bigger.
Turn settled findings into requirements, such as "the bowl can be removed with one hand without looking", in your
[product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html), so they are checked again on later prototypes and not lost.

## Remote or in person

Physical products are usually best tested in person, because you need to see hands, posture and the way people pick things up. Remote sessions can still work well for later rounds:
send a prototype in advance, agree a camera angle that shows the hands and the product, and keep tasks short. Remote testing also suits instructions, packaging and companion apps.

If you are working with Orion Design, early prototypes can be handled and reviewed together in person in Belfast, and later rounds reviewed the same way or remotely; see
[product design in Belfast](https://oriondesign.xyz/product-design-belfast/).

## Accessibility and inclusive design

Products are used by people with a wide range of strength, dexterity, sight, hearing and memory, and by everyone in poor conditions: wet hands, dim light, one hand busy. Designing for the edges often makes a product easier for everyone.

- Include participants with a range of abilities and ages that reflects your real users, and ask what support they need to take part.

- Test in realistic conditions, such as with gloves, at arm's length, or in dim light, where these are part of normal use.

- Check that controls, markings and feedback do not rely on a single sense: combine colour with shape or text, and sound with light or touch.

- Watch grip force, twisting and fine finger actions, which are common barriers.

## Worked example: a handheld kitchen gadget

Illustrative example. A small team has a handheld, battery-powered kitchen gadget with one power button, a speed button and a detachable head that is washed separately.
They test an integrated prototype with five home cooks recruited through a local cookery group, none of whom had seen the product. Tasks: charge it, fit the head, prepare a simple recipe, remove the head and clean it.

|
What the team observed |
Severity |
Change |

|
Four of five pressed the speed button first, expecting it to switch the gadget on |
Slowed the task; caused confusion |
Swap button positions so power sits under the thumb; add a clearer power symbol |

|
Three struggled to remove the head with wet hands; two twisted the wrong way |
Stopped the task for one participant |
Add a textured grip area and a moulded direction arrow; new requirement for wet-hand removal |

|
Two did not notice the charging light while it was face down on the worktop |
Minor; caused uncertainty |
Move the indicator so it can be seen from above |

|
One commented that the colour looked "cheap" |
Opinion, not a usability problem |
Noted for the appearance review; no change from one comment |

The team made the first three changes on a revised looks-like model and ran a short second round with three new participants focused on the power button and head removal. The single colour comment was logged rather than acted on, because one opinion is not a pattern.

## Common mistakes

**Asking "do you like it?"**
Liking is not using. People are polite about prototypes; give them tasks and watch what they do instead.

**Testing with the team.**
People who designed the product cannot forget how it works. Colleagues, friends and family are better than nobody for a first check, but never the only test.

**Fixing the first comment heard.**
One participant's reaction can send the design the wrong way. Wait until the round is complete and look for patterns before changing anything.

**Testing too late.**
Problems found on production-intent parts may need new tooling. A foam model and a few tasks can catch layout problems far earlier and more cheaply.

## Decision rules

- **If you have a shape but no mechanism**, test handling, layout and understanding with a looks-like or foam model now.

- **If several participants fail or hesitate on the same task**, treat it as a design problem, not a user problem.

- **If a problem affects safety**, fix it whatever the number of participants who met it.

- **If findings are mixed after one round**, run another small round with new people rather than a bigger one.

- **Before design freeze**, run a final round on an integrated or production-intent prototype against your usability requirements.

## Next steps

- Write down the two or three usability questions your next prototype should answer.

- Choose the cheapest prototype that can answer them with the [Prototype Strategy Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/prototype-strategy-tool.html).

- Add usability tasks alongside your technical tests in the [Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html).

- See where these rounds sit in the wider journey in the [development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html).

Put usability sessions alongside the technical tests for each prototype round.
[Open Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html)

Match each usability question to the right prototype and method.

## FAQ

### How many people do I need for a usability test?

A handful of representative participants per round usually reveals the main problems with a simple product. Several small rounds, fixing problems in between, generally teach more than one large round. Add more people if your users vary a lot, for example in age, ability or setting.

### Can I usability test before I have a working prototype?

Yes. Card, foam and looks-like models can test size, grip, control layout, labels and the order of steps. Ask people to talk through or act out tasks. Problems found this early are the cheapest to fix.

### How is usability testing different from customer discovery?

Customer discovery explores the problem and how people deal with it today, usually before a design exists. Usability testing checks whether a particular design lets people do the job, by watching them use a prototype.

### Should I pay or reward participants?

A small thank-you, such as a voucher, is common and makes recruitment easier and fairer. Keep it modest and the same for everyone, and make clear it does not depend on what they say about the product.

### What should I do if participants disagree?

Focus on what they did rather than what they said. If behaviour differs, look at whether the participants differ in experience or setting; you may need to design for both groups or decide which matters most, and test again.
