Title: Why Product Lifetime Matters More Than Recycling

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 25 November 2026 · For designers weighing durability, repair and recycling decisions

# Why product lifetime matters more than recycling.

Recycling matters, but it is often overweighted in early sustainability discussions. Lifetime, repairability, energy use, and recovery design usually change the real lifecycle story more.

Quick answer

## For most durable products, lasting longer does more for the lifecycle than being more recyclable.

Impact per year of use ≈ (manufacturing impact + end-of-life impact) ÷ years in service + annual use-phase impact

Doubling a product’s useful life roughly halves the yearly share of its manufacturing impact. Recycling recovers some material value at the end,
but it cannot recover the energy and emissions already spent making the product, and it does nothing about energy used in service.

It is easy to talk about recycled material percentages because they are visible and easy to communicate. It is harder to talk about whether the product lasts long enough, can be repaired, or consumes too much energy during use.
Those harder questions are often the ones with bigger lifecycle consequences.

**Lifecycle principle:** a durable, repairable product with lower use-phase burden will often outperform a shorter-lived product made from a more recyclable material mix.

## Contents

- Why recycling gets overweighted

- Where lifecycle strength actually comes from

- The order of circular design strategies

- Illustrative example: two cordless handheld vacuums

- When recycling does matter most

- Common mistakes

- Practical next steps

## Why recycling gets overweighted

Recycling is a real and useful part of the picture, but it is often asked to carry more weight than it can. Several practical limits apply:

- recycling happens only after the product has already been made, used and discarded, so the manufacturing impact has been spent

- many products are never collected for recycling, and what is collected is not always recovered as useful material

- mixed plastics, coatings and bonded assemblies are difficult to separate, and recycled plastic is often downgraded into lower-value uses

- recyclability on paper depends on infrastructure the designer does not control

None of this makes recycling unimportant. It means a recyclable label is a weak substitute for a product that stays useful for longer.

## Where lifecycle strength actually comes from

- longer useful life that spreads embodied impact across more years of service

- repairability that avoids premature replacement

- upgradeability where performance can improve without a full new product

- lower use-phase energy demand

- recovery design that improves what happens at end of life

## The order of circular design strategies

A widely used rule in circular design is that strategies keeping a product intact retain more value than those breaking it down into materials.

|
Strategy |
What it does |
Design levers |

|
Avoid and reduce |
Uses less material and energy from the start |
Right-sizing, fewer parts, validated need |

|
Extend lifetime |
Keeps the product in service for longer |
Durable materials at stress points, timeless design, robust testing |

|
Repair |
Fixes failures without replacing the whole product |
Standard fasteners, replaceable wear parts and batteries, spare parts and guides |

|
Refurbish and remanufacture |
Restores used products or modules for another life |
Modular architecture, durable housings, accessible components |

|
Recycle |
Recovers materials for new products |
Mono-materials, marked plastics, easy separation, minimal coatings |

## Illustrative example: two cordless handheld vacuums

Two products may share similar material mass. If one is hard to repair, replaced sooner, and consumes more energy during use, its lifecycle performance can be materially worse even if its recycled-content percentage looks better in the brochure.

To make that concrete, imagine two cordless vacuums. The figures are illustrative, not measured data. Design A has a glued-in battery and is typically discarded after about three years when the battery fades.
Its manufacturing and end-of-life impact is 40 kg CO2e. Design B uses screws and a replaceable battery pack, adding a little material for 45 kg CO2e, plus 5 kg for one replacement battery, and lasts six years.

Assuming similar energy use in service, Design A carries about 13.3 kg CO2e per year of use (40 ÷ 3), while Design B carries about 8.3 (50 ÷ 6).
Even if Design A switched to more recycled plastic and cut its manufacturing impact by a tenth, it would still sit at about 12 kg per year. Lifetime is doing most of the work.

Explore it: years of use against recycled material

Illustrative figures, not measured data: 40 kg CO2e to make and dispose of the product (as for Design A above), 2 kg CO2e a year in use, and recycled material cutting the making impact by a tenth. Impact per year of use = 40 ÷ years + 2.

Years of use

3 years

Use recycled material (−10% embodied, illustrative)

- Share of making the product

- Use each year

- Saved by recycled material

- Double the chosen life (up to 15 years)

The interactive chart needs JavaScript. The sentence below gives the figures for a 3-year life.
For this illustrative product, a 3-year life works out at about 15.3 kg CO2e per year of use (13.3 from making it, 2.0 from use). Doubling the life to 6 years would bring that to 8.7 kg (43% lower); switching to recycled material instead would bring it to 14.0 kg (9% lower).

## When recycling does matter most

Recovery design deserves more attention for short-life or single-use items, packaging, and products where materials dominate the footprint and repair is not realistic.
In those cases, using mono-materials, marking plastic types, avoiding unnecessary coatings and making separation easy can make a real difference to what is recovered.

## Common mistakes

**Leading with recycled content.** It is a fair metric but often not the one that moves the lifecycle result most.

**Gluing what will wear.** Batteries, seals, filters and cables are common failure points. Bonding them in shortens the product’s life.

**Ignoring the use phase.** For energy-using products, efficiency in service can outweigh small gains in materials.

**Designing for repair without supporting it.** Replaceable parts help only if spares, guides and tools are actually available.

**Making claims without numbers.** Even a rough concept-stage estimate is better than a general sustainability statement.

The most recyclable product in the world still has to be made again when it is thrown away early.

## Practical next steps

- Estimate the expected useful life and the most likely reason the product will be discarded.

- Identify the wear parts and design them to be replaceable with common tools.

- Check whether use-phase energy or manufacturing dominates, so effort goes where it counts.

- Plan spare parts and repair information as part of the product, not an afterthought; repair and ecodesign rules in the UK and EU increasingly expect this for some product categories.

- Then improve material choice and separation for end of life.

The [Product Lifecycle Explorer](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-lifecycle-explorer.html) helps make those trade-offs visible so teams can see whether the concept is improving through longevity, repair, and recovery rather than relying on narrow recycling claims.

For a first carbon estimate, use the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html) alongside
[Estimating product carbon footprint during design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-product-carbon-footprint-during-design.html).
The wider argument is set out in [The most sustainable product is the one you never make](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sustainable-product-design.html).
When lifetime and repair targets are agreed, the [Product Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) helps carry them into the product plan alongside cost and timing.

[Product Purpose Framework](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-purpose.html)

Typical questions

Product lifetime vs recyclingRepairability and sustainabilityLifecycle design strategy

## FAQ

### Is recycling the most sustainable option for products?

Usually not. Reducing material, extending product life, repairing and remanufacturing generally retain more value than recycling, because they keep the product or its parts intact. Recycling is an important last loop for materials, but it comes after the manufacturing impact has already been spent.

### How does product lifetime affect carbon footprint?

A product’s manufacturing footprint is spread over the years it is used. If the useful life doubles, the share of that footprint per year of use roughly halves, and fewer replacement products need to be made. For energy-using products, use-phase energy must be considered alongside lifetime.

### What is design for repair?

Design for repair means making it practical to diagnose and fix a product rather than replace it. Typical measures include standard fasteners instead of adhesives, replaceable batteries and wear parts, accessible spare parts and clear repair information. It works best when planned from the concept stage.

### Does using recycled material make a product sustainable?

It helps, because recycled material often has a lower footprint than virgin material, but it is only one factor. A product with high recycled content that fails early or uses a lot of energy can still have a worse lifecycle result than a durable, efficient alternative.

### What is the use phase in a lifecycle assessment?

The use phase covers the impacts that occur while the product is in service, such as electricity, fuel, water or consumables. For products that use energy, it can be the largest part of the lifecycle impact. For passive products, manufacturing usually dominates instead.

Related guides

[Design for repair and disassembly](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/design-for-repair-and-disassembly.html)

[Right to repair and ecodesign rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/right-to-repair-and-ecodesign-rules.html)

Title: Working With a Product Design Consultancy

Guide

By [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Last reviewed 26 November 2026 · For founders and teams commissioning product design or engineering help for the first time

# Working with a product design consultancy: what to expect and how to brief one

What a product design consultancy does, how it compares with a freelancer or an in-house hire, how to write a brief that gets useful proposals, what to ask before choosing, and how to agree intellectual property, files and staged work.

Quick answer

## Use a product design consultancy for skills, capacity or experience you do not have, and brief it with the problem, the constraints and the decisions you need, not just the product you imagine.

A good brief covers who the product is for, what it must do (as measurable requirements), the target cost and volume, the timeline and budget range, what already exists,
and what you want delivered at the end of each stage. Choose a partner on relevant experience, how they would tackle your riskiest questions, and clear terms on
intellectual property ownership, and agree the work in stages with a decision point after each.

## Contents

- Consultancy, freelancer or in-house?

- What a consultancy can do for you

- How to brief a product design consultancy

- Choosing a partner: questions to ask

- How engagements are usually structured

- Intellectual property and files

- Worked example: a short brief

- Working well together

- Common mistakes

- Next steps

## Consultancy, freelancer or in-house?

|
Option |
Strengths |
Watch out for |
Often suits |

|
Product design consultancy |
Several disciplines, experience across many products, established processes and supplier contacts |
Often higher day rates than a freelancer; make sure you know who will actually do the work |
Multi-disciplinary products, first products, teams without in-house engineering |

|
Independent designer or engineer |
Direct contact with the person doing the work, flexibility, often lower cost |
Limited capacity and range of skills; plan for illness and holidays |
Focused tasks, simpler products, specific skills such as CAD or DFM review |

|
In-house hire |
Knowledge stays in the business; long-term continuity |
Recruitment time, salary commitment, one person rarely covers every skill |
Businesses with a pipeline of products to develop |

|
Design-and-make (ODM) supplier |
Speed and lower development cost by adapting existing designs |
Less control and differentiation; check who owns the design |
Products close to something the supplier already makes |

Many projects combine these: for example a consultancy for concept and engineering, a freelancer for later updates, and a contract manufacturer for production. [Industrial design vs engineering design](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/industrial-design-vs-engineering-design.html) explains which skills each stage usually needs.

## What a consultancy can do for you

- **Turn an idea into a clear brief and plan**, including what must be learned first and what it is likely to involve.

- **Concept development:** several directions, compared against your requirements.

- **Engineering and CAD:** mechanical design, materials, tolerances and drawings ready for suppliers.

- **Prototyping and testing:** planning rounds that answer specific questions, and managing builds.

- **Design for manufacture:** preparing parts for the chosen processes and reviewing supplier feedback.

- **Manufacturing support:** supplier selection, tooling reviews, first-article inspection and production issues.

- **Independent review:** a second opinion on a design, cost estimate or manufacturing route before you commit.

## How to brief a product design consultancy

You do not need drawings or a finished specification. You do need to be clear about the problem and the constraints. A useful brief covers:

|
Section |
What to include |

|
The problem and the user |
Who it is for, the problem it solves, and the evidence you have that it matters |

|
What it must do |
Essential and desirable requirements, measurable where possible (see [opportunity and concept](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/opportunity-and-concept.html)) |

|
Commercial targets |
Target retail price, route to market, target unit cost and expected volumes |

|
Constraints |
Size, weight, regulations, materials to avoid, brand requirements, existing parts to reuse |

|
What exists |
Sketches, prototypes, competitor products, patents you know about, previous work |

|
Timeline and budget |
Key dates, and a budget range for the next stage, so the proposal can be realistic |

|
Deliverables |
What you want at the end of the next stage: a concept, a prototype, production-ready files |

|
Decisions and people |
Who decides, how quickly, and who the consultancy should talk to |

**Practical rule:**
share a budget range. Without one, proposals range from a two-week review to a year of development, and none can be compared. A range lets a consultancy propose what is realistic.

## Choosing a partner: questions to ask

- What similar products or problems have you worked on, and what did you learn from them?

- How would you tackle the riskiest part of this product first?

- Who will actually do the work, and who will I speak to week to week?

- How do you structure the work, and what decision points are there?

- How do you handle changes to scope?

- Who owns the intellectual property in the work, and when does it transfer?

- What happens to CAD files and documentation at the end, and in what formats?

- How do you work with manufacturers, and do you have any commercial relationship with them?

## How engagements are usually structured

|
Model |
How it works |
Best for |

|
Fixed price per stage |
An agreed scope, deliverables and price for each stage |
Well-defined stages, such as concepts or a DFM review |

|
Time and materials |
Paid for time spent, usually with an estimate and regular reporting |
Uncertain work, such as early exploration or production problem-solving |

|
Retainer or ongoing support |
A set amount of time each month |
Teams that need regular input across several decisions |

|
Short review or advice |
A focused look at one question |
Second opinions before a big commitment |

Staging the work protects both sides: each stage ends with a decision about whether to continue, change direction or stop, based on what was learned.
Costs vary widely with the product's complexity and the depth of work, so compare proposals on scope and approach, not just price.
[How much it costs to develop a hardware product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html) shows the wider budget the design work sits in.

Each stage ends with a decision based on what was learned, so you can change direction or stop before the next budget is committed, rather than discovering a problem at the end of one large contract.

## Intellectual property and files

Unless the contract says otherwise, the designer may own copyright and design rights in their work. Make sure the agreement assigns the intellectual property in work produced for you,
states when ownership transfers (often on payment), and covers delivery of native CAD files, neutral formats such as STEP, drawings and documentation.
A confidentiality agreement before detailed discussions is sensible; see the [IP, partners and compliance hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/ip-partners-and-compliance.html).

## Worked example: a short brief

Illustrative example. "We are developing a wall-mounted charging dock for cordless garden tools, for homeowners who keep tools in sheds and garages.
Twenty [customer interviews](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/customer-discovery-for-hardware.html) and a pre-order page with 140 sign-ups suggest demand. It must hold two tools of different brands, survive an unheated shed (−10 to 35 °C),
mount with standard fixings and cost no more than £14 to make at 3,000 units a year, to sell at £49.99 online. We have foam mock-ups and a list of competitor products.
We need a tested concept and an engineering prototype by June, and have a budget range for this stage. Please propose how you would approach it, who would do the work,
and the decision points." The details are invented for illustration; the structure is the point.

## Working well together

- **Make decisions quickly.** Slow decisions often cost more time than the engineering.

- **Give real feedback early.** "Not sure" on a concept is more useful in week two than in month four.

- **Share what you learn** from customers and suppliers; it changes the design.

- **Keep the requirements list current** so changes in direction are visible and agreed.

## Common mistakes

**Briefing the solution, not the problem.**
You may get exactly what you asked for when a better answer existed.

**Comparing proposals on day rate alone.**
Scope, experience and approach decide the total cost and the outcome.

**Commissioning everything at once.**
Staged work lets you stop or change direction as you learn.

**No agreement on IP and files.**
Fix ownership and deliverables in the contract before work starts.

**Treating the consultancy as a supplier, not a partner.**
The best results come when they understand the business goals, not just the drawing.

- Prepare a confidentiality agreement with the [NDA Generator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/nda-generator.html).

- Shortlist two or three partners and compare their proposals on approach, team and terms.

## FAQ

### What does a product design consultancy do?

It helps turn an idea into a product that can be made: defining the brief, developing and comparing concepts, engineering and CAD, prototyping and testing, design for manufacture and support with suppliers and production. Many also offer shorter reviews and second opinions.

### How do I brief a product design consultancy?

Describe the user and the problem, the requirements (measurable where possible), the target price, unit cost and volume, the constraints, what already exists, the timeline and a budget range for the next stage, the deliverables you want and who makes decisions. You do not need drawings to start.

### Who owns the design when I use a consultancy?

It depends on the contract. Without an assignment, the designer may own copyright and design rights in the work. Make sure the agreement assigns the intellectual property to you, says when it transfers, and covers delivery of CAD files and documentation.

### Should I use a consultancy or a freelancer?

A consultancy brings several disciplines and wider experience, which suits multi-disciplinary or first products. A freelancer can be more flexible and lower cost for focused tasks. Many projects use both at different stages.

### How much does product design cost?

It varies enormously with the product's complexity and how far the work goes, from a short review to full development to production. Share a budget range in your brief and compare proposals on scope and approach as well as price.

Title: Engineering Estimation Formulas

# Engineering estimation formulas.

The formulas behind Orion's free tools and guides in one place, each with its terms, a short worked example, the usual mistake,
and the tool that calculates it for you.

Quick answer

## Use a formula to frame the decision, then check it against supplier quotes and real project figures.

These formulas are for early estimates: comparing options on the same assumptions and finding which input matters most. Each matches the calculation in the linked Orion tool,
so you can check a result by hand. Worked examples use illustrative figures from the guides and tool defaults, not quotes or benchmarks.

|

|

## Unit cost: COGS and the cost to the business

Direct cost = materials + process + bought-in parts + packaging + labour
Labour = build minutes ÷ 60 × hourly rate
Scrap allowance = direct cost × scrap rate
Overhead = (direct cost + scrap) × overhead rate
COGS = direct cost + scrap + overhead
Unit cost to the business = COGS + (tooling ÷ units the tooling will make) + landed-cost additions per unit

**Terms:** process is machine rate × cycle time ÷ parts per cycle, plus finishing; the labour rate is fully loaded; overhead is applied after scrap.
Tooling sits outside COGS so you can see how it changes with volume.

Illustrative figures from the [manufacturing cost guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-estimate-manufacturing-cost.html): £4.80 material, £2.40 process, £5.50 bought-in parts,
£4.80 labour (12 minutes at £24 an hour) and £1.20 packaging make £18.70 direct. A 6% scrap allowance (£1.12) gives £19.82 and a 14% overhead (£2.77) gives a COGS of £22.59
(the tool, which does not round between steps, shows £22.60). £12,000 of tooling over 10,000 units adds £1.20 and freight, insurance, clearance and duty add £1.60, so the unit cost is £25.39.
At 2,000 units the same tool adds £6.00 and the unit cost becomes £30.19.

**Common mistake:** pricing from material, process and bought-in parts alone (£12.70 here), which is about half the real figure.

## Landed cost

Customs value = goods + packaging + origin charges + freight + insurance
Duty = customs value × duty rate
Import VAT = (customs value + duty) × VAT rate
Landed cost = customs value + duty + clearance + delivery + other (+ import VAT if you cannot reclaim it)

**Terms:** the duty rate comes from the product's commodity code and country of origin on the UK Trade Tariff; the customs value usually includes transport and insurance to the UK border.
The import VAT line is simplified, as some costs after the border can also count towards it.

Illustrative figures from the [landed cost guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html): 1,000 units at £6.00 FOB is £6,000; freight and insurance of £760 make a customs value of £6,760;
duty at an assumed 4% is £270.40; clearance and delivery add £300. Landed cost is £7,330.40, about £7.33 a unit, 22% above the factory price. Import VAT of £1,406.08 is reclaimable by a VAT-registered business.

**Common mistake:** comparing suppliers on factory price when their quotes use different Incoterms. Calculate it with the [Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html).

## Crossover volume: when tooling pays back

Total cost of a route = setup or tooling cost + unit cost × quantity
Crossover volume between routes A and B = (setup B − setup A) ÷ (unit cost A − unit cost B)
With no setup cost for A: break-even volume = tooling cost ÷ (prototype unit cost − moulded unit cost)

**Terms:** route A is cheap to start but dear per part (3D printing, CNC, vacuum casting); route B, usually injection moulding, has the higher setup and lower unit cost
and is cheaper in total above the crossover. The third line is the form used in the [injection mould break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html).

Illustrative figures (the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) defaults): a £6,500 mould making parts at £0.70 against 3D printing at £18 with no setup
crosses over at £6,500 ÷ £17.30 ≈ 376 units. But vacuum casting at £950 setup and £4.20 a part only gives way to moulding at (£6,500 − £950) ÷ (£4.20 − £0.70) ≈ 1,586 units.

**Common mistake:** calculating break-even against the most expensive alternative only. The straight-line model is also a simplification: silicone moulds for vacuum casting
wear out after a limited number of parts, as the [processes comparison](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html) shows, and design changes can mean tool modifications.

## Assembly time and labour cost

Assembly time ≈ (parts × handling time) + (joins × fastening time) + (reorientations × turn time) + inspection time
Labour cost per unit = total seconds ÷ 3,600 × hourly labour rate

**Terms:** the [Assembly Time Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/assembly-time.html) assumes 7, 12 or 18 seconds to handle and insert each part (simple, moderate or complex)
and 6 seconds per reorientation; you set the time per fastener and the inspection time. These are planning assumptions, not measured times.

Illustrative figures (the tool's defaults): 12 moderate parts × 12 s = 144 s; 8 fasteners × 14 s = 112 s; 5 reorientations × 6 s = 30 s; plus 20 s of inspection gives 306 seconds, about 5.1 minutes.
At £28 an hour that is 306 ÷ 3,600 × £28 ≈ £2.38 of labour per unit. The [assembly time guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/assembly-time-estimate.html) compares two concepts using its own, lower step times.

**Common mistake:** comparing concepts with different time assumptions. The absolute figure is rough; the difference between concepts on the same assumptions is the useful part.

## Margin, markup and the price for a margin

Margin = (price − cost) ÷ price
Markup = (price − cost) ÷ cost
Markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin)
Price needed for a margin m = cost ÷ (1 − m)
Shelf price = each price in the chain ÷ (1 − that partner's margin), then × (1 + VAT rate)

**Terms:** margin is a share of the selling price; markup is a share of the cost. Retailers and distributors usually talk in margin.

Illustrative figures: a product costing £50 that sells for £100 has a 50% margin but a 100% markup, and a 50% markup is only a 33% margin.
With the [Pricing Ladder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pricing-ladder.html) defaults, an £8.00 landed cost at a 50% brand margin is £16.00 to the retailer; a 45% retailer margin makes £29.09 before VAT, and 20% VAT makes a shelf price of £34.91, about 4.4 times landed cost.

**Common mistake:** adding a percentage to cost when the buyer means margin. A "40% markup" leaves far less room than a 40% margin needs. See
[retail and distributor margins explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-and-distributor-margins-explained.html).

## Target COGS from retail price

Price before VAT = RRP ÷ (1 + VAT rate)
Retained price = price before VAT × (1 − channel's share)
Target COGS = retained price − hidden selling costs − (retained price × target margin)

**Terms:** the channel's share is the retailer's margin or the marketplace fee (zero when you sell direct); hidden selling costs are fulfilment, payment fees, returns, marketing and retail support;
the target margin is the share of the retained price the business needs to keep.

Illustrative figures from the [revenue and margin guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html): a £180 RRP is £150 before 20% VAT. Sold direct with £43 of selling costs and a 30% target margin (£45),
target COGS is £150 − £43 − £45 = £62. Through a retailer keeping 45%, the retained price is £82.50; less £8.13 of costs and £24.75 of margin, target COGS is £49.62.

**Common mistake:** working from the RRP without removing VAT and the channel's share first. Check, too, whether a marketplace charges its fee on the price including or excluding VAT:
the guide's example charges 15% on the VAT-inclusive £180, while the [Target COGS tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) applies the fee to the price before VAT,
which gives a slightly higher retained price (£127.50 rather than £123.00).

## Contribution, break-even and margin of safety

Contribution per unit = net selling price − variable cost per unit
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit (round up)
Contribution margin ratio = contribution per unit ÷ net selling price
Break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio
Margin of safety = (forecast units − break-even units) ÷ forecast units

**Terms:** the net selling price is what you receive after VAT and channel deductions; variable cost is everything that rises with each unit (landed COGS, fulfilment, payment fees);
fixed costs are what must be recovered regardless of volume, such as development, tooling and certification.

Illustrative figures from the [break-even guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html): £65,000 of fixed cost, a £49 net price and £22 of variable cost give £27 of contribution.
Break-even is 65,000 ÷ 27 = 2,407.4, so 2,408 units, or about £118,000 of revenue; the contribution margin ratio is about 55%. Against a forecast of 3,500 units the margin of safety is about 31%.

**Common mistake:** using the shelf price. Sold through a retailer keeping 40%, the same product nets £29.40, contribution falls to £7.40 and break-even rises to about 8,784 units.
Run your own figures in the [Break-even Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/break-even-calculator.html).

## Development budget and contingency

Subtotal = engineering + prototypes + tooling + compliance + first inventory + launch work
Contingency = subtotal × contingency rate
Pre-launch requirement = subtotal + contingency

**Terms:** a common working range for contingency is 15 to 25 per cent of the subtotal: more for new technology, regulated products or a first-time team, less for a simple product on a proven architecture.
The [Startup Cost Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/startup-cost-planner.html) also shows a suggested funding target 10% above the total, as a buffer for delays.

Illustrative figures from the [development cost guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/estimating-hardware-development-costs.html): a subtotal of £148,000 with 20% contingency (£29,600) needs £177,600 before launch.

**Common mistake:** trimming contingency to make the budget look affordable. It does not remove the risk; release it as risks close instead.

## Cash flow, runway and acquisition payback

Closing cash = opening cash + cash received − cash paid
Net burn = monthly operating spend − monthly gross profit
Runway (months) = cash in the bank ÷ net burn
CAC = sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers
CAC payback (orders) = CAC ÷ gross profit per order after fulfilment

**Terms:** cash is counted when it moves, not when a sale is booked, so payment delays and stock bought in advance both matter, and runway should include committed stock orders.

Illustrative figures from the [investor metrics guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-investor-metrics.html): £18,000 of marketing brings 600 customers, so CAC is £30; each order leaves £54 after landed COGS and fulfilment,
so CAC is recovered within the first order. Net burn of £30,600 against £420,000 in the bank gives about 13.7 months of runway.
In the [cash flow guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/calculating-hardware-startup-cash-flow.html), £27 of contribution a unit means about 352 units a month just to cover £9,500 of overhead.

**Common mistake:** reading profit as cash. The [Investor Metrics tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/investor-metrics-kpis.html) divides CAC by gross profit per unit,
so include fulfilment in unit COGS there to match the guide's stricter definition. Model the months in the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

## Tolerance stack-up: worst case and RSS

Nominal gap = Σ dimensions that open the gap − Σ dimensions that close it
Worst case = nominal ± Σ tolerances
RSS (statistical) = nominal ± √(Σ tolerance²)

**Terms:** each dimension in the chain has a nominal size and a symmetric ± tolerance (convert +0.2/−0 to the mid-point ± 0.1). Worst case assumes every part is at its limit at once;
RSS (root sum of squares) assumes independent, random, centred variation.

Illustrative figures (the [Tolerance Stack-up Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/tolerance-stack-up.html) default): a 60.00 ± 0.15 mm opening holds a 59.40 ± 0.15 mm lid, so the nominal gap is 0.60 mm.
Worst case is 0.60 ± 0.30, a 0.30 to 0.90 mm gap; RSS is 0.60 ± √(0.15² + 0.15²) ≈ ± 0.21, about 0.39 to 0.81 mm. With four parts at ± 0.10 each, worst case is ± 0.40 but RSS only ± 0.20.

**Common mistake:** relying on RSS for a short chain, a low volume or a safety-critical fit. Its "most assemblies" prediction holds only when processes are well centred, so many engineers check both.
See [CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html) for what tolerances cost.

**Practical rule:**
change one input at a time and watch which one moves the answer most. That input is where a supplier quote, a test or a customer conversation is worth the most.

## FAQ

### What is the formula for injection mould break-even volume?

Tooling cost ÷ (prototype unit cost − moulded unit cost), when the alternative has no setup cost; otherwise subtract its setup cost from the tooling cost first. A £6,500 tool making £0.70 parts against £18 printed parts breaks even at about 376 units.

### What is the difference between margin and markup?

Margin is profit as a share of the selling price; markup is profit as a share of the cost. £50 cost and a £100 price is a 50% margin but a 100% markup.

### How do I work out target COGS from a retail price?

Remove VAT and the channel's share to find the price you receive, then take away hidden selling costs and the margin the business needs. What is left is the most the product can cost to make and land.

### Should I use worst-case or RSS tolerance stack-up?

Worst case for safety-critical fits, short chains, low volumes or off-centre processes; RSS for longer chains from stable processes in reasonable volumes. Many engineers check both.

### How accurate are these estimating formulas?

Only as good as their inputs. Use them for early comparisons, then replace assumed figures with supplier quotes, test results and real sales data.

Author

## Andrew Hunter

Product design engineer working across manufacturability, sustainability, and hardware commercial decisions in Belfast, Northern Ireland.
