## FAQ

### How do you estimate assembly time during design?

Break the task into handling, joining, reorientation, and checking so design decisions can be compared before final process engineering.

### What increases manual assembly cost fastest?

Repeated joins, awkward part handling, and designs that force operators to keep turning the product all add recurring labour quickly.

### Can this replace a formal DFA study?

No. It is deliberately lightweight. Use it to narrow concepts, then follow with a detailed DFA review once geometry and process are more stable.

### How can I reduce assembly time in my design?

Reduce part count first, then make the remaining parts easy to handle and fit: self-locating features, a single assembly direction, fewer loose fasteners, and parts that cannot be fitted the wrong way round. Snap fits can save time but need careful design if the product must be serviced or repaired.

### Is fewer parts always better?

Usually for assembly time, but not always overall. Combining parts can make tooling more complex, make repair harder, or force a compromise in material choice. Weigh assembly savings against tooling cost, serviceability and sustainability before merging parts.

How this calculator works

## Early-stage estimate, not final quotation

This calculator turns the assumptions you enter into an early engineering or commercial estimate. It is most useful for comparing options, surfacing trade-offs, and deciding what needs deeper validation next.

Source and Attribution

This engineering calculator and supporting analysis were created by Orion Design. Use the result as an early decision aid, then confirm the numbers with suppliers, manufacturing partners, and project-specific data.

Title: Bill of Materials (BOM) Cost Builder

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Bill of Materials Cost Builder

List the parts in your product with their quantities and unit costs, see the cost per product by category, and send the totals straight into the
Product Cost Estimator to add assembly, scrap and overhead. Up to ten lines; group small items, such as fasteners, into one line.

Quick answer

## A bill of materials lists every part and quantity in a product; rolling up its costs gives the parts cost per unit.

Line cost = quantity per product × unit cost
BOM cost = Σ line costs (grouped as material, processing, bought-in and packaging)

The BOM cost is not the full unit cost: assembly labour, scrap, freight and overhead come on top. The link to the Product Cost Estimator carries the four category totals across so you can add those.

## Building a useful BOM

- **List every part,** including fasteners, labels, adhesives, cables and packaging.

- **Use costs for your real order quantity.** A quote for 100 parts and one for 10,000 can differ many times over.

- **Mark where each figure came from** (quote, estimate or guess) in your own records, and firm up the biggest lines first.

- **Separate made and bought parts.** Made parts have material and processing costs, and usually tooling; bought parts have a supplier price.

## How to read your result

Look first at the largest lines: a few parts often make up most of the cost, so that is where design changes, alternative suppliers or volume pricing make the biggest difference.
If bought-in components dominate, supplier choice and order quantity matter most; if made parts dominate, design for manufacture and the manufacturing route matter most
(see the [Manufacturing and cost hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html) and the [DFM checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html)).

Then open the totals in the [Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html) to complete the unit cost, and add freight and duty with the
[Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html) if parts are imported. Save your BOM to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

## FAQ

### What is a bill of materials?

A structured list of every part, material and quantity needed to make one product. It is used for costing, purchasing, stock control and assembly, and it is one of the first documents a manufacturer will ask for.

### Is the BOM cost the same as the product's unit cost?

No. The BOM cost covers parts and materials. The full unit cost adds assembly labour, scrap, testing, freight and duty, and a share of overhead and tooling. Use the Product Cost Estimator to add those.

### What goes in the processing category?

The cost of turning raw material into a made part, such as moulding, machining, cutting, bending or finishing, when you are quoted for it separately from the material. If a supplier quotes a made part as one price, enter it as bought-in.

### Why are only ten lines available?

The tool is for quick roll-ups. Group small items, such as all fasteners or all labels, into one line. For a full BOM with hundreds of lines, use a spreadsheet or product data system and bring the category totals here.

### Are part names saved in the share link?

Yes, if you use the Copy link to this result button: the link carries any part names, categories, quantities and costs you have changed from the example, so anyone you send it to will see them. The address in your browser bar carries only the numbers and categories. Part names are also included in the copied summary and in the result you save to your product plan.

Title: Bracket Deflection Calculator: Beam Bending and Stress

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Bracket Deflection Calculator

Get a first estimate of how far a simple bracket, arm or beam will bend under load, and how hard the material is working.
Choose how it is held and loaded, enter its section and your material's figures, and see the deflection against your limit,
the bending stress against your allowable stress, the safety factor and the thickness you would need.

Quick answer

## A bracket bends in proportion to the load and the cube of its length, and resists it with its stiffness, E × I.

The material sets E and the shape of the section sets I, the second moment of area. Doubling the thickness of a flat bracket makes it eight times stiffer, while doubling its length makes it bend eight times as far. The stress check then tells you whether the material will spring back or take a permanent bend.

Dashed: the bent shape, exaggerated. A cantilever bends 16 times as far as the same beam supported at both ends over the same length.

## How this works

The tool uses the standard Euler–Bernoulli beam formulas for a straight, elastic beam with the same section along its length.
Units are millimetres, newtons and megapascals (N/mm²), so deflections come out in millimetres and stresses in megapascals.
A mass is turned into a force with g = 9.81 m/s². For the spread load, F is the total load along the length, so w = F ÷ L.

Second moment of area, I, and distance to the outer fibre, c:
Solid rectangle: I = b × h³ ÷ 12 c = h ÷ 2
Rectangular tube: I = (B × H³ − b × h³) ÷ 12 c = H ÷ 2
inner sizes b = B − 2t, h = H − 2t
Round bar: I = π × d⁴ ÷ 64 c = d ÷ 2
Round tube: I = π × (D⁴ − d⁴) ÷ 64, d = D − 2t c = D ÷ 2

Cantilever, end load: δ = F × L³ ÷ (3 × E × I) M_max = F × L
Supported, centre load: δ = F × L³ ÷ (48 × E × I) M_max = F × L ÷ 4
Cantilever, evenly spread load: δ = w × L⁴ ÷ (8 × E × I) M_max = w × L² ÷ 2

Bending stress: σ = M_max × c ÷ I
Share of allowable: σ ÷ σ_allow Safety factor = σ_allow ÷ σ
Deflection limit: δ_limit = L ÷ n, or the distance you enter
Thickness needed (solid rectangle, width b held):
for deflection: h = ∛(12 × F × L³ ÷ (k × E × b × δ_limit)), k = 3, 48 or 8
for stress: h = √(6 × M_max ÷ (b × σ_allow))

**The default example.** An aluminium flat bar 30 mm wide and 5 mm thick, held as a cantilever 100 mm long with 20 N (about 2 kg) at the end.
I = 30 × 5³ ÷ 12 = 312.5 mm⁴. δ = 20 × 100³ ÷ (3 × 69,000 × 312.5) ≈ 0.31 mm, against an L ÷ 200 limit of 0.5 mm (62%).
M_max = 20 × 100 = 2,000 N·mm, so σ = 2,000 × 2.5 ÷ 312.5 = 16 MPa: 16% of the 100 MPa example allowable stress, a safety factor of 6.25.

The status takes the worse of the two checks, deflection against its limit and stress against the allowable stress: up to 80% passes,
80–100% is marginal, and above 100% is over. The safety factor is simply your allowable stress divided by the calculated stress,
so it is only as good as the allowable figure you enter.

## Assumptions and limits

- **Small deflections.** The formulas hold while the deflection is small compared with the length. If the result is more than about a tenth of the length, treat it as a sign the part is far too flexible rather than as an accurate figure.

- **Linear elastic behaviour.** The material is assumed to spring back fully. Above the yield stress, metals take a permanent bend and the formulas no longer apply.

- **A fully fixed root.** The cantilever cases assume the root cannot rotate at all. Real joints are less stiff: screws, rivets, welds, thin walls and plastic bosses all let the root turn a little, so a real bracket usually bends more than the estimate, sometimes much more.

- **Self-weight is ignored.** Only the load you enter is counted. For long or heavy beams, add the beam's own weight as a spread load.

- **No buckling, fatigue or stress concentrations.** The tool does not check thin walls or flanges buckling, cracks growing under repeated or vibrating loads, or the higher local stress at holes, slots, notches and tight bends. Keep holes away from the root, and use generous bend and fillet radii, as in [sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html).

- **Plastics creep.** A plastic part under a load that stays on keeps bending slowly over time, and faster when warm. The short-term modulus on a datasheet will underestimate the deflection, so use long-term (creep) modulus data for your load, time and temperature.

- **Confirm by test or FEA.** This is a first estimate. Check the real part by loading a prototype and measuring it, or with a finite element analysis that includes the real joint and any holes.

## How to read your result

- **Pass:** the deflection and the stress each use no more than 80% of your limits. Check the joint at the root, which is usually the weak point, and confirm by test.

- **Marginal:** within your limits, but small changes in thickness, material batch or a less rigid root could push it over. Thicken the section or shorten the length, then test.

- **Over:** the bracket is likely to bend too far or take a permanent set. The thickness needed shows how far a flat bracket is from working; for other sections, try a deeper section.

Depth in the direction of the load is the strongest lever: deflection falls with the cube of the thickness. Shortening the length helps almost as much.
A stiffer material helps only in proportion, which is why an aluminium part often needs thicker sections than a steel one, as
[choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html) explains. For a bent sheet part, a flange or return
along the edge adds depth cheaply. See [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) for plastic brackets,
[product testing and validation plans](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html) for where a load test fits, and the
[development and prototyping hub](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html) for the wider picture.
Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

Related reading

[Choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html)

[Sheet metal design basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html)

[CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html)

[Choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html)

[Designing a product to survive drops and impacts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-for-drops-and-impacts.html)

[Development and prototyping: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

## FAQ

### Which elastic modulus should I use?

Use the figure from the datasheet for your exact material. The buttons fill in typical textbook values only: about 69,000 MPa for aluminium alloys and about 200,000 MPa for steel. Plastics vary much more by grade, temperature and moisture, so the ABS figure is an example only, and a load that stays on needs the long-term (creep) modulus.

### What deflection limit should I use?

Set it from what the bracket must do: a gap that must not close, a display that must not visibly droop, or parts that must stay aligned. Expressing it as a fraction of the length, L ÷ n, scales it with the size of the part; the default of L ÷ 200 is an example, not a rule.

### Why does my real bracket bend more than the estimate?

Usually because the root is not fully fixed. Screws, thin mounting walls and plastic bosses let the root rotate, which adds to the deflection at the tip. Holes and slots near the root, a softer material than expected and, for plastics, creep all add more. Measure a prototype to find out how much.

### What safety factor should I aim for?

It depends on how well you know the loads and the material, and what happens if the part fails. The tool divides your allowable stress by the calculated stress; if you enter the yield strength, a factor of 1 means it is just starting to bend permanently. Shocks, drops and repeated loads need more margin, and fatigue needs its own check.

How this calculator works

## First estimate, confirmed by test

This calculator applies the standard Euler–Bernoulli beam formulas to the load, length, section and material figures you enter. Use it to size a bracket and compare options early, then confirm the design by loading a prototype or with FEA.

Title: Break-even Calculator for Hardware Products

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Break-even Calculator

Calculate how many units a hardware product needs to sell before fixed costs are repaid,
and see whether the current price and variable cost structure make that target realistic.

Quick answer

## Break-even units depend on contribution, not just revenue.

Break-even units = fixed costs / (selling price - variable cost)

If the contribution per unit is weak, the required sales volume rises quickly even when the top-line number looks attractive.

## Use this after product cost is credible

Break-even is useful when the variable cost per unit already reflects reality. If the COGS figure is still optimistic,
the break-even point will be optimistic as well.

## How to read your result

Start with the contribution per unit, then compare the break-even volume with the number of units you have real evidence you can sell.

- **Comfortable:** break-even sits well below the volume you expect to sell in the first year or two, and contribution is a healthy share of the price you receive. A drop in demand or a small cost increase would delay payback rather than threaten it.

- **Borderline:** break-even is close to your realistic sales forecast, or contribution is a thin slice of the price. Small changes in unit cost, discounting or channel terms will move the break-even point a long way, so test a few pessimistic cases.

- **Worrying:** break-even is higher than any volume you can credibly reach, or contribution is near zero or negative. Selling more will not fix this; the price, the unit cost or the fixed cost base needs to change first.

In the first two cases, check that the variable cost includes everything that scales with each sale, such as packaging, fulfilment, payment fees and returns, not just the factory price. In the last case, look at design for manufacture, a different route to market, or a smaller first tooling commitment before adding volume. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the break-even volume sits alongside your cost and cashflow assumptions.

If the result depends heavily on a unit cost that has not yet been quoted by a supplier, it is worth a second opinion before you commit to tooling. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) if you would like to talk it through.

Related reading

[Financial break-even for hardware products](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/financial-break-even-for-hardware-products.html)

[Product Cost Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-cost-estimator.html)

[Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html)

[Route to market and margins: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html)

[How to turn RRP into target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html)

Use it for

Contribution margin
Volume target
Fixed-cost recovery

## FAQ

### What counts as a fixed cost for a hardware product?

Costs you pay regardless of how many units you sell: design and engineering, tooling, certification, and ongoing overheads such as salaries, rent and software. Decide whether you are testing recovery of one-off launch costs or a year of running costs, and keep that consistent when you compare scenarios.

### Should the selling price include VAT or retailer margin?

No. Use the price you actually receive per unit, excluding VAT and after any retailer, distributor or marketplace share. For a product sold through retail, that is usually the wholesale price, which can be roughly half of the shelf price or less.

### What should go into the variable cost per unit?

Everything that is spent each time a unit is made and sold: the bill of materials, assembly, packaging, freight and duty, fulfilment, payment fees and an allowance for returns or warranty. Leaving these out is the most common reason a break-even point looks better than it really is.

### Why does my break-even jump when I change the price slightly?

Break-even divides fixed costs by contribution per unit, so when contribution is small, a modest change in price or cost changes it by a large percentage. That sensitivity is itself useful information: it shows how much margin of safety the plan really has.

Title: Carbon Footprint Estimator

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Carbon Footprint Estimator

Estimate a product's concept-stage carbon footprint using material, process, transport, and use-phase assumptions.
The goal is not perfect certainty. It is to reveal where the biggest carbon drivers are likely to sit.

## What this estimate is useful for

Early carbon decisions are usually directional rather than exact. If a concept carries heavy material burden, energy-intensive use,
or unnecessarily long transport routes, that is enough to justify design changes before detailed LCA work begins.

A relatively small product can still become carbon-heavy if its use phase dominates. Equally, a passive product may be driven mostly by
material selection and transport assumptions.

## Use the estimate to compare

- material substitutions

- manufacturing route changes

- transport assumptions

- durability and energy-consumption trade-offs

## Method and assumptions

Material = mass × material factor × (1 − recycled share × 0.35)
Process = mass × process factor
Transport = mass × distance × transport factor
Use = annual energy (kWh) × lifetime (years) × 0.193
Total = material + process + transport + use (kg CO₂e)

**Assumptions**

- Material factors are typical cradle-to-gate values per kilogram, and process factors are typical allowances per kilogram processed; both are built into the tool for comparison rather than certification.

- Recycled content lowers the material factor by up to 35% at 100% recycled.

- Use-phase electricity uses a fixed grid factor of 0.193 kg CO₂e per kWh, close to a recent UK grid average; official factors are updated each year.

**Limits**

- It is a design-stage estimate, not a footprint to ISO 14067 or an LCA; see [product carbon footprint vs LCA](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-carbon-footprint-vs-lca.html).

- Packaging, consumables, end of life and real supplier data are not included; factors vary by source and region.

- Do not use the result for public environmental claims.

## How to read your result

The total is an estimate of the greenhouse gas emissions linked to one product over its life, in kilograms of CO2 equivalent.
The embodied figure covers material, manufacturing and transport before the product is switched on. The use-phase share tells
you how much of the total comes from the energy the product draws while in service.

- **Use phase above roughly half:** typical of products that plug in or run on batteries every day. Energy efficiency, standby power and lifetime are where design effort pays back most.

- **Material dominates:** common for passive products such as housewares and enclosures. Reducing mass, choosing a lower-impact material or raising recycled content will move the number more than anything else.

- **Transport looks large:** this usually points to air freight. Sea freight is far lower per kilogram, so check whether air is genuinely needed beyond urgent first shipments.

- **Manufacturing stands out:** often a sign of machining or printing parts that could be moulded or formed at volume.

Treat the result as a way to rank options rather than a figure to publish. If you need a number for customers, retailers or
regulators, a formal lifecycle assessment with supplier data is the right next step. Save your result to your
[product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so sustainability choices sit beside cost and production decisions.
If you are unsure which lever to pull first, a [short conversation with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) can help.

Related reading

[Packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html)

## FAQ

### How can you estimate product carbon footprint during design?

Use early assumptions for material mass, manufacturing process, transport, energy use, and recycled content to compare concepts before detailed LCA work.

### Is this a full lifecycle assessment?

No. This is a concept-stage estimator intended to compare options and expose major drivers, not replace a formal LCA.

### Which part of a product's footprint usually matters most?

It depends on the product. For products that use energy, such as heaters, kettles or chargers, the use phase often dominates the total. For passive products such as housewares, furniture or enclosures, materials and manufacturing usually account for most of it. Running both scenarios in the estimator shows which side your product sits on, and therefore where design effort pays off.

### How accurate are the carbon factors for materials and processes?

Published factors vary with the data source, region, recycled content and the boundaries used, so treat the result as a comparison between design options rather than a declared figure. For a formal footprint, use a recognised lifecycle database and method, such as ISO 14040/14044 for lifecycle assessment or ISO 14067 for product carbon footprints.

### Can I use this result in marketing or on packaging?

Not on its own. It is an early design estimate. Public environmental claims in the UK need to be accurate and backed by evidence, and the Competition and Markets Authority's Green Claims Code sets out what that means. Use this tool to make better design decisions, then commission or carry out a proper assessment before making claims.

How this calculator works

## Early-stage estimate, not final quotation

This calculator turns the assumptions you enter into an early engineering or commercial estimate. It is most useful for comparing options, surfacing trade-offs, and deciding what needs deeper validation next.

Title: Cashflow Projection Tool for Hardware Startups

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Cashflow Projection Tool

Project twelve months of startup cashflow so you can see whether growth, payment timing, and upfront spend
are creating a runway problem long before the P&L says the business is profitable.

Quick answer

## Profitable growth can still kill cash.

Closing cash = opening cash + cash in - cash out

For hardware teams, the dangerous gap is often the time between paying for stock and being paid by customers, distributors, or retailers.

## What this tool is showing

The model tracks monthly units, revenue timing, stock cost, fixed overhead, and one-off month 1 spend.
That is enough to show whether the business is on course to dip below zero even if demand looks encouraging.

## Use it for

- estimating runway pressure before launch

- testing the effect of payment delay from channels or customers

- seeing whether higher sales volumes actually increase short-term cash strain

## How to read your result

The most important figure is the lowest cash point across the twelve months, and when it happens, rather than the closing balance.

- **Comfortable:** cash never falls below a buffer of roughly three to six months of fixed overhead, and the curve flattens or turns upwards within the year. The plan can absorb a late payment or a slower sales month.

- **Borderline:** the lowest point comes close to zero, or the buffer drops below about three months of overhead. One delayed customer payment, a larger stock order or a slip in launch timing could tip the business into a shortfall.

- **Worrying:** cash goes negative at some point in the year. Note the month: that is the date by which you need more funding, better payment terms, or a smaller commitment to stock and overhead.

If the result is borderline or worrying, try the payment delay and growth inputs first, because faster growth often deepens the dip when stock is paid for before customers pay you. Then look at staging stock purchases, negotiating deposits or shorter terms, and timing the fundraise so it lands well before the lowest point. Many founders aim to raise with twelve to eighteen months of runway, as fundraising itself usually takes several months. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) to keep the cash picture next to your startup costs and margin assumptions.

If the projection only works with growth or payment terms you have not yet tested with real customers, a second opinion can help. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) to talk through the assumptions.

## FAQ

### Why does faster growth make my cash position worse?

Each extra unit needs stock paid for before the customer pays you, so rapid growth pulls more cash out of the business in the short term. This is normal for hardware and is why profitable products can still run out of cash while scaling.

### What payment delay should I use for retail or distributor sales?

Direct online sales are usually paid in the same month. Retailers and distributors commonly pay 30 to 90 days after invoice. One or two months is a sensible starting point until you have agreed terms in writing; the tool models up to three months, so you can test the longest common terms.

### Does this include VAT, deposits or tooling instalments?

No. The model keeps things simple: month 1 spend is a single lump, and stock and overhead are paid in the month they occur. If your supplier asks for deposits or you pay tooling in stages, adjust the opening cash and month 1 spend to reflect what actually leaves the bank and when.

### How much cash buffer should a hardware startup keep?

There is no single right number, but keeping several months of fixed overhead in reserve is a common rule of thumb, and more if you depend on large stock orders or slow-paying customers. Hardware lead times mean problems take time to fix, so a thin buffer leaves little room to react.

Title: Certification Readiness Checklist (UKCA and CE)

Self-check

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Takes about two minutes · Method and assumptions

# Certification Readiness Checklist

Answer ten questions about regulations, standards, testing, documentation and labelling to see how well certification is planned, and which gaps to close first. It is a planning aid, not legal advice; take specialist advice for regulated categories.

Quick answer

## You are ready for certification when you know the rules and standards, have tested early, and are documenting as you go.

Readiness = Σ (importance × answer) ÷ Σ (importance × 2), where Yes = 2, Partly = 1, No = 0
Critical gap = a most-important question answered No

Knowing which regulations and standards apply carries the most weight, because everything else depends on them.

## Method and assumptions

Each answer scores Yes 2, Partly 1, No 0, multiplied by the question's importance weight
Readiness % = total score ÷ maximum possible score × 100
Gaps are ranked by weight × points missing

**Assumptions**

- Importance weights reflect how much each step usually affects time and cost to compliance.

- A critical gap is a top-weighted question answered No.

**Limits**

- It is a self-check, not a compliance assessment or legal advice, and does not tell you which regulations apply.

- Confirm requirements with official guidance and, where needed, a test house or notified body; see [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html).

## How to read your result

- **About 80% or more with no critical gaps:** ready to go ahead, with the remaining gaps closed in parallel.

- **About 55 to 80%, or one critical gap:** possible, but with avoidable risk. Close the top gaps first if you can.

- **Below about 55%, or several critical gaps:** too early. Work through the gaps in the order listed.

The weights and thresholds are Orion Design's rules of thumb for planning, not a formal standard. Each gap links to the guide or tool that helps close it. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) and repeat the check as you progress.

## FAQ

### When should I start planning product certification?

At the requirements stage. The rules and standards can affect materials, enclosures, circuit design, labels and instructions, and pre-compliance testing on prototypes is far cheaper than redesign after a failed formal test.

### Does this checklist tell me which regulations apply?

No. It checks whether you have worked that out and planned the steps. Product certification basics explains common UK regulations, and GOV.UK guidance covers each category.

### What is a technical file?

The documentation that supports a product's conformity: a description, drawings and circuit diagrams, the risk assessment, the standards applied, test reports and the production controls that keep products consistent with what was tested.

### Do I need a test laboratory?

For most electrical and radio products, formal testing is normally done at a laboratory, ideally one accredited for the relevant standards. Some products also need an independent conformity assessment body.

### Is anything I answer stored?

No. The check runs in your browser and is only saved if you choose to save it to your product plan, which also stays in your browser.

# Change Request Builder

Fill in a short form and get a clear engineering change request (ECR) that follows the five steps in the

## Want a second pair of eyes on the change?

Send the current result context to the contact page, review the generated note, and email Andrew when you are ready.

Quick answer

## An engineering change request records what should change, why, which parts it affects, what it touches, who approved it and from when it applies.

Request → impact check → approval → release → effectivity

A small team needs the same steps as a large company, not the overhead: a numbered request like this one, a change log and a folder per change is enough. The form, fit and function answer decides whether the changed part gets a new revision or a new part number.

## How to use the change request

- Raise the request as soon as a change is proposed. Give it a number and list every affected part number with its current revision.

- Answer the form, fit and function question, then work through the impact check. Use your indented BOM to find every assembly that contains the part.

- Ask the named approver to decide, and record the decision and the date.

- Once approved, update the CAD, drawing and BOM together, release the new revision or new part number, and mark the old revision obsolete or "use up existing stock".

- Set the effectivity, tell suppliers in writing and ask them to confirm. Print the request or save it to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) and keep it with the change log.

## How to read your result

- **Change type** follows your form, fit and function answer: interchangeable parts get a new revision, parts that are not interchangeable get a new part number.

- **Impact areas checked** counts stock, tooling, certification and testing, cost, suppliers and documents. "Not checked yet" is honest; it just means the request is not ready for a decision.

- **Still to complete** lists gaps and contradictions, such as an interchangeable change with a new part number, or an approval with no effectivity.

## Assumptions and notes

- The steps and terms follow the [bills of materials and revision control guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/bills-of-materials-and-revision-control.html): revisions as letters (A, B, C), three release states (draft, released, obsolete) and the form, fit and function test.

- The tool does not decide whether a change is interchangeable, what it will cost or whether test results still hold. It records your answers and points out gaps; the judgement stays with your team.

- If a customer, certification body or contract asks for its own change notification, follow that as well. This tool does not check those requirements.

- The worked examples use the illustrative bike light from the guide. The part numbers, revisions and serial numbers are invented to show the layout.

- Your inputs are kept in your own browser so they are still there when you come back; nothing is sent to a server.

Faults found after launch follow the same steps, with root cause and re-testing added; [after launch: returns, feedback and design changes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/after-launch-returns-feedback-and-design-changes.html) covers that side.

## FAQ

### What is an engineering change request?

A short, numbered record of a proposed change to a released part: what should change, why, and which part numbers are affected. It then carries the impact check, the approval decision and the point from which the change applies, so the whole history of the change is in one place.

### When does a change need a new part number instead of a new revision?

When the old and new parts are no longer interchangeable in form, fit or function. If the new part can replace the old one everywhere without any other change, raise the revision; if mixing them could cause a problem, give the new part its own number, and raise the revision of the parent BOM too.

### What does effectivity mean?

It is the point from which a change applies, given as a date, a production batch or a serial number. Recording it means you can always tell which units contain the old part and which contain the new one.

# Crowdfunding Planner

A crowdfunding target is not the same as the money you need. Work out what each backer actually leaves you after platform and payment fees, VAT,
making the reward and shipping it, and how many backers it takes to cover tooling and campaign costs.

Quick answer

## Only what is left after fees, VAT, making and shipping each reward goes towards tooling and launch costs.

Collected per backer = pledge (+ shipping if charged separately)
Left per backer = collected − fees − VAT in the pledge − reward cost − shipping
Backers needed = (fixed costs + campaign costs) ÷ left per backer

A campaign can hit its headline target and still leave too little to pay for tooling, especially when shipping is under-estimated or the reward is priced like a retail discount.

## How to read your result

- **Comfortable surplus:** the campaign covers fixed and campaign costs with room for surprises. Keep a reserve for manufacturing delays and support.

- **Small surplus or shortfall:** revisit the pledge price, the reward cost, shipping or the fixed costs you expect the campaign to fund.

- **Negative per backer:** each reward loses money. Raise the pledge, charge shipping, or reduce the reward cost before launching; more backers would make it worse.

Fees, VAT treatment and shipping vary by platform, country and product, so the defaults are examples: check your platform's current fees and take accounting advice on VAT.

## FAQ

### How much should a crowdfunding reward cost?

Enough that, after platform and payment fees, VAT, making the reward and shipping it, each backer still contributes towards tooling and launch costs. Many campaigns underprice rewards as a retail-style discount and then find the money runs out before delivery.

### Do I pay VAT on crowdfunding pledges?

Pledges made in return for a reward are usually treated as sales, so VAT can be due if you are VAT-registered. The rules depend on the details, so take advice from an accountant before setting reward prices.

### Should I charge shipping separately?

Often, yes, especially for international backers, because shipping costs vary widely by destination. Either way, get real carrier quotes for your parcel size and weight before launch.

### What fixed costs should the campaign fund?

Typically tooling, certification, the set-up costs of the first production batch and the campaign itself. Include contingency: delays and tool modifications are common in hardware.

### Are the platform fee defaults accurate?

They are example values only. Platforms change their fees and payment providers charge differently by country and card type, so check the current terms of the platform you plan to use.

Title: Injection Moulding DFM Checker for Plastic Parts

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Injection Moulding DFM Checker

Enter the key dimensions of a plastic part and get instant feedback on wall thickness, draft, ribs, bosses, corner radii and undercuts,
based on common design-for-manufacture guidance. Use it on the CAD model before asking for [tooling quotes](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/comparing-manufacturing-quotes.html). Leave rib or boss fields at 0 if the part has none.

Quick answer

## Most moulding problems come from a few features: uneven walls, missing draft, thick ribs and bosses, sharp corners and undercuts.

This checker compares your values with common rules of thumb and explains each result. It is a first pass, not a substitute for the moulder's DFM review or a mould-flow analysis.

## The rules it uses

- **Wall thickness:** compared with an indicative range for the chosen material, for unfilled grades.

- **Uniformity:** thickest section up to about 1.25 times the nominal wall is treated as uniform; beyond about 1.75 times, sink and voids become likely.

- **Draft:** at least about 1 degree for smooth faces and about 3 degrees for textured faces as a starting point; 0.5 to 1 degree on a smooth face is flagged to check, as it can suit shallow features.

- **Ribs:** about 40 to 60 per cent of the wall thick, and up to about three times the wall tall.

- **Bosses:** outside diameter around twice the hole, with a boss wall no more than about 60 per cent of the main wall.

- **Inside corners:** radius at least about half the wall.

- **Undercuts:** each one usually needs a moving part in the tool.

## How to read your result

- **OK:** the feature follows common guidance. It may still need adjusting for your material grade, flow length or cosmetic requirements.

- **Check:** not necessarily wrong, but worth discussing with the moulder before the tool is designed.

- **Fix:** likely to cause sink marks, warping, sticking, cracking or extra tool cost. Change it on the CAD model now, while it is cheap.

The thresholds are rules of thumb collected from common practice, not limits from a standard. Different materials, grades and part sizes justify different values,
so always confirm with the material datasheet and your moulder. The [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html)
explains each rule with diagrams, and [choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html) helps with the material.
Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) to bring it to the supplier conversation.

Related reading

[CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html)

[Injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html)

[Injection moulding explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-explained.html)

[Choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html)

[Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html)

[Development and prototyping: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

[Sheet metal design basics: bends, holes, reliefs, materials and tolerances](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sheet-metal-design-basics.html)

Use it for

DFM
Injection moulding
Design review

## FAQ

### Can this checker replace a moulder's DFM review?

No. It catches common problems early, but a moulder's review considers the specific tool, gate positions, material grade, flow length and cosmetic requirements, and may include a mould-flow simulation. Use the checker to arrive with a better design.

### Where do the material wall thickness ranges come from?

They are indicative ranges of the kind commonly quoted for unfilled grades. The right wall for your part depends on its size, flow length and grade, so check the material supplier's datasheet and ask your moulder.

### What counts as an undercut?

Any feature that stops the part being pulled straight out of the tool in the opening direction: side holes, clips and hooks facing sideways, internal grooves and threads, for example. Each usually needs a side action, lifter or other moving part.

### Why does the checker treat textured surfaces differently?

Texture creates tiny undercuts in the surface, so textured faces need more draft to release without scuffing. Texture suppliers usually specify a minimum draft for each texture depth.

### What should I measure as the thickest section?

The thickest solid area of plastic, such as the base of a solid boss, a junction where several walls meet, or a thickened edge. Measuring the diameter of the largest circle that fits inside the section is a practical way to find it.

Title: Hardware Business Case Builder

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Hardware Business Case Builder

Build a fast commercial view of a hardware concept by linking market size, reachable share,
conversion, price, unit cost, development spend, and annual operating cost.

## What a fast business case should answer

A concept does not need a full spreadsheet model before it deserves scrutiny. It does need a clear answer to whether
the reachable volume and unit economics can support the planned spend.

- How much of the market can the team realistically reach?

- What share of that reachable audience converts into sales?

- How long would it take gross contribution to recover development spend?

## Method and assumptions

Units sold = market units × reachable share × conversion rate
Revenue = units sold × price
Gross profit = units sold × (price − COGS)
Annual contribution = gross profit − annual operating costs
Year-one result = annual contribution − development spend
Break-even units = (development spend + annual operating costs) ÷ (price − COGS)
Payback (months) = development spend ÷ annual contribution × 12

**Assumptions**

- Sales happen at one price and COGS in a steady first year.

- Development spend is a one-off cost recovered from annual contribution.

**Limits**

- Market size, reach and conversion are your assumptions; small changes move the result a lot, so test ranges.

- Timing, cash flow, financing, tax and price erosion are not included; see the [Cash Flow Projection](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html).

## How to read your result

Read the recommendation card first, then look at how much the result depends on the two percentages: reachable share and conversion.

- **Promising:** the case shows positive contribution and development spend is repaid within roughly one to two years, using share and conversion figures you can point to evidence for, such as pre-orders, pilot customers or comparable products.

- **Borderline:** payback stretches beyond two years, or the case only turns positive when reachable share or conversion is nudged upwards. The opportunity may still be worth pursuing, but it needs stronger evidence or a leaner cost base.

- **Weak:** the tool shows a contribution gap, so gross profit does not cover annual operating cost. Revisit price, unit cost, the size of the team behind the product, or whether a narrower first market would be easier to win.

Whatever the outcome, run a cautious version with half the share and conversion you first entered. If the case still holds, it is far easier to defend to investors or a board. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the business case sits alongside your cost, margin and cashflow work.

If the decision depends on a large development or tooling spend, it can help to have someone challenge the assumptions before you commit. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) if that would be useful.

Related reading

[Building a Hardware Business Case](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-business-case.html)

[Hardware Investor Metrics That Actually Matter](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-investor-metrics.html)

[Opportunity and concept: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/opportunity-and-concept.html)

Use it for

Opportunity screening
Internal buy-in
Investor preparation

## FAQ

### How do I estimate addressable market units?

Start from the number of people or organisations who have the problem and could buy the product in a year, not the total population or the whole category. Count bottom-up where you can, for example households with a specific appliance or labs running a specific test, rather than relying on broad market-size headlines.

### What is a realistic reachable share for a new product?

For a new brand, the share of a market you can actually reach through your chosen channels and budget is usually small, often in the low single figures. If the case only works at a high share, treat that as a warning sign rather than a target.

### Should development spend include tooling?

Yes. Include design and engineering, prototypes, injection mould tooling, certification and other one-off costs needed before you can sell. The payback figure then shows how long gross contribution takes to recover that investment once overheads are covered.

### Is this enough for an investor pitch?

It is a screening model, not a financial forecast. It is useful for deciding whether an idea deserves deeper work and for framing the conversation, but investors will expect a monthly model with cash, ramp-up and evidence behind each assumption.

Title: Investor Metrics and KPIs

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Investor Metrics and KPIs

Turn monthly sales, cost, lead, and cash assumptions into the core metrics investors and boards usually ask for first.

## Which signals matter most

Investors do not just look for revenue growth. They look for whether growth is buying time, strengthening margin,
and creating a repeatable acquisition engine.

- Runway shows how much time remains to prove the model.

- CAC and payback show how efficiently demand becomes revenue.

- Gross margin determines whether scale improves the business or just amplifies weakness.

## Method and assumptions

Monthly revenue = units × average selling price
Gross margin = (price − unit COGS) ÷ price
Customers acquired = qualified leads × conversion rate
CAC = marketing spend ÷ customers acquired
CAC payback (orders) = CAC ÷ gross profit per unit
Net burn = monthly burn − monthly gross profit
Runway (months) = cash balance ÷ net burn

**Assumptions**

- One unit per order and one average price and COGS.

- Monthly burn is the total operating spend you enter; gross profit from sales offsets it.

**Limits**

- It is a snapshot of one month, not a forecast; growth, seasonality and repeat purchases are not modelled.

- Investors may define these metrics differently; state your definitions when you share them.

## How to read your result

Look at the three signals together: gross margin, runway and how many orders it takes to recover the cost of acquiring a customer.

- **Healthy:** gross margin is around 45% or more, runway is twelve months or longer, and acquisition cost is recovered within the first order. That combination suggests growth is buying time rather than burning it.

- **Borderline:** margin sits somewhere in the 30% to 45% range, runway is between roughly six and twelve months, or it takes more than one order to recover acquisition cost. The business may work, but you need a clear plan for which number improves next and how.

- **Concerning:** margin is below about 30%, runway is under six months, or acquisition cost is never recovered because gross profit per unit is too small. Prioritise [cost reduction](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html), pricing or a fundraise before spending more on growth.

Most hardware products are bought once, so recovering acquisition cost on the first order matters more than it does for subscription businesses. If you sell consumables or services alongside the device, note that separately, as this tool does not include repeat revenue. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) to track how these metrics change as your costs and channels firm up.

If you are preparing for a fundraise and the margin story depends on cost reductions not yet designed in, a second opinion on the product cost can help. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) to discuss it.

Related reading

[Hardware Investor Metrics That Actually Matter](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-investor-metrics.html)

[Building a Hardware Business Case](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/building-a-hardware-business-case.html)

[Funding and cash: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/funding-and-cash.html)

Use it for

Board updates
Fundraising prep
Commercial discipline

## FAQ

### What gross margin do investors expect from a hardware product?

There is no fixed rule, but many hardware investors look for gross margins of roughly 40% or more at scale, particularly for direct sales; this tool treats about 45% or more as healthy. Lower margins can work with very high volumes or strong recurring revenue, but they leave less room for mistakes.

### What is the difference between operating burn and net burn?

Operating burn is what the business spends each month on salaries, rent, development and marketing. Net burn subtracts the gross profit from sales, so it shows how quickly cash is actually falling. Runway in this tool is based on net burn.

### How is CAC calculated here?

Customer acquisition cost is your monthly acquisition spend divided by the customers it produces, which the tool estimates from qualified leads multiplied by the conversion rate. If some sales come through retail without direct marketing spend, the figure will overstate or understate CAC, so treat it as a guide.

### How often should I update these figures?

Monthly is a sensible rhythm once you are selling, and at least before every board meeting or investor conversation. The trend over several months usually tells a stronger story than any single snapshot.

Title: Landed Cost Calculator: Freight, Duty and VAT

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Landed Cost Calculator

Work out what an imported product really costs by the time it reaches your warehouse: the supplier price plus freight, insurance,
UK import duty, clearance and delivery, with import VAT shown separately. Enter the costs you pay; put 0 for anything the supplier's price already includes.
It is a planning estimate, not tax or customs advice.

Quick answer

## Landed cost is the supplier price plus everything it costs to get the goods into your warehouse.

Customs value = goods + packaging + origin charges + freight + insurance
Duty = customs value × duty rate
Landed cost = customs value + duty + clearance + delivery + other (+ import VAT if not reclaimable)

Use the landed cost per unit, not the factory price, in margins, pricing and break-even. Import VAT is normally reclaimable for VAT-registered businesses, so it affects cash rather than cost.

## How the calculation works

In the UK, duty is normally charged on the customs value, which is the price paid plus the cost of transport and insurance to the UK border.
The calculator adds goods, packaging, origin charges, freight and insurance to get that value, applies your duty rate, then adds the costs after the border:
customs clearance and port charges, delivery to your warehouse and anything else per shipment. Import VAT is calculated on the customs value plus duty.
This is a simplified planning model: some costs after the border can also count towards the VAT value, and special procedures can change the figures, so confirm with a customs broker for real shipments.

## How to read your result

- **Modest uplift (up to about 15 per cent):** the import costs are a small part of the unit cost. Still use the landed figure in your margins.

- **Noticeable uplift (about 15 to 35 per cent):** import costs matter. Check whether a different shipment size, delivery terms or freight mode would help, and confirm the duty rate.

- **Large uplift (above about 35 per cent):** getting the goods here is a big part of the cost. Common causes are small shipments carrying fixed charges, air freight for heavy or bulky goods, or high duty. Compare with a nearer supplier on a landed basis.

These bands are a rule of thumb for interpreting the result, not industry benchmarks. Find your commodity code and duty rate on the
[UK Trade Tariff](https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff), and read
[landed cost explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html) for the method in full.
Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the landed cost sits alongside your margins and cash flow.

[Packaging design for shipping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/packaging-design-for-shipping.html)

[UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html)

[Minimum order quantities and cash](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/minimum-order-quantities-and-cash.html)

[Landed cost explained: freight, duty and VAT](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/landed-cost-freight-duty-vat.html)

[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html)

[Manufacturing and cost: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html)

Use it for

Landed cost
Import duty
Supplier comparison

## FAQ

### What should I enter if my supplier quotes a delivered price?

Enter the delivered price as the supplier price and put 0 for freight, insurance and any other costs the quote already covers. If the quote is DDP (delivered duty paid), set the duty rate and the import VAT rate to 0 as well, because under DDP the supplier normally pays the import duty and taxes.

### Where do I find the duty rate for my product?

Find the commodity code for the product and look up its rate for the country of origin on the UK Trade Tariff on GOV.UK. Rates vary widely between codes, and a trade agreement can reduce the rate if the goods meet the rules of origin.

### Why is import VAT shown separately?

VAT-registered businesses can normally reclaim import VAT, often by accounting for it on their VAT return, so it is not a cost to them, though it can affect cash. If you are not VAT-registered, choose that option and the VAT is included in the landed cost.

### How can I reduce landed cost?

Larger or less frequent shipments spread fixed charges, sea freight is usually cheaper than air for non-urgent goods, smaller and lighter packaging reduces freight, and checking for trade-agreement preferences can reduce duty. Each option has trade-offs in cash tied up and lead time.

### Is this calculator suitable for customs declarations?

No. It is a planning tool for estimating unit cost. Customs declarations must follow HMRC rules on classification and valuation; use a customs broker or the official guidance for real shipments.

Title: Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser

Compare total cost curves across common prototyping and production methods. Adjust setup and unit assumptions,
then inspect which route wins at your target volume and where crossover points occur.

Quick answer

## Injection moulding becomes cheaper when the tooling cost is repaid by the lower unit cost.

Break-even volume = tooling cost ÷ (prototype unit cost − moulded unit cost)

Using the default assumptions against 3D printing: £6,500 ÷ (£18 − £0.70) = roughly 376 units.

## Worked example

If a part costs £18 to 3D print and £0.70 to mould, but the tool costs £6,500, the cheapest route depends entirely on realistic
demand and how confident you are that the geometry is stable enough to tool.

At 200 units: 3D printing costs £3,600, injection moulding costs £6,640 (tooling makes it more expensive).

At 500 units: 3D printing costs £9,000, injection moulding costs £7,350 (tooling is now justified).

At 1000 units: 3D printing costs £18,000, injection moulding costs £8,200 (tooling saves £9,800).

## How this calculator works

The lines show total cost, not unit cost. That matters because early manufacturing decisions are usually distorted by low setup options looking cheaper
at the start, while tooled routes only win once volume justifies the upfront commitment.

- **Use low setup routes for learning and early uncertainty:** 3D printing and CNC let you iterate without tooling risk.

- **Use bridge routes when demand is growing but tooling still feels risky:** Vacuum casting offers lower setup than injection moulding.

- **Use injection moulding when volume and design stability support the investment:** Only commit to tooling when the numbers make sense.

## How to read your result

The top result names the route with the lowest total cost at your target quantity, what that route costs in total, and how far
ahead it is of the next-best option. Below that, the ranking lists every route, followed by the crossover points where one
route overtakes another.

- **A clear winner:** if the gap to the next route is large and your target sits well past the relevant crossover, the decision is fairly robust to small changes in quotes or demand.

- **A narrow gap:** if two routes are close, or your target quantity sits near a crossover, the answer can flip with a modest change in volume or price. Choose on lead time, design stability and cash flow rather than cost alone.

- **Tooling only just wins:** this is the most common trap. If the mould pays back only at your most optimistic forecast, a bridge route such as vacuum casting usually keeps you safer while demand is proven.

Before committing, replace the defaults with real quotes for your part and test a lower volume to see how sensitive the answer is.
Remember that most products have several parts, so run the comparison for the expensive ones individually. Save your result to
your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the chosen route feeds into your cost and launch planning. If a tooling
decision is close, a [second opinion from Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) before you place the order can be worthwhile.

## Key definitions

**Bridge production**

An intermediate manufacturing route (vacuum casting, bridge tooling) used to validate design and market fit before committing to full injection moulding tooling.

**Breakeven volume**

The quantity at which the lower unit cost of tooling offsets the upfront tooling investment.

**Setup cost (fixed cost)**

The one-time investment in tooling, programming, or mould creation that doesn't change with quantity.

**Unit cost (variable cost)**

The per-part cost in material and labour that scales linearly with quantity.

Volume planning
Cost forecasting

## FAQ

### When should a team tool up for injection moulding?

Only when projected demand, part maturity, and cash-flow tolerance justify the tooling commitment, not just when unit cost looks attractive. Use breakeven analysis to support the decision.

### Why compare total cost rather than unit cost?

Total cost reveals when low setup methods stop being the sensible choice and when high-commitment routes finally become economically defensible. Unit cost alone is misleading.

### What if my actual costs differ from these defaults?

Update the inputs with your actual supplier quotes. The tool works best when you plug in real numbers from manufacturers who've seen your design.

### Should I include labour overhead in unit cost?

Yes, but be consistent. Include the fully-loaded cost of labour (wages plus facilities) in your unit cost estimates.

### Can I use this for a die-cast metal part?

Yes. Set the tooled route to die casting, then enter the die caster's quoted die cost (die, trim tool and fixtures) and unit cost (casting plus trimming, machining and finishing). The sums work the same way as for injection moulding. The tool does not suggest die-casting figures, so use real quotes. See [die casting explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/die-casting-explained.html) for what drives those costs.

# Plastic Material Selector

Say how much each property matters for your part and get a ranked shortlist of common plastics, with the ones that miss your essentials ruled out and explained.
It uses Orion Design's relative ratings for typical grades, so treat it as a starting point for conversations with material suppliers and moulders.

Quick answer

## Shortlist from requirements, then confirm with real grades and real tests.

Match % = Σ (importance × rating) ÷ Σ (importance × 5)
Essential = rating of 4 or 5 required, otherwise the material is ruled out

The ratings compare typical unfilled general-purpose grades with each other. They are Orion Design's judgement for shortlisting, not values from a standard or datasheet.

## The ratings used

1 is poor and 5 is excellent; for cost, 5 means cheapest. Fillers, additives and specific grades can move any of these considerably.

|Material |Stiff |Tough |Heat |Chemical |UV |Wear |Finish |Cost |

|PP |2 |4 |3 |5 |2 |3 |2 |5 |

|HDPE |1 |5 |2 |5 |2 |3 |1 |5 |

|ABS |3 |3 |2 |2 |1 |2 |5 |4 |

|PC/ABS |3 |4 |3 |2 |2 |2 |4 |3 |

|PC |3 |5 |4 |2 |2 |2 |3 |3 |

|PETG |3 |3 |2 |3 |2 |2 |3 |4 |

|Nylon (PA) |3 |4 |4 |4 |2 |4 |2 |3 |

|Acetal (POM) |4 |3 |3 |4 |1 |5 |2 |3 |

|Acrylic (PMMA) |4 |1 |2 |2 |5 |2 |4 |3 |

|TPE / TPU |1 |4 |2 |3 |3 |2 |3 |3 |

|PPS, PEEK |5 |3 |5 |5 |3 |4 |2 |1 |

## How to read your result

- **Several good matches:** ask suppliers for datasheets of specific grades of the top two or three, and compare price and availability.

- **Only one or two:** your essentials are demanding. Check each is truly essential, and look at filled or modified grades.

- **None:** relax an essential, consider a specialist grade, or reconsider the design, for example by protecting a part from UV or heat rather than asking the material to cope.

Regulatory needs, such as flame ratings for electrical enclosures or food-contact suitability, depend on specific grades and must be checked separately.

## FAQ

### Where do the material ratings come from?

They are Orion Design's relative ratings for typical unfilled general-purpose grades, based on widely known properties of each plastic family. They are a shortlisting aid, not datasheet values, so confirm with the data for the specific grade you plan to use.

### Why is my preferred material ruled out?

A criterion marked Essential requires a rating of 4 or 5. If a material is rated 3 or lower on that criterion, or does not meet the transparency or feel filter, it is ruled out. Change Essential to Important to keep it in the ranking.

### Does the selector include glass-filled grades?

No. Fillers such as glass fibre raise stiffness and heat resistance considerably, especially for nylon, but reduce toughness and increase tool wear. If a filled grade could be suitable, discuss it with your material supplier.

### Can it tell me if a plastic is food-safe or flame-rated?

No. Food-contact suitability and flammability ratings belong to specific grades, not plastic families. Ask suppliers for the relevant declarations or test data for the grade you choose.

### Should I choose the cheapest suitable material?

Not automatically. Material is only part of part cost: a material that moulds faster, needs no painting or avoids failures in use can be cheaper overall. Compare the whole cost, not just price per kilogram.

Title: Free NDA Generator for Product Discussions

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# NDA Generator

Generate a simple one-way or mutual NDA draft for early product, design, and manufacturing conversations.
Use it to structure discussions, then have the final agreement reviewed for your specific legal context.

When to use this

## Use the NDA generator to prepare early product and supplier conversations.

The draft is intended to help structure confidentiality before sharing product designs, CAD files, drawings,
prototypes, supplier quotes, commercial plans, or manufacturing assumptions. It is a starting point, not legal advice.

## What the draft does

The generated text sets out the agreement type, parties, purpose of disclosure, confidential information,
core obligations, exclusions, term, return or destruction language, and governing law.

For a supplier discussion, keep the purpose narrow enough to match the real conversation: evaluating manufacturing feasibility,
cost, quality, and production route for a defined product. Avoid using an NDA as a substitute for careful staged disclosure.

## How to read your result

**Important:** the generated text is a starting point for discussion, not legal advice and not a finished agreement.
It has not been reviewed for your circumstances, and a qualified solicitor should check it before anyone signs.

The summary cards confirm the three choices that shape the agreement most: whether it is one-way or mutual, how long the
confidentiality obligations last, and which country's law applies. The draft itself sets out who is sharing with whom, why,
what is covered, what is excluded, and what happens to the information afterwards.

- **Looks right:** the parties are correctly named legal entities, the purpose describes the actual conversation, and the information listed matches what you plan to share. A term of two to five years is common for early product discussions.

- **Worth checking:** a one-way NDA when the other party will also share drawings or pricing usually should be mutual. A very broad purpose or a vague list of information can make the agreement harder to rely on.

- **Get advice first:** if you are sharing something that would be hard to protect any other way, such as a process or formulation you plan to keep secret, if the other party is overseas, or if they send back their own terms, have a solicitor review before disclosing anything.

A solicitor may also add clauses this draft leaves out, such as remedies for breach, confirmation that no licence or ownership
is transferred, and how the agreement can be ended. Keep a record in your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html)
of who has signed what and when, so disclosure stays staged and traceable. If you are unsure what to share with a manufacturer
at each stage, [Andrew can talk you through it](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) from an engineering point of view.

## What to do next

- Check that the parties are named correctly before sending anything.

- Keep the purpose specific to the conversation you are actually having.

- Share only the information required for the next decision.

- Have the agreement reviewed for your jurisdiction, project risk, and commercial context.

## FAQ

### Is this legal advice?

No. It is a drafting aid for early product and manufacturing conversations. Have the final agreement reviewed by a qualified legal professional.

### Does an NDA mean it is safe to share everything?

No. Use staged disclosure. Share only what the other party needs to answer the next useful question.

### When should I ask someone to sign an NDA?

Before you share confidential information that is not already public, such as unfiled designs, technical know-how, test results or detailed business plans. A first conversation can often stay at a high level without one, which lets you check whether the relationship is worth pursuing before sharing the detail.

### Does an NDA protect my idea in the same way as a patent?

No. An NDA is a contract with the people who sign it. It does not stop someone else from developing a similar product independently, and it does not give you rights against third parties. Registered rights such as patents and registered designs work differently; the [IP protection guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-protect-product-ip.html) explains the options.

### What if a manufacturer asks me to sign their NDA instead?

That is common, particularly with larger suppliers. Read it carefully: check that it is mutual if you are both sharing information, that the definition of confidential information covers what you will share, and that the duration and permitted uses are reasonable. If the terms matter to your business, ask a solicitor to review them.

Title: Pricing Ladder: From Landed Cost to Shelf Price

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Pricing Ladder

Follow a product's price up the chain: from what it costs you, through your margin, a distributor's and a retailer's, to the shelf price with VAT.
Compare the result with what you hope to sell it for. Use Target COGS by Route to Market to work the other way, from a shelf price down to a target cost.

Quick answer

## Each seller in the chain adds its margin on top of the price it paid, so the shelf price is often several times the landed cost.

Price needed for a margin m = cost ÷ (1 − m)
Your price = landed cost ÷ (1 − your margin)
Distributor's price = your price ÷ (1 − distributor margin)
Retail price before VAT = previous price ÷ (1 − retailer margin)
Shelf price = retail price before VAT × (1 + VAT rate)

Margins here are shares of each seller's selling price, the way retailers and distributors usually quote them. A 50% margin doubles the price; a 45% margin multiplies it by about 1.8.

## How to read your result

- **Shelf price at or below target:** the chain works at that price. Check it still covers promotions, returns and marketing.

- **Close to the target:** little room for discounts or cost increases; test a pessimistic landed cost.

- **Above the target:** reduce landed cost, shorten the chain (for example sell to retailers directly), accept a lower margin, or reposition the product at a higher price.

The multiple of landed cost is a quick sense check when comparing channels. For the reverse calculation and selling costs such as fulfilment and returns, use
[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html); for the full picture, read
[Route to market and margins](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html). Save your ladder to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

Related reading

[Retail and distributor margins explained](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/retail-and-distributor-margins-explained.html)

[How to price a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-price-a-physical-product.html)

[Route to market and margins](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html)

[How to turn RRP into target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html)

[Target COGS by Route to Market](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html)

[Landed Cost Calculator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/landed-cost-calculator.html)

Use it for

Pricing
Margins
Retail

## FAQ

### What is a pricing ladder?

The sequence of prices a product passes through on its way to the customer: your selling price, any distributor's price, the retailer's price and the shelf price with VAT. Each step adds that seller's margin.

### Why is the shelf price so many times the cost?

Because margins compound. If you, a distributor and a retailer each need a healthy margin on their own selling price, and VAT is added at the end, the shelf price is commonly several times the landed cost.

### Should I use margin or markup?

This tool uses margin, as a share of the selling price, because that is how retailers and distributors usually state their terms. A 50% margin is the same as a 100% markup. Always confirm which one a partner means.

### Does the ladder include selling costs such as fulfilment and returns?

No; it shows the price chain only. Your margin needs to cover your selling costs and overheads. Target COGS by Route to Market includes those selling costs explicitly.

### What VAT rate should I use?

The UK standard rate is 20%, which applies to most products; some goods have reduced or zero rates. Check GOV.UK for your product, and use 0 if you are pricing for business customers who see prices without VAT.

Title: Product Cost Estimator for Hardware

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Product Cost Estimator

Build an early manufacturing cost estimate from the bottom up. Model materials, bought-in parts, process cost,
labour, packaging, scrap, and overhead so the first COGS target is grounded in something real.

Quick answer

## A realistic cost estimate includes more than materials and process.

COGS = materials + bought-in parts + process + labour + packaging + scrap allowance + overhead

Early estimates usually fail because the product team only prices the obvious physical parts and ignores the cost of making the product repeatedly.

## Worked example

A simple consumer product might carry GBP4.80 of raw material, GBP2.40 of process cost, GBP5.50 of bought-in parts,
GBP4.80 of labour, and GBP1.20 of packaging. Add 6% scrap and 14% overhead, and the fully loaded COGS reaches roughly GBP22 per unit.

## What this estimator is trying to stop

- Setting a retail price before the recurring build cost is credible.

- Underestimating the effect of bought-in parts, labour, and scrap.

- Sending a product into route-to-market planning with a weak COGS target.

## How to read your result

The first figure is your fully loaded cost of goods sold (COGS): what it costs to make, pack and finish one unit once scrap and
factory overhead are included. The second is the gross margin left at the selling price you entered, and the third is what a
year of production would cost at your stated volume. The breakdown shows which cost lines carry the most weight.

- **Healthy:** a common rule of thumb for physical products is a retail price of roughly three to five times COGS, which leaves room for retailer, distributor and marketing costs. If you are well inside that range, the cost base is probably workable.

- **Borderline:** if retail price is only around two to three times COGS, selling direct may still work, but retail or distribution channels are likely to squeeze you hard.

- **Worrying:** if margin is close to zero or negative, or one cost line dwarfs the rest, revisit the design, the bought-in parts or the volume assumption before going further.

Whatever the result, check the largest cost lines first. Bought-in parts and labour are often easier to reduce through design changes
than raw material. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the COGS figure carries through
to pricing and break-even work. If the numbers look tight and you are not sure where the savings are, a
[second opinion from Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) can help identify where design for manufacture would make a difference.

## Use this before you do margin planning

Start with this bottom-up estimate, then move into the
[Target COGS by Route to Market tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html)
and the [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html) once you need to see whether the channel choice can absorb the build cost.
