## FAQ

### What should be included in an early manufacturing cost estimate?

Materials, bought-in parts, process cost, assembly labour, packaging, scrap allowance, and overhead loading should all be considered.

### Why do early cost estimates come in too low?

Because teams often omit hidden but recurring costs such as packaging, labour burden, rejects, and factory overhead.

### How accurate is an early product cost estimate?

At concept stage, an estimate built from typical rates is a planning figure, and it is common for the final cost to differ by a wide margin, often in the region of 25–50%. Accuracy improves as the design firms up, parts are specified, and real supplier quotes replace assumptions. Record your assumptions so you can see which ones changed.

### Should tooling cost be included in the unit cost?

Keep tooling separate as a one-off investment, then look at its effect when spread over your realistic volume. Mixing the two hides the decision about when tooling is worth paying for. The [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html) shows where a tooled route overtakes lower-setup options.

### What is landed cost, and why does it matter?

Landed cost is the cost of a finished unit once it reaches your warehouse: the factory price plus freight, insurance, import duty and handling. For products made overseas it can add significantly to the ex-works price, so use landed cost, not the factory quote, when checking margins and pricing.

Title: Product Design Process Map

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Product Design Process Map

Translate project context into a practical development sequence. The output highlights where effort should sit across discovery,
prototyping, verification, industrialisation, and launch preparation.

## Why process mapping helps

Many projects fail because everyone assumes the same sequence of work exists in their head. A visible process map
makes dependencies, missing gates, and false urgency easier to spot.

- Discovery and definition reduce wasted build cycles.

- Verification prevents teams from mistaking a prototype for a product.

- Industrialisation should happen before launch pressure forces bad decisions.

## Method and assumptions

Emphasis per stage = starting profile for the project stage + adjustments for complexity, regulation, manufacturing novelty and launch window, kept between 5% and 100%

**Assumptions**

- Higher complexity adds emphasis to define, prototype, verify and industrialise; heavier regulation adds verification and industrialisation; new or complex manufacturing adds prototyping and industrialisation.

- A launch window of 6 months or less adds definition, verification and launch effort; 12 months or more allows more discovery and prototyping.

**Limits**

- The percentages show relative emphasis for planning, not effort, cost or time.

- Turn the map into a schedule with the [Timeline Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/timeline-planner.html).

## How to read your result

The map scores six stages of work, from discovery through to launch, by how much attention each deserves in your next few months.
The two highest become your primary and secondary priorities. The percentages are relative emphasis, not time or budget, so
read them as a ranking rather than a plan.

- **Priorities match your stage:** at idea stage you would expect discovery and definition to lead, and at industrialisation you would expect verification and production readiness to lead. If that is what you see, your plan and your stage line up.

- **Several stages scoring high at once:** this is typical of complex or regulated products. It usually means work needs to overlap, for example planning compliance testing while prototypes are still being refined.

- **Compressed schedule warning:** a launch window of six months or less is flagged because most physical products need longer to move from feasibility to production. Either the scope needs trimming or the date needs testing against supplier lead times.

Use the top two stages to decide what the next three to six months should deliver, and write down the evidence that would show
each one is complete. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the sequence sits alongside
your budget and timeline. If the map suggests a lot needs to happen in parallel, a [conversation with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)
can help you work out a realistic order.

Related reading

[Mapping the Product Design Process](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/mapping-the-product-design-process.html)

[How Engineers Choose Between Concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html)

[Development and prototyping: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

Use it for

Project planning
Gate reviews
Team alignment

## FAQ

### What are the main stages of designing a physical product?

Most projects move through discovery, definition, prototyping, verification, industrialisation and launch. The names vary between companies, but the logic is the same: understand the problem, decide what to build, prove it works, then prove it can be made repeatably.

### How long does product development usually take?

It depends heavily on complexity, regulation and manufacturing route. A simple moulded item with a known process can move in a matter of months, while a regulated electromechanical product often takes well over a year. Supplier lead times for tooling and certification are frequently what set the pace.

### Do I have to finish one stage before starting the next?

No. Stages overlap in practice, and good projects plan that overlap deliberately. What matters is not committing to expensive, hard-to-reverse steps such as production tooling before the evidence from earlier stages is in place.

### When should I start thinking about manufacturing?

Earlier than most people expect. Material, process and assembly choices shape the design from the concept stage, and leaving them until the design is finished often leads to costly rework. A short manufacturing review during definition is usually time well spent.

Title: Product Lifecycle Explorer

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Product Lifecycle Explorer

Explore how durability, repairability, energy use, and end-of-life strategy shape the overall lifecycle performance of a product.

## What lifecycle thinking changes

Lifecycle performance is not only a materials question. Product lifetime, in-use energy, repair access,
and recovery design can all shift the total impact and business resilience of a product.

- Longer life spreads embodied impact across more years of service.

- High use-phase energy can dominate total impact even for lightweight products.

- Repairability and recovery create options at the end of the first ownership cycle.

## Method and assumptions

Longevity = min(100, years × 10 + repairability × 6 + upgradeability × 4)
Repair = repairability × 20 · Upgrade = upgradeability × 20
Materials = min(100, recycled % × 0.9 + 10 with take-back)
Recovery = min(100, recovery % × 0.8 + 15 with take-back)
Circularity = 0.3 longevity + 0.2 repair + 0.15 upgrade + 0.15 materials + 0.2 recovery
Use-phase CO₂e = annual kWh × years × 0.193

**Assumptions**

- Repairability and upgradeability are your 1–5 ratings.

- The weighting favours a long, repairable life, reflecting that lifetime usually matters more than recycling.

- Use-phase electricity uses a fixed grid factor of 0.193 kg CO₂e per kWh, close to a recent UK grid average; official factors are updated each year.

**Limits**

- The scores are a structured comparison for design discussions, not a recognised circularity metric or certification.

- Real impacts depend on materials, use and end-of-life systems; see the [Carbon Footprint Estimator](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/carbon-footprint.html).

## How to read your result

The circularity score combines longevity, repair, upgrade, material content and recovery into a single figure out of 100.
The dominant driver names the factor most likely to shape the product's overall impact, and the use-phase carbon signal
estimates the emissions from electricity used over the product's life. The radar chart shows which of the five areas are
pulling the score up or down.

- **Strong:** as a rough guide on this tool's scale, a score above about 70 with no very weak point on the radar suggests a product designed to last and to be recovered. Check that the lifetime and repair claims can be backed up in testing and service planning.

- **Middling:** scores between about 40 and 70 are typical of conventional products. The weakest point on the radar is usually the cheapest place to improve, often by making the battery or a wear part replaceable.

- **Worrying:** a score below about 40, or a dominant driver of short product life, means the product is likely to be replaced rather than repaired. If use-phase energy dominates, efficiency gains will matter far more than recycled content.

Try changing one input at a time to see which lever moves the result most, then focus design effort there. Save your result to your
[product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so lifecycle goals are recorded before the design is fixed. If you want to design
for repair without adding cost or complexity, a [conversation with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) can help.

## FAQ

### What does circularity mean for a physical product?

It describes how well a product keeps its materials and value in use. That covers lasting a long time, being repairable and upgradeable, using recycled material, and being easy to take apart and recover at the end of life.

### Is a longer product life always better?

Usually, because the impact of making the product is spread over more years of use. The exception is a product that uses a lot of energy, where replacing it with a much more efficient design can sometimes be the better choice.

### How can I make a product easier to repair?

Use screws or clips rather than glue where parts may need to come apart, make batteries and wear parts replaceable, and keep fasteners to a small number of common types. Supplying spare parts and simple repair guidance helps just as much as the design itself.

### Does adding recycled material reduce quality?

Not necessarily, but it can change how a material behaves and looks. Recycled plastics may vary in colour and strength between batches, so test them early and specify an acceptable range with your supplier rather than switching late in development.

Title: Product Purpose Framework: Idea Review Tool

Concept review tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Product Purpose Framework

Evaluate whether a concept earns its place in the world by balancing human value, planetary impact,
economic viability, and technical feasibility.

## Why these four axes matter together

Products can be technically possible and commercially attractive while still offering weak human value or poor planetary outcomes.
This model forces those tensions into one visible frame early enough to change the brief.

A product that scores highly on technical feasibility and economy but poorly on humanity and planet should trigger a harder discussion,
not a faster launch.

## Questions for the review meeting

- Does this solve a meaningful problem for someone?

- Is the material and lifecycle burden defensible?

- Can the product sustain itself commercially?

- Can the team reliably deliver and support it?

## Method and assumptions

Overall score = human value + planet impact + economic viability + technical feasibility (each 0–10, out of 40)

**Assumptions**

- The four axes are weighted equally.

- Benchmark products are scored on the same four axes for comparison; their scores are judgements, not measurements.

**Limits**

- The result reflects your own ratings, so it is only as good as the evidence behind them; ask others to score independently.

- The shape of the radar chart often says more than the total.

## How to read your result

The overall score adds your four ratings together, out of 40. The ranking places your concept among a set of benchmark products
scored the same way, and the radar chart shows the shape of the concept, which is often more telling than the total.

- **Strong:** a total in the low thirties or above with no axis below about 6 suggests a balanced concept worth developing further. The next job is to test those scores with real users, suppliers and numbers.

- **Mixed:** a total in the twenties, or a lopsided radar, usually means one or two axes are carrying the concept. Work out what would lift the weakest axis and whether that change is realistic.

- **Worrying:** any single axis at 3 or below is a warning sign whatever the total. A product that is easy to build and profitable but offers little real value, or carries a heavy environmental burden, tends to struggle later.

Scores are only as honest as the people giving them, so it helps to have two or three people score independently and compare.
Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the reasoning behind the concept is recorded early.
If the team cannot agree on technical feasibility in particular, [talking it through with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)
can help separate real engineering risk from uncertainty.

## FAQ

### What is the Product Purpose Framework for?

It helps teams evaluate whether a product idea is strong enough across value, impact, viability, and feasibility to justify further investment.

### Can a commercially viable product still score badly?

Yes. Commercial viability alone does not guarantee genuine human value or acceptable planetary impact.

### How should I score each of the four dimensions?

Score against evidence rather than hope: what customers have told you, what the materials and energy use actually are, what the numbers say, and what has been proven technically. It helps to have someone outside the project score it too. The value is in the conversation about why scores differ, not in the exact number.

### What should I do if one dimension scores low?

Treat it as a pointer, not a verdict. A low human-value score suggests revisiting the user need; a low planet score suggests looking at materials, lifetime or energy use; a low economic score points to cost or pricing; a low technical score means there is risk to retire before committing more. Re-score after changing the concept.

### Can I compare several concepts with this framework?

Yes. Score each concept separately and compare the shapes on the radar chart. For a more structured, weighted comparison against engineering criteria, follow up with the [Pugh Concept Selector](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/pugh-concept-selector.html).

Title: Production Strategy Planner

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Production Strategy Planner

Stage prototype, bridge, and scale-up choices using expected volume, product stability,
capex, quality criticality, and lead-time tolerance.

## Why production strategy needs staging

Going straight to full tooling can be sensible, but only when demand, geometry, and quality requirements are stable enough to justify the commitment.
Most teams benefit from a deliberate transition through prototype and bridge phases.

- Prototype routes optimise learning speed.

- Bridge routes buy time while demand and design settle.

- Scale routes only pay off when the product is ready to repeat.

## Method and assumptions

Transition risk score = demand certainty (low 2, medium 1, high 0) + product stability (low 2, medium 1, high 0) + quality criticality (high 2, elevated 1, standard 0) + 1 if the lead-time tolerance is 8 weeks or less
Risk: 5 or more high · 3–4 managed · 0–2 favourable

**Assumptions**

- Prototype route: 3D printing and rapid CNC while the design is still changing; rapid tooling and CNC validation once it is stable.

- Bridge route: soft tooling or a bridge cell at about 8,000 units a year or more, or where quality is critical; otherwise machined and fabricated low-volume builds.

- Scale route: hard tooling at about 20,000 units or more with a stable design and a capital budget of at least £150,000; bridge production with selective tooling from about 6,000 units and £60,000; otherwise stay low-volume.

**Limits**

- The thresholds are rules of thumb to start a discussion, not quotes; real break points depend on the part, material, process and supplier.

- Compare actual quotes with the [Manufacturing Payoff Visualiser](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/manufacturing-payoff.html).

## How to read your result

The planner gives three things: a risk profile based on how certain demand is, how settled the design is, how critical quality is
and how much tooling lead time you can absorb; a scale-up posture that says whether committing to production tooling looks
justified; and a suggested route for each of the prototype, bridge and scale phases.

- **Commitment window is favourable:** demand and design are settled enough that tooling is a reasonable next step. Get firm quotes, agree tool ownership and maintenance terms, and confirm the design is frozen before cutting steel.

- **Managed risk:** the most common result. A bridge phase, such as soft tooling or a short low-volume run, lets you sell, gather feedback and fix issues before spending on hard tooling.

- **High transition risk:** several factors are uncertain at once. Spending heavily on tooling now could lock in a design or volume that turns out to be wrong. Focus on reducing the biggest uncertainty first, whether that is demand evidence, design changes or quality requirements.

Remember that tooling lead times are often several weeks to a few months, and modifications add more, so a short lead-time tolerance
narrows your options. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the phased route ties into your
budget and launch date. If you are weighing up a significant tooling spend, a [second opinion from Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)
before committing can save expensive changes later.

Related reading

[Manufacturing processes compared](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-processes-compared.html)

[UK vs overseas manufacturing](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/uk-vs-overseas-manufacturing.html)

[The Risk-Progressive Manufacturing Strategy](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/risk-progressive-manufacturing-strategy.html)

[When Does Injection Moulding Become Cheaper?](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-mould-break-even.html)

[Manufacturing and cost: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/manufacturing-and-cost.html)

Use it for

Scale-up planning
Tooling timing

## FAQ

### What is bridge production?

Bridge production is a stepping stone between prototypes and full-scale manufacturing. It typically uses lower-cost tooling, such as aluminium moulds, or low-volume processes such as vacuum casting, to make sellable units while demand and design are still being proven.

### When is it worth paying for hard production tooling?

When the design is stable, demand is reasonably certain, and the volume is high enough for lower unit costs to repay the tooling. If any of those are still uncertain, a staged approach usually carries less risk, even if each unit costs a little more for a while.

### Who owns the tooling once I have paid for it?

That depends on the agreement with your manufacturer, so it should be written down before the tool is made. Make sure the terms cover ownership, maintenance, storage and whether you can move the tool to another supplier.

### Can I change the design after tooling is made?

Small changes are often possible, particularly ones that remove steel from the mould, but they cost time and money. Larger changes may need new tool inserts or a new tool, which is why it pays to freeze the design and test it thoroughly first.

Title: Prototype Strategy Tool for Hardware Teams

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Prototype Strategy Tool

Match the prototype route to the real job of the build. Compare low-volume processes against quantity, cosmetic fidelity,
functional fidelity, urgency, unit budget, and your willingness to commit to tooling.

When to use this

## Choose the prototype route around the question the build must answer.

A prototype is not automatically better because it looks more production-like. The right route depends on quantity,
fidelity, urgency, budget, and whether the design is mature enough to justify tooling commitment.

## How to read your result

The score is a route-fit signal. A high score means the method is a reasonable match for the current build brief,
not that it is the final manufacturing route. Close scores should trigger a discussion about what evidence the next prototype must create.

- **A clear leader:** when the top route is a few points ahead of the rest, the brief is pointing firmly one way. Get quotes for that route and confirm lead time before planning the build around it.

- **Two routes close together:** this is common and usually means the brief is mixing goals, such as wanting appearance and function from one build. Splitting into a looks-like and a works-like prototype often resolves it.

- **Tooled routes ranking highly early on:** if bridge tooling or pilot injection comes out on top while the design is still changing, treat that as a warning. Tooling changes are slow and costly, so check design stability first.

If CNC and 3D printing score closely for a functional validation build, the better choice may depend on tolerance,
material behaviour, and whether cosmetic finish matters yet. If bridge tooling wins, check that the design is stable enough first.

## What to do next

- Write down the one decision the prototype must unlock.

- Separate looks-like, works-like, and production-like requirements.

- Check whether the selected route creates reusable learning or only a better-looking sample.

- Use production strategy planning before moving from prototype to bridge or pilot production.

Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the prototype route sits alongside your budget and timeline.
If you are unsure what the next build needs to prove, a [short conversation with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) can help shape the brief.

## FAQ

### Should the prototype use the final production process?

Only when the question requires it. Early builds often need speed and learning more than production fidelity.

### When is bridge tooling sensible?

Bridge tooling is useful when demand or test needs exceed one-off prototypes, but the product is not ready for full production commitment.

### How many prototype rounds does a product usually need?

Most products go through several: early looks-like and works-like models, an integrated prototype that combines form and function, and pre-production parts made by or close to the production process. Simple single-material products may need fewer rounds; electromechanical or regulated products usually need more. Plan each round around the question it must answer.

### Is 3D printing good enough for testing?

For form, fit, ergonomics and many functional checks, yes, and it is quick and cheap to iterate. Printed parts can behave differently from moulded or machined parts in strength, stiffness, [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) and tolerance, so final validation, drop tests and certification testing usually need production-intent parts.

### What is the difference between looks-like and works-like prototypes?

A looks-like prototype represents appearance, size and feel; a works-like prototype proves the mechanism, electronics or performance, often without the final form. Splitting them lets you answer design and engineering questions in parallel before combining them into an integrated prototype.

Title: Pugh Concept Selector

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Pugh Concept Selector

Compare three concept directions against the same weighted engineering criteria. This keeps early-stage
decisions explicit instead of burying them in meeting notes and opinions.

## Why this tool matters

Teams often jump between feasibility, user need, cost, and sustainability without a common structure.
A weighted matrix forces the discussion into the open so trade-offs are visible and contestable.

If one concept scores well on value but weakly on manufacturability, the right response may be to derisk the concept rather than discard it.
The matrix should guide questions, not shut them down.

## Use it well

- Keep criteria stable across all concepts.

- Weight only the factors that actually matter to the decision.

- Use the result to identify the next de-risking step, not just a winner.

## Method and assumptions

Weighted score for each concept = Σ (criterion weight × concept score)
Weights and scores are 1 to 5

**Assumptions**

- Each criterion's weight reflects its importance to this product; all concepts are scored against the same criteria.

- The gap between the top two concepts indicates how clear the choice is.

**Limits**

- Scores are judgements; a small lead can come from scoring noise, so test the result by changing weights.

- Use it to structure a discussion and record the reasoning, not to make the decision automatically.

## How to read your result

Each concept's score is the sum of its ratings multiplied by the weight of each criterion. With five criteria scored and weighted
from 1 to 5, the highest possible score is 125. The results show the leading concept, its score, and how far ahead it is of
second place. The recommendation card flags whether that lead looks clear or close.

- **Clear lead:** a gap of 8 points or more is treated as a clear lead here. Carry the leader forward, but look at its lowest-scoring criterion, because that is usually your next de-risking task.

- **Close decision:** a small gap means the answer depends on the weights. Try nudging the most debated weight up or down by one. If the winner changes, the matrix is telling you that the team has not yet agreed what matters most.

- **Worrying:** if every concept scores low, or the leader has a 1 or 2 on customer value or technical feasibility, the right move may be to generate better concepts rather than pick the least weak one.

A quick prototype or a supplier conversation often settles a close call faster than more debate. Save your result to your
[product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the reasoning behind the chosen concept is easy to revisit later.
If the decision carries significant tooling or engineering risk, an [independent view from Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/)
can help before you commit.

Related reading

[Competitor and patent landscape review](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/competitor-and-patent-landscape-review.html)

[How to write a product requirements document](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-write-a-product-requirements-document.html)

[How Engineers Choose Between Concepts](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-engineers-choose-between-concepts.html)

[Product Design Process Map](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-design-process-map.html)

[Opportunity and concept: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/opportunity-and-concept.html)

[How to validate a product idea before you build it](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/how-to-validate-a-product-idea.html)

Use it for

Concept narrowing
Decision framing
Weighted trade-offs

## FAQ

### What is a Pugh concept selector?

A structured comparison matrix that scores concepts against the same criteria so teams can make design trade-offs transparently.

### When should you use a concept selection matrix?

Use it when several options remain plausible and the project needs a shared rationale for prioritising which concept to carry forward.

### How do I choose the criteria and weights?

Draw criteria from the product requirements: what the product must do, cost, manufacturability, reliability, user experience and sustainability. Five to eight criteria is usually enough. Agree the weights as a team before scoring any concept, so the weighting is not bent to favour a preferred idea.

### What should I do if two concepts score almost the same?

Treat it as a tie rather than a win. Look at which criteria separate them, test the uncertainty behind those scores with a quick prototype or calculation, or combine the strongest features of both into a new concept and score that.

### Does the highest score mean the concept is the right one?

It means it best fits the criteria and weights you chose, based on what you know now. Check how sensitive the result is to small weight changes, and remember the matrix structures a decision rather than making it for you.

Title: Am I Ready to Talk to a Manufacturer? Self-check

Self-check

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Takes about two minutes · Method and assumptions

# Ready to Talk to a Manufacturer?

Answer ten quick questions about your design files, quantities, costs, testing and paperwork. You get a readiness score and a prioritised list of what to prepare before approaching suppliers, so their quotes are accurate and comparable.

Quick answer

## You are ready for manufacturers when they can quote from your files without guessing.

Readiness = Σ (importance × answer) ÷ Σ (importance × 2), where Yes = 2, Partly = 1, No = 0
Critical gap = a most-important question answered No

Design files and realistic quantities carry the most weight, because suppliers cannot price accurately without them.

## Method and assumptions

Each answer scores Yes 2, Partly 1, No 0, multiplied by the question's importance weight
Readiness % = total score ÷ maximum possible score × 100
Gaps are ranked by weight × points missing

**Assumptions**

- Importance weights reflect what manufacturers most need to quote accurately.

- A critical gap is a top-weighted question answered No.

**Limits**

- It is a self-check of your preparation; it cannot judge the quality of your files or design.

- Manufacturers' requirements vary; ask what each one needs.

## How to read your result

- **About 80% or more with no critical gaps:** ready to go ahead, with the remaining gaps closed in parallel.

- **About 55 to 80%, or one critical gap:** possible, but with avoidable risk. Close the top gaps first if you can.

- **Below about 55%, or several critical gaps:** too early. Work through the gaps in the order listed.

The weights and thresholds are Orion Design's rules of thumb for planning, not a formal standard. Each gap links to the guide or tool that helps close it. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) and repeat the check as you progress.

## FAQ

### When should I contact manufacturers?

When you can give them 3D CAD, drawings with critical tolerances, a bill of materials and realistic quantities. Earlier conversations can be useful for advice on process and design, but quotes before then are rough guesses.

### Do I need a finished design to get a quote?

Not finished, but defined enough to price. A design that is still changing will be quoted with allowances, and the price will change when the design does.

### Should I sign an NDA with a manufacturer?

It is sensible before sharing detailed designs, especially with new suppliers. It does not replace choosing trustworthy partners and sharing only what is needed.

### What if I do not know my quantities?

Give your best realistic estimate for the first order and the first year, with the evidence behind it. Suppliers price very differently for 100 and 10,000 units, so a range helps.

## FAQ

### When should I invest in injection mould tooling?

When production-intent parts have passed testing, the design is frozen, demand is evidenced well beyond the tooling break-even volume, and you can fund the tools and first stock together. Before then, bridge tooling or low-volume processes usually cost less overall.

### What is bridge tooling?

Cheaper, quicker tooling, often aluminium or soft steel, used for early production while design and demand settle, before committing to hardened production tooling.

### What happens if I change the design after tooling?

Some changes can be made by removing steel from the tool; others need welding, new inserts or a new tool. Changes cost time and money, and some are not possible at all.

### How much should I allow for tool modifications?

Plan for at least one round of modifications after first samples, in both time and budget. The toolmaker can tell you what is typical for your parts.

Title: Launch Margin Planner

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Launch margin planner.

Turn route mix, retail price, COGS, and hidden selling costs into a clearer view of annual contribution,
break-even volume, and whether the launch still works once real operating costs are included.

Quick answer

## Launch margin is what remains after route deductions, COGS, hidden selling costs, returns, and overhead are counted.

Operating profit = annual contribution after variable costs - annual overhead

If a launch only works before marketplace fees, retail terms, packaging, fulfilment, and overhead are included, it is not commercially ready.

## What the planner helps you see

Launch economics often look fine until you add the cost stack that sits between the customer and the factory.
This planner shows how route mix, hidden selling costs, and annual overhead alter the real margin picture.

A product can look profitable at list price and still disappoint once marketplace fees, retailer terms, secondary packaging,
warehousing, and fulfilment are layered in. That is why route choice and cost structure need to be reviewed together.

## Questions to ask after the result

- Is the route mix giving away too much of the retail price?

- Are we undercounting fulfilment, packaging, or account-management costs?

- Does the product need a lower COGS or a different launch route to become resilient?

## Method and assumptions

Price after VAT = RRP ÷ (1 + VAT rate)
Kept per route = price after VAT × (1 − route fee or retailer margin)
Contribution per unit = kept − COGS − route costs − returns reserve
Annual contribution = Σ (annual units × route share × contribution per unit)
Operating profit = annual contribution − annual fixed overhead

**Assumptions**

- Channel shares are normalised so they add up to 100%.

- Route costs per unit are the figures you enter; the returns reserve is a percentage of the amount kept.

- One average price and COGS apply across all routes.

**Limits**

- It does not model timing, payment terms, promotions, price changes or volume discounts.

- Marketplace and retailer terms vary; replace the defaults with quoted figures.

## How to read your result

Start with operating profit and the break-even volume, then look at contribution per route to see which part of the mix is helping or hurting.

- **Comfortable:** operating profit is positive at the volume you can realistically sell, break-even sits comfortably below that volume, and every route makes a positive contribution per unit.

- **Borderline:** the plan is close to break-even, or one route has a very thin or negative contribution that the others are carrying. Consider whether that route is worth its cost at launch or better added later.

- **Worrying:** operating profit is negative and break-even is well above your forecast volume. Look first at unit COGS and the most expensive route, rather than assuming higher volume will close the gap.

It is normal for retail to carry the lowest contribution per unit, as it trades margin for reach. The question is whether the volume it brings is enough to justify it. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) so the launch margin sits alongside your cost, route and cashflow assumptions.

If the plan only works with a COGS figure that has not yet been confirmed by a manufacturer, a second opinion is worthwhile. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) to talk it through.

Related reading

[Selling on marketplaces](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/selling-on-marketplaces.html)

[How to Turn RRP into Target COGS](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/hardware-revenue-margin-planning.html)

[How Route to Market Shapes Product Design and Cost](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-hardware-product.html)

[Route to market and margins: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/route-to-market-and-margins.html)

Hidden costs
Break-even

## FAQ

### Why plan launch margin by route to market?

Because DTC, marketplace, and retailer routes keep very different amounts of the retail price once fees, logistics, and selling costs are counted.

### What hidden costs damage launch margin most often?

Warehousing, packaging, fulfilment, marketplace commissions, retailer margin, site or payment fees, and undercounted operating overhead are the usual leaks.

### What gross margin should a hardware product aim for?

It varies by category and channel, but many hardware businesses aim for a gross margin of roughly 40–60% on the price they actually receive, so there is room for marketing, overheads and profit. Products sold mainly through retail often see lower margin per unit because the retailer's share comes off the top.

### How can I reduce the impact of channel fees on margin?

Price for each channel rather than using one price everywhere, reduce packaging and fulfilment cost per unit, sell bundles or higher-value variants through high-fee channels, and design for a lower COGS from the start. The [Target COGS tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/route-to-market-simulator.html) shows the cost ceiling each route allows.

### Should VAT be included in the retail price I enter?

Yes. Enter the shelf price including VAT, as UK customers see it, and set the VAT rate. The planner removes VAT before working out margin, because VAT is collected for HMRC rather than earned by the business. Forgetting to remove it is one of the most common reasons launch margins look better on paper than in practice.

Title: Target COGS by Route to Market

Live tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Target COGS by route to market.

Start with the retail price you think the market will bear, then see what the product can afford to cost
across direct-to-consumer, marketplace, and retailer routes once the hidden cost stack is included.

Quick answer

## The best route is the one that leaves enough money for both COGS and margin after hidden selling costs.

Target COGS = retained price after VAT and route deductions - hidden selling costs - required margin

Retailer routes usually create the hardest COGS ceiling because wholesale deductions remove the largest share of the RRP before logistics and account costs are counted.

## Why route to market changes what your product can cost

The same product can carry very different economics depending on whether it is sold direct, through a marketplace,
or through retail. The retail price may stay the same while the amount left for COGS changes dramatically.

- DTC keeps more of the selling price, but you absorb warehousing, packaging, delivery, site fees, and customer acquisition.

- Marketplace sales can look simpler, but marketplace fees and fulfilment extras can erode the margin quickly.

- Retail can unlock scale, but wholesale pricing means the product usually needs to be designed to a much harder COGS target.

## Example output

A product that feels healthy at a 180 GBP RRP might afford a very different COGS ceiling depending on whether the sale is direct,
through Amazon or Etsy, or through a retailer taking a standard margin.

## Method and assumptions

Price after VAT = RRP ÷ (1 + VAT rate)
Kept per route = price after VAT × (1 − route fee or retailer margin)
Target profit = kept × target operating margin
Target COGS ceiling = kept − route costs − target profit

**Assumptions**

- Route costs (warehousing, packaging, logistics, fees, marketing) are per-unit figures you enter.

- The target operating margin is taken as a share of the amount each route keeps.

- The marketplace fee is applied to the price after VAT. Some marketplaces charge on the VAT-inclusive price, which leaves slightly less.

**Limits**

- It shows a ceiling for unit cost, not a forecast of sales or profit.

- It does not include fixed overheads, promotions, returns or payment terms; use the [Launch Margin Planner](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/revenue-margin-simulator.html) for those.

## How to read your result

For each route, compare the maximum COGS the route can support with your current COGS. The gap between them is the clearest signal.

- **Comfortable:** your current COGS sits well below the ceiling for the route you plan to launch through, leaving room for cost increases, currency changes or a promotional price.

- **Borderline:** COGS is only just under the ceiling, or it works for direct sales but not for retail. That is common at early stages, but it means the product either needs [cost reduction](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/reducing-the-cost-of-an-existing-product.html) before retail or a launch plan that starts direct.

- **Worrying:** COGS is above the ceiling for every route you are considering. The price, the product cost or the target margin needs to change, and design decisions such as part count, materials and assembly method are usually the biggest lever.

As a rough cross-check, many teams planning a retail launch aim for a landed COGS of around a fifth to a third of the retail price including VAT, because retailer margin, VAT and selling costs take so much of the shelf price. Direct routes can carry a higher COGS, but only if marketing and fulfilment costs are counted honestly. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html) to record the target COGS for each route alongside your cost estimate.

If there is a large gap between current COGS and the target, it is worth a design for manufacture review before tooling is committed. You can [get in touch with Andrew](https://oriondesign.xyz/contact/) if you would like help working out where the cost could come from.

## FAQ

### What retailer margin should I assume?

It varies by category and retailer, but margins of roughly 30% to 50% of the selling price excluding VAT are common for consumer products, and distributors may take a further share. Use the figure from a real conversation with a buyer as soon as you have one.

### Why is the RRP entered including VAT?

Because that is the price customers see on the shelf or website. The tool removes VAT first, since VAT is collected on behalf of the tax authority and is not revenue for the business. For B2B products where customers reclaim VAT, you can still enter the gross price and the standard rate.

### Should DTC marketing really be counted per unit?

Yes. Direct sales avoid retailer margin, but customers still have to be found, and advertising often becomes one of the largest costs per sale. Dividing your planned marketing spend by the units it should generate gives a more honest comparison with retail.

### Can I sell through several routes at once?

Yes, and many hardware brands do. Use this tool to set a COGS target that works for the hardest route you plan to use, then use the Revenue and Margin Simulator to see the combined result of a mixed route plan.

Title: Snap-fit Calculator: Cantilever Strain and Forces

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Snap-fit Calculator

Check a cantilever snap-fit hook before it goes into the tool. Enter the beam size, how far it must deflect and your material's
permissible strain to see whether the root is over-strained, and roughly how hard the hook will be to push together and pull apart.

Quick answer

## A cantilever snap fit works if the strain at the root of the beam stays below what the material can take.

The root strain depends only on the beam's length, its thickness and how far it bends. The material's stiffness then sets how much force that takes, and the hook angles and friction turn that into the force to push the parts together and pull them apart.

Both angles are measured from the beam, so a larger angle means a steeper face and a higher force.

## How this works

The tool uses the standard formulas from published snap-fit design guidance for a cantilever with a constant rectangular cross-section,
treated as a beam fixed at the wall and loaded at the hook. Units are millimetres, newtons and megapascals (N/mm²), so forces come out in newtons.

Strain at the root: ε = 1.5 × t × y ÷ L²
Share of permissible strain = ε ÷ ε_perm
Deflection force: P = (b × t² ÷ 6) × (E × ε) ÷ L
Assembly (mating) force: W = P × (μ + tan α) ÷ (1 − μ × tan α)
Separation force: W′ = P × (μ + tan α′) ÷ (1 − μ × tan α′)
Largest deflection at ε_perm: y_max = ε_perm × L² ÷ (1.5 × t)

Strain is entered and shown as a percentage, but the formulas use it as a fraction (2% = 0.02).
If 1 − μ × tan α′ is zero or less, the formula has no finite answer: friction holds the retention face shut however hard you pull,
so the joint is effectively self-locking and will only come apart if the hook is deflected by hand or with a tool.
The same applies to the lead-in face: if 1 − μ × tan α is zero or less, the hook will jam instead of assembling.

The status compares the root strain with your permissible strain: up to 80% passes, 80–100% is marginal, and above 100% is too high.

## Assumptions and limits

- The beam has the same rectangular section along its length and is rigidly fixed at the root. The load acts at the hook.

- **Tapering the beam or adding a root radius changes the result.** A beam that tapers in thickness towards the hook spreads the strain more evenly and deflects further for the same root strain. A generous root radius lowers the stress concentration that a sharp corner adds; a sharp root can crack well below the calculated strain.

- The material is treated as linear elastic. Past the linear region, published guidance uses the secant modulus at the working strain, which is lower than the flexural modulus, so the forces here are likely to be on the high side.

- The mating part is assumed rigid. If it also flexes, the real forces and strain are lower.

- Permissible strain depends on the material, the grade, temperature, moisture and whether the joint is assembled once or many times. Use your supplier's design data for your conditions.

- Friction varies with the material pair, [surface finish](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/surface-finishes-for-plastic-and-metal-parts.html) and lubrication, and is often uncertain. Try a range of values.

- **3D-printed prototypes behave differently.** Printed parts are weaker across their layers, use different materials and have different stiffness, so a printed hook can break where a moulded one would not, or survive where it would not. Use prints to check fit and feel, not to prove the strain.

- This is a first estimate. Confirm the design by testing moulded parts, including repeated assembly if the joint will be opened.

## How to read your result

- **Pass:** the root strain is comfortably below the permissible strain. Check the forces suit the user: a joint that is too easy may come apart, and one that is too stiff may be hard to assemble by hand.

- **Marginal:** close to the limit. Small changes in moulded thickness or material batch could push it over. Lengthen the beam, thin it, or reduce the undercut.

- **Too high:** the hook is likely to crack or take a permanent set. The largest deflection allowed at your permissible strain shows how much undercut the beam can manage as it stands.

Strain falls with the square of the beam length, so lengthening the beam is usually the strongest lever. The guide to
[designing snap fits and living hinges](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html) covers root radii, retention angles, mould undercuts and testing. See
[snap fits in the joining methods guide](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html#snap-fits) for when to use them
and how to make them releasable, and the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html)
for moulding the hook without a side action. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

Related reading

[Designing snap fits and living hinges](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/designing-snap-fits-and-living-hinges.html)

[Joining methods: screws, snap fits, adhesives and welding](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/joining-methods-for-product-design.html)

[Choosing plastic materials](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-plastic-materials.html)

[From 3D-printed prototype to moulded part](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/from-3d-printed-prototype-to-moulded-part.html)

[Development and prototyping: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

Plastic part design

## FAQ

### What permissible strain should I use for a snap fit?

Use the figure from your material supplier's design data for the exact grade. Suppliers often give a higher limit for a joint assembled once than for one opened and closed many times, and the limit falls with temperature and, for some plastics, moisture. The default in this tool is an example only.

### How do I reduce the strain in a snap-fit hook?

Lengthen the beam first, because strain falls with the square of the length. Then make the beam thinner, reduce the undercut depth, taper the beam towards the hook, and add a generous radius at the root.

### What does self-locking mean here?

When the retention face is steep enough for the friction on it, pulling on the joint can never push the hook out of the way, however hard you pull. The joint will only open if someone deflects the hook by hand or with a tool, or the hook breaks.

### Will a 3D-printed snap fit behave like a moulded one?

No. Printed parts are weaker between layers and are often in a different material, so their strain limit and stiffness differ. Use printed hooks to check fit and feel, then test moulded parts before you rely on the design.

How this calculator works

## First estimate, confirmed by test

This calculator applies the standard cantilever snap-fit formulas to the dimensions and material figures you enter. Use it to size a hook and compare options, then confirm the design by testing moulded parts.

The headline budget combines development, prototypes, tooling, compliance, first stock, launch work, and contingency.

## FAQ

### Should contingency be removed to make the budget look better?

No. A lower contingency does not remove risk. It usually just hides it until the project is harder to change.

### Is this the same as a cashflow forecast?

No. This estimates pre-launch budget. Cashflow also needs timing, payment delay, stock purchases, overhead, and sales ramp assumptions.

### How much contingency should a hardware budget include?

Early in development, a contingency of roughly 15–25% is common, with more for novel technology, regulated products or first-time teams. Reduce it as risks are retired by testing and supplier quotes, rather than removing it to make the plan look cheaper.

### Which costs do first-time founders most often forget?

Not necessarily all at once. Costs fall at different times: design and prototypes first, then tooling and certification, then inventory. Use the [Cashflow Projection Tool](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/cashflow-projection.html) to see when cash is needed, which helps plan funding in stages.

Source: https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/temperature-rise-estimator.html
Title: Enclosure Temperature Rise Estimator: ΔT = P × Rθ

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions

# Enclosure Temperature Rise Estimator

Estimate how hot your hottest component will get inside the housing. Enter its power, your worst-case ambient temperature and the
thermal resistances along the path to the outside air, and see the temperature rise, the margin to your target, the most power the
design can take and the surface area it needs. It uses the same method as the guide to
[managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html).

Quick answer

## The component's temperature is the ambient plus its power multiplied by the total thermal resistance of the path out.

Each step from the component to the outside air resists the flow of heat, and the steps add together. The last step, from the outer surface to the air, is often the largest, so a bigger or metal surface usually helps most. Compare the result with your target, then confirm it by test.

Each box is one thermal resistance in °C/W. They are in series, so they add, and every watt passes through all of them.

## How this works

The tool follows the method in [simple first estimates](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html#estimates):
once the product has settled, all the power going in leaves as heat, and the temperature rise is that power multiplied by the thermal resistance of the path.
Resistances in a chain add together. Lengths entered in millimetres are converted to metres for the area.

Area (from mm): A = length × width ÷ 1,000,000
Surface to air: R_surface = 1 ÷ (h × A)
Internal steps: R_int = R_comp-case + R_pad + R_extra
Total: Rθ = R_int + R_surface
Rise: ΔT = P × Rθ
Component: T_comp = T_ambient + ΔT
Allowed rise: ΔT_allowed = T_target − T_ambient
Margin: T_target − T_comp
Maximum power: P_max = ΔT_allowed ÷ Rθ
Area needed: R_allowed = ΔT_allowed ÷ P − R_int
A_needed = 1 ÷ (h × R_allowed)
Outer surface: T_surface ≈ T_ambient + P × R_surface

**Worked example from the guide.** A 2 W board in a sealed housing, 40 °C ambient and a 65 °C target. An aluminium lid of 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01 m²
with h ≈ 10 W/m²·°C gives 1 ÷ (10 × 0.01) = 10 °C/W. Add the pad and contact surfaces at about 1 °C/W: Rθ ≈ 11 °C/W.
ΔT = 2 × 11 = 22 °C, so the component reaches about 40 + 22 = 62 °C, just under the target. These are the tool's default inputs.

The status compares the rise with the rise your target allows (target minus ambient): up to 80% of it passes, 80–100% is marginal,
and above 100% is over the target. The guide's example uses 22 of 25 °C (88%), so it shows as marginal: under the target, but with little room.
If the internal resistances alone use up the allowed rise, no surface area can meet the target and the tool says so.

## Assumptions and limits

- **Steady state.** The product has run long enough for every temperature to stop rising. Warm-up takes time, so short bursts of power run cooler than this estimate, but a long burst will reach it.

- **A single path.** All the heat is assumed to flow through one chain of resistances. In reality some also leaves through the walls, the base and the cable, so the real temperature should be slightly lower. If another path matters, the estimate becomes pessimistic.

- **The lid is uniform in temperature.** The whole surface is treated as being at one temperature. A plastic or thin surface leaves a hot spot over the component and sheds less heat than its area suggests; metal spreads heat far better.

- **Solar gain is not included.** Sunshine on the housing can add more heat than the electronics produce. For outdoor products, the result applies to shade only; choose the colour and test in sun.

- **h is a rough figure.** The real combined coefficient depends on orientation, size, finish, nearby surfaces and any air movement. Replace the default with better data, or work it out from a test.

- **Touch temperature is a separate check.** The outer surface temperature shown is an estimate only. The limits for how hot a surface may get come from your product's applicable safety standard, which you can identify through [product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html). This tool does not quote them.

- **Confirm by test.** Measure a prototype with thermocouples on the hottest parts and the housing above them, at your highest ambient and heaviest realistic load, until the readings stop rising.

## How to read your result

- **Pass:** the rise uses no more than 80% of what your target allows. Check the outer surface against the touch limits in your safety standard, and confirm by test.

- **Marginal:** under the target, but small changes in power, pad thickness or ambient could push it over. Improve the largest resistance first, then test.

- **Over target:** the component is likely to run too hot. The maximum power and the surface area needed show how far you are from a working design.

The largest resistance in the chain dominates. If it is the surface to air, add area, ribs or fins, or move to a metal lid; if it is the pad, bridge the gap with a
thinner or better pad. The guide to [managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html) covers
venting versus sealing, heat spreaders and testing, and [product testing and validation plans](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-testing-and-validation-plans.html)
shows where the temperature test fits. Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

Related reading

[Managing heat in a product enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/managing-heat-in-a-product-enclosure.html)

[Electronics in a physical product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/electronics-in-a-physical-product.html)

[Sealing and waterproofing an enclosure](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/sealing-and-waterproofing-an-enclosure.html)

[Choosing metals for a product](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/choosing-metals-for-a-product.html)

[Product certification basics](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/product-certification-basics.html)

[Development and prototyping: overview](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

[Product Test Plan Builder](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/test-plan-builder.html)

## FAQ

### Where does the default h of 10 W/m²·°C come from?

It is the rough combined convection and radiation figure engineers often use for a surface in still air, as in the guide's worked example. The real value depends on the surface's orientation, size and finish and on any air movement. Once you have a prototype, measure the power and the surface and air temperatures, and use h = P ÷ (A × (T_surface − T_ambient)) in place of the default.

### What thermal resistance should I use for the pad?

Take it from the pad maker's datasheet for your thickness, compression and contact area, and allow something for the contact surfaces either side. The 1 °C/W default is the illustrative figure from the guide, not a value for any particular pad.

### Why might a measured temperature differ from the estimate?

The estimate assumes one heat path, a lid at an even temperature, steady state and no sunshine. Heat leaking through the walls makes reality slightly cooler; a hot spot on the lid, a dark finish in sun or a higher real power makes it hotter. Use the estimate to choose a direction, then confirm with thermocouples.

### Does this tell me whether the outside is safe to touch?

No. It gives a rough outer surface temperature, but the touch limits depend on the material, how long the surface is touched and the type of product, and they come from your product's applicable safety standard. Check the measured surface temperature against that standard.

How this calculator works

## First estimate, confirmed by test

This calculator adds the thermal resistances you enter in series and applies ΔT = P × Rθ, the same method as the heat management guide. Use it to see early whether you have a problem and which step to improve, then confirm the design by measuring a prototype.

## FAQ

### How long does it take to develop a hardware product?

It varies widely. A simple mechanical product can go from idea to launch in well under a year, while connected or regulated products commonly take considerably longer. Prototype rounds, certification and tooling are the biggest variables, so plan your own stages rather than relying on an average.

### Where do the stage durations come from?

They are typical planning ranges, consistent with the stage durations on the Idea to manufacture page. They are not quotes. Replace them with your own estimates and supplier lead times as soon as you have them.

### How many prototype rounds should I plan?

Many products need two or three rounds before production-intent parts; complex or regulated products often need more. Plan rounds around the questions that must be answered and allow for at least one you cannot yet name.

### How much contingency should a hardware timeline have?

Hardware timelines often slip because of failed tests, tool modifications and supplier delays. A contingency of around 15 to 25 per cent is a common starting point, with more for novel technology or a first product.

Yes, and they usually do. The planner overlaps launch preparation with industrialisation. You can shorten other stages by overlapping work, but overlapping tooling with unfinished testing increases the risk of costly changes.

Title: Tolerance Stack-up Calculator: Worst Case and RSS

Interactive tool

Built by [Andrew Hunter](https://oriondesign.xyz/about/), Product Design Engineer · Free to use · Method and assumptions explained below

# Tolerance Stack-up Calculator

Check whether a gap or fit still works when every part varies within its tolerance. Enter the chain of dimensions that sets the gap,
mark whether each one opens or closes it, and compare the worst-case and statistical (RSS) results with the clearance you need.

Quick answer

## A stack-up adds up the variation of every dimension in a chain to see the range a gap or fit can take.

Nominal gap = Σ (+ dimensions that open the gap) − Σ (dimensions that close it)
Worst case = nominal ± Σ tolerances
RSS (statistical) = nominal ± √(Σ tolerance²)

Worst case assumes every part is at its limit at once, so it is safe but can demand very tight tolerances. RSS assumes variation is random and independent, so it predicts the range most assemblies will fall in.

## How to set up the chain

- Pick the gap or fit you care about, such as a lid clearance or the end float in a bearing stack.

- Trace the chain of dimensions from one side of the gap to the other, through each part that sets it.

- Mark each dimension as opening the gap (+) or closing it (−).

- Enter each nominal and its ± tolerance, then set the minimum (and, if relevant, maximum) gap you need.

## Worst case or RSS?

Use **worst case** for safety-critical fits, small production runs, few parts in the chain, or processes that tend to run off-centre.
Use **RSS** for longer chains in reasonable volumes from stable processes, where every part being at its limit at once is very unlikely.
RSS predicts roughly 99.7 per cent of assemblies within range only when each dimension is normally distributed, centred and has its tolerance set at three standard deviations;
real processes often fall short of that, so many engineers add a safety factor or check both.

## How to read your result

- **Meets the requirement in the worst case:** the fit works even with every part at its limit. Check the other end too, as an over-large gap can rattle or look uneven.

- **Meets it only statistically:** most assemblies will be fine, but some may fail. Decide whether that is acceptable, or tighten the largest contributors.

- **Fails both:** change the nominal gap, tighten the critical tolerances, remove parts from the chain, or add an adjustable or compliant feature.

Tolerances must be achievable by the process: see the [injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html) and ask suppliers what they can hold.
Tight tolerances cost money in tooling, inspection and scrap, so tighten only the dimensions that matter most.
Save your result to your [product plan](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/product-plan-builder.html).

Related reading

[Tolerances and engineering drawings](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/tolerances-and-engineering-drawings.html)

[CNC machining design rules](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/cnc-machining-design-rules.html)

[Injection moulding DFM checklist](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/injection-moulding-dfm-checklist.html)

[Development and prototyping](https://oriondesign.xyz/guides/development-and-prototyping.html)

[Injection Moulding DFM Checker](https://oriondesign.xyz/tools/dfm-checker.html)

[Engineering estimation formulas](https://oriondesign.xyz/knowledge/engineering-estimation-formulas.html)

Use it for

Tolerances
Fits and clearances
Design review

## FAQ

### What is a tolerance stack-up?

A calculation of how the tolerances of several parts in a chain combine to change a gap or fit. It shows the range the gap can take when each part varies within its tolerance, so you can check the assembly will still work.

### What is the difference between worst-case and RSS stack-up?

Worst case adds the tolerances directly, assuming every part is at its limit together. RSS (root sum of squares) combines them statistically, assuming independent random variation, which gives a narrower range that most assemblies will fall within.

### When should I use worst-case tolerance analysis?

For safety-critical fits, low volumes, short chains, or processes that are not well centred. In those cases the statistical assumptions behind RSS may not hold, and a failure could be costly.

### How do I handle unequal tolerances such as +0.2/−0?

Convert them to a symmetric form: use the middle of the tolerance band as the nominal and half the band as the plus-or-minus tolerance. A 10 mm dimension at +0.2/−0 becomes 10.1 mm ± 0.1 mm.

### Does this calculator handle angles or 3D stacks?

No. It handles one-dimensional chains, which cover many everyday fits. Stacks involving angles, form or position tolerances, or several directions at once need a more detailed analysis or specialist software.
